speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, it looks like, from incoming data pertaining to the first quarter, that real GDP growth has declined somewhat below where it was for the last several quarters of last year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that's really why the Committee indicated that growth has moderated somewhat.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There has been a slight downgrading of estimates of growth for this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On the other hand, the strength of the dollar also, in part, reflects the strength of the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The strength of the dollar is also one factor that, as I noted, is holding down import prices and, at least on a transitory basis at this point, pushing inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, we are taking account of international developments, including prospects for growth in our trade partners, in making the forecast we have here.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Nevertheless, it is important to recognize that this is not a weak forecast.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Taking everything into account, we continue to project above-trend growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We continue to project improvement in the labor market by the end of 2015.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The central tendency of the participants is, they're looking for an unemployment rate that will be down to 5. to 5.2, which is consistent with their estimates of its longer-run normal value.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, we do see considerable underlying strength in the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, in spite of what looks like a weaker first quarter, we are projecting good performance for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There is no single thing where I'd say, "We must see such-and-such in order to achieve that level of confidence."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We will be looking at a wide array of data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we've said that we also want to see continued improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And a stronger labor market with less labor market slack is one factor that would tend to, certainly for me, increase my confidence that as slack diminishes, that inflation will move up over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Other things I will be looking at-of course, the inflation data, but as we said, we expect inflation to remain quite low because of the depressing influence of energy price declines and the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we will be looking at the inflation data carefully to see if we can interpret, for example, low levels of inflation-if we see that, which we expect, as reflecting those influences.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We may not see wage growth pick up, I wouldn't say either that that is a precondition to raising rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But if we did see wage growth pick up, that would be at least a symptom that inflation would likely move up over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Survey measures have been stable; I expect that to continue, but we will be watching it carefully.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If they were to move up over time, that would probably serve to increase my confidence.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there are a wide range of things that we will be looking at, including further improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: This is a judgment that the Committee will have to make.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, it's always hard to know exactly why each participant has written down the forecast they have, but certainly there are changes in the assessments of the economy and forecasts for the economy that would point in the direction of downward adjustment in the funds rate path.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: For one thing, you do see meaningful downward adjustment in the inflation forecast, certainly for this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In addition, importantly, a number of participants have marked down their estimates of the normal longer-run unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that range has moved down noticeably from- previously it was 5. to 5.5, and it's now moved down to 5. to 5.2.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And downward revisions to the longer-run normal unemployment rate in a way suggests that participants are seeing more slack in the economy now than they previously did.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think both of those things would point to downward revision in the funds rate path.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, when an economy is operating at the so-called zero lower bound, there-it creates a situation where there are asymmetric risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is possible, if the economy proves stronger than is expected, to respond to that by tightening policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If there are adverse shocks to demand that tend to push inflation and economic performance in an adverse direction, it's not possible to lower rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, that's a reason why, for a number of years, we engaged in active asset purchase programs.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there is a situation there of asymmetric risks, and it does point in the direction of waiting longer to raise rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I would say that this is an influence that we-and a set of considerations-that we have long been aware of and have been taking into account, so that it's not something that just comes into play now.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is a reason that we have held our rates at 0 to ¼ percent for, now, roughly six years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, we are seeing an economy that's growing above trend, the labor market is improving.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think some of the headwinds that have long been holding the economy back are beginning to recede, which is a reason that the Committee wants to be able to evaluate incoming data and consider when it may be appropriate to finally raise rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But that is a consideration we have long taken into account.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in terms of certainty and providing metrics, we provided a metric or a threshold of 6½ percent several years ago and told market participants and the public that we wouldn't consider it appropriate to raise rates as long as the unemployment rate was higher than that level, as long as inflation was well contained.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But our policy needs to be data dependent, and we need to respond to incoming data and our assessment of incoming data in terms of where we think the economy is heading and how close we are to our objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course we can't provide certainty because we're not certain what the data will look like and how the economy will evolve.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And to achieve our objectives, we need to watch the data, continually reformulate our best guesses-our forecasts of where the economy is going-and respond appropriately.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we can't provide certainty and shouldn't provide certainty because economic developments that will unfold are uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And what market participants should be doing is looking at incoming data just as we are and forming their expectations for where policy will be going and should be going just exactly as we will be doing by attempting to understand economic developments as they unfold.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that's-that is what we're trying to say in this statement, that that's what we will be doing going forward.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we don't want to-and don't think it's appropriate at this point-to provide calendar-based guidance.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I guess we said the risks to the outlook are balanced.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, I mean, certainly we could raise rates in a situation where the risks are balanced.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We need to see, as we have said, we want to see further improvement in the labor market, and we want to feel reasonably confident that the economy is on a trajectory where we will achieve our 2 percent inflation objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the mean-often the mean or even the median of those measures does not line up very well with actual inflation, so they seem to be biased.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Nevertheless, they do seem to be useful in predicting actual movements in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And because we think inflation expectations are a determinant of price setting, we need to be looking at the best data that we can, even if it's imperfect, in trying to gauge inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, the fact that survey measures are stable, even if they are stable at levels consistent with inflation objectives that a central bank wants to achieve, that's not a guarantee that inflation will, over time, move to be consistent with those expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: An example is Japan, I would give you, where for many years the households and businesses expected positive inflation but there was a consistent undershoot.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, this isn't a single metric that is perfect, but it's one of many things we'd look at.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We also look at measures of inflation expectations based on market differentials between nominal and real or TIPS yields.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They're also informative but can move around for reasons pertaining to liquidity in the Treasury market and in the TIPS market, and also because of changing perceptions of inflation risk.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we want to look at both things and not take away any simple morals.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I don't want to comment on those particular sectors.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, as we said in the report, overall measures of equity valuations are on the high side but not outside of historical ranges.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In some corporate debt markets, we do see evidence of unusually low spreads, and that's what was referred to in the report.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: More broadly, we do try to assess potential threats to financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And in addition to looking at asset valuations, we also look at measures of credit growth, of the extent of leverage being used in the economy and in the financial sector, and the extent of maturity transformation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And taking into account a broad range of metrics that bear on financial stability, our overall assessment at this point is that threats are moderate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, I believe the Federal Reserve is already one of the most transparent central banks of any around the globe.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We provide an immense amount of information, both financial-about our balance sheet-and our monetary policy operations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If you want to know exactly what's in the SOMA portfolio, it's listed on the New York Fed website on a CUSIP-by-CUSIP basis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have, you know, statements that we release right after meetings and transcripts within five years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, if you put all that together, we are a transparent central bank.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With respect to congressional changes that are under consideration that would politicize monetary policy by bringing Congress in to make policy judgments about, in real-time, on our monetary policy decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Congress itself decided in 1978 that that was a bad thing to do, that it would lead to poor economic performance, and they carved out this one area of policy reviews, of monetary policy decisionmaking, from GAO audits.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The GAO looks at everything else that goes on within the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think that that is a central bank best practice.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The global experience shows that giving central banks independence to make monetary policy decisions that they think are in the best interest of the country and consistent with their mandates leads to lower inflation and more stable macroeconomic outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, I feel very strongly about that, but we are accountable to Congress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, we're ready to provide information that Congress needs to evaluate the Fed's decisionmaking, in monetary policy and elsewhere.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With respect to monetary policy rules, they can be useful, and I find them useful-and long have-as a kind of benchmark for thinking about what might be the appropriate stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But to chain a central bank to follow a simple mathematical rule that fails to take account of many things that are very important in making monetary policy-for example, I was earlier asked about being against the zero lower bound, which is an important special consideration- that would be a very foolish thing to do, and I oppose it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With respect to proposals having to do with voting and the structure of the Fed that you mentioned, a lot of ideas have been mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would say, for my part, I think the Federal Reserve works well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The system we have was put into place by Congress decades ago.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, Congress can revisit the decisions it's made about the structure of the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There were good reasons for making the decisions that were made about how to structure voting and other things, but-and I don't think the system is broken, I think it's working well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, of course, it's up to Congress to review that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, with respect to the impact of the dollar on the U.S. economy, I don't have a quantitative estimate to offer you, but I certainly expect net exports to serve as a notable drag, this year, on the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, remember, we have to put that in context: There are a lot of things that affect the U.S. outlook, and while that is serving as a drag on economic growth, overall the Committee continues to see sufficient strength-particularly in private spending-that we are expecting above-trend growth, even so.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With respect to our neighbors, we look very carefully at what's happening in the global environment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We realize that our own policies affect performance in the rest of the world, and that performance in other countries has an influence on us, so we spend a good deal of time discussing global developments.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is important for us to keep our own house in order, to put in place the policy that's consistent with the objectives that Congress has given us, and I think a strong U.S. economy certainly is something that is good for other countries as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have pledged to communicate as clearly as we can about monetary policy, and I am trying to do that, and will continue to do so.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: What about the risk of waiting too long, especially since it can take a while for Fed actions to work their way through the economy?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Many, many studies over decades and decades have showed that there are lags in the way monetary policy affects the economy, and, therefore, monetary policy does have to be forward looking.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's why we spend so much time preparing forecasts and discussing them, and we want to put in place a policy that will be appropriate for where the economy is heading.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's-that is, you know, a reason that many of my colleagues-most of my colleagues-are anticipating that it will be appropriate to begin to tighten policy sometime this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In spite of the fact that they are projecting that inflation will be low, they're looking forward and they see that, by the end of 2016 or 2017, with the labor market recovering, and assuming that inflation expectations remain stable and transitory influences no longer affecting inflation, they see inflation heading back to our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So just as we don't want to be premature in tightening policy and aborting a recovery that we have worked long and hard to proceed as far as it has, we also don't want to be behind the curve in beginning to tighten given those lags.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, let me say that the Committee and I, personally, take very seriously our responsibility to safeguard confidential information.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a set of policies and procedures that are in place that we're to follow if we believe that there have been leaks of confidential information.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And this is something that doesn't occur very often, but if it does occur, we follow those procedures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It has been reported that our Inspector General is engaged in a review at this time of this matter, and in light of that ongoing review, I'm not going to get into details, but let me just say that we welcome that review and are looking forward to its conclusions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With respect to Congress, congressional inquiries-we have arranged to brief members of Congress who've asked about this, and we'll certainly cooperate in trying to provide them the information that they seek.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, it's certainly been-I mean, it's certainly been very disappointing to see what have been some really brazen violations of the law, and we absolutely expect the banks that we supervise to comply with the law and to have in place controls that ensure compliance in organizations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And while changing the culture of organizations is not something that we can achieve through supervision, we will make sure that the banks that we supervise have appropriate compliance regimes in place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And to the extent that compensation schemes might be incenting such behavior that inappropriately rewards risk-taking, that's something that was-we will, you know, look for in our supervision as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, the agencies-the agencies are working jointly to bring out a rule on this, but we do have supervisory policies in place concerning the structure of incentive pay and compensation, and our supervision covers that topic now.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we have seen, I think, meaningful changes already in the structure of compensation and banking organizations to diminish ways in which it might incent risk-taking.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That is an allegation that I don't believe has any basis in fact.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm not going to go into the details, but I don't know where that piece of information could possibly have come from.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, the focus of regulators-the banking regulators-is safety and soundness, and what we want to see is changes made as rapidly as possible that will eliminate practices that are unsafe and unsound.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We can't-only the Justice Department can bring criminal action, and they have taken up cases where they think that that's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In some situations, when we are able to identify individuals who were responsible for misdeeds, we can put in place prohibitions that bar them from participating in banking, and we have done so and will continue to do so.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, we issued in September a set of normalization principles, and, as you noted, the Committee indicated that we will eventually cease reinvestments or diminish the pace of reinvestments as a way of gradually reducing the size of our portfolio over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We said we would do that when economic conditions were appropriate after we begin raising rates, because we want changes in the-our target range for the federal funds rate to be the main tool by which we shift the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've not made any decision at this point about how long it will be, once we begin to raise rates, before we reduce or cease reinvestment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We will see how things go, and the Committee will revisit that and make a decision at a later time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You also indicated that we have a substantial quantity of Treasuries that will roll off our balance sheet over the next several years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's true, and that will-I think, over the next two years, almost $800 billion will mature-and that they will be short-term, obviously, Treasuries at that point, and that's a way in which we anticipate diminishing the size of our portfolio.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's something for which we've made no plans, and I don't really have anything for you on that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I agree, it has been very low-it's been disappointingly low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: A positive aspect of what is fundamentally a disappointment is that the labor market has improved more rapidly than might have been expected given the pace of economic growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the unemployment rate has come down more rapidly than I would have expected, and the labor market has improved more rapidly than I would have expected.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In the long run, it is a disappointing factor about the ultimate prospects for the U.S. economy if it continues.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would expect it to pick up, and as you can see from the longer-run growth projections, most FOMC participants believe it will pick up above current levels.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it means it's something that would, if it persists, retard living standards and would likely retard real wage growth and improvement in living standards for ordinary households.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I said this previously, and let me reiterate it, that every meeting that the Federal Open Market Committee has is a live meeting at which we could make a decision.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Clearly, if we decided for the first time to raise the federal funds rate, it is something-I think it would be appropriate to answer questions and explain in more detail.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have long had the capacity to call a press conference after a meeting that we would hold by teleconference-by conference call-and that's a capacity that was used on a number of occasions by my predecessor during the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is something that remains a capacity we have and would expect to use if it were necessary.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On the second part of your question, with respect to testimony, you know, it's very important for the Federal Reserve to be accountable to Congress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a wide range of responsibilities, and it's entirely appropriate for me to testify and be quizzed on a range of topics by members of Congress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I-you know, I think I need to be ready to answer questions on any aspect of Federal Reserve behavior, and that's an important principle.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, there are obviously a range of opinions, both in the market and among Committee members, at this time on what the appropriate stance of policy is likely to be later this year and next year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, importantly, the-when the people write down their dots in the SEP, they're making forecasts about what unfolding data is likely to show.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the participants will all be-their views will evolve with unfolding data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: For all of us, the appropriate policy decision is going to be data dependent, and all of us will be looking at incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And our opinions about the appropriate timing of normalization are likely to shift as we look at how the data evolves.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Differences in the appropriate assessments of the appropriate stance of policy-in addition to reflecting different views on the outlook, there are a set of risks that all of us need to weigh in judging on the- judging the appropriate time of the beginning of normalization.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On the one hand, waiting too long to begin normalization can risk significantly overshooting our inflation objective given the lags in the operation of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, on the other hand, beginning too early could risk derailing a recovery that we have worked for a very long time to try to achieve.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I want to emphasize, sometimes too much attention is placed on the timing of the first increase in the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And what should matter to market participants is the entire trajectory, the entire expected trajectory of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, again, while our actual policy decisions will have to evolve in light of what really does happen in the economy, the Committee, as you can see by the SEP projections, currently anticipates that conditions will evolve in the economy in a manner that will make it appropriate to raise the federal funds rate gradually over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, it's a judgment that the Committee is-will have to make, and, as I've said previously and as we've said in the statement, it will depend on a wide range of data and not on any simple indicators.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I can't provide you-it would be wrong for me to provide you a roadmap that said something as simple as, if the unemployment rate declines to X, that then the labor market will have improved enough for us to begin to raise policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Obviously, we have to look at the pace of job creation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have to look at what's happening to labor force participation, to part-time employment for economic reasons, to job openings, to the pace of quits, to wage inflation, and other indicators of the state of the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I did say when we agreed that labor market slack has diminished to some extent in the intermeeting period, and, clearly, over a longer span of time, over the last several years, obviously we've made considerable progress in moving toward our goal of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in spite of the fact that there is some progress on that front, the Committee wants to see some further progress before feeling that it will be appropriate to raise rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On inflation, again, there has been some progress, in the sense energy prices appear to have stabilized.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, inflation is going to-overall inflation is likely to run at a low level for a substantial period of time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The big declines in energy prices came toward the end of last year and the beginning of this year, and they're not going to wash out of the inflation data until late in this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the fact that energy prices have stabilized means that the pressure from that source is diminishing.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, with respect to core inflation, it has been running under our 2 percent objective, but declining import prices have been reducing that pressure.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I believe that as the labor market continues to improve and as our confidence in that forecast rises, at least for me, my confidence will also rise that inflation will move back up toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I expect that to, over time, put upward pressure on core inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Okay, so on the first question you asked about the 2004-06 rate increase cycle.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Throughout that period, the Fed indicated that rates would rise at a measured pace, and that turned out to be, I believe, 17 meetings, with 25 basis point increases at each meeting.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I've emphasized, previously, we have-absolutely do not expect to follow any mechanical 25 basis points a meeting, 25 basis point every other meeting, no plan to follow any type of mechanical approach to raising the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We will evaluate incoming conditions and move in the manner that we regard as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, conceivably, I think, with the benefit of hindsight, it might have been better to raise rates more rapidly or more during the 2004-06 cycle.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, I'm not certain of that judgment, but I think there's a case to be made.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You asked about Audit the Fed and the Shelby bill.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The Shelby bill has a title in it that addresses a number of issues pertaining to the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I suppose I would ask, what exactly is the problem?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We place high priority on being an accountable and transparent central bank, and I think that if you compare the transparency of monetary policy decisions in the Federal Reserve with other central banks, we are one of the most transparent central banks in terms of the information that we provide to the public in a whole variety of ways.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: To my mind, the Fed is accountable, and we work well as an institution.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm not certain what the problem is that needs to be addressed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me start with the balance sheet and our reinvestment policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We issued a normalization statement giving principles of normalizing policy, and what we said at that time is that we expected to reduce or cease reinvestment at some time after we had begun the process of normalizing policy by raising our target for the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We said the timing of that would depend on economic and financial conditions, and the Committee has really not made any further decisions about how it's going to go about doing that, so President Dudley was expressing his own personal point of view.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But this is a matter that the Committee has not yet decided, and I can't provide any further detail.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The last paragraph of the Federal Open Market Committee statement says: "The Committee currently anticipates that, even after employment and inflation are near mandate-consistent levels, economic conditions may, for some time, warrant keeping the target federal funds rate below levels the Committee views as normal in the longer run."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's a long sentence, but I think the spirit of that sentence is consistent with my use of the word "gradual," and it is consistent with what you see in the Summary of Economic Projections.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Participants are projecting-obviously there is a lot of uncertainty, but they're projecting increases that average around 100 basis points per year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, that's not a promise, it's conditional on their economic forecasts, and those forecasts may prove to be wrong and may change.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But at this time, the assessment that participants have of the economy suggest to them that the appropriate pace of normalization to keep the economy on track to meet our objectives will be gradual, in that sense.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So your first question was about a rate increase this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, again, the Committee tries to give an indication in the Summary of Economic Projections about how economic conditions will unfold, their best projections of that and what the appropriate policy will be given in light of those expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, clearly, most participants are anticipating that a rate increase this year will be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, that assumes, as you can see, that they're expecting a pickup in growth in the second half of this year and further improvement in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we will all be-we will be making decisions however that depend on the actual data that we see in the months ahead.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, certainly, we could see data in the months ahead that will justify the expectations that you see in the so-called dot plot.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, again, the important point is, no decision has been made by the Committee about what the right timing is of an increase.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It will depend on unfolding data in the months ahead.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In terms the IMF guidance, you know, I believe the IMF plays a very useful role by undertaking reviews of the economic policies of all of its members.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Obviously, there is a range of opinion among outside observers and market participants as well as among the Committee's participants, as you can see in the SEP, about how economic conditions are likely to unfold and, consequently, the appropriate timing of an initial rate hike.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think, however, we all agree, and the IMF agrees, that policies should be data dependent, and the Committee is always doing its best to assess the implications of incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would point out that we have had incoming data since that report was written.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, again, I want to emphasize-and I think the IMF would agree with this-that the importance of the timing of a first decision to raise rates is something that should not be overblown, whether it's September or December or March-what matters is the entire path of rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I've said, the Committee anticipates economic conditions that would call for a gradual evolution of the fed funds rate toward normalization.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With respect to international spillovers, this is something that we have been long attentive to.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Obviously, we have to put in place a policy that is appropriate to evolving conditions in the U.S. economy, but we can't promise that there will not be volatility when we make a decision to raise rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: What we can do is to do our very best to communicate clearly about our policy and our expectations to avoid any type of needless misunderstanding of our policy that could create volatility in the market and potential spillovers as well to emerging markets, and I have been trying to do that now for some time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've been doing my best to make good on that pledge.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think our experience suggests that it's hard to have great confidence in predicting what the market reaction will be to Fed decisions, and there have been surprises in the past.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I don't think the Committee anticipated that its decision would cause the taper tantrum.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And all I can say is that uncertainty in the markets at this point about long-term rates doesn't appear to be unusually high, and we can only do what is in our power to attempt to minimize needless volatility that could have repercussions for other countries or for financial stability more generally, and that is to attempt to communicate as clearly as we can about our policy decisions, what they will depend on, and what we are looking at.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think it's clear that the market is also responding to incoming data, and you can see that in daily market reactions to surprises in the economic data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, of course, none of us can quite forecast what incoming data will be.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we are-productivity growth has been-is a factor that affects the pace of improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Productivity growth has been extremely slow for the last couple of years, and I think, in part, the pace of improvement in the labor market that we're projecting reflects the notion that there's likely to be some pickup in the pace of productivity growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Obviously, that's something that's quite uncertain, and it's conceivable that if productivity growth disappoints-something I hope that we won't see, because that has very negative implications for living standards-we could conceivably see faster improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, in addition, there are other margins of slack that don't show up in the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Labor force participation that has, at least, is-appears to be depressed, at least to some extent, because of cyclical weakness, and the fact that labor force participation rate has remained roughly stable for the last year or so when there's an underlying downward trend suggests that some slack is being taken up by, in a sense, improved or diminished cyclical impact on labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I expect that to continue, and I would expect also to see some improvement in the degree of part-time employment that's for economic reasons.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the Committee estimates that the longer-run normal level of the unemployment rate is 5. to 5.2.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: At 5. percent, where we have an unemployment rate that still exceeds the Committee's best attempts to estimate what is a normal unemployment rate for this economy, and, as I mentioned, there appear to be unusually large elements of slack over and above that in the form of somewhat still-depressed labor force participation and part-time work for economic reasons.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think it's fair to say that most members, most participants on the Committee, wouldn't judge yet-although some might-that most wouldn't judge us to be at, quote, "maximum employment."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Wage increases are still running at a low level, but there have been some tentative signs that wage growth is picking up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have seen an increase in the growth rate of the employment cost index and a mild uptick in the growth of average hourly earnings.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would call these tentative signs of stronger wage growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think it's not yet definitive, but that is a hopeful sign.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Still, however, inflation-not only headline, but, stripping out food and energy underlying inflation, core inflation-is still running below the Committee's objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think we need to see additional strength in the labor market and the economy moving somewhat closer to capacity-the output gap shrinking-in order to have confidence that inflation will move back up to 2 percent, but we have made some progress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I mean, the house-the increase in house prices is restoring wealth of many households who have that as their major asset.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is an important part of the wealth of American household-the American household sector.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And for all of the households that were underwater, those house price increases are improving their financial condition, although, of course, at the same time, it's making housing less affordable for those who look to buy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: At the same time, housing overall, given the low levels-still low level of mortgage rates, remains quite affordable.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Anyone who doesn't have a pristine credit rating is-finds it very difficult at this point to qualify for a mortgage, and I think we're seeing quite a bit of reluctance, given the job market and given what the history of what's happened to house prices, of young people to want to buy homes.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've seen them delay marriage and wanting to have the flexibility to move.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the demand for multifamily housing to rent is very high, and rent prices are moving up, I think, because of that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well I-unfortunately, Greece and its creditors are faced with very difficult and consequential decisions at this point and in the days ahead, and my hope is that they will continue to work together to try to find a solution to the, you know, current difficulties and impasse.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Obviously, European leaders place great value on preserving European monetary, economic, and political integration, and the Greek people have made clear that it's important to them to remain in the euro area.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In the event that there is not agreement, I do see the potential for disruptions that could affect the European economic outlook and global financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would say that the United States has very limited direct exposure to Greece, either through trade and financial-or financial channels.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But to the extent that there are impacts on the euro-area economy or on global financial markets, there would undoubtedly be spillovers to the United States that would affect our outlook as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think in recent weeks we have received data that suggest that consumer spending is growing at a moderate pace.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'd say, you know, car sales, for example, were very strong.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Part of it probably represents payback for weak sales during the winter months, but, nevertheless, the pace of car sales has been strong.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And recent readings on retail sales and on spending on services have suggested an improvement in the pace of consumer spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are questions at this point about just how much impact we've seen of lower energy prices on consumer spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The decline in oil prices translates into an improvement in household income, on average, of something like $700 per household, and I'm not convinced yet by the data that we have seen the kind of response to that that I would ultimately expect.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think it's hard to know at this point whether or not that reflects a very cautious consumer that is eager to add to savings and to work down borrowing.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Or, in part, some survey evidence suggests that consumers are not yet confident that the improvement they've seen-the decline in their need to spend for energy, for gasoline-that that's going to be something that will be permanent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They may think it's a transitory change and not yet be responding.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the jury is out there, but I think we have seen some pickup in household spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the Federal Reserve strongly believes that its actions with respect to AIG in 2008 were legal, proper, and effective, and it believes that they were necessary, given the threat that a disorderly failure of that company would have likely implications for the economy, for the flow of credit to households, in businesses in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it believes that the-we believe that the terms of that intervention were tough, and appropriately so, in order to protect taxpayers from the risks that those rescue loans presented at the time they were made.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, I should emphasize that Dodd-Frank changed our 13(3) authority and said that the Federal Reserve may not in a future crisis intervene to attempt to address the issues of a particular company.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: At the same time, it gave the government a set of new tools that it could use in a situation like the AIG situation or Lehman to try to resolve such a situation that poses systemic risks in an orderly way.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The-I'd just say at this point, the Federal Reserve under Dodd-Frank can continue, if necessary, in some future crisis to engage in broad-based programs similar to the program we had in effect-the programs we had in effect in 2008 to provide support for the issuance of asset- backed securities that enabled loans to small businesses and to students and for credit cards and, you know, for credit throughout the economy, or to support the issuance of commercial paper.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: At this point, I believe we are working with the Department of Justice to decide on next steps.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me say, to my mind, the most important positive is that it-I believe a decision to raise rates would signify very clearly that the U.S. economy has made great progress in recovering from the trauma of the financial crisis and that we're in a different place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think, hopefully, that would be something that would be confidence-inducing for many households and businesses.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: From the point of view of savers, of course this has been a very difficult period.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Many retirees-and I hear from some almost every day-are really suffering from low rates that they had anticipated would bolster their retirement income.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: This, you know, obviously has been one of the adverse consequences of a period of low rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The-you know, we have a good reason for having kept rates at the levels that we have.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We-our charge from Congress is to pursue the goals of maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And obviously there are benefits from a strong economy to every household in the economy, including savers, from having a better job market and a more secure economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, yes, when the time comes for us to raise rates, I think there will be some benefits that flow through to savers.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I can't give an ironclad promise, but I think it's clear from our Summary of Economic Projections that we anticipate that the economy will grow, that the labor market will improve, that inflation will move back up to 2 percent as we-is our objective over the medium term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if economic conditions unfold in the way that most of my colleagues and I anticipate, we see it as appropriate to raise rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as you can see, the largest number of participants anticipate that those conditions should be in place later this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Obviously, we have to-you know, there can be surprises-that might not happen.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's not an ironclad guarantee, but we anticipate that that's something that will be appropriate later this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, with respect to-you asked first about overnight reverse repos.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we communicated in our minutes that the Committee has an intention to make sure that they are available-overnight repos are available in large quantity at liftoff to ensure that we have a smooth liftoff, that there will be an elevated level of provision of overnight RRP.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: However, it is our expectation and plan that fairly quickly after liftoff we will reduce the level of the overnight RRP facility, and we have a variety of ways in which we can do that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With respect to market reactions, we always, in evaluating the economic outlook, have to take account of financial conditions, whether it's the level of long-term interest rates or the value of the dollar in assessing the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: To the extent that there are market reactions and market movements, whether they're in reaction to decisions of ours or in reaction to other events-foreign events or unfolding economic conditions-we will always take those into account in deciding on the appropriate path of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I think we still are, since last summer-have seen an appreciable increase in the value of the dollar vis-à-vis most of our trading partners, including emerging markets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it is a significant appreciation of the dollar, and I think we have seen that it's had a negative effect on net exports and so served as something of a drag on the economy, and probably that drag is going to continue for some time to come.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In addition, import prices for non-oil imports continue to fall, and I think that's serving to push down core inflation a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Eventually, I expect that impact to ebb, but it is a factor affecting the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That said, we obviously have no target for the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We take movements in the dollar and its economic impact as one of many factors affecting the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, in spite of the appreciation of the dollar, the Committee obviously thinks that the economy is likely to do well enough to call-likely call for some tightening later this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we take CRA very seriously and evaluate for those banks that we supervise.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a set of guidelines and are very conscientious in attempting to evaluate CRA performance.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's something that we certainly take into account in assessing applications that we receive for mergers, and we have very active programs to try to bring together community groups with banking organizations to try to provide them with information about how they can assess community needs and best address them.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we are looking at CRA and continue to look to see whether there are ways in which implementation could be improved.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, Steve, I think you can see from the SEP projections that most participants continued to think that economic conditions will call for or make appropriate an increase in the federal funds rate by the end of this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Four participants moved their projections into 2016 or later, but the great majority of participants continued to hold that view.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, in light of the developments that we have seen and the impacts on financial markets, we want to take a little bit more time to evaluate the likely impacts on the United States.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I mentioned, the inflation outlook has softened slightly.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've had some further developments-namely, lower oil prices and a further appreciation of the dollar-that have put some downward pressure in the near term on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we fully expect those further effects, like the earlier moves in the dollar and in oil prices, to be transitory.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there is a little bit of downward pressure on inflation, and we would like to see some further developments.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And this, importantly, could include-is likely to include-further improvements in the labor market that would bolster our confidence that inflation will move back to 2 percent over the medium term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, as I've said before, every meeting is a live meeting where the Committee can make a decision to move to change our target for the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As you know, and I've stressed previously, were we to decide to do that, we would call a press briefing, and you've participated in an exercise to make sure that you would know how to participate in that press briefing should it happen.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we will be looking at incoming developments, both financial and economic, to try to make sure we feel, really, that the U.S. economy is doing well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, I want to emphasize, domestic developments have been strong.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We see domestic demand growing at a solid pace, the labor market continuing to improve.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, we will watch incoming data to confirm our expectation that that will continue.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we, of course, will watch global financial and economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I can't give you a recipe for exactly what we're looking to see, but, as we say, we want to see continued improvement in the labor market, and we would like to bolster our confidence that inflation will move back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, of course, a further improvement in the labor market does serve that purpose.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There could be other things we would see that could bolster that confidence, but further improvement in the labor market will serve to do that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, we have been receiving advice from a large number of economists and interested groups, and that's of course appropriate, and we value hearing the opinions of many-you know, many different groups and individuals with different perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, look, at the end of the day, it's the Committee's job to come together to analyze the data that we have on the economy, to decide how it affects the outlook, and to try to deliberate and arrive at a Committee judgment about the appropriate path of policy, and that's what we did today.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I said, although we are close to many participant's [estimates] and the median estimate of the longer-run normal rate of unemployment, at least my own judgment-and this has been true for a long time-is that there are additional margins of slack, particularly relating to very high levels of part-time involuntary employment and labor force participation, that suggest that, at least to some extent, the standard unemployment rate understates the degree of slack in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I've said in the past, we don't want to wait until we've fully met both of our objectives to begin the process of tightening policy given the lags in the operation of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, your first question was, have we come closer or moved further away from our inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we've used the same language, which is that we expect to achieve our 2 present goal over the medium term, and I would say, although we-as we say in our statement, recent developments seem likely to put some downward pressure.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But an important reason for that is that declines in import prices reflecting the appreciation of the dollar and declines in energy prices are holding down inflation well below our target and well below core inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We expect those effects to be transitory, and with well-anchored inflation expectations, we expect inflation to move back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, in the intermeeting period, we have seen some further appreciation of the dollar and some further downward pressure on energy prices, and that creates a bit of further drag on inflation that I would view as transitory-is very likely to be transitory.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I continue and the Committee continues to expect that inflation will move back to 2 percent, so this should be a small thing.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, in the meantime, the labor market has continued to improve, so a tighter labor market, a labor market moving toward full employment, is one that historically has generated upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On the other hand, we've had a long period in which inflation has been running below our objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I consider it, and the Committee does, very important that we-we achieve our inflation objective and defend against inflation that is persistently above our inflation objective and also persistently below our inflation objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we want to have not only an expectation, but a good degree of confidence that that will occur.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We did take note in the statement of a decline in inflation compensation, and it's hard to get a direct read on inflation expectations out of these measures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They can be pushed down by factors pertaining to liquidity in the Treasury-in the TIPs market and other issues pertaining to risk premia, but we have taken note of that, and I would say that that's something that has caught our attention and is a factor that we're watching.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we'd like to have a little bit more confidence, but I would not interpret developments during the intermeeting period as significantly undermining confidence.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the labor market is really important that as it continues to improve-it has, and we want to see it improve further-that serves to bolster confidence.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Oh, I'm sorry, you asked about the September 2012 leak.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are working very closely with House Financial Services Committee that's requested information to satisfy their request.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, we have been very focused, Binya, on doing everything we can to revive this economy and to achieve our maximum employment objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And after we took the funds rate down to zero, as you know, we put in place a number of other extraordinary measures-including forward guidance and large-scale asset purchases-in order to speed the recovery and attain both our inflation objective and our maximum employment objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, I mean, when you look at the projection, you see, as you mentioned, that we see sufficient growth to push the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's already very close to participants' estimates of its longer-run normal level.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We expect the unemployment rate to fall slightly-or, at least, participants project that it will fall slightly below that level.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As that occurs, we would expect labor force participation, the cyclical component of that, to diminish over time, and we would hope to see some decline in the portion of slack that's reflected in high levels of part-time involuntary employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, inflation is going back in our projection to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's awfully close in 2017, and it's not terribly far away even next year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have very large drags from import prices and energy prices, and over the next year or so, those things should dissipate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the behavior of inflation should mainly-if we-if our understanding of the inflationary process is correct and if inflation expectations are well anchored at 2, which I believe they are, as the labor market heals and as that healing progresses, we will see further upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, it's a slow process, it's characterized by lags, and that's why it takes a few years as the inflation-as the unemployment rate falls and even overshoots its longer-run normal level, it just takes some time for inflation to get back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the overshooting helps it get back faster than it otherwise would.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it's certainly important for us, and I think our credibility hinges on defending our inflation target not only from threats that it rises above, but also that we not have-that over the medium term, that we want to see inflation get back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we believe the policies we're following are designed to accomplish that and will do so.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We want to see inflation go back to 2 percent; 2 percent is not a ceiling on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we're not trying to push the inflation rate above 2.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's always our objective to get back to 2, but 2 percent is not a ceiling.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if it were a ceiling, you would have to be conducting a policy that, on average, would hold the inflation rate below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We want to see the inflation rate get back to 2 percent as rapidly as we can.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there are lags in the impact of monetary policy on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if we waited until inflation is back to 2-and that would probably mean that unemployment had declined well below our estimates of the natural rate- and only then did we start to-begin to-and, you know, the word "tighten" monetary policy I don't think is really right because we have an immensely accommodative monetary policy in place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, let me say, just to begin to diminish the extraordinary degree of accommodation for monetary policy, we would be overshoot-we would likely overshoot substantially our 2 percent objective, and we might be faced with then having to tighten policy in a way that could be disruptive to the real economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I don't-I don't think that's a desirable way to conduct policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, that's a very hard question, and, you know, it's why we come together and have very careful evaluations of a wide range of factors.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, at the end of the day, what we're focused on are two things: the path for employment and whether or not we feel confident that we're on a road that will take us to our maximum employment objective and whether or not we see the risks around obtaining that as balanced.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, there will be uncertainty around it and whether or not we have reasonable confidence that inflation, will, over the medium term, go back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it's really through that filter that we're trying to look at uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, there are many uncertainties in the global economy, but we're asking ourselves how economic and financial developments in the global economy affect the risk to our outlook for our two goals and whether or not they create unbalanced risks that we want to wait to resolve, to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, with respect to global developments, we reviewed developments in all important areas of the world, but we're focused particularly on China and emerging markets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we've long expected, as most analysts have, to see some slowing in Chinese growth over time as they rebalance their economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And they have planned that, and I think there are no surprises there.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The question is whether or not there might be a risk of a more abrupt slowdown than most analysts expect.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think developments that we saw in financial markets in August in part reflected concerns that Chinese-there was downside risk to Chinese economic performance and perhaps concerns about the deftness with which policymakers were addressing those concerns.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In addition, we saw a very substantial downward pressure on oil prices and commodity markets, and those developments have had a significant impact on many emerging market economies that are important producers of commodities as well as more advanced countries, including Canada, which is an important trading partner of ours that has been negatively affected by declining commodity prices, declining energy prices.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, there are a lot of countries that are net importers of energy that are positively affected by those developments, but emerging markets-important emerging markets-have been negatively affected by those developments.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we've seen significant outflows of capital from those countries, pressures on their exchange rates, and concerns about their performance going forward.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So a lot of our focus has been on risks around China, but not just China- emerging markets, more generally, and how they may spill over to the United States.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In terms of thinking about financial developments and our reaction to them, I think a lot of the financial developments were really-so, we don't want to respond to market turbulence.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The Fed should not be responding to the ups and downs of the markets, and it is certainly not our policy to do so.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But when there are significant financial developments, it's incumbent on us to ask ourselves what is causing them.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, of course, while we can't know for sure, it seemed to us as though concerns about the global economic outlook were drivers of those financial developments.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so they have concerned us in part because they take us to the global outlook and how that will affect us.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, to some extent, look, we have seen a tightening of financial conditions during- as I mentioned, during the intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the stock market adjustment, combined with a somewhat stronger dollar and higher risk spreads, does represent some tightening of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, in and of itself, it's not the end of story in terms of our policy because we have to put a lot of different pieces together.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are looking at, as I emphasized, a U.S. economy that has been performing well and impressing us by the pace at which it's creating jobs and the strength of domestic demand.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have some concerns about negative impacts from global developments and some tightening of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're trying to put all of that together in a picture.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think, importantly, we say in our statement that in spite of all of this, we continue to view the risks to economic activity and labor markets as balanced.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it's a lot of different pieces, different cross currents, some strengthening the outlook, some creating concerns, but overall, no significant change in the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I would be very-I would be very surprised if that's the case.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That is not the way I see the outlook or the way the Committee sees the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, really, that's an extreme downside risk that in no way is near the center of my outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, if we maintain a highly accommodative monetary policy for a very long time from here and the economy performs as we expect-namely, it's strong and the risks that are out there don't materialize-my concern will be that we will have much more tightening in labor markets than you see in these projections.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the lags will be probably slow, but eventually we will find ourselves with a substantial overshoot of our inflation objective, and then we'll be forced into a kind of stop-go policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We will have pushed the economy so far it will have become overheated, and we will then have to tighten policy more abruptly than we'd like.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And instead of having slow, steady growth, improvement in the labor market, and continued improvement and good performance in the labor market, I don't think it's good policy to have to then slam on the brakes and risk a downturn in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, let me be clear that negative interest rates was not something that we considered very seriously at all today.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But one participant in the Committee would like to see additional accommodation, is concerned by the inflation outlook, and thinks that we need additional stimulus, additional accommodation to provide that, and proposed doing so by moving interest rates negative.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Look, if-I don't expect that we're going to be in a path of providing additional accommodation, but if the outlook were to change in a way that most of my colleagues and I do not expect and we found ourselves with a weak economy that needed additional stimulus, we would look at all of our available tools, and that would be something that we would evaluate in that kind of context.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So you ask me about my own expectation, and I'd say-I don't want to-I speak on behalf of the Committee and try to explain Committee decisions, and we don't identify who's who in terms of our projections of the funds rate, and I don't want to change that and have the focus be on my personal views on the path.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, I have characterized the Committee view as, you know, a forecast that will likely, if it prevails, if that's how the economy evolves, call for a funds rate increase later this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think that's a fair summary of the Committee's assessment of things.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You asked me, I think, also about uncertainty about our own policies?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the main drivers of the turbulence have been concerns about the global outlook, that's how I read it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I know that, of course, there is uncertainty about Fed policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I mentioned, we're well aware that there's been a huge focus on the decision today.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, you know, I would ask you to appreciate that there are a lot of cross- currents in economic and financial developments that we need to take into account in deciding on what the appropriate course of policy is.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we don't make continuous decisions every single day about our policy, we meet periodically.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We do our darndest to pull together the best analysis we can and to exchange views and to arrive at Committee decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I do understand that, during this intermeeting period, that every word that an FOMC member has said has been parsed for its potential implications for what our decision will be.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think it's, you know-that's an unfortunate state of affairs, but I understand, and I think it's natural when you're at a point when conditions may be falling in place for there to be a shift in policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's natural that that should happen, and it does, to some extent, contribute to uncertainty in financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, monetary policy-U.S. monetary policy is directed toward trying to achieve the goals the Congress has laid out for us.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: When we-when monetary policy tightens and interest rates rise, it commonly is the case, either when it happens or in expectation-the expectation that that's coming-interest rate differentials globally do tend to reduce capital flows that have impacts on exchange rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So monetary policy often has some effect on the exchange rate, and it's not, in my view, the main channel by which monetary policy works.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's one of a number of different channels by which monetary policy works, but it does have some impact on exchange rates, and, of course, yes, we need to take that into account.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: 1 Chair Yellen intended to say that "interest rate differentials globally do tend to induce capital flows that have impacts on exchange rates."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we are envisioning further improvements in the housing market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It remains very depressed-housing starts below levels that seem consistent with underlying demographics, especially in an economy that's creating jobs, and we have lots of people who are still doubled up, and demand for housing should be there and should materialize as the job market improves and income growth improves.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Housing is now a very small sector of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is not the driver of-it is not the key driver in my own forecast of ongoing improvements in the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It plays a supporting role, but consumer spending is the main driver, bolstered by, you know, a decent outlook for investment spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, remember, we're envisioning, if things go as we anticipate, a pretty gradual path of increases in short-term interest rates over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: To some extent, that's already embodied in longer term rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On the other hand, as time passes and we move beyond the window in which short rates are zero, it will be natural for long rates to rise some.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, of course, we recognize that the housing market is sensitive to mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But that's something that, of course, we are taking into account in thinking about what's the appropriate path of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You mentioned you've gotten a lot of unsolicited advice-the folks outside.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there is another side that says the Fed should raise interest rates because keeping rates so long-so low for so long has actually exacerbated the wealth gap.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Do you think the Fed has widened the wealth gap with its low interest rate policy?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: These people say low interest rates mainly benefit the wealthy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I guess I really don't see it that way.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is true that interest rates affect asset prices, but they have a complex effect through balance sheets, through liabilities and assets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: To me, the main thing that an accommodative monetary policy does is put people back to work.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And since income inequality is surely exacerbated by a high-having high unemployment and a weak job market that has the most profound negative effects on the most vulnerable individuals, to me, putting people back to work and seeing a strengthening of the labor market that has a disproportionately favorable effect on vulnerable portions of our population, that's not something that increases income inequality.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There have been a number of studies that have done-been done recently that have tried to take account of many different ways in which monetary policy, acting through different parts of the transmission mechanism, affect inequality.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And there's a lot of guesswork involved, and different analyses can come up with different things.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But a pretty recent paper that's quite comprehensive concludes that Fed policy has not exacerbated income inequality.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I believe it's the responsibility of Congress to pass a budget, to fund the government, to deal with a debt ceiling so that America pays its bills.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a good recovery in place that's really making progress, and to see Congress take actions that would endanger that progress-I think that would be more than unfortunate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Congress charged us with forming an economic outlook that is focused on the medium term and taking appropriate policy actions based on that outlook, and that's what we have done in the past and will continue to do going forward.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have been-and this was reported in the minutes of our July meeting-we have been discussing reinvestment policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Our normalization principles indicated that we would not begin to either reduce or eliminate reinvestments until after we have begun to raise the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Our principles said that the exact timing of that would depend on economic and financial conditions and our evaluation of them, and that guidance continues to be accurate-we don't have anything further on it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it is certainly true that we have committed to wait to begin running down our balance sheet until after we've begun the process of normalization.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, yes, if we defer, this is not a very large matter that we're talking about from a stimulus point of view.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it is, to some extent, true that if we delay raising the rate, it probably-maybe delays the timing at which that process will begin.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there's no fixed- we've not given some fixed amount of time at so many months after we start.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we're continuing to discuss what the appropriate timing would be of that policy and haven't made any further decisions on that just yet.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We decided to move at this time because we feel the conditions that we set out for a move-namely, further improvement in the labor market and reasonable confidence that inflation would move back to 2 percent over the medium term-we felt that these conditions had been satisfied.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have been concerned, as you know, about the risks from the global economy, and those risks persist, but the U.S. economy has shown considerable strength.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Domestic spending that accounts for 85 percent of aggregate spending in the U.S. economy has continued to hold up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And while there is a drag from net exports, from relatively weak growth abroad, and the appreciation of the dollar, overall, we decided today that the risks to the outlook for the labor market and the economy are balanced.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We would like to be able to move in a prudent and, as we've emphasized, gradual manner.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's been a long time since the Federal Reserve has raised interest rates, and I think it's prudent to be able to watch what the impact is on financial conditions and spending in the economy, and moving in a timely fashion enables us to do this.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Again, I think it's important not to overblow the significance of this first move.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have indicated that we will be watching what happens very carefully in the economy in terms of our actual and forecast- our projected conditions relative to our employment and inflation goals and will adjust policy over time as seems appropriate to achieve those goals.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
