text: Our expectation, as I've indicated, is that policy adjustments will be gradual over time, but, of course, they will be informed by the outlook, which in turn will evolve with incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's a benchmark that I think is usual-is useful for assessing the stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Neutral is essentially a stance of policy, a level of short-term rates, which, if the economy were operating near its potential- and we're reasonably not quite at that, but reasonably close to it-it would be a level that would maintain or sustain those conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, at this point, policy we judge to be accommodative.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The Committee forecasts that the unemployment rate will continue to decline, and I think that's important and appropriate for two reasons.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: First of all, as I've indicated, I continue to judge that there remains slack in the economy, margins of slack that are not reflected in the standard unemployment rate, and, in particular, I've pointed to the depressed level of labor force participation and also the somewhat abnormally high level of part-time employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So a further decline in the unemployment rate and strengthening of labor market conditions will help to erode those margins of slack.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But also we want to see inflation move up back to our 2 percent objective over the medium term, and so seeing above-trend growth and continuing tightness- greater tightness in labor and product markets-I think that will help us achieve our objective as well with respect to inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have kept rates at an extremely low level and had a high balance sheet for a very long time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have considered the risks to the outlook and worried about the fact that with interest rates at zero, we have less scope to respond to negative shocks than to positive shocks that would call for a tightening of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That is a factor that has induced us to hold rates at zero for this long.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we recognize that policy is accommodative, and if we do not begin to slightly reduce the amount of accommodation, the odds are good that the economy would end up overshooting both our employment and inflation objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: What I-we would like to avoid is a situation where we have waited so long that we're forced to tighten policy abruptly, which risks aborting what I would like to see as a very long-running and sustainable expansion.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So to keep the economy moving along the growth path it's on with improving and solid conditions in labor markets, we would like to avoid a situation where we have left so much accommodation in place for so long that we overshoot these objectives and then have to tighten abruptly and risk damaging-damaging that performance.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, we recognize that inflation is well below our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The entire Committee is committed to achieving our 2 percent inflation objective over the medium term, just as we want to make sure that inflation doesn't persist at levels above our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The Committee is equally committed-this is a symmetric goal-and the Committee is equally committed to not allowing inflation to persist below our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, I've tried to explain-and many of my colleagues have as well-why we have reasonable confidence that inflation will move up over time, and the Committee declared it had reasonable confidence.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Nevertheless, that is a forecast, and we really need to monitor over time actual inflation performance to make sure that it is conforming, it is evolving, in the manner that we expect.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it doesn't mean that we need to see inflation reach 2 percent before moving again, but we have expectations for how inflation will behave.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And were we to find that the underlying theory is not bearing out, that it is not behaving in the manner that we expect, and that it doesn't look like the shortfall is transitory and disappearing with tighter labor markets, that would certainly give us pause.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we have indicated that we're reasonably close-not quite there, but reasonably close-to achieving our maximum employment objective, but we have a significant shortfall on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so we're calling attention to the importance of verifying our-that things evolve in line with our forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm not going to give you a simple formula for what we need to see on the inflation front in order to raise rates again.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We'll also be looking at the path of employment as well as the path for inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But if incoming data were-led us to call into question the inflation forecast that we have set out, and that could be a variety of different kinds of evidence, that would certainly give the Committee pause.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I don't want to say there's a simple benchmark.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We-you know, the Committee expects inflation-over the next year, the median expectation is for inflation to be running about 1. percent, and-both core and headline.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we do expect it to be moving up, but we don't expect it to reach 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: First, let me say with respect to oil prices, I have been surprised by the further downward movement in oil prices, but we do not need to see oil prices rebound to higher levels in order for the impact on inflation to wash out.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I believe there is some limit below which oil prices are unlikely to rise.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If we look at market expectations, market expectations are for stabilization and then some gradual upward movement.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I certainly grant that we've had a series of shocks pushing them down, but we're not looking for them to revert back to the-to higher levels that they were at merely to stabilize.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We-I would point out, you asked me, would we tolerate overshoots.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: For a number of years between 2004 and 2008, we had a series of increases in oil prices that for a series of years raised inflation above-again, we didn't have a 2 percent objective then, but-raised it above 2 percent, and we judged those increases to be transitory as well and looked through them.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If we saw in a meaningful way that inflation expectations were either moving up in a way that made it-them seem unanchored or down, that would be of concern.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we have called attention to some slight downward movements in survey measures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are watching that, but I still judge that inflation expectations are reasonably well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, yes, we have tolerated inflation shortfalls that we thought would disappear over the medium term just as we did overshoots of inflation that we also judged to be transitory.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we do need to monitor inflation very carefully because if energy prices and the dollar were to stabilize, import prices, our expectation is that both headline and core inflation would move up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if we failed to see that occurring in the manner that we expect, of course we need to take further action to reconsider the outlook and to put in place appropriate policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, you know, if the economy were disappointing, we-you know, our actions wouldn't purely be based on inflation, we would also take employment into account.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I can't give you a simple answer, but we would pursue a more accommodative policy because we do-certainly are committed to achieving 2 percent over the medium term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, there are number of different channels through which monetary policy is transmitted to spending decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The behavior of longer-term-longer-term interest rates, short-term interest rates matter.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The value of asset prices and the exchange rate, also- these are transmission channels.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We wouldn't be focused on short-term financial volatility, but were there unanticipated changes in financial conditions that were persistent and we judged to affect the outlook, we would of course have to take those into account.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we will watch financial developments, but what we're looking at here is the longer-term economic outlook: Are we seeing persistent changes in financial market conditions that would have a bearing, a significant bearing, on the outlook that we would need to take account in formulating appropriate policy?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Yes, we would, but it's not short-term volatility in markets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, look, you know, we-this is not an unanticipated policy move, and we have been trying to explain what our policy strategy is.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it's not as though I'm expecting to see a marked, immediate reaction in financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Expectations about Fed policy have been built into the structure of financial market prices, but we obviously will track carefully the behavior of both short- and longer-term interest rates, the dollar, and asset prices, and if they move in persistent and significant ways that are out of line with the expectations that we have, then of course we will take those into account.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me start by saying that I feel confident about the fundamentals driving the U.S. economy, the health of U.S. households, and domestic spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are pressures on some sectors of the economy, particularly manufacturing and the energy sector, reflecting global developments and developments in commodity markets and energy markets, but the underlying health of the U.S. economy I consider to be quite sound.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think it's a myth that expansions die of old age.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I do not think that they die of old age.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the fact that this has been quite a long expansion doesn't lead me to believe that it's one that has-its days are numbered.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the economy does get hit by shocks, and there are both positive shocks and negative shocks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so there is a significant odd, you know, probability in any year that the economy will suffer some shock that we don't know about that will put it into recession.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so I'm not sure exactly how high that probability is in any year, but maybe at least on the order of 10 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, yes, there is some probability that that could happen, and of course we'd appropriately respond, but it isn't something that is fated to happen because we've had a long expansion, and I don't see anything in the underlying strength of the economy that would lead me to be concerned about that outcome.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, during the years in which we were-you know, the economy was recovering from the Great Recession and we put further policy and measures in place, we studied our policy options quite carefully.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As you know, communications policy to affect market expectations about the path of interest rates played an important role.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Obviously, we lowered our overnight interest rate effectively to zero.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we have seen some foreign central banks, Europe-the ECB and others-that have taken their overnight rate into negative territory, and that's something that-I don't contemplate that we will need to do this, but it is something that we could study.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, we have balance sheet policies, and there might be a range of direct policies that we could use as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But this is something that we have thought about, our range of options.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, in our normalization principles, which are in effect, the Committee stated that we eventually want to operate with a much smaller balance sheet of-than we have at present.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The-we would reduce the size of the balance sheet to essentially whatever size we needed to manage monetary policy effective-in an effective and efficient way.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, a lot has changed since pre-financial crisis in terms of the financial system, and we are studying- we are engaging in a project at this time to consider what our long-run operating framework should look like.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I can't tell you exactly what size of balance sheet we will determine is the best to operate in an efficient and effective manner.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It might be somewhat larger than the very tiny quantity of reserves that we had in pre-crisis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have also said that we will-we expect to reduce the size of our balance sheet over time by cease- diminishing or ceasing entirely reinvestments.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, beyond that, we haven't given additional guidance other than to say that the timing of reductions in reinvestment will depend on economic and financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I suppose the additional guidance we're giving today, when we say "well under way," we want to see-as I mentioned, there are number of considerations, and the Committee has made no further decisions about this, but as we've discussed, the factors that will be relevant to the decision-one factor that we've talked about is the desirability of having some scope to respond to an adverse shock to the economy by lowering the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so it would be nice to have a buffer in terms of having raised the federal funds rate to a certain extent to give us some meaningful scope to respond.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, I don't have in mind any particular level of the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It would depend on the entire economic outlook, how robust the economy is.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But that is an important consideration for the Committee, and it means that this is not something that we expect to be turning to, to cease reinvestment very quickly.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, risk spreads in the high-yield bond market have been widening since last year, partly reflecting falling oil prices-only partly, but partly-and redemptions in high-yield bond funds have been increasing in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But Third Avenue Focused Credit Fund was a rather unusual open-end mutual fund.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It had very concentrated positions in especially risky and illiquid bonds, and it had been facing very significant redemption pressures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My understanding is that the SEC is in touch with Third Avenue.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as you probably know, the SEC has proposed some reforms to address what's a structural problem of liquidity mismatch in open-end mutual funds.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we continue to believe that financial conditions are supportive of economic growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We will be-we have been and will continue to track developments in financial markets very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would say that I think we have a far more resilient financial system now than we had prior to the financial crisis and highly capital[ized] banks that are well situated to support corporate lending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'd also point out that many corporations during these years have reduced their interest payments and extended their debt profiles, and I think that should help to mitigate spillovers, but we will be evaluating this carefully.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, when you say that central banks often kill them, I think the usual reason that that has been true when that has been true is that central banks have begun too late to tighten policy, and they've allowed inflation to get out of control.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And at that point, they have had to tighten policy very abruptly and very substantially, and it's caused a downturn, and the downturn has served to lower inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, if you don't mind my flipping the question on you, I would point out that it is because we don't want to cause a recession through that type of dynamic at some future date that it is prudent to begin early and gradually.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, it is true that some central banks have raised rates and later turned around.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Not in every case has that reflected a policy mistake.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Sometimes when they have raised rates, it hasn't been the wrong thing to do, but conditions have changed in a way that they have had to reverse policy to respond to shocks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm not denying that there are situations where central banks have moved too early.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have weighed that risk carefully in making today's decision.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, look, you know, as I've-as the Committee has said, we're watching economic developments closely, and we will adjust policy in whatever way is necessary to support the attainment of our objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the first-the first thing that Americans should realize is that the Fed's decision today reflects our confidence in the U.S. economy, that we believe we have seen substantial improvement in labor market conditions, and while things may be uneven across regions of the country and different industrial sectors, we see an economy that is on a path of sustainable improvement.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in thinking about their labor market prospects and their financial prospects going forward, I hope they will take this decision as one that signals the FOMC's confidence that conditions will continue to strengthen and job market prospects will be good.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It will be reflected in some changes in borrowing rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Longer- term interest rates-loans that are linked to longer-term interest rates are unlikely to move-to move very much.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Some-for example, some corporate loans are linked to the prime rate, which is likely to move up with the fed funds rate, and those interest rates will adjust.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are some consumer borrowing rates, I think credit card rates, that are linked to short-term rates that might move up slightly.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, remember, we have very low rates, and we have made a very small move.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Interest rate risk at banks is something that we have been monitoring very carefully for quite a long time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The community banks and smaller banking organizations that we work with-part of our supervision has been ensuring that they manage appropriately for interest rate risk.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the larger banking organizations that are subject to the stress tests and capital planning-the scenarios that we have presented in each of the last three years look at their ability to withstand what would be much sharper increases in interest rates than we're envisioning would happen.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we want to make sure that if there were sharper increases- unlike our expectations-that they would be well positioned to handle it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we have concluded that-that their capital positions are sufficient for them to weather it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, we have said that we will carefully monitor both actual and expected progress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, I think that standard Fed policy has been to look through shocks that are transitory.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have had some further declines in energy prices, and, you know, as I said previously, I do expect there is a bottom to that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If we-if we analyze inflation data and conclude that, clearly, transitory influences are holding down inflation, I do not want to say that we would respond to that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But if we concluded that there were structural factors or that there were a problem with our theory or some global deflationary force that were simply persistently holding down inflation in a way that was not transitory-and I don't want to attach any simplistic meaning to what we would need to see to conclude that in the inflation data, but if we concluded that, we certainly would take action to make sure we adjusted policy so that we attain our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we would need to feel that what we were seeing in the data suggested a sustained departure from our 2 percent objective that we really needed to address.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, starting with the median CPIs, we look at a range of statistics that bear on the inflation outlook, and the median CPI has been somewhat more stable and running closer to 2 percent than the PCE, but there is a systematic gap between these two measures, and our objective is 2 percent on the PCE price index, and so there's no simple translation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I-there are upside risks to the economy, and I think, you know, we tend to focus on the downside risk.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Housing has been recovering very slowly, but the demographics would point to considerable upside for residential investment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My mainline forecast is for gradual recovery, but there is upside risk there.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have seen that the decline in drilling has been depressing investment spending, but there's upside risk too.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The global economy-we tend to focus-there are many countries that are undergoing very difficult adjustments or slowing growth, especially with declining commodity prices.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But even recently, we've seen growth in emerging markets strengthen.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And-so it is not only downside risks, but, you know, we do pay attention to downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the Committee said they regard the risks overall as balanced.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I do want to emphasize that while we have said "gradual," gradual does not mean mechanical, evenly timed, equally sized interest rate changes.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that is not what the Committee means by it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My guess is that the economy will progress in a manner that is not sufficiently even that we will decide to make evenly spaced hikes.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I recognize we want to do what's appropriate, and I recognize that's a danger.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I do want to assure you that we will be data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I strongly doubt that it will mean equally spaced hikes, and it certainly is not the intention of the Committee to follow any mechanical formula of that type.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, so the reason-the main reason that we revised down our projection ever so slightly-it's hardly revised for core inflation-is because we have seen further appreciation of the dollar that's holding down import prices that spills over into core inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, my own estimation is that core inflation will pick up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are various idiosyncratic factors that affect core inflation-for example, nonmarket price increases, which are a little bit hard to understand, have been running at a slow pace.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There were factors that have been affecting inflation in medical care prices that may change over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I personally don't think we're in a world where inflation is being determined in a different way than it has historically.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I see import prices and energy prices as holding down headline but also core, and I do believe it will pick up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But as we've said, if that theory is wrong and we do not see inflation is unfolding in the way the Committee expects, we will make adjustments over time in policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, we have many people who are studying inflation models.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've, you know, tried to-let me express some humility about them.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are theories of how the economy works that govern many aspects of economic forecasting.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Whether it's consumer spending or residential investment or inflation, the underlying theories are not perfect, and they are subject to uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And this is true in all aspects of forecasting, which is why we change our forecasts and our models.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm not aware, I will say, of a different model of inflation that would be superior to the one that we employ.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we have to verify that inflation is moving in the manner that we expect, and if it's not, we need to adjust policy accordingly.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we are constantly monitoring foreign economic developments, including those in emerging markets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We understand that in the global economy, with integrated product and capital markets, that our fates are very much linked, and that the performance of the U.S. economy has important spillovers onto emerging markets and vice versa.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have been trying very carefully-we've made a commitment to emerging market policymakers that we would do our best to communicate as clearly as we could about our policy intentions to avoid spillovers that might result from abrupt or unanticipated policy moves.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think this move has been expected and well communicated-at least, I hope that it has.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: This action takes place in the context of a U.S. economy that is doing well and is a source of strength to the emerging markets and other economies around the globe.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so-that is, there can be negative spillovers through capital flows, but remember, there are also positive spillovers from a strong U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My general view is that many emerging markets are in a stronger position than they would have been in the 1990s-for example, that they have stronger macroeconomic policies.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They have taken steps to strengthen their financial systems and are better positioned to deal with this.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On the other hand, there are vulnerabilities there, and there are countries that have been badly affected by declining commodity prices, so we will monitor this very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we have taken care to avoid unnecessary negative spillovers.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Wage growth is not quite where you would like it to be-

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Wage growth is not quite where you would like it to be.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: How much is that going to play into your thinking next year as you're trying to decide whether to raise interest rates more and when?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So my expectation is that in a strengthening labor market that we would see faster wage growth, and I believe there is, with the 2 percent inflation objective, space for wage growth to be higher than it's been.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We may be seeing some incipient signs of faster wage growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've seen a pickup in measures of hourly compensation and some slight firming in recent months in average hourly earnings.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I hesitate to say that this is a firm trend.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Wage growth is not-there are many factors that affect it-it's not definitive in any sense in determining our policy, but it does have a bearing on the inflation outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It also has a bearing on assessing how much slack there is in the labor market, and I think a number of my colleagues looking at the slow pace of wage growth have-you've seen that their estimates of the longer-run normal unemployment rate have come down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think that is one of the factors that has prompted those adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, it does affect views about just how much slack there is in the labor market and the inflation outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, let me start-let me start with the question of the Fed's credibility, and you used the word "promises" in connection with that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I tried to emphasize in my opening statement, the paths that the participants project for the federal funds rate and how it will evolve are not a preset plan or commitment or promise of the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Indeed, they are not even-the median should not be interpreted as a Committee-endorsed forecast, and there's a lot of uncertainty around each participant's projection.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And they will evolve-those assessments of appropriate policy are completely contingent on each participant's forecast of the economy and how economic events will unfold.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And they are, of course, uncertain, and you should fully expect that forecasts for the appropriate path of policy on the part of all participants will evolve over time as shocks, positive or negative, hit the economy that alter those forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So you have seen a shift this time in most participants' assessments of the appropriate path for policy, and, as I tried to indicate, I think that largely reflects a somewhat slower projected path for global growth-for growth in the global economy outside the United States-and for some tightening in credit conditions in the form of an increase in spreads.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And those changes in financial conditions and in the path of the global economy have induced changes in the assessment of individual participants in what path is appropriate to achieve our objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, I guess you asked me also what would we need to see to continue raising rates, and I think it's worth pointing out here that the Committee-most participants do continue to envision that if economic developments unfold as they expect, that further increases in the federal funds rate will prove appropriate over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Most participants anticipate that, and that the pace will be gradual.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I emphasized, most empirical work attempting to assess what the equilibrium level of the fed funds rate is, a level that would be neither expansionary nor contractionary is-those assessments are quite low at this time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there is accommodation in the stance of policy, and we do expect, over time, that neutral rate to move up, but, you know, we're not positive what rate-what the pace of change of that will be over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, given that the economy is now close to our maximum employment objective, you know, hopefully inflation is moving up-I mentioned, as you mentioned, recent readings on inflation have moved up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There may be some-you know, I want to warn that there may be some transitory factors that are influencing that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, certainly, our projections are for a gradual increase in inflation, and the Committee-at least, most participants continue to expect that if we follow along this course, that some further adjustments in the federal funds rate will be appropriate but gradual.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I want to make clear that our inflation objective is 2 percent, and we are projecting a move back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we are not trying to engineer an overshoot of inflation, not to compensate for past undershoots, so 2 percent is our objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it is a symmetric objective, and we certainly don't seek to overshoot our objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But some undershoots and overshoots are part of how the economy operates, and our tolerance for those is symmetric with respect to under- and overshoots.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We did take note in the statement of the fact that inflation has picked up in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I see some of that as having to do with unusually high inflation readings in categories that tend to be quite volatile without very much significance for inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I'm wary and haven't yet concluded that we have seen any significant uptick that will be lasting in, for example, in core inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we note-the Committee notes, as it did in December, that we continue to monitor development trends and developments closely, and that would include both the fact that recent inflation readings have been on the high side, and, as I mentioned, on the other side, that readings on measures of inflation compensation and some survey measures have been on the low side.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in that sense, there are risks around the inflation forecast in both-in both directions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there has been a slight downgrading of the assessment of economic growth for this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, nevertheless, growth is expected to run in-somewhat in excess of potential, so that the labor market is expected to continue to tighten, and by the end of the year, even edge below levels that-of the unemployment rate-that are estimated to be longer in the normal run, and inflation is expected to gradually move back to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We still have, weighing on inflation, the influence of earlier declines in energy prices and a prolonged effect from the appreciation of the dollar, but we do expect those transitory influences to fade.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And with a continuing-continuing improvement in the labor market, I think we'll see upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, in that context, the Committee sees it appropriate to-if things unfold in that way, to have some further increases in the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I indicated in December-the Committee indicated in December, we want inflation to go back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we also want to be careful not to see some significant overshoots, so that we would get behind the curve and potentially be faced with a need to tighten in a very rapid fashion later in a way that could undermine the sustainability of the employment gains we have had.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we do see some continued tightening in monetary policy to be appropriate in that event.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there has been, by many forecasters, a slight downgrading of forecasts of global growth in-over the coming several years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The IMF has slightly downgraded their forecasts, and other international agencies have as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've anticipated that it would slow over time, and it seems to be slowing as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Japanese growth in the fourth quarter was negative, and that was something of a surprise.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And with respect to the euro area, recent indicators suggest perhaps slightly weaker growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there's been a number of emerging markets-as you know, we're suffering under the weight of declines in oil prices that are affecting their economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Our neighbors both to the north and south, Canada and Mexico, are feeling the impacts of lower oil prices on their growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So our projection for global growth, for those reasons, is slightly lower-not dramatically lower, but enough lower to make some difference to our forecast.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I indicated, I think that's part of the reason, along with the associated increase we have seen in some spreads that are involved in-enter into corporate borrowing rates, and can affect investment decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's a reason to think that a slightly lower path for the federal funds rate will be appropriate to achieve our objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so what you see here is a virtually unchanged path of economic projections and a slightly more accommodative path that most participants are writing down for what's necessary to achieve that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I will say again that every meeting is a live meeting.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: April remains a live meeting, and we will be tracking incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have six weeks, but there will be additional data on the labor market and on various factors that pertain to inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that's, you know, that's-that is certainly a live possibility.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me start with the impact of oil prices on consumer spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I have to say, it's very difficult when you look at patterns of consumer spending to-there are many factors that influence it, and to definitively say that lower oil prices have not boosted consumer spending, I'm not sure we can really arrive at that conclusion in any-in any rigorous way.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The typical-the average household in the United States with oil prices where they are now is probably benefiting around $1,000 a year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And some very detailed microdata that I've seen on household spending patterns suggest that there may be a link, as you would expect, from reduced bills-you know, reduced amounts that people pay at the pump to other spending, like eating out at-for restaurant meals and other things.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the aggregate data, I-you know, is not as strong as it-and spending is not as strong as it could be, given the decline.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, of course, on the other side, we are-and, you know, it may be that it will take a while, and it's something that will slowly strengthen over time if oil prices stay low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On the other side, of course, we have seen a marked decline in drilling activity, which has depressed investment spending, and, of course, very substantial layoffs in the energy sector.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With respect to impact of oil prices on inflation and what would happen if they move up, the Committee has generally tended to look through movements in oil prices, whether they were on the upside or on the downside, viewing it as a factor that should have a transitory influence.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And when I say that, what I mean is that if oil prices move up during the time that it's moving up, it raises inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But they don't need to move down again to their previous levels for that influence to disappear, they only need to stabilize at a higher level.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, similarly, oil prices have obviously moved down a great deal over the last year, and we're not expecting them to move back to their previous levels but to stabilize at some level.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They're obviously volatile, but, as they stabilize, the influence will move out of both headline-of headline inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that's what you see in the forecasts of participants.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So if oil prices were to increase to 50, I mean, that would probably slightly move up our expected path for core inflation, maybe speed how rapidly we would move back to 2 percent, but I wouldn't think that that would be something alone that would have great policy significance.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me say that, in recent weeks, I think the Committee certainly thinks that risks to the outlook have diminished.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, I would point out that we decided not to describe the balance of risks as weighted to the downside.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the Committee did not reach that judgment, and there is no collective judgment in this statement on whether the risks are balanced or not.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, my guess is that some participants see them as balanced, and some see them as weighted somewhat to the downside.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I think it is important to note a couple of things.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: First of all, the U.S. economy has been very resilient in recent months in the face of shocks, and we highlighted that right at the beginning of our statement, where we said that "economic activity has been expanding at a moderate pace despite the global economic and financial developments of recent months."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that-that is important, that the U.S. economy continues to do well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Second, I would say that while global developments do pose some downside risks, the risks are not all one sided.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: A number of countries-including China, the euro area, the Bank of Japan-have taken measures to stimulate the economy, so there is also upside risk to the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, in addition, oil prices have rebounded from their lows, and that eases concerns about the financial condition of some energy firms and the stresses facing some oil-producing economies.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, at the same time, low oil prices continue to boost household purchasing power.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have not described them as unbalanced to the out-to the downside, and they are two sided.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I must say I'm-I do see broad-based improvement in the labor market, and I'm somewhat surprised that we're not seeing more of a pickup in wage growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But at least-and I have to say, in anecdotal reports, we do hear quite a number of reports of firms facing wage pressures and even broad-based, slightly faster increases in wages-wage increases that they're granting.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But in the aggregate data, one doesn't yet see any convincing evidence of a pickup in wage growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I do think, consistent with the 2 percent inflation objective, that there is certainly scope for further increases in wages.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The fact that we have not seen any broad-based pickup is one of the factors that suggests to me that there is continued slack in the labor market, but I would expect wage growth to move up some.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Let me start with your second question, if I might.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So in trying to judge the outlook for the economy, we do look at measures pertaining to consumer sentiment, and they are in solid territory.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Gains in inflation- adjusted disposable income are running at a healthy pace.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I mentioned, households have benefited pretty significantly from lower oil prices, and measures of consumer sentiment do reflect-do reflect that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, really, the labor market, I think, has improved a great deal.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And every demographic group that, you know, we track regularly has seen improvement in their labor market situation-perhaps not all equally, but almost all demographic groups have seen improvement.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I-I think it's right to say the economy is improving, and most groups are seeing benefits.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That said, we know that inequality has been rising in the United States over many years, not just the last several but going back to the mid-'80s.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There has been downward pressure on real wage groups-on real wage gains for groups, particularly those that are less skilled and educated, and those longer-term trends that may be associated with a number of factors- technological change and globalization-have been a concern for many, many years, and that may be part of what you're-we're seeing expressed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me start with the question pertaining to exchange rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In-in a world with highly integrated capital markets, monetary policy actions in any country have effects-spillovers to other countries.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's true of our monetary policy, and it's true of other countries' monetary policies.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In part, that shows up through movements in exchange rates, and those movements are a factor that any country needs to take into account in deciding what is the appropriate stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the fact that there are these linkages is an important factor in designing a monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it does not mean that monetary-U.S. monetary policy is somehow constrained in a way that makes it impossible for our monetary policy to diverge from policies abroad.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are many periods when monetary policies in different countries have moved in different directions, and, you know, the United States has been growing more strongly and had better success in the labor market than many other advanced countries.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, at this point, it's natural that there should be some divergence in our monetary policies.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I wouldn't want to endorse the notion if, you know-that you're suggesting, that our policy is in some way crippled by the fact that there are these interlinkages.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We-this is one reason we meet-meet frequently with other economic policymakers in other countries, exchange notes about how we see economic developments evolve, and try to keep one another apprised of economic developments and likely policy responses.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I want to start by saying that I've been involved for many years in the Federal Reserve System, and we are a nonpartisan, independent institution devoted to pursuing our congressionally mandated objectives, and I have never seen political views in any way influence the policy judgments that are made inside the Federal Reserve.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The political activities of Governors, participants, government employees are governed by the Hatch Act.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are all subject to that, and the Hatch Act does allow campaign contributions to be made.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I would say, within that, so it is each-it's up to each individual to decide what is appropriate, in their point of view.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the Federal Reserve is not-is not a partisan political organization.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I should point out that I think what you're talking about is the slight decline in the median estimate of the longer-run normal unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I-the path of rate increases maybe slightly reflects the modest decline in estimates of the longer-run normal unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That, I would say, reflects, for those who brought it down, an estimate of greater slack in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's also, as I mentioned, a reflection of shifts in other views about, for example, the likely pace of global growth that affects what we need, as a policy path, to achieve our objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the slow pace of wage growth, the fact that part-time employment for economic reasons and voluntary part-time employment remains high-we have seen an upward move in labor force participation, which is heartening and suggests that there was scope there for further improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My guess is that those things influenced individuals who wrote down a slightly lower number for the longer-run unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've heard a lot of talk today about President Obama's pick for the Supreme Court, but there are a number of vacancies on the Fed Board of Governors, and there's a new position, the Vice Chair[man] for Supervision, that the President hasn't even nominated anyone for.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Would you like the President to nominate someone for that position, and what effect are those vacancies having on the Fed?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I think Congress intended for the Federal Reserve Board to have seven members, and that tends to bring on board people with a wide spectrum of views and experience and perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think that's valuable, and I would like to see the Senate move forward and consider these nominees so that we could operate with a full complement.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With respect to the nomination for Vice Chair[man] [for] Supervision, that's a question that I think you need to pose to the White House.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I, you know, would say that we are doing a very good job on supervision, and, you know, we are very focused on and devote a great deal of time to that issue.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, really, it's-the nomination question is one for the White House.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have been working at this for a number of years, and I believe we have made very substantial progress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a-much more capital, higher-quality capital, liquidity in the banking system.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Our supervision has-we have made very meaningful changes for-in our supervision, for example.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The stress tests-the stress-test methodology that we use routinely to evaluate the robustness of the capital positions and plans of the largest institutions constitutes a quantum leap in terms of, I think, the quality of the supervision we are providing, especially of the largest firms.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have finished writing most of the Dodd-Frank rules.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are working very hard on "too big to fail," which is of grave concern to the American people.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In addition to having a financial system that is more robust and less likely to experience a failure, we have also worked very hard, continue to work on making sure we have the ability to resolve a firm if it were to fail in spite-in spite of having more capital and liquidity.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And there, too, I think, we have made very substantial progress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: A month or so ago, we came out with a rule-so-called TLAC rule-that would require the largest firms to hold a substantial buffer of long-term debt that, in the event that they were to fail, could be bailed in to protect the taxpayer from having to bear any burden in terms of injecting capital into the firms-it would provide loss absorption in that event.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And working jointly, closely with the FDIC, firms have made a great deal of progress with their living wills.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're in the process of evaluating the most recent submissions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And working with the FDIC, I think, potential techniques that could be used in the event of a failure of a significant financial institution, we have also made a lot of progress there.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think I was at the meeting of financial regulators with the President when he made those comments, and I understood that what he was trying to tell the American people, that they should understand there really has been very substantial progress, and that's something they should be aware of.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I think-I think it's our job as we make these improvements to explain what we're doing and to try to educate the public about what's happened, and they may not understand how much has changed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's certainly part of my own responsibility to try to explain that to the American people.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Okay, so that was a complicated question, and there-let me start with the Phillips curve.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the Phillips curve posits that there is a relationship between the degree of slack in the labor market and inflation, and it is an empirical relationship that, while not absolutely tight, has been a consistent relationship over time, and I believe that relationship still holds.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the impact of shifts in the unemployment rate on inflation should not be overstated.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The Phillips curve has become, according to most estimates, quite flat in the sense that movements in unemployment have only a modest impact on inflation, so we shouldn't overblow how large that is.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In addition, the Phillips curve theory suggests that inflation expectations are also an important driver of actual wage- and price-setting decisions and inflation behavior, and I believe there's also solid empirical evidence for that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it's one of the reasons that I highlighted in my statement, and we continue to highlight in the FOMC statement, that we are tracking indicators of the inflation expectations that matter to wage and price setting.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, unfortunately, we don't have perfect measures of these things.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We know that household measures, even when households are asked about longer- term inflation-at longer-term inflation, they tend to move in response to salient changes in prices that they see every day.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In particular, when gas prices go down, which is very noticeable to most households, you tend to see a view-you tend to see responses about long-term inflation marked down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that's kind of an overresponse to something that's transitory.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it's difficult to get a clear read from those survey measures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Inflation compensation as measured in financial markets also embodies a variety of risk premia and liquidity premia.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so, it's also-we monitor those closely and discuss them in the statement in paragraph one, but, again, there's not a straight read on what's happening to the expectations that influence wage and price setting.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But this model continues to at least influence my own thinking, and it certainly is a factor that I and at least some of my colleagues are incorporating in these projections.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So what I would like to make clear is that this is not actively a subject that we are considering or discussing.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The Committee continues to feel that we are on a course where the economy is improving and inflation is moving back up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I indicated, if events continue to unfold in that way, we are likely to gradually raise rates over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're prepared to respond if things transpire differently, but we are not spending time actively debating and considering things we could do for additional accommodation and certainly not actively considering negative rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are looking at the experience in other countries, and I guess I would judge they seem to have mixed effects, you know, some positive and some negative things.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, look, if we found ourselves in the unlikely situation where we needed to add accommodation, we have a range of tools.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we know from the things we did in the past that we have a number of options with respect to the maturity, for example, of our portfolio, with respect to asset purchases or forward guidance that remain available to us, that are tools we could turn to in the unlikely event that we need to add accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So negative rates is not something that we're actively considering.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, Brexit, the upcoming U.K. decision on whether or not to leave the European Union, is something we discussed, and I think it's fair to say that it was one of the factors that factored into today's decisions-clearly this is a very important decision for the United Kingdom and for Europe.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is a decision that could have consequences for economic and financial conditions in global financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If it does so, it could have consequences in turn for the U.S. economic outlook that would be a factor in deciding on the appropriate path of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it is certainly one of the uncertainties that we discussed and that factored into today's decision.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, there is really a great deal of uncertainty around each individual's assessment of the appropriate level of rates, particularly as we go further out in the forecast horizon and when we come to the long term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think what we can see, and what many econometric and other studies show, is that the so-called neutral rate-namely, the level of the federal funds rate that is consistent with the economy growing roughly at trend and operating near full employment-that rate is quite depressed by historical standards.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Many estimates would put it, in real or inflation-adjusted terms, near zero.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, the path that you see in the dot plot for rates over time is importantly influenced-there is accommodation, and as we achieve our objectives, I think most participants feel that the accommodation in the current stance of policy needs to be gradually removed, but a very important influence in the out years is, what will happen to that neutral rate that will just keep the economy operating on an even keel?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I've often in my statements and remarks talked about headwinds that reflect lingering effects of the financial crisis; to the extent that there are headwinds, I think many of us expect that these headwinds would gradually diminish over time, and that's a reason why you see the upward path for rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there are also more long-lasting or persistent factors that may be at work that are holding down the longer-run level of neutral rates-for example, slow productivity growth, which is not just a U.S. phenomenon but a global phenomenon.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, obviously, there is a lot of uncertainty about what will happen to productivity growth, but productivity growth could stay long for a prolonged time, and we have an aging-aging societies in many parts of the world that could depress this neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think all of us are involved in a process of constantly reevaluating where is that neutral rate going, and I think what you see is a downward shift in that assessment over time, the sense that maybe more of what's causing this neutral rate to be low are factors that are not going to be rapidly disappearing but will be part of the new normal.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, 1 Chair Yellen intended to say, "You know, obviously, there is a lot of uncertainty about what will happen to productivity growth, but productivity growth could stay low for a prolonged time, and we have an aging-aging societies in many parts of the world that could depress this neutral rate."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: you still see an assessment that that neutral rate will move up somewhat, but it has been coming down, and I think it continues to be marked lower.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it is highly uncertain, for all of the dots.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I'm not going to comment on participants versus voters.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, monetary policy-the Committee feels that monetary policy-when we are looking at several years, we should show the public what the views are of all the participants in the Committee, especially given that voting-voting rotates every year, and so that's a decision we made.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But you asked me what it would take to have two increases.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, the Committee as a whole never discusses, how many increases should we have this year or next year-that's not a decision we're making as a Committee.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're making decisions on a meeting-by-meeting basis and trying to give a sense to the public of what we're looking for and what the basis of a decision will be.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I indicated, first of all, international uncertainties loom large here; we mentioned Brexit, the U.K. decision, obviously how that turns out is something that will factor into future decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we're also looking at the prospects for economic growth and continued progress in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The forecast that you see in the SEP and the statement indicate the Committee continues to expect we will have moderate growth, 2 percent growth-so, you know, suggests healthy growth for the rest of the year and a pickup in growth in the second quarter, and we expect to see continuing progress in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we had questions about the growth outlook because we did see slower growth in the fourth quarter and in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I have to say there, with respect to the slowdown we saw in consumer spending, that seemed to be out of line with fundamentals.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We expected it to pick up, and we've seen very good evidence that it has picked up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But now, the labor market appears to have slowed down, and we need to assure ourselves that the underlying momentum in the economy has not diminished.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, as I said, we will be carefully assessing data on the labor market to make sure that job gains are going to continue at a pace sufficient to result in further improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we will be watching the spending data to make sure growth is picking up in line with our expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, with respect to inflation, we're constantly evaluating whether or not incoming information is roughly in line with our expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we will be evaluating that at every meeting; every meeting is live, and we could make a decision at any meeting to adjust the funds rate, but that's the kind of thing that we will want to see to make such decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, let me just say the labor market conditions index is a kind of experimental research product that's a summary measure of many different indicators, and, essentially, that measure tries to assess the change in the labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I look at it, and as that index looks at things, the state of the labor market is still healthy, but there's been something of a loss of momentum: The 200,000 jobs a month we saw, for example, in the first quarter of the year, that's slowed in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Exactly what the reasons are for that slowing, it's difficult to say.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It may turn out-you know, again, we should never pay too much attention to, for example, one job market report.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There's a large error around that, we often see large revisions, we should not overblow the significance of one data point, especially when other indicators of the labor market are still flashing green: Initial claims for unemployment insurance remain low; perceptions of the labor market remain fine; data from the JOLTS on job openings continue to reach new highs.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there's a good deal of incoming data that does signal continued progress and strength in the labor market, but, as I say, it does bear watching.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, the Committee doesn't feel and doesn't expect, and I don't expect, that labor market-progress in the labor market has come to an end.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have tried to make clear to the public and through our actions and through the revisions you see-have seen over time in the dot plot-that we do not have a fixed plan for raising rates over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We look at incoming data and are prepared to adjust our views to keep the economy on track, and, in light of that data dependence of our policy, I really don't think that a single rate increase of 25 basis points in December has any-has had much significance for the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we will continue to adjust our thinking in light of incoming data in whatever direction is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the levels of longer-term rates reflect essentially two things.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: One is market expectations about the path of short-term rates over, if we're considering, say, a 10-year Treasury security, what would be the path of short-term rates over the next 10 years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the second factor is the so-called term premium, or the extra yield that investors demand in order to hold a longer-term security instead of to invest short term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And clearly, market expectations for the path of short-term interest rates over the next 10 years remain low, and that is a factor.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That is an important factor that's, I think, holding down the level of longer- term yields.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, perhaps as important, or maybe even more important, the term premium is also low and has probably come down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, when we engaged in longer-term asset purchases, our very purpose in doing that was to drive down longer-term yields by making these assets scarce- scarcer and, hence, more valuable to the public that wants to invest in long-term securities, and we were consciously attempting to drive down that term premium.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we continue to hold a large quantity of those securities, but we're not adding to them.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, in many parts of the world-the ECB, for example, and the Bank of Japan are also engaging in quantitative easing, buying longer-term assets and pushing down those term premia.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think term premia are very low as well as the expected path of short rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, so I want to say again, we're quite uncertain about where rates are heading in the longer term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We write down our best estimates at this time of what is a longer-run normal level of the federal funds rate, and those are numbers about which there is great uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I said, we have good reason to believe that the so-called neutral rate or rate compatible with the economy operating at full employment is low at the present time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And many of us believe, as a base case, it's reasonable to assume that those rates will move up over time, but we're not certain of that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is-it's one of the uncertainties that-and there could be revisions in either direction, but thus far, in recent SEPs, I'd say the revisions have mainly been-have been in the downward direction.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The idea that a low neutral rate may be more- closer to the new normal, but you still do see some reversion.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I can't give you a formula, I know you would probably like to have a number that's a cutoff for what we need to see in a particular report.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are a lot of different indicators of the labor market-for example, the labor market conditions index that Binya referred to has 19 different indicators.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Clearly, we will be looking at the next job report, and if we were to see a healthy pace of job growth, you know, above that needed to kind of maintain the status quo in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, I should say, over time, we should expect to see, as the economy comes closer to maximum employment, the likely pace of job gains is probably going to slow down somewhat.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the recent couple of months was very low and, arguably, not even at the pace we need to see to maintain stable labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we want to see an adequate pace of job creation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There might be revisions to previous months that would change our views, but there will be other surveys of employment intentions and other indicators of the labor market that we'll focus- we'll be focusing on.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, there is no formula for what it takes, but we will be looking at the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, we do need to make sure that there is sufficient momentum.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I don't know what the timetable is going to be to gain that assurance.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Every meeting is live; there is no meeting that is off the table, that-no meeting is out in terms of a possible rate increase.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, we really need to look at the data, and I can't prespecify a timetable.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I'm, you know, not comfortable to say it's in the next meeting or two, but it could be, it could be, it's not impossible.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's not impossible that by July, for example, we would see data that led us to believe that we're on a perfectly fine course, and that data was an aberration, and other concerns would have passed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we are very focused on assessing the economic outlook and making changes that are appropriate without taking politics into account.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Look, if the data- incoming data were, in the coming months, to justify the kind of gradual increases that we have long discussed, that we see as appropriate in light of the outlook, I think markets should not be surprised by such a decision if we make it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it's obviously consistent with the data that we've seen, and the Committee will feel free to move in the coming months if we think it's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, I would say, with respect to the behavior of inflation, inflation is behaving roughly in the manner I would have expected; I have really not seen significant surprises there.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've long said that an important reason that inflation is as low as it's been is because of past declines in energy prices and increases in the value of the dollar, and as those factors began to dissipate, we would see inflation moving up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, that's exactly what we're seeing, what we're-that's in line with our thinking and with the data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And with respect to core inflation, which-now, that's partly influenced also by the dollar, but trying to pull out the dollar and import price influence-core inflation seems to be behaving roughly as one would expect with well-anchored inflation expectations and in improving labor markets.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I'm not seeing anything-inflation, even core inflation, is running under 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I continue to think the evidence supports a projection that it will move up over the next couple of years back toward our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, we've seen in the past, and economic theory suggests, that inflation expectations are relevant to price and wage setting decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, it's very hard to know exactly what inflation expectations are relevant to actual price and wage decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so, for example, we have seen the Michigan survey, a measure of household inflation expectations, move down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's hard-that's a preliminary number, it's hard to know what to make of it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But survey-based measures that- where forecasters are queried-have really all been quite stable.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And measures of inflation compensation-I always try to be careful to call it "inflation compensation" rather than "inflation expectations" because they're not inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Inflation expectations influence those market measures, but there's also an inflation risk premium.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And there are actually good reasons to think that the inflation risk premium could have declined significantly and may be depressing those measures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we watch them, we've taken note in the statement that they've moved down, but actual inflation is behaving more or less as would be expected.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the minutes are always-have to be an accurate discussion of what happened at the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So they're not changed after the fact in order to correct possible misconceptions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There was a good deal of discussion at that meeting of the possibility of moving in June, and that appeared in the minutes.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I suppose in the April statement, we gave no obvious hint or kind of calendar-based signal that June was a possibility.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I think if you look at the statement, we pointed to slower growth but pointed out that the fundamentals-there was no obvious fundamental reason for growth to have slowed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we pointed to fundamentals underlying household spending decisions that remained on solid ground, suggesting that maybe this was something transitory that would disappear.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We noted that labor market conditions continued to improve in line with our expectations, and we did downgrade somewhat our expressions of concern about the global risk environment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I do think that there were hints in the April statement that the Committee was changing its views of what it was seeing in a direction.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We continue to say that we think, if economic developments evolve in line with our expectations, the gradual and cautious further increases we expect to be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I suppose I was somewhat surprised with the market interpretation of it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the June meeting minutes-the minutes of the April meeting were an accurate summary of what had happened.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think that the minimum wage increases that have gone into effect-estimates that I've seen suggest it's a relatively minor influence on the aggregate level of wage inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would take somewhat faster wage increases to be a sign that labor market slack is diminishing and that the labor market is approaching conditions that are consistent with maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, I think, you know, I think we have seen some hints, perhaps preliminary indications, that wage growth is picking up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And as much as anything, I think it's a sign of a generally healthy labor market, which is what our mandated objective is, to achieve maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in normal times, I think it's very important that there be a separation between monetary and fiscal policy, and it's a primary reason for independence of a central bank.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have seen all too many examples of countries that end up with high or even hyperinflation because those in charge of fiscal policy direct their central bank to help them finance it by printing money, and maintaining price stability and low and stable inflation is very much aided by having central bank independence.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, that said, in unusual times where the concern is with very weak growth or possibly deflation-rather rare circumstances-first of all, fiscal policy can be a very important tool.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it's natural that if it can be employed that, just as monetary policy is doing a lot to try to stimulate growth, that fiscal policy should play a role.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And normally, you would hope, in an economy with those severe downside risks, monetary and fiscal policy would not be working at cross purposes to get-but together.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, whether or not in such extreme circumstances, there might be a case for, let's say, coordination-close coordination, with the central bank playing a role in financing fiscal policy; this is something that academics are debating, and it is something that one might legitimately consider.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would see this as a very abnormal, extreme situation where one needs an all-out attempt, and even then it's a matter that academics are debating, but only in an unusual situation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, it is conceivable in a scenario when-where growth and inflation really surprise us to the upside that we would have to raise short-term interest rates so rapidly that the rates we would be paying on reserves would exceed what we're earning on our portfolio.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now even then, we have about $2 trillion of liabilities, namely currency on which we pay no interest.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So this does requires an extreme scenario with very rapid increases in short-term interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it is conceivable but quite unlikely that it could happen.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, you know, if it were to happen, we would have an economy that would be doing very well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
