text: This is probably an economy that everybody would feel very pleased-was performing well and better than expected, and where monetary policy-you know, our goal is price stability and maximum employment, and we would probably feel that we had done very well in achieving that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, we usually make money-we've been making a lot of money in recent years, but the goal of monetary policy is not to maximize our income.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, you know, in a very strong economy like that, the Treasury would be seeing a lot of inflows in the form of tax revenues, too.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the state of foreign economies, both their growth outlooks and the stance of monetary policy, those are factors that influence the U.S. outlook and influence the appropriate stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, of course, we do look at foreign rates, the prospects-and the prospects for growth in those economies in considering the stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Differentials between countries in likely policy paths do tend to spill over into exchange rates-that is a standard part of how monetary policy works-and a stronger dollar, those have a both-a depressing effect.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: At the moment, net exports-well, for quite some time and probably going forward, they will be somewhat of a drag on U.S. growth, so that's a factor that we take into account.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And increases in the dollar that we've seen since mid-2014 have served to push inflation down as well; it can also have impacts on commodity prices that are relevant.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, it's-it is certainly relevant to the stance of U.S. monetary policy and a factor, but when one says "a constraint," I really would not go so far as to say it is a constraint on monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: When we have an outlook for continuing above-trend growth-that if we held rates absolutely flat, we have reason to believe inflation would overshoot our target-we would see a case to gradually raise rates over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: At the moment, I think markets do expect, and this is factored into market prices, a gradual path for rates to increase over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, for example, if we were to see upside surprises to growth and to inflation and had to raise short-term rates faster, thought we should, one of the channels by which that would work would be the associated impact on the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That is a standard channel through which the monetary policy transmission mechanism works, and we would take it into account and would not feel constrained, but that would be part of how it would work.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: How much are you watching oil prices and their impact on inflation, and how that could affect the timing of future rate increases and how much you might increase rates?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, oil prices have had many different effects on the economy, and so we've been watching oil prices closely.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, it takes falling oil prices to lower inflation on a sustained basis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Once they stabilize at whatever level, their impact on inflation dissipates over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Not only have they stabilized, they have moved up some, and their inflation is-their impact on inflation is waning over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But oil prices have also had a very substantial negative effect on drilling and mining activity that's led to weakness in investment spending and job loss in manufacturing and, obviously, in the energy sector.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, you know, it has different effects in different countries and different sectors.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've estimated that since mid-2014, the decline in energy prices and oil prices has probably resulted in gains of about $1,400 per U.S. household, and that's had an offsetting positive impact on spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But in many countries around the world that are important commodity exporters, the decline we've seen in oil prices has had a depressing effect on their growth, their trade with us and other trade partners, and caused problems that have had spillovers to the global economy as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Let me try to set out again how the Committee sees the economy and what we're looking for.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're generally pleased with how the U.S. economy is doing.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Growth was weak in the first half of the year; we're seeing definite evidence that the economy is now expanding more strongly.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I mentioned, payroll gains in recent months have been solid, averaging around 180,000 per month, which is less than the pace in 2015, but, as I mentioned, it's well above what's needed to provide jobs for new entrants into the labor force over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The unemployment rate is pretty close to most FOMC participants' estimates of its longer-run equilibrium value.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, as I mentioned, that rate and other measures of labor utilization are little changed since the beginning of the year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I don't see that as bad news, because it may reflect that the strong labor market is attracting people from outside the labor force back into employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The labor force participation rates increased on balance since late last year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It has-it is on a declining demographic trend, and the fact that it's increased shows a substantial number of people are being attracted into the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we were not really certain that this is something that would happen as the labor market strengthened, and it's good to see that development has taken place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that is some news that we've received in recent months, that the labor market does have that potential to have people come back in without the unemployment rate coming down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we're not seeing strong pressures on utilization suggesting overheating, and my assessment would be, based on this evidence, that the economy has a little more room to run than might have been previously thought.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Remember that inflation continues below 2 percent, although we expect it to move up over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the Committee agrees that risks to the outlook have become roughly balanced.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we are generally agreed that gradual increases in the federal funds rate to remove what is a modest degree of accommodation will be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My colleagues and I exchanged views at this meeting on the appropriate timing of the next step in reducing policy stimulus.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Most of us judged that the case for an immediate increase in the federal funds rate is stronger, but that it would be sensible, given the finding of a bit more running room, to wait to see some continued progress-evidence that we continue to progress toward our objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, for the time being, we're going to watch incoming evidence, and you can see from the SEP that most participants do expect that one increase in the federal funds rate will be appropriate this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I would expect to see that if we continue on the current course of labor market improvement and there are no major new risks that develop and we simply stay on the current course.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it is true that our estimates of the neutral rate are coming down, and that's what's largely responsible for that shift.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: At the same time, we generally agree that the stance of monetary policy is somewhat accommodative.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So 180,000 jobs a month is a faster pace of employment growth than is sustainable in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we have seen people come into the labor force and maybe more than would be expected, which is why the unemployment rate hasn't fallen.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But that's probably not something that is possible without the economy overheating on an indefinite basis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We don't want the economy to overheat and significantly overshoot our 2 percent inflation objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think we generally agree that some gradual increases to remove that accommodation will be appropriate if we stay on this course.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, as I emphasized, it's not that much accommodation, and the economy has shown evidence that there are more people who are being attracted back into the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in that sense, I would characterize it as, we found the economy has a bit more running room.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Nevertheless, we don't want the economy to overheat, and if things continue on the current course, I think that some gradual increases will be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, mainly, what we discussed today were issues affecting the timing of such increases.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I did say at Jackson Hole that I thought the case for a rate increase had strengthened, and that assessment is included in today's statement.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think most of my colleagues agree-agree with that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think we are trying to understand some difficult issues.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There is less disagreement among participants in the Committee than you might think, listening to speeches and commentary.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think we all agree that the economy is making progress, that we are close to an unemployment rate that is one that's sustainable in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We all agree we are undershooting our inflation goal, and that we want to make sure we stay on a course that raises that to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we're struggling with a difficult set of issues about what is the "new normal" in this economy and in the global economy more generally, which explains why we keep revising down the rate path.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, you know, it's very important that in a body like ours that a whole range of views are expressed, that we have independent- minded people who gather together and discuss these issues.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My colleagues do explain, in their individual speeches, their own perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: These are complicated, complex issues, and it just isn't straightforward exactly how to interpret what is appropriate policy and exactly what is going on in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My-my sense is that market participants and the public more generally learn more about the issues that we're grappling with as they listen to this set of speeches.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think it's a very good thing that the FOMC is not a body that suffers from groupthink.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And you see that-you see that's one of the, you know, real worries in an organization, that everybody thinks identically.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there's a lot that we share in common and express, both in our statement and in our speeches.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we are debating and discussing issues pertaining to timing.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I think Congress very wisely established the Federal Reserve as an independent agency in order to insulate monetary policy from short-term political pressures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I can say emphatically that partisan politics plays no role in our decisions about the appropriate stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are trying to decide what the best policy is to foster price stability and maximum employment and to manage the variety of risks that we see as affecting the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We do not discuss politics at our meetings, and we do not take politics into account in our decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I said, we're generally pleased with the progress of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the decision not to raise rates today and to wait for some further evidence that we're continuing on this course is largely based on the judgment that we're not seeing evidence that the economy is overheating, and that we are seeing evidence that people are being drawn in-in larger numbers than at least I would have expected-into the labor market, and that that's healthy to continue, but that, nevertheless, we do need to be forward looking.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if we continue along this course, it likely will be appropriate to raise the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, every meeting is live, and we will again assess, as we always do, incoming evidence in November and decide whether or not a move is warranted.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So you asked, first: What evidence would suggest that the neutral real rate is moving up?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I think if you saw us revising up our growth forecasts, revising down our estimates, well, with an unchanged path for policy, you know, if you saw this, you would see revisions in the funds rate path.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But if unemployment were moving down faster than we had anticipated, if we saw faster growth or upward pressure on inflation, that would be suggestive of the appropriateness of reevaluating whether or not the neutral funds rate had increased.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, the downward revisions reflect the fact that, while the economy has made a lot of progress, it's only made that progress in the context of a monetary policy that has been characterized by extremely low interest rates and negative real yields for a very long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in most advanced nations now, we have highly accommodative policies, and they seem to be necessary for countries to be able to achieve their inflation and employment objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that's characteristic of a-an environment in which the neutral rate-interest rates both here and in advanced countries around the globe appear to be very low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that is an environment that, if we do have to live with that for a long time, we have to be aware that it does give rise to a reach for yield as individuals and investors seek to, perhaps, take on risk or lengthen maturities to seek higher-to seek higher yields.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think we should be concerned about that to the extent it creates financial stability risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We engage in regular assessments of financial stability factors that bear on financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Overall, I would say that the threats to financial stability I would characterize, at this point, as moderate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In general, I would not say that asset valuations are out of line with historical norms, but there are areas my colleague President Rosengren has focused on: commercial real estate, where price-to-rent ratios are very high or cap rates are very low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a variety of tools other than monetary policy to address such risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've recently issued new supervisory guidance pertaining to commercial real estate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would say, in the area of commercial real estate, while valuations are high, we are seeing some tightening of lending standards and less debt growth associated with that rise in commercial real estate prices.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, more generally, we're not seeing signs of leverage building up or maturity transformation in the way that we saw in the run-up to the crisis, and we're keeping a close eye on it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, starting with the issue of political uncertainty and investment, investment spending really has been quite weak for some time, and we're really not certain exactly what is causing that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Part of it, of course, has been the huge contraction in drilling activity associated with falling oil prices, but the weakness in investment spending extends beyond-beyond that sector, and I'm not certain of exactly what explains that, whether-I'm not aware of evidence that suggests that it's political uncertainty, but it certainly-I would agree with the finding that it has been weak.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're seeing a lot of strength in consumer spending, and consumer sentiment certainly seems to be solid.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I indicated we have a number of tools that we've used before and could use again.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I did indicate that I do have concerns about the scope for monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Nevertheless, at this point our balance sheet is large, and we're not at what we see as the normal level-longer-run level of interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, at the moment, the funds rate is very low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, at the moment, I would say the zero lower bound is a concern, and we have less scope than I would like to see or expect us to have in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, I think it would be-it would be worthwhile for other policymakers to think about what role they could play in addressing negative shocks should they come.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I mentioned specifically automatic stabilizers because I think that's an important way in which fiscal policy serves to cushion shocks to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it would seem to me, without getting into specifics, that there are ways in which the response of fiscal policy to shifts in the economy could be strengthened, which would help take some burden off monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we are very focused on evaluating, given the way the economy is operating, what is the right policy to foster our goals, and I'm not going to get into politics.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm just-those are factors that we don't consider, and I don't-I'm not going to get involved in commenting on the election.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In terms of the dissents, as I indicated, the notion that we do have some accommodation, that if we continue on the current path, it's something we will need to remove over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There's general agreement among participants on that, but the precise timing of what is the right-what is the right timing for removing that accommodation is something on which we had active discussions, and there are a range of opinions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the dissents represent a judgment on the part of some of my colleagues that it's important to begin that process now.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I certainly agree, and I've said myself, that there are risks in waiting too long to remove accommodation, and we need to take a forward-looking approach.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've always advocated making policy based on forecasts of where the economy is heading and taking account of risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And there are two particular risks that we need to think about and balance.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: One is the risk that the economy runs too hot, that unemploy-the labor market tightens too much, that unemployment falls to a very low level, that we need to tighten policy in a less gradual way than would be ideal, and in the course of doing that, because that is a very difficult thing to accomplish, to gently create a bit more slack in the labor market, we could cause a recession in the process.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so that's something my colleagues and I certainly wouldn't want to be responsible for.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We would all like to have a very long expansion, with the labor market operating well for many years to come, and the prospect that we could create-create downside risk for the labor market is something we would like to avoid, and taking "a stitch in time" might be essential to avoiding that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On the other hand, inflation is running below our 2 percent objective, and it's also important that we make sure we get back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I have routinely indicated a number of measures of inflation expectations that are running at the low ends of their historical range, and we're watching that as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And there would also be risks from not seeing inflation move back to our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And exactly how to balance these two risks, which is more serious-which is a more serious risk-can affect one's judgment about the appropriate timing, and we're all struggling to understand the magnitude and nature of those two risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I can't recall any meeting that I have ever attended where politics has been a matter of discussion.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think the public, if they had been watching our meeting on TV today, would have felt that we had a rich, deep, serious, intellectual debate about the risks and the forecasts for the economy, and we struggled mightily with trying to understand one another's points of view and to come out at a balanced place and to act responsibly.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that's my commitment to the American people, that I want to lead an institution that is not political and is-that we are striving to do our very best to pursue the goals the Congress has assigned to us, which are important ones of price stability and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I have no concern that the pol-the Fed is politically motivated, and I will assure that you will not find any signs of political motivation when the transcripts are released in five years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We-I-it is important that we maintain the confidence of the public, and I do believe that we deserve it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I know that these are difficult decisions, and everybody may not agree with them, but I hope the public will understand that we're striving to do our best to pursue these goals that do matter to all of us.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Are you worried that bubbles could form in the economy because of our prolonged low interest rates?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, we-we are worried that bubbles could form in the economy, and we routinely monitor asset valuations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: While nobody can know for sure what type of valuation represents a bubble-that's only something one can tell in hindsight-we are monitoring these measures of valuation, and commercial real estate valuations are high.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Rents have moved up over time, but, still, valuations are high relative to rents.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We called this out in our Monetary Policy Report and in other presentations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we are-we are, in our supervision with banks, as I indicated, we have issued supervisory guidance to make sure that underwriting standards are sound on these loans, and we're aware-this is something also that we look at in stress tests of the large-the larger banks to see what would happen to their capital positions and to make sure that they hold sufficient capital.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, of course, I think the soundness and state of the banking system has improved substantially, but, of course, we are focused on such things.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in this specific case, the abuses that occurred took place in a national bank.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And on the consumer side, it is the CFPB that has responsibility, but we work cooperatively and closely with those organizations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And in terms of our overall supervisory responsibility for Wells and other large banking organizations, we are very focused, and this will be a particular focus of our supervision going forward over the next year or so on the compliance environment to make sure that the controls, that the senior management oversight, that the involvement of the boards of directors are appropriate to control these kinds of risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have been distressed to see banking organizations responding when a particular problem arises, and what we'd really want to see is robust procedures that ensure that employees are always acting in a legal and ethical manner, and that the incentives that are put in place in these organizations are appropriate and don't serve to foster behavior that could harm the public.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And this has been and will be a focus of our supervision.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, that's a political issue that's currently being debated that I really don't want to get into.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, so-I'm going to-I'm going to pass on that one.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have high expectations for what we expect to be in place in a large organization or in any banking organization.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We expect there to be robust systems of risk management, strong audit functions, a board of directors that is monitoring and supervising and holding senior management accountable for things that happen throughout the organization in a strong compliance environment, and I don't think that these are impossible standards to meet.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They may be challenging, but I wouldn't at this point arrive at the conclusion that just because an organization is large, it can't live up to those standards.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And those are our expectations, and we intend to hold banking organizations responsible for putting in place that kind of-that kind of risk-management and compliance environment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I'm not-I'm not endorsing a general conclusion that banks are- banks of that size are too big to manage.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I believe they can be, but it may be challenging, and that's what we expect.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the projections-I agree, the projections for growth are slow.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have further written down our estimate of the longer-run normal growth rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And what that reflects is an assessment that productivity growth is likely to remain low for an extended time, although it does embody an expectation that it will pick up from the miserable ½ percent pace per year that we have seen over the last five years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, why we would never-and slow growth is a factor.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Slow productivity growth is a factor that influences the longer-run normal level of interest rates, and writing down the likely pace of productivity growth is one factor that is responsible for the downward shift in the path that you see for the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's an important reason for revising down the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But now, let's go to your-the part of your question about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In spite of having such slow growth, disappointing productivity growth, we have a labor market that last year generated an average of about 230,000 jobs a month and so far this year has been generating about 180,000 jobs a month.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that is a very solid pace of job growth and a pace that likely is not sustainable in the longer run, although we've been pleased to see people come back in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it certainly is sustainable for some further amount of time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I think what ultimately drives inflation, both wage and price growth, is that tightness in the labor market and pressure on resource utilization.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the sad fact is that we are getting that healthy pace of job market growth with very slow growth in output.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So this is-I don't think it bears on the inflation outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It has prompted a downward shift in the projected path for the neutral and actual federal funds rate, but it is a huge concern because slow productivity growth ultimately means slow growth in living standards.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that's a big concern that policymakers should be focused on.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, as I mentioned, we are going to be focusing on compliance risk management and board oversight not only at Wells, but also across bank holding companies.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, consumer issues and issues that involve harm of consumers can become safety and soundness issues.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if there was-at least one of the lessons from the financial crisis, I think, is that abuses of consumers of the sort that we see-saw in subprime lending ultimately did become-become safety and soundness issues.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so, of course, we need to have that concern, and we'll focus there.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think-I can't really at this point give you specifics beyond that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have a system that Congress did set up in the Federal Reserve Act in which the governance of the Reserve Banks involves banks contributing capital and serving on the boards of directors.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have long recognized inside the Federal Reserve that when we're charged with supervision of banks, having bankers involved in that obviously presents conflict of interest.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we have put in place very strong measures to ensure that those conflicts of interest are not allowed to play out in any-in any way, that bankers are not allowed to be involved in supervision.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Dodd-Frank changed the arrangement so that only the Class B and C, or nonbanking, directors can participate in the selection of the president as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think-I want to make sure the public has confidence that, in spite of the fact that we do have this banker involvement in our boards of directors, that it is not giving rise to any conflicts in our actual conduct of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, that setup-if that setup is changed, it raises which-it's up to Congress to decide what to do here.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It raises complex issues about the governance-the whole governance arrangement in the Reserve Banks in the Federal Reserve, and I would simply caution that if that is looked at, as Congress is entitled to do, that they think through carefully what the ramifications of making changes would be.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the notion that monetary policy operates with long and variable lags-that statement is due to Milton Friedman, and it is one of the essential things to understand about monetary policy, and it has not fundamentally changed at all.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that is why I believe we have to be forward looking, and I'm not in favor of a "whites of their eyes" sort of approach.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the global economy and the U.S. economy have changed a lot.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Many of the-those of us sitting around the table, we learned the lesson that if policy is not forward looking, that inflation can pick up to highly undesirable levels, that inflation expectations can be dislodged upward, and the consequence of that can be that, endemically, higher inflation takes place, which-it is very costly to reduce.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And absolutely none of us want to relive an episode like that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so I believe, and my colleagues, that it is important to be forward looking.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the structure of the economy changes, things do change.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The nature of the inflation process has changed, I think, significantly since the bad days of the '70s when the Fed had to face this chronic high-inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've seen inflation respond less to the economy, to movements in the unemployment rate-that's sometimes said, "The Phillips curve has become flatter."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Inflation expectations appear to be better anchored, and perhaps that's been a result of a long period of low and stable inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, in addition, we have to be attentive to the fact there we've now had a long period in which inflation is actually undershooting our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we see some signs that I-we conclude inflation expectations are reasonably well anchored at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we are seeing signs suggesting possible slippage there, and we're a long way from being-facing the problems that Japan faces.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there always a remi-should be a reminder to us that we also would not want to find ourselves in a period where inflation is chronically low-running below our objective, inflation expectations are slipping.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And with a low neutral rate, that becomes more important.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So things are changed, but the principle of "forward looking" absolutely holds.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I do think job training and job skills are important.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we do work in community development, trying to-in the local communities where the Reserve Banks operate, to try to foster broader understanding of what kinds of programs work and how community organizations in state and local governments can put in place programs that will be helpful.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've recently visited a program that was very impressive in Philadelphia.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I do believe it's possible to design programs that will help people overcome obstacles in getting jobs that are available.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I definitely think that, you know, while we can play some role in facilitating understanding of what works and what doesn't work that can be helpful, it's certainly worthwhile for policymakers at the federal level, at state and local levels, to be focusing on this, because I think it is an area that would be helpful in making progress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think we have seen some modest pickup in wage growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's running a little bit higher than it was over the last two years by a number of important measures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think the Census report was encouraging, showing that there are income gains, both because of more jobs and higher-paying jobs, and that that's occurring throughout the income distribution.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I do expect-we expect the unemployment rate to decline further, we expect labor market conditions to continue to improve.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And my hope and expectation is that we will see some further pickup in wage growth, and that it will be broadly beneficial to American households.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I would like to emphasize that this is a very modest adjustment in the path of the federal funds rate and involves changes by only, you know, some of, you know, some of the participants.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So in thinking about the paths and the revisions, there are a number of factors that were taken into account by participants.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The unemployment rate is perhaps a touch, as I said, a touch lower than previously; you've seen some modest downward revisions in that- in that projection.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: For this year, there was a slight upward revision to inflation, and some of the participants, but not all of the participants, did incorporate some assumption of a change in fiscal policy into their projections.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that may have been a factor that was one of several that occasioned these shifts, but I want to emphasize that these-the shifts that you see here are really very tiny.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the statement that I made, that it would be useful to increase the productive capacity of the economy, reflects my concern that productivity growth has been very low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's the ultimate determination of the evolution of living standards.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Policies that would improve productivity growth would include policy changes that enhance education, training, workforce development; policies that spur either private or public investment to enhance the quality of capital in the United States that workers have to work with; and policies that spur innovation or competition or the formation of new firms.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I don't think there's anything that I could say in general about what tax policy would do, but that-and I really can't tell you what the Fed's response would be to any policy changes that are put into effect.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I wouldn't want to speculate until I were more certain of the details and how they would affect the likely course of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I-you know, it's something I really just can't generalize about because, while it would be desirable to have tax policies that do increase the productive capacity of the economy, an increase in the pace of productivity change is one of the factors that does affect the economy's neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As we have been saying, we estimate that the value of the neutral federal funds rate is quite low-has-and one of the reasons for that is slow productivity growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so it's very hard to generalize about it because it could affect that neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me say that our decision to raise rates is-should certainly be understood as a reflection of the confidence we have in the progress the economy has made and our judgment that that progress will continue.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it is a vote of confidence in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As you know, this was a decision that was well anticipated in markets, and I think it will have relatively small effect on market rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It could boost very slightly some short-term interest rates that could have an effect on borrowing costs that are linked to them, but, overall, I think that households and firms will see very modest changes from this decision.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, certainly, it's important for households and businesses to understand that my colleagues and I have judged the course of the U.S. economy to be strong, that we're making progress toward our inflation and unemployment goals.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a strong labor market, and we have a resilient economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I would agree that-and as we said in our statement-policy remains accommodative.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I've emphasized and said in the statement, we currently judge the neutral level of the federal funds rate to be pretty low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The Committee projects-at least the median projection shows a very modest undershoot of estimates of the longer-run normal rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The median unemployment rate here gets down to 4½ percent, which is just a few tenths below the estimated longer-run normal level of the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we think that that's appropriate because we want inflation to rise to our 2 percent objective in a timely fashion.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there is not a substantial undershoot of the natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're not seeing evidence in labor markets of very substantial upward pressures on labor that could signify extreme shortages of labor that could propel inflation higher in a very rapid way, and inflation is still operating below our objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I do not judge that we are behind the curve.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've-my judgment is that we're on a good path to reaching our objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We recognize that there are many sources of uncertainty affecting the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we will have to adjust our thinking as things evolve, as conditions-conditions evolve, and we learn more about economic policy changes that could affect the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I believe my predecessor and I called for fiscal stimulus when the unemployment rate was substantially higher than it is now.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, with a 4. percent unemployment and a solid labor market, there may be some additional slack in labor markets, but I would judge that the degree of slack has diminished.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I would say at this point that fiscal policy is not obviously needed to provide stimulus to help us get back to full employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, nevertheless, let me be careful that I am not trying to provide advice to the new Administration or to Congress as to what is the appropriate stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are many considerations that Congress needs to take account of and many bases for justifying changing fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've continued to highlight the importance of spurring productivity growth, that I think that would be something that's beneficial for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, it's also important for Congress to take account of the fact that, as our population ages, that the debt-to-GDP ratio is projected to rise, and that needs to continue to be taken into account.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so there are many factors that I think should enter into such decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I want to be clear that what I said in that speech in Boston is that an important research question is whether or not, in an economy with a very strong labor market, there might be changes that took place that permanently raised the labor force participation, training, and other things of the labor-of the labor force that would be positives for the productive potential of our economy on a long-lasting basis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I never said that I favor running a high-pressure economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, you know, as you can see in the SEP projections of the participants-and this has long been true not just in this forecast, but in earlier ones as well-you see a modest undershooting.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The under-unemployment rate is projected to modestly undershoot, for several years, levels that are deemed to be normal in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's an appropriate policy purely on the grounds that inflation is running below our objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And while we don't want to overshoot our 2 percent objective, we also don't want a persistent undershoot of our 2 percent objective, and that does involve a labor market that may succeed in attracting more people off the sidelines into the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's something we will see as we examine experience over the next couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I do want to make clear that I have not recommended running a "hot" economy as some sort of experiment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I'm not going to offer the incoming President advice about how to conduct himself in policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm a strong believer in the independence of the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have been given the independence by Congress to make decisions about monetary policy in pursuit of our dual-mandate objectives of maximum employment and inflation, and that is what I intend to stay focused on.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have been-our staff have been in touch with the Trump transition team.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we, of course, share the objective that the whole government has to work constructively to ensure a smooth transition.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've not been in touch beyond that, and it's not something that I would expect.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, okay, on financial regulation, I feel that we lived through a devastating financial crisis that took a huge toll on our economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And most members of Congress and the public came away from that experience feeling that it was important to take a set of steps that would result in a safer and stronger financial system.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That has been our mission since the financial crisis for the last six or seven years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think it's very important that we have reduced the odds that a systemically important firm could fail by requiring higher capital, higher liquidity, by performing stress tests that provide us another way of ensuring that the firms we count on to supply credit to households and businesses would be able to go on doing that even in the face of a severely adverse shock.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The firms-the largest firms have a great deal more capital than they did before the crisis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have placed the toughest regulations on those firms that are systemically important.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would advise that-and we have been trying to do this-that it's important to look for ways to relieve regulatory burden on community banks and smaller institutions, to tailor regulation so that it's appropriate for the systemic risk profile of the particular institutions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think there was broad agreement also that we should end "too big to fail," and that means not only reducing the odds of the failure of a systemically important institution, but also making sure that, should such a firm fail, that it could be resolved in an orderly way.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the living wills process has been about that, and I think we've made considerable progress in making sure that the largest and most systemic firms conduct their businesses in a day-to-day way with some thought about-with important thinking in place about whether or not the way they are conducting their business would aid resolution in the event that they encountered a severe negative shock.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So this is progress, I would say, it's very important not to roll back.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There may be some changes that could be made, and we've suggested a few, like eliminating the burden of compliance with the Volcker rule, or incentive compensation, regulations for smaller banks, or modestly raising the threshold for banks that are subject to enhanced prudential supervision.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I would urge that it's important to keep this in place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we did discuss these topics in our meeting today.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would simply summarize by saying that all the FOMC participants recognize that there is considerable uncertainty about how economic policies may change and what effect they will have on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And in so far as that will affect monetary policy, of course we will have to factor those policies along with many other things, including the global environment and oil prices and other matters.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We will have to factor that into our outlook and figure out what is an appropriate response.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we're operating under a cloud of uncertainty at the moment, and we have time to wait to see what changes occur and to factor those into our decisionmaking as we gain greater clarity.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I see the market moves as implicit forecasts about what impact these policies are likely to have on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The changes-the financial market changes that you described, particularly the increase in stock prices, the increase in longer-term rates, and the strengthening of the dollar, suggest that many market participants anticipate expansionary fiscal policies that would raise interest rates somewhat in the United States relative to abroad and would cause a strengthening in the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But market participants were uncertain too, and I would expect changes in our understanding of what is going to happen to also affect market prices in financial markets as we move forward.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Wondering about slack, when do you think the slack in the labor market will have worked its way through so we're no longer talking about it at press conferences and it's not such a big issue?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So this is not something that it's possible to judge precisely.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My colleagues write down their best estimates of a normal longer-run unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The median stands at 4. percent, so we're close, possibly-the unemployment rate right now is ever so slightly below, but in the neighborhood.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If we look at larger, broader measures of slack, like the U-6 measure that includes involuntary part-time employment and those who are marginally attached to the labor force, they're slightly higher than pre-recession levels, but they've come down considerably.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We look at a broad array of indicators of the labor market, and if you look at job openings or the hires rate or the quits rate or difficulty of hiring workers as reported in business surveys, you know, I would say the labor market looks a lot like the way it did before the recession, that it's-we're roughly comparable to 2007 levels when we thought the, you know, there was a normal amount of slack in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The labor market was in the vicinity of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I guess the way I think about it is that I was confirmed by the Senate to a four-year term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The term of the Fed Chair was not meant to coincide with that of the President, and there were good reasons for that, too.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so I do intend to serve out my four-year term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I, you know, I recognize I might or might not be reappointed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's a decision that I don't have to make and don't, you know, don't have thoughts on at this time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as you said, I recognize too that I could stay on as a Board member, and that's a decision for another day.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, I really don't want to comment on the level of stock prices.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They may have been boosted by expectations about tax policy; possible cuts in corporate tax rates that have been much discussed; or by expectations about growth, possible reductions, and downside risk to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, you know, these are things that market participants are trying to view, along with the likely path of-paths of interest rates, and I think all of that factors into movements and stock valuations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I don't-I don't want to offer a view as to whether they're appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I think rates of return in the stock market relative to- remember that the level of interest rates is low, and, taking that into account, I believe it's fair to say that they remain within normal ranges.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, there have been many ways in which there have been compliance failures at large organizations, and you've seen a series of enforcement actions by the banking regulators over a range of practices that suggests some breakdown of compliance or culture, whether it involves violations of sanctions or foreign exchange or LIBOR or other matters.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So this is something that we've discussed and emphasized, the importance of a culture of compliance.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've already begun this year, broadly, of compliance and management of compliance risk in the largest corporations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the failings that we have seen in a number of institutions suggest there is certainly room for improvement.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I want to make clear what I said and what I didn't say.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: One of the things we've learned from our financial crisis and from a series of financial crises in history and around the globe is that, very commonly, when the economy takes a hit and falls into a recession, that productivity doesn't pick up to pre-recession levels and that there looks like there is a permanent hit to the path of potential output for the economy, which is called "hysteresis."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I raised the question as to whether or not this might operate in the opposite direction as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have seen quite a few people who lost their jobs during the Great Recession drop out of the labor force and, you know, lose their ties and become discouraged and not reenter.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I raised the question as to whether or not hysteresis could operate in the opposite direction.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that was a research question for economists to see if there is any evidence, because it could be important in determining policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I didn't-I didn't draw any policy conclusions from that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I indicated, I think the path that you see-that the Committee has laid out in a tentative way that involves a modest degree of undershooting of normal longer-run levels of unemployment going down to around 4½ percent would remain for a couple of years-might provide some insight.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I was not recommending a substantially easier policy in order to test that hypothesis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's not a prerequisite, but we do try to explain our evolving views as clearly as we can.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's important for market participants to have a sense of how we think about the economy and the appropriate path of policy, to look at incoming data, and to form their own judgments as to whether or not changes in policy would be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And while it's not a prerequisite, if we're in good sync in terms of explaining what goes into our policy judgments, it's not surprising that it would often be true that moves are well anticipated by the market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I said, in thinking about today's move, we've indicated that we thought we were making progress on our objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think anyone looking at incoming data can clearly see that we have enjoyed further progress both in the labor market and on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, therefore, there are good reasons why the market should have anticipated a moved today.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I haven't weighed in on either fiscal policy, specifics of evaluating policies.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm not going to weigh in either on the details of particular trade policies.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, more generally, I'd say, you asked me about manufacturing.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There were a lot of manufacturing jobs lost over a long period of time and particularly after-during the Great Recession.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've had some recovery in manufacturing employment as the economy's recovered.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, to some extent, manufacturing employment depends on the progress of the economy, and we have seen some recovery.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Over a long period of time, technological change is something that has been important in reducing manufacturing employment absolutely and as a share of jobs in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: For decades, the pace of technological change in manufacturing has outstripped that in the economy as a whole.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, so, firms-manufacturing firms have found it easier to continue producing by-with reducing their workforces.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that's a change that I would expect to continue.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So some of the forces that are acting on manufacturing and other sectors, including technological change and globalization-even though most economists would judge the overall consequences of these developments for the economy to be positive, certainly there are groups of workers who were harmed by developments pertaining to globalization and technology.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think most economists and policymakers recognize that it's important to provide ways for workers who were harmed by these kinds of developments to be retrained for jobs so that they can succeed in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so, I mean, I would agree-without getting into any particular program and whether it's sufficient, I do think that it's important to recognize there are those who were harmed by these developments, and their concerns, I think, need to be addressed by policymakers, certainly.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we've indicated in our normalization principles that we expect to diminish the size of our portfolio over time largely by ceasing reinvestments of principal rather than by selling securities.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've indicated that once the process of normalization of the federal funds rate is well under way, we would probably begin to allow our portfolio to run off.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've not yet made any precise decisions about when that will occur.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We want to feel that if the economy were to suffer an adverse shock, that we have some scope through traditional means of interest rate cuts to be able to respond to that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, there's no mechanical rule about what level of the federal funds rate we might deem appropriate to begin that process.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's not something that only depends on the level of the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It also depends on our judgment of the amount of momentum in the economy and possible concerns about downside risks to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we've not yet made this decision, but it is something that we have long planned, to begin to allow our balance sheet to run off.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we would end up, if all goes well, with a substantially smaller balance sheet than we have at present.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I mean, we've long been aware, and I've spoken about previously disturbing trends in the economy, particularly rising wage inequality, income inequality, and the fact that a significant share of our population hasn't been enjoying significant real wage gains, if any.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: These are not new phenomenon, but the recession was very severe and probably exacerbated developments that had long been affecting many American workers and households.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, they're ones that the Fed is not well positioned-I think our policies can affect the general level of economic activity and slack in the labor market, the level-the rate of inflation, which we focus on.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I think it's important for policymakers more broadly to be attentive to these trends and to think about policies that could address them.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've been quite attentive with respect to particular demographic groups in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Particularly, minorities tend to be very badly affected by downturns.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've been focused on it-it's not just since the election-and are pleased to see that they are enjoying gains.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: For example, the African American unemployment rate at this point is now rough-about back to 2007 levels as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But these are important trends, and I think it's important for policy to address them.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've emphasized for quite some time that the Committee wishes to use variations in the fed funds rate target-our short-term interest rate target-as our key active tool of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We think it's much easier in using that tool to communicate the stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have much more experience with it and have a better idea of its impact on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So while the balance sheet, asset purchases are a tool that we could conceivably resort to if we found ourselves in a serious downturn where we were, again, up against the zero bound and faced with substantial weakness in the economy, it's not a tool that we would want to use as a routine tool of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think the right-the right way to look at it is in qualitative and not quantitative terms.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It doesn't mean some particular cutoff level for the federal funds rate that, when we've reached that level, we would consider ourselves well under way.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think what we want to have is confidence in the economy's trajectory, a sense that the economy will make progress, that we're not overly worried about downside risks and adverse shocks that could hit the economy that could quickly-after setting it off on the path to shrinking the balance sheet gradually over time- cause us to want to begin to add monetary policy accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think it has to do with the balance of risks and confidence in the economic outlook and not simply the level of the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I'm not sure that I can tell you what "a rapid rate of increases" is.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think the trajectory that you see is the median in our projections, which, this year, looks to a total of three increases.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My comfort in using the term "gradual" comes back, in part, to my judgment that the neutral level of the federal funds rate- namely, the level of the federal funds rate that would keep the economy operating on an even keel, that it's a rate where we neither are pressing on the brake nor pushing down on the accelerator-that level of interest rates is quite low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, at present, I see monetary policy as accommodative-namely, the current level of the federal funds rate is below that neutral rate, but not very far below the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As we reach those objectives, and particularly in light of the fact that we see the risks to the outlook as roughly balanced at this point-and that's been our assessment for the last several meetings-it looks to us to be appropriate to gradually raise the federal funds rate back in the direction of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, the SEP gives you a sense of what Committee participants envision in a concrete sense.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, you know, if it's one more or one less, I think that still-that still qualifies to my mind as gradual, I think, if you compare it with any previous tightening cycle.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I remember when rates were raised at every meeting starting in mid-2004.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think people thought that was a gradual pace, a measured pace.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have not discussed in detail potential policy changes that could be put into place, and we have not tried to map out what our response would be to particular policy measures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We recognize that there is great uncertainty about the timing, the size, the character of policy changes that may be put in place and don't think that that's a decision, or a set of decisions, that we need to make until we know more about what policy changes will go into effect.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I do want to emphasize that, while some participants have penciled in some fiscal policy changes into their projections, that the basis for today's decision is simply our assessment of the progress of the economy against our long-established goals of maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There's nothing that we have done or anticipate that is a speculation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think it's fair to say, there's nothing that's a speculation about preemptive responses to future policy moves.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We did remove the word "only" in the statement today from "gradual."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I regard it as a relatively small change and think it's appropriate for you to consider it in the context, for example, of the fact that our economic projections are virtually identical to those that we issued in December.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They're essentially unchanged both in terms of the path of the economy and the path of the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have carried out a modest adjustment of the federal funds rate because we've seen the economy progressing over the last several months in exactly the way that we anticipated.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We haven't in any way changed our view about where the economy is heading or the risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We had long said that if the economy progressed, and-it's, you know, it's been doing nicely, I think, in making progress, in showing resilience, and we have, you know, have some confidence in the path the economy is on.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if we continue to feel that, we will likely regard it as appropriate to make some further moves to scale back accommodation to move toward neutral, along the lines in the SEP. Now, obviously, there are surprises.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But the word "gradual," I think, emphasizes that if things continue in the manner that we've been going, as we have said now for quite some time, we think that gradual-some gradual increases in the federal funds rate-will be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And this is not a, you know, this is not a significant-this is not a significant change.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've met a couple of times with the Treasury Secretary, and I'm getting to know him.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think, you know, it's traditional for Fed Chairs and Treasury Secretaries to meet on a regular basis, and I fully expect to have a strong relationship with Secretary Mnuchin.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have had very good discussions about the economy, about regulatory objectives, the work of the FSOC, global economic developments, and I look forward to continuing to work with him.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I had a very brief meeting and appreciated that as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I've given a number of recent speeches on this topic where I've developed my views more fully.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would say, over the longer run-that means going several years out-I think the evidence suggests that the neutral rate may be something, in real terms, that might be close to 1 percent or a little bit under that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That would be consistent with the median longer-run value of the federal funds rate in our economic projections for the last several meetings.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Three percent is the longer-run normal federal funds rate that participants estimate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In real terms, with a 2 percent inflation objective-that's 1 percent in real terms.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I think there's very strong evidence that's accumulated that this rate has been falling not just in the United States, but in many advanced nations, and the decline probably predates the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think in part it reflects slowing population growth and also slow productivity growth here and in many other advanced nations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But some recent work suggests that, at the present time, the neutral real rate is yet lower than that, and some estimates place it around zero in real terms.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the lower current rate arguably reflects headwinds that are left over from the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: One form of headwind, I think, has been caution and restraint and risk aversion on the part of households and businesses that's held back spending decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, I suppose, my judgment that it'll move up over time reflects a notion that part of that will gradually dissipate over the years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that's a sense of where I think-now, there is uncertainty about the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as you mentioned, it is-it can be affected by shifts in fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: How the neutral rate is affected by fiscal policy-that really depends importantly on the nature, the size of the fiscal shift and the effect it has both on demand and supply in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, when I look at our sequence of communications, they seem to me to have been reasonably consistent over this entire period.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We had indicated in December that we expect-we saw the risks as balanced, and if the economy continued to progress along the lines we expected, that several rate increases would likely be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The minutes of our January meeting indicated that many participants thought that an increase in the funds rate would be appropriate fairly soon if things continued along those lines.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I indicated in my congressional testimony that I thought that, indeed, the economy was progressing in line with our expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I think all of us-having that expectation and that if the economy continued to progress along the lines that we expected and we continued to see the risks as balanced-do regard it as appropriate to gradually remove accommodation that's in place by having several interest rate increases this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As we saw the data continue to come in in line with our expectations, my colleagues and I spoke out and indicated that, indeed, that had been and continued to be our expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, you know, when you ask me, how did we get out of sync with the market, this is something I tried to reflect on a bit in the remarks I made in Chicago.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, of course, it is true that in 2015 and in 2016 each, we raised the federal funds rate only once, and perhaps market participants have been influenced by that pattern.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I did try to explain the reasons why we had moved so slowly during those two years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it reflects, I think, a set of shocks partly emanating from the global economy and risks that we saw to the outlook as well as more fundamental assessments-reassessments pertaining to the neutral level of the federal funds rate and the longer-run normal level of the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think there are reasons, but it is important for the public to understand that we're getting closer to reaching our objectives; that policy is accommodative; that although the level of the neutral federal funds rate is probably quite low, we nevertheless have an accommodative stance of policy; and it will be appropriate to gradually move toward a neutral stance if we continue on the path we're on.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, we do look at financial conditions in formulating our view of the outlook, and stock prices do figure into financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the higher level of stock prices is one factor that looks like it's likely to somewhat boost consumption spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We also noticed that, in the last several months, that risk spreads, particularly for lower-grade corporate issuers, have narrowed, which is another signal that financial conditions have become somewhat easier.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, on the other side, longer-term interest rates are up some in recent months, and the dollar is a little stronger.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are private-sector analysts that produce financial conditions indices that attempt to aggregate all these different factors affecting financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And for some of the more prominent analysts and indices, I think the conclusion they have reached is that financial conditions, on balance, have eased, and that's partly driven by the stock market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, we always exchange views on the economic outlook and developments in our country, and it will be my objective to explain-explain U.S. monetary policy and to try to make the same points to them that I've made here already today about what the outlook is for monetary policy in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think it's fair to say that the global economy is doing better.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's growing a bit more strongly than it was, perhaps, the last time I got together that the-with my counterparts in the G-20-that the risks do look somewhat more balanced.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there remain a set of very significant risks, medium term, facing the global economy, and I'm sure that those will be discussed as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we recognize-our statement actually last time noted that there had been an improvement, a marked improvement in business and household sentiment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's uncertain just how much sentiment actually impacts spending decisions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I wouldn't say at this point that I have seen hard evidence of any change in spending decisions based on expectations about the future.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We exchange around the table what we learn from our many business contacts, and I think it's fair to say that many of my colleagues and I note a much more optimistic frame of mind among many-many businesses in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, I'd say, most of the business people that we've talked to also have a wait-and-see attitude and are very hopeful that they will be able to expand investment and are looking forward to doing that but are waiting to see what will happen.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, of course, if we were to see a major shift in spending reflecting those expectations, that could very well affect the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm not seeing it-I'm not seeing that at this point, but the shift in sentiment is obvious and notable.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I don't believe it is a point of conflict.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We would certainly welcome stronger economic growth in a context of price stability.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if policies were put in place to speed growth that I've certainly urged Congress and the Administration to consider- policies that would boost productivity growth and raise the economy's so-called speed limit or potential to grow-I think that those would be-those would be very welcome changes that we would like to see.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If one averages through several quarters, I would describe our economy as one that has been growing around 2 percent per year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And as you can see from our projections, we-that's something we expect to continue over the next couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, that pace of growth has been consistent with a pace of job creation that is more rapid than what is sustainable if labor force participation begins to move down in line with what we see as its longer-run trend with an aging population.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, unemployment hasn't moved that much, in part because people have been drawn into the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Labor force participation, as I mentioned in my remarks, has been about flat over the last three years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in that sense, the economy has shown over the last several years that it may have had more room to run than some people might have estimated, and that's been good.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's meant we've had a great deal of job creation over these years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And there could be- there could be room left for that to play out further.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We expect the unemployment rate to move down further and to stay down for the next several years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we do expect that the path of policy we think is appropriate is one that is going to lead to some further strengthening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is data dependent, and we're-we're not locked into any particular policy path.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Our-you know, as you said, the data have not notably strengthened.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I-there is noise always in the data from quarter to quarter, but we haven't changed our view of the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We think we're on the same path, not-we haven't boosted the outlook, projected faster growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We think we're moving along the same course we've been on, but it is one that involves gradual tightening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would describe some measures of wage growth as having moved up some.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Some measures haven't moved up, but there's some evidence that wage growth is gradually moving up, which is also suggestive of a strengthening labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we expect policy to remain accommodative now for some time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we're-we're talking about a gradual path of removing policy accommodation as the economy makes progress moving toward neutral.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we're continuing to provide accommodation to the economy that's allowing it to grow at an above-trend pace that's consistent with further improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I've not seen any concrete proposals along this line.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I don't really know what a "21st century Glass-Steagall" would look like.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think my reading on the financial crisis is that that wasn't the major source of the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In fact, many of the problems emanated from firms that were investment banking units.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
