text: To me, an important reform in the aftermath of the crisis was to make sure that investment banking activities where-that were a core part of the shadow banking system where leverage had built-that those were appropriately capitalized, had appropriate liquidity, and their management was strengthened, and that's what we have tried to do.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, obviously, we would look at any proposals that are put forward.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I don't think it was the cause of the financial crisis, and I do feel that we have significantly strengthened supervision of bank holding companies that incorporate investment banking activities.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the simple message is, the economy is doing well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have confidence in the robustness of the economy and its resilience to shocks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have created, since the trough in employment after the financial crisis, around 16 million jobs.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The unemployment rate has moved way down, and many more people feel optimistic about their prospects in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're seeing more people who are feeling free to quit their jobs, getting outside offers, looking for other opportunities.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the job market, which is an important focus for us, is certainly improving.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's not to say that it's a-good labor market conditions for every individual in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We know there are problems that face, particularly, people with less skill and education and in certain sectors of the economy, but many Americans are enjoying a stronger labor market and feel better-feel very much better about that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And inflation is moving- moving up, I think, toward our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we're operating in an environment where the U.S. economy is performing well and risks seem pretty balanced.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think people can feel good about the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, a couple of years ago, we included the word "symmetric" in our statement of longer-run goals, and this seemed like an appropriate time to introduce that word into the statement because we had previously indicated that there was a shortfall of inflation from our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, headline inflation has moved almost back up to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I indicated, a better forward-looking measure of inflation, core inflation-that's not our target, but I think it's worth looking at because it's a better forward-looking predictor of headline inflation-I think that's still running a little bit under 2 percent, but we expect it's going to move up to 2.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And this seemed like a good time to remind Americans that what our objective is is 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Inflation is not always going to be at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Sometimes it's going to be below 2 percent, sometimes it's going to be above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've had a long period in which inflation has run under 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As we move back to 2 percent, which is where we're heading, there will be some times when it's above 2 percent as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it's a reminder-2 percent is not a ceiling on inflation, it's a target.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And there will be some times when inflation is above 2 percent, just like it's been below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're not shooting for inflation above 2 percent, but it's a reminder that there will be deviations above and below when we're achieving our objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, we would-if there were an overshoot and it appeared to be persistent, we would put in place policies to try to bring inflation back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's the core set of principles that we have adopted in our statement on longer-run goals and strategy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And exactly how long it would take to get back to 2 percent would depend, in part, on what was happening with respect to employment and our other objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You asked that question not in an isolated way: What would the impact of a large appreciation of the dollar be?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, as I understand it, you asked about it in the context of a border tax adjustment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Because the argument that is made is that what a border tax would do without an exchange rate adjustment is to raise the price of imported goods into the United States.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that large movement in the dollar that analysts claim would occur would essentially-if it were complete, would fully offset the impact of the border tax on U.S. import goods.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, it wouldn't end up having an impact on U.S. inflation or GDP growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But a question that's a very different-that's a very different matter than if, suddenly, for some reason, the dollar were simply to begin appreciating by a large amount, say, because there were flight-to-safety flows into the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, if-if the latter were to occur, there were just a big boost in the dollar, it would tend to put downward pressure on inflation and would have a negative effect on U.S. export growth and tend to boost imports.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But that's a, that's a different- that's a different exercise.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would just say, it's very uncertain exactly what would happen to the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There has been a lot of discussion of that, and I think it's complicated and uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So at this point we don't have a lot of time-sensitive regulations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There is nothing right now that we need to get out that's a significant rule.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have a relatively light regulatory agenda at this point.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We recognize, of course, that we do have an obligation to write the rules that Congress, you know, dictates in laws that they pass, and so that is an ongoing obligation-obligation that we have.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Some Fed critics have said it's too soon to raise interest rates because wages haven't risen enough to justify a rate increase.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I don't-I would like to see wages increase and think there's some scope for them to increase somewhat further.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But our objectives are maximum employment and inflation, and we need to consider what path of rates is appropriate to foster those objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Unfortunately, one of the things that's been holding down wage increases is very slow productivity growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think we are seeing some upward pressure as the labor market tightens.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I take that as a signal that we're coming closer to our maximum employment objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But productivity is-for those focusing on wage growth, productivity is an additional important factor.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that is something that we've said for some time, and I've previously-when I've been asked what "well under way" means-said that I don't want to define that in purely quantitative terms but rather in qualitative terms.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there's no specific level of the federal funds rate that means we're well under way.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it's also a question of not only the current level, but our confidence in the outlook and our projections for the future path of the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have increased our federal funds rate target now several times.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Our outlook is that we anticipate further increases this year and next year for the federal funds rate, and our statement indicates that if the economy continues to evolve in the manner that we expect, that we would feel the conditions are in-will be in place to begin this process this year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So what I've said about my own situation is that I fully intend to serve out my term as Chair, which ends in early February.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I have not had conversations with the President about future plans.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I do very much hope-I know that they have been working hard to identify appropriate nominees for the open slots, and I do very much hope that there will be nominations in the not-too-distant future, and that the Senate will take those up expeditiously.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I really don't have anything for you at this point.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me just say, as I emphasized in my statement and always say, monetory policy is not on a preset course.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We indicated in our statement today that we're closely monitoring inflation developments and certainly have taken note of the fact that there have been several weak readings, particularly on core inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Our statement indicates that we expect inflation to remain low in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, on the other hand, we continue to feel that with a strong labor market and a labor market that's continuing to strengthen, the conditions are in place for inflation to move up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, obviously we need to monitor that very carefully and ensure, especially with roughly five years of inflation running under our 2 percent objective- that is a goal to which the committee is strongly committed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we need to make sure that we have in place the policies that are necessary to achieve 2 percent inflation, and I pledge that we will do that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But let me say, with respect to recent readings, it's important not to overreact to a few readings, and data on inflation can be noisy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I pointed out, there have been some idiosyncratic factors I think that have held down inflation in recent months, particularly a huge decline in cell telephone service plan prices, some declines in prescription drugs.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We had an exceptionally low reading on core PCE in March, and that will continue to hold down 12-month changes until that reading drops out.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we are-this morning's reading on the CPI showed weakness in a number of categories, and it's certainly something that we will be closely monitoring in the months ahead.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We will-we're focused on making our policy decisions on the medium-term outlook, and we will, you know, be looking carefully at incoming data and, as always, revising our outlook and policy plans as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So-continue, as today's actions show, to feel that the economy is doing well, is showing resilience.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a very strong labor market, an unemployment rate that's declined to levels we have not seen since 2001.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, even with some moderation in the pace of job growth, we have a labor market that continues to strengthen and policy remains- remains accommodative.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, I-it's important that inflation move up to our 2 percent objective, as our projections show we continue to expect that and believe the conditions are in place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we will monitor incoming data, obviously, and be attentive to rethinking our outlook if it seems appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, we are closely looking at the actual performance of inflation and altering our views on the basis of discrepancies between what we see and our expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, well, it is very difficult to pin down what is the longer-run normal rate of unemployment, and there's a great deal of uncertainty about it, and it's hard to pin down, especially given the fact that the so-called Phillips curve appears to be quite flat.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That means that inflation doesn't respond very much or very quickly to movements in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, in the face of very low unemployment that we have seen, while wage growth has picked up somewhat, it remains low, and inflation is influenced by a number of different factors, but we certainly haven't seen much or any evident upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In light of that, the Committee has successively moved down its estimate of the normal longer-run rate of unemployment, and in this projection, it's moved down to 4. percent, a tenth lower than it was last time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, while the unemployment rate is below that, it's not that much-it's not that much below it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I would say that business and household sentiment remains quite strong, although many forecasters have pushed back somewhat the timing of the expected policy changes, such as changes to tax policy or fiscal policy more generally.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would say that, based on my observation of actual spending behavior and my discussions with our wide range of contacts, that I haven't seen very much evidence that, thus far, expectations of policy changes have driven substantial changes in either consumer spending or investment spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Many of our business contacts-I think their confidence remains high.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They've not really changed their plans yet, and they have a wait-and- see attitude.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, in deciding what the appropriate path of rates is, we take many different factors into account.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have certainly noticed the stock market is up considerably over the last year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That usually shows up in financial conditions indexes and is an important reason why some of them show easier financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There's been a modest decrease recently in the value of the dollar, although it's up substantially since mid-2014.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we take those factors into account in deriving our forecasts and deciding the appropriate stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have done that, and-but other things also affect the stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're trying to set a path of the federal funds rate, but taking account of those factors and others that don't show up in a financial conditions index.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're trying to generate paths for employment and inflation that meet our mandated objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I don't think central bank credibility-at least the Fed's credibility-has been impaired.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We look at a whole variety of indicators of inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Professional forecasters-whether it's in the Blue Chip or the Survey of Professional Forecasters, those expectations have remained quite steady and in close alignment with our 2 percent inflation target.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: TIPS-based measures of inflation compensation do not provide straight reads on market participants' estimates and expectations about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They embody other elements-risk premia and liquidity premia as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They had moved down and now have moved-they remain at low levels, but they have moved back up again.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is true that some household surveys of inflation expectations have moved down, but overall I wouldn't say that we've seen a broad undermining of inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But you asked also, I guess, about have structural changes perhaps impacted the inflation process, and that certainly is possible.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And estimates of the normal longer-run unemployment rate-they are quite uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And policy is not being-is not based on some firmly held preconceived notion.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, you know, I continue to believe, though, that with job growth running well in excess, even with the moderation of the level that's needed to provide for new entrants in the labor market, we do have a strengthening economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With policy accommodative, all that we're doing in raising rates is moving- removing a bit of accommodation heading toward a neutral pace.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're not moving so aggressively as to put a brake on continued improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I think that that's a prudent move, to move in a gradual way to remove accommodation, with unemployment now-and not only, I should say, the unemployment rate, but I think any indicator of labor market performance and tightness that you could look at, whether it's household perceptions of the availability of jobs, difficulty that firms report in hiring workers, the rate at which workers are quitting their jobs, the rate of job openings, all of these indicators do signal a tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, with inflation below 2 percent, I think it's appropriate that the labor market be that tight.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, on the other hand, I think we want to avoid the risk.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We want to keep the expansion on a sustainable path and avoid the risk that at some point we need-we find ourselves in a situation where we've done nothing and then need to raise the funds rate so rapidly that we risk a recession.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So moving to some extent in a timely way to remove accommodation with a strong economy and continued labor market strength, the Committee believes, is an appropriate management of risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we are attentive to the fact that inflation is running below our 2 percent objective, that we've faced that situation now for a long time, and it's really quite essential that we put in place policies that will succeed in moving inflation back to our 2 percent objective, and it's a symmetric objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The Committee believes we have conditions in place for inflation to move up, but that's also a risk.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And those things point, I think, to a gradual pace of reducing accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Recently, a group of economists sent the Fed a letter earlier this month disagreeing with your 2 percent inflation target and saying they would like the economy to run a bit hotter.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You say you're committed to the 2 percent target, but what do you say to them?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, at the time that we adopted the 2 percent target-it was back in 2012-we had a very thorough discussion of the factors that should determine what our inflation objective should be.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, you know, I believe that was a well-thought-out decision.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, at the moment, we are highly focused on trying to achieve our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we recognize the fact that inflation has been running below, and it's essential for us to move inflation back to that objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we've learned a lot in the meantime, and assessments of the level of the neutral likely level, currently and going forward, of the neutral federal funds rate have changed and are quite a bit lower than they stood in 2012 or earlier years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that means that the economy is- has the potential where policy could be constrained by the zero lower bound more frequently than at the time that we adopted our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it's that recognition that causes people to think we might be better off with a higher inflation objective, and that's an important set-this is one of our most critical decisions and one we are attentive to evidence and outside thinking.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's one that we will be reconsidering at some future time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it's important for our decisions to be informed by a wide range of views and research which is ongoing inside and outside the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But a reconsideration of that objective needs to take account not only of benefits of a higher in-potential benefits of a higher inflation target, but also the potential costs that could be associated with it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I would say that this is one of the most important questions facing monetary policy around the world in the future, and we very much look forward to seeing research by economists that will help inform our future decisions on this.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me first say, it's not straightforward to determine exactly what expectations are embodied in market prices because there are term premia that affect these rates, and they may not really be as low as one would infer from a straight read.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That said, in part, expectations reflect estimates of what the neutral federal funds rate is and how it's likely to evolve over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And views have changed about that over time, and there is a good deal of uncertainty about it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have recently put out charts that try to show what the range of uncertainty is around our path for the federal funds rate, especially as one goes further out.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There's a good deal of uncertainty and-that reflects the, like-all the shocks that can affect the evolution of the economy, and also the fact, we're quite uncertain ourselves about what the likely-what the evolution will be of the neutral federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we do try to write that down and provide the public with information about our current expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the median now stands at around 3 percent, but we have uncertainty about that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Many of my colleagues and I think that the current neutral level is lower than that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And as I said in my opening statement, the fed funds rate path reflects an expectation that that neutral rate will be moving up some in future years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But that remains uncertain, and I think that's something that market participants are trying to assess, and we will be as well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, the projections we released today are essentially identical to those.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think the market is aware of the views of participants and is assessing evidence itself to form their own views.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it's important that the market take an independent look, and that we get to understand and see how market participants are interpreting evidence on the evolution of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it's not an unhealthy thing to have such a gap.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, as I just said, our own views are not set in stone but are likely to evolve as well over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have indicated for quite some time, I guess, since our-at least since our 2014 normalization principles, that we wanted to reduce our balance sheet in a gradual and predictable way.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we have tried systematically to communicate more about how we would do that as our plans have evolved.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And today's announcement is another step in providing further details about how we plan to proceed so that when this plan does go into effect, no one is taken by surprise and market participants understand how this will work.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think that we-the plan is one that is consciously intended to avoid creating market strains and to allow the market to adjust to a very gradual and predictable plan.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: My hope and expectation is that when we decide to go forward with this plan, that there will be very little reaction to it, that it's clear how we intend to proceed, and that this is something that will just run quietly in the background over a number of years, leading to a reduction in the size of our balance sheet and in the outstanding stock of reserves, and that it's something that the Committee will not be reconsidering from time to time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We think this is a workable plan, and it will, as one of my colleagues, President Harker, described it, it will be like watching paint dry, that this will just be something that runs quietly in the background.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Look, of course, if it turns out that there is a surprise and a substantial reaction, that is something we would have to take into account in deciding on the appropriate stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, with respect to the impact of credit conditions and bank regulation on slow growth, I've previously, in testifying, indicated that I don't think that our regulations have played an important role, at least broadly speaking, in impeding credit growth and the growth of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I've pointed in the past to a number of statistics suggesting that credit growth continues to be healthy, including among small-smaller community banks that are most concerned with regulatory burden.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think when banks are undercapitalized and weak, that impedes credit growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And when banks are strong, they're in a much better position to lend.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, in terms of regulation, the Treasury recently issued, on Monday, a detailed report.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that's quite a complicated document with lots of recommendations in it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I haven't had a chance to review it thoroughly, so I don't want to comment on too many details.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I would say it underscores the importance of capital, liquidity, stress testing, and resolution planning in having a safe and sound banking system, which are views that I and my colleagues have long espoused.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Regulatory burden, when it's possible to ease it, and a good deal of the Treasury report is focused on regulatory burden, that's something that all regulators should be looking to do.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We strongly believe in the importance of tailoring our regulation to the size and complexity of institutions, of finding ways to relieve burden for community banks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have been focused and had a number of initiatives already in that direction, looking for ways, for example, to simplify capital requirements for community banks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we'll continue in that direction and, in that sense, in those areas certainly share the views expressed in the Treasury report.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there are a number of areas and suggestions where our thinking aligns well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There is probably some areas where we're likely to have differences but quite-you know, quite a number of areas where we're, you know, likely to be able to and already are taking actions that are consistent with those recommendations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I have felt that it's been appropriate for interest rates to remain low for a very long time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are in the process of, as the economy strengthens, normalizing interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, certainly, we've had a lot of years in which interest rates have been low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I thought it was necessary to support the economy at that time and was strongly in favor of those policies.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have tried as meticulously as we can to provide advanced warning to markets about how we would go about doing this so that market participants can prepare.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we certainly wanted to get this information out before we actually undertake the beginning of this plan.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, you know, as the statement says, we've made no definite decision on the timing of the plan, but-the timing of initiating the plan.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But if the economy evolves in line with our expectations, which, you know, we will be watching-always are-we could put this into effect relatively soon.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You asked about whether or not we would do that and raise rates at the same meeting, and I would say, we've made no decision about that, and it really hinges on the outlook and our assessment of conditions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have previously suggested exempting community banks, smaller banks, entirely from the rule.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And a number of my colleagues have spoken about the Volcker rule.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Implementation of it is frankly complex, and I'm certainly open to looking at ways to reduce regulatory burden in that area.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, in that sense, it endorses the main objective of the Volcker rule, which I was pleased to see.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But on implementation, it's true that the rules were-in part reflecting the way the legislation is written-were, I think, necessarily complex, but we do have some ideas for how we might simplify the rule, and certainly it's something we're quite open to looking at.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I mean, Treasury has a-set out a list of objectives for regulation that I'm sympathetic to and endorse.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think looking for ways to reduce regulatory burden, when it can be done without sacrificing safety and soundness or creating systemic risk, that's something that all regulators should want to do.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've done an awful lot of rule writing over the last five or six years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And coming back and looking at where we have created burdens and ways in which we can simplify to reduce, that is an objective that is core to the Treasury review and that we are very sympathetic with.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, while we may not agree on every detail, certainly the suggestions that are made there are ones that we will pay attention to and in many cases are already on our own list of things we should review.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, staff in the Federal Reserve and outside economists have done a great deal of work trying to evaluate QE.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think the general conclusion is that it has worked in that it has put some downward pressure on longer- term interest rates, so-called term premiums embedded in longer-term interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There's disagreement among economists about exactly how large those effects are, and it's something that's difficult to pin down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, obviously, it has not caused runaway inflation, quite the contrary.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, that was never my expectation, but I do remember when people were afraid that that would happen.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have, you know, even with a large balance sheet-we intend to shrink our balance sheet now, but even with a large balance sheet, we retain the ability to move the fed funds rate and set it as appropriate for the needs of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's something that, if we were to encounter an episode in the future of extreme weakness where-I've said we want the fed funds rate and movements in short-term interest rates, that's our go-to number one main policy tool- but if we were to hit the zero lower bound and constrained in our use of that tool, certainly balance sheet policies and forward guidance of the type that we provided, I believe, based on the evidence of how they worked, ought to remain part of our toolkit.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we have said in the bullets that we released today on our balance sheet that in such of-an episode of such extreme weakness in the future, those are things we would consider going forward.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, we've had no discussion of that issue, you know.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And our focus now is on getting it back to a more normal size.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I would say, the use of QE in the United States relative to the size of our economy is not as high as it's been in some other countries that have employed it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I'm not going to comment on the President's budget, and these programs can be undertaken at many different levels.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've seen many nonprofits and states and local authorities put in place programs that looked to me to be successful.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I do think we have a tight labor market and one where employers have jobs where they're finding difficulty identifying workers with the appropriate skills.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In my own discussions with businesses, what I hear more of-and this is something I think is a great aspect of a tight labor market-larger firms are spending more on training and trying to, given that they can't hire workers with the ideal skills, are training people to fill jobs that they have available.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: What I hear from CEOs of smaller firms is that they don't have the ability to launch such programs.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They would really very much like to participate along, for example, with community colleges or nonprofits to see such programs launched and have jobs that people could fill if they received the appropriate training.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I do think that this is an important area, and, especially given the pressures that have, you know, existed for a long time-downward pressure on wages and job opportunities, especially for those with less skills-I think that this is something that deserves priority.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me first say that employment is a very important part of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're charged by Congress with trying to pursue maximum employment, and we have taken that very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm very pleased and heartened by the improvement we have seen in the labor market, and at 4. percent, the unemployment rate has really fallen to quite a low level.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As that's happened, the unemployment rates for less advantaged groups in the labor market, particularly African Americans and Hispanics, has fallen more dramatically than that for the nation as a whole, reversing the outsized increases that those groups experienced when the financial crisis and Great Recession hit.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we certainly seek a strong labor market, but we have a dual mandate, which is inflation and unemployment, and we also have to be mindful of our obligation to achieve a 2 percent inflation objective over the medium term.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, I recognize and it's important that inflation has been running under our 2 percent objective for a number of years, and that is a concern, particularly if it were to translate into lower inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: For a number of years there were very understandable reasons for that shortfall, and they included quite a lot of slack in the labor market-which, my judgment would be, has largely disappeared-very large reductions in energy prices, and a large appreciation of the dollar that lowered import prices starting in mid-2014.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: This year, the September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 7 of 25 shortfall of inflation from 2 percent, when none of those factors is operative, is more of a mystery, and I will not say that the Committee clearly understands what the causes are of that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, we do, in our regular projection, show fan charts indicating the typical size of forecast errors.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: All of the variables-GDP, the unemployment rate, and inflation-are forecast by ourselves and private forecasters with errors, and so there is variation in these economic variables from year to year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would say our judgment, as I said in the statement, is that the shortfall is not largely related to cyclical considerations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You can see from the projections that the Committee participants submitted that we anticipate that core and headline inflation will move up close to our 2 percent objective next year-namely, that the shortfall this year is due to transitory factors that are likely to disappear over the course of the coming year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I want to emphasize that we do have a commitment to raising inflation to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And as we watch incoming data, the assessments that you see participants write down about the path of the federal funds rate, they are not set in stone.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We will look at incoming data on inflation and on other economic variables, including the labor market, in deciding what we should actually do going forward.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if it proves contrary to our expectations that the shortfall is persistent, it will be necessary to adjust monetary policy to address that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I want to point out that while there are risks that inflation could continue below 2 percent, which we need to take account of in monetary policy, monetary policy also operates with a lag.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And experience suggests that tightness in the labor market, gradually and with a lag, tends to push up wage and price inflation, and that's also a risk, that we want to be careful not to allow the economy to overheat in a way that would force us later on, somewhere down the road, to have to tighten monetary policy rapidly, which could cause a recession and threaten the very desirable labor market conditions that we have now.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 8 of 25

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So at every meeting we try to assess the economic outlook and take account of information that's been accumulated about the real economy and also developments in financial markets and put all of that together in assessing the course of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So developments affecting asset prices and longer-term interest rates, the exchange rate-all of those aspects of financial conditions factor into our thinking.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it's not easy to get a clear read on the implications of asset prices for the overall outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Sometimes movements-upward movements in asset prices can, for example, reflect a change in market participants'-reduction in market participants' estimates of the longer-run level of interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there has been-there have been downward revisions both to the Committee's and to market participants' estimates of the longer-run normal level of interest rates, which in turn reflects in some sense a view that, going out many years, aggregate demand globally is likely to be weakened by continuing low productivity growth and aging populations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, of course, we don't know if that view is correct, but that's a factor that could be reflected- could be one reason why asset prices have moved as they have.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's important in determining the impact on the overall outlook, but, certainly, we are taking account of movements in asset prices in evaluating the appropriate stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 9 of 25

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we have two policy tools that are available to us to use: the balance sheet and adjustments in short-term interest rates-our federal funds rate target.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, historically, the Committee has operated to adjust monetary conditions to meet our economic goals when there are shocks to the economy by adjusting the federal funds rate-our short-term interest rate target.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And that's something-a technique of monetary control that we have used for a very long time that we are familiar with, we believe we understand pretty well what the effects are on the economy, market participants understand how that tool has been used and would likely be adjusted in response to shocks to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And our preference is, when we have two different tools that we could use to actively adjust the stance of policy, to prefer and to make a commitment that, to the maximum extent possible, the federal funds rate will be the September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 10 of 25 active tool of policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That is what we intend to use unless we think that the threat to the economy is sufficiently great that we might have to cut the federal funds rate- after all, we've moved it up to 1 to 1¼ percent and expect it to go up further-but a very significant negative shock to the economy could conceivably force us back to the so-called zero lower bound.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have said if there were that type of material deterioration in the outlook where we could face a situation where the federal funds rate isn't a sufficient tool for us to adjust monetary policy, we might stop-we might stop roll-offs from our balance sheet and resume reinvestment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But as long as we believe that we can use the federal funds rate as a tool, that is what we intend to do.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, if there are small changes in the outlook that require a recalibration of monetary policy, we will change our anticipated path and setting of the federal funds rate, but not, for example, change the caps on reinvestment or stop-continue reinvestment for a few months and then change it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We think that provides greater clarity to market participants about how policy will be conducted and will be, will be less confusing and more effective in terms of conducting policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the only thing I would object to there, is you said that we are "locked in," and I would say that we are not locked in.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We believe that economic conditions will evolve in a way that will warrant gradual, further increases in our federal funds rate target, but if conditions evolve differently than that, whichever direction that might be-it might be that growth is more rapid, the labor market tightens more quickly than we assume, and inflation appears to be picking up more rapidly than we had expected-we have not promised, no matter what, that the path of interest rate increases will be gradual.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We believe that that will be appropriate, but we always watching the economy and will adjust policy as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, as I said, the hurdle to changing our plans with respect to the balance sheet, in some sense, is high.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If conditions were to weaken, we would really only consider resuming reinvestment if it were what we refer to as a material deterioration, and I tried to explain why that is.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: What you see in the dot plot is each participant's best guess, based on the information they have today, about what will be appropriate in light of their expectations about how the economy would evolve.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we think it's helpful to show the public some sense that it helps in understanding our evaluation of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But we're assessing incoming data, and these plans are subject to change.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: What's not subject to change is our commitment to doing everything in our power to achieve the goals that Congress has assigned to us, which are price stability or 2 percent inflation and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, certainly, if growth is stronger or if inflation picks up more rapidly, we have room.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a certain amount of room now, and we have raised the funds September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 12 of 25 rate four times.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We believe that we are on a path where there will likely be further increases over the next couple of years, which will give us greater room, and we think the recovery is on a strong track.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the reason for our actions today in beginning to run down the balance sheet is, we think the economy is performing well and we have confidence in the outlook for the real economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, of course, there are shocks, and if the negative shock to the economy were sufficient, we recognize that we might be unable to pursue objectives purely by cutting the federal funds rate, and that is why we say explicitly that we would be prepared, in that event, to resume reinvestment, and other tools that we used in the financial crisis-forward guidance- would also be available to us.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the term "trend inflation"-usually there are a variety of statistical techniques that can be used to extract a trend from a series.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Exactly what that means is, in some sense, a statistical thing, and there are methodologies that would show some modest decline in recent years in the trend.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: After all, we've had a number of years in which inflation has been low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I said in answer to an earlier question, I think if you go back to, say, 2013 and consider the- until this year, the reasons why inflation was low are not hard to understand.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's a combination September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 13 of 25 of slack in the labor market, declines in energy prices, and a strong dollar that pulled down import price inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So what's important in determining inflation going forward is inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: By some-by many-by some survey measures of professional forecasters, those have been rock solid.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We do also look at household expectations, which have come down some.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Market-based measures of inflation compensation, as we mentioned in the statement-they have declined, and they've been stable in recent months, but they've declined to levels that are low by historical standards.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That might suggest that inflation expectations have come down, but one can't get a clear read-there are risk premia built into inflation compensation that make it impossible to extract directly what inflation expectations are.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I can't say I can easily point to a sufficient set of factors that explain this year why inflation has been this low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've mentioned a few idiosyncratic things, but, frankly, the low inflation is more broad based than just idiosyncratic things.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The fact that inflation is unusually low this year does not mean that that's going to continue.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Remember that in January and February, core inflation was running over a 12-month basis at around 1. percent, and we look to be very close to 2 now.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've had several months of data that have meaningfully pulled that down, and what we need to do is figure out whether or not the factors that have lowered inflation are likely to prove persistent or they're likely to prove transitory, and that's what we're going to try to be determining on the basis of incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Of course, if we determined our view changed, and instead of thinking that the factors holding inflation down were transitory, we came to the view that they would be persistent, it would require an alteration in monetary policy to move inflation back up to 2 percent, and we would be committed to making that adjustment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 14 of 25

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I'm not really going to try to explain what market participants are thinking.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think all of us-both market and FOMC participants' paths have come down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Not in the last couple of quarters, but over the last several years, there's been a growing recognition that the so-called neutral interest rate, consistent with the economy operating at maximum employment, that that rate seems to have come down, and most of the economic papers and research bearing on this topic suggest that it's quite low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Market-SEP-the FOMC participants-you can see by their estimates of the longer-run normal rate of interest, it is-this time it came down from-the median came down from 3 percent to 2. percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that shows that even in the long run, FOMC participants, in light of incoming data, are adjusting their views.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would say they still believe that, in real terms, that neutral rate will be rising somewhat over the next few years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: With a 2 percent inflation rate, that long-run estimate in real terms amounts to 75 basis points, which is higher than the zero or slightly positive rates now.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that's one factor that explains the path in the SEP. Market participants may have lower estimates or believe that a low neutral rate may be more persistent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, let me emphasize that, as I said before, there's nothing set in stone about the policy paths that you see in the summary of projections.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Not only is there disagreement, there's also uncertainty, and FOMC participants have been revising their views over time, and they will continue to do so.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 15 of 25 I'd also point out a couple of technical reasons why it's difficult to compare what you see in the SEP and market-implied paths.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: One is that FOMC participants are writing down what they think is the most likely, or modal, outcome for rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the mean rate, if they were asked to write that down, would take account of weighing all possible outcomes and likely would be lower than what participants are writing down as their most likely outcome.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In addition, in markets, many economists have suggested that there are term premia that can affect moving from the so-called market-implied path to the view for what the future federal funds rate path is, and if those term premia are negative, as many economists think they likely are, there's a little bit less difference between what you see in the FOMC plot and the market-implied plot.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I have said that I intend to serve out my term as Chair, and that I'm really not going to comment on my intentions beyond that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I will say that I have not had a further meeting with President Trump.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I met with him early in my term, and I've not had a further meeting with him.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So you asked me, what was the main-first, what was the main message of my speech, and I would say it's that we put in place, since the financial crisis, a set of core reforms that have strengthened the financial system, and, in my personal view, it's important they remain in place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And those core reforms are more capital, higher-quality capital, more liquidity-especially in systemically important banking institutions-stress testing, and resolution plans.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And those four prongs of improvements in banking supervision have really strengthened the financial system and made it more resilient, and I believe they should stay in place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I also tried to emphasize-and I believe that they have contributed to growth and the availability of credit.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've also tried to emphasize that all regulators should be attentive to undue regulatory burden and look for ways to try to scale that back.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And this is especially true after years in which we have implemented a large number of complex regulations, and we have been committed to doing that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would point out particularly community banks that are laboring under significant regulatory burden.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have been looking for ways to scale back burdens, running the EGRPRA process, where we've listened to concerns among community banks and are looking September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 17 of 25 for ways, for example, to simplify capital standards and reduce burdens, and that's very important.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: More generally, we want to tailor-we want to, and we would like to see Congress as well-we can do things to appropriately tailor regulations to the risk posed by different kinds of banking organizations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are some things that Congress could also do to help that process, and we have made some concrete suggestions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And then some of the regulations that we have put in place with other regulators since the crisis, like the Volcker rule, are really quite complex, and we're working-we believe we should-and we're working with other regulators to try to see if we can find ways, while carrying out what Dodd-Frank intended, that banking organizations not be involved in proprietary trading.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Your second question asked about what impact the Fed has had on income distribution because of the fact that stocks and homes tend to be disproportionately owned.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, I would say, look, we were faced with a huge recession that took an enormous toll in terms of depriving large numbers of people-and disproportionately lower-income people who are less advantaged in the labor market-found themselves without work.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We had a 10 percent unemployment rate, and our congressional mandate is maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So we set monetary policy not with a view toward affecting the distribution of income, but toward pursuing those congressionally mandated goals.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I am pleased to see the unemployment rate and every other measure that I know of pertaining to the labor market show dramatic improvement over these years, and that is hugely important to the economic well-being not at the top end of the wealth and income distribution, September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 18 of 25 but to the bottom end of the income distribution.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we have seen this year median income in real terms rise significantly, with gains throughout the income distribution.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So first let me say that I will greatly miss Vice Chair Fischer.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: He's made enormous contributions to the FOMC and to the broader work of the Federal Reserve, and I have really enjoyed working with him and appreciated his wise counsel and friendship.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is conceivable that we will be down to three Governors.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I have full confidence that even if that happens, we will be able to carry out our complement of responsibilities.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There's-every action that we are allowed to take under the Federal Reserve Act can be taken, even if we are a Board of three, although we will have to abide, as we always do, by the restrictions that are part of the Government in the Sunshine Act.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a lot of work to do, and it would be nice to distribute it over more people.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, perhaps more important than that, I think it's very important to have a broad range of views around the table as we deliberate on policy actions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've had very good interactions with Randy Quarles and hope he will be confirmed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I look forward to working with him, and, you know, I hope that the Administration will make other nominations to fill our slots.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 19 of 25

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Look, that's something that's a matter for Congress and the White House to decide.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, I've put forward a few principles about fiscal policy that I would reiterate, that one of the problems that the American economy suffers from, along with many other economies around the globe, is slow productivity growth, and I think it would be very desirable if a fiscal package had the potential in it to create incentives that would raise productivity growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We do face, in terms of longer-term deficits as the population ages, an unsustainable debt path that will require, I believe, some adjustments to fiscal policy, and I hope Congress will keep that in mind.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But beyond a few core principles, it's really-I don't want to weigh in on details.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: When you testified before Congress last July, you said that you might be prepared to take enforcement actions against Wells Fargo if it proved to be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Do you think it's appropriate, and what actions could you take?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me say that I consider the behavior of Wells Fargo towards its customers to have been egregious and unacceptable.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We take our supervision responsibilities at the company very seriously, and we are attempting to understand what the root causes of those problems are and to address them.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm not able to discuss confidential supervisory information and not yet able to tell you what actions we may take, but I do want to say that we are committed September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 20 of 25 to taking the actions we regard as necessary and appropriate to make sure that the right set of controls are in place in that organization.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, starting with the last part of the question, I mean, my own judgment, based on my experience and the economic research that has tried to estimate the effectiveness of our balance sheet actions starting in 2008 and has also looked at the similar balance sheet actions in other parts of the world, including the euro area, is that these actions were successful in making financial conditions more accommodative and, I believe, in stimulating a faster recovery than we otherwise would have had.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: A recent Fed working paper estimated that the full set of balance sheet actions that we took during the crisis may have lowered long-term interest rates by about 100 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Obviously, there are different-there are different estimates around-of what difference it made, but I would say that it's effective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It will be up to future policymakers to decide, in the event of a severe downturn, whether they think it's appropriate to again resort to balance sheet-to adding assets to a balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would say that if economists are correct that we're living in a world where the level of neutral interest rates not only in the United States, but around the world is likely to be low in the future September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 21 of 25 due to slow productivity growth and demographics-now, we don't know that that view will bear out to be correct, but it is a view that many people adhere to when there is evidence of it- then future policymakers will be faced with the question of, in the event of a severe downturn where they're not able to provide as much stimulus as they would ideally like by cutting overnight interest rates, what other actions are available to them?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And during the crisis, we bought longer-term assets and used forward guidance, and for my own part, I would want to keep those things in the toolkit as being available.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It will be up to future policymakers to decide how to rank those, or whether or not there might be other options that are available to them, but I don't think this issue will go away, although perhaps it's only- well, this could well be a decision that future policymakers will have to face in the event of a significant asset-economic shock.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, you asked me what would it take for us to resume reinvestment, and I can't really say much more than we said in the guidance that we provided, which is that if there is a material deterioration in the economic outlook and we thought we might be faced with a situation where we would need to substantially cut the federal funds rate and could be limited by the so-called zero lower bound, it is that type of determination that our Committee is saying would-might lead us to resume reinvestment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that's-our Committee has been unanimous in affirming this statement of intentions, so, you know, I think that's where our Committee stands.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So that is a somewhat high bar to resume reinvestments, and that's why, in answering previous questions, I would say, well, you know, if there's some small, negative shock, our first tool-our most important and reliable tool-will be the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But if there is a significant shock that's a material deterioration to the outlook, we would consider resuming reinvestment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 22 of 25

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So during the time that I've been on the FSOC, only one firm was-several firms were designated before I participated.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: MetLife was designated during the time that I was there, and I have seen how the designation process works.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We saw during the financial crisis that some systemically important nonbanking organizations like Lehman and AIG-that their distress produced broad systemic consequences that were adverse for the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And having the ability to designate firms when the FSOC makes the determination that their distress or failure could have systemic repercussions, I believe that's an important-that's an important policy tool for FSOC to have available.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, it's not meant to be a one-way street, in the sense that a firm that's designated-the procedures require annual reviews.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Firms may change their business models or just how they conduct their business, and we should welcome de-designation of firms if their business model is changed in a way that leads us to believe that their failure or distress would no longer be systemically important and those are decisions that we make every year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, I'm satisfied with that process so far.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: GE Capital dramatically changed its business model and was de-designated, and, you know, I believe it's a process that works.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 23 of 25 know that the Treasury is looking at this and may make recommendations, and if they do, I'd be, you know, glad to consider them as, you know, part of the FSOC process, but I think it's been important and basically working.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You asked about Equifax and, you know, of course that is a very serious data breach.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We would really urge consumers now to be very careful in monitoring their credit reports and financial situation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, through our supervision, we're working with the banks that we supervise to make sure that they take appropriate actions with respect to their business processes in light of the fact that there could be breaches or fraudulent transactions or information that they received that they might use-for example, in credit determinations-could be contaminated by bad data.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: More generally, it points to the importance of strong cybersecurity controls and attention to cybersecurity risks, which we do see as one of the most significant risks to the financial sector.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we are very focused in our banking supervision in making sure that banks have appropriate controls in place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the Equifax breach, I think, highlights the importance of that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, first of all, let me say that the decisions that we've made this year about rates and today about our balance sheet are ones we've taken because we feel the U.S. economy is performing well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are working down our balance sheet because we feel that's stimulus that in some sense is no longer needed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the basic message here is, U.S. economic performance has been good.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Every measure of the labor market, whether it's the narrow unemployment rate, the broader unemployment rate, the number of people working in part-time jobs who want full-time work, the level of job openings, the quit rate, the difficulty that firms are facing in hiring workers, the level of confidence we see in surveys about the labor market-all of that is pointing to vast and continuing improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And we see sufficient strength in the economy, in terms of spending-that growth, with its ups and downs, but nevertheless is strong enough-looks to be strong enough in the medium term to support ongoing improvement in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And all of that is good, and I think that the American people should feel the steps we're taking to normalize monetary policy are ones that we feel are well justified, given the very substantial progress we've seen in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, inflation is running below where we want it to be, and we've talked about that a lot during this-the last hour.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: This past year, where it's not clear what the reasons are-I think it's not been mysterious in the past, but, one way or another, we have had four or five years in which inflation is running below our 2 percent objective, and we are also committed to achieving that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the monetary policy path that we follow and the paths that my colleagues are writing down in our projections as ones they think will be appropriate given economic conditions are ones that September 20, 2017 Chair Yellen's PressConference FINAL Page 25 of 25 we think are necessary to move inflation back up to 2 percent and to maintain a strong labor market on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And in making these judgments about the path of policy, we have to balance various risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: One risk is that if we tighten policy too quickly, we may find out that, although we don't think this now, that the inflation shortfall is something that's going to be persistent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if we tighten too quickly, we could undermine inflation performance-leave it at too low a level- inflation expectations could fall, and that could become ingrained, and that would be dangerous.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so that's a reason to be cautious about raising interest rates when inflation is as low as it is.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, on the other hand, we have a strong labor market and a low unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And although the pace of job gains is not quite as strong this year as, for example, as it was in 2016, we're still averaging 175,000 jobs a month this year, which is quite a bit above the pace of maybe 100 to 120,000 that would be consistent with a stable unemployment rate if labor force participation begins to move down in the manner we expect.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So if we don't do anything to remove policy accommodation, and the labor market tightens and just continues to tighten, as you mentioned, arguably-we could, you know- arguably, financial conditions overall haven't tightened that much.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We think the economy could overheat, inflation could rise more quickly and above our objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That's something that would occur with a lag, and that would force us later on to tighten policy more rapidly than would be ideal, and we could risk a recession if we did that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there are risks on both sides to our objectives, and most of my colleagues and I have concluded that a gradual path of rate increases-while constantly watching incoming data, being open to revising our views on the outlook, and revising our expectations about policy-is the best way to manage that set of risks.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, yes, we did discuss tax policy, and let me say that most of my colleagues factored in the prospect of fiscal stimulus along the lines of what's being contemplated by Congress into their projections.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, I should emphasize that some have been incorporating those expectations into their projections throughout the year, so changes to the projections that you see since September should not be viewed as an impact-an estimate of the impact of the tax package.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, in particular, broader expectations of changes to fiscal policy have been reflected in financial market conditions, I think, over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: For example, we have seen a significant increase in the stock market, and at least some portion of that, I would judge, likely partly reflected expected tax changes, and that effect-along with other financial market effects, which affects, for example, projected consumer spending and would have affected wealth-that's been part of participants' forecasts now for some time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think my colleagues and I are in line with the general expectation among most economists that the type of tax changes that are likely to be enacted would tend to provide some modest lift to GDP growth in the coming years, and you see that-in part, that's one of the reasons, I think, for the uptick you see in estimated growth and decline in the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The views of participants, I believe, have been informed by a wide range of analysis, including that of the Joint Committee on Taxation and other outside evaluators, and my sense is that their estimates are essentially in the same ballpark, although they recognize, as I emphasized, that there is considerable uncertainty about the impacts, and that will have to be monitored over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: More specifically, they tend to see the package as boosting both consumer spending and capital spending, to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, to the extent that the changes do have positive impact on the growth of potential GDP and longer-run growth, let me just say that this is something that, should it occur, would be very welcome to participants, as long as it's consistent with the attainment of our employment and inflation objectives.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I guess I would also urge you to remember that when you look at the projections, that there are many factors that affect those projections, and changes in tax policy- that's only one of a number of factors, including incoming data that has, to some extent, altered the outlook for growth and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I think, bottom line, when you look at assessments of the funds rate path, participants continue to see gradual increases in the target range for the federal funds rate as being appropriate to sustain a strong labor market and bring inflation back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, look- importantly, there is a lot of uncertainty about what the likely effects will be, and my colleagues and I will be committed, as always, to evaluating incoming data and altering the outlook as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So it is true that incoming wage data suggests only modest upward pressure on wages.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That leaves me-that's one factor, along with the fact that inflation remains low-with feeling that even though we have a 4. percent unemployment rate, that the labor market is not overheated at this point.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Remember, the modest pace of wage gains also probably reflects slow productivity growth.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But when you ask me about the outlook for inflation, you know, I've talked in detail about this in the past and recognize that there is uncertainty about what's holding inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But my colleagues and I continue to believe that the factors that are responsible this year for holding inflation down are likely to prove transitory.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: That said, we all agree that our inflation objective is extremely important.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: This is a symmetric 2 percent inflation objective, and we continue to indicate that we'll be monitoring inflation developments closely.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so this is on the horizon and recognized to be one of the risks facing policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think my colleagues and I mainly see the likely tax package as boosting aggregate demand, but also having some potential to boost aggregate supply.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So changes on the corporate tax side-the reduction in the corporate tax rate, expensing-will lower the cost of capital.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And while there are a range of estimates and uncertainty about how much stimulus that will provide to investment, in general I would see some stimulus to investment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In terms of aggregate supply effects, a stronger pace of investment could boost capital formation and thereby raise productivity growth and potential GDP or output to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Exactly how large those effects might be remain uncertain, but that is a channel.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I suppose it's also possible-I'm uncertain how significant this would be-that lower marginal effective tax rates for those groups that will see them could boost labor supply.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, again, there are a range of estimates in the literatures.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I indicated I think participants have reviewed a number of pieces of analysis, including the Joint Committee on Taxation estimates, and the many outside analysts who have weighed in on this and been influenced by that kind of analysis-but there is a good deal of uncertainty about what the impacts would be.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, to the extent that there are larger impacts than those analyses assume on aggregate supply or potential GDP, in the context of an economy that has had disturbingly low productivity growth, that would be welcome and could support faster GDP growth, at least for some period, without-you know, without creating a need to tighten monetary policy to offset that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there are potentially both demand and supply effects here.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, importantly, you really don't, at the end of the day, see very much change in the federal funds rate path.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Participants do recognize that the unemployment rate is lower than their estimates of its long-run sustainable rate, so I think we are in the vicinity of full employment.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm sorry, remind me of the first part of your question.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I think, generally, in a strong labor market where many firms are having difficulty finding qualified workers, we would expect, just through normal demand and supply channels, to see some upward pressure on wage growth over time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And as the labor market is tightened, we've seen some very gradual drift upward in wage gains.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: They remain-it remains at a low level, but I would expect, in the context of an ongoing strong labor market, to see some upward pressure.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I believe that's the main thing that my colleagues are factoring in.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: On your question on advice to women and minorities, in the Federal Reserve, my colleagues and I are very focused on wanting to see and do what we can to foster greater participation of women and minorities in economics.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We would love to, if we could, increase our hiring ourselves of women and minorities, and we see that both women and minorities are studying economics in disproportionately and disturbingly low numbers.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Although the women in STEM fields generally are about even with men-represent about 50 percent-in economics, women majors constitute something like 30 percent of undergraduate majors, and there is disproportionate low enrollment of minorities.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I will just say, from my own experience, I think economics is a terrific field.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've thoroughly enjoyed my career in economics and think there are many different paths that people can follow that lead to satisfying careers, and that there are very interesting and important questions that economics addresses.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it is a great field, and I would like to encourage greater involvement and think that people will find that satisfying.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, just in terms of the kinds of research that's done in the field, I think also a greater diversity, more women and minorities, may change the focus to some extent of the questions that people choose to look at and the analysis that they bring and a range of thinking that bears on research.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me start, Steve, with the stock market generally.
