speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, of course the stock market has gone up a great deal this year, and we have in recent months characterized the general level of asset valuations as "elevated."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: What that reflects is simply the assessment that, looking at price/earnings ratios and comparable metrics for other assets other than equities, we see ratios that are at the high end of historical ranges-and so that's worth pointing out.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But economists are not great at knowing what appropriate valuations are.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We don't have a terrific record, and the fact that those valuations are high doesn't mean that they are necessarily overvalued.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We are in a-I've mentioned this in my opening statement, and we've talked about this repeatedly-likely a low interest rate environment, lower than we've had in past decades.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And if that turns out to be the case, that's a factor that supports higher valuations.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We're enjoying solid economic growth with low inflation, and the risks in the global economy look more balanced than they have in many years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think what we need to and are trying to think through is, if there were an adjustment in asset valuations or the stock market, what impact would that have on the economy, and would it provoke financial stability concerns?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think when we look at other indicators of financial stability risks, there's nothing flashing red there or possibly even orange.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a much more resilient, stronger banking system, and we're not seeing some worrisome buildup in leverage or credit growth at successive levels.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, this is something that the FOMC pays attention to, but if you ask me, is this a significant factor shaping monetary policy now, well, it's on the list of risks, it's not a major-it's not a major factor.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And then you asked about bitcoin, and there I would simply say that bitcoin at this time plays a very small role in the payment system.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is not a stable source of-store of value, and it 1 Chair Yellen intended to say that credit growth is not at excessive levels.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is a highly speculative asset, and the Fed doesn't really play any role-any regulatory role with respect to bitcoin other than assuring that banking organizations that we do supervise are attentive, that they're appropriately managing any interactions they have with participants in that market and appropriately monitoring anti-money- laundering Bank Secrecy Act, you know, responsibilities that they have.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I don't believe there's been anything specific about that, just, generally, banks have Bank Secrecy Act anti-money-laundering responsibilities, and this applies to bitcoin as it does in every other realm.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, look, I will just say that it is up to the Administration and Congress to decide on appropriate fiscal policy, and our job is to maintain our focus on employment and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We continue to think, as you can see from the projections, that a gradual path of rate increases remains appropriate even with almost all participants now factoring in their assessment of the impact of the tax-the tax policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, it is projected that the tax cut package will lead to additions to the national debt and boost, by the end of the horizon, the debt-to-GDP ratio.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I will say-and this is nothing new, this is something I've been saying for a long time-I am personally concerned about the U.S. debt situation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's not that the debt-to-GDP ratio at the moment is extraordinarily or worrisomely high, but it's also not very low.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And it's projected, as the population continues to age and the baby boomers retire, that that ratio will continue to rise in an unsustainable fashion.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So the addition to the debt, taking what is already a significant problem and making it worse, is-it is of concern to me, and I think it does suggest that in some future downturn, which, well, could occur just for whatever reason, the amount of fiscal space that would exist for fiscal policy to play an active role, it will be limited-may well be limited.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So right now the FOMC is not discussing or considering its inflation target.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We do see inflation as likely moving up to target over the next couple of years, and I would say-you said our stimulus tools are limited.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I would want to emphasize that if there were a negative shock to the economy, we do have some scope to cut the fed funds rate, and there are other tools available, ones that we have used previously: forward guidance and asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think we're not-I wouldn't say that we're out of ammunition, but certainly it's been recognized-and I've emphasized myself that, in the longer run, we may be-and we'll have to see how this works out, but we may be in low interest rate environments where it could prove useful to have additional scope to conduct monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, in that context, I think additional research-the academic economists and others are thinking hard about what more could be done, and I think these are matters that are certainly worthy of further study.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, I mean, on that I would say we have-that's not something that we have studied inside the Fed to any considerable extent and haven't seriously thought about using ourselves during this last downturn and recovery.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I would say it's an area that academics may have interest in in the future and is worthy of some study, but it hasn't been part of the Fed's agenda.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I mean, you know, I think I'm not familiar with every detail of the bill, but I think the bill does address a wide range of issues that, you know, we've highlighted in the past as being ones where perhaps additional flexibility to tailor our supervisory requirements would be worthwhile.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I don't have additional things on the congressional list.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, we continue to work seriously on resolution and the resolution plans, the living wills, and the structure of systemic firms to ensure that it would be possible to resolve a firm-under the bankruptcy code would be the top choice of methods, or, alternatively, under the Orderly Liquidation Authority.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I think it's fair to say that, over time, we have learned more ourselves and more clearly detailed our expectations for the firms that file living wills.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And the firms themselves have made considerable progress in, you know, changing what they do, whether it's adopting financial contracts that would facilitate a resolution rather than a disorderly unwinding of contracts, making sure that they're appropriately dealing with shared services so that key services would be able to continue, governance arrangements, legal entity structures-the firms have all made progress in adapting to our expectations of what would enable a successful resolution.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think it's an ongoing process, and I believe we have made substantial progress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, you know, the projections that we're showing you today, many factors went into that, fiscal policy being one of a number of different factors.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, you know, you're looking at 16 participants who have made adjustments to their economic outlook for a whole variety of reasons, including, in some cases, rethinking some of the fundamentals that went into their original forecast.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there have been modifications in different directions by different participants.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I would caution you about the dangers of looking at the median and acting like that is one individual who has made a change to their forecast.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, look, generally, you see modestly faster growth over the next couple of years, which is consistent and, I said, I think for most participants, reflects partly an impact from taxes stimulating consumer and investment spending.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it's not a gigantic increase in growth that since-relative to September.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You do see a lower path for unemployment, but remember that inflation has also been running low on a persistent basis, and the Committee does have a concern about inflation and wants to see it moving up.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, on balance, you see only modest changes, slight revisions to the path for the fed funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, okay, growth is a little stronger, the unemployment rate runs a little bit lower-that would perhaps push in the direction of slightly tighter monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, again, counterbalancing that is that inflation has run lower than we expect, and, you know, it could take a longer period of a very strong labor market in order to achieve the inflation objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I want to distinguish carefully between digital currency and cryptocurrency.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: This is-there is a discussion going on among central bankers about the potential merits of adopting-a central bank itself adopting a digital currency.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And there might even be a central banker or two around the globe that might go in that direction.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I really want to caution that this is not something the Federal Reserve is seriously considering at this stage while we're looking at research on this topic.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are, I think, to my mind, limited benefits from introducing it, a limited need for it, and some substantial concerns.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And so I would really doubt that the Federal Reserve would soon go in that direction.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it is something that central banks are looking at to see if there could be benefits from doing it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I would agree with you that these are important appointments.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Under the Federal Reserve Act, the nonbanking directors of the Reserve Banks have responsibility for conducting a search, and the Board of Governors has to sign off on the candidates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've made very clear and we monitor ongoing searches very carefully to make sure that absolutely every effort is made to create a pool that is diverse, and that there be a national search, and that every attempt should be made to create a diverse pool.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: At the end of the day, we cannot guarantee that the outcomes of these searches will result in an increase in diversity.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I mean, I've been very pleased to see that there's been some success in that regard, but we have signed off on the individuals who were appointed and have held the view that these are individuals who were qualified to serve in these positions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I would hope-I would hope to see greater diversity.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I think the process has become more open, and in a number of the recent searches there has been outreach-public outreach, information on websites, acceptance of potential names and nominees, and those have gotten careful consideration.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There has been-there have been meetings in some cases with community groups to try to enlarge the pool and get suggestions, and I think that's appropriate, and I think it has moved in the direction you're suggesting.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I'm wondering if you have any advice for incoming Chair Powell?

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, my colleague-I've had the pleasure of working with him now for many years, and he is somebody who understands the Federal Reserve very well and shares its values.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And as I mentioned in my opening statement, he is committed to the mission of the Fed; to its independence; and to its acting in a nonpartisan, nonpolitical way.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: He is somebody who has participated in the FOMC now for many years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: To the best of my knowledge, he has been part of the consensus.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think there is strong consensus in the Committee for the gradual approach that we have been pursuing, and Governor Powell has been part of that consensus, so I feel he's very well positioned and very knowledgeable of all the ins and outs of everything that the Fed does.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: In supervision, in the payment system-he's played an active role there-and in monetary policy, and I have confidence that he is very capable of steering the Federal Reserve in the years ahead.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I would say that all of my colleagues on the Board have expressed a strong commitment to keep in place the core reforms that have produced a stronger financial system.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I'm considering there stronger capital, particularly for the most systemic institutions-higher-quality capital, stronger liquidity requirements, a rigorous stress-testing program, and resolution planning that will make it more possible to resolve a firm that encounters significant distress.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I have heard broad-based commitment to those things, and I think they are the core of the reforms we have put in place.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think all of us agree that it is appropriate to tailor regulatory requirements in all of those areas and others to the systemic footprint of firms.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have done a lot to do that, and I think there is more that could be done, and in some areas it would require legislation in order to do that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I believe all of my colleagues and I are in agreement on that, and we're also focused on community banks and want to find ways to relieve burdens.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So in those important ways, I do think that all of my colleagues are in the same place with respect to their priorities.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I have not seen anything emerge at this point that I would describe as a significant difference.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We tend to focus in our own evaluation on economic risks, and we've characterized them as "balanced."

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: You know, I can always give you a list of, you know, potential troubles, international developments that could result in downside economic risk.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, look, at the moment the U.S. economy is performing well.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The growth that we're seeing, it's not based on, for example, an unsustainable buildup of debt as we had in the run-up to the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: This is the first time in many years that we've seen this.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the risks are balanced, and there's less to lose sleep about now than has been true for quite some time, so I feel good about the economic out-the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I feel, you know, good that the labor market is in a very much stronger place than it was eight years ago.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We've got a good, strong labor market and a very low unemployment rate, and I think that's been tremendously important to the well-being of American households and workers.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I feel very pleased when I hear anecdotes from firms that tell me they're having a hard time finding workers, and they talk about, given that they're taking on people with skills that don't quite match what they want, but they're training them, and, you know, giving them the training that they need in order to be able to fill jobs.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think that's a development that is a natural one that occurs in a strong labor market that tends to build human capital and worker skills, and that that's a strong positive.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: As I mentioned, I think the financial system is on much sounder footing, and that we have done a great deal to put in place greater capital, liquidity, and so forth that make it less crisis prone, and that has been an important objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We have a 2 percent symmetric inflation objective, and, for a number of years now, inflation has been running under 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And I consider it an important priority to make sure that inflation doesn't chronically undershoot our 2 percent objective, and I want to see it move up to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So most of my colleagues and I do believe that it's being held down by transitory factors, but there's work undone there, in the sense-we need to see it move up in line with our objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, I think for a number of years-so we've had an undershoot of inflation for a number of years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: First we had a good deal of slack in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, beginning in mid-2014, there was a marked depreciation in the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And those three factors held down inflation for a number of years.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, in 2016, core inflation came very close to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: We seemed to be on a path of inflation moving up, and this year, beginning in March, there seemed to be a sequence of negative surprises.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Some reflect one-time factors that were easily identifiable, like a marked decline in quality-adjusted cell phone plans.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There may be other factors that are not so easy to name, but we would judge-you know, inflation doesn't always follow exactly.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: There are errors and many factors that affect it beyond the key influences of labor market slack: exchange rates and import prices and oil prices.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But there are other factors that affect inflation too, and our judgment at this point is that transitory factors that are unrelated to the broader macroeconomic outlook are holding inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I have tried to be straightforward in saying that this could end up being something that is more ingrained and turns out to be permanent.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's very important to watch it and, if necessary, rethink what's determining inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: A possibility is that the longer-run sustainable 2 Chair Yellen intended to say that, beginning in mid-2014, there was a marked appreciation of the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's conceivable that they need to come down even more.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It's not my judgment that inflation expectations have slipped, but that also remains a possibility that needs to be monitored.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So there are-you know, there could be a rethink of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I think it's important to watch inflation outcomes carefully and, if we don't see inflation moving in the manner that the Committee anticipates, to alter policy so that we do achieve our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But, at the moment, most of my colleagues and I believe we are on track to achieve it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, on my plans, I don't have anything definite for you, I guess.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I have a home in Berkeley and expect to maintain it.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But I would say, my spouse is on the faculty-he's a professor at Georgetown and would like to stay in his job, and we expect to maintain Washington as our base.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So let me just say that I have served in senior positions in the Federal Reserve now for quite a long time.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I became president in San Francisco in 2004, and I've participated in the FOMC since that time as president, as Vice Chair, and as Chair, and it's been an immensely rewarding experience for me.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I feel very positive about what we've been able to accomplish and feel tremendous, you know, loyalty to the institution.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I did make the judgment that this is the right time for me to leave, but I feel I have served in senior positions at the Fed for a long time, and it's really been an honor and a privilege for me to have had a chance to do so.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, I certainly agree that it's important for the Fed to attempt to understand emerging risks to financial stability and to be looking not just in the banking system but outside it for developments that could pose financial risks, and we are doing that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And, I would say, one of the changes during my tenure is, we devoted-decided in the aftermath of the crisis that we needed to devote considerable resources to financial stability to monitor for emerging threats, and now we have at the Board a full-blown division of financial stability that's involved in doing that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, when you ask about bitcoin, I still see the financial stability risks from it as limited.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Often, risks threatening financial stability arise when there's exposure of the banking system to fluctuating asset valuations, and I really don't see any significant exposure of our core financial institutions to threats from bitcoin if its value were to fluctuate.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I don't see a threat to our core financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, undoubtedly, there are individuals who could lose a lot of money if bitcoin were to fall in price, but I really don't see that as creating a full-blown financial stability risk.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: I've never been willing to reveal which dot is mine, and I'm not going to change that now.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So, you know, my assessment, and I think most participants' assessments, as I said, of the impact of the tax policy on growth has been informed by work by the Joint Committee on Taxation and other analysts.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And everyone recognizes that there's uncertainty about what the economic effects would be, and I wouldn't want to rule anything out.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It is challenging, however, to achieve growth of the levels that you mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Look, if the package were to stimulate growth of that magnitude, let me just say again, the Federal Reserve would welcome that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If it's a supply-side-favorable supply-side developments that would be compatible with the attainment of our employment and inflation objectives, that's something that would be very, very welcome.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: But it would be challenging to achieve numbers like that.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Let's see, I think you also then asked me about the yield curve, and-I mean, there is much discussion about yield curve inversions and whether or not a flattening yield curve could signal a recession.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So this is something that we discussed and have looked at.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The yield curve has flattened some as we have raised short rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: It mainly-the flattening yield curve mainly reflects higher short-term rates.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: The yield curve is not currently inverted, and I would say that the current slope is well within its historical range.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, there is a strong correlation historically between yield curve inversions and recessions, but let me emphasize that correlation is not causation, and I think that there are good reasons to think that the relationship between the slope of the yield curve and the business cycle may have changed.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And one reason for that is that long-term interest rates generally embody two factors.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: One is the expected average value of short rates over, say, 10 years, and the second piece of it is a so-called term premium that often reflects things like inflation-inflation risk.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So when the yield curve has inverted historically, it meant that short-term rates were well above average expected short rates over the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So with the positive term premium, that's what it means.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: And typically that means that monetary policy is restrictive, sometimes quite restrictive, and some of those recessions were situations in which the Fed was consciously tightening monetary policy because inflation was high and trying to slow the economy.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Well, right now the term premium is estimated to be quite low, close to zero, and that means that, structurally-and this can be true going forward-that the yield curve is likely to be flatter than it's been in the past.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: If the Fed were to even move to a slightly restrictive policy stance, you could see an inversion with a zero term premium.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: So I think the fact the term premium is so low and the yield curve is generally flatter is an important factor to consider.

speaker: CHAIR YELLEN
text: Now, I think it's also important to realize that market participants are not expressing heightened concern about the decline of the term premium, and, when asked directly about the odds of recession, they see it as low, and I would concur with that judgment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you're right that the outlook did improve, as I mentioned and as you-as was in your question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The Committee's estimates of growth went up, the Committee's estimates of unemployment went down, and there was a very slight increase in inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I think that reflects, essentially-if you think back to the era after the crisis, unemployment was 10 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You've only seen very gradual upward pressures on inflation and wages despite that very large increase.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And that suggests that the relationship between changes in slack and inflation is not so tight.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I think when you see those small changes in unemployment, that simply reflects the, you know, the flatness of the Phillips curve, if you will.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, I think we're trying to, we're trying to be, to take the middle ground there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you know, on the one hand, the risk would be that we wait too long, and then we have to raise rates quickly, and that foreshortens the expansion.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The-on the other side, if we-if we raise rates too quickly, inflation, then, really doesn't get sustainably up to 2 percent, and, that will hurt us going forward.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We need that, and it's, you know, we need to make sure that inflation expectations are anchored at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we're trying to take that middle ground, and the Committee continues to believe that the middle ground consists of further gradual increases in the federal funds rate as long as the economy is broadly on this path.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, so as you noted, the-what we've said in the longer-run statement of goals and monetary policy strategy is that we would be concerned with sustained or persistent deviations of inflation either above or below.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've also said-in minutes and in speeches and things like that-that that is a symmetric objective.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, I think it's-I wouldn't characterize what we've done over the last five years as tolerating, you know, an undershoot of inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We were always pushing toward 2 percent, and I think that is how we look at it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It just, you know, it, we haven't agreed on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It just is that we're always going to be seeking 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And in doing that, we're going to be considering, by the way, the other side of the mandate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we have to balance that against the deviation of employment from- unemployment from its goal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the Summary of Economic Projections is really a compilation of the individual rate forecasts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The Committee made really one decision at this meeting, and that was to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The Summary of Economic Projections is individual forecasts compiled and written down.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would also say that the central tendency is interesting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So you have a range of views around the table.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: One of the great benefits of our system is that we do have Reserve Banks with their own staffs and Governors with different views, and so we discuss these things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the Committee doesn't vote or agree upon the medians, so you're going to have a range of views.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: just happens to be the median for '18, but it doesn't really say, you know, what we think is possible.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, I would say it's hard to say, but it would take-you know, that is well above almost all estimates, current estimates of potential long-run growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It would take, you know, significant increases in productivity and labor force participation to get there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I guess I'd start by saying that the natural rate of unemployment is not something that we can observe directly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We look at a wide range of indicators on that-you know, 15 or 20 of them at least.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And also, I think we all understand that any point estimate is surrounded by very wide uncertainty bands.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So as the-as the actual unemployment rate has declined from 10 percent to 4. percent, the Committee's median estimate of the natural rate of unemployment has also declined by a full percentage point.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the Committee-and, I think, people-are generally influenced by data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As they see unemployment going lower, they're looking at a variety of aspects of the labor market, including wage inflation and price inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I don't think we, we-we're mindful of the uncertainty of that, and we'll be looking at that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, as-if inflation-if unemployment does continue to go down, we'll continue to do that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As I mentioned earlier, there is no-there's no sense in the data that we're on the cusp of an acceleration of inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We have seen moderate increases in wages and price inflation, and we seem to be seeing more of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I guess the idea-the theory would be that if you get below the sustainable rate of unemployment for a sustained period, you would see an acceleration of inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we would know that then, and we're very alert to it, but it's not something we observe at the present.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Longer-run values like the neutral rate of interest, the natural rate of unemployment, the potential growth rate of the economy are pinned down by slow- moving forces over time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I wouldn't expect the Committee's, you know, predictions or projections or estimates of those values to move quickly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So is it possible that the neutral rate of interest would move up because of, for example, greater fiscal expansion?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In fact, it did tick up one-tenth, as you all know, in the-in the median at this time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But it's-I think, generally speaking, the Committee sees the neutral rate of interest as still quite low and is not-is not seeing it as having moved up and is open to the possibility that it will.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's something that I'm going to be carefully considering.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: My colleagues and I are committed to communicating as clearly as possible about what we're doing and why we're doing it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would want to think very carefully about it and make sure that no one would take more frequent press conferences as a signal of the path of policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so, it is something that I'll be thinking about.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, in terms of the balance sheet, we've said that, you know, we carefully developed this plan.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We carefully socialized it in a series of meetings last year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We announced it, and we said we wouldn't change it, really, unless there were a significant downturn that required, you know, meaningful reductions in interest rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're going to use monetary policy as the principle tool of adjusting, you know, our policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, on the second question, on tariffs, a number of participants in this FOMC did bring up the issue of tariffs, and if I could summarize what came out of that, it was, first, that there's no thought, I think, that changes in trade policy should have any effect on the current outlook.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Second thing is, I would say, is that a number of participants reported in-about their conversations with business leaders around the country and reported that trade policy has become a concern going forward for that group.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So fiscal stimulus is a, you know, a meaningful input into, you know, into the SEP and particularly in the changes over the course of last year and this year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And individual policymakers went through, with their staffs, a range of estimates, a range of literature, and did their own thinking and came up with their own estimates and submitted those as their Summary of Economic Projections-as their projections.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would go back to the thought that, you know, we made one decision at this meeting, and that decision was to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The projections are really just individual projections that are submitted and then compiled.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, you're mentioning the median as being, you know, three and four being close, but, you know, I think, like any set of forecasts, those forecasts will change over time, and they'll change depending on the way the outlook for the economy changes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I wouldn't want to-for now, these are the best forecasts that people could make, and, you know, it could be that if the economy's a little bit stronger or a little bit weaker, then the path could be a little less gradual or a little more gradual.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, for trade, what I mentioned is that our FOMC participants reported in that they had heard, you know, concerns, which were relatively new, about-about future trade actions, really.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And they're seeing it as a risk-to-the-outlook kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So-and the kind of things people are talking about would be, you know, more widespread retaliation and more widespread actions back-and-forth kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In terms of productivity-productivity, as I'm sure you know, has been very weak since the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's averaged only about 0. percent a year for the last six years, I guess.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's well below, you know, longer-run averages, and it would certainly be a good thing to see it move up.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It has moved up just a little bit but not, kind of, decisively.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, you asked me about fiscal policy and the connection to productivity.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think in the tax bill there's-there are incentives for-there-a tax cut bill that allows expensing of investments should encourage additional investment that should encourage productivity.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In theory, an individual tax bill that lowers tax rates should encourage more labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I do think it's very important that we have a focus on productivity in the country.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's not something that we can really do at the Fed, but, you know, we're certainly hopeful that there will be supply-side effects like that from the tax bill.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think estimates are really all over the place in terms of the amount and the timing of those.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, I would say that-remember that forecasts three years out-so, you're right, in 2020 there's a-I think it's 3. percent is the median of the SEP dots for 2020, which is 40 basis points above the estimates of the neutral rate, which I would characterize as, you know, modestly restrictive, modestly tightening policy, but that's three years in the future.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we don't have the ability to see that far into the future, so I really wouldn't put a lot in that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You could imagine narratives in which that would make sense, but I honestly I wouldn't put too much on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we've been through many years of growth around 2 percent, and I've given a number of public remarks where I've called on, you know, the country to focus more on potential growth and productivity and labor force participation, which drive potential growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you know, I think it's really important that we do something-do what we can as a country to increase our potential growth rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would say in the bill that passed Congress, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, there were elements that should encourage productivity, as I mentioned-sorry, encourage investment, which should help productivity, encourage labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't know how big those effects are going to be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think, as you look around the table at the FOMC, there's a wide range of views on the amount and the timing of those.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think all of us would agree that we hope that they will be large.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Our current framework for implementing monetary policy is working very well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We haven't made a decision to keep that as our longer-run framework.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've had meetings where we've talked about it, and we've agreed that it's working well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But it's-and it's not something I see us as needing to urgently address.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: For example, one-in the long-run, the size of the balance sheet is going to depend on the public's demand for our liabilities, including currency and reserves.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we don't know what the demand is for reserves in a world where you have-you know, you have regulations that require banks to hold lots of high-quality liquid assets, and reserves are one of those.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it's not something we're looking at resolving in the near term.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You mentioned the question of interest on excess reserves, and I think it's a little bit of a misnomer to think that there's a subsidy there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We can't pay interest on excess reserves that are-is above the general level of short-term interest rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we're paying rates that banks can get from other interest rates from other-any other investment in the short-term money markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The assets that we have on the other side are Treasury securities and mortgage-backed securities, which yield much higher than interest on reserves.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, in fact, it's not a subsidy, and it's not a cost to the taxpayer.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Since the financial crisis, we've been monitoring financial conditions and financial stability issues very carefully, and the FOMC receives regular briefings about the staff framework and, sort of, measures of various aspects of financial-financial stability risks, and the current view of the Committee is that financial stability vulnerabilities are moderate, let's say.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I'll go through a couple of pieces of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, if you look at the banking system, particularly the large financial institutions, you see higher capital.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You see them more aware of their risks and better able to manage them with stress testing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And if one-if something does go wrong, you've got-you've got better ability to deal with the failure of those institutions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You don't see excess risk-taking in great quantity the way you did see before the crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you look at households, household balance sheets are in much better condition.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you look at nonfinancial corporations, you see-you do see relatively elevated levels of borrowing, but nothing that suggests, you know, serious risks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I should mention also that for large financial institutions, they're no longer funded by a lot of short-term wholesale funding, which can disappear very quickly, so they're far less vulnerable to liquidity issues.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Overall, those aspects, I think, suggest low levels of vulnerability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You identified the-really, one area where-which is an area of focus, which is asset prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, in some areas, asset prices are elevated relative to their longer-run historical norms.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You can think of commercial real estate prices in certain markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But we don't see it in housing, which is key.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so, overall, if you put all of that into a pie, what you have is moderate vulnerabilities, in our view.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In terms of whether we have the tools, you know, we have some tools, and I think we certainly-we use them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We have-I think the stress test is a really important tool that we have for the largest financial institutions and for the smaller financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We regularly use that to-as a way to test against various, you know, market shocks, certainly for the larger institutions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, this is a matter that Congress has under consideration.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's not something-so Congress is looking at raising the threshold for applying enhanced financial standards to-from $50 billion to $250 billion, while leaving us with the ability to reach below $250 billion and apply those standards where we think it's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, we haven't been shy about doing that, because, of course, one of the eight SIFIs is below 250 already.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But this is a decision that's in the hands of Congress.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The version of the bill, I think, that passed the Senate did have-did give us the ability to do supervisory stress tests periodically, as opposed to annually, is the language.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We would want to think very carefully about that, and, you know, we would-whatever we do decide to do, we'd put that out for comment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would think it would be, but it's certainly not something that we've decided to do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Well, it's-I guess the next thing on the list would be activities.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you know, we-regular way commercial banks that do deposit taking and lending and don't speculate in markets, you know, that's one business model.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Another business model might be, you know, if you think of a hedge fund, right?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: They're speculating on markets, and-you know, so very different business models and different levels of risk and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, that's-that would be the next thing on the list.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I mean, there would be a range of things, you know-how well capitalized is the institution, but mainly those things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Remember that there are 15 FOMC participants, and we-each of us has his or her own forecast.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So there's a real diversity of views on this, particularly on these fiscal issues.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If I could try to summarize, it would be that, I think, broadly speaking, participants believe there will be meaningful increases in demand from the new fiscal policies for at least the next, let's say, three years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think there's a general view as well that supply-side issues-that there could be supply-side effects as well, and you would see that again through higher investment, driven by lower corporate tax rates and the expensing of some investment, which would drive-tend to drive productivity over time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you make investment more attractive, companies should do more of it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I mean, I spent many years of my life working with companies and discussing-and, you know, the cost of capital is one of many factors that they'll consider.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It isn't the only factor or the principle factor, but it should result in more investment, and investment should drive productivity.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: At the same time, the-you know, I mentioned labor supply.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You should see some labor supply effects over time from lower individual effective tax rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The whole thing is very uncertain, and particularly the supply-side effects should and would be expected to take longer to appear and would be less certain in amount.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, we've all looked at the literature carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've discussed it with our in-house experts and come up with our own views, and they're disparate, but that's- I'd say that's about where the-where the views are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, at this stage, what our FOMC participants discussed-it wasn't-it was-it was just that this is a new risk that had been probably a low- profile risk, which has become, you know, a more prominent risk to the outlook.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: They didn't get into talking about particular-you know, whether it's inflation or growth or whatever it would be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As I mentioned, you know, we've had unemployment decline sharply since, I guess, 2010, when it peaked at 10 percent and down to 4. percent now, and we've seen only modest increases in wages.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, on the one hand, what wages should in theory represent is inflation plus productivity increases.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So these low wage increases-in a sense, they do make sense in that-from that perspective.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: On the other hand, as the market has tightened, as labor markets have tightened, and we hear reports of labor shortages and we see that, you know, groups of unemployed are diminishing, and the unemployment rate is going down, we haven't seen, you know, higher wages-wages going up more.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I would-I think I've been surprised by that, and I think others have as well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In terms of what's the right level, I don't think I have a view on what the right level of wages is, but I think we will-we will know that the labor market is getting tight when we do see a more meaningful upward move in wages.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we-we're looking very carefully at our assigned responsibilities of maximum employment, stable prices, and that's really our focus.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You can count on us to stay focused on the jobs that Congress has assigned us and count on us to use the tools we have to achieve them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: By the way, I'm hearing this, the 10-year thing a few times these days, and it's true that rates are higher than they've been in 10 years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: On the other hand, the economy's healthier than it's been since-since before the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, it's a healthier economy than it's been in 10 years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The financial crisis, of course, was just really getting going 10 years ago.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, it's an interesting question, and there are a range of views there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think it's true that yield curves have tended to predict recessions if you look back over many cycles, but a lot of that was just situations in which inflation was allowed to get out of control, and the Fed had to tighten, and that put the economy into a recession.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That's really not the situation we're in now, so I don't know that that's-I don't know that-I don't think that recession probabilities are particularly high at the moment, any higher than they normally are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, having said that, I think it's-there are good questions about what a flat yield curve or inverted yield curve does to intermediation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's hard to find in the research data, but nonetheless, I think those are issues that we'll be watching carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So since-I wouldn't say anything has happened since March to really change the way I'm thinking about inflation or the way the Committee's thinking about inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've seen inflation move very gradually up toward our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And part of that has been just idiosyncratic things dropping out from last March, which were holding inflation-measured inflation-down.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Part of it is just that continued tightening in the labor market and the economy more broadly is pushing inflation up.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we continue to think, and the Committee continues to think, that we are just about at our 2 percent goal but, as I mentioned, not ready to declare victory until we sustain that over time, which we haven't done yet.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You also asked about fiscal policy, and there's a range of views on the Committee and, I think more broadly, a range of views among economists generally.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But I can say that the Committee members-Committee participants-generally believe that the fiscal changes-and that includes both the tax cuts, individual and corporate, and the spending changes-will provide meaningful support to demand, significant support to demand over the course of the next three years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And the question-the other question is, what about the supply side?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it is-it makes sense that if you lower corporate tax rates and allow faster expensing of investment, you will encourage greater investment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think the amounts and the timing of that coming in are also quite uncertain.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There's also the possibility that there would be more labor supply from lower individual tax rates, again, in amounts and in timing that might be more uncertain.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's how the Committee generally is thinking about-about fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So for many, many years, we've been far from maximum employment and stable prices, and so the need for accommodative policy has been-has been clear.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As the economy has strengthened and as we've gradually raised interest rates, the question comes into view of, how much longer will you need to be accommodative?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: How will you know where-at what point policy will be neutral?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Neutral meaning that interest rates are neither pushing the economy up nor trying to restrain it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we know that we're getting closer to that neutral level.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't have an exact sense of how that will be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the Committee is discussing, very actively, the questions that you raise.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, really, it boils down to a question of, what is appropriate policy?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I think we'll be very carefully looking at incoming data on inflation, on financial readings, and on the labor market.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We have to acknowledge that there are always wide uncertainty bands around the level of, for example, the natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: What is that rate of interest that pushes neither up nor down?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I think we- we'll be guided by incoming data on the economy and try to keep our minds open as we move forward.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, the-our target for-our medium-term objective for inflation is 2 percent PCE inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We feel that that target has served the economy well, and I'm strongly committed to it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The sort of barriers to making a material change to that would be-would be very high because, again, we think it's fundamental, and we think it's worked.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You asked about price-level targeting and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, there are some ideas that sort of take cognizance of the fact that rates are lower, we're near the zero lower bound, and that could put downward pressure on inflation expectations if we're going to be down at the zero lower bound and, therefore, sort of undermine the credibility of the 2 percent inflation objective.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the idea is to have kind of a makeup.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you-if you're below target for a while, you have a-you have a time of being above target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And the idea is to enhance the credibility of that 2 percent-that 2 percent target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: This is an idea that's been written about for many years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's not something that the Committee has looked at seriously.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I imagine we will be having discussions about it, but-not something that we have on the calendar right now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I ought to start by saying that, you know, Congress has assigned us very important jobs and-you know, maximum employment, stable prices, we have a role in financial stability that we share with other agencies.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Congress has very specifically given authority over trade to the executive branch, so I wouldn't comment on any particular specific trade actions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I will say that we, of course, have-we have broad contacts in-among business leaders around the country.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so they report in the Beige Book and then in person at the FOMC meeting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And they do come back and they say that concerns about changes in trade policy are arising, I think it's fair to say, and also that you're beginning to hear reports of companies holding off on making investments and hiring people.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So right now we don't see that in the numbers at all.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But-so I would put it down as more of a risk.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, first of all, that's a-that's a reasonable range, I think, of-it's not that we're all on the same number, but there are a range of views about potential growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we don't-the thing about fiscal policy is, you don't have thousands of incidents to, you know, to-you don't have big data, in a way.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You've got only a few instances here, so you have a lot of uncertainty around what the effects will be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But I think our approach is going to be to watch and see and hope that, in fact, we do get significant effects to, you know, to potential growth out of the tax bill, and we're just going to have to see.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think we're looking at a reasonable range of estimates and we're putting every-different participants are putting different estimates in and we're going to be waiting and seeing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, what we've said in our Statement of Longer-Run Principles and Monetary Policy Strategy is that the Committee would be concerned if inflation were to run persistently above or below 2 percent, persistently above or below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're looking at it equally on either side and it's a matter of persistent overruns.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: For example, as I mentioned, later this summer there's a good chance that headline inflation will move up above 2 percent because of oil prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Things buffet inflation back and forth, but-so we acknowledge that, we understand that-and if inflation were to persistently run above or below 2 percent, then we would be using our tools to try to move inflation back in the direction of the target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We do understand, though, that we don't have the ability to precisely hit that target, so we expect that inflation will be above or below.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we just hope that that is-happens on a symmetric basis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think what you should see is that the economy is continuing to make progress.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The economy has strengthened so much since I joined the Fed, you know, in 2012 and even over the last couple of years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We- unemployment was 10 percent at the height of the crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So really what you-the decision you see today is another sign that the U.S. economy is in great shape.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Growth is strong, labor markets are strong, inflation is close to target, and that's what you're seeing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: For many years, as I mentioned-many years-we had interest rates held low to support economic activity.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And it's been clear that as we've gotten closer to our statutory goals, we should normalize policy, and that's really what we've been consistently doing for some years now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Earlier in the recovery, they were-there are many different wage measures, of course, but-so just-but just to generalize, wages were running roughly around 2 percent and they've moved gradually up into between 2 to 3 percent as the labor market has become stronger and stronger.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think it's fair to say that some of us-and I certainly would have expected wages to react more to the very significant reduction in unemployment that we've had, as I mentioned, from 10 percent to 3. percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Part of that can be explained by low productivity, which is something we've talked about at the Committee and elsewhere.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, I think we had anticipated, and many people have anticipated, that wages-that in a world where we're hearing lots and lots about labor shortages-everywhere we go now, we hear about labor shortages-but where is the wage reaction?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I wouldn't say it's a mystery, but it's a bit of a puzzle.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, frankly, I do think there's a lot to like about low unemployment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And one of the things is-you will see-pretty much people who want to get jobs-not everybody-but people who want to get jobs, many of them will be able to get jobs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You'll see people at the, sort of, the margins of the labor force having an opportunity to get back in work.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So there are a lot of things to really like, including higher wages, as you asked.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Our role, though, is also to, you know, to make sure that-that maximum employment happens in a context of price stability and financial stability, which is why we're gradually raising rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You mentioned that unemployment moved down and inflation moved up by truly small amounts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you look at the Summary of Economic Projections, things are moving by just a tick or even a semitick between now and March.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And you asked, you know-I mean, I think we take a longer-run view that we're shooting for-we're aiming for- 2 percent inflation-inflation around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're not going to-we didn't overreact, I think, to inflation being under 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I think we'll always be using our tools to move inflation in the direction of the target, if it-if it leaves-if it moves away from the target persistently, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In terms of unemployment, you know, you have to acknowledge that we are-no one really knows with certainty what the level of the natural rate of unemployment is, the rate that is sustainable over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we know that probably that rate has declined as the U.S. population has become more educated, as it has become older.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've got to be looking at data and informed by what's coming in.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And as I mentioned, I think at the last press conference, estimates by the-by members of the Committee have moved down by a full percentage point since maybe 2012 as we've learned-as unemployment has dropped and inflation hasn't really reacted.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I can't give you a precise number, but I just-you know, we will be very much informed by incoming data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And this uncertainty is why-the fact that we live in that uncertainty is why we've been gradually raising rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're going ahead and moving gradually and trying to navigate between two risks, really.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: One would be moving too quickly-inflation never gets back to target if we do that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And the other is moving too slowly, and then we have-we have too much inflation or financial instability, and we have to raise quickly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I would say that-remember the important thing is that we want the federal funds rate to trade in the target range.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: IOER is the principal tool by which we assure that that will happen.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we've said in our, you know, basic documents that we will adjust the use of our tools, as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't expect to have to do this often or again, but we're not sure about that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If we have to do it again, we'll do it again.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And yes, you know, we-of course, we're looking carefully at that and, you know, the truth is we don't-we don't know with any precision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's-you can't run experiments, you know, with one effect and not the other.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, I think there's a lot of probability on the idea of just high bill supply leads to higher repo costs, higher money market rates generally, and the arbitrage pulls up federal funds rate towards IOER.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't know that that's the only effect and, you know, we're just going to have to be watching and learning.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: What we really need is to have the federal funds rate trade in the range, and that's what this minor technical adjustment accomplishes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Your question-your first question, really, is, do we think the natural rate of unemployment is lower?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I think we do believe it has moved down significantly over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't think that the natural rate of unemployment- you know, it's not one of those variables that moves around a lot.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It tends to be driven by slow- moving variables, like the education level, the population, like the functioning of the labor market, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you know, it may-it may have moved down too, on a cyclical basis, lower.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As the economy gets hotter and hotter, there's some possibility of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, you know, the thing is, if you look back, there have been a lot of studies done and, you know, real- time estimates of the natural rate of unemployment have uncertainty bands, which are-which are quite wide, so we have to remember that and very much be guided by the-by the incoming data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, inflation we look about-we look at the 2 percent inflation objective as something that central banks, the Fed, really control.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we have to be strongly committed to achieving that using our tools to do that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think in-in recent years the dominant force has been, you know, disinflationary-have been pushing down on inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Of course, all those years when we were growing up, it was the opposite.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Inflation was too high and central banks were constantly pushing down.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's really important that inflation not fall below 2 percent, that inflation expectations remain well anchored at 2 percent-very important-because the implications of inflation below 2 percent are that you're closer to the zero lower bound, meaning the Fed has less room to cut, meaning that we'll spend more time there and we won't be able to do the job that we're assigned to do for our citizens.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would just-would-I would just emphasize, emphasize that-a couple things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: First, we're learning about the real location of the natural rate of unemployment as we go.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it's moved down by more than a full percentage point since 2012.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it's not so simple as thinking, oh boy, we've just got to go ahead and get that rate up.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you-if you look at the forecast, two years from now, end of 2020, you're still seeing inflation very close to target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So there's no sense that inflation will-no sense in our models, or in our projections, or forecasts-that inflation will take off or move unexpectedly quickly from these levels, even if unemployment does remain low.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's-that's what-so it's important to know that the-the unemployment rate forecasts go with the inflation forecasts and go with the rate forecasts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so each person who's submitting them is submitting accommodate-you know, appropriate monetary policy that fits with that person's assessment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And their assessments generally are to support maximum employment and stable prices around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So if we thought that inflation were going to take off, obviously, we'd be showing higher rates, but that's not what we think will happen.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, the best estimate that we have, over the longer run, is that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Although, you know, there's a range of views, you know.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Some people are in the low 4s, and, again, I said the uncertainty bands are, you know, not quite a full percentage point on either side, but ¾ of a percent, that kind of thing, so it's very possible.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We have to be, you know-we can't do-we can't be too attached to these unobservable variables.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we-I think we have to be practical about the way we think about these things and we do that by being grounded in the data and what we see happening in the real economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the countercyclical capital buffer gives us the ability to raise capital requirements on the largest institutions when financial stability vulnerabilities are meaningfully above normal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I wouldn't say that-I wouldn't look at today's financial stability landscape and say that risks are meaningfully above normal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You have-you know, households are well-you know, are in good shape.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: They're-they've paid down their debt, incomes are rising, people have jobs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And banks are highly capitalized, so that's not really a concern.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We see-there's some concern with asset prices in a couple of pockets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But overall, if you-if you bake it all in, I think we see, generally, financial vulnerabilities as moderate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Could that change, you asked, over a couple of years?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So this is a very difficult area because we have state law-many state laws permit the use of marijuana and federal law still doesn't.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it puts, you know, federally chartered banks in a very difficult situation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think it would be great if that could be clarified.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't have-you know, it puts the supervisor in a very, very difficult position.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, of course, this isn't our-our mandate has nothing to do with marijuana, so we don't really-we just would love to see it clarified, I think.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You mentioned a number of the things, but I would-I would point out-we're having, I guess, a public Board meeting tomorrow on the single counterparty credit limit provision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've also got quite a lot of work to promulgate rules to-after S. 2155 that Senator Crapo's bill passed-we've got a lot of work to do under that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've got to think about how we would reach below that $250 billion threshold to assess and supervise, regulate, you know, financial stability risks below that level.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There's-there-oh, oh, net stable funding ratio is out there to be done.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So there's a lot of work to do, I think.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, and if I can just take this opportunity to say, you know, the financial system all but failed 10 years ago.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We went to work for 10 years to strengthen it-stronger capital, stronger liquidity, stress testing, resolution planning.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We want to make it, you know, even more effective and certainly more efficient.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We want the strongest provisions to apply to the most systemically important institutions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so we're committed to preserving and enhancing that structure.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But we-we're finding a lot that we can do in the way of tailoring regulations for the smaller, less systemically important institutions, and that's a lot of what we're working on right now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, I would say that the economy is in great shape.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you ask-if you survey workers about the job market, they'll say that it's a really good environment to find jobs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you survey businesses, they'll say that workers are scarce.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I think overall, we have-we have a really solid economy on our hands here.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so what we're doing is, we are trying to conduct monetary policy in a way that will sustain that expansion, keep the labor markets strong, and keep inflation above-right at-sorry, not above, but right at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That's really what we're trying to do and, you know, I would say I like the results so far.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're-we've been very, very careful not to tighten too quickly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think that patience has borne fruit and I think it continues to.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We had a lot of encouragement to go much faster and I'm really glad we didn't.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, at this time, the- continuing on that gradual pace seems-continues to seem like the right thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If we get a sense that the economy is reacting badly, then we'll certainly react to that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I would just point you to the range of estimates at the Committee, which I think is 2¼ to 3½, and the median is 2.9, right in there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's the range of estimates of the nominal neutral rate of interest.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we do understand that there's high uncertainty around the level, but that's kind of-so you can think of 2. as being-which is sort of a full percentage point away from where fed funds is going to trade after today's decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You asked, is the-is the neutral rate moving up because of fiscal policy?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I mean, there's-there should be an effect if you have increased deficits that should put upward pressure on, you know, a few tenths, let's say.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's one of these unobserved variables so it's very hard to-we shouldn't try to speak about it with a- with a lot of precision or confidence.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You've got to look at-you've got to look at all of the indicators in the economy and look at inflation, look at unemployment, look at what's happening in the job market.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's worth noting that the last two business cycles didn't end with high inflation-they ended with financial instability-so that's something we need to also keep our eye on.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As you know, we made a-we made a significant number of changes at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So language gets in the statement and then, you know, the economy changes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, as I mentioned earlier, for a long time, the economy has needed accommodative monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As the economy has recovered, we've been gradually raising rates and we will-we will be at a place relatively soon when, again, assuming we stay on this path, when interest rates will be in the zone of what FOMC participants think is roughly neutral.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, at that point, it would no longer be accurate for us to say that the Committee thinks that policy is accommodative.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We kind of don't think it's here yet, but it's certainly coming.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I mean, the real message is that you're getting close to the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's not a statement, really, that should upset the markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, you know, we'll obviously discuss it carefully in meetings and communicate about it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you know, as I mentioned earlier, I'm really committed to staying in our lane on things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We have very important jobs assigned to us by Congress and that's maximum employment, stable prices, financial stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Trade is explicitly assigned to the executive branch by Congress and not to us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we don't really-we don't really seek to play a role in trade policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Those are-those powers and decisions are given to others and so we want to stick to what we do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, I-as I mentioned earlier, we do hear from our business contacts, which are extensive in the United States, and we do report on that in the minutes, and I've just mentioned what those are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There is -there is concern that trade changes could be disruptive.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I also-as I also mentioned, we don't see it in the numbers yet.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We see a very strong economy across a bunch of fronts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But most people who want a job can find one.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're well aware that there are pockets out there of people who have not felt the recession yet, but, broadly speaking, it's a good economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I mean, I- the yield curve is something that people are talking about a lot, including FOMC participants.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's something we're going to continue to be talking about.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's-but it's only one of many things, of course, that we talk about.
