speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think that that discussion is really about what is appropriate policy, and how do we think about policy as we approach the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And what are the consequences of being above or below it?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That's really what-when people are talking about the slope of the yield curve, that's really what they're talking about.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We know why-we know why the yield curve is flattening.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It makes all the sense in the world that the short end would come up.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think you asked-the harder question is, what's happening with long rates?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And there are many things that move long rates around.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Of course, there's an embedded expectation of the path of short rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There's the term premium, which has been very low by historical standards.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so arguments are made that a flatter yield curve has less of a signal embedded in it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In 1 Chairman Powell intended to say that there are pockets of people in the United States who have not yet experienced the economic recovery.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: addition, I think what you saw most recently that you referred to, Steve, was just risk-on, risk- off.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In a risk-off environment, people want to own U.S. Treasuries, and you see-you know, Treasury prices go up, rates go down quite a lot.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So-but I think ultimately, you know, what we're-what we really care about is what's the appropriate stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And there's a- there may be a signal in that long-term rate about what is the neutral rate, and I think that's why people are paying attention to the yield curve.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Companies are buying back their shares at a record rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So if you look at households, you do not see excess credit growth, you don't see high levels of credit going out.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And that really was where the problems were before the financial crisis, was particularly in-among household borrowing, particularly around mortgages.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: With-if you take banks, then, of course, their leverage is significantly lower.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Or, to say it differently, their capital is significantly higher.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you ask about nonfinancial corporates, that's really where leverage is at levels that are high relative to history.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But defaults are low, interest rates are low, you know, so it's something- that's something we're watching very carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, again, I don't think we see it as-I think there are a range of views on that, but we are watching nonfinancial corporates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Households are in good shape, though, and that is-that is so important because that's where-you know, that's where we got into trouble before.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And that's-it's often around property, and particularly housing, where you see real problems emerge.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't really see that now, so we take some solace from that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it doesn't play any part in my thinking and I'll tell you why.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you raise rates too quickly, you're just increasing the likelihood of a recession, and that's exactly what you don't want to do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the best thing you can do, I think-I think the incentives actually run in the other direction.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you're-if you're worried about going back to the lower bound, then risk management would suggest that you go a little slower in raising rates and tolerate-that's likely to be a more sustainable strategy to get further away from the zero lower bound.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think we're far enough away now, though, that the risks are kind of balanced.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so I think it's more just-we're just looking at the economy, and what does it need, and how do we- how do we sustain the expansion, keep the labor market strong, and try to keep inflation near 2 percent?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we don't-we don't have the tools to control that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If companies choose to-companies in our system are free to do what they can-what they need to do once they've-once they've made profits and have cash to distribute.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: They can distribute it to their shareholders, they can buy-either through dividends or through buybacks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, the part-and, you know, we don't play a role in those decisions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we view maximum employment as the maximum sustainable level of employment, meaning it's not so much that it will cause the economy to overheat.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, over time, when-when labor markets are strong and companies are hiring, we should see higher wages.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, again, we don't really have the tools that will address the distribution of profits and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we've been given a really important job to do on behalf of the American people by Congress, and we've been given the tools to do it, and my colleagues Page 4 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL and I are focused exclusively on carrying out that mission.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We consider the best thinking, the best theory, and the best evidence.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We have disparate points of view, which we debate extensively and come to a perspective and try to set monetary policy to achieve maximum employment in a context of price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so that's who we are, that's what we do, and that's just the way it's always going to be for us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So in terms of financial markets and monetary policy, we-as we say in our statement every cycle, we do take financial conditions into consideration because financial-broader financial conditions do affect the broader economy, and they're one of the many things that we take into account.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The part of it that we control, though, is what we do with the federal funds rate and that has-that has effects out through, you know, out through the full interest rate curve and into financial asset prices generally.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the answer is, we take everything into account, but, you know, broader financial conditions are just one of the things that we take into account.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In terms of '20 and '21, why-your question was why the funds rate needs to be above neutral?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Some of-some of the participants have mostly very modest Page 5 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL overshoots of their personal estimates of neutral a couple-three years out.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think it's hard to be confident that that's-that that's the way things are going to be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: What we're going to be doing as we-as we go through time is asking at every meeting whether monetary policy is set to achieve our goals.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I think that that's an assessment of where policy will need to be some years down the road, and I'll leave it at that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The Committee forecasts what they-what they show, in general, is an economy where unemployment remains in the high and middle 3s throughout the entire forecast period and inflation remains very close to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And that is based on our understanding of the way the inflation process works now and on the fact that the inflation seems to be fairly nonreactive to changes in slack- that is to say, a flat Phillips curve.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And it's just-it's a-it's a world of strongly anchored inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So you may ask-I mean, the sense is, what does the longer-run natural rate of unemployment mean?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so that really is a longer-run concept that we think the economy will return to over the longer run.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, obviously, that longer run, you know, isn't- it's not creating problems in the short run for that forecast.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Page 6 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL Now let's just admit that the inflation process has changed dramatically from where it was in the 1960s to where it is now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We can't take for granted that it will remain the way it is, and, you know, we will be, of course, watching carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If inflation reacts more strongly or more weakly to the strong economy, then we'll adjust policy appropriately.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Well, interest rates, of course, have effects on growth, have effects-I mean if-I guess the-your question was, what are you buying with by raising interest rates?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The question is, what would the economy look like if you didn't raise rates?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It would look very different, I think, if we didn't raise rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're always trying to, you know, work our way between the-sort of the two-the two problems we face.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: One is that if we move too quickly, we can, you know, snuff out a recovery unnecessarily, and inflation falls short of its 2 percent target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Or if we move too slowly, we have an economy that can overheat.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't see any signs of that now, but we're always trying to navigate between those two shoals.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we think that gradually, you know, raising interest rates is the way that we kind of take both of those risks seriously.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As I said, I think I'm in the camp of seeing vulnerabilities as relatively moderate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think the financial system-I think another thing that we learned in the crisis is that we need to be alert to the buildup of vulnerabilities as a long expansion continues.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I don't see that in troubling-troubling amounts at this point, but, you know, I think it's appropriate for us to monitor that very carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I guess I need to start by saying that we're not responsible for trade policy, and we don't comment on particular, you know, trade actions and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But you will have seen that we have this very extensive network of business contacts around the country through the Reserve Banks largely, and we've been hearing a rising chorus of concerns from businesses all over the country about disruption of supply chains, materials costs and increases, and loss of markets, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we've been hearing quite a lot of that, and we-the Reserve Bank presidents talk about it in the meeting, and it goes in the minutes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we, you know, that's-we're very transparent about hearing all that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think if you look at the aggregate perform-the performance of the U.S. economy at an aggregate-at Page 9 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL a national level, it's hard to see much happening at this point.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And-or you can look at it the other way: You can ask, if all of the tariffs that have been announced are applied, what would be the effect at the aggregate level?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: One is loss of business confidence, which could reduce investment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Again, we don't really see effects that we could measure yet.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Also, the possibility of a financial market reaction over time to unexpected trade developments.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: More than anything, though, I would worry, in the longer run, where this is going, you know.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If the- if the end place we get to is lower tariffs, that would be good, you know.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, fair trade-fair trade under internationally accepted rules can be a good thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think if this, perhaps inadvertently, goes to a place where we have widespread tariffs that remain in place for a long time-a more protectionist world-that's going to be bad for the United States' economy and for American workers, and families, and also for other economies.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: This year has-we've kept raising our forecast for this year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: This-as the year's gone on, the economy has come in stronger than we expected, and that's a really good thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And the economy, as I mentioned at the beginning, is strong, and there's good reason to expect that to continue.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, some of it is, no doubt, the effect of the fiscal policy changes, the tax cuts, and the spending increases-that's got to be part of the story.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Part of it may be higher oil prices, which are calling for more investment in the Page 10 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL oil patch.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, you know, the growth picture is very much supported by very high readings of household confidence, business confidence, so it's a-it's a-it's a-it's a pretty particularly bright moment, I think.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you look back over the last decade, this is a pretty good moment for the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, the idea is, you cut-you reduce taxation on corporations and particularly-and allow faster expensing for investment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The idea is to encourage more investment, and that is one of the things that drives productivity, which is one of the main things that drives rising incomes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the effects are very uncertain, they're-you know, they're-the literature is-it's-there's no clear answer to exactly how these mechanisms work or how effective they are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And it would be soon to be seeing supply-side effects.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The other-supply­ side effects are probably both more uncertain and they're probably slower to come in.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, you know, as I said, we-I certainly hope-I hope that we'll be marking up our estimates of potential growth as well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You mean-you mean, where's the point at which inflation- unemployment is too low?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, so we've been-I think the perform-labor Page 12 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL force participation has surprised us on the upside.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There is a long-run trend there, and we've now had basically five flat years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you look-if you look at labor force participation, since the fourth quarter of '13 till now, you really have a-kind of an oscillation that basically is a sideways movement in the face of a significant downward trend, thanks to aging and other factors.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That's a gain of well more than a percentage point in participation, so that's really- that's really a good thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Those are people who are remaining in contact with the labor force and looking for jobs, finding jobs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's one of the things that has allowed the unemployment rate not to fall further.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And it's a-it's a signal, too, that there may be more there on the supply side, that there may be more labor supply than the prior trend would indicate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it's a very positive thing to see people staying in the labor force.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, we don't know how long it can continue.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We have models, and we look at this-we look at this question all the time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, admittedly, we've been surprised on the positive side here, so we're open to the idea that that may continue or not.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You don't see it yet, but we-you could see retail prices moving up.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The tariffs Page 13 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL might provide a basis for companies to raise prices in a world where they've been very reluctant to and unable to raise prices, where raising prices is really difficult, you know, with the ability to shop on the internet.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: This could provide, you know, a way for-again, we don't see it in the numbers.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, until we see it in the numbers, it's hard to say how one would react.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And the other question would be, if you're just talking about the effect on inflation is, is it just a one-time increase in the price level, or is it actually fueling higher inflation going forward?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And that's a real-that's an important question in, in how we would think about the appropriate response.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, don't see it yet, but we-you're hearing-I mean, broadly across the economy, it's not just tariffs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You're hearing-we're hearing a lot of talk of labor shortages, of material costs in particular industries.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're hearing a lot, you know, what amount to supply-side constraints and things like that, but we're not seeing it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're seeing a sort of modest increase in wages, inflation right around 2 percent, no sense of it moving up really, so we're not seeing it yet.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, we just aren't, and we're watching very carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I don't think it's a new point that forecasts two and three out-two or three years out are fairly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The dot plot is individual FOMC participants who are writing down their individual views on the evolution of the economy and of appropriate monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think market participants generally find that interesting information, and so it seems to me to be serving a purpose.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think the point with "accommodative" was that its useful life was over.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we put that in the statement in 2015, just when we lifted off, and the idea was to provide assurance that we weren't trying to slow down the economy, but, in fact, we were still-interest rates were still going to be pushing to support economic activity.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Well, that-you know, that purpose has been well served, and the language now doesn't really say anything that's important to the way the Committee is thinking about policy going forward.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Did I get- did I get all of your ques-?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Yeah, you know, it's-if you look at a broad financial conditions index, that's pretty much the answer you'll get.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't control that, and, as I mentioned earlier, we do take financial conditions into account in what we do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And financial conditions are affecting the broader economy, so, by definition, we're taking them into account.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But if you look at-look at interest rates, you know, interest rates-look at long-term interest rates this year and short-term interest rates this year, there's very significant increases.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you Page 15 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL know, with your long and variable lags, that should be-that should be having an effect over time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Okay, so in terms of nominations to the Fed, those are entirely, completely under the control of the White House and, ultimately, the President.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And traditionally, the Fed Chair has been consulted on those, and I'm happy to say that that has continued.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But these are-these are really decisions for the White House, and, you know, we are-think of us as just being consulted.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I will say that I'm very happy and excited about the team that we're putting together, and I'm very much looking forward to having those offices up and down our hall filled.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's been pretty quiet, more quieter than usual, which is saying something on the Board hall.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In terms of corporate debt, so this is a-this is a-you know, I was an investor for a long time in areas that were very close to the leveraged lending markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you know, I have had a lot of experience in that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That market has evolved really significantly since before the crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, the banks take much less risk than they used to.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: They're-the-they're Page 16 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL essentially in the business of distributing these loans and bonds rather than keeping them on their balance sheet, to a much greater degree.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But it's also true-and there's significant research on this-that excessive risk-taking in the leveraged lending markets does have channels for affecting the real economy, if there's overheating and that kind of thing in those markets, so we monitor that carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, the guidance is-isn't binding, as you pointed out, that the leveraged lending isn't binding, and that's just-that's just the way that the law is interpreted.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it's something we're monitoring, and, as I mentioned, we think overall vulnerabilities are moderate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I think if you look at the-look at the dot plot in the SEP, you'll see that the federal funds rate, even after today's move, is below the longer-run neutral estimate of every single participant that-who submits a- an estimate of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's why this is the perfect time to take the language out, because, you know, it's perfectly clear that there can't be a signal because, you know, by definition, that means an accommodative policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The thinking was more, as I mentioned, it's more that the language has run its useful life.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There's another point, though, too, which is, you know, we don't want to suggest either that we have this precise understanding of where "accommodative" stops or suggest that that's a really important point in our thinking.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, what we're going to be doing, assuming we Page 17 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL stay on this path, is, we're going to be carefully monitoring incoming data from the financial markets and from the economy and asking ourselves whether our policy is achieving the goals we want to achieve-you know, sustain the economy, maximum employment, stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That's the way we're thinking about it, and that does kind of amount to thinking less about one's precise point estimate of the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, many of the participants have written that down, and they've written down really modest overshoots, you know, amounting to one rate hike kind of thing, which wouldn't have a big effect on the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, it-I would just say, you know, it really depends on what happens.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It depends on if we keep going-you can think of it different ways.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Maybe we'll be raising our estimate of the neutral rate and we'll just go to that, or maybe we'll keep our neutral rate here and then go one or two rate increases beyond it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think it's very possible, but I mean, ultimately, isn't really the question we're answering.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The question we're answering is, how do we provide the economy just the right amount of support- not too much, not too little-to sustain the recovery and achieve our statutory goals?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The first thing is the single biggest thing I think that we learned was the-as I mentioned, I think, earlier, the importance of maintaining the stability of the financial system.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I think if you look-if you look back at the way the models worked and the way people thought about risk in the economy, that's what was missing, and I think it's not missing anymore.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we-you know, we put a tremendous focus on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We have stress tests, which force banks to understand-the largest banks particularly-to understand and better manage their risk and have enough capital to survive a really substantial shock that's at least as bad as the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And if all that doesn't work, we've got resolution plans, which we've, you know, through many cycles, have made really substantial progress, more than I had thought was likely.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Nobody's-you know, nobody is, I think, overconfident that we've solved every problem.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, now we're going back and kind of taking a hard look at everything and, you know, trying to make-trying to-trying to keep at it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I think those are the really important lessons, and, you know, we-we're determined not to, you know, not to forget them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And that's, I think, a risk now-is to-is to forget things that we-that we learned.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I saw the article you're talking about; the question is, did Congress take things away, emergency powers from the Fed?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So there was sort of a trade for taking away our power under Page 19 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL 13, section 13(3), to provide support to individual nonbanks, which is really holding companies and other companies.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In exchange for that, we got orderly liquidation authority and a resolution authority.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I don't think there's any sense that Congress would seriously look at changing that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I have real doubts about whether it was wise to take away our crisis-fighting tools.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think you put them away, and you hope you never need them, but-and I certainly strongly oppose efforts to take away more of our tools.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, the third thing you mentioned is the designation power.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In my mind, it should be used-my thinking, it should be used sparingly, and that means, you know, in situations where you have-I mean, in principle, you could have another Lehman Brothers come up out of the ground that's not a bank, and it could be very threatening-or it could be capable of creating systemic risk.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so I think it's a critical power to have.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, again, I would use it-I would tend to use it fairly sparingly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Are you worried about the effect of rising interest rates on consumers?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Credit card rates have jumped to more than 17 percent since the Fed started raising interest rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Yeah, we look-of course, we look at that very carefully, and interest rates are going up across a broad range of consumer borrowing, as they would when we raise short-term interest rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And the other thing I'll say is, take-if you take housing, if you look at the NAR Affordability Index, housing is still more affordable now than it was before the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So you're right that the cost of borrowing is going up, but it's going up from what were extraordinarily low levels, and it is Page 20 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL something that we watch carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, the effect on consumer spending is a very important channel through which interest rates work, and so we do monitor the effects.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Well, at the Fed, we are, you know, deeply committed to the mission of CRA, which is for banks to provide credit and other banking services in the communities they serve.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we have also been of the view for some time that with the evolution of technology particularly and changes-changes in the nature of banking, that it's an appropriate time-it's past an appropriate time, but now it's certainly an appropriate time to revisit the way we think about CRA.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But we don't want to lose that focus on community, and, you know, we definitely want to see that fundamental purpose of the law sustained.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Many of the issues that we had were reflected in the OCC's ANPR, and we're-we're hopeful that, over time, there will be a joint proposed rulemaking with the OCC, the FDIC, and the Fed.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's a process, and, you know, we're very much interested in continuing to push it forward.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you know, some of the things that we'd be looking at to tell us whether we're getting close to supply-side limits would be, first, does job growth slow down?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: A slowing down in job growth would be an indicator, you know.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: An unexpectedly sharp increase in wages or inflation could tell you that you're reaching those points.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, if headline growth slowed down, that's another one.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So all of those things would be worth taking into consideration.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think also, though, we've seen sometimes sharp tightening in financial conditions, as we saw at the beginning of 2016, can have a substantial effect pretty quickly on our economy if it's a broad and significant tightening.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we would be looking for those kinds of things and many other things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the U.S. economy is, as I mentioned, is strong and is at a pretty positive moment, you know, with strong growth, healthy labor market, inflation right on target, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So-and we've seen growth abroad, but growth, I think, both in advanced economies and in some emerging economies has slowed down a little bit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And in that world, you know, if the U.S. is stronger, then that's just part of the context, part of the environment that could mean a higher dollar.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It could be-it could therefore mean that some of our demand will wind up being shared with other economies.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So you could see that, and, you know, it's just-it's just all of the-all things that go into thinking about, you know, the path of the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Page 23 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL I would say, you know, we're not responsible for the dollar.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Of course, the Treasury is responsible for managing the dollar, but the dollar has only partly recovered the decline that it had in 2017.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's moved up off its lows, but it's not as high as it was at the beginning of last year yet by a significant margin.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we've said that we would use our tools to assure that the federal funds rate trains-trades within the target range.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And the principal tools we use have been interest on excess reserves and then, at the bottom end, a reverse repo facility.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we-in June, when we raised rates, we only raised the interest on excess reserves by 20 basis points and raised the range by 25, and that moved federal funds sort of back into the range.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The federal funds rate traded in the low 190s, well within the range.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we-again, we have our tools, and we will use them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We think it's principally a function just of a number of things, but particularly high Treasury supply, and-which is showing up in repo rates and then showing up in fed funds as well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we don't see it as a-as a big problem.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We see it as a problem we can address with our tools, and we'll use them if we have to.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We regulate financial institutions, financial stability, that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But in the longer-run, fiscal policy will have a significant effect on the economy, so for that reason, I think my predecessors have commented on fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But they've commented on-at a high level rather than trying to get involved in particular, you know, particular measures.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so-and I-my plan is to kind of stick to the same approach and stay in our lane.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know-so I would just say, it's-it's no secret, it's been true for a long time that with our uniquely expensive health-care delivery system and the aging of our population, we've been on an unsustainable fiscal path for a long time, and there's no hiding from it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In the end, we will have to face that, and I think, you know, the sooner, the better.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: These are, you know, this is-this is the economy at nearly full employment or in the range-in the neighborhood of full employment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's a-it's a good time to be addressing these things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I just-I put that out there and leave it at that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Well, we serve a domestic mandate, which is assigned to us by Congress, and that is to have maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: About half of global GDP is outside the United States, and way more than half of the growth is outside the United States and in emerging markets, I should say.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so the performance in the emerging market economies really, really matters to us in carrying out our domestic mandate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I'd also say that, you know, a strong U.S. economy, where Americans are buying things and the economy is growing and our-you know, that's going to support demand all around the globe, so that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Now, we do understand, though, that when we-when our economy is strong and we're raising rates, that puts upward pressure on interest rates around the world and can affect countries, particularly countries that have significant external dollar borrowing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And what we try to do is be very transparent about what we're doing and why.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we have been, I believe, and we've also moved quite gradually.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I-you know, I think we've been performing well on that front.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There are some countries that are-that are undergoing severe stress, a handful of them, and-but not most emerging market countries.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's a relatively small number, and those particular countries have, you know, have particular vulnerabilities, which are well known in the form of budget deficits, and significant external dollar borrowings, and high inflation, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, again, we'll continue to conduct U.S. monetary policy as transparently as we Page 27 of 29 September 26, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL possibly can, and that's really the best thing we can do, along with supporting U.S. growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I don't comment on the appropriateness of the level of stock prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I can say that by some valuation measures, they're in the upper range of their historical value ranges.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, you know, I wouldn't want to-I wouldn't want to speculate about what the consequences of a market correction should be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we would-we would look very carefully at the nature of it, and I mean, it-really-really what hurts is if consumers are borrowing heavily and doing so against, for example, an asset that can fall in value.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's a really serious matter when you have a housing bubble and highly levered consumers and housing values fall.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: A simple drop in equity prices is- all by itself, doesn't really have those features.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It could certainly feature-it could certainly affect consumption and have a negative effect on the economy, though.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Inflation has come in just a touch below where we expected it to be-not by a big amount, but by a small amount.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: More broadly, 2018 has been the strongest year since the recov-since the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And during that period we've had low unemployment and strong growth, and inflation has still remained just a Page 5 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL touch below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I do think that gives the Committee the ability to be patient in moving forward.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As I mentioned, there's significant uncertainty about the-both the path and the ultimate destination of any further rate increases.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you go back some years, I think we-people who were working at the Fed in 2013 and '14 took away the lesson that the markets could be very sensitive to news about the size of the balance sheet, the pace of asset purchases, the pace of runoff, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we thought carefully about this, on how to normalize policy, and came to the view that we would effectively have the balance sheet runoff on automatic pilot and use monetary policy, rate policy, to adjust to incoming data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think that the runoff of the balance sheet has been smooth and has served its purpose.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I do think that we will continue to use monetary policy, which is to say rate policy, as the active tool of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, we monitor a broad range of economic conditions, including financial conditions-a broad range of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we took on board the tightening in financial conditions, which-not any one condition, but, broadly speaking, financial conditions have tightened since the September meeting, really.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That's why the forecast for growth and inflation went down a little Page 7 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL bit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, remember, that's in a context of a more accommodative path.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we definitely did take that into account, and, as you can see from the statement language, we acknowledged those risks in the clause about monitoring developments.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we're going to be watching carefully to see as those things develop.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think, more broadly, there's been a sense of concern among business people and market people about global growth, and, you know, that may be partly about trade tensions, it may be partly about a variety of things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you just mechanically drop into a model of the U.S. economy tariffs, you don't see very large effects.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The large effects would have to come from financial market changes or from losses in business confidence.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And those are things that are very difficult to model.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: On your third factor, you know, political considerations have played no role whatsoever in our discussions or decisions about monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're always going to be focused on the mission that Congress has given us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We have the independence, which we think is essential to be able to do our jobs in a nonpolitical way.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And you know, we are-we at the Fed are absolutely committed to that mission, and nothing will deter us from doing what we think is the right thing to do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, again, I go back to the health of the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you look at 2018, as I mentioned, this the best year since the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we also have a positive forecast, as I mentioned, and, in that context, we think this move was appropriate for what is a very healthy economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Policy at this point does not need to be accommodative.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're now at the bottom end of the range of estimates of neutral.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's the basis upon which we made the decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I also think we took on board, you know, the risks to that, and, you know, we're certainly cognizant of them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Page 9 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference **FINAL MARTIN CRUTSINGER** Mr. Chairman, Marty Crutsinger with the AP.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You've established for this coming year a communications panel to look at how the Fed communicates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Could you talk a little bit about what you expect to get from that panel, and will the dot plot be involved in that at all?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Are we dealing with it the way that you want us to be handling the dot plot, or is it something that you might tweak a bit?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So this review, what it really is-it's coming at a time when the economy is strong, and it's a good time to take a step back, we think, and ask whether our strategy and our tools and our communications around monetary policy are doing the job that Congress has assigned us to do on behalf of the American people.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And what we're going to do is, we're going to open ourselves up and have a discussion with many outside groups of all different parts of the economy, including, you know, an academic conference in June in Chicago.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, again, the idea is to, you know, listen to new ideas, better ideas, old ideas-many of them have been around-and try to assess whether there are better ways we can do things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: One of the overarching facts is that rates have been really coming down overall for more than three decades now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We may be in a world where interest rates are just lower for the time being, and, therefore, we'll have less policy space to react to economic downturns.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we'd want to be evaluating ideas for-again, for better achieving the goals that Congress has given us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're not looking at law changes at all, and we're not looking at changing the inflation target, for example.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We are looking for better ways to achieve the inflation goal-for example, on a symmetric basis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As I mentioned, on the dot plot-you asked about the dot plot.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think the dot plot generally does provide useful information about the reaction function of Committee participants-sometimes more useful than others, I'll admit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, in general, I think people sort Page 10 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL of have it figured out and understand what it is and what it isn't.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But that doesn't mean we don't like to repeat what it isn't, which-it's not a consensus forecast.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's something that each of us writes down, and we always update it as-you know, as data come in and as we update our outlooks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we do watch all of that, but the amount of-the amount of runoff that we've had so far is pretty small.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And if you just run the quantitative easing models in reverse, you would get a pretty small adjustment in economic growth and real outcomes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we don't think, you know, things that are happening at the short run-at the short end-are driven by many other factors other than the balance sheet runoff.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: For example, just-very large bill supply has pushed up short-term rates, has pushed up repo rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Tightening of the federal funds rate has raised short-term borrowing costs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But we don't see, you know, the balance sheet runoff as creating significant problems.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we're watching-we have a strong forecast, generally, for next year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That forecast involves growth, you know, between 2 and 2½ percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It involves growth at a strong enough level to continue driving unemployment down and inflation near 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, to make further moves, I'll be looking for data that suggests that that's, in fact, the path that we're on.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As I mentioned, once you-once you're, broadly speaking, in the range of neutral, I think it's appropriate to be putting aside individual estimates of that and be looking at what the incoming data are telling you about the outlook, updating your estimates of what neutral might be, of what the natural rate of unemployment might be, of the state of the economy, so-and letting that lead you to adjust your outlook and, therefore, your appropriate path for policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's what we mean when we say we're "data dependent."

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Of course, we're always data dependent, but I think it has a particular meaning in this context, which is that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Page 13 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference **FINAL ANN SAPHIR** Next year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I guess I would just go back to this: The individual forecasts are not something that the Committee votes on.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We vote on the rate increase, and we write down our-you know, our own personal paths.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So people have disparate views on what the endpoint could be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Ultimately, it's going to depend on what the circumstances are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There would be circumstances in which it would be appropriate to go past neutral, and there would be circumstances in which it would be wholly inappropriate to do so.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I don't-I wouldn't put too much on-it does inform you, the way people are thinking about things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But don't-I wouldn't take it as a signal about current policy or about near-term policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, if you look at the Tealbook, or-you know, we get the Tealbook in person from the Reserve Bank presidents who come in, and they share their discussions not just with their directors, but with literally hundreds of business and nonprofit, you know, and labor union people around the country.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I personally find it really 1 Chairman Powell was referring to the Beige Book, not the Tealbook.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Page 14 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL interesting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: My background is very much working-starting with, you know, a small group of people, maybe a company, and working out.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that kind of anecdotal data really helps me capture the picture better.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So-and, you know, what-what you're picking up now, I think, is, there's, you know, a mood of concern, or it's a mood of angst about growth going forward, if I could just capture it in one thought.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There are many reasons that are given for that, but, generally speaking, it's-it's a concern about, is growth going to be as strong as it was?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That doesn't mean that it'll come into the real data in a big way-it may, but-or that financial conditions will tighten further.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've taken that on board both in the outcomes, in our forecast, but also in a lower rate path to-you know, to provide some accommodation to push back against that tightening.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, financial conditions-broadly speaking, we don't look at any one market.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We look at a really big range of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And what matters for the broader economy is material changes in a broad range of financial conditions that are sustained for a period of time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: A little bit of volatility-speaking in the abstract-some volatility doesn't probably leave a mark on the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, what we've seen here is a tightening.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There's been a tightening since right around after-a week or so after the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, that-we tried to factor that into our models of the economy and to the results that come out of those models.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Page 15 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL That's how we think about it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, remember, from a macroeconomic standpoint, no one market is the single dominant indicator and it really matters if changes are sustained over time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Do you still think core PCE is a good measure of whether the economy is overheating?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: What do you think of other measures like setting a target for economic growth and relying more on that?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Well, I think we look at both, but core PCE is a good indicator.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It has-what's happened over, really, 50 years is that inflation has become much less reactive to changes in growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There was a time when inflation reacted really quickly to changes in growth and changes in unemployment, and that time is behind us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And that is often attributed to the success of central banks in anchoring inflation expectations so that people believe that inflation will come back to the target or around the target so it doesn't go down as much-inflation doesn't go down as much in a downturn and doesn't go up as much when the-you know, when the economy is strong.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's really true, though, that inflation has not reacted a lot on a road from 10 percent unemployment to now 3. percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But in terms of just targeting growth, you know, I think-I actually think our dual mandate works very well, which is maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: When they work temporarily in different ways, we take a balanced approach.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But I think that approach has served us well, and I think we can work well with it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think having regular press conferences will be a big gain for communication.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so, being able to come out after each meeting and explain the Committee's thinking and relate that to the state of the economy and expectations for policy and global developments, I think it'll be-the idea is that it'll be helpful in explaining how we're thinking and, you know, explaining what we're thinking about policy going forward.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think it'll also become the case, over time, that there will be no "prior" as to whether we would move at a quarterly meeting or one of the meetings at which we do not file an SEP. As you know, we only update our projections under the current approach quarterly, whereas we have eight-eight meetings.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I think we'll move to a more-we'll have the ability to move eight-at eight different meetings.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Not eight times, but at eight different meetings on the year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If we, you know-if we're-if we want to communicate something about something that's going to happen in a future meeting, I think we know how to do that in speeches, in press conferences, and such.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Page 17 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference **FINAL DON LEE** Don Lee with the L.A. Times.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You mentioned broad-based wage gains this year, and I'm wondering if you see further acceleration in wage growth and just how much slack there is in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So what we've seen is, is a very gradual-and, I think, ongoing-increase in wages.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you go back a few years, you'll see that we look at many, many indicators of wages and compensation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And they were all kind of clustered around 2-if you go back five years ago-2 percent increase per year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Now they are all at 3, and they've just continued to gradually move up-not perfectly in sync, but-and that's a number that is, you know, right in keeping with 2 percent inflation and 1 percent productivity growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I do expect, and I think many forecasters expect, that wage increases will continue, and that would be a welcome development.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There's plenty of evidence of situations-for example, in the very tight labor market of the late 1990s of a-I think I mentioned in a speech a month or so ago, we had wage increases above productivity plus inflation, and we didn't have high inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We hear a great deal of anecdotal information about labor shortages, along with other, you know, bottlenecks and things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I would expect that wages will keep moving up, and it doesn't necessarily mean inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you know, by most indicators-we look at a very wide range of indicators on the labor market.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, by most indicators, we are at or even above longer-run normal levels.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But I would point to one particular pocket, and that is, labor force participation by younger prime-age workers, particularly prime-age males, is still, Page 18 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL you know, meaningfully below its pre-crisis level.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Most other age groups in both genders have moved back up pretty close to where they were at the last cyclical peak.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, there's a question, can we go above that cyclical peak?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And-or, or are the problems more structural than cyclical, and that there isn't-so we'll have to find that out.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think, given the strong economy, we've had the luxury of finding out that labor force participation can be higher than we had thought.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So you're right that a big focus of what we have been doing has been tailoring regulations.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And the sense of "tailoring" is that we want to look below the level of the G-SIBs at the large regionals and then on down to the community banks at various steps and ask whether we have appropriately tailored regulation and supervision to account for the fact that smaller and less complex organizations present a much less significant threat to the economy and to the community should they fail-should they experience material difficulty.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, in the nature of that, you're focused more on the smaller institutions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Page 19 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL I think, with the larger institutions, we want regulation and supervision to be effective and efficient.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I know that the larger institutions tend to be the ones who care about the Volcker rule.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we-we think that things need to be looked at carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, again, I wouldn't want to materially change capital levels, because, I think, you know, it's important that the largest financial institutions, the largest and most complex-the systemically important ones be held to the highest standards and higher expectations.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And while we may tailor some regulations, those fundamentally high expectations are not going to change.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Again, we do focus on a broad range of financial indicators, and I-really, we don't obsess about any particular one.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, we look at a whole range of them, and we ask ourselves, what's really going on in the broad picture out there?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, if you ask what's going on with the long-certainly the long, longer-maturity Treasury market has come in some.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That's consistent with, you know, a risk-off feeling in the stock market as well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Really, the longer Treasury has moved in a range above 3 percent and down 3 percent as the risk sentiment has changed.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, I think if rates were to stay low for a longer period of time, that could be thought of as a signal of expectations of lower growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As I Page 20 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL mentioned, our forecast for next year is-I think, in keeping with most other forecasts-is that we'll still have solid growth next year, declining unemployment, and a healthy economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, monetary policy is a forward-looking exercise, and I'm going to-I'm just going to stick with that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's-where we are right now is, we're at the lower end of the range of neutral.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've arrived effectively at the bottom end of that range.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: For that, as I mentioned, going forward, there's real uncertainty about the path-the pace, rather, and the destination for further rate increases.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we're going to be letting incoming data inform our thinking about the appropriate path.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, if you go back a year, 2017 was a year of kind of ongoing upside surprises in global growth.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And people raised their forecasts for growth around the world kind of throughout 2017 and, in some sense, expected that to continue into 2018.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: What has happened instead has been a modest retracing of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So you have still healthy levels of growth in the aggregate around the world but close to the potential growth rate of, you know, the Page 21 of 22 December 19, 2018 Chairman Powell's Press Conference FINAL global economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But you no longer have the really strong levels of growth you had in 2017.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We also monitor, you know, event risks like Brexit-like, you know, like the negotiations between Italy and the EU over their budget.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, as far as those are concerned, we monitor them very carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Our financial institutions have had a long time now to get ready for the full range of possible exits from the EU by the U.K. And they've had supervisory involvement from U.S. supervisors, from U.K. supervisors, from EU supervisors-we think they are fully prepared for the full range of outcomes that may come out of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I was very happy to see the developments around central counterparties today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That was a big issue that seems to have been satisfactorily, for the time being, resolved.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Honestly, it shouldn't have major implications for the United States, but, you know, there's a lot of uncertainty because it's not something that's happened before.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We think that our policy is at the appropriate point right now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We also know that our policy rate is now in the range of the Committee's estimates of neutral.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we'll be-again, we think our policy stance is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We had an extensive discussion of the baseline and also of the risks to the baseline, and the risks are, of course, the fact that financial conditions have tightened, that global growth has slowed, as well as some, let's say, government-related risks like Brexit and trade discussions, and also the effects and ultimate disposition of the shutdown.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we looked at-we look at those, and the way we think of it is that policy-we will use our policy, and we have, to offset risks to the baseline.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we view the baseline as still solid, and part of that is the way we adjusted our baseline to address those risks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, generally speaking, we think the outlook is favorable, and we think that these crosscurrents that I referred to-these risks-are going to be with us for a while.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We think there's no pressing need to change our policy stance and no need to rush to judgment there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would say that we'll be looking at a full range of data, and that will include inflation data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It will include all data relevant to our dual mandate of stable prices and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Remember that our inflation objective is a symmetric one, meaning that we are- we're always trying to get to 2 percent, and we don't look at-we look at inflation equally on both sides.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I can't get into specific hypotheticals, but I do believe that we have a symmetric objective, and I believe we'll act that way.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I'm just going to say that the-it's going to depend entirely on the data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We will be- we will patiently wait and let the data clarify.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Some of the crosscurrents that I refer to may be with us for a while, and I think we'll be looking at seeing those clear up as it relates to-as they relate to the outlook for the U.S. and that will be an important aspect as well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We'll be looking at everything, but I do think that, you know, muted inflation pressures-you know, you would want-I would want to see a need for further rate increases, and, for me, a big part of that would be inflation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It wouldn't be the only thing, but it would certainly be important.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So today I'm here to talk about decisions and also discussions about decisions that haven't been made.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we're talking about the latter thing, which is discussions, and so I can't get ahead of where decisions are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But so the Committee is- what we're looking to do is create a whole plan that will bring us to our goal, our longer-run goal, which is a balance sheet no larger than it needs to be for us to efficiently conduct- efficiently and effectively conduct monetary policy, but to do so in a way that doesn't put our goals at risk or result in unnecessary market turmoil.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So there are a lot of pieces to that, and we've learned over time that it's-when making these-when designing these plans, like, for example, the original normalization plan, it's good to take your time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Let them stand the test of time and argument and then move when you're really comfortable with what you've got and when you feel you can communicate it clearly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So I don't want to get ahead of that process today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But-so we've discussed-there are a number of pieces to that puzzle.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There are several different pieces to them, and I think they're coming-and I'm very pleased with the progress that we've made, and, you know, the piece that you mentioned is something that is in those discussions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I'm not going to give our estimate or ratify anybody else's estimate of what the equilibrium balance sheet is here today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There are estimates out there, but I'm not at a point today where I'm going to be giving out numbers on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But there are estimates, and I think they're consistent with what I said, broadly speaking.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There are different pieces of the thing, and that is in the discussion as one of many pieces that is in the discussion.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Let me say that the question of the ultimate composition of our balance sheet in the longer run is a very important one, and it's one that we see ourselves as coming to, you know, fairly soon, as in, in coming meetings.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It won't be the first thing we work on, but it will be one of the first things that we try to resolve.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We had discussions at one of the last two meetings on this, and we haven't come to a judgment on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, you know, I wouldn't comment beyond saying that we understand that's a key question, and there are, you know, there are issues to be decided.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There are benefits and costs to doing- to taking different approaches, and I wouldn't want to prejudge them today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: First, the narrative of slowing global growth continues, if you will.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've seen that both in China and in Western Europe, and so that's an important-that has important implications for us, and that story has-let's just say it continues.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, in addition-I mean, I think important-possibly less important now-probably less important now, but-has been the shutdown, which will leave some sort of imprint on first- quarter GDP.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If that's all there is, and the shutdown is gone and there isn't another shutdown, then we'll get most of that back in the second period-second quarter.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So those things-in addition, you know, you have to look back.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And they now have persisted and remain tighter- significantly tighter, let's say-than they were, and that's something that we have to take into account as well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, patience-I think we're going to know in hindsight, because the length of this patient period is going to depend entirely on incoming data and its implications for the outlook.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that's going to be-so it's hard to say, you know, it's hard to think of what to call it at this point or how to label it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So really, your second question is about how do we think about financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I would say this: We think about a broad range of financial conditions, not just one or two things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, it's interest rates, it's risk spreads, it's currency, it's the stock market, it's credit availability, it's many, many factors.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And what matters for financial conditions is, when there are changes and those changes are sustained for a period of time, then they become important for us because they have important macroeconomic implications.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we don't react to, you know, to most things that happen in the financial markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But when we see a sustained change in financial conditions, then that's something that has to play into our thinking.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In fact, our policy works through changing financial conditions, so it's sort of the essence of what we do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, on the first question, I can-we don't comment on individual investigations or whether they're happening.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I will say that we take our enforcement powers very seriously, and we put them to work when we feel it's justified.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In terms of real-time payments, it's something we're very actively working on.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As you obviously know, we have some proposals out, and we're considering them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, the thing is, it's very important in that space to consult with the full range of market participants and interest groups, consumer groups, and we've done that, as I'm sure you know, over a period of years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't have plenary authority to just do things, for the most part, in the payment space.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We've been more of a convener, bringing industry and the public-public interest groups-and all those groups around the table.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we've-I think we've played a constructive role in that respect, and I believe that will continue.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So what we care about-and, really, the only thing we care about at the Fed-is doing our job for the American people and using our tools appropriately.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think anyone who knows the Fed or who has worked at the Fed would recognize that description.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we're always going to do what we think is the right thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're never going to take political considerations into account or discuss them as part of our work.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But we're not going to make mistakes of character or integrity.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I would want the public to know that, and I would want them to see that in our actions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I guess the sense of your question is that we could be in a situation in the future-we hope not, but-we could be in a situation where we'd like to cut rates more than we can effectively, and we hit the zero lower bound.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't think anything like that is in the cards.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Now, there's no reason to think that it would be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But as we said in today's release, if that happens, then we'll use the full range of our tools, and that includes the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But we would use it after using our conventional tools, which would be the interest rate and forward guidance about the interest rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So let me give you the economic side of it first-is that, even with a fairly long shutdown, as long as that's the end of it and everyone gets their backpay-except the contractors, I guess, the private-sector contractors, but-some people get their backpay, then the lost GDP will be regained in the second quarter.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would say that the-you know, we all see the suffering and the heartbreak and all the pain people go through.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I see, you know, federal employees doing their work, and I'm, you know, really grateful they did.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I mean, to be doing your work while you're not getting paid, it's something we should all be grateful for.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: As I mentioned, there wouldn't be if there isn't another shutdown.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If there were going to be a permanent effect or a lasting effect, let's say, it would be from a longer shutdown or perhaps a second shutdown, and that would be through the channel of a loss of confidence in our ability to make policy in the United States.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And I think that was something that we and many others were worried about as there was talk of an even longer shutdown.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In terms of ideas for not having more shutdowns, I know Congress is actually looking at some of those, so I think that could be a profitable thing to explore.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, trade-you sound like you're an avid reader of the Beige Book, and that's great-the trade, as you will know, then-trade has been a big feature in the Beige Book for some time now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The Beige Book is a collection of all of our-of the comments that our Reserve Bank presidents get from their Districts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's incredibly valuable, because you're getting actual reports from people who are on the line.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And there have been real concerns about trade right along the line, both in terms of availability of materials and costs and retaliation and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would say the longer-term concern, though, is the negotiations that are going on.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If they linger, then there could be more and more uncertainty, and you worry over time that that could have an effect on business confidence.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So far, the actual amount of tariffs that have been applied both here and in China is not enough to have material effects on GDP either here or in China.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the concern is more a longer-for me-a longer, drawn-out set of negotiations back and forth, which could result in sapping business confidence.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Are you worried that by taking a pause in raising interest rates-we've had low interest rates for so long-are you contributing to a bubble in corporate debt?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, we did-we've called out corporate debt as a risk-more of a macroeconomic risk, I think, than a financial stability risk, the sense of that being that if you have companies that are highly levered and we do go into a downturn, they're going to be less able to weather that and keep serving their customers and, you know, may have to do layoffs and things like that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We also watch carefully for the exposure of the financial system to these companies.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: In other words, banks are arranging a lot of these loans.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Do they have obligations to underwrite loans which build up in a pipeline?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And, frankly, the banks monitor them much better with our support and help than they did before the crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Of course, you know, November, December, and January were much slower months for those sorts of things.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, you know, it'll be something that we're always paying close attention to.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, I would point to all the continuity here.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, the thing we did on the balance sheet is something we've been working on for, frankly, years- the thing we announced today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: My-honestly-only motivation is to do the right thing for the economy and for the American people-that's it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And this situation, I think, calls for patience-I think it does.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And it's just the stance of policy we think is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We see these uncertainties, and we see a time when we can afford to-we have the luxury of being able to wait and watch, and that's what we're planning to do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I'm not going to be able to help you much on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Those are great questions, and those are questions that are, you know, that our great supervisory people are looking at.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think we're open to these ideas, but I don't have any news for you on that today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: Ultimately, though, you know, a strong global economy is good for us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I mean, part of the story of 2017, for example, was that European growth kept coming in stronger and stronger, and that meant the euro was strong, and that supported our exports.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, ultimately, I think we benefit from having strong growth abroad, although you point to an interesting case.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't advise the government or Congress on fiscal policy, so I'll limit myself to more high-level comments and say that it is not a secret-it is a long-known fact that the U.S. federal government budget is on an unsustainable path, and that needs to be addressed.
