speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And that is driven principally by the combination of health-care costs-really, due to our health-care delivery system-and the aging of the population.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And there's no time like now-when the economy is healthy, growing, people are working-to go after that problem.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I have no reason to doubt CBO's numbers on this.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I haven't actually looked at that report, but my general experience with them is that it's a professional outfit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, you know, first of all, our-the work that we do relates more to the medium term rather than the long term.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so I don't see this, in particular, as a threat to this business cycle or to the economy this year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: It's more in the longer run, we'll be spending all of our money on paying interest and not on the things that we really need to be doing for future generations and for our own generation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it's a serious problem, but it's not a problem that is something that either helps or prevents the Fed from doing our job today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the range of estimates on the Committee starts at 2½ percent, and that's kind of roughly where we currently are.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And as I've said a couple of times, when you get to that range-you know that we can't directly observe the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so we have to put aside our own priors of what that rate might be and let the data speak to us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: There are a number of Committee members who are, you know, right around that range.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't-I don't-again, I think that our policy stance today is appropriate for the state of the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We're going to be watching data to see whether that's right, and we're also going to be watching data to see how these crosscurrents resolve themselves and how the U.S. economy performs this year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we've been monitoring the Brexit situation very carefully for a long time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And for us, that starts with U.S. financial institutions that have a presence either in the U.K. or in the EU or both.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we have worked with those institutions alongside U.K. and EU regulators to assure ourselves that those firms have plans and have liquidity and have all of the things they will need to deal with the full range of Brexit outcomes.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So we've done a lot of work on that, and, generally speaking-again, a lot of work has been done-we have to be humble and say that this is an unprecedented event.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If there is a hard Brexit, then that would very likely involve disruptions both to the continental economy and certainly to the U.K. economy, and we would feel that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The question for us-it wouldn't be a huge first-order thing, the economic effects, unless you saw financial disruptions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So, if you saw financial turmoil and that kind of thing, that would be the way it would reach us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would expect that we would feel some of this, and it's very hard to have great confidence that you know what that would be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But it would be something-probably not material to our economy, but it's something we'll be watching very carefully and certainly hoping that there is a resolution short of a hard Brexit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I don't know that demand for reserves has risen over the past years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think our understanding of demand for reserves-remember that the banks have more reserves than they need.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So the question is, how much of that amount is actually going to be needed in the end after, you know, after the firms adjust to our very gradual decrease?

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And so our understanding, really, of the distribution of reserves and how much will be needed has moved up over the past year.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And then there would be a buffer on top of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And then we would want to be-we would want to have a buffer, as I mentioned in my remarks, because we want to be operating in an abundant reserves regime where we operate through our administered rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If you operate too close to that point of scarcity, then you wind up having to have these big, ongoing interventions in the market.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't want the Fed to have a, you know, a large ongoing presence in the market around this.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We'd rather just, you know-in managing the federal funds rate, we'd rather have it set by our administered rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that implies you'd want to be a bit above what that equilibrium demand for reserves is.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: The only way you can figure it out is by surveying people and market intelligence and then, ultimately, by approaching that point quite carefully.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't take-you know, we don't think we have a precise understanding of this at all.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So if you think that the level of demand for reserves is here [gesturing with hands together, in the middle], all you can say is, it's probably somewhere in this range [gesturing with hands apart, equidistant from the middle].

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: If banks want to use reserves for a good and sufficient reason-which is to say, to hold liquidity as we require them to do to meet the liquidity coverage ratio, to meet their resolution requirements and resolution planning-we're not going to discourage them from holding them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: They are, in fact, a very safe asset-in a way, the safest asset.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we want the banks to be safe and sound.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We didn't create the reserves, you know, with that in mind, but, you know, since-in the post-crisis, you know, regulatory regime, we have brand-new and quite substantial liquidity requirements, which are very good and which have great public benefit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So it's not a bad thing that banks hold onto these reserves or another safe asset.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We don't-we're not encouraging them to hold reserves instead of Treasuries.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I would say that, you know, our mandate is maximum employment and stable prices, and that's about, you know, hard, real-side economic data.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We- as I mentioned earlier, we-our tool, you know, our interest rate tool operates on the economy through financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So financial conditions matter, and they matter in the way that I suggested earlier-which is to say, broad financial conditions changing over a sustained period-that has implications for the macroeconomy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So if you lower interest rates and they stay low, every borrower in the country ultimately has a lower interest rate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: That'll have an effect on-over time, an effect on the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: But, again, the entire focus we have is on maximum employment and stable prices, not on any particular financial market or financial conditions generally.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: You know, I'll quickly go back-in 2017, we were-in designing the normalization plan, we were concerned at not having two active tools of policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: We learned during the taper tantrum, frankly, in 2013 that was-that would be confusing to markets.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So what we did was we set up the normalization of the balance sheet in a way that was very transparent so that you could look and know really, certainly as to Treasuries, pretty much the exact amounts and the timing in which we would be returning these assets to private hands.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: And we put that out there very publicly and in the hope that it would be priced in and understood, and that then we could put the balance sheet on the side and have interest rates be the active tool of policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: So that went along that way very well, and I think that division of labor was a good one for our policy and for the benefit of the country.

speaker: CHAIRMAN POWELL
text: I think that there's-I think the market is now looking for more clarity around that, and I think we'll be providing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on the outlook, our outlook is a positive one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, FOMC participants continue to see growth this year of around 2 percent, just a bit below what we saw back in-at the end of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And part of that is seeing that economic fundamentals-underlying economic fundamentals are still very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You have confidence surveys for households and also for businesses that are at attractive levels, and you also have financial conditions that are more accommodative than they were a couple of months ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As far as balance sheet-the balance sheet plan, the answer to that is, you asked whether that's related to our monetary policy, in effect, and the answer is really "no."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are-we still- we think of the interest rate tool as the principal tool of monetary policy, and we think of ourselves as returning the balance sheet to a normal level over the course of the next six months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're not really thinking of those as two different tools of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the global economy was a tailwind for the United States in 2017.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we began 2018 expecting and hoping for more of the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What happened instead is that the global economy started to gradually slow, and now we see a situation where the European economy has slowed substantially-and so has the Chinese economy, although the European economy more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And just as strong global growth was a tailwind, weaker global growth can be a headwind to our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's hard to be precise about it, but, clearly, we will feel that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is an integrated global economy, and global financial markets are integrated as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what's causing it, it seems to be a range of different things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In China, you have, you know, factors that are very specific to China.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The main point, though, is that, I would say, the outlook-let's look at the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Chinese authorities have taken many steps since the middle of last year to support economic activity, and I think the base case is that, ultimately, Chinese activity will stabilize at an attractive level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in Europe, you know, we see some weakening, but, again, we don't see-we don't see recession, and we do see positive growth still.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, tariffs may be a factor in China.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the main factors are the delevering campaign that the government undertook a couple of years ago and also just the longer-term slowing to a more sustainable pace of growth that economies find as they mature.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of our own economy, the level of tariffs is relatively small in the size of our economy-relative to the size of our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have, since the beginning of the year-and before, really-been hearing from our extensive network of business contacts a lot of concerns about tariffs, concerns about material costs on imported products, and the loss of markets and things like that, depending on which industry, so there's a fair amount of uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's hard to say how much of an effect that's having on our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I will say, it's been a prominent concern among our business contacts for some time now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what happened at Wells Fargo really was a remarkably widespread series of breakdowns, really, in their risk-management apparatus, which resulted in significant consumer abuses, let's say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as it's gone on and on, it's become clear that-I think some time ago it became clear that these are deep problems that needed to be addressed in a fundamental kind of a way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's a lot of work to do on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we put in place, really, an unprecedented sanction in the form of an asset growth cap, and we will not lift that until Wells Fargo gets their arms around this, comes forward with plans, implements those plans, and we're satisfied with what they've done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, our main supervisory focus is on the company fixing its risk-management approach and fundamentally rebuilding that approach.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do supervise boards of directors for, you know, for having a set of compensation practices that don't reward short-term risk-taking and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, first, the data are not currently sending a signal that we need to move in one direction or another, in my view.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say it this way: We see a positive outlook for this year, a favorable outlook for this year, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in our SEP projections, Committee members, participants, generally see growth of around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they see growth, as I said, around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also very mindful-and we have been, of course, all along-of what the risks are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the limited data that we have do show a slowdown.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other hand, as I mentioned, we see the underlying economic fundamentals for growth this year as still very positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can think of growth as being composed of two things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And one is really growth in the workforce-more hours worked.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can really think of growth as those two things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I've been calling-often mentioning these days that it would be great if we had national-level policies to support higher labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The United States is now one of the lowest countries among the advanced economies, in terms of our labor force participation by prime-age workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we can bring more people into the labor force and give them a chance to contribute to and benefit from our overall prosperity, that will be a great thing for the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's very difficult to project productivity over long stretches of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I guess I would say, what is the potential growth rate?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's quite hard to know with any precision, and I just would like to see us, you know, undertake an effort to make it be as high as it can sustainably be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's clear that the tax and spending policies that were adopted early last year supported demand in a significant way last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's also the case, I think, that they should have some supply-side effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's hard to know, it's hard to identify those with any precision, and we hope they're-we hope they're very large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the idea would be that lowering corporate taxes would spur more corporate investment, which would spur more productivity, and lowering individual taxes would spur greater labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't want to be handing-you know, assigning credit or blame for that, but I do think that the performance of labor force participation over the last, really, three or four years has been an upside surprise that most people didn't see coming, and it's extremely welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, the data that we're seeing are not currently sending a signal which suggests moving in either direction for me, which is really why we're being patient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We feel our policy rate is in the range of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a great time for us to be patient and watch and wait and see how things evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And U.S.-the large U.S. financial institutions have made significant progress there and are now much better at the capital planning process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And for, really, some time now, for a couple of years, we've talked about moving supervision of that process-moving to a supervisory approach to that rather than having a pass/fail in the stress tests.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, given the level that the banks have moved to in capital planning, we did that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It shouldn't be a big surprise-something we've been talking about doing for a couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For banks that are newer to CCAR and haven't made that kind of progress, then they're still going to be part of-they're still going to have a qualitative test until they can reach similar levels of achievement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of having disparate views, I-look, we try-we are very much a consensus- driven organization.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the end, it's very healthy to have disparate views and to state them publicly and put them on the record.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll always be trying to reach consensus, and, you know, I'm committed to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on the household side, what we saw was a very weak reading on retail sales in December and then a bounceback in the January reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it was a surprise, I would say, and inconsistent with a significant amount of other data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not dismissing it in any way, but I would go back to, what is it that supports consumer spending?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's 70 percent of the economy, as you point out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's strong economic underlying fundamentals, so, rising wages, high levels of employment, low levels of unemployment, high levels of job creation, confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The household confidence surveys have moved back up to where they were last summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at those fundamentals, and we think that looks like a setting in which consumption will have support from underlying economic fundamentals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we're also patiently watching and waiting and not assuming.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not taking no signal from the incoming data; that's why we called it out in our statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're in a very different world today and post-crisis, because we now very carefully monitor financial conditions and financial stability concerns on an ongoing basis, and we publish a report twice a year, and we have quarterly Board meetings and briefings where we look deeply into these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is something we have very much on our radar screen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, overall, we don't see financial stability vulnerabilities as high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are some aspects of the financial markets that we're carefully monitoring, and those are in the nature of things that might be amplifiers to a downturn-as opposed to a financial stability concern, which might lead to a financial crisis and that kind of thing, which we don't see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would also say, you know, that the whole question of monetary policy and financial stability is an unsettled and difficult one in our world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do think that the principal tools for, you know, for managing financial stability are regulation, supervision, macroprudential tools, and those sorts of things as opposed to changing the interest rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're certainly very mindful of financial conditions and those risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-in our system, we mainly rely on "through the cycle" tools like high capital and stress tests.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our financial stability system is built on those tools: high capital, high liquidity, resolution planning, stress testing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also have some tools, like the countercyclical capital buffer, which we can deploy at times when vulnerabilities are meaningfully above normal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're far better capitalized and better aware of their risks and more liquid than they were before the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So they'll be more resilient in, you know, in difficult states of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think that deficits matter, and I do think-I think it's not really controversial to say that our debt can't grow faster than our economy indefinitely and that's what it's doing now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is something we will have to deal with, and I think we can't really lose sight of that, and I'd like to see a greater focus on that over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not in the nature of a near- term debt crisis or anything like that, and I wouldn't want to try to predict when that would happen, but it is something that it's important that the public discussion really come back to, if I can say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, we're watching Brexit carefully and hoping that it can be resolved in an orderly way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: From our standpoint, the part of it that we can control is that we've been involved with supervising our financial institutions that are active either in the United Kingdom or the European Union or both to make sure that they're ready for the full range of possible outcomes to the-to Brexit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and in doing so, we've also had-we've also worked alongside regulators from the United Kingdom and the EU.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do, again, hope that that can be resolved well, but we know that our banks are well capitalized and resilient to different kinds of events.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the size of the balance sheet, the balance sheet will be of a size of approximately 17 percent of GDP around the end of this year, down from 25 percent of GDP at the end of 2014-so, significantly smaller relative to GDP than it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm guessing you're looking for a dollar number, though, probably, and that would be-so, for the size of the balance sheet, it looks like it'll be a bit above $3.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So wages have moved up in the last couple of years and are now running at healthier, higher levels, and that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, a lot of the wage gains have been going to lower-paid workers, as can happen late in the cycle, which is also a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what I see is inflation that's close to 2 percent but that sort of keeps bumping up against 2 percent and then maybe moving back down a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't feel that we have kind of convincingly achieved our 2 percent mandate in a symmetrical way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we really mean is that we would look at-we know that inflation will move around on both sides of the target, and what we say is that we would be equally concerned with inflation persistently above as persistently below the target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't think we've quite achieved that yet, because we're really 10 years deep in this-almost 10 years-in this expansion, and inflation is still kind of, I'd say, not, you know, clearly meeting our target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's one of the reasons why we're being patient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, as I've said before, I think inflation that is a little bit below our target- particularly headline inflation this year will be, you know, meaningfully below our target for most of the year because of lower oil prices, but we project that core will be too-that gives us the ability to be patient and not move until we see that our target goals are being achieved.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One of them is just that the natural rate of unemployment is lower than people think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's one way to think about it, that there's still more slack in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Another is that expectations play a very-inflation expectations play a very key role in our framework and other frameworks, and, you know, there is the possibility that some people discuss of expectations being anchored but below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, either way, inflation itself has kind of bounced around a little below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's one of the major challenges of our time, really, to have inflation-you know, downward pressure on inflation, let's say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It gives central banks less room to, you know, to respond to downturns, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if inflation expectations are below 2 percent, they're always going to be pulling inflation down, and we're going to be paddling upstream in trying to, you know, keep inflation at 2 percent, which gives us some room to cut, you know, when it's time to cut rates when the economy weakens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that's something that central banks face all over the world, and we certainly face that problem too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's one of the-one of the things we're looking into as part of our strategic monetary policy review this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The proximity to the zero lower bound calls for more creative thinking about ways we can, you know, uphold the credibility of our inflation target, and, you know, we're open minded about ways we can do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, we-I think we were-we wanted to be careful to go ahead and acknowledge the things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's relatively little hard data so far this year, but we were careful to point out lower retail sales-the weak November meeting-BFI, all those things, and I think that was the right thing to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Notwithstanding that, we do have a positive outlook for the year for the reasons I mentioned-you know, solid underlying economic fundamentals, et cetera.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and in terms of what it would take, I'd say, again, today we don't see any-we don't see data coming in that suggests that we should move in either direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They suggest that we should remain patient and let the situation clarify itself over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, let me say that we've had, you know, a significant move up in wages and compensation over the last few years, and I-which does not trouble me from the standpoint of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had-also had-in other cycles, we've had situations where, you know, unit labor costs were moving up above inflation, and that didn't lead to price inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It does-you know, in theory, it can squeeze corporate margins, and, you know, that can't go on indefinitely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, I don't see the current wage picture as concerning from an inflation standpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think we look at-I understand what you're asking, but we're looking at-our mandate is price inflation and maximum employment, and that's what we're looking at with setting interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we also monitor financial stability very carefully across all meaningful asset categories.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think we tie it particularly to the relationship you're talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You mentioned that you're making sure that U.S. financial institutions are ready for whatever outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm wondering, can you be a little more specific about that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, how are you preparing for any pressures that a hard Brexit would put on the U.S. dollar?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, as I mentioned, you know, with the stress tests that the largest financial institutions-and those are the ones that tend to be active internationally-that they undergo every year, we put them through very large financial shocks with large losses and big changes in markets every year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a pretty good-you know, having done that for a number of years now, that's-and having them be required to have adequate capital and liquidity even after all that happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a good thing to have done, knowing that you're going into something that's quite unknown, which may prove stressful, it may not prove stressful, depending on what the outcome is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think all that has probably prepared our institutions well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That said, nothing like this has happened in recent years, and so it's really hard to be confident.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't-you know, we-the dollar is really the business of the Treasury Department.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's certainly a financial condition unto itself that plays into our models, but we don't, you know, seek or model or attempt to affect the dollar directly with our policies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not motivated by a particular view of industry structure that we're trying to achieve through our regulation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we want to have banks of all different sizes and with different business models out there carrying out their functions in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would also say, when banks merge and move into a larger asset category, they get stronger regulation, not weaker regulation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you think about it, you know, if you're a medium-sized bank and you merge with another medium-sized bank, you wind up being more than a medium-sized bank, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the sense of our tapering is that-"tailoring," sorry-our tailoring policy is that the highest expectations fall upon the largest, most systemically important, most complex institutions, and then at every step along the way, the expectations become more tailored to the risks that that institution actually presents to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we take-we take fiscal policy as, you know, as exogenous to what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, in other words, whatever happens with fiscal policy, we take that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't evaluate it, we don't criticize it, and we don't overreact to it either.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just an external fact about the economy for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, our policy is-the reason we're on hold is that we think our policy rate is in a good place, and we think the economy is in a good place, and we're watching carefully as we see these events evolve around the world and at home, and we think that's what we need to be doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are-the decision about the maturity composition of the Fed's balance sheet in the longer run lies ahead of us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have not made that decision, and we're-we really haven't begun to have a serious series of discussions over a series of meetings to grapple with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, I think, will be something we turn to reasonably soon, but I think it will take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a consequential decision and one that needs some thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had a lot of balance sheet discussions, as I mentioned, over the last four meetings, but this is the next big one that-big decision that we'll face.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I think we're not going to be in a rush to resolve it, but we'll turn to it soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, isn't it just that as securities roll off, you wind up investing in-you know, as a 10-year rolls off, you wind up investing in a 10-year, and automatically that lengthens things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not at all a plan to lengthen the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just been-we try to have a practice that we don't deviate from, and it's transparent, and-no policy message in that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I-as I mentioned, the balance sheet runoff will stop at about-at September 30.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if it is our view at that time that we're still a ways away from-a ways above a balance sheet that is what we need to efficiently and effectively conduct monetary policy, at that time we will hold the balance sheet constant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then what'll happen is, organically, very gradually, currency and other nonreserved liabilities will grow, and reserves will shrink.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the question you're asking is, how long will that go on?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The truth is, we don't know, and we don't really know that we'll move past September 30th.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The level of reserve demand is something that we've put a lot of effort and time into creating estimates, based on market intelligence and surveys and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't want to put a time out there for that, but-so I'll just leave it there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I'm just going to say that I think we're in a good place right now, which is, we're being patient, we're watching, we don't see any data pushing us to move rates in either direction, and we're going to watch carefully and patiently as we allow events to evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, first, we are strongly committed to our 2 percent inflation objective and to achieving it on a sustained and symmetric basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, we think our policy stance is appropriate at the moment, and we don't see a strong case for moving in either direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would point out that inflation actually ran-including core inflation-actually ran pretty close to 2 percent for much of 2018.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you point out, both headline and core, though, did come in on the soft side in the first quarter, and that was not expected as it relates to core.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we say in our Statement of Longer- Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy that the Committee would be concerned if inflation were running persistently above or below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So "persistent" carries the sense of something that's not transient, something that will sustain over a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in this case, as we look at these readings in the first quarter for core, we do see good reasons to think that some or all of the unexpected decrease may wind up being transient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'd point to things like portfolio management, service prices, apparel prices, and other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, the trimmed mean measures of inflation did not go down as much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But to go back to your question, if we did see a persistent-inflation running persistently below, then that is something the Committee would be concerned about and something that we would take into account in setting policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as I mentioned, we've just come through a two-day meeting, and we've done a deep dive on economic and financial conditions in the United States and around the world and thought about our policy, and we do think our policy stance is appropriate right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't see a strong case for moving in either direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So- we do, of course, though-as a routine matter, as you well know-we look not only at our baseline, but we also look at alternative simulations, both better and worse, and we ask ourselves what the appropriate policy response would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would just say that we're comfortable-the Committee is comfortable with our current policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a small, temporary deviation outside of the range would really carry no-wouldn't be important, as your question suggests.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do think it's important that we be able to control the federal funds rate and generally keep it within the range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think it's important, and we have the tools to do that, so we've used them again today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, I mean-so, generally speaking, the federal funds rate-we control only directly the federal funds rate in terms of the market rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the transmission of the federal funds rate into other short-term rates-money market rates-has been very good over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's important, because it's really broader financial conditions that matter, not so much precisely the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the Fed controlling the federal funds rate is actually important from that standpoint, and I don't see us not controlling it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we'll continue to control it, and it will continue to transmit well into broader financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We actually have a financial stability briefing and opportunity for comment every other meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we had our quarterly briefing today-yesterday, as a matter of fact-and had that discussion as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think there haven't been a lot of changes since the last meeting, but I'll just go through the way we think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, we've developed and published our framework for assessing financial stability vulnerabilities-put it out for comment and welcome any feedback that we get from the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that enables us to focus our assessments regularly on the same things so that we can be held accountable and be transparent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there are four aspects of it that I'll go through quickly, but I'd say that the headline really is that while there are some concerns around nonfinancial corporate debt, really the finding is that, overall, financial stability vulnerabilities are moderate, on balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in addition, I would say that the financial system is quite resilient to shocks of various kinds with high capital and liquidity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the four things we look at are, first, asset prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as for asset prices, some asset prices are somewhat elevated, but I would say not extremely so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Leverage in the financial sector-I mentioned households are actually in good shape from a leverage standpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonfinancial corporates is an area that we've spotlighted and focused on for attention, and there are concerns about that-not so much from a financial stability standpoint, but from the standpoint that having a highly levered corporate sector could be an amplifier for a downturn.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then the last two-the last two things are really about the leverage in the financial system and funding risk, and those are both very, very low by historic standards in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do say that risks to the financial system-we say in our longer-run statement of goals and monetary policy strategy that risks to the financial system that could prevent us from achieving our goals are something that we do take into consideration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that, though, that really the tools for addressing those concerns are better-capital liquidity, good supervision, good stress testing, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are better first-order tools to deal with these kinds of issues than monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, to your first question, if you go back and think about the middle of last year, inflation was at 2 percent and appeared to be staying there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the economy was quite strong and was growing strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The fiscal changes were hitting the economy in a very positive way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think the expectation was that inflation would remain up around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The weak first quarter performance was not expected-of core was not expected, and I don't think is related to anything we did, in terms of raising rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It appears to be more-we don't know this, but you never know until-with hindsight, with perfect hindsight, but some of it does appear to be transient or idiosyncratic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, I mean-so, as I said earlier, we do address this in our, sort of, constitutional document.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If inflation were to run persistently below 2 percent or persistently above 2 percent, that would be a concern for the Committee, and the Committee would take that into account in making policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think it's important that inflation run close to and sustainably -for a sustained period of time-and symmetrically around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Because if it doesn't, you run the risk that inflation expectations can-it has been the case, most of the misses are on the downside-inflation expectations over time could be pulled down, and that could put downward pressure on inflation and make it harder for us to react to downturns and harder for us to, you know, support the economy in difficult times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So probably the biggest single factor driving it is the rate of underlying inflation or the closely related idea of where inflation expectations are anchored-the thought being, that's where inflation will go in the long run if it's not been pushed by those other factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we also think that slack-the level of slack in the economy does play some small role.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's nothing like it was in the 1960s when the Phillips curve was quite steep, so that's also something that plays a role.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we take all those things into account, and the part of it that we can control is the slack part.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we do expect that this reading will be transient and inflation will move back up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if it isn't and if it runs persistently below 2 percent for a sustained period, then that's something we'd take into account in setting policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think, generally, I'd have to see the data on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think men and women should make the same for the same work, by and large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we're getting in here to commenting on a nominee to the Fed indirectly, and that's something I'd rather avoid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's really not my role to engage with potential nominees to the Fed, so I'm really not going to go there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I haven't seen this research either, so I don't really-really know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I want to say it was April 1, but it may have been April 2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In any case, the Fedwire® did go down for a few hours, in the three- or four-hour range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were able to quickly identify the problem: It was an internal problem, and we were able to correct it and make changes so that that problem and other problems like it cannot repeat themselves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're fairly rare, but we learn from them, and in this case it was internal, and it's been corrected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's always the example of Australia that everyone, I think, is aware of, where I think they're in year 28 of their expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All I can see is that we have an economy where the expansion is continuing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation is low, which gives us the ability to be patient, and we do expect it to move up, and we want it to move up to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I see us on a good path for this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This was before inflation really was under control, but, you know, it's very interesting to look at the history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I find it quite interesting to look at different periods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think, in our own cycle, we face a particular set of challenges that are really what's relevant for us now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, so, as you know, we are a nonpolitical institution, and that means we don't think about short-term political considerations, we don't discuss them, and we don't consider them in making our decisions one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we're always solving for in our process, in our work, is to carry out our mission, which is to extend the economic expansion, keep the labor market strong, and get inflation around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So to give you an idea of what our process is like, maybe as a way of putting all that in context-so for the past maybe 10 days, all 17 FOMC members will have made extensive preparations: catching up on the latest data, reading all the memos, talking to their colleagues and their staff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you also are I'm sure aware, Marty, we talk to literally thousands of businesspeople and market people and people in the nonprofit sector and the educational sector just to get a better sense of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We put all that together, and we come together for two days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first day begins with an economic briefing, which is, sort of, economic and financial developments in the United States and around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That takes up most of the first day, and we talk about this in great detail.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We go away, we think about that, and we come back, and the next day we talk about monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in this particular case, we came to a unanimous decision, after an extensive discussion, that our monetary policy stance is appropriate where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think our monetary policy stance is in a good place, and we're going to be patient as we consider adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we also see, by the way, the evolving-risk picture as very consistent with that outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't feel like the data's pushing us in either direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we'll not hesitate if we do feel that the data justify moving in either direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're pointing to, really, the fact that in recent years inflation has moved down and down, and, really, many major central banks have struggled to reach their inflation goals from below.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that includes us, although we've actually done- we've come closer, I think, than most others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's just a question, I think, of demographic and other large and, in some cases, global forces that are disinflationary to some extent, and it creates significant challenges.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One, I would say, is, it means that interest rates will be lower- will be closer to the effective lower bound more of the time because that means lower interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's one of the reasons we're having a review of our monetary policy strategies, tools, and communications this year-to think about that problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You mentioned the connection to financial stability of lower-for-longer rates, and that is another challenge.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned earlier, we do consider financial stability concerns to the extent they threaten achievement of our goals, but we also view, and I do take the view that macroprudential and supervisory tools, regulatory tools, things like the stress tests that we can do right through the cycle-those are really the best defense against financial instability so that the financial system is highly resilient to the kinds of financial shocks that can happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is the ISM reading, I guess from this morning, on manufacturing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, we see that reading as-it's still a positive reading and consistent with what we expect from the manufacturing sector, which is moderate or perhaps modest growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-yes, it's something that we are watching carefully, but we do expect a positive contribution to growth from the manufacturing sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our outlook and my outlook is for-is a positive one, is a healthy one for the U.S. economy for growth for the rest of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say that the basis for that, really, is consumer spending and business investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at consumer spending, you saw stronger retail sales, stronger motor vehicle sales in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, the conditions, the broader economic fundamentals, are strong in support of consumer spending-that's more accommodative financial conditions, high confidence readings, high levels of employment, wages going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a significant part of the outlook this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And business investment should also be positive in that sort of direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the effect of trade deals, I think one thing would be that the resolution of the uncertainty around these trade negotiations would, I would guess, be a positive for business sentiment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have been hearing from our business contacts, really, a lot since the beginning of the trade negotiations that uncertainty is a concern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you import metals or whatever for your product or export your product, then it's been a challenge for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, most of the gains, though, I would expect, even from a successful trade negotiation, would come in over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I don't think-it wouldn't be the kind of thing where you'd immediately feel big effects right away, but they could be quite important over a longer period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I haven't seen-none of us, at least I haven't seen, the details of what's been negotiated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let me say, I don't mean to diminish concerns about too-low inflation, but I think there's good reason to think that these readings are particularly influenced by some transitory factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One that I would mention is portfolio management services, which would tend to go down when asset prices go down, with a lag.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so when asset prices went back up, probably there'll be a swing around there, a positive contribution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Other ones that get mentioned are things like apparel, and apparel prices were very, very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't know until, again, until we see, but there's reason to think that those would be transient and would turn around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And another way to look at it is, there are models that look at inflation in different ways, like-not models, but measures, like the Dallas trimmed mean, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So trimmed mean-it cuts off the big movements on the upside and the downside and looks at just the mean movements in inflation of various product categories and service categories, and it didn't go down at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's at 2 percent-or it's at, I don't know whether it went down or was above that, but it's at 2 percent now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's reason to think that these will be transient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, of course, will be watching very carefully to see that that is the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would point to the case of cell phone services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many of you will remember, in March of 2017, there was a very low reading for cell phone services-mobile phone services-and it was kind of a price war, and it dragged down core inflation for a full year, but it did not look like something that would be repeated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we kind of thought so and said so, and then, sure enough, in 2018, we had those months of 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be watching-really, I'd like to say we're going to be watching inflation carefully to see that these things are transient, and I'll end by saying we are strongly committed to the 2 percent inflation objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You were saying if inflation does stay low and these low inflation rates are not transient, you said a couple times you'll take that into account with monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, it's hard to say, because there's so many other variables.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, there are many variables to be taken into account at any given time, but that's part of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Stable prices is half of our mandate, and we've defined that as 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we would be concerned, and we'd take it into account.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't really be any more specific than what I've said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we need to, and as needed, we will use our tools to keep the federal funds rate somewhere in the target range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Don't expect to need to do it again, but we don't know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we're-with-the balance sheet is now-the size of it is going to be driven by demand for liabilities, principally reserves, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're right at that point where we're starting to learn more and more about what the real demand for reserves is over the next few months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just have to do it, and that's why we're moving so very gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's why we tapered the roll-off to only $15 billion in Treasuries per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Effective, I guess, today, we're cutting the roll-off rate for Treasuries in half just because we want to take our time and move gradually here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of other tools, we're actually-I'm sure at an upcoming meeting we will be looking at the idea of a repo facility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't have any presupposition that it's something we would do, but we'll be taking a look at it as a possible addition to our toolbox.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I wouldn't say-it would just be a way for us to do what we do, which is to do a deep dive on it, think carefully about it, look at the pros and cons, look at the different possible ways to do it, and then go away and think about it for a little while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's something we'll do at an upcoming meeting, I would imagine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we put out a proposal on Volcker some time ago, and we got a lot of comments, and we're reviewing them carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in terms of what all it's going to be, it's not something I can say with any certainty yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, we don't see any evidence at all of overheating, for one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see inflation below 2 percent now-as I mentioned, pretty close to 2 percent for most of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the labor market, for a long time now there have been anecdotal reports of labor shortages and difficulty in finding skilled labor and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, you have very strong job creation, and you have wages moving up at a rate that is appropriate, given inflation and given productivity, but not at all signaling any overheating at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not higher than that rate that would incorporate both inflation and productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, really not seeing signs of overheating at the moment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes-in terms of wages getting over 4 percent, wages have moved up pretty steadily over the last five years and are now-wages and benefits are now between 3 and 3½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just for the last couple of years, the biggest part of the gains have come for people at the lowest end of compensation and education, which is kind of a welcome thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one has been able to predict it successfully, so I won't really try.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I will say this: Productivity was very, very low in the wake of the crisis for six or seven years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Last year, we had 1. percent productivity, which is much higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know if that level can be sustained, but we really- it's driven, to some extent, by technological developments and, really, the diffusion of technology through the economy, and it's very hard to predict.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, I'll mention, if we're talking about the supply side, labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, there has been a significant positive supply-side development over the last year and a half between the uptick in labor force participation, which goes back several years, but also productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It suggests that a less tight economy, a less, you know-may be part of the explanation for lower inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the Committee had, you know, our usual long discussion of global and domestic economic and financial conditions and then spent this morning talking about monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I came to the view that I expressed to you, which is that we're going to be monitoring-monitoring the crosscurrents and the other items that we've mentioned, but that we'd like to see more going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Particularly, we'd like to see whether these risks continue to weigh on the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, generally, as I mentioned, many on the Committee do see a strengthened case-eight of those, a strengthened case for cutting rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A number of others see that the case has strengthened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the Committee wanted to see more, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I also mentioned that some of these-some of these developments have been of quite recent vintage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we do expect that we'll be learning a lot more on all of these issues in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm sure that things will change before the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I expect a full range of data and information on all of these issues that we are looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we'll learn a great deal more about them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's-we think that that's the right way to move here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, many of these developments happened, you know, part of the way through the last intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Only seven weeks ago, we had a great jobs report and came out of the last FOMC meeting feeling that the economy, and our policy, was in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we want to see-we want to see and we want to react to developments and trends that are sustained, that are genuine, and not react just to data points or just to changes in sentiment, which can be volatile.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we are-we're quite mindful of the risks to the outlook and are prepared to move and use our tools as needed to sustain the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so I would say that we're not looking at any one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess I would start by agreeing with your premise that news about trade has been an important driver of sentiment in the intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's really trade developments and concerns about global growth that are on our minds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're not exclusively focused on one event or one piece of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, we have incoming data in the United States that's been pretty good, particularly for the consumer: Consumer spending is solid supported by, you know, a healthy job market, high levels of employment, wages going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do see, though, some areas that we're looking at, such as, I mentioned, business fixed income.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-also, the prolonged shortfall in inflation and perhaps job growth-we don't like to look at one job report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We like to average over three or six months, but still that bears watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll be monitoring the implications of all of those developments for the U.S. economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We expect to learn a good deal more, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be asking the question whether those risks are going to continue to weigh on the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, in the end, we'll use our tools as appropriate to sustain this long expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the law is clear that I have a four-year term, and I fully intend to serve it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're always trying to balance that risk, but I would say that, given the quite recent nature of some of the events, I think the Committee felt, though, that the right thing to do was to wait and see more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will see a lot more on all of these issues in the very near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't think the risk of waiting too long is prominent right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, as a general matter, it's always something that we have to weigh.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think we believe that the right thing here is to watch carefully in the near term and see how these risks unfold and see whether they continue to weigh on the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In this case, you know, there's always some judgment in these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would just say that the risks that we see having emerged are risks that have gotten our attention and that have called a number of us to write down rate cuts, and a number of those who haven't to see that the case has strengthened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let me let me say the same thing as I said the last time, before there had been any dissents, and that is that I think the process of careful, thoughtful dissent is a very healthy one, and I've always believed that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I feel like you make better decisions when you hear a disparity of views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would add, though, that the support for the path we took for the policy statement that we adopted was quite broad.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, first, I think all central banks are focused on their domestic- their mandates are domestic, and they're focused on economic conditions from a domestic standpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that goes for the European Central Bank, it goes for the Fed, it goes for all central banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I would think that, to the extent you see stronger financial conditions and stronger activity in the ECB after a rate cut, that would support-tend to support activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're really focused on, you know, the risks to our-on the baseline outlook, which is still a pretty favorable one, and the risks to those outlooks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me let me answer the inflation question first.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're saying that we know-I noted in the statement and also in my-what I said here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We saw that market-based measures of inflation expectations, breakevens, dropped.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I noted it as a reason for us to-one of several reasons why it feels to us that the case for more accommodation has strengthened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not only that, the actual forecast for inflation for this year, among FOMC participants, dropped a couple of tenths.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let me say, on inflation, it's something I've been concerned about for quite a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's one of the principal reasons why I called for the review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In a world where policy rates are going to be closer to the effective lower bound, then, just as a general matter, we need to be really strong on 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, you know, we certainly don't want to be seen as weak on inflation, and I don't believe we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the dots, you're right, this is the first time, I believe, we've had-we've talked about cutting in the "dot era."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know that my view on the dots is that they, overall, provide useful information for people, but that we need to do our absolute best to explain what they are and what they are not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Speaking of which, they are not a forecast of the group, they're not discussed or debated at the meeting, they're an input to policy more than an output of policy, and they're also only the most likely case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in a situation where there's relatively high uncertainty, there's the most likely case, but the second most likely case might only be a little bit less likely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I just would say that, if you pay too close attention to the dots, then you may lose sight of the larger picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the specific question of that, that's just something we haven't really engaged with yet, and it will depend very heavily on incoming data and the evolving risk picture as we move forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it would be-so nothing I can say about that is specific to the near-term question that we face.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: More generally, though, the research you refer to essentially notes that, in a world where you are closer to the effective lower bound, it's why-research kind of shows this-it's wise to react, for example, to prevent a weakening from turning into a prolonged weakening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other words, sort of, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that is a valid way to think about policy in this era.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know-and it's always in the-I think it's in the minds of policymakers, you know, during this era, because it's well understood to be correct.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I don't know what that means in terms of the size of a particular rate cut going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's going to depend heavily upon, you know, the actual data and the evolving risk picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The U.S. Treasury has responsibility for exchange rate policy, not the Fed, and we don't comment, in that sense, on the level of the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have the responsibility for maximum employment and stable prices, and we use our tools to achieve that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we do that through changing financial conditions, and one of those is the dollar, but we don't target the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, central banks-or, rather, nations, when they get together, routinely adopt a communique that says we will target our domestic, economic, and financial conditions and not our exchange rate in using monetary policy, and that includes the United States, that includes the G-20 communique that we adopted 10 days ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm not the right person to ask about that sort of dollar policy intervention.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I would say, there was not much support for cutting rates now at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was, as you see, a number of people wrote down rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But all of those, but apparently one, felt that it would be better to see more to-before moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I gave a couple of reasons why that is the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, it's just the fact that some of these developments are so recent that we want to see whether they'll sustain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we felt that it would be better to get a clearer picture of things, and that we would, in fact, learn a lot about these developments in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, the question we're going to be asking ourselves is, are these risks going to be continuing to weigh on the outlook?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will act as needed, including promptly, if that's appropriate, and use our tools to expand-to sustain the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it's a complicated picture, and, you know, the answer is, we look at all of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say, the big pieces of it are this: The baseline outlook has been a good one, and that has basically been consumer spending coming back up in the second quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And consumer spending is at a healthy level, and that makes sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got companies in surveys saying that labor is scarce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got workers in surveys saying that jobs are plentiful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, all of that, underlying fundamentals for the consumer spending part of the economy, which is 70 percent of the economy, is quite solid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job creation, if you take a three-month average, is still well above, you know, the entry-level of entry into the workforce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You mentioned manufacturing, and we're seeing this all around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not solely a domestic issue, and it may be that there are a range of factors that are contributing to that, including, for example, what China has done over the last couple of years in working to bring down its leverage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of it may be uncertainty over your supply chains due to trade developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Boeing 737 issues may be contributing in their own way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there-lower oil prices are contributing to lower investment, although they're also leading to lower gas prices, which supports spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you do see growth in services, so you-this pattern around the world of weak manufacturing but growth in the far larger part of the services economy, which has led to low unemployment, good job creation, rising wages, that's kind of the two big pieces of it that you see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you lay the crosscurrents on top of that-concerns about global growth and trade developments-you have the full picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think what that picture-what we took away from that picture is that we'd like to see more, that we do see these risks, and what we want to do is, we want to watch and see whether they continue to weigh upon the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, we have the tools we have, and we're committed and sworn to use them to support economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they do support economic activity through a number of channels that are reasonably well understood-some more directly tied to interest rates than others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do generally believe that-that our interest rate policy can support demand and support business investment as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we will use those tools and use them as we see as appropriate to achieve our objectives, which really are to sustain this expansion, and I would just make a note of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The reason why we say "sustain the expansion" is, you're seeing now, for the first time, you know, communities that are being brought into the benefits of this expansion that hadn't been earlier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're 10 years deep into this, and that's something we heard quite a lot at the conference in Chicago on the review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I just would say, that's why we think-it's one of the reasons why we think it's so important to sustain the expansion, keep it going, because we really are benefiting groups that haven't seen, you know, this kind of prosperity in a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we take the-you know, we take the crosscurrents as a given, and we have our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we don't-we react to anything in principle that could undermine our achievement of our dual-mandate goals-maximum employment, stable prices-is worthy of our attention and can call forth a policy response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I don't-I don't discuss elected officials publicly or privately, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would just say that we are-at the Fed, we're deeply committed to carrying out our mission, and also that our independence from direct political control we see as an important institutional feature that has served both the economy and the country well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Chair Powell, are you concerned that new digital currencies like Libra, which Facebook unveiled this week, could undermine the Fed and erode your power to influence the economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And did anyone from Facebook talk with anyone at the Fed before Libra was unveiled this week?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on your specific question of digital currencies replacing central bank currencies, I think we're a long way from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, the-so I think we're a long way from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, essentially, not too concerned about, you know, the central banks no longer being able to carry out monetary policy because of cryptocurrencies or digital currencies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, Facebook, I believe, has made quite broad rounds in-around the world really with regulators, supervisors, and lots of people to discuss their plans, and that certainly includes us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We meet with a broad range of private-sector firms all the time on financial technology, and there's just a tremendous amount of innovation going on out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are also potential risks, particularly of a currency that could, you know, that could potentially have large application.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would echo what Governor Carney said, which is that we will wind up having quite high expectations, from a sort of safety and soundness and regulatory standpoint, if they do decide to go forward with something.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Do you think the Fed will be involved in regulating Libra then?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we have-we don't have plenary authority over cryptocurrencies as such.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They play into our world through consumer protection and money laundering and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, I would say that, you know, through international forums, you know, we have significant input into the payment system and, as you know, play an important role in the payment system here in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have-we've said that we wouldn't look at raising the target rate for inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason is, it's become a global norm, 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're actually taking a less-we're looking at less radical ideas, such as how to make the 2 percent inflation objective more credible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This gives me a chance to say a couple things about the review and Chicago, in particular.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's something that-I thought it was both appropriate and important for us to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll be a yearlong, or even longer, process, looking at our strategy, tools, and communications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's meant to be a way to open ourselves up, to let the sunshine in, and have dialogue and criticism with the constituencies that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had a series of Fed Listens around the country at every Reserve Bank, and we had an academic conference earlier this month, with seven papers written and criticized, and leading global experts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I'll just say, again, that the heart of the conference was the two panels on-with practitioners in low and moderate income-who live in low- and moderate-income communities and are part of those communities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they were-there, I think, people were quite struck by their intervention, which was really uniformly around how important maximum employment is and what it means in their communities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the idea being, they haven't had, you know, a bull market in these communities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What they have had is low unemployment, lots of social problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And just now, you have, you know, companies who want to hire and are bringing people into the-providing opportunities for people to come into the labor force to an extent not seen in quite a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
