text: And that is, I think, you know, for someone who does this work, that was very focusing and motivating, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think everybody thought, you know, that's-that was really quite worth doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, there was some thought at the beginning that we should-some people recommended that we just talk to, you know, econ Ph.D.'s about this, but, no, that's not what we chose to do, and we're glad this is the choice we made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think it's-I don't think it's a practical alternative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see central banks having a hard time getting inflation up to their-close to their objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've done better than other large central banks that are not, you know, open economies, like the U.K., where you have big currency moves that move inflation around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but it's quite challenging to get inflation- it's been-even with very high levels of resource utilization, inflation has been lingering and not getting back up to target in a sustained, symmetric kind of a way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So saying that you're going to go for 4 percent-I wonder how credible that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the 2013 guidance is not binding, and that's what came out of the GAO review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we have the authority we need to examine the banks for safety and soundness exposure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, this-the first thing you start with as a bank supervisor is the risks that the banks are taking to themselves through their portfolio, through the risks that they're running and the pipeline-you know, the obligations that they've undertaken to underwrite deals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we monitor that very carefully-so do the banks-and you see exposures that are much smaller than they were before the crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, we test that regularly in the stress tests.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We impose very large losses on those portfolios, so we kind of have a sense of what that is, whereas before the crisis, there was a lot of lack of knowledge about what the losses would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's where it starts for us in supervision, is the risks that the banks are running-you know, running on their own books and to themselves and to each other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in that, I feel-I feel like that is-that's in a good place, but we never-we never say "Mission accomplished" on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's happened, though, is, the paper is now owned by market-based vehicles: collateralized loan obligations, mutual funds, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we now have-you know, we have a good sense of, domestically, of where that paper is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, internationally, not as much, and the Financial Stability Board is actually looking more carefully at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we- you know, we monitor those vehicles to see what they are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they're actually pretty stably funded, in the sense that there's no run risk, but there's still macroeconomic risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, this is something that we take very seriously and that the FSOC, the Financial Stability Oversight Council, is looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we call it out as a macroeconomic risk, but it's not really a financial stability risk, in the sense that it could undermine the ability of the financial system to do its job of intermediating credit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think the issue isn't that the banks don't understand what the rules are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The issue is that the risk isn't in the banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't, I don't-you know, I no longer am day-to-day involved in this as I was before I took this job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But my sense is, though, that that's really not the problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not saying it's perfect, but I think we do understand what risks the banks are running.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And really the question is, how concerned should we be about large holdings by market-based vehicles that I mentioned, and what risks do they present?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I gave a whole speech about this a few weeks ago, so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we have to be closer, because more jobs are being created than people are entering the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, by just lots and lots of numbers, the labor market is in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the level of wages is very consistent with what it should be, in the sense that it's approximately equal to inflation plus productivity increases on an hourly basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what's, I guess, a little surprising, though, is that you could reach these levels of unemployment late-you know, long into a cycle, let's say, and not see even higher wages that are pushing up on inflation, because wages at this level, even though they're growing at a healthy rate, at an appropriate rate, they're not growing at a rate that would provide much upward thrust for inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we watch-we watch all of this very carefully, and I think we're very careful about not assuming that we're, you know, that would-that there's no more slack in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've all lived through-you know, when I got to the Fed, we were in the 8 percent-plus range, and it's just gone down and down and down, and you haven't seen wages picked up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You haven't seen real signals that we're at maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it-the surveys that I mentioned will all show that the labor market has tightened, but not overtightened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Balance sheet runoff is very close to the end of its planned life.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say this: If we do provide more accommodation-again, we haven't really addressed this-but if we do provide more accommodation, we'll certainly keep in mind what we said earlier this year, which is that we'll always be willing to adjust balance sheet policy so that it serves our dual-mandate objectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think you have to look at not just the 25 basis point cut, but look at the Committee's actions over the course of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I noted in my opening statement, we started off expecting some rate increases, we moved to a patient setting for a few months, and now we've moved here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think what you've seen over the course of the year is, as we've moved to a more accommodative policy, the economy has actually performed just about as expected with that gradually increasing support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think-I wouldn't take credit for all of that, but I do think that increasing policy support has kept the economy on track and kept the outlook favorable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the rest of your question, the Committee is really thinking of this as a way of adjusting policy to a somewhat more accommodative stance to further the three objectives that I mentioned: to insure against downside risks, to provide support to the economy, that those factors are-where factors are pushing down on economic growth, and then to support inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do think it will serve all of those goals, but again, we're thinking of it as essentially in the nature of a midcycle adjustment to policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The position of the economy is as close to our objectives as it's been in a long time, and the outlook is also good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we've been monitoring since the beginning of the year is, effectively, downside risks to that outlook from weakening global growth, and we see that everywhere: weak manufacturing, weak global growth now, particularly in the European Union and China.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, we see trade policy developments, which at times have been disruptive and then have been less so, and also inflation running below target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we see those as threats to what is clearly a favorable outlook, and we see this action as designed to support them and keep that outlook favorable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, frankly, it is a continuation of what we've been doing all year to provide more support against those very same risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I-I really think it does, and I think the evidence of my eyes tells me that our policy does support-it supports confidence, it supports economic activity, household and business confidence, and through channels that we understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Since-you know, since we noted our vigilance about the situation in June, you saw financial conditions move up, and you saw-I won't take credit for the whole recovery, but you saw financial conditions move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see confidence, which had troughed in June-you saw it move back up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just-it seems to work through confidence channels as well as the mechanical channels that you are talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think we-of course, you know, what we do at every meeting, as I noted, is, we do a deep dive into U.S. economic activity and global activity and, certainly, carefully went through U.S. economic activity, which there has been some positive and some negative, but, overall, the U.S. economy has shown resilience during the intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, the-the issue is more the downside risks and then the shortfall in inflation, and we're trying to address those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in addition, going forward, I would say, we're going to be monitoring those same things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be monitoring the evolution of trade uncertainty, of global growth, and of low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll also, of course, be watching the performance of the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, it had shown some resilience here to those issues, and we'll be putting all of that together, and that's how we'll be thinking about policy going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I gave three reasons for what we did, and that is to insure against downside risks to the outlook from weak global growth and trade tensions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is-in a sense, that is a risk-management point, and that is a bit of insurance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we also feel like weak global growth and trade tensions are having an effect on the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see it now in the second quarter: You see weak investment, you see weak manufacturing-so support demand there and also to support return of inflation to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't-you know, the thing is, there isn't a lot of experience in responding to global trade tensions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is a-it's something that we haven't faced before and that we're learning by doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it is not-it's not exactly the same as watching global growth, where you see growth weakening, you see central banks and governments responding with fiscal policy, and you see growth strengthening, and you see a business cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With trade tensions- which do seem to be having a significant effect on financial market conditions and on the economy-they evolve in a different way, and we have to follow them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, I want to be clear here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We play no role whatsoever in assessing or evaluating trade policies other than as-as trade policy uncertainty has an effect on the U.S. economy in the short and medium term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I actually think different people have different-different weightings has been my experience on those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You mentioned lower r*, trade slowdown- and I would actually add, lower natural rate of unemployment too has moved down, all of which kind of point to more accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, I don't think asking about a ¼ point is really the right question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you have to look back over the course of the year and see the Committee moving away from rate increases to a neutral posture to, now, a rate cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we've been providing-and that affects the forward rate path, and it affects financial conditions, and financial conditions affect the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see an economy which is actually performing pretty well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Growth in the first half of this year is about the same as it was in all of '18 and actually a little better than our forecast for growth in 2019-at the end of 2019.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, in a way, that's monetary policy working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, I wouldn't just look at the 25 basis point cut as the right question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, as we noted-we noted at the bottom of the statement that language, which really says how we're thinking about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it says, as we're contemplating the future path of the target range for the federal funds rate, we'll continue to monitor the implications of incoming information-and it talks about that language.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I can't- all I can tell you is, we'll be looking at weak global growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be looking very carefully to see how that's happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you see-you learn-every cycle you learn about these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we will see whether growth is picking up, whether it's bottoming out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're going to be seeing-I think we've learned a lot on trade in this cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we'll continue to learn more, and on inflation we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in addition, the U.S. economy itself is-the performance of the U.S. economy will enter into that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would love to be more precise, but with trade, it is a factor that we have to assess in kind of a new way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are the things that we'll be looking at, and-you know, in making our decisions going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They don't come in and say, "We're not investing because, you know, the federal funds rate is too high."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you hear is that demand is weak for their products.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I wouldn't lay all of that at the door of trade talks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's a-there's a global business cycle happening with manufacturing and investment, and that's-that's been, you know, definitely a bigger factor than, certainly, we expected late last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think global-global growth started to slow down in the middle of last year, but that has gone on to a greater extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, trade policy uncertainty has also been, I think, more elevated than we anticipated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of, is this the-we believe this is the right move for today, and we think it's-we think it will serve the three ends that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I've already gone over how we're thinking about going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, the sense of that is-I mean, that refers back to other times when the FOMC has cut rates in the middle of a cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'm contrasting it there with the beginning-for example, the beginning of a lengthy cutting cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so our policy is-will depend on the implications of incoming data for the economic outlook as well as evolving risks to that outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're going to be monitoring the implications of incoming information for the outlook, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, so I-that's really where I would leave you with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on the first, I would say that I view the level of capital requirements and the level of capital in the system as being about right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The idea that you're talking about is one that's-that Vice Chair Quarles has talked about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The idea being, in a sense, we've chosen, in the United States, to have high through-the-cycle capital requirements by doubling the SIFI surcharge, which is the surcharge that the largest banks have in their capital requirements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've, in effect, already put in place substantial countercyclical buffers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, conceptually, you can think of-I'm not saying it's the same thing as a countercyclical capital buffer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-that's really the point-is that we don't rely-our system doesn't rely on our ability-it doesn't mainly rely on our ability to identify the right time in the cycle to trigger a countercyclical tool.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We rely on through-the-cycle, always-on high capital and liquidity requirements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The idea of putting it in place so you can cut it, that's something some other jurisdictions have done, and it's worth considering.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the United Kingdom, in particular, has a countercyclical capital buffer that's always on, but the one point of it is that you can cut when there's a downturn and therefore give the banks more room.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the real-time payment system, your second question, so this is something we-the United States is far behind other countries in terms of having real-time payments available to the general public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Fed, really, coming out of the Reserve System-the Reserve Banks and the Board together-convened all of the stakeholders around the table to talk about how we can move forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is consumer groups, technology companies, banks, card companies-pretty much all of the groups who would be interested-and worked on a project for several years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And one of the things that came out of that was a recommendation that the Fed should build a 24 x 7 x 365 real-time settlement system to solve that problem-to address that problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We put out a proposal in October of last year about, you know, should we do this, and we got quite a lot of comments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would point out that in our payment system, in many places, the Fed operates alongside private-sector operators-for example, in wholesale payments, in ACH, and in check-so it wouldn't be unusual or out of keeping with-with how we've done things in the past.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have not made a decision on this, but it's something we're looking at carefully and something I do expect we'll make a decision on soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is-as I mentioned, it's going to depend on the evolving data and the evolving risk picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as we look at the situation now and the outlook now, what we see is that it's appropriate to make an adjustment in policy to a somewhat more accommodative stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's what we're going to be looking-you know, we'll be looking at incoming data, at all of the-at the risks that I mentioned, and the performance of the U.S. economy, and at low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be looking at that to make our decisions going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think the best thing for people who are-who are feeling that-and we are getting lots of feedback from people who work and live in low- and moderate- income communities to the effect that they're now feeling the recovery, and, in fact, they haven't felt a better labor market in anybody's memory, so this is great to hear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I guess my view is, the best thing we can do for those people is to sustain the expansion, keep it going, and that's one of the overarching goals of-of this move and all of our policy moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There really is no reason why the expansion can't keep going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the-at the U.S. economy right now, there's no sector that's booming and therefore might bust.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, the engine, though, is really a consumer economy, which is 70 percent of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The manufacturing economy-the investment and manufacturing part of the economy-is more or less not-not growing much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and we hope to help that with this rate cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, I would say, overall, we're trying to sustain the expansion and keep, you know, close to our statutory goals, which are maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I gave my-my reasons for-our reasons, really-for doing this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, just to touch on that again, this action is designed to insure against downside risks to the outlook from weak global growth and trade tensions, offset the negative effect that those factors are already having, and promote a faster return of inflation to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we've been talking about all year long, and we've gradually moved our policy in the direction of more accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think what you see is an economy that has reacted well to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's what we're doing, and that's why we're doing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also don't conduct monetary policy in order to prove our independence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We conduct monetary policy in order to-to move as close as possible to our statutory goals, and that's what we're always going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, at the end, we'll-you know, we'll live with the results.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the balance sheet, that was really just a matter of simplicity and consistency.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, first, let me say-I'll just speak for myself, but I understand those concerns very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've-you know, I've studied them, I've spoken about them, and I take them very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as I look at today's situation, I don't see them as a reason not to take this action today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And one of the reasons why I think that is, if you look-if you look-so we have a financial stability framework now for the first time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Before the crisis, we didn't have this, but now we have it, and we publish it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we look at, really, four big things so that we know we can-you know, the public can hold us accountable and compare us meeting to meeting, and-you know, and see whether we got this right, because it's transparent now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the four things we look at are valuation pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do see notable valuation pressures in some markets but, you know, honestly, not at a highly troubling level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of household borrowing, household and business borrowing is the second thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Leverage in the financial system is low, and funding risk is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, staff's view has been-and my view has been-that if you look overall, financial stability vulnerabilities are moderate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The place that gets all the attention right now-a lot of attention-is business borrowing, and we look very carefully at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's happening with business borrowing is, the loans have moved off the balance sheets of the banks and into market-based vehicles, which tend to be stably funded.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, it's clear that the highly leveraged business sector could act as an amplifier to a downturn.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, I think if you look overall at the U.S. financial system, what you see is a high level of resilience-much higher than it was before the crisis-and that's something to take comfort from.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think all of that gives us the ability to use monetary policy for its purposes and rely on supervisory and regulatory tools to-you know, to keep the financial system resilient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are very few things that I don't worry about at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have-every quarter we have an extensive briefing on financial stability, and we had that yesterday.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, one of my colleagues is the head of the Financial Stability Board globally, so we're very, very much monitoring these things all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're always looking at the-we're looking for that thing that we may have missed a lot of the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the things we haven't missed, I think they paint a mixed picture, but not one that should prevent us from taking monetary policy actions that we think are appropriate to support the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I said was, it's not-it's not the beginning of a long series of rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I didn't-I didn't say it's just one or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I said is, when you think about rate-cutting cycles, they go on for a long time, and the Committee is not seeing that-not seeing us in that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You would do that if you saw real economic weakness and you thought that the federal funds rate needed to be cut a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're seeing is that it's appropriate to-to adjust policy to a somewhat more accommodative stance over time, and that's how we're looking at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I said was, it's not a long cutting cycle-in other words, referring to what we do when there's a recession or a very severe downturn.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, if you look back at other midcycle adjustments, you'll see-you know, I don't know that they'll be, in the end, comparable or not, but you'll see examples of these.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I wouldn't bring it down to any one trade thing or any one factor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we look at a broad range of factors, and trade uncertainty-trade policy uncertainty is one of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That certainly includes the discussions with China, but I wouldn't-I wouldn't be able to tell you how much of it is due to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And without knowing-you know, I think we-with trade, we have to react to the developments, and we don't know what they'll be, and so it's hard to exactly say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Certainly, we've seen, though, that when there's a sharp confrontation between two large economies, you can see effects on business confidence pretty quickly and on financial markets pretty quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But then we saw them unwind after that, to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've seen it returning to-to a much lower temperature, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, with-with trade policy, we're just going to be watching and trying to assess the implications for the-for the U.S. outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the mechanical effects of the tariffs are quite small.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're not large as it relates to the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The real question is, what are the effects on the economy through the-through the confidence channel-business confidence channel?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've seen some research, which-you know, which says that they are meaningful-meaningful effects on-on output.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that that sounds right, but it's quite hard to get-there is no way to get an accurate measure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You have to look at a range of estimates, and I think businesses will tell you that it's a factor, particularly businesses that have-manufacturing businesses that have supply chains that cross international borders will all tell you that it's been a challenge.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many of them have made adjustments, and they've gotten to a place where it's okay, but it's-it's been a challenge.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a range of views on the Committee, and-but the Committee is unified, completely unified on our dedication to making the best policy decisions that we can make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means people have a responsibility to do their best thinking and to present that thinking, and I wouldn't have it any other way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the way forward, we will be monitoring the factors that I mentioned, and we laid that out in the-you know, in the postmeeting statement, and that's the roadmap we're going to be following going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be, as we always are, doing what we need to do-what we believe we need to do to support the economic expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the problems at Wells Fargo-that arose at Wells Fargo around risk management and consumer-the way they dealt with the consumer were actually pretty deep, and I think the company realizes that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they're not going to be fixed-they haven't been fixed quickly, and, frankly, we didn't expect them to be fixed quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So they're-you know, they-they will be under the growth cap, our enforcement action, until the Board votes to lift it, and that's not something we're considering doing right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the Committee-I mean, the company is working away to address these issues, but, as I said, they're deep-seated issues, and it just takes time to address them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think they do see it as we do, as something that has to go deep.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we'll lift the growth cap when we're satisfied.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when we have our next recession, the Fed will have less room-it will happen-the Fed will have less room to maneuver cutting interest rates since you're cutting now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the premise is not-I will question your premise for a second.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you remember whether-again, one of the purposes of our-of our cut today is to support the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't know when-and if it really works-if that works very well and the economy gets going again, you know, you don't know where the-where the funds, in other cycles-and I don't know whether this will happen or not, but in other cycles, the Fed wound up raising rates again after a midcycle adjustment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I'm not predicting that, but I don't think that we know that we won't have-that we'll have less ammo because of these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you won't be able to cut as much if-if rates are low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, you will have-have less ammo, in that sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, but you're assuming that we would never raise rates again, that once we've cut these rates that they can never go back up again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just as a matter of principle, I don't think that's right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other-in other long, long cycles, long U.S. business cycles have sometimes involved this kind of event where the Fed will stop hiking-in fact, will cut-and then will go back to hiking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't seem-it doesn't seem like something that's in-you know, particularly likely, frankly, but we don't know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the other thing is, I think by extending the cycle, you-you do have a lot of benefits from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, you know, we will use the tools that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A couple of rate hikes one way or the other isn't going to matter so much if there is a downturn.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll use all of our tools aggressively, as we need to, when that time comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the monetary policy review is really for-it's really there to look at the way we make policy in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something that enters directly into our discussions today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had-so far we've had a series of meetings, called Fed Listens, at almost all the Reserve Banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we meet there with the constituencies that we serve, and they've been very, very successful, hearing from people-not just-not just economists, but people who are not economists, how-how their lives interact with the Fed's work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've got to say, it's been even better than I hoped it would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're just now beginning the process of incorporating all of that feedback, and we're going to be having a series of meetings, beginning today and yesterday, as we evaluate, you know, the questions that we're asking about our framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's very early to say where that's going, but, you know, we're setting the table now and looking at what our framework is and looking at how it's performed, looking at how all frameworks performed around the world during the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's opened us up to sunlight and perspectives that we might not have gotten otherwise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you have-10 years after the crisis, you're really living in a new normal for the economy and monetary policy, and it's a really good time to step back and ask whether there are some things that we can do to improve our framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we did today was-was very consistent with what we had said we were going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They've been well telegraphed, and I think-you know, I think they will-they will achieve their goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do know that monetary policy works through communications and then actions that are consistent with those communications, and we think that the changes that we've made this year have really worked.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we always retain the flexibility to adjust our communications and our actions to-in light of incoming data and the evolving risk picture, but-I'll leave it there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so again, I see the U.S. outlook as being a positive one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do-we have had these global, really, risks to the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There really-there really is nothing in the U.S. economy that presents a-you know, a prominent near-term threat to the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, there's no-there's no segment that's really-or sector that's really boiling over and overheating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-and, by the way, those risks from abroad are affecting the manufacturing sector here and business investment-fixed investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you can see from our policy statement and from the SEP, we see a favorable economic outlook, with continued moderate growth, a strong labor market, and inflation near our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, that view is consistent with those of many other forecasters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you can see, FOMC participants generally think that these positive economic outcomes will be achieved with modest adjustments to the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the last press conference, I pointed to two episodes in, I guess, 1995 and 1998 as examples of such an approach, which was successful in both of those instances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As our statement also highlights, though, there are risks to this positive outlook due particularly to weak global growth and trade developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if the economy does turn down, then a more extensive sequence of rate cuts could be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't see that-it's not what we expect-but we would certainly follow that path if it became appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other words, as we say in our statement, we will continue to monitor these developments closely, and we will act as appropriate to help ensure that the expansion remains on track.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the idea of having a bias is something that was a longtime practice, and we don't actually have that practice anymore, so I can't really adopt it right here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we did-we made one decision today, and that decision was to lower the federal funds rate by ¼ percentage point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We believe that action is appropriate to promote our objectives, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our decisions are going to depend on the implications of incoming information for the outlook, and I would also say, as we often do, that we're not on a preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Sometimes the path ahead is clear and sometimes less so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to be looking carefully, meeting by meeting, at the full range of information, and we're going to assess the appropriate stance of policy as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I said, we will act as appropriate to sustain the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, what we do going forward is very much going to depend, Rich, on the flow of data and information.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen-you know, if you look at the things we're monitoring, particularly global growth and trade developments, global growth has continued to weaken.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Trade developments have been up and down and then up, I guess-or back up, perhaps-over the course of this intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do see those risks as actually more heightened now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also going to be watching the U.S. data quite carefully, and we'll have to make an assessment as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, let me just say, on the general point of diverse perspectives, you're right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Sometimes the-and there have been many of those times in my now almost eight years at the Fed, many times when the direction is relatively clear and it's relatively easy to reach unanimity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a time of difficult judgments and, as you can see, disparate perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I really do think that's nothing but healthy, and so I see a benefit in having those diverse perspectives, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that the idea that if you see trouble approaching on the horizon, you steer away from it if you can-I think that's a good idea in principle, and I think history teaches us that it's better to be proactive in adjusting policy if you can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think applying that principle in a particular situation is where the challenge comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I told you where the Committee-the bulk of the Committee is going, meeting by meeting, and I think the main takeaway is that this is a Committee that has shifted its policy stance repeatedly, consistently, through the course of the year to support economic activity as it has felt that it's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the beginning of the year we were looking at further rate increases, then we were patient, and then we cut once, then we cut again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you've seen us being willing to move based on data, based on the evolving risk picture, and I have no reason to think that will change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-but it will continue to be data dependent, and depend-data includes the evolving risk picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's where I am, and that's where I think the bulk of the Committee is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so I would say I doubt that anyone is closer to and has more invested in carefully following the-you know, the behavior of these markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, we were well aware of the-you know, the tax payments and also of the settlement of the large bond purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we were very much waiting for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we didn't expect-the response to that was stronger than we expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, our sense is that it surprised market participants a lot, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, people were writing about this and publishing stories about it weeks ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It wasn't a surprise, but it was-it was a stronger response than-certainly than we expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, no, I'm not concerned about that, to answer your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can go on a little bit about how we're looking at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, it doesn't-we don't see this as having any implications for the broader economy or for the economic outlook, nor for our ability to control rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The strains in the money markets reflect forces that we saw coming, and they just had a bigger effect than I think most folks anticipated-strong demand for cash to purchase Treasuries and pay corporate taxes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We took appropriate actions to address those pressures, to keep the fed funds rate within the target range, and those measures were successful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we experience another episode of pressures in money markets, we have the tools to address those pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And since we're talking about this, let me take a step back and say this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Earlier in the year, as you will all recall, after careful study over a period of years, actually, the Committee announced the decision to implement monetary policy in an ample-reserves regime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've been operating in that regime for a full decade.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it works well to implement our rate decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The main hallmark of that regime is that we use adjustments in our administered rates-the IOER and RRP rates-to keep the fed fund rates in the target range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's designed specifically so that we do not expect to be conducting frequent open market operations for that purpose.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, going forward, we're going to be very closely monitoring market developments and assessing their implications for the appropriate level of reserves, and we're going to be assessing, you know, the question of when it will be appropriate to resume the organic growth of our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'm sure we'll be revisiting that question during this intermeeting period and certainly at our next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've always said that it's-that the level is uncertain, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's something we've tried to be very clear about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as you know, we've invested lots of time talking to many of the large holders of reserves to assess their-what they say is their demand for reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We put it out so the public can react to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, yes, there's real uncertainty, and it is certainly possible that we will need to resume the organic growth of the balance sheet earlier than we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's always been a possibility, and it certainly is now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, we'll be looking at this carefully in coming days and taking it up at the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think to provide a little context, Fed economists do research all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not an official finding of the Federal Reserve Board or the Federal Reserve System.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just-and, by the way, they put it out for public review so that you can see their econometrics, so you can see all of it- their whole work is exposed to critique by the whole profession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, what this particular piece of work did is, it went after measuring trade policy uncertainty through a couple of channels, including concerning tariffs, also concerning the threat of more tariffs, and it looked deeply at the data to try to assess the effects on output.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And while I would say, directly answering your question, there's real uncertainty around these- around these effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To try to isolate the effects of certain things is very challenging, but we do the best we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and this piece of research found significant effects, and that's frankly consistent with a number of other research projects that economists have undertaken.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also consistent with what we've been hearing in the Beige Book.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I mean, I think if you take a step back from that, we do feel that trade uncertainty is having an effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see it in weak business investment, weak exports-hard to quantify it precisely, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, honestly, I think it's hard to have hardened expectations about where rate policy is going to be a year from now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the closer you get to the current day, the more confidence you can have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But even then, knowing where the-knowing what the data will say and the way geopolitical events and other events are going to evolve in the next 90 days and the implications of that for the economy, I would say there's a lot of uncertainty around that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Particularly, if you look at 2020, I think the use of this is, individual participants write down their forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It should give you a sense of how people are thinking about the likely path of the economy and the appropriate path for monetary policy in that individual person's thinking, and I think that's a good thing to know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think I'd be very reluctant to look at it as hardened views or a prediction, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, well, I think, if you look at the U.S.-look at the U.S. economy, the U.S. economy has generally performed roughly as expected-roughly: The consumer is spending at a healthy clip, I'd say business fixed investment and exports have weakened further, and I'd say the manufacturing PMI suggests more weakness ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market is still strong, though, so generally that is the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if you look at-the global economy, I think, has weakened further in the EU and China, and I think, you know, trade policy developments have been a big mover of markets and of sentiment during that intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's why I think what's-that's what's happened over the intermeeting period, and, you know, different people around the table have different perspectives as you obviously know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think it's hard to deal with every hypothetical possibility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, for the foreseeable future, we're going to be looking at, if needed, doing the sorts of things that we did the last two days-these temporary open market operations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the question will be, then-as we go through quarter-end, as we learn more, you know, what really-how much of this really has to do with the level of reserves?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we'll learn quite a lot in the next six weeks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so I think if we concluded that we needed to raise the level of required reserves for banks to meet the LCR, we'd probably raise the level of reserves rather than lower the LCR.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it's not impossible that we would come to a view that the LCR is calibrated too high, but that's not something that we think right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other hand, it might be that more reserves are needed, in which case we are in a position to supply them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the net stable funding ratio, it's-I believe we put it out for comment and got comments, and I believe we're looking at-at finalizing that in the relatively near future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we want banks to, you know-to use their liquidity buffers in times of stress rather than pull back from the markets and pull back from serving their clients as a general rule.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So my point, really, was that-to start, that trade policy is not the business of the Fed, it's the business of Congress and the Administration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're talking about it because anything that affects the achievement of our goals can, in principle, be something that monetary policy should take into consideration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And our discussions and the research we have suggests that trade policy is something that's weighing on the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I pointed out in recent remarks that the thing we can't address, really, is what businesses would like, which is a settled roadmap for international trade.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do have a very powerful tool which can counteract weakness, to some extent, by supporting demand through sound monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think our policy tools support economic activity through fairly well-understood channels: by reducing interest burden and encouraging consumer purchase of durables, of homes, and other interest-sensitive items; by creating broadly more accommodative financial conditions, which support spending and also investment by businesses; and also by boosting household and business confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I don't want to be heard to say that our tools don't have an effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I was making the point that there is a piece of this that we really can't address.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no simple bottom-line answer where I can say, yes, I've got it for you here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what it amounts to is this: What you see is probably the kind of volatility that's typical of an important, complex, ongoing negotiation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think what we need to do is to try to look through the volatility and react to the underlying forces, the underlying things that are happening that are relevant to our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't-we have nothing to do with setting trade policy or negotiating trade agreements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're supposed to be reacting on behalf of the American economy to support maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we need to look through what's a pretty volatile situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I would say, the outlook is positive in the face of these crosswinds we've felt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, to some extent, I do believe that our shifting to a more accommodative stance over the course of the year has been one of the reasons why the outlook has remained favorable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we are looking for through all of the data, all the events that are going on around the world, we'll be looking at, you know, the evolving geopolitical events, we'll be looking at global growth, we'll be looking at trade policy uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Most importantly, we'll be looking at the performance of the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be looking for things that are affecting the outlook for the U.S. economy, particularly the outlook as it relates to maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So all of those things in principle can affect the achievement of our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's an unusual situation, because, you know, the U.S. economy itself-the largest part of it, the consumer part of it-is in strong shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, overall, you see an economy that-I think, generally, forecasts show growth similar to our own, forecasts coming in about 2 percent, which is a good, solid year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the difference here is, we have significant, really, risks to that outlook from not just the geopolitical events, but also from slowing global growth and trade policy uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll be looking at all of that and also financial market conditions and how they are affecting the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't-it's a challenging time, I admit it, but we really have to be open to all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be making decisions meeting by meeting as we see this, and, you know, we'll try to be as transparent as we can as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, in terms of firepower, I think the general principle, as I mentioned earlier, is, it can be a mistake to try to hold onto your firepower until a downturn gains momentum, and then-so there's a fair amount of research that would show that that's the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, I think that principle needs to be applied carefully to the situation at hand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we believe we're facing here-what we think we're facing here is a situation which can be addressed and should be addressed with moderate adjustments to the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, we are watching carefully to see whether that is the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, in fact, the economy weakens more, then we're prepared to be aggressive, and we'll do so if it turns out to be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So negative interest rates is something that we looked at during the financial crisis and chose not to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We chose to-after we got to the effective lower bound, we chose to do a lot of aggressive forward guidance and also large-scale asset purchases, and those were the two unconventional monetary policy tools that we used extensively.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if we were to find ourselves at some future date again at the effective lower bound-again, not something we are expecting-then I think we would look at using large-scale asset purchases and forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do not think we'd be looking at using negative rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just don't think those will be at the top of our list.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: By the way, we are in the middle of a monetary policy review where we're looking through all of these questions about the longer-run framework-the strategy, tools, and communications-and we expect that to be completed sometime around the middle of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of how our rate cuts will affect the real economy, first, we think monetary policy works with, as Friedman said, long and variable lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the real effects will be felt over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we think that lower interest rates will reduce interest burden for borrowers, so that interest-sensitive things like housing and durable goods and other things like that-cars-it supports purchases of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-the models and the data show that that's another powerful channel.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see-you see household and business confidence turn up when financial conditions become more accommodative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, through all of those channels, monetary policy works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It isn't, you know, precisely the right tool for every single possible negative thing that can happen to the economy, but, nonetheless, it broadly works, and, you know, we're going to use the tool we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if it comes to it, we'll use all of our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's how we think it works and how we think it's working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll- we'll use our tools to offset negative-that's really the job of monetary policy, is, to the extent it can, to offset, you know, things that drive us away from maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Chair Powell, are you worried that the low interest rates are adding to, or could create a bubble of, consumer and corporate debt that could make it more difficult for, especially, consumers to recover from the next recession or survive the next recession?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so, if you look at-if you actually look at households, households are in very strong shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they're in very good shape-much better shape than they were in before the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the household sector as a sort of aggregate matter is in very good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That doesn't mean that every single person in the household sector is in good shape, but, overall, it's really not a concern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The business sector is something that, you know, we've talked about a lot and studied a lot, and the situation there is that the level of debt relative to GDP in the business sector is at a high level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, actually, the business sector itself is not materially higher leveraged than it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, there are a lot of highly levered companies, and that's the kind of thing that happens during a long cycle when there aren't downturns for, now, into our 11th year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You get-you know, you do get that kind of phenomenon in a long cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's something we're monitoring, and I think our view still is that that's a real issue, but what it really represents is a potential amplifier of a macroeconomic downturn.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It does not have the makings of anything that would undermine the workings of the financial system, for example, or itself create a shock that would turn the economy down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We take it very seriously, though, and, you know, we're monitoring it carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're actually looking-the Financial Stability Board is actually conducting a project right now to identify where these loans are held all around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's the subject of a lot of study and work, and, you know, we're trying to keep on top of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so, I think-and my colleagues and I, I think, all think that the most likely case is for continued moderate growth, continued strong labor market, and inflation moving back up to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's, by the way, widely shared among forecasters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the issue is more the risks to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You have downside risks here, and we've talked about them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's that global growth will have an effect on U.S. growth over time- less so than for many other economies, but, still, there's a sector of our economy that's exposed to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and you can see some weakness in the U.S. economy because of all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless-so the job of monetary policy is to adjust both to ensure against those downside risks, but also to support the economy in light of the existing weakness that we do see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're not-as I mentioned, we're not-we don't see a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we are adjusting monetary policy in a more accommodative direction to try to support what is, in fact, a favorable outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, we do-so we monitor the yield curve carefully, along with a large, wide range of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't-so, it's not-there's no one thing that is dispositive among all financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, based on our assessment of all the data, we still think it's a positive outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The thing-so, just to talk about the current situation, you see-you saw long-term rates move down a whole lot and then retrace two-thirds of that move in the space of a few days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think what really matters for all financial conditions generally is when there are changes- material changes that are sustained for a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are a number-there can be a signal about expectations about growth there for sure, but there can also just be low term premiums.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For example, just-well, it can just be that there's this large quantity of negative-yielding and very low-yielding sovereign debt around the world, and, inevitably, that's exerting downward pressure on U.S. sovereign rates without really necessarily having an independent signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, that is a signal about weak global growth, probably, and weak global growth would affect us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So global capital markets and the global economy are quite integrated, so this is something we pay careful-we're not going to be dismissive about the yield curve, but-and I think you can tell, on the Committee, there's a range of views-there are some who are very focused on the yield curve, others not so much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, from my perspective, you watch it carefully, and, you know, I think you need to be asking yourself a lot of questions if the yield curve is inverted as to why that is and how long it's sustained.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I'd love to be able to articulate a simple, straightforward stopping rule, but it's really just going to be when we think we've done enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've moved, really, through the course of this year, as I discussed, and, you know, we see ourselves as taking actions to sustain the expansion and thereby achieve our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look at sort of the things that are happening in the economy, I think I personally see a high value in sustaining the expansion, because we really are reaching-this positive economy is reaching communities that haven't been reached in a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There would be great benefit in having that last as long as possible, that's all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't have a specific stopping rule for you, but I think we're watching carefully, and there will come a time, I suspect, when we think we've done enough, but there may also come a time when the economy worsens, and we would then have to cut more aggressively.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The incoming data and the evolving situation and-that's what's going to guide our-guide us on that path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the morale of the institution, I would say it's very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We feel like we're doing the best job we can in serving the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so I saw the headline, like, this morning during all of the preparation and everything and this morning's meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say about Wells Fargo that, you know, there were quite wide breakdowns in risk management which resulted in, you know, mistreatment of consumers that we know was quite harmful to the consumers and to the image of the institution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I have no idea whether that's what happened at Bank of America.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we try to be clear about that, but, really, I think our job is to use our tools as best we can to achieve-you know, to do the jobs that Congress has assigned us, which is achieve maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of giving the fiscal authorities-who, by the way, are the ones who created us- advice about how to do their job, you know, we keep that at a high level, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, at a high level, yes, I would say, and I've said before, that it's really fiscal policy that is more powerful and that has much more to do with-fiscal policy can do those things that will increase the longer-run growth rate of the United States by improving productivity and labor force participation and the skills and aptitudes of workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of that comes from the private sector, but also from more of the kinds of things that can be done with fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Over the long run, we can't really affect the growth rate of the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The potential growth rate of the United States is not a function of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-I try to be clear about that, and so-but, ultimately, fiscal-fiscal authorities will do what they seem-deem appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going to change my practice here today of not responding to comments or addressing comments made by elected officials.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will just say that I continue to believe that the independence of the Federal Reserve from direct political control has served the public well over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I assure you that my colleagues and I will continue to conduct monetary policy without regard to political considerations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to use our best judgment based on facts, evidence, and objective analysis in pursuing our goals, and that's what I have to say on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's really-that's really Treasury's job and Congress's job, in terms of, well, there's how much to spend, and how big the deficits are, and then there's how to finance it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, none of that really calls for advice from the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We take-we take fiscal policy pretty much as exogenous to our work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, that doesn't stop us, from time to time, from saying that we think it's important that the U.S. fiscal picture return to a sustainable footing, and, you know, right now it's not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's been the case for a long time, and that's something we will have to address, and a good time to do it is when the economy is strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, so I guess I would say it this way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Global capital markets are highly integrated, and, you know, our rates-our long rates are definitely being pulled down by the very, very low rates that are abroad.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the way I would characterize it is this: that low rates abroad are a symbol-or a sign, rather, of weak global growth, expectations of low inflation, low growth, and, you know, just kind of a lack of policy space to move against or ideas about how to break out of that low equilibrium.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we-in a world where economies and financial markets are tightly integrated, that matters for the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's going to pull down U.S. rates, and U.S. financial conditions can tighten because of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think we put all-all of that goes into our thinking and into our models.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do understand how the-you know, how the international sector interfaces with the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We take that into account in setting our interest rate policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we've said, to repeat, is that we see the current stance of policy as "likely to remain appropriate as long as incoming information about the economy remains broadly consistent with our outlook."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we say that, really, because both of the performance of the economy and the stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The performance of the economy has been-particularly the household sector-has been strong, has been resilient, with low unemployment, attractive levels of job creation, wages moving up, labor force participation moving up, household confidence, and solid gains in many measures of consumer spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The manufacturing sector, particularly manufacturing, and also investment and exports have been weaker.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, overall, we've seen moderate growth, a strong labor market, inflation moving up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see the outlook as for more of the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also see the risks to the outlook as perhaps having moved in a positive direction over the course of this intermeeting period, although, some remain-some things remain to be seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Turning to policy, we've moved the stance of policy over the course of the year to a more accommodative stance, and, after the cuts at the last three meetings, the federal funds rate is now in a range between 1½ and 1¾ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We feel that policy is well positioned to support the outlook that I described.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you asked what it would take, you know, to move, and, as I mentioned, we're going to be watching all factors, And if developments emerge that cause a material reassessment of our outlook, we would respond accordingly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's what it would take: a material reassessment of our outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be looking at a full range of data about the economy and about the risks to the outlook, and I've given you a sense of what our outlook is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's for moderate growth, a strong labor market, and inflation near our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If something happens to cause us to materially reassess that outlook, that's what would cause us to change our views on the appropriate stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of risks, what I was referring to there-the principal risks that we've been monitoring have been, really, slowing global growth and trade policy developments as well as muted inflation pressure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have that phase-one potential agreement with China, which, if signed and put into effect, could have the effect of reducing trade tensions and reducing uncertainty, and that would bode well, we think, for business confidence and perhaps activity over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that has the potential for being an improvement in the risk picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Brexit, I would say, as well-it appears that the risk of a no-deal Brexit seems to have materially declined.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think on both situations there's plenty of risk left, but I'd have to say that the risks seem to have subsided.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Business investment has been weak, and today's reading was weak as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it was broad across equipment and other parts of-all parts of business fixed investment were weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's consistent with what we've seen, but that's the economy we've had this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we've had is an economy where the consumer is really driving growth, and, you know, personal consumption expenditures were almost 3 percent in this quarter-in this first reading for the quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, we see the economy as having been resilient to the-you know, the winds that have been blowing this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a risk that we've been monitoring, but we don't see it yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't see rising initial claims or layoffs or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the risk you mention of the weakness in the manufacturing-in export investment, business investment, parts of the economy getting into the consumer side of the economy, we really don't see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Unemployment has declined again, and the household survey is now at a 50-year low-has been, you know, very close to 50-year lows for 18 months now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The consumer-facing companies that we talk to in our vast network of contacts report, you know, that consumers are doing well and are focused on, you know, the good job market and rising incomes, and that's their principle focus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is the thing that's pushing the economy forward, and it doesn't seem to have been affected so far by weakness in the other areas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the reason why we raised interest rates is because-generally is because we see inflation as moving up-or, in danger of moving up significantly, and we really don't see that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation moved down in the first quarter of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We thought that that was due, to some extent, to idiosyncratic or transient factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That turns out to have been the case, so it's moved back up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it seems to be settling in below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And inflation expectations have also kind of moved down and sideways-both surveys and market based over the course of this-of, really, the recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we think that inflation expectations are very important in driving actual inflation, and we're strongly committed to achieving our 2 percent inflation objective on a symmetric basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There obviously will be times in the future where that will be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're really thinking now is that our current stance of policy is appropriate and will remain so as long as the outlook is broadly in keeping with our expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think that the current stance of policy is likely to remain appropriate-likely to remain appropriate-as long as incoming information about the economy is broadly consistent with our outlook, which is a positive one of moderate economic growth, strong labor market, and inflation moving close to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also say, of course, if developments emerge that cause a material reassessment of that outlook, we would respond accordingly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't point to one data point or one thing that would change our minds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It really-it would be a reassessment of-a material reassessment of our overall outlook, which is what I described.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, there's-there's a lot of, you know, practice and science and history, in terms of how much you put in the actual postmeeting statement as opposed to what we say in the press conference statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, we do think that inflation expectations are- they're quite essential, quite central in our framework of how we think about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need them to be anchored in a level-at a level that's consistent with our symmetric 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that we need to conduct policy in a way that supports that outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also, as part of our review, looking at potential innovations, changes to the way we think about things, changes to the framework that would lead us-that would be more supportive of achieving inflation on a 2 percent-on a symmetric 2 percent basis over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's at the very heart of what we're doing in the review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're in the middle of thinking about ways that we can make that symmetric 2 percent inflation objective more credible by achieving symmetric 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it comes down to using your policy tools to achieve 2 percent inflation, and that is the-that is the thing that must happen for credibility in this area.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're in the middle-we're really quite in the middle of it now, and my thinking is still that it will run into the middle of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are-you know, these changes to monetary policy frameworks happen-they don't happen really quickly, let's say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we'll wrap it up around the middle of next year, would be my guess.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would just say that a-if we were to have a sustained reduction in trade tensions-broad reduction in trade tensions and a resolution of these uncertainties, that would bode well for business sentiment, which is-trade uncertainty's been weighing on business sentiment, in our judgment, in the judgment of many analysts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't expect that the effects on activity or confidence would be immediate, or-would there be immediate effects in economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it would take some time after the recent things, but I do think it would be quite positive over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you know, we haven't yet-we just touched 2 percent core inflation, to pick one measure-just touched it for a few months, and then we've fallen back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we would need to see a really significant move up in inflation that's persistent before we would consider raising rates to address inflation concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think we're keeping-I think we've made very substantial adjustments to policy over the course of this year, if you think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We entered the year expecting some further rate increases, we went to "patient," now we've done three rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a very substantial shift, and the effects of it will be felt over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
