text: So we feel like those shifts are appropriate to support exactly the outcomes you're talking about, which are a continuing strong labor market, continued strong job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You have a synchronized slowdown in economic activity around the globe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been building for just about 18 months now, and that's having an effect on U.S. activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's part of the weakness in manufacturing, export, and business investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had trade policy uncertainty, which we think also has been weighing on activity and investment and sentiment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've had inflation, which-we've called out the risk of inflation running persistently below 2 percent as a risk that we needed to address.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've been doing it to address all of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, the gains in the labor market have been great to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's particularly the fact that people at the lower end of wages have been getting most of the benefit of most of the wage gains in the last couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know from our Fed Listens events that we've been hearing from people who live and work in low- and moderate-income communities that this is the best labor market they've seen in their lifetime, things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, that there's also-there's still so many people who are, you know, still not in the labor market yet, and that-there's just a lot more good that can be done there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we have to think about the whole economy, and-but, yes, those gains are very positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They are a reason for us to want to extend the expansion, and that's something we're committed to doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on the "how long," what we've said is that we expect bill purchases to continue at least into the second quarter of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've said that temporary open market operations we expect to continue, I think, at least until the end of January, I believe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the causes, so there's a lot of forensic work going on by us and by market participants and all kinds of analysts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, one thing is that we think we need reserves to be back up to the level-the minimum level of reserves that we can have during the various fluctuations that you see with reserves is something like $1.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: trillion or a little higher, and that's the level in early September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to be adding reserves to get back to that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are also-it may be-one thing that was surprising about the episode was that liquidity didn't seem to flow as one might have expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had surveyed the banks carefully about what was their lowest comfortable level of reserves, and many banks that were well above that level did not take that excess cash and invest it in the repo market at much higher rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They just-they didn't do that, and so the question is why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And are there things that we can do that would-adjustments that we could make that would allow liquidity to flow more easily in the system without in any way sacrificing safety and soundness or financial stability?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are not things that can happen that can really address the situation in the short term, but those are a range of things that we're looking at as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's really the whole range of economic data and also what we see as-about our stance of policy, which we believe is the appropriate stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, if you look at the performance of the economy through this, the consumer sector has been quite resilient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's just-again, all the things I went through earlier suggest that that sector continues to be strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that the manufacturing, investment, trade, export sector has been weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That continues, but nonetheless, overall, we've got an economy that is showing moderate growth, and we think that today's setting-we're now at 1. to 1. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is, we believe, an accommodative level and a level that will support that outlook that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we see is-what we see is that the consumer sector continues strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's all-the data we monitor, obviously, is a very broad range of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also see now, I think, more clearly the effects of more accommodative monetary policy on various kinds of consumer activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're seeing housing now contributing to growth for the first time in a while-two-tenths, I think, this quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you're seeing retail sales-the retail sales number, the PCE number, as I mentioned, in today's release was 2. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, more broadly, monetary policy is also supporting household spending and home buying by keeping the labor market strong, keeping workers' incomes rising, and keeping consumer confidence at high levels, where it currently is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think monetary policy works through the channels that we understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the effects are clear in what we think of as the interest-rate-sensitive sectors, which are the ones-some of the ones that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's-I think interest rates are a factor in business investment, but I don't believe they're the main factor and main driver.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, you know, what one would like to see for-to support greater manufacturing activity, business investment, and exports would be a global recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there's a lot of monetary policy accommodation and some fiscal accommodation, maybe, in the global economy now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that should turn-that should support growth in the global economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, resolution of our trade issues would contribute to that over time as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think-we think that Fed Listens has been a great success for us, and I'm sure we will repeat it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, I would imagine that this entire monetary policy review will become institutionalized and be done every few years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say this: In the Beige Book, we talk to educational institutions, health-care institutions, community groups, labor groups-it's not just businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, all of those groups are also represented on the boards of our regional banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also meet quite regularly at the Board with representatives of low- and moderate- income communities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're-we're very conscious of-you know, that we represent all Americans, and we need to hear all of their perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's why we-you know, we talk about how low the unemployment rate is, the aggregate unemployment, but we also talk about groups that haven't experienced that yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're-we try to remind ourselves that we serve everybody.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is-our outlook overall is for moderate growth of around 2 percent, which is pretty close to trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we feel like our current stance of policy is appropriate as long as that remains broadly our outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can see that we had our usual range of perspectives, range of views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in the end, we had a strong vote in favor of this action.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I strongly believe that the actions we've taken over the course of this year have been the right things to do for this economy and are supporting economic growth and will do so in the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we can't-obviously, we can't raise interest rates some place and lower them other places.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first thing to know is to understand that, that-and we've called that out, as you, I'm sure, know, in one of our recent Monetary Policy Reports to Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The sort of rural-urban disparities in-you know, in employment, in growth, in all kinds of things, in health outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's a big and growing difference-set of differences.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't really have, you know, the tools to address that, but we call things out that are important to our economy that we may not be-that we might have-may not have the right tools to best address them, but we call them out because, you know, we're spending all of our time with the economy, and those are issues that maybe have to be addressed by legislatures and, you know, by-at the national level and at the state level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let me put it this way: We do what we do, which is, we're assigned a job, which is maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The U.S. economy faces significant longer-term challenges around potential growth, around labor force participation, around disparities of income and wealth, around all kinds of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those are issues for Congress, and they're not issues for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you really want the U.S. economy to be all it can be and raise the potential growth rate of the United States, you need-you need proper monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, it's fiscal policy that supports, you know, inclusive growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, I know, that's-I wouldn't-that's not how I would characterize it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just-I noted that it may be that there's been progress there toward- away from bad outcomes and confrontational outcomes, and it seems like there's the makings of a possible settlement there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I didn't say we're baking that in or anything, but I'm just noting that that's the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As with Brexit-it's still quite uncertain what will be the result of the election and what the ultimate result will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that the tail risk of a nonnegotiated no-deal Brexit seems to have decreased, just as I would say that the situation in our trade negotiations with China seems to have taken a step closer to resolution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's one factor among many, many factors that factor into our assessment of the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we see-if we have-if we-if things happen that cause us to materially reassess the outlook, change our assessment of the outlook in a material way, then we would act accordingly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, not for us to say what the appropriate labor arrangements will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will just say, on the General Motors strike, it's-it's likely to have taken away a couple of tenths of growth this quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's likely to come back, maybe, over the first half of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I'm not going to comment on what the appropriate labor arrangements are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a little bit far afield from our task here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at where the federal funds rate is trading, it should be in the middle of, or maybe the lower half of, the range of 150 to 175.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that means the real rate is probably modestly below zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think my own sense would be that that's somewhat accommodative policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, though, that there's a range of plausible estimates of what the neutral rate of interest is, and I think many of those who make such estimates have moved their estimate down over the course of many years, and that process continues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, that seems to me to be very likely to be an accommodative stance of policy, and an appropriate stance, given the situation we're in with continuing downside risks and-that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we monitor financial stability risks very carefully all of the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's what we do since the financial crisis, as I've mentioned before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This long expansion is notable for the lack of large financial imbalances like the ones we've seen certainly before the crisis happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first is leverage in the financial system, which is low by historical standards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second is funding risk, which is the risk of runnable funding, and that risk is also quite low for banks but also for, you know, the nonbanking financial sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at asset prices, we see some high asset prices but not broadly across a range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that leaves the fourth, which is leverage in the nonfinancial sector, and that's households and businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see them actually getting in very good shape financially in the aggregate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Obviously, plenty of households are not in great shape financially, but in the aggregate, the household sector is in a very good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That leaves businesses, which is where the issue has been.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Leverage among corporations and other forms of business, private businesses, is historically high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's what I would say, but it's-corporate debt is one part of a larger part of our framework, and it is something that we're paying quite a bit of attention to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's been part of the last couple of Shared National Credit exams, and we've been monitoring it carefully and taking appropriate action.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Have the problems in the repo market led you to look into whether the liquidity and capital requirements for banks are too high?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're-I think, again, I think the most important basic thing is to get the level of reserves back up so that-reserves move up and down with some volatility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't want them to move below the level they were at in the beginning of September, which is, again, between $1.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're on a path to do that, between our temporary open market operations and also our bill purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition to that-in addition to that, we're looking at-there are-it's a big, complicated marketplace, and there was the-one of the surprises, as I mentioned, was that banks that had told us that their lowest comfortable level of reserves was here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They were well above that, and yet they didn't deploy that liquidity when there seemed to be great opportunities to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You ask, would we lower capital and liquidity requirements because of this?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think where it may go, though, is to look at, for example, intraday liquidity, which used to be a common thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It used to be a common thing for banks to have intraday liquidity from the Fed, what are called "daylight overdrafts."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Also, there are just a few technical things that we can look at that would perhaps make the liquidity that we have-which we think is ample in the financial system-move more freely and be more liquid, if you will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those are things we would do, but only if we can do it without compromising safety or soundness or financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-we, of course, have watched the situation in Japan and now the situation in Europe, and we-we note that there are significant disinflationary pressures around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, of course, if you look at our current inflation performance, it hasn't been anything like what we've seen in those other places.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we don't think-again, we don't think we're exempt from those pressures, and we are, therefore, strongly committed to having inflation expectations anchored at the level that is consistent with the symmetric 2 percent inflation objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we're committed to, and we'll use our tools to achieve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-the risk isn't that inflation might run a couple tenths below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The risk is that what we've seen is other economies getting on a disinflationary path, that it's been very hard for them to get off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You have less-interest rates move down as well, because there's an inflation component in interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we think that the right thing to do is to do what we can now to hold and really move inflation expectations up so that they're squarely and firmly anchored at a level that's consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's a-it's an issue, but it's not an issue that we're currently working on and-or reaching a decision on or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question of the longer-run maturity composition of the balance sheet is a-is a big one, and it's one we'll return to over time, but not-not imminently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I'm going to maintain my longtime practice of not-not commenting on anything any elected official would say, but thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, that's-what's happening there is the fact that the relationship between resource utilization, or unemployment, and inflation has just gotten weaker and weaker over the years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go back 50 years, you would have seen that, when there was-when labor markets were tight and unemployment was low, inflation moved right up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then as the Fed got control of inflation, the connection got weaker and weaker and weaker, to the point where there's still a connection, but it's-it's a very faint one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-what that suggests is that you 1 Chair Powell intended to say the repurchase operations were announced in October.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we believe that policy is somewhat accommodative, and we think that that's the appropriate place for policy to be in order to drive up inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we-the-again, the relationship between slack in the economy and inflation is weak, has been weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's much, much lower than it used to be, but I don't know that it's gone down any more in the last decade.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look-look at where wages were three or four years ago, they were running around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now the whole group of different wage measures that we monitor has moved up to 3 and 3½ percent, and that suggests tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The same thing is true, but much less true, of inflation, the relationship between-in a way, the wage Phillips curve has a higher coefficient than the price Phillips curve does.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do still see some relationship, and that's what you're seeing in those numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's similarities, conceptual similarities, I think, between the two instances during that long expansion, I guess in '95 and '98, when the Fed cut three times only to resume raising rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the notion just is that it's a-the economy needed slightly more accommodative policy, but it wasn't the end of the expansion, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's the same situation we believe we're in here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is that we did, in fact, turn out to do three rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That wasn't in the plan, you know, in any kind of specific way at the beginning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's different is, you have a very different-you have very different structural characteristics in the economy, particularly around inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So now, as you can see, inflation is barely moving up, notwithstanding that unemployment is at 50-year lows and expected to remain there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, this is-it's a good thing that, you know, we think we can-I think we've learned that unemployment can remain at quite low levels for an extended period of time without unwanted upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, we need some upward pressure on inflation to get back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's quite different in '95 and '98 when there were those two adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm going to take a little step back, and I will-I will get to your specific questions on the year-end and on T-bills.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I want to start by stressing that these are very important operational matters but that are not likely to have any macroeconomic implications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'd decided back in January to remain an ample-reserves regime, and that means we will be setting the federal funds rate-the range for the federal funds rate through our administered rates and not through active management of the level of reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're committed to robustly implementing that framework, as you can see by our actions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the purpose of all this, let's remember, is to assure that our monetary policy decisions will be transmitted to the federal funds rate, which in turn affects other short-term rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have the tools to accomplish that, and we will use them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The purpose of all this is not to eliminate all volatility, particularly in the repo market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, taking you back, this-as you know, we had very gradually allowed the balance sheet to shrink, we slowed that gradual pace by half in March, and then we ended it in July.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Meanwhile, we had surveyed all of the banks, and particularly the large banks who hold a lot of the reserves, and said, "What's your lowest comfortable level of reserves?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We got those numbers, we added them up, we added a buffer, and it came out sort of at a level that was well below where we were in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And yet we saw, actually, in September that reserves-the markets acted as though reserves had become scarce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what had happened was that liquidity, which actually existed, didn't flow into the repo market, and that had effects on the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've been very carefully looking at the reasons why that might have happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are-there are payments issues, there have been a number of supervisory and regulatory issues raised-we're looking carefully at those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're open to ideas for modifying supervisory and regulatory practice in ways that don't undermine safety and soundness, and a number of ideas are under-under examination there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To go through it sort of by-in time, we started off, really, on September 17 with overnight operations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: By October 11 we had created and put into effect a plan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, for the last couple of months, repo markets have been functioning well, short-term rates are stable, markets are functioning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Temporary upward pressures on short-term money market rates are not unusual around year-end.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And our-both our repo operations and Treasury bill purchases are intended to mitigate the risks that such pressures pose to our control of the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that the pressures appear manageable, and we stand ready to adjust the details of our operations as necessary to keep the federal funds rate in the target range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our strategy has been-essentially, the key to our strategy is to supply reserves in the near term through-through both overnight and term repo, and, at the same time, we're raising the underlying level of reserves through bill purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've also said that we were willing to adapt our strategy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not at this place, but if it does become appropriate for us to purchase other short- term coupon securities, then we would be prepared to do that if-if the need arises.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It looks-it very much looks like the bill-so those bill purchases are going well, just according to expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the other thing I'll say is that we're in, you know, very regular contact with market participants all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be providing-we'll be continuing that, and we're prepared to adjust our tactics.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-we're focused on-on year-end as well and prepared to adjust our operations as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on the standing repo facility, as you know, we've actually had a couple of meetings where we've discussed that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the standing repo facility is something that'll take some time to evaluate and create the parameters of and put into place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the moment what we're focused on is, you know-we're now focused on year-end.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I should also mention that after the year-end, the sense of it is that as the underlying level of reserves moves up because of bill purchases, as that happens, there will come a time when it will be appropriate for overnight and term repo to gradually decline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know-we can't know today what the timing of that will be, but that's the way-that's the way we see it going over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, as I mentioned, actually, at the last press conference, we think our policy rate is appropriate and will remain appropriate as long as incoming data are broadly in keeping with our-with our outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in order to move rates up, I would want to see inflation that's persistent and that's significant-a significant move-up in inflation that's also persistent before raising rates to address inflation concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't-we haven't tried to turn it into some sort of, you know, official forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It happens to be my view that that's what it would take to want to move interest rates up in order to deal with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think what you're seeing is, you've got a full year of the median being flat, which is, we think, accommodative, modestly accommodative, and inflation not moving up very much, as we've discussed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that underscores, I think, the challenge of getting inflation to move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Committee has wanted inflation to be at 2 percent, squarely at 2 percent, for-ever since I arrived in 2012.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it hasn't happened, and it's just-it's because there are disinflationary forces around the world, and they've been stronger than, I think, people understood them to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of those out-year rate increases, what's you're-you're looking at rate increases more than a year into the future, and, you know, people will have their own explanations for why they do that, but we-really, none of us have much of a sense of what the economy will be like in 2021.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think what may be behind some of that is just the thought that, over time, it would be appropriate-if you believe that the neutral rate is 2½ percent, it would be appropriate for your rates to move up in that direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will also say to you that a number of people wrote down, and you can't see this at this level of detail, but-today-but a number of people did write down overshoots of inflation as appropriate-under appropriate policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, it's just that there is still, empirically, by many, many different-by the work of many different analysts, there is a relationship between resource utilization, by which I mean unemployment, and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That means that we can run at low levels of unemployment and have a historically good-in some dimensions-labor market without having to worry about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It also means, though, that it's not easy to move inflation up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I would say there's more humility than there is confidence in this at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been very challenging to get inflation to be at target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look around the world, the United States, of all major economies, has been closest to it but still hasn't quite been able to achieve it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would also point out that this year, which has been a good year for the economy, inflation-core inflation is actually running at 1. percent, whereas it ran close to 2 percent most of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-it's a real challenge, and-but I think we're using our tools as best we can to meet that challenge.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I-you know, I think the answer to the question of whether saying it is enough to create credibility, the answer to that is "no."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you have to back that up with policy that supports the outcome, and that's what we're trying to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so the- the changes that we're looking at to the framework are-I think they take all of that on board, and-but they're-what they're-what they are designed to do is to strengthen the credibility of that-of that inflation target, but only if followed by policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, it will take time to establish-to move inflation expectations up from where they are, which appears to be a bit below 2 percent, will not happen overnight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll have to happen over time as credibility is built.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the Fed has great inflation credibility, but inflation expectations are anchored at about their 25-year average, which is a few ticks below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I did see the news today that it appears there's an agreement to move forward to vote on USMCA, and, of course, it's not our role to comment on particular trade policies or criticize them one way or the other or evaluate them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, though, that getting-if the deal were to be enacted, then it would certainly remove some of the trade policy uncertainty, and that would be, I believe, a positive for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'll say the same thing about the negotiations with China, which haven't reached that point yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've been hearing from our people that we talked to-the many, many people and businesses that we talked to in-through the Reserve Banks that wind up being written up in the Beige Book, and they've been telling us all year-for a year and a half, really, that trade policy uncertainty is weighing on the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think that, again, without commenting on it- in any way on the process or the content of the agreement, I think that uncertainty-removal of uncertainty around that would be a positive for the economy as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think you can-you know, it's-I think you can see that what's been moving-one way to look at it is, what's been moving financial markets?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been news about the negotiations with China, not so much USMCA.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the difference between NAFTA and USMCA is-is smaller than the difference between current, you know, arrangements with China and what's being negotiated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-you know, the focus really is on how to use our strategies, tools, and communications to achieve both sides of the mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you're right, though, that we've talked here a lot about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that the-I think, more broadly, over a period of years-many years-we've been learning that the natural rate of unemployment is lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just been-it's in estimates not just at the Fed, but among-broadly among economists-labor economists have seen that the connection-that we can sustain much lower levels of unemployment than had been thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, that's a good thing because that means we-we don't have to worry so much about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-and you see the benefits of that in today's labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-you know, the Fed Listens events are about inflation to a much lesser extent than they are about maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you've-if you've listened to or attended any of those, the discussion-we always focus on inflation as well, but the discussion is really around what's happening in low- and moderate-income communities and among small businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you-you get a perspective, which-you know, we were already getting that from our extensive outreach to community groups and such.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it was help to get-helpful to get it in the context of a monetary policy review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that the fact that these communities have so much- such high levels of unemployment and low levels of labor force participation tells you that there is slack out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that does also inform our understanding of what we mean by "maximum employment."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's been a very positive-I would say that the Fed Listens events have been-have been extraordinarily positive, and they're certainly something we'll repeat.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You also see from the business perspective that companies are taking all kinds of measures to-you know, to look through things on people's résumés that would have perhaps disqualified them in other kinds of environments, training is moving up-you hear just a lot-there are a lot of things going on that suggest that people at the margins of the labor force are being pulled in and being given chances, which is a great thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I-I think we have kind of internalized-and this isn't- this isn't news for today, this is something we've been saying for, you know, for several years- you've seen us moving down our estimates of the-of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, it's already-it's already understood, I think, that-that there's more-even though we're at 3½ percent unemployment, there's actually more slack out there, in a sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-and the risks of, you know, using accommodative monetary policy, our tool, to explore that are relatively low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we know that, and I think the review certainly underscores that, but that's-that's a very important insight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on Treasuries versus reserves, we've done a ton of work on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've talked to supervisors, and-it's interesting, if you look at the banks, they're all over the place on the composition of their-of their buffer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you have to have-you have a business model, and that business model suggests what your stress outflows will be, and that suggests what your buffer should be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of them have lots of reserves and, you know, fewer Treasuries, and then they change their mind and they switch, so it's not obvious that there's one thing happening there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Notwithstanding that, we have-we've gone out to try to understand that, talking to supervisors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the-the TGA, you know, we have not tried to pull the TGA into this yet; we've taken it as exogenous.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know that at some point we won't have those discussions, but, you know, Treasury-we want Treasury to be able to have the cash that it needs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we should-we are essentially taking that as exogenous to our-to our work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there may come a time when we-when we talk about that, but we haven't done much of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Standing repo facility-so your question on that is, what are we thinking about it?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What are we-I mean, I-so I think we're-we are more focused, frankly, on the T-the bill purchases, the year-end, and also the review of supervisory and regulatory issues that we're digging into, and-because we think, you know, there's-these are structural things-right?- where you could, without sacrificing safety and soundness, just allow the-allow the liquidity that is already there to flow more freely, perhaps by making fairly straightforward, noncontroversial changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think there is some of that, though-and so we're working hard and fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But those are things, you know, the-if they take rule changes, it'll take, you know, a notice of public rulemaking-it'll take three months and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These things that we're working on now, though-like, you know, going through year-end with the overnight facilities and the bill purchases and the term repo-those are-those are things we have to do right now and are doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, we did, actually-if you look at the statement, you'll notice that we-we did call out global developments and muted inflation pressures later in the statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, those are the things that we've been monitoring all year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've put now in place policies that we think are appropriate to address those things, so we're not revisiting that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But those are-those are just key things, and they haven't gone away, so we thought it was appropriate to mention them there-still subject to the idea that, for us to change our stance, we would want to see a material reassessment of the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I mean, one thing that we're mindful of is that we've cut rates three times since July.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do believe that monetary policy operates with long and variable lags, and that it will take some time before the full effects of those actions are seen in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, if you look at-more broadly at the Treasury yield curve, it has moved more than 75 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you've-you've had quite a significant move in the direction of higher accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what's-you know, what is material at the end of the day, well, I would just say, whether or not a change in the outlook merits a policy response will be a collective judgment of the FOMC.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There isn't any single factor that will determine our decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll- we'll look at a full range of data and other information bearing on the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-this wouldn't be a-my response will not be about Paul Volcker, but-so, well, you started with Paul Volcker.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, if you look back at 2018-I'll just take you back to the beginning of 2018.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had an economy growing at 3 percent, we had inflation at 2 percent, and we had a trillion and a half dollars' worth of stimulus arriving, and the federal funds rate was 1. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it wasn't that-so we moved-we moved policy up during the course of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We never got policy even at the level of what we thought the neutral rate was at the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We took steps to make it less accommodative, and that seemed to be the right thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It still seems to me to be the right thing in hindsight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The idea that we were trying to, you know, slow the economy down-we were really just trying to get near neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And even with the last rate increase a year ago, we were still meaningfully below the median estimate on the Committee of what the neutral rate was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So policy was always accommodative during the course of that year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think what's happened is, the-obviously, the facts on the ground have changed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw the global economic slowdown begin in the middle of last year, gather force, and then continue to go on this year, so you've seen a continual weakening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just look at the IMF's forecasts of growth from, you know, the spring of 2018 and compare them to now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, also, the trade situation was just beginning in the middle of '18, and I think it had-has had-you know, I think there'll be a very, very wide range of estimates of the effect, but I think it's had a meaningful effect on output just through the uncertainty channel and, to a lesser extent, through-through, you know, the tariff effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not up to us to make a judgment about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I wouldn't want to speculate on-on a hypothetical.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-we look at a range of factors and we've-as I've said before, we try to look through the volatility in trade news and trade negotiations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Monetary policy is not the right tool to react in the very short term to volatility and, you know, things that can change back and forth and back and forth as this has happened, as is probably typical of a-of a large complex negotiation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of-you know, I-again, I don't want to get into hypothetical outcomes, though, if that's all right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I-I'm going to stick with my and my predecessors' longtime practice of not discussing private meetings with elected officials-or other officials, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With-I think properly understood, it can be useful, but that's been a challenge.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think "properly understood" to me means looking at what it is and not at what it isn't.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what it is is, it's an expression of the thinking about individual Committee members about appropriate monetary policy and the path of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Remember that we write all that down, and we send it in, and it gets compiled.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we don't discuss it at the meeting, and we don't negotiate a plan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, particularly at inflection points, it's hard to convey the reality, which is that policy is always going to depend on the economic outlook and changes in the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when the economic outlook is changing, the dots are-they're just not a consideration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to do what we think is the right thing for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if the fact-dots that we did six months ago or three months ago don't agree with that, that's not even in the conversation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So its more-but it can it be useful if-and I think-but, as I said, it's been a challenge, and so I-I do-I do like to say, if you focus too much on the dots, you can-you can miss the broader picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say, we're-we've been working on this all year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're just at the stage where we've had a really interesting discussion about the various tools that we have at the October meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At this meeting, we talked about the way monetary policy affects different groups in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we had a-we talked about the Fed Listens events and some very interesting research.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're just getting to the stage where we're looking at conclusions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what do we take away from all this?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those things- many of those things would wind up as changes, if you will, modifications to the "Statement of Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that process will take until the middle of the year where-but we want to approach it very thoroughly and very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that is- in effect, that is our framework document.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one-I believe we will be able to-to reach a successful conclusion and make meaningful improvements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of "4 percent"-so that's-I think it's premature for people to be saying that this isn't going anywhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know-and if you define going anywhere as a 4 percent inflation target-let me talk about the 4 percent inflation target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'll go back to the point that just saying words is not itself credible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you said, "We're raising the inflation target to 4," what would be the effect of that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we-I think you need to lower your sights a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also think, is 4 percent-you'd have to ask the question, is that really, you know, price stability?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I think-I'd like for this review to come out with very-a set of positive results-you know, meaningful improvements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't mean it has to solve every problem going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to-we want to have this be a successful exercise where we meaningfully improve our monetary policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These things don't tend to move in- you know, in a lurchy way, they tend to evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think-and if we do this, then in a few years, again and again and things like that, then we can-at least we're moving in a good direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, you know, I have to say, my total focus is on right now and getting policy right and thinking about next year-you know, thinking about what's the economy going to be doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I like where we are on policy, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think our policy stance is appropriate and likely to remain so as long as the outlook is broadly like this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I don't know how to get after that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's- there's a lot of learning that comes into-from the economy every year and in the way we do our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're always going to be trying to learn lessons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I didn't-obviously, you know, didn't see and I don't think anybody saw coming the-the challenges that we faced this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that, toward the end of 2018, there was still a sense the economy was growing at around 3 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I didn't expect the-to face the challenges, but I think we did face them, and I think we-I'm pleased that we moved to support the economy in the way that we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, I think both the economy and monetary policy right now, I think, are in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages are growing more slowly now than they were toward the beginning of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look back three, four years, you'll see wages are growing around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now you see them moving up, you know, more at 3, 3½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So why aren't they growing higher, at a faster rate?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For instance, one would be that productivity has just been low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So wages should go up to cover inflation and productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Productivity has been low, and that-that is very likely to be holding back wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also think there are other possible potential explanations, such as, you know, globalization can be-the idea that you can make, manufacture, or even provide services anywhere in the world to anywhere in the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that hangs over the wage-setting process-and everywhere, pretty much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You don't see- there isn't the kind of traction in the wage market that-even in a tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Another thing is, though, that the labor market may not be as tight as we had thought it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I think there-there are many, many possible explanations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, though, if you look, for example, at nonsupervisory employees in the labor report, there are- their wages are going up at 3. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, you do see-and wages are going up the most for people at the lower end of the-that's been true for the last couple of years-lower end of the wage spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, at the end of the day, that probably has most to do with productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just as far as the market not being as tight as you thought, are you saying there are still more people on the sidelines who could join the labor force?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would also say that we-if you ask people, and we did ask people, what do you think the natural rate of unemployment is?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People were writing down numbers in the fives, and then they were writing down numbers in the fours.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now, unemployment has been in the threes for a year and a half, and we still see wage inflation, as you mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The level of wage inflation has actually moved down, although, there may be compositional effects in that number that may-that may be, to some extent, about younger workers coming in at lower wages that-than retiring workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you wouldn't-that shouldn't have much of an effect, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It may just be that there's more slack in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For many years, we've thought that there's a trend decline in participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Notwithstanding that, against that trend, we've seen prime-age participation moving up pretty steadily over the last two or three years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's a very positive thing, but it does sort of provide more labor supply, meaning a less tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we think the CRA-we know the CRA is a very important law, and we're strongly committed to the mission of ensuring that banks provide credit to their-throughout their communities, particularly addressing the needs of low- and moderate- income households and neighborhoods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've thought that for some time, and we worked very hard to try to get aligned with the OCC, really, on-on a proposal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And my hope is that we can still do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I don't know whether that'll be possible or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It will have to-well, we'll just have to see, but-and if we-if we can't, I don't-I'm not sure what the path forward would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would certainly not want to create confusion or, you know, sort of tension between the regimes if they do turn out to be slightly different regimes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's something we-I hope we don't have to face, but we will if we have to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we-there's so many other measures that suggest that the labor market is-I like to say the labor market is strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Someone asked me a question about a hot labor market-that was in the Humphrey-Hawkins hearings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know that it's tight, because you're not seeing wage increases, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, if it's tight, those should be-should be reflected in higher wage increases, so it does come down to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we look at countless measures of labor market-you know, labor utilization, and there's so many- it's too many to count.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the one that has-that is kind of suggesting that you're-it's a healthy number that, you know, the sort of 3. percent average hourly earnings number is a decent number-3.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, though, we'd like to see-to call it "hot," you'd want to see heat.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in making that change, our goal was, really-that was, changing "near" to "returning to"-was to avoid possible misinterpretation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you may remember, in the December minutes we noted that a few Committee members suggested that the language that stated that monetary policy would support inflation near 2 percent could be misinterpreted as suggesting that policymakers were comfortable with inflation running below that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we thought about that in the intermeeting period and concluded that it would be appropriate to adjust that language to send a clearer signal that we're not comfortable with inflation rising persistently-running persistently below our 2 percent symmetric objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just that we wanted to underscore our commitment to 2 percent not being a ceiling to inflation running around-symmetrically around 2 percent, and that we're not satisfied with inflation running below 2 percent, particularly at a time such as now where we're a long way into an expansion and a long way into a period of very low unemployment when, in theory, inflation should be moving up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Why don't I say a few things about repos, since I know that'll be of interest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, just to bring you back, after last September's brief turmoil, we took prompt and decisive action, and a result-as a result, money markets have been operating smoothly since then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just to review, those two adjustments were Treasury bill purchases of at least-of $60 billion-sorry-at least into the second quarter, and term and overnight repo at least through April.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The purpose of the adjustments has been to assure that our policy is transmitted smoothly to the federal funds rate, which requires well-functioning money markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't mean we're trying to eliminate all volatility in the repo markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that some volatility is normal and expected in well-functioning markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, these adjustments have been successful in supplying an ample quantity of reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Money markets operated smoothly, including right through year-end, and the fed funds rate has remained in our target range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we know-we will know when these adjustments have run their course when reserves are durably at a level that enables us to control the federal funds rate using our administered rates, the interest on reserves and reverse repo, without the need for frequent use of open market operations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Based on current projections, we expect that the bill purchases will durably bring the underlying level of reserves to the ample level sometime in the second quarter of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when we see that we've reached that level, we'll begin to gradually reduce our asset purchases to the level of the underlying trend growth of demand for our liabilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As our bill purchases bring the underlying level of reserves up to an ample level on a sustained basis, the necessary quantity of overnight and term repo will gradually decline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've already begun the gradual reduction in the quantity of repo, and we'll continue to reduce those offering amounts gradually as conditions permit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At some point, we'll also raise the minimum bid rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Even after we reach an ample level of reserves, it's possible that repo operations might play a role as a backstop and support effective control of the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll continue to discuss that issue and review it under our implementation framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Coming to your question, in terms of the actually desired reserve level, we know that reserves will continue to move up and down over the course of the calendar year in a wide range depending on volatility in nonreserve liabilities, particularly the Treasury General Account, or TGA.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In particular, reserve levels will need to be at a level high enough to remain ample even when the TGA peaks during the April tax season.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Effectively, what that means is that we need reserves at all times to be no lower than they were in early September-and, I would say, around $1½ trillion, subject to learning more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Reserves are going to move in a broad range, as I mentioned, and we want to be clear, that will be the bottom end of the range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want $1½ trillion or thereabouts to be the bottom end of the range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, most of the time, reserves will be moving in a range substantially higher than that but not going below $1½ trillion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not an-it's not something that we're aiming at all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that reserves will fluctuate and be substantially higher than that most of the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also want interest on excess reserves and the fed funds rate to be well within the FOMC's target range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that'll be the case now that we made our technical adjustment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Last points-we're committed to making this adjustment process a smooth one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll provide more details as we go, and we expect to learn as we go, as we always have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're prepared to adjust the details of the plan as necessary to foster efficient and effective monetary policy implementation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'll just-I'll repeat that-we think that the-we think we need to continue purchases until the-until reserves are at a level at which they will not go below $1½ trillion, roughly, during the course of the calendar year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we know that the TGA will move up and down there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So they'll be much higher than that some of the time, but that's kind of the number, and we think we'll reach that sometime in the second quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll know it because we'll be able to be-to control the federal funds rate without use of-without active use, ongoing use of open market operations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, our intention of these-for these adjustments is just to raise the level of reserves and to allow us to conduct monetary policy in an efficient and effective manner.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I pointed out on other occasions, more than once, the differences-the really specific differences between this and the large-scale asset purchase programs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what affects markets, you know, I think many things affect markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's very hard to say with any precision at any time what is affecting markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I can tell you is that you know what our intention is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And our plan as we do that is, as those purchases get to that level, we believe we can gradually reduce them, and we believe we can also gradually reduce repo as-as we reach an ample level, as we're satisfying demand now more from underlying reserves from bill purchases rather than from repo.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, the last thing I'll say is, we're prepared to adjust the details of this plan as we've shown ourselves willing to do depending on conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Very importantly, we see labor force participation continuing to move up, really, against expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go back a few years, you will not find a lot of forecasts suggesting that we could have been at 63. percent overall labor force participation or the levels of employment to population that we're seeing now, let alone the unemployment level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we've learned quite a lot of good things about the labor market, good things suggesting that there's been more room to run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The performance of wages, I think, has to be seen in that context.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We saw-if you go back four or five years, the four or five major wage statistics that we track were running at around 2 percent, and now they're running at around 3 percent, which is theoretically about where they might be at full employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The-it's a bit surprising that, with sustained levels of historically low unemployment, we haven't seen wages moving up above that level as we have in other long expansions and other periods of low unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, one thing can be that the natural rate of unemployment is still lower than we think, that the labor market is not as tight as it would appear just from the 3½ percent number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the other can be, I think, that-as I mentioned, the sort of supply-side shock or surprise that we're receiving from higher labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People are coming in to the labor market and providing more labor supply, and that is-that's a great thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're a country that has low labor force participation compared to essentially all of our advanced-economy peers, and it's a very good, positive thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, it represents more labor supply, and it may be holding down wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll just say that we undertook the review because we felt, and I felt, that it was time to incorporate the realities of what we could call the "new normal" into our policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And some aspects of that new normal would include ongoing powerful global disinflationary trends, which have led to lower-than-target inflation many places in the world; secondly, a flat Phillips curve, by which I mean low levels of sensitivity of inflation to resource utilization-for example, low unemployment; and, thirdly, a much lower neutral real interest rate here and around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those are challenging conditions for monetary policy to deliver on our statutory goals of maximum employment and stable prices, although I would say that, under our existing framework, we've been able to succeed or get close to succeeding it for most of the time lately to achieve those goals, although we do struggle, as other central banks do, with the inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is about reviewing our strategy, tools, and communications to assure that they're the best that we can do to achieve those goals in this environment on a sustained basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's included the 14 Fed Listens events around the country, at which we've engaged with a full range of people and groups across American society.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That was a very, very positive experience, and I think we learned a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've now had a series of-a number of FOMC meetings at which we've reviewed what we've learned and also dug deeply into strategy, tools, and communications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I expect that we will conclude the review and announce our conclusions around the middle of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, we are just at the point of coming together to put all that together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think I'm not the person who should be telling you my personal preferences right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm trying to-and we were trying to come together as a group around a set of answers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I feel very positive about-that we're going to come up with some good results, and I'm just going to have to wait until we get to that point to announce them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me talk about the coronavirus specifically, and then I'll turn more to global growth more generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, it's a-it's a very serious issue, and I want to start by acknowledging the significant and considerable human suffering that the virus is already causing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There is likely to be some disruption to activity in China and possibly globally based on the spread of the virus to date and the travel restrictions and business closures that have already been imposed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, the situation is really in its early stages, and it's very uncertain about how far it will spread and what the macroeconomic effects will be in China and its immediate trading partners and neighbors and around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in light of that uncertainty, I'm not going to speculate about it at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will just tell you that, of course, we are very carefully monitoring the situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, as you suggested, our framework ultimately is, what are the potential ramifications for the U.S. economy and for the achievement of our dual mandate?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: More broadly, though, if I can talk about the global economy for a second-and if you look at the backdrop, you know, if you go back to 2017, that was the year of synchronized growth that lasted into the middle of 2018, and then you saw slowing in growth, which lasted right through the end of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The fourth-quarter growth globally was quite weak last year, and a number of factors played into that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was trade policy uncertainty, absolutely, but also there was the decision by the Chinese authorities to try to rein in leverage and financial excesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was a turn-downturn in the global high-tech manufacturing cycle in global auto production.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There were some idiosyncratic strains in some countries like Argentina, Turkey.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, later, in Hong Kong and Chile, you had social unrest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, all of those things were playing into that cycle of weakening growth over the course of 2019 and the last half of '18.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, now there are grounds for what I would call "cautious optimism" about the outlook now for the global economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many analysts are predicting a pickup in growth this year, although still to relatively modest growth rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would-people are pointing to, and we would point to, supportive financial conditions, the easing of trade tensions, the lower odds of a hard Brexit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The high-tech manufacturing industry does appear to be rebounding well in Asia, including in China.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The latest indicators-manufacturing PMIs, for example-suggest that manufacturing may have bottomed out, that they're still below 50 in many jurisdictions, but they have moved up off of their lows.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would-I would just say, none of this is assured.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, we saw the fourth quarter of last year came in quite weak-weaker than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are not at all assured of a global rebound, but there are signs and reasons to expect it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then comes the coronavirus, which, again, it's too early to say what the effects will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There will clearly be implications, at least in the near term, for Chinese output and, I would guess, for some of their close-in neighbors, and we'll just have to see what the effect is globally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our stated goal is to keep IOER and the federal funds rate well within the range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, clearly, you know-5 basis points from the bottom or from the top isn't that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Last year we were-we saw some tightness as reserves were draining out of the system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With ample reserves, we see-we see that it's possible to bring the interest on reserves rate up to 10 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So now we're-now we are well within the range, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we'll continue to adjust it to the extent it's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, what we're trying to do is deliver a federal funds rate that's well within the range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we-if we need to make changes to keep it well within the range, we'll do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just means-I mean, the thing that matters for the economy is that we keep the federal funds rate-which is the rate that, of course, transmits into other money market rates, which ultimately transmit into all kinds of financial conditions-that's what we care about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, ultimately, we will-we will use that tool to keep it well within the range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we-when we make decisions about the steps we're going to be taking in that adjustment process that I described at some length, we'll be making them as early as we can and as transparently as we can-and specifically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's January, and we're several months away from- from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the standing repo facility, as I mentioned in, I guess, in my answer to an earlier question, there may well be a role for repo in this system even after we're at an ample- reserves level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, we haven't decided what that role is, we have not decided-we haven't at all made a decision on a standing repo facility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had a couple of discussions about it, as you know, back in, I guess, June and October.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to return, I would say, fairly soon to this question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it was wise to wait, because we're still getting a better sense of what that- what that world looks like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's really going to be a question of, how useful will it be?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And my thinking is, we will return to that fairly soon, and I wouldn't assume a decision one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, we haven't made one, because we haven't had to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you-when you delay, you get more information by waiting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't have any urgency in making that decision, because we're still trying to find that sort of stable equilibrium where we're in an ample-reserves regime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's an interesting question-the question being, is there a systemwide financial stability risk?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'd say, over-over the longer term, it's certainly possible, and I would say that sort of feeds into the way we're thinking about climate change as an institution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I've mentioned, climate change is an important issue, a very important issue, but it's essentially assigned to many other agencies in the federal government and state governments for leadership on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, importantly, society's overall response to climate change needs to be decided by elected officials and not by the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of that said, if you look at our mandate, we've got a monetary policy mandate and, more immediately perhaps, a supervisory mandate where we're supervising financial markets, utilities, and financial institutions, banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we haven't-we share overall responsibility for financial stability with a number of agencies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that latter part-I think the public has every right to expect and will expect that we will assure that the financial system is resilient and robust against the risks from climate change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are in the very early stages, as are other central banks, in understanding just what that means.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's quite a lot of work going on around the world at other central banks and at the Fed, too, to think that through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I do think it's-in that sense, it has to be part of our role, and-but not the overall response of society to climate change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've attended all of their meetings and taken part in them, and we've been looking at joining in one form or another and talking to them about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're very much attending those meetings and taking part in them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I'd start by saying that the fact that we've reached a phase-one deal with China and the fact that we've moved ahead closer to getting USM[C]A agreed-those are potentially positive things for the economy without question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And financial markets-the reaction of financial markets is very consistent with that perception.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A sustained reduction in uncertainty over time should improve business sentiment, investment, which would provide some additional support for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's important, though, to bear in mind a couple of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We still have two or even three active trade discussions that are going on in the public square right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it hasn't gone away, and we've just come through a round of talking to our vast network of comments- sorry, contacts in the business world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, clearly, these are seen as positive developments going forward, but there's a bit of a wait-and-see attitude-is this going to be sustained?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The agreements have to be implemented, too, and that'll take quite some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I would say, we need to be a little bit patient about the effect on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You could-you could well see manufacturing-as I mentioned, manufacturing PMIs have started to tick up consistently among both advanced economies and emerging market economies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do not see a decisive recovery, but it's possible that this mix of positive developments and also accommodative financial conditions could spur further growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As for those forces, so, as we indicated, we would undertake a, you know, serious review of that question and look at both our regulations and also supervisory practices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'd be prepared to adjust those in ways that might encourage liquidity to flow more easily in the system as long as it didn't undermine safety and soundness.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we've undertaken that, and we've done a ton of work, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't have anything to announce here today, but I feel good about the-what we've learned there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going to give you a time, but we're- we're well along in that assessment at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we also found out, though, that the level of reserves that we need in the system to conduct our operations without frequent resort to open market operations was higher than we had thought and was higher than others had thought, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We learned that we can't let reserves-we shouldn't let reserves go below $1½ trillion-roughly, the level of early September-at any point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means that reserves will move through in a range over the course of the year that will be substantially higher than $1½ [trillion], but they won't ever go below.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is the bottom of a range in which reserves will be expected to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, let me just stress that we have a very specific and important reason for caring about money market operations generally, and that just is that we are-our monetary policy decisions are transmitted through the financial markets-through the money markets into other financial markets and into broader financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a one-time thing that we're doing to adjust the level of reserves so that the money markets will be able to operate smoothly on an ongoing basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Repo markets are important, because that's where Treasury securities-the purchase of Treasury securities, which is the way-you know, the federal-part of the way the federal government is funding its operations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
