text: So these are largely Treasury securities that have been purchased by dealers to-for distribution to-and buyers, to a substantial extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, again, we don't-that activity is a-is a market activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not looking to eliminate volatility or protect anybody from volatility at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we care about is that volatility in the repo market can affect the transmission of-of our policy decisions to federal funds rate, and that really is important for the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Chair Powell, is the Fed going to vote tomorrow on changes to the Volcker rule restrictions on banks investing in venture capital funds?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What can you tell us about what the Fed is considering?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we will be looking tomorrow and voting on a-a new part of-part of the existing Volcker rule, and that is the covered fund provisions of the rule.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be making a bunch of proposed revisions that we believe are faithful to both the letter and the spirit of the law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to put those proposals out for public discussion, and we're going to listen carefully, as we always do, to public comments on those proposals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, we believe that they will be-and you'll see them tomorrow-will be public-you know, will be publicly-we have a Board meeting tomorrow to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, is this just the venture capital funds, or are also you changing the rules for hedge funds and private equity funds?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-so it's that covered-so it's not the proprietary trading part of Volcker.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And is there a chance that banks could take this and run and maybe even get involved in mortgage-backed securities again and risky investments?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we'll-we think that what we're doing is-is very consistent with safety and soundness and absolutely consistent with the letter and spirit of the Volcker rule.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be-we'll be getting comments from people, and we'll be looking into that question, among many others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, China has had a problem for some years, including from that period-2014 up until, I guess, '17 or '18, and I thought-which was essentially just a lot of debt for an emerging market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For an economy at the-at the stage of evolution of the Chinese economy, they had very high levels of debt-not sovereign debt the way we think of it, but more business debt-debt of state-owned enterprises and also just private businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And a couple of years ago the authorities decided to try to get that under control-to stop the growth and to control it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that-as I mentioned, that's one of the reasons why Chinese growth slowed, and it's one of the reasons why global growth slowed, because we felt that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they've actually stuck to that even during this difficult period when they were experiencing, you know, strains from trade negotiations and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The authorities have stuck to that and have, again, continued to try to do that, so-to try to control the growth of debt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think that-that there's any imminent risk there, although you-as you point out, the coronavirus thing is a significant thing, which will-will have some effects on the Chinese economy, at least in the short term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Chinese economy is very important in the global economy now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we-when China's economy slows down, we do feel that-not as much as countries, though, that are near China or that trade more actively with China, like some of the Western European countries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We still have-you know, 85 percent of our economy is domestic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have a much smaller external sector, trade sector, than other economies just because of our physical location.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, in terms of liquidity, I think what we're doing is what I said: We're trying to raise the level of reserves back up to a level so that banks can meet their reserve requirements, and that there's enough reserves in the system that we don't see reserve scarcity, and we don't have to use repo operations to provide additional reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, as I mentioned, we believe we can get to that state at the current pace sometime in the second quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of effects on risk assets, as I said earlier, it's very hard to say what is affecting financial markets with any precision or confidence at a given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not our intention to change the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These were designed to provide more reserves and, really, to do that in order to enable better transmission of our-of our rate decisions into the economy under our chosen framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, as you know, we're comfortable with our current policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it'll remain appropriate as long as data coming in are broadly in keeping with our outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Over time, an average inflation-targeting framework would be different than our current framework, in the sense that it wouldn't be a-there would be some aspect of trying to make inflation average 2 percent over time, which means, if it runs below 2 percent for a time, it has to run above to bring the average up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our current framework is one where we say-or we'd be equally concerned with deviations of inflation from target on either side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that isn't-that doesn't suggest an intention specifically to have those deviations be symmetric.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other words, that would- consistent with that would be having all the deviations be on one side, which is what we've had, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it is a change in framework, and over time it would lead to a different approach to policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I'm not trying to-I don't want to comment on the current stance of policy, which we do think is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-we look at a very broad range of financial conditions where-there isn't any one financial condition that we-that we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when we look at financial conditions, what matters for the real economy is substantial changes in-or, material changes in financial conditions that are sustained over a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If I can, maybe I'll-maybe I'll answer that in the context of our overall financial stability framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at-when we look at financial stability, we look at-really, we've got four pillars to that, the first of which is leverage in the financial system that is at a comfortable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our banks, particularly our large banks, have high levels of capital.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second is leverage in the nonfinancial sector, and that divides into households and businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Households' debt to GDP is-has been coming down since the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's at low-low levels compared to what it was before the crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So not every household-but, in the aggregate, household debt is in a good place, a very good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've been calling that out for more than a year-substantially more than a year, and it's something we're focused on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we think it's not something that would threaten financial stability, but more be an amplifier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other one is asset purchases, getting to your-sorry, asset prices, getting to your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do see asset valuations as being somewhat elevated-I do-somewhat elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the way to think about-a good way-one way to think about equity prices, though, is, what's the premium you're getting paid to own equities rather than risk-free debt?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's also at fairly low levels, but not extremely low levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Are big financial institutions and other players in the financial system funded with stable funding, or is there a lot of run risk?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the answer is, very stable funding, for the most part.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at, overall-what you see, in my view, is, vulnerabilities to the financial-to financial stability are moderate overall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wanted to know, do you support Governor Brainard's vision for the Community Reinvestment Act reform?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And is this something that we could see the Fed formally propose at some point?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say that I think this is a good time to do-to update CRA, really, in a way that is a win-win both for the intended beneficiaries-low- and moderate- income communities-and also for banks that would like to have more certainty about-about what does and doesn't qualify and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The law can both be more effective and more efficient is-it comes down to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also just a good time to take on board the way the delivery of banking services has changed through technology and demographic change as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We worked very hard to try to get on the same page with the other two agencies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that an interagency final rule together would be the best outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're sorry we haven't been able to get there, and we still hold out some hope that we will be able to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We spent a lot of time on research and analysis and looking at meaningful reform.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw Governor Brainard's recent speech presenting some of the thinking and the analysis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we haven't made any decisions about what we're going to do, about whether we'll propose-I mean, our focus has been entirely on trying to get to agreement with the OCC, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we haven't made any decisions about what we're going to do going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of, you know-Governor Brainard led our oversight committee over these activities for many years, and I asked her to take the lead on CRA modernization, which is a high priority for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I was comfortable with her speech, and I'm comfortable with the work we've done and with the Fed's position on this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I said, we haven't chosen to bring a proposal forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're not going to comment on the other proposal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do agree that-the principles that he articulated of firm and fair supervision and effective transparency in communications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also think it's a good thing that we would have brighter lines to define our LISCC supervisory portfolio, which we haven't really had to date.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Remember that when a firm moves from one portfolio to another, that doesn't mean that its level of scrutiny or supervision will change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and I also thought that, you know, the-he's raising some very interesting questions about, if you-in the first part of the speech, where he's talking about regulation and supervision and, you know, how to-how to balance the desire for transparency and due process in everything the government does with the needs of confidential supervision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as far as the specific, you know, proposals, there's-you know, they're interesting, you know, and need further development and will need lots of comment and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-we are assigned a job by Congress, and that is to use our tools to pursue maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, monetary policy is a blunt instrument, but it's a powerful one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you look- look at the time since the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That was-in the week [wake] of fairly modest growth, it was a powerful recovery in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And part of that just is the effect of lower interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, if-so many, many people benefit from low interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, you don't hear-when you talk to the low- and moderate-income communities, one thing you don't hear is, "You ought to raise rates."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You hear quite the opposite, which is, you know, "Please do whatever you can to keep this expansion going."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you're living on just the interest in a bank or on fixed-income generally, then that's a challenging thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other hand, if you own a home, home values-the housing market has recovered, other financial assets have recovered, so-but, yes, for some people who are limited to those sources plus whatever other help they get, it can be challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we have to do what's best for the-for the overall society and the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we've been carefully monitoring the situation since it first became known and waiting to see how it would evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we've come to the view now that this-that it is time for us to act in support of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And once you reach that decision, we decided to go ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what changed, really, was, I would say, over the course of the last couple weeks, we've seen a broader spread of the virus-we've seen it begin to spread a bit here in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, for us, what really matters, of course, is not the epidemiology, but the risk to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we saw a risk to the outlook for the economy and chose to act.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of my confidence that we will return to-what was your question?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think anybody knows how long it will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do know that the U.S. economy is strong, and we will get to the other side of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I fully expect it will return to solid growth and a solid labor market as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-we're in active discussions with central banks around the world on an ongoing basis, as you would guess.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've been in regular contact with central bank leaders from around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Central banks are doing what makes sense in their particular institutional contexts, but we're all talking to each other on an ongoing basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And our action today represents what we think is the right policy for us in our particular institutional context under our domestic mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw this morning's G-7 statement of finance ministers and governors, and I think that statement does reflect coordination at a high level in the form of a commitment to use all available tools, including health-care policy, fiscal policy, and monetary policy as "appropriate."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of fiscal policy, again, not our role.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not our role to give advice to the fiscal policymakers, but you saw the mention in the G-7 statement-as "appropriate" as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the sense of the G-7, you know, is to-we have seven countries, obviously, and different policies, different situations, different mandates-a lot of overlap.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the sense of that is to get together as a group and say at a high level that "These are the things we're going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are going to use our tools-all of our tools in a strong way to-to try to support the economy."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it's up to individual countries-individual fiscal policies and individual central banks-to do what they're going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would think it will be- it's possible there will be some more-more formal considered coordination as we move forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of-in terms of moving forward, I would say that we do like our current policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think-we think it's appropriate to-to support achievement of our dual-mandate goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as I said in my-in my statement, we're prepared to use our tools-tools and act appropriately, depending on the flow of events.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't-we don't see any of that happening yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we are-we are thinking about what we can do should those things happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, we do hear concerns, particularly from those most directly exposed, but there's nothing in that nature: Financial markets are functioning in an orderly manner and all that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think when it-when it comes to those sorts of issues, though, we will be-the supervisors will be working with banks to assure that they work with their-with their borrowers and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I can imagine us doing those sorts of things, but it's-those things are not upon us at the moment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, as you know, we're in the middle of a review of all of our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you go back a few meetings, we've talked about what our toolkit is, and we've put that in the minutes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we discussed is the current stance of policy, is it appropriate-came to the view that it was appropriate to make a change and went ahead and did that today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the virus outbreak is something that will require a multifaceted response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that response will come, in the first instance, from health- care professionals and health policy experts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It will also come from fiscal authorities should they determine that a response is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it would be-come from many other public- and private-sector actors: businesses, schools, state and local governments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Monetary policy can be an effective tool to support overall economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do recognize that a rate cut will not reduce the rate of infection.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do believe that our action will provide a meaningful boost to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: More specifically, it will support accommodative financial conditions and avoid a tightening of financial conditions which can weigh on activity, and it will help boost household and business confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's why you're seeing central banks around the world responding as they see appropriate in their particular institutional context.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on your first question, we're always going to set monetary policy at a given time in a way that we think best serves our dual-mandate goals, and it's as simple as that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we'll-if we get to a place where we think it's an appropriate time to change the stance of monetary policy, we won't hesitate to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would also say that it's-it's very important that people understand that we will always make our decisions based on the best thinking we have, based on our-what we learned from our outreach to businesses, nonprofits, educational institutions that we get every cycle through the Reserve Banks, and the best analysis, the best research.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're always going to make our decisions in the interests of the American people to carry forward and try to achieve the mandates that Congress has given us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're never going to consider any political considerations whatsoever.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will not do that, and it's very important that the public understand that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're-we are hearing-I would just say, the effects are at a very early stage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you are hearing concerns from people-for example, in the travel business or the hotel business and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you don't see things showing up in actual data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You do see them showing up in, sort of, sentiment forecast indicators and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's one of the reasons why we've come to the view that it would be appropriate for us today to move to support the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, based on our discussions today and many conversations with participants, it's fair to say that we have a range of views about the path of the economy, as is always the case with the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in general, I'd say that we see the U.S. economy as having been in quite a strong position before the arrival of the virus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see that it is likely that the measures we take to protect ourselves from the virus will involve withdrawing from or reducing certain activities-thinking there of travel, leisure, hospitality, those things- and that's going to mean lower economic activity for a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are choices that we make to protect ourselves-appropriate choices that we make to protect ourselves from the virus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that means that the second quarter is probably going to be weak-in fact, in the view of many, output declining-output lower in the second quarter than it was in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: After that, it's very hard to say how big the effects will be or how long they will last.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's going to depend, of course, on how widely the virus spreads, which is something that is highly uncertain, and I would say, in fact, unknowable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do know that the virus will run its course and that the U.S. economy will resume a normal level of activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, the Fed will continue to use our tools to support the flow of credit to households and businesses and support demand with monetary policy- ultimately, to do what we can to see that the recovery is as vigorous as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would point out that we have, of course, responded very strongly not just with interest rates, but also with liquidity measures today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we believe that what we did today will be beneficial to financial markets generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as I said in my statement, we're prepared to use our full range of tools to support the flow of credit to households and businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I've noted on a number of occasions, really, the Committee- as you know, we did a year-plus-long study of our tools and strategies and communications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we, really, at the end of that, and also when we started out, we view forward guidance and asset purchases-asset purchases and also different variations and combinations of those tools as the basic elements of our toolkit once the federal funds rate reaches the effective lower bound- so, really, forward guidance, asset purchases, and combinations of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we looked at negative policy rates during the Global Financial Crisis, we monitored their use in other jurisdictions, we continue to do so, but we do not see negative policy rates as likely to be an appropriate policy response here in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me tell you how, I think-what our tools can accomplish, and-and really what they're not designed to accomplish.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what our liquidity operations-and I'll talk specifically about the Treasury and MBS purchases-are designed to do is to assure the proper functioning of the Treasury and MBS markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Treasury market is one of the most important, perhaps the most important, market in the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's probably the most liquid large market in the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The MBS market is very important: It's closely linked to the Treasury market, and it's the way that our monetary policy decisions flow through to borrowers in the real economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they had reached levels of very high illiquidity, and-to the point where we-as you know, last week we offered financing-very large amounts of financing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And after that, we bought assets across the curve to try to support liquidity and return to normal function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we found that that helped, but, nonetheless, we thought we had to do more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we knew what we had to do, which was the asset purchase programs that we did today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those are designed to restore those key markets to normal function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These markets are part of the foundation of the global financial system and of the United States financial system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if they are not functioning well, then other markets-then that will spread to other markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those are the markets that-that amount to-that-where households and businesses typically get credit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we know that dysfunctional financial markets-a dysfunctional financial system, really, can have very big negative effects on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a very different situation, but, nonetheless, we thought it was quite important for us to take strong measures to support-to support proper market function in these important markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's true, we don't have the tools to reach individuals and particularly small businesses and other businesses and people who may be out of work or whose businesses may not-may experience a period of very low activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have the tools that we have, and we use them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we've used them quite aggressively for the benefit of the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But this is a multifaceted problem, and it requires answers from different parts of the government and society.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think that, by far, the most important is the response of the health-care workers and health-care policymakers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think fiscal policy is a way to direct relief, really, to particular populations and groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Monetary policy has a role, and it really is in, you know-our original role was providing liquidity to financial systems when they're under stress, and that's-that's really part of what we did today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other role is to support demand through lower interest rates, and we did that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You-you asked about fiscal as well, and I guess I've sort of covered that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do think fiscal response is-is critical, and we're happy to see that those measures are being considered, and we-we hope they are effective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on-on inflation, you know, the-the economy's performed so well, really, over the last few years, and right up through January: historically low unemployment-50-year-low unemployment for a couple of years, 11 years-almost 11 years of expansion so far, and yet inflation lingered below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've been concerned that inflation not move down further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was a question of not getting inflation up to our target on a robust, symmetric kind of a way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, with this coronavirus arriving, we judged that the-the net effects of this will be to- to have inflation move down even a little bit more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-it's not a question-it's not-it's not an issue of deflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, it's just an issue of inflation probably falling even a bit further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We expect, with uncertainty, that, you know-that it will fall a little bit further, at least, below where it has been.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are-of course, we don't have the legal authority to buy other securities other than the ones we already buy, and we're not seeking authority to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't discussed that at the-at the FOMC, and it's not-it's not legal authority that we're seeking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what-what I can tell you definitively is what the purpose of the asset purchases was, and I mentioned this in my statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it really is to support the availability of credit in the economy-households and businesses-and thereby support the overall economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They do that by supporting proper market functioning in the Treasury market and the MBS market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you see-and I think you'll see-as these purchases roll forward, you will see the Treasury market and the MBS market returning to normal market function, and that will actually support economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what it's labeled, that's of less interest to me.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I really think we are very clear in our minds what we're doing this for and what the logical effects would be, which would be- which would be both better market function and-and-you know, when there's better market function, it will be-you know, policy will be supporting the economy better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Desk is going to go out, and it's going to buy at a strong rate that is-that we think will restore market function-restore liquidity as quickly as it can be restored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that language is open ended, and it's meant to send a signal to the market that-that, you know, we're not going to be bound by, for example, $60 billion a month or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to go in strong starting tomorrow, and we're going to buy across the curve, and we're going to buy MBS, and we're really going to use our tools to do what we need to do here, which is restore these important markets to normal function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As far as-as the policy rate, what we've said is that we will maintain the rate at this level until we're confident that the economy has weathered recent events and is on track to achieve our maximum employment and price stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you can see, that's the test we've written down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you-if you look at it, you'll see that some things have to happen before we'd consider-we'd have to become confident of-that the economy has weathered these recent events and also is on track to achieve our maximum employment and price stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a test we'll be looking at, and I think it suggests that, you know, we're going to be watching and willing to be patient, certainly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we do, actually, work pretty closely with the Treasury Department and-and cooperate with them on things, with clear lines of delineation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For example, the Treasury Department has authority over fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have sole responsibility for monetary policy and strong instructions from Congress to conduct it in an independent, nonpolitical way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in the middle there, there are areas where we-where we can cooperate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You would want the finance ministry and the treasury [and the central bank] to be talking in every major economy in the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You would want them to be regularly exchanging information-professional relationships not just at the, you know, the Chair-to- Treasury-Secretary level, but also through the organization.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For example, the New York Fed is the Treasury's agent-fiscal agent, as you know, so there's a lot that goes into debt management and the issuance of debt, which happens at the New York Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we do, actually-we have professional, good working relationships up and down the chain there, and, you know, that-that seems to me to be working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there is-there's also quite a lot of coordination in other respects with-of course, with foreign central banks, but you didn't ask about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I feel very well, and so there's no reason for me to be tested.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are observing-we're trying to model good behavior here, so we're observing quite a lot of teleworking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, we're-you know, we're not having a lot of big, crowded meetings-we're not having any big, crowded meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're trying to observe all of the things that the professionals tell us to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do expect to do some teleworking because I want to model that-that it's okay for the people to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of our-of our toolkit, let me say first that, you know, I think we do have plenty of space to adjust our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mentioned our liquidity tools-you know, we have a lot of power in our liquidity tools, and, as I mentioned, we're prepared to use them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, we've got plenty of space left to offer forward guidance, asset purchases, and adjust those policies, so I think we do have room.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-we have not at all made a decision to request further-further tools or authorities from Congress, no.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So why no-I guess you're asking, why no SEP, and what's our forecast?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a couple reasons we didn't do an SEP. First, we decided on Thursday to move the meeting up by three days to today, and that's before the SEPs are generally filed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They hadn't been filled out, and we-frankly, we spent our time focused on getting ready to make these announcements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Second, and, you know, a number of FOMC participants had already reached out to make the point that the economic outlook is evolving on a daily basis, and it really is depending heavily on the spread of the virus and the measures taken to affect it and how long that goes on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, actually, writing down a forecast in that circumstance didn't seem to be useful, and, in fact, it could have been more of an obstacle to clear communication than a help.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do expect that we'll return to the quarterly- regular quarterly cycle in June, however.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the forecast, so, as I mentioned, you know, we see the U.S. economy starting out strong-from a strong position, different-different as we-as we talked through it today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People have a range of perspectives on the way the year is going to go, but I think there's a pretty broad sense that the second quarter will be a weak quarter, with probably out-you know, output declining a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: After that, it becomes hard to say, you know, what'll happen in the third and fourth quarters and thereafter, and it's going to depend, again, on-on the path of the virus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the thing we do know is that we'll be here doing our job and supporting the flow of credit and there to do what we can when the recovery comes to make it as vigorous as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of fiscal policy, I think in the first instance-and you're-you're seeing some of this now-is the thing that fiscal policy and, really, only fiscal policy can do is reach out directly to affected industries, affected workers, and we've seen some of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: More broadly, after that, there's the question of-of fiscal-broader fiscal stimulus, and I think that'll depend on the path of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I think there is such a wide range of possibilities here that it's some-it's very hard to predict.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there could certainly be-there could certainly be, you know, a need for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think, in the very near term, we're going to be looking at, you know, the Treasury market function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're really going to be looking to see that financial markets are returning to more liquid, more normal functioning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is-actually, you know, that is the thing that central banks were originally designed to do, was to provide liquidity to financial systems in stress, so we take that job very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's probably the most important thing we're doing now is that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll be watching that and we'll be prepared to use our tools when and as appropriate to address-to-to support market functioning and really to support the flow of credit to households and businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, in terms of economic data, I think it's just so early.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're really looking-I mean, the economic data will follow the data on the spread of the virus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think what happens-what happens during the spread of the virus is probably not going to tell you a lot about where the economy will be in six months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's going to be- because you may have a-you probably have a bad quarter in the second quarter, but if things get better in the third quarter, that probably won't matter so much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If it lasts longer-so that's really what I'll be looking for, is-is what is going to be the spread of the virus and what's the path it's going to take and what are the effects on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess your first question is, how-how do we think about the time-the time for this thing?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know-and the truth is, we just don't know, and, you know, the experts we talk to will say that they don't know, and that it's, in fact, unknowable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, it's the measures that we take to, you know, to-with the social distancing, and the-all the things businesses and school and everyone's doing now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that will depend, to some extent, on how compliant people are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can see that some countries have had a-have been able to, through aggressive measures and really high compliance-have been able to bend the curve and-and do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And whether we succeed or-you know, that's really the question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I wouldn't-I wouldn't, you know-I'll resist the impulse to guess.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the toolbox, as I mentioned, we think we have plenty of policy space left, plenty of power left in our tools, and I would point in particular to the liquidity tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, I think, is-is right now the most important thing that we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our interest rates will matter-cuts will matter now to borrowers who will get some relief from our cuts, but they'll matter a lot more when the economy begins to recover.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but in the forefront now are the liquidity tools and-and getting that job done well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, as I mentioned, we-you know, we have room to provide forward guidance, to do more asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there-there is room for us to do what we need to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I would just close, though, by saying that, you know, typically, fiscal policy does play a major role when-when there are downturns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw-you've seen that in many past downturns, and that's beyond just the automatic stabilizers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Sometimes fiscal policy comes in on a discretionary basis, and that-that will probably need to be the case here as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's a big group-it's got a lot of people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, you should know that we are, of course, in regular contact with the other regulatory agencies, constantly talking about what's going on in markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a lot of information and conversation on an ongoing basis there, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and the same is true with our central bank contacts around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're in ongoing contact with all the major central banks around the world, talking about what's going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're having group calls, we're calling one- on-one, so there's quite a lot of information being exchanged there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, again, that's a judgment for the-that's a judgment for the FSOC.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-you know, I'm comfortable with the actions that we've taken, and if-if we do identify, you know, a systemically important nonbank institution, then we wouldn't hesitate to designate it, but-although I guess now we're working more on activities, but we do still have the power to designate institutions, so-

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, you know, that's-that's something that happens when markets are as volatile as they are, when you're having these big market movements while markets are trying to understand what's going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're trying to reach a view on-in high uncertainty, and that's why you see lots and lots of volatility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's more risk to financial stability in an era like-like that than there is when things are really placid, and, you know, we're going home at 4 o'clock and kind of bored over here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, financial stability-I would say those-those risks do rise at a time of high volatility, particularly a time where we're presenting-presented with a challenge that is-is kind of unique, really-it's not something we've all done before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also want to add, though, that, you know, we're strongly focused on financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The banks are highly capitalized, lots of liquidity, much better at understanding and managing their risks, their resilience to stress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our financial stability focus-our focus on an event like this over the last 10 years will pay dividends, in the sense that you have a much more resilient financial system than you've had before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, so we saw, and everyone saw, that liquidity had become very strained in Treasury and MBS markets, and we decided to offer very large quantities of term and overnight repo to address that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That makes it easier to finance the purchase of repos-sorry, of Treasuries and MBS.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we did that, and as you pointed out, the take-up was not as high as many had expected, and I did-we did learn something from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We thought that was worth doing, and what we learned was that we needed to go direct here rather than trying to intermediate through the dealers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we realized at that point that we would need to actually purchase securities for our portfolio, so we did that on Friday.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We bought-the next day, Friday, we went in and we bought across the curve, and we bought, I think, $37 billion worth of securities, and then we saw what happened with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We saw that market function improved a little bit, but still it wasn't what we needed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why we brought together the full FOMC and had our meeting this afternoon and announced these measures this evening, which are strong measures, with the broad support of the Committee to provide really substantial amounts of liquidity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-I think you can see us working through different solutions and-and finding the one that we think really will work and then acting quite vigorously, quite aggressively tonight to implement it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'd like them to use their buffers to provide-you know, to provide loans and-and also to work with their borrowers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you can see, we're providing a lot of guidance to them across a wide range, and they're saying they have every intention of doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There-there are a lot of discussions going on, and, you know, we hear the banks saying, that's exactly what they're going to do, so that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're-of course, we've-we're-we have nothing to announce on-on 13(3) powers, but, you know, of course, we-that's part of our playbook in-you know, in any situation like this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I said, we're-we're prepared to use our authorities as is appropriate to-you know, to support borrowing and lending in the economy, and, hence, to support the availability of credit to households and businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say that we're-we're committed to using our full range of tools to support the economy in this challenging time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to use them, as I mentioned, forcefully, proactively, and aggressively until we're confident that we're solidly on the road to recovery and also to assure that that recovery, when it comes, will be as robust as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would just say, we have a number of dimensions on which we can still provide support to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, our credit policies are not subject to a specific dollar limit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They can be expanded as appropriate, and we can do new ones.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we can continue to be part of the answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, Congress has also reacted quite aggressively and strongly with the Cares Act and other laws-several other laws.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With enhanced unemployment insurance and the Paycheck Protection Program, we've seen an extraordinary, historically large reaction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that it may well be the case that the economy will need more support from all of us if the-if the recovery is to be a robust one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me-let me start-I'll take the questions in the order you- you gave them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in terms of, if I can say, legislative priorities, we don't-we're not responsible for fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that policies that protect workers, businesses, and households from avoidable insolvency, that keep businesses going so that they're able to produce goods and-and to either hold on to their employees or quickly rehire them, those are going to be key policies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They'll come with a hefty price tag, but we would come out of this event eventually with-with a stronger economy and with less long-run damage to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-that's a key thing that-that, really, Congress could do over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what we can do, I mentioned, we have our-our credit facilities are-are wide open.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, you know, we've had-we've had extensive discussions, as I've mentioned-done a lot of thinking about what monetary policy might look like over-in coming months over a range of potential scenarios for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do think that our-our policy stance today is right where it should be for now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, we cut rates to the effective lower bound, we-and we've said that we'll keep them there until we're confident that the economy has weathered the effects of the outbreak and is on track to achieve our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With asset purchases, we're continuing to purchase Treasury securities and agency MBS in the amounts needed to support smooth market functioning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're doing those things, and I would say that we'll continue to use our tools as needs be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, let me say again, in terms of-of asset purchases and-and other measures, we-we do think our-our policy stance is appropriate now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had discussions, as I've mentioned, over time and done quite a bit of thinking about what we might do in the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're really waiting to see more from the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are a range of potential paths the economy could be on, and I think as-as the time approaches for-then we'll-you know, we'll address your first question, which is about asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-it's something that we have talked about, and, you know, for now, we like our current policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of risk, so, you know, we operate under the laws that Congress passes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are a number of aspects under section 13(3), and you can see that they've permitted us to, I think, move very quickly and move into areas where we've never been before and do so quite aggressively.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-I think we're going places and providing help in places where we never have, and I'm glad that we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you read section 13(3) of the Dodd- Frank-or, the Federal Reserve Act, and I know you have, it does require that-that we be secured to our satisfaction, and-and we can't lend to insolvent companies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's clear these are lending powers, and we are-we are ultimately bound to-to implement the laws that Congress gives us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-the reason I raised that in my remarks is that I just want to be clear on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-you know, we can do what we can do, and we will do it to the absolute limit of those powers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you-I just want people to know that we'll-we will be at it with-with the legal authorities that we have until we get through this thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there are authorities that we don't have, and there may be a need for those authorities to be used as well as ours.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of those facilities, the corporate credit facilities are near being finalized and will be operating, I would say, soon-fairly soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Main Street facility is-we're close to announcing-to issuing a new term sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, we put out a term sheet for comment a while back, and we got a couple thousand comments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've tried to reflect those in what we're doing now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, with Main Street, there'll be at least a couple of different kinds of lending going on there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It-this is a broad area of the economy with many different kinds of credit needs, so we're going to keep at that for some time, I think, adding in sectors and lending products.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we'll be at-we'll probably be continuing to work and expand Main Street for some time, but it won't be done quite as quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the first part of it, I think, will be done fairly quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of our statement, so what we said was that we-I'll just read the sentence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It says: "[The] ongoing public health crisis will weigh heavily on economic activity, employment, and inflation in the near term and poses considerable risks to the economic outlook over the medium term."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the "medium"-but what we meant by that, "over the medium term"-so, obviously, what we're talking about is, you know, not right now, in the very near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's between now and the long term, so the next year or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would point to a couple of-of risks to the outlook that-what we were thinking of.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: How long will it take to get it under control?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Will there be drugs that can either treat it or-or a vaccine of some kind?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's-all of that is very much shrouded in uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second issue-and this is a very substantial one-is just the possibility of-of damage to the productive capacity of the economy through a couple of channels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first is just workers who-if one is unemployed for an extended period, that person can-can lose the skills that are needed, can lose touch with the labor force, and have difficulty restarting his or her career.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a-that's a feature of deep and long recessions, and that's something we've got to watch out for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Another is just businesses-you know, these thousands of great medium- and small-sized businesses that we have all over the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're worth so much more to the economy than the sum of their net assets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we see an unnecessary-unnecessary insolvencies, a wave of those, that could be damaging to the performance of the economy over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the good news is that we have policies, as I mentioned in my remarks-we have policies that can address those things, but not perfectly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The third thing I would point to is just the global dimension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a very global phenomenon, and you are-we're seeing economic data from around the globe which is very, very negative, and that, too, can weigh on U.S. economic performance over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-you know, I would say, just on the U.S.-on the U.S. economy, there are things you can say, one can say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first is that, in the near term, we're going to see, you know, significant declines in economic activity, significant declines in employment, and increases in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to see that as a consequence of the virus and the measures we're taking to protect ourselves from it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The next phases are more uncertain, highly uncertain, but we will go through a phase starting fairly soon where we begin to reopen the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And probably the economic activity will pick up as consumer spending picks up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Consumer spending, as I mentioned, has gone down quite a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll begin to pick up as people start to return to their normal patterns of spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the chances are that it won't go right back to where we were, because people will-until they're confident of-that the virus is well and truly under control, then they will be somewhat probably reluctant to-to undertake certain kinds of activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it may take some time for us to get back-it probably will take some time for us to get back to-you know, to a more normal level of unemployment and-and, ultimately, to maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on the first, as I mentioned, you know, we moved very quickly, very aggressively.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were the first to return to the effective lower bound, where we are now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We got there essentially right away, and we think that's the right place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think, if you look at surveys, you look at market pricing, the market expects us to-to be there for a good while, and that's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, it's not as though the market is pricing in a near-term liftoff or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And let me just say, we're going to not be in any hurry to withdraw these measures or to lift off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to wait until we're-we're quite confident that the economy is-is well on the road to recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't see-we see our current stance and our current guidance-and I would say the same thing about asset purchases-we see them as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've-I've also mentioned now a couple times that we have done a lot of thinking about what monetary policy might look like over coming months, and that would, you know, depend on-on where we are in-in a range of potential economic scenarios.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-we were thinking about that all the time, but right now, for now, we think our current stance is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Second question was, how-so the thing about our facilities is, Treasury still has plenty of equity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've said that if-if demand for our facilities is greater than we've estimated, then we'll expand them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it won't be the way the-the Paycheck Protection Program is, where there's a specific amount allocated-appropriated for it, and-and then there's no more money.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-that will be unlikely to happen here unless we exhaust Treasury's equity, and we're a long way from doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second thing I would say is-and you've all seen this-is when we announce these facilities-and I mentioned this in my remarks-it's not just the actual lending we do, it's the- we build confidence in the market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And many companies that would've had to come to the Fed have now been able to finance themselves privately since we announced the-the initial term sheet on-on these facilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Companies are out there financing, they're out there raising liquidity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've made the short-term money market loans, but-we haven't made any of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And yet there's a tremendous amount of financing going on, and that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-for that reason, the ultimate demand for the facilities is quite difficult to predict, because there is this announcement effect that really gets the market functioning again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will follow through to validate that-that announcement effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, as you know, economic forecasts are always uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Today they're unusually uncertain, and that's-that's really because so much of the performance of the economy depends on the path of the virus and the success of the measures we take to control it, our success in reopening the economy, and also the time it takes to develop new drugs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And our tools, the things that we do, don't affect any of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not experts on those things either, but what the experts tell us is that the outcomes are highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is an unusual, new kind of uncertainty added on top of our-our regular uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I-I will say, there-I think there are a few things that you can say about-about the path ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, this time, now, is going to be a time of sharp contraction in economic activity, high unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Personal consumption expenditures have declined sharply, business investment as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to see economic data for the second quarter that's worse than any data we've seen for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they're a direct consequence of the disease and the measures that we're taking to protect ourselves from it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So then we will enter this new phase, and we-we're just beginning to maybe do that, where we will-formal measures that require social distancing will be rolled back gradually and at different paces in different parts of the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in time, this-during this period, the economy will begin to recover.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People will come out of their homes, start to spend again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll see unemployment go down, we'll see economic activity pick up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But let's just say, for this purpose, that it's in the third quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned earlier, that-that could be a fairly, you know, a large increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Given the- given the size of the fall, the increase could also be substantially large, although it's unlikely that it would bring us quickly, quickly all the way back to pre-crisis levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, this is the period as well that carries the risk of new outbreaks of the virus, something we really want to avoid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think then, after that period, at some point you will have-you know, the kind of formal social-distancing measures will-will be gone, but you'll still be left with, probably, a level of caution on the part of people who will-who will worry and probably keep worrying for some- for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You would think that behavior will change as people gain confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the- the sooner we get the virus under control, the sooner people can regain that confidence and regain their economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think trying to be really precise about when that might happen and what the numbers might look like is-I think it's very tough to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So unemployment has tended to go up much faster for minorities and for others who are-tend to be at the low end of the income spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it tends to come down-come down faster as well, but it tends to go up faster and be much, much higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we were in a place-only two months ago, we were well into-beginning the second half of the 11th year is where we were, and every reason to think that it was ongoing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were hearing from minority-low- and moderate-income and minority communities that this was the best labor market they'd seen in their lifetime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it is heartbreaking, frankly, to see that all threatened now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All the more need for our urgent response-and also that of Congress, which has been urgent and large-and to do what we can to avoid longer-run damage to the economy, which is what I-I mentioned earlier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is an exogenous event that-you know, just, it happened to us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It wasn't because there was something wrong with the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it is important that we do everything we can to avoid that longer-run damage and try to get back to where we were, because I do very much have that concern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think everyone is suffering here, but I think those who are least able to-to bear it are the ones who are, you know, losing their jobs and losing their incomes and have little cushion to-you know, to protect them in times like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is different from the PPP, the Paycheck Protection Program, in two ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't know that the demand will be quite as strong as-as it has been for the PPP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the second thing is, we won't run out of money.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's not a limited pot, so there won't be this incentive to try to get there first and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm-I'm hopeful we-we will very much try to learn as much as possible from that facility and from all the other ones, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have a lot to learn here, so we'll certainly be trying to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of fiscal concern, so I-you know, I'm-for many years, I've been, before the Fed, I have longtime been an advocate for the need for the United States to return to a sustainable path from a fiscal perspective at the federal level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have not been on such a path for some time, which means-just means that the debt is growing faster than the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is not the time to act on those concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is the time to use the great fiscal power of the United States to-to do what we can to support the economy and try to get through this with as little damage to the longer-run productive capacity of the economy as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The time will come again-and reasonably soon, I think-where we can-where we can think about a long-term way to get our fiscal house in order.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But this is not the time to be-in my personal view, this is not the time to-to let that concern, which is a very serious concern, but-to let that get in the way of us winning this battle, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so we don't-we're not in a position to make, you know, a reliable assessment of when a vaccine or a therapeutic drug would be ready, and so we're not going to set our policies based on-on our estimate of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to just provide the support that we can with the tools that we have, and we're going to keep doing that until-until the recovery's well under way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of Main Street, so you know the story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We put out a term sheet, we got a lot of comments, we took those very much to heart.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a challenging space, because it's many different kinds of borrowers-they have different needs, different sizes of companies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, we're-as I mentioned, we're very close to announcing a new term sheet, which will then become operative fairly quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: My guess is, though, that we'll keep-we'll keep looking to add products and add different kinds of borrowers to that as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're-we're well aware of the importance of-of doing it as quickly as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, here, you know, we're very much in touch with-with the urgency of that need.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So unemployment's going to go up to a high number in the second quarter-uncertain what the number will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When-and that's because so much economic activity has been shuttered, really, as we take social-distancing measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the- so sometime fairly soon here, and probably gradually and at different paces at different parts of the country, we'll see the social-distancing measures rolled back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And once that starts to happen, people will get hired back and unemployment will go back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think it'll get anywhere near the historically low levels that we had in-as recently as February, 3½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it will take some time for that to happen, for us to get back to anything that resembles maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, I mean, the main thing we want is, we want to get back on that road.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to get that-that recovery going and get people back to work as fast as we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not faster than we can, but as fast as we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The main thing is to get into that stage where the economy's healing, where we have the disease under control, where we don't, you know, take too much risk of-of second and third waves and that sort of thing, and get people back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's-again, the path of it is highly uncertain, but we will-we will be there with our tools, supporting the economy and supporting that recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Can you just say that part-you're a little bit low volume.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's an extraordinary, extraordinary shock, unlike anything, certainly, that's happened in my lifetime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I think the time will come for a careful assessment of the answers to those questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we'll be at that for a while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, but I'd point to a couple of directions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we worked hard to strengthen the banks: much higher levels of capital, liquidity, far greater sense of what the risks are they're running and how to manage them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the breakdowns that we've seen in market function have really been in the capital markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't-I wouldn't rush in with prudential regulation into the capital markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think-and we did plenty of things-you know, triparty-you know, we did a lot of reform in the capital markets: money market reform, triparty repo reform, central clearing, all these important things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there-there will no doubt be- with this-the size and force of this shock will no doubt reveal weaknesses in the financial architecture, and we'll have to go to work on those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I also think it-you know, it tells you the importance of-of getting your fiscal house in order.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The U.S. really hadn't-really hadn't gotten back to where we needed to get on fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so we-we had an already high level of debt to GDP, and rising quickly, when this shock arrived.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, we have the fiscal capacity to deal with it, I believe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we will need to-ideally, you would go into an unexpected shock like this with a-with a much stronger fiscal-fiscal posture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of inflation, we think that inflation is very closely and strongly related to inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And during the Global Financial Crisis, there was a concern that we might see deflation, but it didn't happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation expect-inflation tended to move down a little bit, as it will when demand is weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but inflation expectations did not move strongly down here in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They have in other places in the world, though, over the past 25 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's been downward pressure on inflation, really, for several decades now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I would say, as long as inflation expectations remain anchored, then we shouldn't see deflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the Federal Reserve is strongly committed to maintaining 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If- if low energy prices-very low energy prices were to-were to drop headline inflation negative, I-I would hope that people would see through that-and we'll be monitoring it very carefully- would see through it, though, and look to core, which is a better predictor of future inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, needless to say, we'll be keeping very close track of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the markets, you know, our-our concern is that they be working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-we're not focused on the level of asset prices in particular, it's just-markets are trying to price in something that is so uncertain as to be unknowable, which is the path of this virus globally and its effect on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's why you see volatility the way it's been, market reacting to-to things with a lot of volatility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, what we're trying to assure, really, is that the market is working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The market is assessing risks, lenders are lending, borrowers are borrowing, asset prices are moving in response to events.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-that is really important for everybody, including-including, you know, the-the most vulnerable among us, because if-if markets stop working and credit stops flowing, then you see-that's when you see, you know, very sharp negative-even more negative economic outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think our measures have-have supported market function pretty well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're going to stay very careful, carefully monitoring that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think it's been good to see markets working again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Particularly, the flow of credit in the economy has been a positive thing, as businesses have been able to build up their liquidity buffers and households have been able to be home-you know, people have been home, you know, concerned about their jobs, but they're not concerned about the financial system collapsing as they were in 2008 and '09.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of the labor market, the-the risk to-of damage to people's skills and their careers and their lives is a function of time to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the longer one is unemployed, the harder it gets, I think-and we've probably all seen this in our lives-the harder it is to get back into the workforce and get back to where you were, if you ever do get back to where you were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, longer and deeper downturns have had-have left more of a mark, generally, in that dimension with the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's why-as I mentioned, that's why the urgency in doing what we can to prevent that longer-run damage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We won't be able to limit all of it, but we do have the tools to-to do what we can to-to keep people in touch with the labor force and working and also out of insolvency, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't seem fair that people should lose everything they have, including their homes, over this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the-so in terms of the-the money, you know, the $454 billion, it's a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, the Treasury Secretary really has-has authority over that, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know-but I do think we are-we're clearly moving into areas where there is more risk than there has been in the past.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so-but in terms of the-of the way to think about that money, I think that's really a question for the Treasury Department.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we are-we set up the facilities, and we work very, very closely and successfully and collaboratively with the Treasury on this, but that-that particular aspect of it falls more to the Secretary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think that low interest rates affect the economy through a number of channels in a positive way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Lower interest rates support economic activity through channels that we-overall, through channels that we understand reasonably well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They make it cheaper to borrow, they make-they drive, you know, your costs of borrowing down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They do-they do raise asset prices, including the value of your home.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If your saver owns a home or has a 401(k), your saver will benefit from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But for people who are really, really just relying on their bank savings account earnings, this is-you know, that's-that's-you're not going to benefit from low interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we-you know, we have to look out for the overall economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Low interest rates support employment, they support economic activity, and those are our mandates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think for the overall good of the economy, low interest rates are a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's not to say they're good for every single person, but that shouldn't stop us from doing what we think is-is good for the whole.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of how low, I really don't want to speculate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we will turn to questions like that soon enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the-in terms of how long we'll stay and under what conditions we'll stay at the effective lower bound, those are just exactly the things we're thinking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've said that we'll keep our rates where they are until we're confident that the economy has weathered the effects of the outbreak and is on track to achieve our-our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're leaving-we're not changing that guidance today, you know, but it'll be-that means we're going to be very patient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That means we're-we're not going to be in any hurry to move rates up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, first, I would say that we think that monetary policy today is currently well positioned to support the economy in this challenging time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we didn't think that, of course, we would change our policy now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, we-we lowered our policy rate very quickly, [more] quickly than others, to the effective lower bound.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
