text: And we've said that we'll keep it there until the economy has weathered the effects of the virus and is on track to achieve our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can see that in-in the dot plot, as I think you pointed out, that overwhelmingly, FOMC participants expect, as their baseline expectation, no rate increase at least through 2022.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look at surveys of more forecasters and market participants, financial market prices, et cetera, those also appropriately reflect a long spell with rates at the effective lower bound.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the first thing is, monetary policy is in a good place, and it's-that's well understood in the markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Secondly, we've also taken strong measures to support the flow of credit in the economy, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, third, we're continuing asset prices in coming months at-at a- at a relatively high level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So for all those reasons, we feel like policy is now in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as we look ahead, we see that the path for the-ahead for the economy is highly uncertain and continues to depend to a really significant degree on the path of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, at this meeting, what we did was, as I mentioned, we-we looked in some depth at forward guidance and asset purchases and looked carefully at those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also received a briefing on the historical experience with yield curve control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll continue those discussions in upcoming meetings and evaluate our stance and communications as more and portion-more- more information about the trajectory of the economy becomes available.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I would just say, in terms of-of what we're looking for, we-we expect to get a better understanding of the economy's trajectory and, particularly, how we should best deploy those tools to achieve those goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's really what we're looking to achieve, and, as you can see, we're-we're actively at work on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: 1 Chair Powell intended to say "asset purchases" rather than "asset prices."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And remember, we're using-we're using our-our emergency 13(3) lending tools to an unprecedented extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have asset purchases, and we've now said that we won't go any lower than this, and-but-but that we're prepared to adjust as appropriate, and rates are at the effective lower bound.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have all of our tools in-in use in a strong way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so what we're-what we're waiting for is to-is to learn more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I think, actually, if you look at the May employment report, it's a pretty good-probably the biggest data surprise that anybody can remember.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a pretty good illustration of just how uncertain these times are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to learn a whole lot about the-the path of the economy in the next-in coming months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of inflation, you'll know that we-we had a 128-month expansion, and we never did quite get inflation back to 2 percent on a symmetric, sustained basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We got close for the last couple of years, but we never did quite get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we have to be humble about our ability to move inflation up and particularly when unemployment is-is going to be above most estimates of the natural rate for-certainly above the median in our-in our-in our SEP well through the end of-past the end of 2022.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do-I think we're in the right place now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We- we are looking carefully at what the-as we learn more and-and better understand the-the path of the economy, we will be assessing, what's the best way to deploy all of our tools to achieve our goals in the best possible way?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'll-I'll just say again that we are-the-the May employment report, of course, was a-was a welcome surprise, very pleased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-it's, depending on how you count it, well more than 20 million people displaced in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we are going to be deploying our tools-all of our tools, to their full extent, in pursuit of that-of those goals, however long it takes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, you know, we were-we just had a period of unemployment, as you know, that was in the-well below 4 percent, hanging around 3½ percent, that lasted two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And during that period of time, we saw a lot of great things happening in the labor market, things that we'd love to get back to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I would say, you know, we'd be looking to get inflation back up, and we-we'd be prepared to tolerate pretty low-welcome, in fact, not tolerate but welcome very low readings on-on unemployment just based on what we-what we saw in the last-in the last expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we're thinking about is-is providing support for this economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do think this is going to take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would be great if-if we got a whole bunch more months of job creation like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not- notwithstanding that, as I mentioned, there are-there are just a lot of people that are unemployed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it seems quite likely that there will be a significant group at the end of- even-even after a lot of strong job growth, that'll still be struggling to find jobs, and we'll still be providing strong accommodation for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think that the-that the Great Depression is a good example or a likely outcome or a model for what's happening here at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, the government response has been so fast and so forceful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This was a very-an economy that was in a healthy place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, every economy has longer-run challenges, not-and that-that includes our economy, notwithstanding that 50-year low in unemployment and the longest expansion in our history and every reason to think it could continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's different from what was happening around the time of the Great-the Depression started.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The financial system this time was in- was in-was in very good shape, much better capitalized.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, every month that passes, we're seeing more, we're learning more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think particularly the next few months will be very important in learning what the-what the real story will be, because we'll see the-the significant incoming data about the opening of the economy-the reopening of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know-and I would say, assuming that the-that the-that the disease remains or becomes pretty much under control, I think that what you see is a-is a very weak second quarter, historically weak, and then an-an expansion that builds momentum over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People will adjust, probably a little bit gradually, to some of the activities that would- that involve getting together in small-in large groups in close quarters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those will be the harder parts of the economy to recover.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, we do see a full recovery over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really what, you know, what I think I'm-I'm personally seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you could see significant job growth in-in coming months as people return to their jobs, but you're still going to face probably an extended period where it will be difficult for many people to find work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And for-and that's what you see in-in-in, really, many, many forecasts at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That doesn't mean it's right, but that's sort of a-a broad expectation, certainly not the Depression forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it's-it's not the risk for the next few months, but it's the risk over time of-of lasting damage to the-to these- you know, to the productive capacity of the United States, typically in two forms.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One, through extended periods of unemployment, people lose contact with the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They get out of touch with the skills and-that they need, and-and they have a hard time getting back in, and that drives that-that, you know, it's very damaging to people's lives and their working lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it also just lowers, in a way-it can-it can increase the-you know, the unemployment rate, but it can also lower the labor force participation rate, which is almost worse, in a way, to have people dropping out of the labor force where we need them in the-in the labor force working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, a shock like this that just comes in, it's like a natural disaster.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You wouldn't want a lot of perfectly good businesses, particularly the smaller and medium-sized businesses that may not have a lot of resources to sustain them to- you know, to go out of business permanently in a situation like that-like this where, really, there was no reason for it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, you know, businesses are going to go in and out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're going to fail all the time, and that's a healthy thing in capitalism.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a way-potentially-so those are the things we've been worried about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't change our longer-run estimate of-of potential growth or of the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-I would say, in my thinking, the reason I didn't change mine is that I still-I-I think we can avoid that or avoid much of that, most of that even.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-and we do that with measures that-that, you know, keep people in their homes; that-that support hiring; that support growth; that avoid unnecessary, avoidable business insolvencies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's all the things that we're trying to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Basically, if you look at what's happened, as I mentioned, there's something-somewhere short of 25 million people have been displaced, even after the good May employment report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're trying to do is create an environment in which they have the best chance either to go back to their old job or to get a new job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-that's kind of the most important part of this exercise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And maybe these-it's probably hopeful at this point to say that-that we won't have longer-run damage to the economy, and these numbers won't change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but I think it's way too early to be-to be changing the longer run-see, these are-these are not meant to be short- run numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're called-they're longer-run assessments, so I-I would-I have not changed mine, and I'm hopeful that-that I won't have to change it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There have been gains in market function, although not fully back to where you would say they were, for example, in-in February, before the pandemic arrived.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a-this is a highly fluid situation, and we're- we're not taking those for granted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in addition, as I pointed out in my-in my statement, those purchases are clearly also supporting highly accommodative-or accommodative financial conditions, and that's-that's a good thing, so that's why we're doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Turning quickly to Main Street, so I would say that the thing-what we've done on Main Street, I think to a greater degree, is, we've listened to feedback.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've been out repeatedly for feedback in trying to create a-a much more difficult product than, really, the other facilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think this-this last set of changes we made have actually been very positive for the facility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's going to be better able to achieve its goals, and, you know, so we've used the time well, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that-we are now in the-in the-in the final run-up to starting the facility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we did, as you saw earlier-I guess it's early this week or late, whenever we did it in the last few days-was we lowered the minimum loan size and we increased the maximum loan size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, I think, even more importantly, we lengthened the maturity and we stretched out the repayment schedule significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So borrowers will get a-a two-year delay until they have to make any principal payments-repayments and a one-year delay on interest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we had been hearing from both borrowers and lenders that these would be very helpful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Shortly after that, the facility itself will be up, and those facilities can be-those loans can be sold-95 percent of the loans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's 95 percent across the board now in the Main Street facility can be sold.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think this has-this has been a challenging project, but I think we've come to a-to a better place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, we're-we're going to be prepared to adapt further, if we need to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You-you have to draw this up and then try it out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've-we've been, you know, very willing to adapt and will continue to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can-we can make changes to bank regulation and supervision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know that we have the ability to make changes, for example, in mortgage payments, if that's what you're thinking of, or credit card payments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's really-that's something that could be legislative, or it could just be what the-what the banks themselves are doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's been a tremendous amount of forbearance on the part of the banks, and I guess our role there would be to encourage it, but those are not decisions that we hold any legal authority to make, and we-by the way, we have encouraged those decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we try to keep our comments on fiscal policy at a high level, and I'll-I'll come to your specific question, but I would just say this: This is the biggest economic shock in the U.S. and in the world, really, in living memory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We went from the lowest level of employ-unemployment in 50 years to the highest level in close to 90 years, and we did it in two months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, appropriately, the response from fiscal authorities has been large, forceful, and very quick by-by the standards of these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Roughly $3 trillion Congress has authorized, and that's benefiting households; laid-off workers; small, medium, and large businesses; hospitals; state and local governments-14 percent of GDP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is-it's in a class by itself, in terms of both the size and the speed of it, and it's also pretty innovative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the-both the PPP and the unemployment insurance are quite innovative in the American context, and there were difficulties in implementing it, but that's really a function of-of their novelty, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those programs-by the way, let me add: The Fed also-we both innovated and acted forcefully, progressively, proactively, and aggressively as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you put those together, all of that is making a difference now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The expanded unemployment insurance and also the stimulus checks have gone a long way to replacing lost income from-from job loss.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you're seeing it in the job market data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many are giving the PPP credit on that front and-and in keeping small businesses going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-so far, it's a good response, and it's having-it's having a big effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You-you get to-the question is, it's big-everyone can see that it's big.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-and the question for-for-the question that I've been concerned about, really, is this issue of longer-run damage to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-we're-we're doing a fair job of getting through these first few months, more than a fair job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question, though, is, that group of people who won't be able to go back to work quickly, what about them?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that could be many millions of people, you know, parts- who worked in parts of the economy that will be the slow ones to recover.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we want those people back in the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and-and they're going to need possibly-probably will need further support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I will just say this: It's possible that we will need to do more, and it's possible that Congress will need to do more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the $600 unemployment insurance, I wouldn't-I wouldn't try to give Congress advice on the specifics of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I know they're looking at-I mean, I-I know from both talking to people and-and reading the papers that they're looking at a whole bunch of different possible approaches going forward, and some of those seem kind of promising.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we're happy to give advice if people ask for it but-but probably not-not publicly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't offer any advice, but I will provide a little context for the- for-I want to be clear about the picture-one way to look at the picture, really, and that is this: You can-you can get at this by looking at, you know, the-the-the widest measure of unemployment, of labor market slack, if you will, is the U-6 measure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the U-that's the- the one we look-talk about all the time is called U-3, by economists.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the-the one that has a much broader measurement of slack in the economy is U-6.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in-in-in U-6, the U-6 level of unemployment has tripled from 7 percent to 21 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That-that amounts to 22 million additional people who are-who've-who've lost work in the economy either by going to part time or something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's in the low 20s, and that's post the May employment report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can take the 21 [million]-people who have-had-are listed as unemployed right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can add more on for the ones who were miscoded.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can also take those people who are suddenly out of the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You put those together, and that has gone up by about 24 million.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the question is, 20, 22, 24 million people-got to get them back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Somehow, we've got to all, as a country, get those people back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They didn't do anything wrong; this was a natural disaster, and I-I really-I do think the responses so far have been great.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if-if you think we-I would just, in terms of the May employment report, it's-it's so nice to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think what people were thinking was that you'd start to get those back- to-work kind of numbers in June and July and August.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, almost no one saw that happening as early as mid-May, but it did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, you know, and we-we don't know fully what that means, whether it's just a timing change or whether it will prove to be much more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is a-as I mentioned earlier, it is clear evidence of just how uncertain things are, and-and how humble we have to be about our ability to-to really have confident predictions as opposed to just predictions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, bottom line, I would just say, that-that-the key thing people need to understand is that there's just a lot of work to do in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to stick with this and support that until the work is done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That you-you can-that is something we're going to do with all of our tools, and I think it may require Congress to help as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-you know, we have major responsibilities and powerful tools, but the decision about when to reopen the economy is one for elected officials at the state and local and federal level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, if they ask, we-we don't have any particular expertise here at the Fed in pandemics or coronaviruses or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We talk to experts, but-you know, so we don't have anything special to add on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just say, it's-you know, it's kind of self evident, I think, that if a-if it happens, you know, the-the issue would be, first of all, people's health, but secondly, you could see a public loss of confidence in-in parts of the economy that will be already slow to recover.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it could hurt the recovery even if you don't have a national-level pandemic, just a-just a series of-of local ones, of local spikes could-could have the effect of undermining people's confidence in traveling, in restaurants and entertainment, anything that involves getting people together in small groups and feeding them or flying them around-those things could be hurt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it would not be a positive development, and I'll just leave it at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, remember, lots and lots of companies are getting financed, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you have a-a-a much better lending climate than-than certainly than we had in February and March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-we- and we do expect it to be up quite soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the timing of these things, so, you know, we'll leave them open as-we'll leave them open for new loans as long as they need to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That'll be a decision we make, of course, with our colleagues at the Treasury Department.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, at a certain point, there won't be a need for further loans, and-and then the assets will-will be there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so if that's-I don't know if that's a part of your question too, but I would just say that, at that point, you know, the-the useful role of the-of the Federal Reserve is probably close to an end at that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't have any expertise in managing pools of credit assets, loans-if you will-or bonds, and we, you know, we don't want to be made-we don't really want to be part of the decisions that have to be made to manage such a portfolio, so we'd be looking to have that done either someplace else or, you know, by-by a third party or at the Treasury Department or something.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're, you know, we're working on ideas for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But our real focus now is on-is getting these facilities going and-and getting them to do the job that they-they need to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that many forecasters had been expecting a bottom for the economy in-around the middle of the year, with-with a huge range of uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the labor market-the evidence of one jobs report is that the labor market may have hit bottom in May.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, many forecasters widely expect a-a recovery over the second half of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it-it is possible, but the thing is, we're not going to overreact to a single data point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be very careful about reaching any conclusions about-about good data or bad data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I think, you know, we're going to be here with our tools supporting this economy for as long as it's needed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but I think there's a possibility that-that the bottom has come in the labor market, but we don't know that yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of the-you know, the effect of the pandemic on inequality, what you see- the pandemic, of course, hits everybody, but in an economic sense, it hits those industries that are-that involve groups of people in tight groups, either in places where they're-it's the travel, leisure, restaurant, bars, those kinds of service-economy jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so a lot of the lost jobs were from people who work in the service economy, dealing with the public, for example, and relatively-compared to other jobs, relatively low wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and if-if you just look at what that is, unemployment has gone up more for Hispanics, more for African Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And women have borne-borne an extraordinary-a notable share of the burden beyond their percentage in the workforce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's really-really, really unfortunate, because if you just go back two months, where we were was, we had, effectively, the first tight labor market in a quarter-century.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And for the last couple of years before the pandemic hit, you were seeing wages go up the most for people at the lower end of the wage spectrum, and that was great.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we were meeting with people from low- and-low- and moderate-income communities all over the country and hearing, "Don't change this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we had every expect-every expectation, every reason to expect that this would continue, and then this comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-it's heartbreaking, and, you know, we want to get it back, so-we really want to get it back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think we learned a number of things over the course of the last few years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One of them is that, you know, I-you-you can have 3, 3½ percent unemployment for a couple of years, and, really, you see modest moves in wages and relatively almost invisible moves in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that was not anybody's understanding of the structure of the economy, I think, or most peoples', anyway.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we can use our tools to-to support the labor market and support the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can-we can use them until we do fully recover, and that-that's what we're planning to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What-what we are-we are cognizant of the fact, though, that late in the last cycle, late in the last expansion, the benefits really do go more to people at the lower end of the wage spectrum for-for the first time in many years when labor markets are tight, when unemployment is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we would really like to get back to that- get back to that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the way-the way we do forecasts is, we-we don't- the-we don't tend to incorporate things we're highly uncertain about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the-the forecast would not have included substantial additional-you know, big additional fiscal support for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Maybe-maybe a modest amount, something that looks like a-a low-end guess on what might come out of the current negotiations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, if there were more fiscal support, you'd see-you'd see better results sooner, but that's a question for Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're-we're spending a lot, and that's really what they get to decide.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of Main Street and our willingness to expand it further, I think we're-one thing we're looking at-very strongly looking at is-is nonprofits, and is there a way to-to incorporate them into-into that facility or a similar facility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I- you know, if we had a great idea for changing Main Street, we would've done it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-and we have done some things that I think are really very positive lately here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if we-as we learn more, it could be-it could be in terms of size, it could be in terms of lots of different things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I-I think we have a good product to go to market with now, and I think it'll get- it'll get out there soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we'll see, and-and we'll be willing to continue to adapt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-and I-I would say, many will go back, but what's-what's going to be the remainder when-you know, when we reach sort of what is the new normal?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-it's so uncertain, but it-it could be a good number of millions of people, I think, in many-in many estimates, but these-I'd say you're so early in the process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People are-for example, people are going back and looking at other significant changes in the economy, and they've seen how many people go back when, for example, there's a technological change, and things like that-you may have seen some of this research-and you come up with an estimate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-you know, it's just going to be very hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I, but I-my-my assumption is that there will be a significant chunk-chunk well into the millions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I don't want to give you a number, because it's going to be a guess, but well, well into the millions of people who-who don't get to go back to their old job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in fact, there isn't a-there may not be a job in that industry for them for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There will eventually be, but it could be some years before we get back to those people finding jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, when-when people lose a job, if they can find a job in their own industry, that's usually the fastest way, is-is they know other people in that industry, different kinds of jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you have to go to a different industry and start over again, it's much harder, and that's where you start to lose people's-who are-just fall out of the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We all know people who-to whom that happened in the Global Financial Crisis, and, hence, our desire to-to do what we can to support this and-and-and support this recovery with-with the tools that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do track all unemployment by all kinds, as you know- all kinds of different demographics, including particularly the African American unemployment rate, which reached an all-time low since the data started being kept in the modern era.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, it's still close to twice the white unemployment-it is twice the unemployment rate, or it was back in the-back then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the-the best thing we can do with our monetary policy tools is to-is to look at, you know, the evidence of what we saw-that we saw with our own eyes so recently, which is that the economy can have very low unemployment-very low unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It could be lower than 3½ percent without seeing financial imbalances, without seeing inflation going-getting out of control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, frankly, didn't even get inflation back up to target-without seeing wages getting out of touch with-with where they should be, so that's the-that's the biggest thing we can do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, in-in-inequality is something that's been with us increasingly for more than four decades, and it's-it's not really related to monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, or-or it's more related to-there are a lot of theories on-on what causes it, but it's been something that's more or less been going up consistently for more than four decades.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are a lot of different theories, one of which is-just is that it-globalization-globalization and technology call for rising levels of skills and aptitudes and education, and that U.S. educational attainment kind of flattened out, certainly relative to our peers-flattened out over that period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so a lot-so that means if you're-if you're on the right side of those trends, then those things are good for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you're not, then your wages are going to stagnate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And wages for the bottom, you know, 10 percent really haven't gone up in real terms in a very long time, and-over a long period of time, whereas wages for the people at the top, compensation, any way you cut it-before taxes, after taxes, after transfers, all of those, any way you cut it-wages have-compensation has gone up a whole lot for people at the top, and it really hasn't gone up for people at the bottom.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look more in the middle, then it's-then-then it has gone up for most other groups, but at the bottom, not so much in real terms, in inflation-adjusted terms.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we-we call it out as a-as an important factor in the economy, and we will use our tools to support maximum employment and take that, you know, definition to heart.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, obviously, that's something that's going to require an all-of-society, all-of-government response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go back to the end of February and early March, you had-basically, the world markets realized at just about the same time-I remember that Monday-that there was going to be a global pandemic, and that this possibility that it would be contained in one province in China, for all practical purposes, was not going to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It all-it was-you know, it was Iran, Italy, Korea, and then it became clear in markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: From that point forward, investors everywhere in the world, for a period of weeks, wanted to sell everything that wasn't cash or a-a short-term Treasury instrument.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They didn't want it to have any risk at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-that's the kind of situation that can be very-financial turbulence and malfunction-a financial system that's not working can greatly amplify the negative effects of what was clearly going to be a major economic shock.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what our tools were-were put to work to do was to restore the markets to function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, you know, some of that has really happened, as I-as I mentioned in my opening remarks, and that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-we're not looking to achieve a particular level of any asset price.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we want is investors to be pricing in risk like markets are supposed to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think our-our principal focus, though, is on-on the state of the economy and on the labor market and on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, inflation, of course, is-is low, and we think it's very likely to remain low for some time, below our target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, really, it's about getting the labor market back and getting it in shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, you know, we-if we were to hold back because-we would never do this, but-the idea that, just the concept that we would hold back because we think asset prices are too high-others may not think so, but we just decided that that's the case-what would happen to those people?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what would happen to the people that we're actually legally supposed to be serving?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're supposed to be pursuing maximum employment and stable prices, and that's what we're pursuing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also pursuing financial stability, but there you have a banking system that is so much better capitalized, so much stronger, better aware of its risks, better at managing its risks, more highly liquid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say that, you know, we're tightly focused on our real economy goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And- and, again, not-we're not-we're not focused on moving asset prices in a particular direction at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just we want markets to be working, and I think, partly as a result of what we've done, they-they are working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so our-our dollar swap lines-we introduced those back at the beginning of-of this episode after the pandemic made itself present.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And dollar funding markets were in very difficult shape at the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the introduction of the swap lines has really restored dollar funding markets around the world to fairly normal levels of activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we extended them-I guess, yesterday morning- really to facilitate planning by other central banks and just so people will know that those facilities are still there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want them to remain in place and be available as long as they are needed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And since, you know, the crisis and the economic fallout from-from the pandemic are far from over, we're going to leave those in place for the time being.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll leave them in place until we're confident that they're no longer needed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's nothing that's going on in the market right now that raises any concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just, we want them to be there as a backstop for markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They-they appropriated that money, and-$454 billion for our facilities, and it's really a question for them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right that our facilities have not-we haven't done as much lending as we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in very substantial measure, that's because markets started working again fairly soon after we announced the facilities, particularly in the corporate credit facilities, also in the muni-in the muni space, and also in the short-term funding facilities-the three of those that we set up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we didn't turn out to need the kind of funding that we thought we would.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other hand, it's important that the facilities stay in place, and that's why we extended them yesterday.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's important that they still stay in place until we're, you know, very confident that the turmoil from the pandemic and the economic fallout are behind us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-I can't really speak to what Congress should do with it, but it's important that the facilities be there and be fully funded in case the needs do arise down the road.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't see them now, but, in case they do arise, they should be there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on your first question, I wouldn't want to be giving very detailed, specific advice on particular programs and the level they should be at and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just will say the following, that, you know, this-this pandemic and its fallout really represents the biggest shock to the U.S. economy in living memory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We went from the lowest levels of unemployment we'd had in 50 years to the highest levels we've had in 90 years, and we did it in the space of two months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say that the response from the fiscal authorities was strong, it was fast, it was broad-and appropriately so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we are seeing the results of the earlier strong fiscal actions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When you see the spending that's happening, when you see small businesses staying in business even though the economy hasn't fully, successfully, sustainably reopened yet in many places, you are seeing what happens with that-that money.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, in-in a broad sense, it's been well spent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, in the broad scheme of things, that there will be a need both for more support from us and from more fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it suggests to me that there's-you know, that both sides, they're wrangling over-over various provisions but nonetheless believe that there is a need for some additional fiscal support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the last thing I'll say is that if the expansion-even if-sorry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Even if the reopening goes well and many, many people go back to work, it's still going to take a fairly long time for the parts of the economy that are-that involve lots of people getting together in close proximity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means that many of the people who were laid off from those industries-and that's restaurants, you know, bars, hotels, public entertainment, all of those places, travel and accommodation-many of those people are going to find it hard to go back-they can't go back to their old job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think those people are going to need support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But they're going to need support if they're to be able to pay their bills, to continue spending money, to remain in their current rental house or-or apartment or a house if they own it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of inequality, really-so I think it's fair to say that the burdens of the pandemic have fallen on, heavily-they've fallen on everyone, but they've fallen very heavily on people who work in the service industries in relatively low-paying jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there was a-a figure that came out of some of our research that was that if you make $40,000 a year or less, then 40 percent-you had a 40 percent chance of losing your job in April and May.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's falling very heavily on-on people who have the least financial wherewithal to, you know, to bear that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that happens to be heavily skewed to minorities and to women.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, in terms of what we're doing, what we're trying to do is create an environment in the financial markets and in the economy where those people have the best chance they can have to go back to work to their old job or to a new job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the-I would say-I would say one last thing on inequality.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is, inequality is a-is an issue-has been a growing issue in our country and in our economy for four decades.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see it in the relative flattening-out of-of incomes for people in low and-lower and middle incomes as compared to those at the top.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see it in low mobility where people-where the chances of moving up from the bottom to the middle or the top have declined and are lower than they are in other comparable wealthy countries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a serious economic problem for the United States, but it's-it's got underlying causes that are not related to monetary policy or to our response to the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's about the flattening-out of educational attainment in the United States compared to our other competitor countries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you're on the wrong side of those forces, it's been-your income has stagnated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-it's a critical, critical problem for our society, but one that really falls mainly to fiscal policy and other policies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our part of it is to-is to push as hard as we can on our employment mandate while keeping price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We saw what happened to people at-at the lower end of the income spectrum late in the last expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was the best labor market in 50 years, they told us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We saw that the biggest wage increases were going to people at the bottom end of the-of the wage spectrum for the last couple of years of that 10-year, 8-month expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a tight labor market is probably the best thing that the Fed can foster to-to go after that-that problem, which is a-a serious one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right, the asset purchases in-in their current size really sprang from severe dysfunction in the Treasury and MBS markets at the beginning of the market reaction to the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And thanks to those purchases, we have substantially restored-not fully, but substantially restored functioning markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That market is really one of the-it's part of the absolute bedrock of the global financial markets, and it's-it's essential that it-that it work well, and it is doing so now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've always said, though, that we understand, accept, and are fine with the fact that-that those purchases are also fostering a more accommodative stance of monetary policy, which would tend to support macroeconomic outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's doing both, and-and, you know, we've understood that for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-the programs are not structured exactly like the-the QE programs were in the last-in the last financial-in the aftermath of the last financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of our strategy, you know, that just remains to be seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-as you know, we've spent a lot of time in meetings this year looking at the tools that we have to adjust our current stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do feel that our current monetary policy stance is the appropriate one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we cut rates close to zero right at the beginning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-we ramped up asset purchases, and those-those have really helped.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we gave forward guidance on-on both of those things, which the markets appear to understand, and market pricing is consistent with those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think we're-we think that our-our policy stance is a good one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, of course, prepared to adjust that stance as appropriate and when we deem it as appropriate to-to better foster achievement of our goals, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we make the policy decisions in conjunction with our colleagues, and they just execute our-our plans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I actually don't remember exactly what I would have been talking with him about, but he's a-you know, he's the head of a major service provider.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: He generally checks in to find out whether we're okay with the quality of the service that-that BlackRock is providing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't have the daily face-to-face interaction with anybody else at BlackRock or-or, as you can see, three phone calls in the course of a few months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, you know, their conflicts are managed extremely carefully in the contractual arrangements we have with them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, I would have-I-I can't recall exactly what those conversations were, but they were-they would have been about what are you seeing in the markets and things like that too-you know, generally exchanging information.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And he's-he's typically trying to make sure that-that we are getting good service from the company that he founded and leads.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-the situation with coins is that the-the quantity of coins is going up but was adequate before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The problem is, the circulation kind of stopped because stores were closed, banks were closed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just-customers weren't spending, they were-so the coins stopped moving in the system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've been working for-ever since that began to happen, we saw it happening right away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've been working to try to-try to reverse that disruption of the supply chain and restore normal circulation for our coins.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're working with the U.S. Mint, which is the issuing authority, to address the issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just last week, the Mint-you may have seen-issued a statement asking for the public's help in keeping coins circulating, and various people, you know, went and put their coins back into circulation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also created a coin task force with all of the stakeholders-you know, banks and, you know, the armored carriers, the banking community, credit unions, everybody in the-in the coin supply chain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're in frequent communication with the banks and with the-with the armored carriers trying to get back to where we need to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the Mint-the Mint is making coins as fast as they can, but-but, you know, things happen with-in the factory environment: Someone will come to work with COVID-I think this has happened in-in almost every factory environment around the country-and then they'll shut down for a day, and then they come back, and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've-we've got a lot of resources on it, and we do feel like we're-we're making progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So maybe I'll talk more broadly about the-the outlook and include your-include your question in it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, economic activity and employment picked up beginning in May and right through June and remained well below their levels because, I'd say, job gains have reversed about a third of the job losses from March and April, and consumer spending has reversed about a half of the drop.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but, nonetheless, those were-those were sooner and stronger than we expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but what happened then was, along with that positive data, we got-we got the virus increases starting in the middle of June in lots and lots of states around the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that brings us to a new-a new point here, which is, we need to-in addition to dealing with the health crisis-we have to remember, this is really a health crisis, and these are people who are having the coronavirus, and it's taking a terrible toll, so we've got to deal with the economic ramifications of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we're seeing is that we monitor quite a lot of what we-what we think of as sort of nonstandard, high-frequency data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's become a very important thing, even more important than usual in the work that we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what that data show, on balance, is that the pace of the recovery looks like it has slowed since the cases began that spike in June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So some measures of consumer spending based on credit card and debit card data have moved down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Recent labor market indicators point to a slowing in job growth, particularly among smaller businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People aren't going out to restaurants, bars, gas stations, pharmacies, and beauty salons as much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Consumer surveys, by the way, which had dropped very sharply when the pandemic arrived and then moved back up sharply- they look like they may be softening again now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, on balance, it looks like the data are pointing to a slowing in the pace of the recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I want to stress, it's-it's too early to say both how large that is and how sustained it will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just don't know yet, because we have to wait for-to see the, you know, the actual data on spending and employment come in, and-but this-this is what we're seeing, and, of course, we're monitoring it very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The path of the economy is going to depend to a very high extent on the course of the virus and on the measures that we take to keep it in check.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is just a very fundamental fact about our economy right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, social-distancing measures and fast reopening of the economy, they actually go together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think we feel that it-it might be, the most central fact or the most central driver of the path of the economy right now is the virus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw that in the-during the lockdown when we got cases way down, and you saw the economy reopening, and you saw spending go up and hiring go up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now that the-that the cases have spiked again-again, the early data, the high-frequency data suggest that there is a slower pace of growth, at least for now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know how deep or how long that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just decided that it needed to be in our-in our postmeeting statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I think we can't say it enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-you know, you can think of it as three stages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's the lockdown, and we know what that looks like, and we'll get the data, I guess, later this week on GDP being down very historically large amounts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then there was the reopening, and we would expect that many, many people would go back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those whose jobs could be done without-you know, without exposure to lots of people in tight groups, they should have been-they should be able to go back to work during that phase fairly quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that would depend on being able to keep the virus under control, which will depend on wearing masks and other social-distancing measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-it's in-we're all talking about it, so we thought it really had to be in the statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are committed to using our full range of tools to support the U.S. economy at this difficult time, and we will always remain committed in that sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We feel like we have ways to further support the economy certainly through our credit and liquidity facilities, which are effectively unlimited.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-we feel like we have the ability to do more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would not disagree with the-with the importance of fiscal policy-with your statement about the importance of fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Fiscal policy can do-can address things that we can't address.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If there are particular groups that need help, that need direct monetary help- not a loan, but an actual grant as the PPP program showed-you can save a lot of businesses and a lot of jobs with those in a case where lending a company money might not be the right answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The company might not want to take a loan out in order to pay workers who can't work because there's no business.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So lending is a particular tool, and we're using it very aggressively.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But fiscal policy is essential here, and I would say, again, Congress's action early in the pandemic-historically large by any standard around the world, and certainly by U.S. standards-it's really helping now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's going to stand up very well to-to scrutiny down the years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This Congress's very fast and very open-handed response, I think, has really helped.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think-I know that, as I've said, very likely more will be needed from- from all of us, and I see Congress negotiating now over-over a new package, and I think that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-of course, the concept of vaccines comes up in our discussions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I have to say, you know, we're-our job is not to plan for the upside case, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our job is to plan for all-the full range of things that could happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're assuming-we're going to continue to assume that our facilities are needed, that our policies are needed, and that the public needs-you know, needs the support that we're giving the public until-until shown otherwise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's great uncertainty around the development of therapeutics and vaccines.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of us want them to happen as soon as possible, but we can't plan on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got to hope for the worst-hope for the [laughs]-hope for the best and plan for the worst, I guess it goes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I-you know, I think, fundamentally, this is a disinflationary shock.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I know there-there is a lot of discussion about how this might lead to inflation over time, but, you know, we're-we're seeing disinflationary pressures around the world going into this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now we see a big shock to demand, and we see core inflation dropping to 1 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think for quite some time we're going to be struggling against disinflationary pressures rather than against inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, as we've said, we're carefully monitoring the situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We moved very quickly and very aggressively early, and we've been monitoring the situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the markets and-and the economy-you know, I think our policy is in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we've looked at-at ways of adapting our policy as time goes by, and we're ready to do that when we think it's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It really just is when we think it would help: Would it help more than what we're doing now to foster maximum employment and stable prices?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as I-as I said earlier, or a while back, we're not even thinking about-thinking about raising rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-we're totally focused on providing the economy the support that it will need.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that the economy will need highly accommodative monetary policy and the use of our tools for an extended period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're absolutely committed to staying in this until-until we're very confident that that is no longer needed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't look for us to be sending signals about cutting back on facilities or anything like that for a very long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think this-you know, I think the picture is, you have the-you have the lockdown, then you have the reopening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's probably going to be a long tail where a large number of people are struggling to get back to work because those-those heavily affected areas of the economy are going to be challenged, really, to employ the millions of people who are now out of work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think 14 million people are now out of work who were working in February, something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's going to take a while, I think, in everyone's reckoning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I just-everyone should know that we're going to be there for all of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we always point this out in our-in our remarks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: While the aggregate unemployment rate was 3½ percent, every-every economy-every market in every economy has longer-run issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And one of ours is just the disparate level of unemployment between-between Blacks and whites.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's generally sort of twice as much-twice as high for Blacks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So even-but this was the lowest, you know, Black unemployment rate in 50 years-or, actually, since we started keeping records, which was less than 50 years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's just a fact, and it's-it's not a good fact, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have started, though, in recent years to focus considerable time and attention on disparate levels of unemployment-for example, among-among different racial groups and demographic groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We call them out in testimony and in speeches and in our Monetary Policy Report to Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You'll see it everywhere, in all the things that we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-you know, I think what we learned is that a tight labor market really does a lot of good things for minorities and people at the lower end of the income spectrum generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it-you know, tight labor markets, it took 8 years-it took sort of the 8th and 9th and 10th years of that expansion to get to those benefits.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's not a good strategy, waiting 8, 9, 10 years to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're-we're going to get back there as fast as we can, because that's what we can do, but society more broadly can affect these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we don't really have tools that can address distributional, disparate outcomes as well as fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And just policy generally-education, health care, all those things are much better at doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of-so we do-you will see that-you will see that discussed-the Black unemployment rate discussed all the time in what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we clearly understand now that it's something to weigh when you get a tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's something that you want to be focused on and weigh.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is very much in our thinking-again, in a world where we don't really have the best tools to address that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I have not seen that-I did not see that blog post yet, although someone did mention it to me.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, of course, have been in meetings until just before this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I-without having had a chance to think about it, read it, understand it, I'll just say a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, I think it's fair to acknowledge that there's been a lot of pain and injustice and unfair treatment that women have experienced in the workplace-not just among economists, but among economists and at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, like every other organization, the Fed could have done more and-and should have done more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, though, that we-you know, we have made it a very high priority to have as diverse and inclusive an organization as we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we've made a lot of progress on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we want a place where it's free to speak, where views are welcome, where people can disagree but must do so respectfully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think a lot of organizations are coming around to understanding the importance of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-my experience has been, you know, from my career in business too, is that organizations-the really successful organizations in our society get this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They-mostly, they get it that if you want to attract the best people, this is what you-you're going to attract the best people by having a diverse and inclusive workforce, so-and workplace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We actually-you know, this has been a big issue for the economics profession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had the-the two heads of the AEA task force on this-who happen to be named Ben Bernanke and Janet Yellen-come here, and I cohosted a-an event with them, I guess, last year or the year before, which had several hundred-500 people or something like that listening in about-about these issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're doing a lot to-you know, to foster a respectful climate-particularly for women, but for-for all people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-it's a very high priority for us as an organization.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will look into-into that and-when I-you know, when this is over.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as I mentioned earlier, you know, we're watching this high- frequency data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, the official labor market reports come out once a month, and no one has had a very good record lately of predicting what they're going to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They've been, in May and June, stronger than anybody expected, particularly in May.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say, some humility is appropriate here in terms of thinking we understand exactly where this is going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think all we can say today is that there's-there's evidence in the high-frequency data, the surveys, and, you know, you're tracking-you get pictures of spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we-it looks like we're seeing a slowdown in the rate of growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-and that might be-it might be short lived, it might not be, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it seems to be related to-and the timing of it seems to be related to the spike in cases that began in the middle of June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, I really don't want to get ahead of where the data are on this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to have to-the data over the next couple of months will answer that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And recent experience suggests we-we need to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In any case, there's clearly a risk that we're going to see a slowdown in the rate of growth in economic activity and in hiring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Honestly, we-we will not know until we start to see more data come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we haven't-we haven't looked at that, and we have no-no intention.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't done any work or thought about buying equities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we-we're bound by the-by the provisions of 13(3), which requires that we make, you know, facilities-programs or facilities of broad applicability, meaning we have to have-it can't just be focused on one entity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it has to be a broad group of entities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a lot in 13(3) about-about the solvency of the borrowers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, remember, it was rewritten or amended after the financial crisis, and it was written in a way that was-that was to-meant to make it challenging to bail out large financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's- there was a lot in there to make sure that, you know, that they were going to be solvent and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we haven't looked and said-tried to say, "What can we buy?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we felt that, using these facilities, that we could buy corporate bonds and-and municipal bonds, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The statute doesn't say that, but, yeah, you could read the statute that way if you want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Honestly, we haven't tried to push it to, you know, what's the theoretical limit of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think, clearly, it's-it's supposed to-it's supposed to replace lending, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're stepping in to provide credit at times when the market has stopped functioning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-and so I think you've got to-you've got to sort of work within that framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I-I think that the main thing that tells you is that the-the labor market has a long way to go to recover.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are always going to be issues within an economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the labor market really has a long way to go now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Even with two very strong months of job creation-7½ million jobs between the two months-we still have 14 million people unemployed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as-and that leads to a situation where there are so many people looking for jobs, and we have the economy only partially reopened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there aren't, you know-until the economy-or as the economy fully reopens, people can go back to work, but-so it's a tough situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, of course, the reported wages went up because of the composition effect-you know, it's low-paid workers didn't go back to work, so-they were the ones that got laid off-so average hourly earnings went up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But clearly, clearly the pressure-there will not be much upward pressure on wages and compensation at the aggregate level here in a world where there are just an awful lot of people looking for work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the main-so it just underscores again the-the urgency of doing everything we can to restore the labor force and-and to support those who are-who want to be in the labor force but whose jobs have gone away for some period of time as they find other work due to this natural disaster.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a great discussion that we-we've talked about that at past meetings, and I imagine we will at future meetings and haven't made any decisions yet on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, you've got a couple ways to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can say we will-for a specific period of time, we will keep rates at X level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Or you can say we'll keep them there until you achieve a certain macroeconomic goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it can either be inflation or it could be an employment goal, as you pointed out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that, you know, there's attraction in all of those depending on the situation, I think, for obvious reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can imagine situations where, you know, where you'd really want to be targeting macroeconomic outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also the case, though, that sometimes- sometimes date-based guidance works too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it really is very fact specific, and it's not something we've-you know, we haven't made any decisions on that, so I wouldn't be standing here telling you we're going to go this way or that way, you know, should the time come for us to-to change our forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think what the stress tests showed is that, under the "regular way" stress test, the banks passed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But right in the middle of the-of the stress test came the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we quickly dropped in three other scenarios, which were, you know, really bad scenarios.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we pivoted, and we used the provision that says we can-that says there's been a material change, and we're going to ask them to resubmit their capital plans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're working through the details of how all of that will work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're going to-I think we're going to send out the-the stress scenarios on September 30th.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I would say, that's-you know, that-that process is working that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but you're making a connection to it, to the Collins Amendment fix.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what's going on there is that, like many other supervisors and regulators around the world, what we found is that our-we have found our banks are strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they've really been a source of strength in this-in this crisis so far.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they've written off bad loans and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're still well capitalized and strong and will be, I think, a source of strength in this situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but what-what we did earlier was, we-what happens is, the banks run up against their leverage ratio, which is a non-risk-sensitive measure just of the amount of assets on the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people put cash in-on deposit at the banks, and they reached the limit of how-how much they could grow or made loans-you know, they-companies drew down loans and deposited cash.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we gave some leverage ratio relief earlier by temporarily-it's temporary relief-by eliminating, temporarily, Treasuries from the calculation of the-of the leverage ratio.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If Congress chooses to do this, we would want it to be explicitly temporary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-in other words, this will not be a permanent change in capital standards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't decided to do it, but it would give us the ability to allow banks to grow their balance sheet and, in doing so, to serve their customers better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I have to tell you, if you look around the world, bank regulators-many, many bank regulators around the world have given leverage ratio relief.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, Swiss National Bank, the Bank of Japan, the European Commission did, the Bank of Canada did, we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-it's not, it's not-what it's doing is, it's allowing them to grow their balance sheet in a way that serves their customers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, I would want it to be explicitly temporary if-if we do do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so I do think that completion of the review would-first of all, it's something that was a very high priority for-we were really looking forward to completing it, probably, at the June meeting, but it might have been the meeting before that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were right on track, and then we got distracted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it is important to go back and finish that, and I do think that will inform, you know, everything we do going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would also tell you, though, that, to-to a very large extent, the-the changes we'll make to the Statement of [on] Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy are really codifying the way we're already acting with our policies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To a large extent, we're already doing the things that are-that are in there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is just a way of-of acknowledging that and putting them in the document.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't tell you what the exact timing of that will be, but I do think that's a-that's a sensible way to think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we say in our postmeeting statement that we'll continue to increase our securities holdings "at least at the current pace" over coming months "to sustain smooth market functioning and help foster accommodative financial conditions."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That latter part is an updating of our guidance to reflect what I've been saying in these press conferences for some time and what other central banks have acknowledged, which is that the purchases are fostering accommodative financial conditions as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That amounts to roughly $80 billion a month of Treasuries and $40 billion net per month for MBS.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do-we do think that these purchases have been effective in, in restoring orderly market conditions and have supported the flow of credit to households and businesses, including by fostering more accommodative financial conditions, which, of course, we think is a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of going forward, I would just say this: There are various ways and margins that we can adjust our tools going forward, and we'll continue to monitor developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we think our-we think our policy stance is appropriate today, and we're prepared to adjust it going forward as we, as we see appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And today we believe that particularly this very strong forward guidance-very powerful forward guidance that we've announced today will provide strong support for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Effectively, we're saying that rates will remain highly accommodative until the economy is far along in its recovery, and that, that should be a very powerful statement in supporting economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now we're buying $120 billion in securities per month across the-across the Treasury curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do have the flexibility to adjust that tool and, and the rate tool and, and other tools as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as for right now, we think-we think that our policy setting is appropriate to support the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did-we said from the beginning that we would first try to provide some support and stability and relief in the first phase of the crisis, the acute phase, and then we would support the expansion when it came.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's why we changed our guidance today, and we do have the flexibility to do more when we think it's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
