text: So what we said in our Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy was that the Committee's policy decisions reflect "its longer-run goals, its medium-term outlook, and its assessment[s] of the balance of risks, including risks to the financial system that could impede the attainment of the Committee's goals."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And today we said that we'd "be prepared to adjust the stance of monetary policy as appropriate if risks emerge that could impede the attainment of our [the Committee's] goals."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One thing I would say is that financial-that monetary policy should not be the first line of defense-is not the first line of defense on financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look to more appropriate tools in the first instance as a first line of defense, and those would be regulation, supervision, high capital, high liquidity, stress testing-all of those things, macroprudential tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of those things are, are really the first line of defense on financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we always leave open the idea that we will not ignore those kinds of risks and other kinds of risks, more broadly, that could impede the attainment of our goals in, in setting monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's really how we think about it, but principally that, you know, other tools are the-are the frontline, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, what we said again in the [Statement on] Longer-Run [Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy]-you know, in our consensus statement is that we, you know-"policy decisions reflect … the balance of risks, including risks to the financial system that could impede the attainment of the Committee's goals."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the test would be, you know, does a majority of the Committee feel that, that monetary policy is, is triggering that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do monitor financial stability concerns, of course, intensely and regularly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We try to use our other tools on them, but we, we do keep them in mind as we think about monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, you don't-you also don't see people, by and large, lifting off or raising interest rates above zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess there are 4 exceptions out of a Committee of 17 during that-during the forecast period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't reach 2 percent, but we get very close to it in the forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We reach 2 percent-I guess the median is 2 percent at the end of 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It says that we expect that the current setting of, of our rates will be-what we expect [is] that it will be appropriate until such time as we reach 2 percent inflation, that we feel that labor market conditions are consistent with our assessment of maximum employment, and that we're on track to achieve inflation moderate-inflation moderately above.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't think there's any conflict between those two because, you know, the, the way they're set up, the projections don't show the out years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You asked about confidence, and I would say that this, this very strong, very powerful guidance shows both our confidence and our determination.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It shows our confidence that we can reach this goal and our determination to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Because it-we think, looking at everything we know about inflation dynamics in the United States and around the world over recent decades, we expect it will take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We expect that the economy will recover quickly now, but that that pace will slow as, as people go back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll still have an area of the economy-a big area of the economy-that struggles.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy will be below maximum employment, below full demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that will tend to wear-to put downward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think that once we get up closer to maximum employment, we think that inflation will come back, generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, that's sort of what happened during the last long expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a slow process, but-but there is a process there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do expect that will continue today, and we expect that our, our guidance is powerful and will help that outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that-that effectively saying that policy will remain highly accommodative until the economy is very far along in its recovery should provide strong support for the economy and get us there sooner rather than later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, first, if you look at the Summary of Economic Projections that my colleagues and I filed for this meeting, what you'll see is an expectation that the recovery will continue-that it will continue at a reasonable pace through 2021, '22, and '23.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do expect that that pace will slow just because you would expect that the, the pace would be fastest right at the beginning of the-right at the beginning of the recovery, because you had such a sharp decline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You would expect that the third quarter should be the fastest gains, and that, after that, the pace should slow down to a more normal pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, one thing-I guess I would start by saying that the initial response from fiscal authorities was rapid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're seeing the results of that in-today in income and household spending data, in the labor market data, in the construction data, in the data for business equipment spending, and the fact that businesses are staying in business, and, you know, the pace of default and things like that has really slowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That said, my sense is that more fiscal support is likely to be needed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, the details of that are for Congress, not for the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would just say, there are still roughly 11 million people still out of work due to the pandemic, and a good part of those people were working in industries that are likely to struggle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those people may need additional, additional support as they try to find their way through what will be a difficult time for them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've also got struggling small businesses, especially those in the business of facing directly to the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have state and local governments dealing with a drop in revenue at the same time spending has gone up, much of it related to the pandemic and economic effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, I would say, the fiscal support has been essential in, in the good progress we see now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, finally, I'll note that just about all-the overwhelming majority of, of private forecasters who, who project an ongoing recovery are assuming there will be substantial additional fiscal support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so we think that the forward guidance we adopted today is appropriate and, as I mentioned, powerful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Effectively, what it says is that we'll, we will keep policy where it is now-keep the rate policy where it is now until unemployment reaches the Committee's assessments or levels that are-sorry, not unemployment, labor market conditions reach levels that are consistent with the Committee's assessments of maximum employment, until inflation reaches 2 percent, and until it's on track to go above 2 percent moderately for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's very strong forward guidance, and we think that that will be durable guidance that will provide significant support to the economy in coming years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's really our thinking on, on forward guidance on rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you know, maximum employment is not-is not something that can be reduced to a number the way inflation can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It really always has been and, really, a substantial number of factors that we've indicated we would look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's broader labor conditions, consistent with our Committee's assessment of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that would certainly mean low unemployment, it would mean high labor force participation, it would mean wages-it would be a whole range of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking at a judgmental assessment, which I think we'll be very transparent about as we-as we go forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of inflation, you know, this is a Committee that is both confident and committed to-and determined to reach our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the idea that we would look for the, the quickest way out is just-it's just not who we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would not be looking for one month of 2 percent inflation; we said return to 2-to achieve 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So just understand that, you know, we're strongly committed to achieving our goals and the overshoot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Oh, in terms of-okay, in terms of-so, what does "moderate" mean?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of-in terms of "for a time," what it means is not permanently and not for a sustained period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're, we're resisting the urge to try to create some sort of a rule or a formula here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the, the public will understand pretty well what we want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to achieve inflation that averages 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we do that, inflation expectations will be right at 2 percent, and that'll help us achieve 2 percent inflation over time and avoid the situation where the central bank loses its ability to support the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of the effects, so I think what we've done is-is more or less aligned with the consensus statement today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it's in line with what, what might have been expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, I think over time it will provide very powerful support for this economy as we move forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In a sense, it's consistent with expectations, so I don't-I'm not looking for a big reaction right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think, over time, again, guidance that we expect to retain the current stance until the economy is-has moved very far toward our goals is a strong and powerful thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that will be supportive of the economy over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of additional fiscal support, I guess your question is, what would happen if- yes, so, people have different assessments, and, and different participants in the FOMC made different assessments on their own.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think broadly, though, there is an expectation among private forecasters and among FOMC participants that there will be some further fiscal action.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there does seem to be an appetite on the part of all the relevant players to doing something.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I would just say that if-and it's very hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so far the economy has proven resilient to the-to the lapsing of the-to the, of the CARES Act unemployment- enhanced unemployment benefits.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's, there's certainly a risk, though, that, that those who are unemployed have saved-appear to have saved some of those benefits, and they'll, they'll now spend them, and that, as the months pass, if, if there's no follow-up on that, if there isn't additional support and there isn't a job for the-some of those people who are, are from industries where, where it's going to be very hard to find new work, then you'll-that will start to show up in economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll also show up in things like evictions and foreclosures and, and, you know, things that will scar and damage the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think the real question is, is, when and how much and what will be the-what will be the contents?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, no one-no one has any certainty around that, but, broadly speaking, if we don't get that, then there would certainly be downside risks through the- certainly through the channel I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-you know, we monitor everything we think is important in the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in that-in a broad sense, all of it goes into thinking about monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, disparities in, in income and in financial well- being by various demographic and racial categories is something we monitor carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would point to the relative stagnation of incomes for people at the lower end of the income spectrum and also lower mobility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The thing is, we don't really have the tools to address those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we have interest rates and bank supervision and financial stability policy and things like that, but we can't-we can't get at those things through our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we lower the federal funds rate, that supports the economy across a broad range of, of people and activities, but we can't-we don't have the ability to target particular groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Notwithstanding that, we, we do talk about it, because these are important features of our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-you know, I, I think those are-those distributional issues are, are issues that are really for our elected officials.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, I take them seriously as holding back our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The productive capacity of the economy is limited when not everyone has the opportunity, has the educational background and, and the health care and all the things that you need to be an active participant in our workforce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we can-if we want to have the, the highest potential output and the-and the best output for our economy, we need that prosperity to be very broadly spread in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-again, I would just say, the Fed-you know, we can talk about those things a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in, in-when we think about maximum employment in particular, we do look at individual groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So high unemployment in a particular racial group like African Americans when-you know, we would look at that as we think about whether we're really at maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would look-we would look at that along with a lot of other data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the answer is, we do look at all those things and, and do what we can with our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we think our-we think that our asset purchases are doing both the thing-both those things today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think, clearly, there's been great progress, in terms of market function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you remember, early in the spring when the acute phase of the pandemic hit, market function was very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's improved rapidly and, and in many respects is, is in a good place now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also, though, think that these asset purchases, which total $120 billion a month-you know, which is much larger than, for example, the last asset purchase program during the Global Financial Crisis and the recovery therefrom-we think that that's also providing accommodative financial conditions and supporting growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also aware that we, we-there are ways we can adjust that, you know, to do various things-you know, make it smaller, make it larger, and also target different sectors of the-of the curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're, we're going to continue to monitor developments, and we're prepared to adjust our plans as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on the first one, what's happening is basically we're learning to live with-right now, we're learning to live with COVID, which still spreads.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of this recovery that we've seen is in a context where-you know, where people are still at risk of, of catching it, and yet we're able to resume lots and lots of economic activities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that involves, as I mentioned, you know-I think the more social distancing we can preserve as we go back into the workforce-wearing masks, keeping our distance, that kind of thing-the better we'll be able to get economic activity back up close to where it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think, though, there are areas of the economy that are just going to really struggle until we have an-a vaccine that's, that's in wide-you know, wide usage and is, is widely trusted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those are the ones where people were getting really closely-close together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also think testing-to the extent you have cheap and rapid testing, you can do a lot with that in the workforce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can-you can build confidence in the workforce if you have regular-very regular testing that doesn't cost very much and you get the results really quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you do that, you'll be able to open a lot of workforces, particularly in cities where the overall case numbers are quite low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we're, we're going to be finding lots and lots of ways to get out towards-you know, as far as we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's always going to be that-for, for some time, there's going to be certain activities that will be-that will be hard to, to resume.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think that's the only way I can say it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think trying to-you know, we all-when we make a forecast, we make assessments about that, but it's really hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, frankly, for the last 60 days or so, the economy's recovered faster than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we should do those things that we control to make sure that we can recover as quickly as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the main thing, again, is wearing a mask and keeping your distance while you're in the workforce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's something we can all do that will limit the spread and let people go back to work, avoid major outbreaks, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In, in terms of the stress tests, so I really don't have any-you know, we're getting ready quite soon to be making announcements and saying things publicly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's not much I can say with you-nothing, really, that I can say that's-on that today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's got more than half of the banking industry assets signed up among the banks that are part of it, and it's making loans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The number is more like-it's close to $2 billion now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's relatively small now, but it can scale up in response to economic conditions, should that be- should that be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, if you look out in the lending world, surveys generally find that, that firms are not citing credit constraints as a top problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, that is a lot of PPP, bank credit lines, and syndicated loans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking at-some lenders are concerned about the underwriting expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So banks are going to-their approach is likely to be that they're going to underwrite this loan roughly the same as they underwrite any loan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're keeping part of it, and, you know, what, what we want to do is make sure that-that they know that they should take the payment deferrals and other things in, in place, and also that-you know, it's, it's really-it's really a, a facility for, for companies or borrowers that, that don't have access to, to "regular way" borrowing now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be doing some, some-we'll be making some changes in that respect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just would say that, you know, this is 13(3).

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the law under section 13(3), it's very clear that we are to make loans only to solvent borrowers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and the CARES Act is quite specific in keeping all of the terms of, of section 13(3) in effect, including the requirement that we, you know, gather good evidence that the borrower is solvent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This was-this law was amended in, you know, under-in Dodd-Frank, and the idea was, was to make it challenging and put hurdles in place before we made loans-at the time, the thinking was to banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So now we-now we're using that same law for, for smaller business borrowers, and, you know, it doesn't-it's not a perfect fit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, I would also just say, for many borrowers, they're in a situation where their business is still relatively shut down, and they won't be able to service a loan, and so they may need more fiscal support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Having said that, we're, we're continuing to work to, to improve Main Street, to make it more broadly available-make it pretty much to any company that needs it and that can service a loan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, again, if you think about it, we, we weren't-we're, we're going to have to go through the banking system to do this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-we're not going to have a hundred thousand or a million loan officers working for the Fed and the Treasury.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to go through the banking system, and the banks-banks like to make good loans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you should expect that they-and we expect that they will do some underwriting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also want them to take some risk, obviously, because that was the point of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the question is, how do you dial that in?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're getting some loans made, and we're hopeful that we'll, that we'll clarify this and that credit will continue to flow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, we-of course, we can't be-we can't be really sure we know the answers to those questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say, the, the likely path is that the-that the expansion will continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's, as I said, it's well along, and it'll move most easily through the parts of the economy-it'll still take some time, but the parts of the economy that weren't exactly directly affected, that didn't involve getting people in large groups together to feed them, to fly them around, to put them in hotels, do entertainment, things like that-those are going to be the places that are-that are very challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there will also be the-you know, the places that are affected that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's going to be challenging for, for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't really know how long that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, we had 11 million-something like 11 million people in the payroll survey have gone back to work out of 22 million who went-who lost their jobs in March and April.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, 11 million- particularly if the pace of, of returning to work slows down, it's going to leave a large-a large group of people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, we want-you know, the sense of our forward guidance is that policy will remain, as we've said, highly accommodative until the- until the expansion is well along-really, very close to our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And even after, if we do lift off, we will keep policy accommodative until we actually have a moderate overshoot of inflation for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those are powerful commitments that we think will, will support the full recovery, including those people, as long as it takes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, no, I wouldn't-I certainly would not say that we're out of ammo.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, first of all, we, we do have lots of tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got the lending tools, we've got the balance sheet, and we've got further forward guidance-further forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we-there's still plenty more that we can do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do think that our-that our, our rate policy stance is an appropriate one to support the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, you know, this is the kind of guidance that will provide support for the economy over time, the idea being that policy will remain highly accommodative until the recovery is well along-really, very close to our goals-and then will remain accommodative even after we lift off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that's, that's a really strong place for, for rate policy to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, we have the other margins that we can still use.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so, of course we monitor financial conditions very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These were questions that were very much in the air a decade ago and more when, when the Fed first started doing QE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I would say, if you look at the long experience of, you know, the 10-year, 8-month expansion, the longest in our recorded history, it included an awful lot of quantitative easing and low rates for 7 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I would say, it was notable for the lack of the emergence of, of some sort of a financial bubble-a housing bubble or some kind of a bubble, the popping of which could threaten the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, frankly, it hasn't really happened around the world since then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That doesn't mean that it won't happen, but-and so, of course, it's something that we monitor carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: After the financial crisis, we started a new-a whole division of the Fed to focus on financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the Board here, we talk about it more or less on an ongoing basis, so it is something we monitor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I don't know that the-that the connection between asset purchases and, and financial stability is a particularly tight one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but again, we won't be-we won't be just assuming that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, the kinds of tools that we would use to address those sorts of things are not really monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would be more tools that strengthen the financial system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I mean, I think the overall picture-take a step back from this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The overall picture is clear, and that is that the labor market has been recovering, but that it's a long way-a long way from maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The number of claims, the quantity of claims, and, frankly, the fact that PUA claims are new-the Pandemic Unemployment Assistance claims-that's a new system that had to be set up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The actual counting of the claims is, is volatile, and, and it's very difficult to take much signal about the particular level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, because people were setting those systems up, and when they got them set up, they counted them all at once and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, though, what you've seen is that the level of-certainly the level of initial claims has declined very sharply from the very high levels of March and April and is now at a lower level-continues either to be flat or gradually decline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's worth noting-and that's good-it's worth noting that that level is maybe five times the level of what claims were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Claims were around 200,000; now they're 900,000, in that range, weekly for, for initial claims.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that just tells you, the labor market has improved, but it's a long, long way from maximum employment, and it will be some time getting back there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that's the best way to think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In many parts of the economy there's just a lot of disruption, and it's, it's really hard to say precisely where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll give you another example with-you know, we say unemployment's 8. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you count those who are-who are misidentified as, as employed when they're actually unemployed and you add back some part of the participation number-so if you were-if you had a job and you were in the labor force in February and you lost it because of the pandemic, some of you are now being reported as out of the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I-you know, I would-I would more look at those people as unemployed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you add those back, the level of unemployment's probably 3 percent higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other hand, by that metric, the, the unemployment rate would have been in the-in the 20s in, in April.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the improvement has been quite substantial under any measurement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I, I can't be precise about a particular number, but let me just say, there was a lot to like about 3½ percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one would say that number is the touchstone or that is, you know, maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A 3½ percent unemployment rate showed, you know, gains being shared very widely across the income spectrum-in fact, going more to people at the bottom end of the spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It showed labor force participation coming up as-up above many estimates of its trend, as people who'd been out of the labor force were being pulled into a tight job market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a lot to like about a tough-a tight job market, particularly in a world where we didn't see inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I would say, we would like to get back-rather than to a particular number, we'd like to get back to a strong labor market where wages are moving up, where people can find work, where labor force participation is holding up nicely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, of course we would-we need inflation to perform in line with, with our framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the good news is, we think we can have quite low unemployment without raising troubling inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we do-we are gifted with a, a substantial group of researchers who really cover the waterfront.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do a significant amount of research on racial disparities in-across multiple variables, including wealth, as you asked about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we also-remember, we have our Division of Consumer and Community Affairs, which is present in communities around the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the Reserve Banks all have very active community affairs groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's more, just, over a long period of time we, we are in contact with people in those communities to understand their experience of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to use our tools to, to reflect that fact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do quite a bit of research, and I suppose we could do more, but we really do a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we contribute to those fields and those assessments of, of the state of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do that not just because it's interesting and important, but because it's important for the economy and important for our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned earlier, it doesn't mean a particular headline unemployment number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we look at-look at that in many, many different variables, and we ask ourselves whether those variables are-those labor market conditions are consistent with our assessments of what would constitute maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that would include all of the things that we're talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't-I don't want to comment particularly on, on the two dissenters, but they, they consent-they dissented from, of course, different perspectives, and, and that should be clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's their-they're not-they're sort of on, on two sides of the, of the discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say this: I am blessed with having a Committee of highly thoughtful people who bring diverse life experiences and diverse careers, and, of course, diverse views to our work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so I would just say, the right-in our discussions the last couple of days, the whole Committee, everybody on the Committee is very supportive of the Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy and what's in there-very, very broad support, unanimous support for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Everyone sees the, the changes in the underlying economy and sees, in their own way, the need to address those-and including the changes we made to the employment mandate and to inflation so that we're now at flexible average inflation targeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, there would be-this is-you know, we're the first major central bank to adopt this framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no cookbook, and we-you know, this is the first guidance under our new framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course there would be a wide range of views, and you would expect that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would also say this: You know, this is all about credibility, and we understand perfectly that we have to earn credibility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This, this facility-this, this framework has to-we have to support it with our actions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think today is a very good first step in doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is-it ties in very nicely with the Statement of [on] Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had quite a robust discussion, and there are, there are different ideas on how to do this, but I-that's just, that's just the way it is when you have a diverse group of highly thoughtful and effective people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've actually spent quite a bit of time on this as Secretary Mnuchin, I think, mentioned the other day.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, you know, our facilities are essentially always-they have to be, under the law-broad based and not so much targeting any single sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Also, it's important to remember that CRE, commercial real estate, benefits from several of our existing facilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the TALF takes commercial mortgage-backed securities and SBA commercial real estate deals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, I would say, Main Street helps businesses pay their rent, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're helping real estate, you know, in a number of other ways-commercial real estate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One is just that commercial properties with CMBS loans often have covenants-uniformly, I think, have covenants that forbid them to take on more debt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you have a situation, and you have a situation where, where you-without a legal change or some kind of an innovation that defies discovery so far, you're-you have a hard time providing mass relief with regard to real estate that's in, in commercial mortgage-backed securities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, it may be that further support for commercial real estate will require further action for Congress-from Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a very, very important question, and I actually spoke about that in my Jackson Hole remarks a couple weeks ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is intuitive that, that high inflation is a bad thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the way I would explain it is, is that inflation that's too low will mean that interest rates are lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's an expectation of future inflation that's built into every interest rate, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And to the extent inflation gets lower and lower and lower, interest rates get lower and lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then the Fed will have less room to cut rates to support the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you, if you look at many, many large jurisdictions around the world, you are seeing that phenomenon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we want inflation to be-we want it to be 2 percent, and we want it to average 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if inflation averages 2 percent, the public will expect that, and that'll be what's built into interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means that, you know, in a downturn, these days, what happens is, inflation, as has happened now-it moves down well below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means that we've said for, for-we would like to see and we will conduct policies so that inflation moves, for some time, moderately above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it won't be-these won't be large overshoots, and they won't be permanent but to help anchor inflation expectations at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, yes, it's, it's a challenging concept for a lot of people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, the economic importance of it is, is large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, those are the people we're serving, and, you know, we serve them best if we can actually achieve average 2 percent inflation, we believe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In February, we had an economy that was performing well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then the pandemic hit, and we had a record decline in activity in March and April, and then we had a record bounceback in May and June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so as I think would have been expected and was expected, the pace of improvement from May and June has now moderated, so it's not unexpected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if you look at just about anything, you know, for example, the payroll readings, the payroll job gains in May and June were just outsized.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they're certainly still very large, but they've-but the pace of improvement has moderated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's the case for, for all different measures in the labor force-in the labor market, rather.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But then, as you would expect, when, when you sort of had people-a lot of people go back to work at once, the pace will moderate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Most forecasts call for, you know, still a significant growth in the fourth quarter but not at the 33 percent annualized pace that we had in the third quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in a sense, that would be-that would be as expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have been concerned that the downside risks, though, are, are prevalent now, which are-which are really the risk of the further spread of the disease and also the risk that, that households will run through the savings they've managed to accumulate on their balance sheet and that that could weigh on activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what we see up to the present, really, is, continued growth, continued expansion, but at, at a gradually moderating pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is-obviously, it's for Congress to decide the timing, size, and components of further fiscal support for the economy, and I will say that the support provided by the CARES Act was absolutely essential in supporting the recovery that we've seen so far, which has generally exceeded expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think it's likely that further support is likely to be needed for monetary policy and fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just mentioned the two risks that I think we, we face, and those would be well addressed through more fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One is the further spread of the virus, and the other is the lapsing of the CARES Act benefits and the savings on people's balance sheets that will dwindle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, you know, I think it's appropriate for us not to try to prescribe for Congress exactly what they should do or what the timing of it should be or what the size of it should be and leave it at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on your first question, you know, we'll take into account all external factors and, and do what we think we need to do with the tools that we have to pursue our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I've said it on a couple of occasions that that will go better and move more quickly if we have a broad set of policies from across the government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've said this in the very beginning: It's really, first and foremost, health-care policy, getting the-getting the spread of the virus under control and working on therapeutics and vaccines and that kind of thing, getting-so that-those are absolutely critical to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Fiscal policy can do what we can't, which is to replace lost incomes for people who are out of work through no fault of their own.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we-what we can do is, we can obviously support financial stability through our lending programs, and, and we can support demand through, through interest rates and asset purchases and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're going to take the economy as it comes, including all external factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think all of us lived through the experience of the-of the years after the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And for a number of years there, in the middle of the recovery, fiscal policy was pretty tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: and I think I just would say that I think we'll have a stronger recovery if we can just get at least some more fiscal support when it's appropriate, you know, when it's appropriate and in the size Congress thinks is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think that that will likely-and, by the way, you see, you know, a lot of discussion on both sides of the aisle, on both sides of the Hill that suggests generally that there will be something.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on the first-the first question, it's-our asset purchases are serving both purchases, both-sorry, both purposes: financial market function and support for economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and that's really been true-I think in the very beginning of the crisis, the main focus was, obviously, financial, financial market function, particularly in, in, you know, some of the major markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But after that period, we've, we've understood all along that our purchases are also supporting economic activity, and that's important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in terms of what they can do, first I would just say, the purchases that we have in place are providing strong support to economic activity still.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, they're sustaining the gains we've made in financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, we have a habit of keeping things in place for a while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're not taking our gains in financial market function for granted, although, admittedly, they've been very large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the asset purchases are just another very important piece of the accommodative policy stance that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, as you know, these-we're buying $120 billion a month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's just providing a lot of support for, for economic activity and, by the way, removing just about the same amount of duration risk from private hands as QE3 did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is a big program, and it's doing a lot of good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we also, today, you know, we had a full discussion of the options around quantitative ease-not quantitative easing, the asset purchase program, and, you know, we understand the, the ways in which we can adjust the parameters of it to deliver more accommodation if it turns out to be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, we think that this very large, effective program is delivering about the right amount of accommodation and support for the markets, and so it continues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you did-you laid out nicely the, the risks of damage to the supply side of the economy, or "scarring," as you put it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've been talking about those since the very beginning of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The risk is that, for example, people are out of the labor force for an extended period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They lose their attachment to the labor force, and it's harder to get back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the record is, if you don't get back in very fairly quickly, it can be harder to get back in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, it also-it places enormous burdens on individuals who may have this happen to them at an important stage in their career.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know-so that is one of the reasons why our response was so strong and so urgent at the beginning and why we called this, this set of risks out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know how we could be much more vocal about it than we have been.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Fortunately, for-you know, the economic recovery has exceeded, certainly, the downside cases that we were very concerned about and even, even exceeded-sort of exceeded the baseline expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're, we're sort of halfway there on the labor market recovery at best.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and there are parts of the economy where it's going to be hard until there's a vaccine-you know, the parts of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's sort of the third thing that we talk about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first, at the beginning, it was to provide relief and comfort.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second-then the second part was to provide support when-to the expansion when it came.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the third was to avoid longer-run damage to the economy, and that's, that's all of these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we'll, we'll try to continue to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and those are-that's again-that goes to keeping this episode as short as it can be and avoiding unnecessary business bankruptcies, unnecessary household bankruptcies, and unnecessary long- term stays of unemployment or supporting people through them so that they can maintain their financial footing and their lives and be able to go back to work in a productive way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's very important that-you know, there is a real threat here of those things, and, and, you know, we're trying to do everything we can to minimize that threat.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, first, let me say, we do think that the facilities have, have generally served their purposes well, particularly in supporting the flow of credit, particularly acting as backstops to private markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, we think that the, the programs have, have gone well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the extension, we are, we are just now turning to that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've had a lot of things to work our way through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now we're just in the process of turning to that question and, of course, not made any decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in terms of the process, this is a decision that, of course, we have to make and will make jointly with the Treasury Department.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, I, I take the sense of your first question to be, is monetary policy out of power or out of ammo?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the answer to that would be "no," I don't think that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-I think that we are strongly committed to using these powerful tools that we have to support the economy during this difficult time for as long as needed, and no one should have any doubt about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do not doubt the power of the things that we've already done or the things that we may, may do in the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I also think, if you look at the stock of assets that we've bought, if you look at the facilities and, and the way we've been able to keep accommodative financial- financial conditions accommodative, I think we've been able to do a lot of things that are providing very strong support for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've said-we've said from the very beginning, though, that this is particular-that the particular situation we find ourselves in is one where there is a sudden loss of income on, on the part of millions and tens of millions of people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not so much a typical recession where demand weakens, the Fed cuts interest rates, interest rates stimulate demand, and the economy recovers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a sudden shock where tens of millions of people are out of work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the fiscal response was, was frankly, I think, very good and very robust in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's certainly one of the main reasons why the recovery has been as good as it's been so far.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do think fiscal policy is absolutely essential here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, stimulating aggregate demand is one thing, but where there's a part of the economy that kind of will be resistant to that, you also need fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I didn't see Madame Lagarde's comments this morning, but I, I took the sense of that question to be the spread of the disease in Europe, and what do we think about that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned in my-in my opening remarks, it's a concern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have a widespread spike in cases across the country, more in some regions than others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And even if we don't have-and I don't expect that we would-sort of government-imposed restrictions, it does seem likely, though, that people who have maybe begun to engage in activities that they had in flying, staying in a hotel, going to restaurants, going to bars, and, and things like that, that they may pull back in a situation where suddenly the cases are everywhere in your city, your state, your community.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do think that that's a risk that we have as we go into the fall now and, and the cases spike.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We thought the same thing, in fairness, about the wave we had this summer in the South and the West.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the economy, you know, seemed to move right through that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In any case, it's a risk, is what I would characterize it-I would characterize it as a risk, as I did in my-in my comments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me-let me say, in the first instance, our, our main focus is on doing our job, and that is really what we're, we're focused on is using the tools that Congress has given us and the assignment they've given us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we're, we're-that is the thing that we think about night and day.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just know from, from the experience of the last cycle, it helps to have the whole government working on these things, and this one is particularly that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I don't-I think-you know, I, I don't want to say whether I feel like I'm being heard or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, sure, I think there are plenty of people on Capitol Hill who, on both sides of the aisle, on both sides of the Hill, who see a need for further fiscal action and understand perfectly why that might be the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't really have a specific hypothetical I would-I would put to you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just say that we, we understand that there are a number of parameters that we have where we can shift the composition, the duration, you know, the size, the life, life cycle of the program.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of those things are, are available to us as ways to deliver addition-you know, more accommodation if we think that's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, we, we like the amount of accommodation the program is, is delivering.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it will just depend on the-on the facts and circumstances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We may reach a view at some point that we need to do more on that front.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Today's meeting was about analyzing the-one of the things it was about was about analyzing the various ways and having a, you know, good discussion about how to think about those, those various parameters, which I, I thought was quite a useful discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I do think that the public, public will expect and has every right to expect that we-that in our oversight of the financial system, we will account for all material risks and try to protect the economy and the public from those risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a relatively-the science and art of incorporating climate change into our thinking about financial regulation is relatively new, as you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we are, you know, very actively, in the early stages of this, getting up to speed, working with our central bank colleagues and other colleagues around the world to try to think about how this can be part of our framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're active participants, as you know, in the CG-no, the greening the financial system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we haven't, we hadn't actually formally joined, but we're there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're in the working groups, and we're doing all of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're very much working with and monitoring the things other central banks are doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You hear-you know, there's lots of research going on at the various Reserve Banks and here at the Board in trying to understand this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, of course, the longer term does arrive over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we take it as our obligation to-you know, to understand these risks and incorporate them into our- into the way we supervise and, and think about the, the overall financial system and the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on your first question, we, we really are just turning to this issue now, and we have not made any decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we are just getting started on it, and, and it's a decision that we'll make jointly with the Treasury Department.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the tail risks, I mean, I think clearly the tail risks that we were worried about have, have subsided.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we were worried about very negative potential outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that-you know, that's, that's-what is to be expected of us is, is to think about how things can go wrong as well as the way things that can go right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, we have to-we do make policy from a risk-management standpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we ask, "How do you make policy in light of the risks?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: and often it's downside risks in a situation like this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would not say that anybody's feeling comfortable about this, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've gotten through the first five, six months of the-of the expansion better than expected, but we do see in Europe-look what's happening in Europe, look what's happening here-another spike in cases as the cold weather arrives and people are inside more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we have to be humble about where we are relative to this-to this disease.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Clearly, you know, therapeutics are advancing, research on vaccines are advancing, death rates are way down, hospitalization rates are, are lower now, but-so we're learning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, I mean, we, we are so- we're very far from saying that we think we've got this and eliminated the tail risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think, clearly, the tail risks have, have diminished since-at least our perception of them has diminished since earlier in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say why it's such an important-you know, in a world where so many payments are made digitally and all that, coins and currency are very important for the relatively low-income people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so it's a really incredibly important part of the payment system, and we do pay a lot of attention to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I actually just-I just caught up this morning with the-with the person who heads that operation here who, who says that, yes, things have really gotten significantly better on the coin front.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we worked very hard to increase the supply of coins and, even more than that, the distribution of coins around the System and are happy to say that that situation is well on the way to normalizing itself.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm very reluctant, as you will imagine, to comment on the election directly, indirectly, at all, other than just to say that it's a good time to take a step back and let the institutions of our democracy do their jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, at the Fed here, we will, as always, continue to do our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Every day we'll continue to serve the American people using our tools to support the economy during this difficult time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, you know, the meeting we just finished, for example, what we do is we talk about the economy and markets, domestically and around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We hear reports on how households and businesses are doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We talk about what the right policy response might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the election comes up in some-you know, it comes up now and again, but it is not at all a central focus of the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, very reluctant to get into anything more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, we have had very little demand below $1 million in loans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And part of that just is that the fee structure is what it is, and that's the compensation that the banks get.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's a certain amount of work that they have to do to get-to get into the loan program and do-and to document the thing, the loans that they make because these are loans that, you know, go on their balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They keep 5 percent, so they actually have to underwrite the credit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're relying on them, to some extent, for, for doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We moved the minimum down to $250,000, and we were reluctant to go below that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we heard, over and over again, that it would be great if we could reduce it to $100,000.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and, you know, we've been saying we'd have to redesign the program.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I got the question in a-in an oversight hearing a month or so ago with the Secretary and said that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I went back to the office and thought, you know, okay, so what would that look like if we were to redesign the program in a way-what's the least thing we could do to redesign the program so that we could move to a lower level?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it-basically, we concluded we could just change the fee structure to create incentives for that, so we did that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want, you know, qualifying businesses to be able to borrow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, with, with these programs, why did it-why didn't we do it right away?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We tend to-it's-there's more work than one might-certainly than I imagined in setting up one of these facilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you, you just try to get it out there and get it working and not try to do everything before you start it because you'll never start it if you do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's the most recent set of ones that we've done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we hope-we hope that it will help some companies, and I guess we'll find out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when I say we're not out of ammo, I'm looking at, you know, a couple of our tools, mainly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, the asset purchase program-there's a number of dimensions in which we can adjust that if we deem it to be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We could, you know, if, if the facilities are extended, we could certainly look at new facilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If-you know, if things deteriorate, that would be the case where you'd want to maybe continue the facilities and, and, and maybe change them and maybe have new ones.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, certainly, the facilities have been doing a lot of work and been very successful, I think, overall in accomplishing that job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do think there, there are things that we can do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, remember, we've always said this will take a whole of government approach, including health-care policy and fiscal policy too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it really is, if you-if you want to get the economy back as quickly as possible to where we want it to be, then, then really it should be all of government working together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that the, you know, the corporate-the larger corporate market-based lending program has been very successful without making a single loan-I think, unambiguously, has been a big success.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the success-I think the state and local government program has also restored market function so that-whereas, you know, there were the, the sort of individual investors who wind up funding loans in the muni market through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: through mutual funds, they, they had withdrawn a lot of money, and, and that-we've had many weeks of consecutive, I believe, of, of inflows there, and you're largely back to a normal functioning market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the other-certainly the, the funding market programs have been a big success.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The-Main Street is just-is just a bigger challenge than all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Reaching out to small and medium-sized businesses through the banking system, which we had to do, is, is quite challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think, you know, the grant programs, the PPP, were, were a great way to reach smaller companies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what you hear out there is that demand-you talk to banks, and they'll say demand for loans is very, very low right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and the reason is that, you know, activity's at a relatively low level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so I-we put, we put an awful lot into Main Street, and it is very challenging to reach a lot of those companies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I-you know, I think we, we are reaching many of them now, and, and I hope that the new changes will help us reach more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so I'm going to take your question literally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so if the idea is money-financed fiscal policy, that's not something that we would consider.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that- what I mean by that is, is really, you know, the, the central bank is really funding fiscal activities of the government fairly directly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That separation between those jobs is absolutely critical in our system of government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The-you know, the job of taxation and spending goes to people who have stood for election and been elected, and that's the way it should be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have a specific, you know, job to do with, with a specific set of tools to support maximum employment, stable prices, financial stability, help the payment system, supervise banks-all the things we're assigned to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, we, we're not going to get into financing the government and, and-by the way, when we buy government bonds, we don't-it doesn't actually, as you probably know, doesn't change the amount of government debt outstanding.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We issue a reserve to, to purchase a Treasury security, and that's just another form-on the consolidated balance sheet of the federal government, that's just another obligation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You change the-you change the, you know, the nature of the obligation, but not the total quantity of debt that the government has when you do these asset purchase programs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, to-again, to take your question literally about financing fiscal activity, it's really not something that we think the central bank should do and, and not something we're looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, we're doing that with the Municipal Liquidity Facility now, so we're, we're buying, you know, with, with our own funds and with the CARES Act funds that, that we've gotten through Congress and the Treasury.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're doing that now as part of an emergency facility under section 13(3), you know, which has to meet the emergency requirements of exigent circumstances and which is all clearly laid out in the law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, I see-what that is, from our standpoint, is a rare thing that we do under section 13(3) when regular intermediation in the capital markets or in the banking system has broken down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we step in under 13(3), and we provide liquidity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What turns out to happen is, we announce a program, and the market starts working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The amount of financing that's happened in the municipal markets this year is much higher than it was the prior year, and, and we didn't do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did-we've done a very small number of, of loans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But just the fact that we're there as a backstop seems to-seems to get the private parties to get back together and, and get the market working again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-that shouldn't be a permanent thing where we're just another federal financing agency that's available to direct credit to-you know, to very worthy borrowers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That would be more along the lines of a GSE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're there to provide emergency liquidity when intermediation has broken down and then to pull back on that when- you know, when-as the markets normalize, we pull back and we put those tools away, as we did after the Global Financial Crisis and as we will here when the time comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so we're not-we're not going to be identifying specific-associating that test with, with specific numbers at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, really, the question is, what do we mean by, by that language?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, really, the overarching message, Rich, is that our guidance for both interest rates and asset purchases will keep monetary policy accommodative until our maximum-employment and price-stability goals are achieved, and that's, that's a powerful message.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It means we'll be looking for employment to be substantially closer to assessments of its maximum level and inflation to be substantially closer to our 2 percent longer-run goal before we start making adjustments to our purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would also point out that by increasing our asset holdings, we see ourselves as adding policy accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There will come a time when the economy does not require increasing amounts of policy accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when that time comes-and that will be uncertain and, in any case, is, is some ways off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I can't give you an exact set of numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will-of course, as we approach that point, we'll be evaluating that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when we see ourselves on a path to achieve that goal, then we will-we will say so undoubtedly well in advance of any time when we would actually consider gradually tapering the pace of purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, again, I would start with what we actually did at the meeting, which, which was, we provided this, this guidance about the path of asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I just went through what, what they-what they-the guidance that we put forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so I guess since September we've now adopted a flexible average inflation-targeting framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have provided rate guidance that is tightly linked to the goals as expressed in that new framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now we've done the same for, for asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we've, we've been sort of-as, as the future has become clearer and as we've absorbed new developments in medical-in the medical sphere and also in, in the economy, we have-began to be able to see further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've, we've started to be able to provide further important guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that the-that the asset purchase guidance, guidance is very important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that the, the prior language of "in coming months" was obviously temporary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This links that guidance, those purchases, to actual "substantial further progress" toward our, our mandated goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that that is important to have done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I would just add, though, that we also continue to think that our current policy stance is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it's providing a great deal of support for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we monitor a range of financial condition indexes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are many of them, and they'll, they'll all pretty much tell you that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can-you can also look at the interest sensitive parts of the economy-for example, housing, durable sales, vehicle sales-those parts of the economy are, are performing very, very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The parts of the economy that are weak are the service-sector businesses that involve close contact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are not being held back by financial conditions, but rather by the spread of the virus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'll close by, by just saying, we do have the flexibility to provide more accommodation through the channel you mentioned and through other channels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we recognize that circumstances could shift in a way that warrants our, our doing that, including by adjusting purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are committed to using our full range of tools to support the U.S. economy to achieve our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will continue to use our tools to support the economy for as long as it takes until the job is well and truly done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, Nick, I-on, on the first part of the question, I, I don't-I wouldn't want to sort of talk about hypothetical situations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we look at our overall stance of policy, we look at overall financial conditions, we look at what's going on in the economy-different parts of the economy, and we ask ourselves, should we change our policy stance?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we look at where financial conditions are now, and, and we, we feel that they are appropriate for now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Anytime we feel like the economy could, could use stronger accommodation, we would be prepared to provide it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-but right now, we're providing a great deal, and we think-we happen to think it's the right amount.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, you, you mentioned-I think you're referring to the idea of maintaining the duration but, but reducing the quantity, which is sort of what the Bank of Canada did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, that is something that we-you know, that we talked about in the last meeting and was addressed in the minutes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, the views on that were mixed: Some thought it was an interesting idea, others not so much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I wouldn't say that that's something that's, that's high on our list of, of possibilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on your-on your first question, we really have not thought about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're very focused on-we have a lot to do now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we have not focused on, on that question, and I, I really have nothing to add on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, we, we would have the ability-certainly, we would have the ability to do facilities under 13(3) in some cases with no backing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we can't do any 13(3) facilities without the approval of the Treasury Secretary, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we did some facilities-I think one of our facilities this time didn't have any Treasury backing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think some in the-in the round of-during the Global Financial Crisis also didn't have any.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that we are-you know, we're-we have the authorities we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will use them if, if they're needed and if-and if the law permits us to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we do not have any plans for, for the future about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've been very focused on, on the issues that are right in front of us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, honestly, we're not-we're not planning on anything or having any discussions about what we might do down the road.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on, on fiscal policy, I would just say a couple of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The case for fiscal policy right now is, is very, very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that is widely understood, I would say, now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But with the expiration of unemployment benefits-some of the unemployment benefits, the expiration of eviction moratoriums with the virus spreading the way it is, there's a need for households and businesses to have, have fiscal support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think that-again, I think that is widely understood.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it would be-I, I certainly would welcome the work that Congress is doing right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I don't have a view for you on, on the size of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the surge, you know, so it's a really interesting question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have, and others too, have consistently expected there to be more economic-that, that cases would hold-growth in cases would hold back the economy more than it actually has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've overestimated the, the effects on the economy of, of these spikes we've been having.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, this spike is so much larger that I think-and I think forecasters generally do think that there-that this will have an effect on suppressing activity, particularly activity that involves people getting together in bars and restaurants, on airplanes and hotels and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the-in the high-frequency data, you're now beginning to see that show up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if this is-the case numbers are so high and so widespread across the country that that, that seems like it must happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you'll see the first quarter could well be-what, what we said is that coming months are going to be challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first quarter will, will certainly show significant effects from this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And by the end of the first quarter into the second quarter, you're going to be seeing significant numbers of people vaccinated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so then what will be-how will that play into economic activity?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You have to think that sometime in the middle of next year, you will-you will see people feeling comfortable going out and engaging in a broader range of activities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And some people will be probably quick to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some are doing it now without a vaccine-right?-in many parts of the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, nonetheless, my expectation-and I think many people have the expectation that the second half of next year should-the economy should be performing strongly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
