text: We should be- you know, we should be getting people back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The issue is more the next four or five months-getting through the next four, five, six months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, clearly there's going to be need for help there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, my sense and hope is that we'll be getting that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so we monitor basically just about every asset price in the economy, and housing prices are something that we've been monitoring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This, this is the housing market that people have been expecting since, you know, 2010.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and then, you know, not many, when the-when the pandemic hit, thought, "Oh, this is what-this is what will produce that housing market," but it has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, I would say, from a financial stability standpoint, housing prices are not-are not of a level of concern right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, builders are going to bring forth supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's also a sense that this-some of this may be pent-up demand from when the economy was closed, which would imply that demand-once that demand is met, that the real level of demand will be more manageable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we met recently with a bunch of homebuilders, and many of them in the business 30, 40 years said they've never seen the likes of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, no, housing prices themselves are not-are not a financial stability concern at the moment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in the near term, I wouldn't think that that's an issue that we'd be concerned about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are a number of options we would have to provide more support to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would-I would say, though, that in the near term, the help that people need isn't just from low interest rates that stimulates demand over time and works with long and variable lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As the-as-we've, we've talked about this as all of these government policies trying to work together to create a bridge across this chasm, economic chasm that was created by the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And for many Americans, that bridge is there and, and they're across it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's a group for, for which they, they don't have a bridge yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's the 10 million people who lost their jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-you know, you see the, the-many, many millions of Americans are, are waiting in food lines in their cars these days all over the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know there are small businesses all over the country that, that have been basically unable to really function, and they're just hanging on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and, by the way, now that we can-we can kind of see the light at the end of the tunnel, it would be-it would be bad to see, you know, people losing their business, their life's work in many cases, or even generations' worth of work, because they couldn't last another few months, which is what it amounts to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll-I, I think more the issue is, we're going to need to continue to provide support to this economy for quite a period of time, because the, the economy will be growing in expectation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We should be growing at a fairly healthy clip by the second half of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's going to be a while before we really are back to the levels of, of labor market-the, the sort of conditions in the labor market that we had in early this year and for much of the last couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of the vaccine, yes, you know, we do estimates of, of when the United States would reach herd immunity, and they're, they're going to be similar to what other people think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it depends on your assumptions, such as how many people will actually take the vaccine and how fast will the rollout be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, sometime-it's possible sometime in the middle or second half of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going to try to be precise, because it's just another estimate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, our people are very good, but they're looking at, at the same data as other people are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, you know, all the estimates are-it depends on what your assumptions are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But under a normal set of assumptions, it could happen as, as soon as the middle of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the, you know, inflation, a couple things-your second question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're-I think you have to be honest with yourself about, about inflation these days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are-there are significant disinflationary pressures around the world, and there have been for a while, and they persist today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, is not going to be easy to have inflation move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it isn't going to be just a question-it's going to take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It took a long time to get inflation back to 2 percent in the last crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're, we're honest with ourselves and with you in the SEP that even with the very high level of accommodation that we're providing both through low rates and very high levels of asset purchases, it will take some time, because that's what we believe the underlying inflation dynamics are in our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's sort of why we're-one reason why we're concerned about inflation is that we see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and that's why we have adopted the flexible average inflation-targeting framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're, we're honest with ourselves and with the public that it will take some time to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of, you know, would, would it really speed it up a lot to, to move asset purchases, you know, I don't think that would really be-I think it's going to take a long time however you do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we've been having very long expansions since-in, in the last several decades because inflation has not-really, the old model was, inflation would come along and the Fed would tighten, and we'd have a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now inflation has been low, and we haven't had that dynamic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the result has been three of the four longest expansions in, in modern history, in recorded history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we're, we're thinking that this could be another long expansion, and that we'll keep our-what we're saying is, we're going to keep policy highly accommodative until the expansion is well down the tracks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're not going to preemptively raise rates until we see inflation actually reaching 2 percent and being on track to exceed 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a very strong commitment, and we think that's the right place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm just going to add, markets have actually found this fairly credible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at what-at inflation compensation and at the survey measures of, of when the Fed will lift off, everything has moved.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There have been significant movements since we announced the framework in the direction that is consistent with the-with the framework being credible to market participants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I don't think it's something that-I, I mean, I'm actually pleased by, by the reception it's gotten in markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And markets have moved in ways that suggest it is credible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-you're, you're talking about the-sorry, the Network [of Central Banks and Supervisors] for Greening the Financial System, which we joined this week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'll just-I'll just say a couple things about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, first, I'll just start by saying that we're going to move carefully and thoughtfully on developing an understanding of how climate change affects our work, including the areas you mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to do so with a great deal of engagement with all of our external constituencies, including the public and their elected representatives who are charged with our oversight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Remember that we are a nonpolitical agency whose goals and authorities to achieve those goals are set by Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have great responsibilities and strong authorities that we'll use vigorously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not the forum where all the great issues of the day are to be hashed out, debated, and addressed unless and only to the extent that those issues are directly relevant to our statutory goals and are addressable through our legal authorities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And because we have a narrow remit, and because we stick to it, Congress has given us a precious grant of independence from direct political control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So society's broad response to climate change is for others to decide-in particular, elected leaders.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What does all that mean for an issue like climate change?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So Congress hasn't explicitly assigned us or other financial regulators a role, and we're not among the agencies who contribute to the National Climate Assessment-Climate Assessment, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But climate change is nonetheless relevant to our existing mandates under the law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One of our jobs is to regulate and supervise banks and to look after the stability of the financial system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The public will expect that we will-we will do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll, we'll expect that, that those important institutions will be resilient against the many resists-risks that they fake-face: credit risk, market risk, cyber risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Climate change is an emerging risk to financial institutions, the financial system, and the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we are, as so many others are, in the very early stages of understanding what that means, what needs to be done about it, and by whom.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's why 83 central banks have joined together to share research and identify best practices in this important emerging area.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've been attending NGFS meetings as an observer for more than a year, taking part in the work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had discussed that it was probably time to join as a member.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll just say that the financial system is really a global one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's important that we work and discuss best practices with peer agencies around the world, especially in a field where we're just beginning to develop our, our understanding.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we have historically shied away strongly from taking a role in credit allocation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, our agreement with Treasury during the financial crisis from back in 2009 or '10 says that we will avoid credit allocation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I would be very reluctant to see us move in that direction, picking one area as creditworthy and another not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's, it's-for now, I would say the real-the real concern is-the real place to focus, for me, is supervision of financial institutions and then financial stability concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Monetary policy, maximum employment, stable prices-it's less obvious to me.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can-I can, you know-I can make the argument, but it's less obvious to me that those should be first-order things that we would look at in connection with climate change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think there's-I think there's work to be done to understand the connection between climate change and the strength and resilience of financial markets and financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be thorough and transparent and, and engage with the public on all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the state and local governments, they provide important critical services: safety, fire, police, health, all kinds of things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're, they're really involved in people's lives, state and local governments are, to, to a large extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The decision whether to, to provide more fiscal support to them is entirely in the hands of Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, they're in the middle of these discussions, and, and those, those are issues for them to decide.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's happened is, if you're a state that has a significant exposure to tourism or to extracting energy from the ground-oil from the ground, or gas-you are probably, at least in those industries, feeling a significant loss of revenue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A number of other states have been surprised on the upside, where-and that's because goods sales, for example-property taxes are-don't move much year to year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the kind of sales taxes on goods-goods sales have been very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Income has been more or less replaced by, by the CARES Act-fully replaced, more than, in many cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the concerns that we had at the very beginning of really serious, deep shortfalls and massive budget cuts on the part of state and local governments have not yet-have not yet occurred.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're seeing is, is that it's different state to state.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And some states are having significant difficulties, others not so much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The real concern, though, that still emerges is, state and local governments are very large employers, and-one of the largest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so far, since the pandemic began, employment has dropped by 1. million in-of state and local government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it's a very large number of people to be-to be out of work from just that one source.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's actually significantly more than lost their jobs during the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is-that is a significant-a significant part of that group is, is in education.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when the schools reopen, a significant part of that 1. million would go back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're watching carefully to understand why that-why that many people have been let go and what are-really are the sources.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're monitoring it carefully, and it's a mixed picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I just have to leave the question of what to do with fiscal policy on this to Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I could go back, James, to what I said earlier, which is, this is-this is a very, very large asset purchase program.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's providing a tremendous amount of, of support for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the interest-sensitive parts of the economy, they're performing very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The parts that are not performing well are not struggling from high interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're struggling from exposure to, to COVID, in a sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are-these are the businesses that, that are really hit hard by people's reluctance to gather closely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so we, we do have the ability to-you know, to buy more bonds or to buy longer-term bonds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But also, I would remind-I would also note, though, monetary policy works with "long and variable lags," is the famous statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think that the big effects from monetary policy are, you know, months and months into the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this looks like a-you know, it looks like a time when what is really needed is fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and that's why it is, is a very positive thing that, that we're getting that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we remain open to doing-you know, to, to either increasing the size of our asset purchases, if that turns out to be appropriate, or to just moving the maturities, moving to buying longer maturities, because that had-that also increases accommodation by taking more duration risk out of the market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that our- you know, that our, our guidance on asset purchases today will also provide support to the economy over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, what we've-what we've done is, we've laid out a path whereby we're going to keep monetary policy highly accommodative for a long time, really until-really until we reach very close to our goals, which is not, you know, not really the way it's been done in the past.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's providing significant support for the economy now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think the economy suffers from a lack of, of highly accommodative financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it's suffering from the pandemic and people wanting to not engage in certain kinds of economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we expect that, that with the virus, that that will improve-that condition will improve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, again, we will-are prepared to use our tools, and we will use them at such time and in such amounts as we-as we think would, would help.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that, that has all the markings of a transient increase in the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you can imagine that as people really want to travel again-let's say, you know, that airfare, airfares-I'm just imagining this, right?-that they go up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what inflation is, is a process whereby they go up year upon year upon year upon year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if-given the inflation dynamics that we've had over the last several decades, just a single, single sort of price-level increase has not resulted in ongoing price-level increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, that was-the problem back in the 1970s was, it was the combination of two things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One, when unemployment went down and resources got tight, prices started going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the second problem was that that-that that increase was persistent, there was a level of persistence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if prices went up 6 percent this year, they'd go up 6 percent next year, because people would internalize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, really, really, that's what happens is, people internalize that they can raise prices, and that it's okay to pay prices that are going up at that rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that was the inflation-those are the inflation dynamics of that era.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There-the connection between low unemployment or other resource utilization and inflation is so much weaker than it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's still there, but it's a-it's a faint heartbeat compared to what it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the persistence of inflation, if you-if you get a-for example, oil prices go up, and that'll send a temporary shock through the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The persistence of that into, into inflation over time is just not there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So they- what you describe may happen, and, of course, we would watch it very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we understand that we will always be learning new things from the economy about how it will behave in certain cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would-I would expect, though, going in that that would be a one-time price increase rather than an increase in underlying inflation that would be persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-I think I got the sense of it, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, I, I don't think it's at all a foregone conclusion that there needs to be a permanent Fed presence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we certainly don't-you know, that's not something we're planning on or intending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now we're buying assets because it's a-you know, it's a-it's a time when the economy needs highly accommodative monetary policy, and we think our asset purchases are, you know, one of the main delivery mechanisms for that, the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, there's lots of demand for, for U.S. Treasury paper all-from all over the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think we need to be thoughtful about the structure of the Treasury market and look at ways to make sure that the capacity is there for it to be handled by the private sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's, there's quite a lot of work going on on that front.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, I don't presume at all that, that this is something that needs to be-where the Fed needs to be in there at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I would think that this should be handled by the private sector and can be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there may be-there may be a central clearing angle that would, you know, net a lot of risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are a lot of things that are being looked at right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the main thing that those companies need is a-is a robust recovery-a strong, robust recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we, we contribute to that through highly accommodative monetary policy, through accommodative financial conditions that are supporting economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Health authorities are contributing to that through, through, you know, management of the spread of the virus and now through vaccines and the delivery of those vaccines.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And Congress contributes, contributes to that by helping them make it through this very difficult time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and I think my understanding is that there's support for small businesses in, in what's being discussed on Capitol Hill.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would certainly think that would be something well worth looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we've had a-and I've had sort of the typical meetings with the transition team for Treasury.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They've met with quite a lot of people in our agency and other agencies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I really have only spoken to former Chair Yellen to congratulate her on being nominated and just to say that I look forward to working with her.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I did work very closely with her for five years before she left and have stayed in touch, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I have not discussed, you know, policy with her.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I'm not going to do that until she's confirmed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You, you were breaking up, but I, I think I got that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, financial stability-we, we look at a broad range of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We actually have a framework so that we can, you know, be-evaluate changes in financial stability over time, and so that the public can evaluate whether we're doing a job-a good job at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we published a report a few weeks ago on that-maybe it was month or so ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It depends-with equities, it depends on whether you're looking at P/Es or whether you're looking at the premium over risk-free-over the risk-free return.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at P/Es, they're historically high, but, you know, in a world where the- where the risk-free rate is sustain-is going to be low for a sustained period, the equity premium, which is really the reward you get for taking equity risk, would be what you'd look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's not at, at incredibly low levels, which would mean that they're not overpriced in that sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Admittedly, P/Es are high, but that's-you know, that's, that's maybe not as relevant in a world where we think the 10-year Treasury is going to be lower than it's been historically, from a-from a return perspective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we look at-we also look at borrowing-leverage of financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We spent 10 years and the banks spent 10 years building up their capital.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So far, they've been a source of strength through this crisis, and their capital has held up well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at leverage in the nonfinancial sector-that's households and nonfinancial corporates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and so companies have been able to handle their debt loads even in weak periods, because rates are- rates are quite low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Defaults and downgrades have, have declined since earlier in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Households came into this very strong, and there certainly has been a hit there for people who are unemployed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, with the CARES Act, Congress replaced a lot of lost income.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's very important that, that the economy gets strong again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the, the ultimate thing to support financial stability is a strong economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We found that there was a lot of unstable funding for companies, particularly financial companies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's down to a-to a very low level these days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the broad financial stability picture is, is kind of mixed, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, you know, asset prices are, are a little high in that metric and in my view.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You, you don't have, you know, a lot of red flags on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and it's-again, it's something that we monitor essentially ongoing, almost daily.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're, we're monitoring these prices for that and, and have published our, our framework, and, you know, we'll be held accountable for what we saw and what we missed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people who-people who run for elected office and win, they're the ones-their reward is they get to make those very difficult decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-you know, so we're not charged with providing fiscal advice to, to Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, I would just say, as a general-as a general rule, it is important to be on a sustainable fiscal path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For my way of thinking and many others', the time to focus on that is when the economy is strong and when unemployment is low and taxes are-you know, are, are pouring in, and there's, there's room to get on-get on a sustainable path, because the economy's really doing well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're still now in the-in the, you know, some part of, of an economic crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the fact that Congress is debating a fairly large bill today suggests that, that-you know, suggests that something fairly substantial is going to get done, we hope-that what's being discussed is, you know, is, is of some size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what is a sustainable level, I think, you know, it's-the question is-we've always looked at debt to GDP, and we're very high by that measure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In particular, you can look at the real interest rate payments, the amount of, what does it cost?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And from that standpoint, if you-if you sort of take real interest costs of the federal deficit and divide that by GDP, we're actually-you know, we're actually on a more sustainable fiscal path if you look at it through those eyes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, I'll just say in the near term, I think fiscal-the case for, for fiscal is, is strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'm certainly hoping-I think it will be very good for the economy if, if we did get something soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, I mean, that's-I think we're a very, very long way from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the Congress has given the Fed independence on the condition that we stick to our knitting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think that's, that's what people call fiscal dominance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think we're just a very, very long way from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, if we-if we do our jobs well and support the economy and achieve maximum employment and stable prices, keep the financial system stable, I don't think that that is something that will-that I would worry about, certainly not in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on, on your first question, I don't want to comment on a particular company or, or day's market activity or things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just not really something that I would typically comment on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of macroprudential policy tools, so, as you know, no doubt, we rely on sort of always-on, through-the-cycle macroprudential policy tools, particularly the stress tests and also the elevated levels of liquidity and capital and, and, and also resolution planning that we-that we impose on the largest financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't use time-varying tests and tools as some other countries do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think it's a good approach because-for us to use ones that are always-on-because we don't really think we'd be successful in every case in picking the exact right time to intervene in markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And while we don't have jurisdiction over, over many areas in the nonbank sector, other agencies do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we do coordinate through the Financial Stability Oversight Council and with other agencies who have responsibility for, for nonbank supervision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in fact, as you know, in the last crisis, the banking system held up fairly well so far.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and the dislocations that we saw from the outsized economic and financial shock of the pandemic really appeared in the nonbank sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-right now we are engaged in, in carefully examining, understanding, and thinking about what, what in the nonbank sector will need to be addressed in the next year or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I'd start by saying that the, the fiscal response that we've seen to this downturn has been strong, and I think we can say now that it's been sustained after the passage of the-of the, the most recent act in, in late December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really a key reason why the recovery has been as strong as it's been.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we look back on, on the history of this period, we'll see a strong and sustained fiscal policy response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would-I would add that we're, as I mentioned, a long way from a full recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Something like 9 million people remain unemployed as a consequence of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's as many people as lost their jobs at the peak of the Global Financial Crisis and the Great Recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many small businesses are under pressure, and there are other needs to be addressed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, all of that said, the judgment on how much to spend and in what way is really one for Congress and the Administration and not for the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's a discussion, as you know, right now around, around those precise questions, and, and that's appropriate, but not for us to play a role in talking about specific policies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The shock that the-from the pandemic was unprecedented both in its nature and in its size and in the amount of unemployment that it created and in the shock to economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's nothing close to it in our modern economic history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-we've done what we could, first, to restore market function and to provide a bit of relief, then to support the recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, hopefully, we'll be able to do the third thing, which is to avoid longer-run damage to the-to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our role assigned by Congress is maximum employment and stable prices and also look after financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in a world where, almost a year later, we're, we're still 9 million jobs, at least-that's one way of counting it; it can actually be counted much higher than that- short of maximum employment and people are out of the labor force who were in the labor force-the real unemployment rate is close to 10 percent if you include people that've left the labor force-it's very much appropriate that monetary policy be highly accommodative to support maximum employment and price stability, which is getting inflation back to 2 percent and averaging 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on, on matters of financial stability, we have a framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at-and we made that framework public after the financial crisis so that it could be criticized and understood and we could be held accountable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the things that we look at are-we do look at asset prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at leverage in the non-the nonbanking system, which is to say, corporates and households.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look at it across that range of, of, of readings, they're each different, but we monitor them carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say that financial stability vulnerabilities overall are moderate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our overall goal is to assure that the financial system itself is resilient to, to shocks of all kinds, that it's strong and resilient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that includes not just the banks, but money market funds and, and all different kinds of nonbank financial structures as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when we get to the nonfinancial sector, we don't-we don't have jurisdiction over that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-so I would just say that our-that there are many things that go in, as you know, to, to setting asset prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at what's really been driving asset prices, really, in the last couple of months, it isn't monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are-those are the news items that have been driving, driving asset purchases-sorry, asset values in, in recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I know that monetary policy does play a role there, but that's how we look at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, you know, I think that the connection between low interest rates and, and asset values is probably something that's not as tight as people think, because a lot of-a lot of different factors are driving asset prices at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, that's-as you know, that's one of the very difficult questions in all of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't rule it out as a theoretical matter, but we, we clearly look to macroprudential tools, regulatory tools, supervisory tools, other kinds of tools rather than monetary policy in, in addressing financial stability issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-you know, the, the monetary policy we know strengthens economic activity and job creation through fairly well- understood channels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And a strong economy is actually a great supporter of financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That will mean strong, you know, well-capitalized institutions, and, and households will be- will be working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't actually understand the tradeoff between-the sense of it is, would you-if you raise interest rates and thereby tighten financial conditions and reduce economic activity now in order to address asset bubbles and things like that, what-will that even help?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Will it-will it actually cause more damage, or will it help?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think it's, it's something we, we look at as not, not theoretically ruled out but not something we, we-we've ever done and not something we would plan to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would rely on macroprudential and other tools to deal with financial stability issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on inflation, a couple of things-there are a couple of things that are worth mentioning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One is just that we know that we measure inflation on a trailing 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as we-as we lap the very low inflation readings of March and April of last year, we'll see measured 12-month inflation move up a few tenths.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is just-they're called base effects, and, and that's a-that's a transient thing that we think will pass.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's also the possibility-indeed, it's in some forecasts-that as the economy fully reopens, there'll be a burst of spending, and-because people will be enthusiastic that the pandemic is over, potentially, and that that could also create some upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, again, we would see that as something likely to be transient and not to be very large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In both cases, we don't see those as either lasting or particularly large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the way we would react is, we're going to be patient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Expect us to wait and see and not react if we see small and what we would review-we would view as very likely to be transient effects on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if you-you know, it helps to look back at, at the inflation dynamics that the United States has had now for some decades and notice that there has been, you know, significant disinflationary pressure for some time, for a couple of decades.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation has averaged less than 2 percent for a quarter of a century.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the inflation dynamics, with the flat Phillips curve and low persistence of inflation, is very much intact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We understand that inflation dynamics evolve constantly over time, but they don't change rapidly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think it's very unlikely that anything we see now would result in, you know, troubling inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, if we did get sustained inflation at a level that was uncomfortable, we have tools for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's far harder to deal with, with too low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know what to do with higher inflation, which is, you know, should the need arise, we, we would have those tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of how much, you know, what we've said is we'd like to see-because inflation has been running persistently below 2 percent, we'd like to see it run moderately above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to-we, we use policy rules and formulas in everything we do, consult them constantly, but we don't set policy by them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're going to preserve an element of judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we'll seek inflation moderately above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll, we'll show what that means when we get inflation above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the way to achieve credibility on that is to actually do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of the rollout of the vaccines, we see what everyone else sees, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see that we're, we're vaccinating people and at a rate of about a million a day, apparently, and that it'll take quite a while to get-to get to the numbers that the experts say are required to get to herd immunity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You'll notice that we, we said that the, the pandemic still, still provides considerable downside risks to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's one of the reasons why, is that-is the slowness of the rollout.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other-another reason why is just the arrival of these new virus strains.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know how to-we don't know how to model that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we can have a base case, but we realize no one knows how the-how this new vaccine will roll out, how successful it will be, how high we'll be able to drive vaccination, and those sorts of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have a base case, and we-but we always-we always look at, at the range of possibilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In this case, we particularly look at the downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, that's really what we do is, we, we set policies so that we're, we're, you know, we're going to remain accommodative until we actually see improvement in the economy and not just in the outlook, in the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would-I would also add, there's nothing more important to the economy now than, than people getting vaccinated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, if you-if you, you think about the places where the economy is weak-I mentioned bars and restaurants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's 400,000 jobs we lost last month, and that's all because of the spread of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many other areas of the economy- actually, there was actually job creation in-you know, in goods production and in some service parts-industries as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're just not going to be able to get that last group of people back to work-and it's a big group of people-until we get the pandemic behind us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't succeeded in doing this yet, and we need to stay focused on it as a country and, and get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we clearly can, but we're going to have to stay focused.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that includes-you know, that includes us at the Fed, monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I have been vaccinated once, and I expect to get my second vaccine sometime soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, remember, we're, we're focused on maximum employment, price stability, financial stability as I defined it-the broad financial sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and that-that's not, you know-over the years, we, we consult the fact that we have that authority.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, no, it's not something we're looking at right now at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, first, I-we, we think our policy stance is, is just right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it's providing significant support for economic activity and hiring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, you know, we, we adopted a new monetary policy framework of flexible average inflation targeting in August.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In September, we, we implemented rate guidance that, that was consistent with and based on that new framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we now have, you know, strong guidance on, on rates and on asset purchases that's providing very strong support for economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the sectors of the economy that are interest sensitive, you will see very strong activity: housing, durable goods, automobile sales.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that, that they are-we think our policy stance is, is right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With asset purchases, for example, we can, you know-that's, that's a tool we can do more-we can strengthen our guidance, too, if we were to think that that were appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you see is an economy where what's holding it back is not the lack of, of policy support from the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's the spread of the disease and people's reluctance or, or inability to partake in certain kinds of economic activities, which amount to a, a meaningful part of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We certainly have things that we can do, but we think we're-we think we're in the right place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, in terms of-in terms of tapering, it's just premature.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We said we'd want to see substantial further progress toward our goals before we modify our, our asset purchase guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just too early to be talking about dates, which we should be focused on, on progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when, when we see ourselves getting to that point, we'll communicate clearly about it to, to the public so nobody will be surprised when the time comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll do that well in advance of actually considering what will be a pretty gradual taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I, I was here-we had all the same questions back in-after the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We froze the balance sheet size, and then we shrank the balance sheet size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's no reason why we, we won't be able to do that again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we, we understand-as we understood then, but even more so-we understand that the-that the way to do it is to communicate well in advance, to, to do predictable things, and to move gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, honestly, no-you know, the whole focus on exit is premature, if I may say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're focused on finishing the job we're doing, which is to support the economy, to give the economy the support it needs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's essential that we get them back to work as quickly as possible, and we want to do everything we can to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's, it's too soon to be-to be worried about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, when we come to exit, we have a-we have an understanding of how to do that, and we'll do it very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in the meantime, our focus is on giving the economy the support it needs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I would say that, again, we have been struggling with disinflationary forces for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look around the world-look in Western Europe, look at Japan-around the world, large economies have, have felt much more downward pressure on inflation, have fallen short of their inflation goals, for some time now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is the broad global macroeconomic context that we all live in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we believe that those global forces-which are, you know, aging demographics, advancing technology, and globalization-those, those forces are still in effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, they may slow down, and, and it's, it's an interesting question, the extent to which, for example, globalization may slow down or even reverse.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Notwithstanding that, inflation dynamics in the United States have, have consisted of a flat Phillips curve and low persistence for, for a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do not expect in the near term that that will change significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, these things are-these things are, are changing, but they don't change at a rapid rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't-I'm, I'm not-I'm much more worried about falling short of a complete recovery and losing people's careers and lives that they-that they built because they don't get to work-back to work in time and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm more concerned about that and the damage that will do not just to their lives, but to the United States economy, to the productive capacity of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm more concerned about that than about the possibility, which exists, of higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The kind of troubling inflation that people like me grew up with seems, seems far away and unlikely in, in the both domestic and global context that we've been in for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I have the highest respect and admiration for Secretary Yellen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'm, I'm sure that we're going to have a, a good working relationship together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll also have a good institutional relationship between the Fed and the Treasury.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I expect that that'll be very good and, and very productive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, the way that works is, is that, you know, we know-the agencies know each other well, and this is true of finance ministries and central banks around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that we work together on some things to-you know, for the benefit of the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'm, I'm absolutely sure that we're going to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, you know, haven't-I haven't spoken to, to Secretary Yellen-I'm going to be calling her "Chair Yellen" most of the time, so you just have to be patient with me-Secretary Yellen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I haven't spoken to her since I congratulated her on being nominated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do expect very soon to begin our regular calls or-and, and ultimately meetings, which have gone on, really, for, you know, 70 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Treasury Secretary and the, and the Fed Chair have had weekly or so meetings, lunches, breakfast, calls, depending on the situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And just, you know, I, I, I don't-I don't have any comment on your-on your last question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't want to comment one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-I'll just say that I think our facilities were very successful in supporting the economy during its darkest moments and I believe saved-protected the loss of millions of jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to continue to monitor financial and credit conditions throughout the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and if the kind of emergency conditions arise that are required under that law, then our emergency lending tools will remain available.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, I've had no discussions with anybody at Treasury on that, because I haven't had any discussions with anybody at Treasury other than meet-you know, high-level meetings with the-with the transition team a month or so ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And once we start having those, those meetings, of course, I'll observe, you know, the long-standing practice of not talking about confidential discussions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as of now, there haven't been any discussions at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in the statement, on the language, we dropped "in the medium term," because, really, the risks are, are in the near term, frankly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, as I mentioned, it's the rollout of the vaccine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's the arrival of new strains that, that are more contagious and perhaps more virulent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those are the-those are the-and also just the ongoing-third thing, of course, is the ongoing spread of the virus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were thinking-when we were thinking "medium term," we were thinking of longer-term scarring and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, I mean, I think what-to go to your, your second question, and as I mentioned in my, in my opening remarks-there is good evidence to, to support a stronger economy in the second half of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, if you look at, at-as we do-look at a range of private forecasters, what was their forecast in, in December, and what's their forecast now?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right across the board: much higher forecasts for 2021 growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's because of the ongoing rollout of the vaccines and also because of fiscal policy, expectations, and the reality of, of the CRRA Act [Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021] getting done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that-think of that as-the sort of base case is, is a strong economy in the second half of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The language says that there's still-I forget the exact language-downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there are considerable risks, risks to the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really how, how I would-I would parse that for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know when we're going to come back to work, and I'm, I'm actually in the Eccles Building here today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we-I can't wait to be working in person again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we-we've been able to work successfully remotely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're not going to push people when they're uncomfortable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to wait till people are comfortable and wait till it's well and truly time to get back together in person.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're monitoring that on an ongoing basis, continue to-continuing to evaluate our, our restrictions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we haven't made a decision about whether to continue them in the second quarter or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're just going to look at bank-we're going to look at the whole range of, of information, including economic activity, banking activity, the, the success in vaccination.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of those things will go into our assessment of what the right answer is to that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we've been careful about, about rolling back those restrictions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let's remember that the banks-that the banks that are subject to the stress tests have taken very, very large reserves-very large loss reserves, and also increased their capital.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They've actually had-they have higher capital ratios now than they had at the beginning of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and-but, you know, we're going to be careful about this and, you know, move based on data, and all of the data, when we make that decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on housing, you know, housing is now-the level of housing activity is at its highest level since before the Global Financial Crisis, in some measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of the, the tightness in housing markets, we think-which has led to the, the significant price increases this year-we think is, is a passing phenomenon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a one-time thing happening with people who are spending all of their time in their house, and they're thinking either "I need a bigger house" or "I need another house and a different house-or a second house," in some cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's just-there's a-there's a one- time shift in demand that we think will get satisfied-also, that will call forth supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that will-that will, we think-we think that those price increases are unlikely to be sustained for, for all of those reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we monitor pretty much all of the big financial markets pretty carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, what's happened in, in the corporate debt market, beginning with the announcement of our corporate credit facility, has been, you've seen lenders lending and borrowers borrowing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've seen relatively significantly fewer defaults than we-than we expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There were a lot of downgrades and some defaults at the beginning, and those have really slowed down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, the same is true for bank loans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Banks are not experiencing the kinds of defaults that, that we all were concerned about in the early months of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So they're having to reverse some of their loss reserves, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They were very broad-high-wide, of course, at the-during the acute phase of the pandemic, and they've- you know, they're now at the lower end of their typical range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's, it's not something we can control or operate on directly, but we do-we do watch those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, in a sense, it's good that companies have been able to finance themselves during this period, because they-they've been able to stay in business.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the, the big thing is that the jury's out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this has been a concern since the very beginning, is the concern that people-if, if they become disconnected from the industry or the job where-that they used to work in, it, it can be years or never when they get back into the labor force, particularly for people who are well along in their careers-the same kind of scarring for small businesses, which don't have the kind of resources that you need to get through this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've, we've had a big concern about, about both of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't seen as much of it as we-as we feared.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as I said that, you know, the jury is out here-9 or 10 million people still out of work because of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're-a big chunk of them are people who worked in public-facing jobs in the service sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, they've gotten a lot of support from fiscal policy and some from monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's, it's harder if you're-it takes longer, empirically, to find that next job if you're looking at a brand-new industry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that just, again, stresses the urgency that we feel and others feel at, at, you know, fully defeating the pandemic, finishing the job and getting back to a place where it's safe to have these-you know, to, to, to stay in hotels, to fly on airplanes, to go to sporting events and movie theaters, and all of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're, we're very, very focused on that group of people with our policy and, and, and, you know, the way we look at the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So many people have had that bridge across the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For many people, it's clear that they've made it across, and their job is okay, and their house is okay.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's been terribly inconvenient and painful, and schools are closed and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there, there's a bunch of people yet who haven't found that bridge yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, the other thing is, we're going to a different economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to be learning more about that as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, clearly, we're, we're learning that things can be done from remote locations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're learning that technology can replace people even more than we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think as we, you know, as we get into this, you know, the phase after-even after the economy fully reopens, I think we're still going to need to keep people in mind whose lives have been disrupted, because they've lost that-the work that they did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it would be wise as a country, for the longer-run productive capacity of the country, if we were to look out for those people and help them find their way back into the labor force even if it means continuing support for an additional period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I strongly agree with that, as a matter of fact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if you look at either-look at employment gaps or unemployment gaps or wage gaps, wealth gaps, homeowning gaps, all of those persistent gaps that exist even controlling for many other factors, you will see that they're, they're persistent, they're-and they're very difficult to explain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so it's-the reason we talk about inequality and, and racial inequality in particular, is that it goes to our job, which is to achieve maximum employment, which, which links up with, with-we want-we want the potential output of the United States to be as high as it can possibly be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want-we want an economy where everybody can take part and everybody, everybody can put their labor in, and they can share in the prosperity of our great economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's how the U.S. economy can be bigger, stronger, growing faster, is if we can achieve a more-a broader prosperity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, now, in terms of our tools, you know, of course, that project that I just mentioned is one for the broader society, for the private sector, for fiscal policy, but we have a role to play.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and that is, how we think about the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Principally, when we say that the maximum employment is a, a broad and inclusive goal, what we're-what we're saying there is, we're not just going to look at the headline-and we never did, really, but-we're not going to just look at the headline numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to look at different demographic groups, including women, minorities, and others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're not going to say that we've reached maximum employment, which is our statutory goal, until we've reached maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you haven't if, if there's lots of pockets of, of people not participating in or not employed in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also do a tremendous amount of research on these issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we do-we, we have such a focus on these issues now that we actually-we, we have a new, a webpage, relatively new, where you can access all of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's a lot of activities in our Division of Consumer and Community Affairs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's lots of research, and, and it's also, you know, our enforcement of the fair lending laws and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think everybody's got a role to play here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a-it's a national goal and a national job, and we're just going to do our part of the job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, if you go back to the-to the beginning, there was a real concern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, just, just take the financial markets, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Suddenly, all of those big buildings all over the, the-New York City and all around the world where people work in the financial markets with terminals and everything, everybody had to go home, and they had to take their terminals with them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think there was a real concern that there would be a tremendous loss of functionality just at the time when the financial markets were under historically difficult conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think people-many people in the financial sector are still working with their terminals at home, including people on trading floors or on virtual trading floors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we have definitely learned that we can do more work from home in many, many different lines of work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, that's not possible if your job involves being at a place, doing personal services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's very much something that skews to higher-income, higher-educated people being able to work from home and others not so much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other thing, though, even conditional on that, when we saw the wave in the South and the West, the wave of cases this summer, I think, intuitively, having seen what happened in March and April, we expected there to be a significant hit to economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people kind of just got on with their lives and went and, and dealt with it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and it didn't actually-it had a much smaller effect on economic activity than we expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then comes the fall wave, which is just so much larger-a very, very large wave as, as was very much forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And even there, if you look at-I would say, look at the December jobs report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, big job losses in, you know, in that part of the service sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you go-if you look elsewhere, it's not having an effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, even purchasing manager index and sentiment indexes on, on areas of the economy that are not directly-really directly-exposed to the pandemic in their economic activity, they're doing okay.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the way-the way-the way the housing industry worked, that when you buy a house, there was a lot of in-person contact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They managed to pretty much immediately go to a more virtual-you know, with all the technology.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the housing market has been really strong, notwithstanding that it's, it's now quite virtual rather than in person.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's been a lot of adapting, and-but you can't adapt, you know, hotels, sporting venues, movie theaters, restaurants, bars.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You just-you know, those are just going to-and that's-again, that's millions and millions of people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so you're just going to have to defeat the pandemic, which, as I mentioned, you know, we, we have a plan to do that, but we haven't done it yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-it's, it's within our power to do that as a country this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would just urge that-and I know people are working hard on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that, that is really the main thing about the economy, is, is getting the pandemic under control, getting everyone vaccinated, getting people wearing masks, and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's the single most important economic growth policy that we can have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you-as you pointed out, we've said that we would continue asset purchases at this pace until we see substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and what we mean by that is, is pretty straightforward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is, we want to see that, that the labor markets have moved-labor market conditions have moved-you know, have made substantial progress toward maximum employment, and inflation has made substantial progress toward the 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we also understand that we, we will want to provide as much advance notice of any potential taper as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when we see that we're on track, when we see actual data coming in that suggests that we're on track to perhaps achieve substantial further progress, then we'll say so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll say so well in advance of any decision to actually taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we have a, a range of perspectives on the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we, we have-we debate things, we discuss things, and we always come together around a-around a, a solution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, the, the strong bulk of the Committee is, is not showing a rate increase during this forecast period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, as, as data improve, as the outlook improves very significantly since the December meeting, you would expect forecasts to move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's probably not a surprise that some people would bring in their estimate of the appropriate time for liftoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, you know, the bulk of the Committee-the, the largest part by far of the Committee is, is-doesn't show a rate increase during this period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, part of that is wanting to see actual data rather than just a forecast at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do expect that we'll begin to make faster progress on both spending-you know, labor markets and inflation as the year goes on because of the progress with the vaccines, because of the fiscal support that we're getting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Victoria, we'll have something to announce on that in coming days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Why don't you-why don't you ask another question if you'd like to?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Because, because that one-I'm just going to say that we'll have something in coming days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, let me say, as we say in our Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, we look to a range of indicators on the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We never only looked at the unemployment rate, which is the only indicator of, of labor market outcomes that's in the SEP. We look at a very broad range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You hear us talk all the time about participation; about employment to population, which is the combination of the two; about different measures of, of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's wages, it's, it's the job flows, it's, you know, all of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the-trying to incorporate all of that into the Summary of Economic Projections would not be practical.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, obviously, the thing that we do include is just the unemployment rate, and that's a very insufficient statistic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-it, it doesn't include a lot of other things that we-that we do look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I wouldn't want to say that we're looking to include the other dozen things that we look at into the SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But at time-from time to time, we do look at, at adding different things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, I would just say the SEP is, it's a summary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not going to include all of the things that we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you know the things that we look at-we, we talk about them all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're not actually looking actively at significantly broadening those indicators in the SEP right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess the first thing to say is that the, the SEP is not a Committee forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's not something we sit around and debate and discuss and approve, and say, "This represents our, you know, our reaction function as a Committee."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-since we don't debate it or discuss it, it would be hard for me to say why-exactly why each participant did what they were going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So all I would say about this is that we've-we laid out what I think is very clear guidance on liftoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's really three things: labor market conditions that are consistent with our estimates of maximum employment-and, as I mentioned, we consider a wide range of indicators in assessing labor market conditions, not just the unemployment rate; inflation that has reached 2 percent, and not just on a transitory basis; and inflation that's on track to run moderately above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first two of those three are very much data based; the third does have a little bit of a-of an element of expectations in it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we are very much determined to implement this guidance in a robust way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is the guidance that we chose carefully to implement our new framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And to meet these standards, we'll need to see data, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It says that we're committed to our framework and to the guidance we've provided to implement that framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will wait until the requirements set forth in that guidance are clearly met before considering a change in our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the last thing I'll say is this: The state of the economy in two or three years is highly uncertain, and I wouldn't want to focus too much on the exact timing of a potential rate increase that far into the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's how I would think about the, the SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've said we'd like to see inflation run moderately above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've resisted, basically, generally, the temptation to try to quantify that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of that just is, talking about inflation is one thing; actually having inflation run above 2 percent is the real thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-you know, over the years we've, we've talked about 2 percent inflation as a goal, but we haven't achieved it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I would say we'd like to, you know, perform.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we'd really like to do, is to get inflation moderately above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't want to be too specific about what that means, because I think it's hard to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, when we're actually above 2 percent, we can do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The fundamental change in, in our framework is that we, we're not going to act preemptively based on forecasts for the most part.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it will take people time to, to adjust to that-and to adjust to that new practice.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the only way we can really build the credibility of that is by doing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on, on herd immunity, I, I'm really going to leave that question to the experts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll, we'll leave that whole discussion to the experts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we're-what we're focused on is, is the part that we control, which is the support that we provide to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in the case of asset purchases, it's at their current level until we make substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There is an element of judgment in that, and we'll, we'll- therefore, we'll supply clear communication well in advance of, of actually tapering, and we just went through, you know, the, the criteria for raising interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're, we're very much committed to having them fulfilled robustly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I would agree with you that the, the path of the virus continues to be very important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we have these, you know, new strains with-which, which can be quite virulent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I-we're clearly on a good path with, with cases coming down, as I mentioned, but we're not done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'd hate to see us take our eye off the ball before we actually finish the job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People may be, for example, going into spaces that, that, you know, that involve close contact with others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, though, remember, there are-there are 10 million people-in the range of 10 million people who need to get back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's going to take some time for that to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it can-it can happen maybe, maybe more quickly than it has in the past, because it involves the reopening of a sector of the economy, as opposed to stimulating aggregate demand and waiting for that to produce job demand for workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's, it's just a lot of people who have-who need to get back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No matter how well the economy performs, unemployment will take quite a time to go-to go down, and so will participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the faster the better; we'd love to see it come sooner rather than later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, realistically, given the numbers, it's going to take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we monitor a broad range of financial conditions, and we're always attentive to market developments, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're still a long way from our goals, and it's important that financial conditions do remain accommodative to support the achievement of those goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look at various indexes of financial conditions, what you'll see is that they generally do show financial conditions overall to be highly accommodative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would add, as I've said, I would be concerned by disorderly conditions in markets or by a persistent tightening of financial conditions that threaten the achievement of our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think the stance of our-of monetary policy remains appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our guidance on the federal funds rate and on asset purchases is providing strong support for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're committed to maintaining that patiently accommodative stance until the job is well and truly done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we-the tools we have are the tools we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
