text: What I'm telling you is that the stance of monetary policy we have today, we believe, is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that our asset purchases in their current form-which is to say, you know, across the curve, $80 billion in Treasuries, $40 billion in mortgage-backed securities on net-we think that that's, that's the right place for our asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, we can-we can change them, of course, in, in a number of different dimensions should we deem that that's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, for now, we think that our policy stance on that is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we do monitor and communicate very regularly about different labor market-disparities in the labor market, let's say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the African American unemployment rate is substantially elevated, and so is the Hispanic unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at those and we see those as, you know-it's, it's slack in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's sad to see, because those disparities had really come down to record lows since we started keeping the data that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As recently as a year ago, February of last year, we had those, those disparities quite low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What happens in a downturn, though, is they move up at twice the speed of white unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-our tools, of course, affect unemployment generally, but we're going to look at those as, as a form of slack in the labor market and hope that, you know, that there's progress there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and this particular downturn, of course, was just a direct hit on, on a part of the economy that employs many minorities and lower-paid workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The public-facing workers in the service industries in many cases don't have a lot of financial assets, they're not tremendously well paid, they might have other jobs, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this was a direct hit on that part of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's the slowest part of the economy to recover.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we'd like to see those people continue to get supported, you know, as we-as the broader economy recovers, which, which it's very much doing now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of disparate levels of vaccination, that's-those are facts and unfortunate facts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're really not something we, we have within our policy toolkit to address.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it is-it is true, though, that the data we have suggests that there are-there are significant disparities between different ethnic groups and-you know, but that's, that's not for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's for fiscal authorities and the government more generally to, to work on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do think that fiscal policy overall will have really helped us to avoid much of the scarring that we were very, very concerned about at the beginning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's just the size and the speed with which Congress has delivered-you know, with the CARES Act and since then, has-is going to wind up very much accelerating the return to full employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's going to make a huge difference in people's lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned in my remarks-opening remarks, the recovery has been faster than we expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of that just is, it's very hard to predict, given we've never seen an event like this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But part of it is just the strength of the fiscal response, which I think will, will look good over the years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Longer term, you know, to, to really-that's-the first part of it is about avoiding scarring, and I think we've not avoided all of the scarring, but we've probably avoided the worst cases there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and I hope we keep at it, and we will keep at it with our policies, of course, to do whatever we can to make sure that's-that continues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Longer term though, what it takes to drive productive capacity per capita or per hour worked, to raise living standards over time, is investment: investment in people's skills and aptitudes, investment in plant and equipment, investment in software.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It takes a lot of investment to, to support a more productive economy and raise living standards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-you know, that hasn't been the principal focus with these measures-our measures, certainly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what Congress has been doing has mainly been replacing lost income and beginning to, you know, support people as the economy returns to normal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there should be a focus on-a longer-term focus, I think, would be healthy on, on the investment front.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're right that the pace of the recovery is that we're having diverging recoveries here, as we did after the last crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in this case, as well as the other one, the U.S.'s recovery is, is leading the global recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our, our focus is on-our, you know-our, our objectives are domestic ones.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's maximum employment and price stability here in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We monitor developments abroad, and we know-because they know we know that they can-those can affect our outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think U.S. demand-very strong U.S. demand, if, if-as the economy improves is going to support global activity as well over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, when the U.S. economy is strong, that strength tends to be-tends to support global, global activity as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'd love to see the vaccine rollout going more smoothly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I don't worry too much about us in the near term, because we're, we're on a very good track.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Very strong fiscal support coming, now vaccination going quickly, and cases coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's all ahead of us, but the data should, should get stronger fairly quickly here and remain strong for some time here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, we're going to continue our data-driven approach.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know that we restricted buybacks and dividends, so the firms are preserving capital.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Through 2020, the banks actually increased their level of capital and their level of reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the December stress tests showed that banks are strong and well capitalized under our hypothetical recessions that we-that we used in December, which were quite stringent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're right in the middle of our 2021 stress tests, and we'll release those results before the end of June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that layers, you know, very significant additional stress on top of the stress the banks have already absorbed over the past year, with the unemployment rate going to 11 percent and stock prices falling more than 50 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but all of that, you know, the results of the stress tests and the decision on distributions-all of that is to come fairly soon, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've set out very clear criteria for liftoff, right, where we've said we want to see labor market conditions that are consistent with our estimates of, of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that doesn't just mean unemployment, it means a much broader set of criteria.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want inflation at 2 percent, and not on a transitory basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we want inflation on track to be moderately-to run moderately above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it comes down to, what's your projection for the economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you want to-if you want to-you know, people will have a range of, of assessments for how good the economy is going to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we, we don't-I would say that we're in a relatively highly uncertain situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the uncertainty, people, people on the Committee broadly say that uncertainty about the forecast is, is very high compared to the normal level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't had this kind of fiscal support before, totaling it all up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're going to have different perspectives from Committee participants about how fast growth will be, how fast the labor market will heal, or how fast-sorry, inflation will move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those things are going to dictate where people write down an estimate of liftoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, this isn't a decision to lift off now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's an estimate based on-based on assumptions about growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's, it's meant to be a tool to generally show the public how, how our objective function works, how we think about the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It isn't meant to actually pin down a time when we might or might not lift off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-you know, we're not going to make that decision for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The chances are that the economy in that time and place will be very different from the one we think it'll be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-sometimes with the dots, I have to be sure to point out that they-they're not a Committee forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you know this, but it's-they're not a Committee forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not meant to, to actually be a promise or even a prediction of when the Committee will act.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That will be very much dependent on economic outcomes, which are highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, Brian, it's not up to us to decide what, what Congress should spend money on or when.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I was answering Jeanna's question, which really was, how do we assure lack of damage to-scarring, for example, or lack of damage to the productive capacity of the economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think what's happened so far has done a pretty good job of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, really, I wanted to make the longer-run point that if-to work on the productivity-on productivity over longer periods, that is-that is-comes down to a number of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But one of those things is investment: investment in people, in their skills, education, aptitude, all of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not in any way suggesting that that's something Congress should work on right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Or that, you know, that's just not my-that's not our job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm just saying, that, that is what fiscal policy can do that, really, monetary policy can't do-is, is invest in the future productive capacity of the economy, raise potential growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, I wasn't making a comment at all on the current fiscal setting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you know, financial stability for us is, is a framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not a particular market or a particular asset or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We report on it semiannually, the Board gets a report on it quarterly, and we monitor every day.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it has-it has four pillars, and those are four key vulnerabilities: asset valuations, debt owed by businesses and households, funding risk, and leverage among financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at asset valuations, you can say that by some measures, some asset valuations are elevated compared to history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of households and businesses, households entered the, the crisis in very good shape by historical standards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Leverage in the household sector had been just kind of gradually moving down and down and down since the-since the financial crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, there was-there was some negative effects on that, people lost their jobs and that sort of thing, but they've also gotten a lot of support now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the damage hasn't been as, as bad as we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Businesses, by the same token, had a high debt load coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's-they've done so much financing, and there's a lot of cash on their balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So nothing in those two sectors really jumps out as really troubling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Short term-I mentioned funding risk as the-as the last one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we saw, again, in this crisis, breakdowns in parts of the short-term funding markets-came under a tremendous amount of stress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we shut down our facilities and all of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, we don't-we don't feel like we can let the moment pass without just saying again that we-that those-some aspects of the short-term funding markets and, more broadly, nonbank financial intermediation didn't hold up so well under great stress-under tremendous stress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we need to go back and look at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a very high priority for us as regulators and supervisors is going to be to go back-and this, this will involve all the other regulatory agencies; it does involve all of them as well-and see if we can strengthen those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, again, I wouldn't read too much into, into the, the March 2021 SEP dot plot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Remember what it is: It's a compilation of individual projections by individual members.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they're-also remember that the SEP doesn't actually include all the things that go into maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I would just say, we've set out clear guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The-the message from the SEP that I would like to leave with people is, we set out clear guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's inflation up to-no, sorry, it's, it's labor market conditions consistent with our estimates of maximum employment-and that's not just unemployment, it's all the other indicators, but, overall, totaling up to maximum employment; it's inflation at 2 percent, and not on a transient basis; and inflation on track to exceed 2 percent for-moderately for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, you know, the, the state of the economy in two or three years is highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I wouldn't want to focus too much on the exact timing of a potential rate increase that far into the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what I would say is, we're committed to giving the economy the support that it needs to return as quickly as possible to a state of maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, to the extent having rates low and support for monetary policy broadly, to the extent that raises other questions, we think it's absolutely essential to maintain the strength and stability of the-of the broader financial system and to carefully monitor financial stability questions if that's what you're getting at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I would point out that, over the long expansion-the longest in U.S. history, 10 years and 8 months-rates were very low for-they were at zero for, you know, 7 years and then-and then never got above, you know, 2. percent, roughly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: During that, we didn't see, actually, excess buildup of debt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't see asset prices form into bubbles that would threaten the progress of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't see the things you-we didn't see a housing bubble.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the things that have tended to really hurt an economy and have in recent history hurt the U.S., we didn't see them build up despite very low rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of that just is that you're in a low- rate environment, you're in a much lower rate environment, and the connection between low rates and the kind of financial instability issues is just not as tight as people think it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We say there is, but it's not quite so clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We actually monitor financial conditions very, very broadly and carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we didn't do that before the Global Financial Crisis 12 years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've also, you know, put a lot of time and effort into strengthening the large financial institutions that form the core of our financial system-are much stronger, much more resilient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want it to be true of, of other nonbank financial intermediation, markets, and, and institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that's, that's-you know, monetary policy should be, to me, for, for achieving our macroeconomic aims.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Financial regulatory policy and supervision should be for strengthening the financial system so that it is strong and robust and can withstand the kinds of things that it couldn't, frankly-and we learned that in 2008, '09, '10.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This time around, the regulated part of the financial system held up very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we found some other areas that need strengthening, and that's what we're working on now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was a time when there was a tight connection between unemployment and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had low unemployment in 2018 and '19 and the beginning of '20 without having troubling inflation at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were bouncing around with unemployment 3. percent to 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that has not- what, what happens is that when wages move up because unemployment is low, companies have been absorbing that increase into their margins rather than raising prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that seems to be a feature of late-cycle behavior.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're not-when, when we-when we seek to achieve low unemployment, high levels of employment, which is our mandate, you know, we think we have the freedom to do that based on the data without worrying too much about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, if you go back, October, November-sorry, November, December, and January, progress in the labor market slowed very sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you had an average of 29,000 jobs per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go back and look at the, the level of job creation before that, it was very, very high-very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we weren't making any progress on the labor market from November through January.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: February, we saw a nice-a nice pickup, a good jobs report-379,465 private sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, it would be nice to see-to really make faster progress that's different from substantial progress, we'd like to see it be, be higher than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-the expectation is, you'll see now, I think, really strong job creation return-not as high as it was in the very early days of the recovery, the reopening of the economy, but, nonetheless, very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what, what I'm saying is, to achieve substantial progress from where we are, having had three months of, of very little progress, is going to take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-we don't want to get into-I don't want to get into trying to put a pin on the calendar someplace, because it's going to be data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we see-when we see ourselves on track to make substantial further progress, we're going to-we're going to say so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We understand fully that that test is one that involves judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you remember, during the Global Financial Crisis recovery, we said quantitative easing, number three, was-the test was a substantial improvement in the outlook for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, it means a substantial improvement in the outlook for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It meant we would communicate when we thought we had that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're saying is, substantial further progress toward our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll tell people when we think-until we-until we say-until we give a signal, you can assume we're not there yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as we approach it, well in advance-well in advance-we will give a signal that, yes, we're on a path to, to possibly achieve that, to consider tapering.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we've learned-what we've learned from the experience of these last dozen years is to communicate very carefully, very clearly, well in advance, and then follow through with, with your communications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In this case, it's, it's an outcome-based set of guidance, as our rate guidance is, and it's going to depend on the progress of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's why it's not appropriate to start pointing at dates yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, you know, we and everyone who's forecasting these-what, what we're all doing is, we are looking at the-at the amount of savings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking at-you know, we have reasonably good data on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're looking at the government transfers that'll be made as part of the various laws.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're trying to make an assessment on what will be the tendency of people to spend that money, the marginal propensity to consume.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And from that, you can develop an estimate of the impact on spending, on growth, on hiring, and, ultimately, on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have, you know, we have-we can look at history, and we can make estimates, and those are all very transparent and public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we've made very conservative assumptions and sensible mainstream assumptions at each step of that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what, what it comes down to is what I said before, which is, there very likely will be a step-up in inflation as March and April of last year drop out of the 12-month window, because they were very low inflation numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll wear off quickly, though, because it-just the way the numbers are calculated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Past that, as the economy reopens, people will start spending more, and then, you know, you can only go out to dinner once per night, but a lot of people can go out to dinner.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That part of the economy-and travel and hotels-that part of the economy is, is really not functioning at, at full capacity, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also-wouldn't be surprising if-and you're seeing this now, particularly in the goods economy-there'll be bottlenecks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They won't be-they won't be able to service all of the demand maybe, maybe for a period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those things could lead to-and we've, we've modeled that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've-and what we see is relatively modest increases in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what'll, what'll happen is-the supply side-the supply side in the United States is very dynamic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People start businesses, they, they reopen restaurants, you know, the airlines are, will be flying again, all of those things will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so it'll turn out to be a one-a one-time sort of bulge in, in prices, but it won't change inflation going forward, because inflation expectations are strongly anchored around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there was a time when, when inflation went up, it would stay up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think it won't-it won't-we won't suddenly change to another regime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they tend to-tend to change when the central bank doesn't understand that having inflation expectations anchored at 2 percent is the key to it all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the-having them anchored at 2 percent is what gives us the ability to push hard when the economy's really weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we saw inflation expectations moving materially above 2 percent, of course, we would conduct policy in a way that would, would make sure that that didn't happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're committed to having inflation expectations anchored at 2 percent, not materially above or below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-I think if you-if you look at the savings, look at all of that, model it, that's, that's kind of what comes out of our assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's, it's a relatively unusual-very unusual situation to have all these savings and this, this amount of fiscal support and monetary policy support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you know, as the-as the data come in and the economy performs, we'll of course adjust.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our outcome-based guidance will immediately adapt, we think, to meet whatever the actual path of the economy is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I have to say, I think it's impossible to say, frankly, with any confidence, but I, I would expect it's very possible-let's put it that way-that you will see bottlenecks emerge and then clear over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you'll probably see that over a period of time, because, you know, really, the, the strong data are ahead of us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you're, you're-right now the, the checks are going out just, just now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the really strong economic data is coming.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It should be coming, assuming we stay on this track.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's when you'll really know where, where the bottlenecks are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you can see, though, that they're not-these are not permanent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not like the supply side will be unable to adapt to these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and some of the answer to that may be price.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's a little bit the story about, you know, the wage-the wage Phillips curve does show that as unemployment goes down, wages move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But companies choose not to try to, to pass that, that price increase along to their customers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you'll see a lot of that here too, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've said that we would let the public know when it is time to have that conversation, and we said we'd do that well in advance of any actual decision to taper our asset purchases, and we will do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, we'll be monitoring progress toward our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We first articulated this "substantial further progress" test at our December meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Economic activity and hiring have just recently picked up after slowing over the winter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it will take some time before we see substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, so we have to leave questions about herd immunity and what that looks like to the health experts, but, but I would certainly say that what matters the most to the economic recovery continues to be controlling the virus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy can't fully recover until people are confident that it's safe to resume activities involving crowds of people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There may be people who are around the edges of the labor force who won't come back in unless they feel really comfortable going back to their old jobs, for example, and there, there may be parts of the economy that will-that just won't be able to, to really fully reengage until the pandemic is decisively behind us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we've articulated particular guidance for tapering our asset purchases and for lifting off and raising interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So for, for asset purchases, we've said that we would continue at the current pace of asset purchases until we see substantial further progress toward our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and that is, that is what it is, substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For interest rates, as I-as I said a moment ago, we want to see labor market conditions consistent with maximum employment, we want to see inflation at 2 percent, and we want to see it on track to exceed 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't have an independent test to do with the virus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, though, as I-as I started with, you know, the, the path of the virus is going to have an effect on our ability to achieve both of those tests.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it seems unlikely, frankly, that we would see inflation moving up in a persistent way that would actually move inflation expectations up while there was still significant slack in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I won't say that it's impossible, but it, it seems-it seems unlikely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's much more likely that we would-having achieved maximum-employment conditions-we'd also be seeing 2 percent inflation and be on track to see inflation moving above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's not to say inflation won't-might not move up, but for inflation to move up in a persistent way that, that really starts to move inflation expectations up, that would have to-that would take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you would think that, that it would be quite likely that, that we'd be in very strong labor markets for that to be happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If it-if that actually were to happen, though, there is a-there's a paragraph in the-in the Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy which says that when the two goals are somewhat in conflict, we weigh various factors, including the, the time it would take to get back and [so] forth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do-it doesn't really tell you what to do, but it tells you that we will weigh those two factors and how far we are away from them and how long it would take to reach them were we to reach that sort of pretty unlikely state.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we really have-just articulated the goals that I've-that I've just mentioned a couple of times, which is substantial further progress toward our goals before we taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, that's very likely-for us to achieve that, it's very likely going to be the case that we've also made really significant progress on controlling the virus through vaccination and, and other-it, it-you know, those two things should more or less coexist.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't articulated a separate test for a state of the virus that we'd like to achieve because we're not-you know, we're not experts in that area.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're really focused on the economic outcomes, and, again, my, my guess is that we-it's very likely, it seems to me, that for us to achieve the economic outcomes, we would need to taper or to raise interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would also have to have made very substantial progress in getting the virus under control-not, not necessarily fully under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There is a, a possibility, of course, that we will, will have ongoing outbreaks over the summer and various regional outbreaks and potentially next winter as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we'll be looking for substantial progress toward our goal-substantial further progress toward our goals as we think about tapering asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say that we were very worried about scarring, both in the labor market from people being out of-out of the labor market for an extended period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The evidence is clear that it becomes much more difficult if you're out for a long time to get back in and get back to the life that you had.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Same thing with these small businesses, many of which are the work of generations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Were we going to wipe out many of those unnecessarily?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that, so far, you know, here we are in late April of 2021.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't experienced that level of scarring either in the labor market or among smaller businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're not living that, that downside case that we were very concerned about a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-you know, payroll jobs are 8. million below where they were in February of 2020.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've been hearing a lot from companies that they are-they've been looking at deploying better technology and perhaps fewer people, including in some of the service industries that have been employing a lot of people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it, it may well be-it seems quite likely that a number of the people who, who had those service-sector jobs will struggle to find the same job and may need time to find work and get back to the working life they had.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These were people who were working in February of 2020.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those people are going to need-they're going to need help.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, while I would say we haven't seen really highly elevated levels of unemployment for-you know, up in the teens that we thought we might have for an extended period of time, we've still got a lot of people who are out to-out of work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to get them back to work as quickly as possible, and that's really one of the things we're trying to achieve with our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do monitor the housing market very carefully, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say that, before the pandemic, it's a very different housing market than it was before the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And one of the main differences was that households were in very good shape financially compared to where they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, most people who got mortgages were people with pretty high credit scores.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There wasn't the subprime-you know, low-doc, no-doc lending practices were not there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't have that kind of thing where we have a housing bubble where people are overlevered and owning a lot of houses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no question, though, that housing prices are going up, and so we're watching that carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's partly because there's, there's clearly strong demand, and there's just not a lot of supply right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So builders are, you know, struggling to keep up with the demand, clearly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you're-if you're an entry level housing buyer, this is-this is a problem, because it just is going to be that much harder for people to get that first house, and that's a problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we-it's part of a strong economy, with people having money to spend and wanting to invest in housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's clearly the strongest housing market that we've seen since the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, my hope would be that, over time, housing builders can react to this demand and, and come up with more supply and workers will come back to work in that industry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, it is-it's not an unalloyed good to have prices going up this much, and we're watching it very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't see the kind of financial stability current concerns, though, that really do reside around the housing sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So many of the financial crackups in all countries, all western countries, that have happened in the last 30 years have been around housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't see bad loans and unsustainable prices and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Chris, you were breaking up a little there, but I think I did get your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think there are a number of-a number of things going on there: the tension between a high level of unemployment and yet many, many companies saying they can't find- an elevated number of companies saying that they can't find workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are workers who don't actually have the specific skills that the employers are looking for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It, it may also be that, for example, there-one big factor would be, schools aren't open yet, so there are still people who are at home taking care of their children and would like to be back in the workforce but can't be yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are people afraid of-there are virus fears that are weighing on people, so some-some people don't want to go back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are also a significant number of people who say they've retired-a large number of people that say that they're retired.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, it's hard to say whether they will come back in as the labor market strengthens and as COVID, you know, becomes a-in the rearview mirror, in the history books, if you will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but clearly there's something going, going on out there, as, as many companies are reporting labor shortages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't see wages moving up yet, and presumably we would see that in a real-you know, in a really tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think-so what will happen-what we saw during the last expansion, and it may be a different expansion, we don't know, but, but what we saw was that labor supply generally showed up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other words, if you were worried about there-about running out of workers, it seemed like we never did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So my guess would be that you will see people coming back into the labor force, and these jobs will be-the labor market will reach equilibrium.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I do think that-and I do think also that unemployment insurance benefits will run out in September, so to the extent that's a factor, which is not clear, it will no longer be a factor fairly soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So my guess is, it will come back to this economy where we have, you know, equilibrium between labor supply and labor demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I actually have a couple things I'd like to say about inflation, including addressing your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me start with just saying that we're very strongly committed to achieving our objectives of maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our, our price stability goal is 2 percent inflation over the longer run, and we believe that having inflation average 2 percent over time will help anchor long-term inflation expectations at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With inflation having run persistently below 2 percent for some time, the Committee seeks inflation moderately above inflation for two times-above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, with a, a little bit of context, we're, we're making our way through an unprecedented series of events, really, in which a synchronized global shutdown is now giving way to widespread reopening of economies in many places around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the United States, fiscal and monetary policy continue to provide strong support: Vaccinations are now widespread, and the economy is beginning to move ahead with real momentum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: During this time of reopening, we are likely to see some upward pressure on prices, and I'll discuss why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But those pressures are likely to be temporary as they are associated with the reopening process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In an episode of one-time price increases as the economy reopens is not the same thing as, and is not likely to lead to, persistently higher year-over-year inflation into the future- inflation at levels that are not consistent with our goal of 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Indeed, it is the Fed's job to make sure that that does not happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, if, contrary to expectations, inflation were to move persistently and materially above 2 percent in a manner that threatened to move longer-term inflation expectations materially above 2 percent, we would use our tools to bring inflation and expectations down to mandate-consistent levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, if I may, that is a principal difference from-we're all very familiar at the Fed with the history of the 1960s and '70s, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we know that our job is to achieve 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're committed to that, and we will use our tools to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a very different situation than you had back in the 1960s-or many, many differences, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me talk quickly about the two reasons-two, or you could say three, but really two main reasons why we think inflation will move up in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Twelve-month measures of inflation are likely to move well above 2 percent over the next few months as the very low inflation readings recorded in March and April of last year drop out of the calculation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw it in the March CPI reading, and you'll see it later this week in the PCE price data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These base effects will contribute about 1 percentage point to headline inflation and about 0. percentage point to core inflation in April and May.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, significant increases, and they'll disappear over the following months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They carry no implication for the rate of inflation in later periods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other big one I would talk about is bottlenecks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is what we're seeing in supply chains in various industries, and we're, we're in close touch with all of these industries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the Fed has a network of contacts that is unequaled in businesses and in nonprofits for that matter, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A bottleneck really is a temporary blockage or restriction in the supply chain for, for a particular good or goods, something that slows down the process of producing goods and delivering them to the market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think of bottlenecks as things that, in their nature, will be resolved as workers and businesses adapt, and we think of them as not calling for a change in monetary policy since they're temporary and expected to resolve themselves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that the base effects will disappear in a few months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's much harder to predict with confidence the amount of time it will take to resolve the bottlenecks, or for that matter, the temporary effects that they will have on prices in the meantime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I'll just sum up and say, we understand our job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we are, we are focused-as you've seen, for many years, we've been focused on inflation deviating below 2 percent, and we used our tools aggressively to keep it back up at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, if we see inflation moving materially above 2 percent in a persistent way that risks inflation expectations drifting up, then we will use our tools to guide inflation and expectations back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But no one should doubt that, in the event, we would be prepared to use our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I would say, what we have right now is one really good-I can tell you what it's not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not one really good employment reading, which is what we got in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We got close to a million jobs in March and a very strong labor market reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I was just suggesting that we'd want to see more like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're 8½ million jobs below where we were in February of 2020, and that doesn't account for growth in the labor force and growth in the economy, that trend we were on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have-we're a long way from our, our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't have to get all the way to our goals to taper asset purchases, we just need to make substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I was really thinking-we were thinking of the base effects and also the energy effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wasn't meaning to say there are some real effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, there are always-there are always relative prices going up and down within inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are, you know, many, many, many factors that go into it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This, this-we think it's, it's very fair to say that the increases we see and, frankly, are about to see later this week are largely due to base effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would have been more contentious to say "entirely due to base effects" because there are some things that are always going up, and so we just said "largely."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we, we supervise banks to make sure that they have risk- management systems in place so that they can spot these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't manage their companies for them or, or try to manage individual risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the grand scheme of these large institutions, the Archegos risks were not systemically important or were not of the size that they would have really created trouble for any of those institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What was troubling, though, was that this could happen in a business for a number of firms that is thought to be-to carry relatively well understood risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The prime brokerage business is, is a well understood business, and so it was surprising that a number of them would have had this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it was essentially, I believe, the fact that, that they had the same big risk position on with a number of firms, and they weren't-some of the firms were not aware that there were other firms that had those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I wouldn't say it's in any way an indictment of our supervision of these firms.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It, it-in some cases, it may be they were-it seems as though there were risk-management breakdowns at some of the firms, not all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I have not had a chance to do it yet, but I've been very busy, but I will visit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't want to visit it at a time of a lot of media attention, because I don't want that to be part of the story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I will-I will go visit when, when it's no longer a, a news story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-you know, I-I've met with homeless people many times, a number of times, anyway, let's say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think it's always good to talk to people and hear what's going on in their lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, they're, they're-these are people who, in many cases, had jobs and, you know, they have lives, and they've just, they've just found themselves in this place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, there are many, many facets of it, and I'm well aware that this is not something that the Fed has all the tools for or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, I will do that when, when the need arises and when, when it's not so much, you know, in the public eye.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And is there anything specifically that you would be looking to learn there?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I, I think I know what I'll find there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think you, you connect with these people and what you-again, what you find is, they're like you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You, you always feel that way in that sort of an encounter, and, you know, it just is a-it's a-it's an important thing to engage in, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, you know, we bring that understanding into our lives and, frankly, into our work-the work that we do as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the first thing to say is that we feel an obligation to understand the technology and all of the policy issues very, very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Central bank digital currencies are now possible, and we're going to see some of them around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we need to understand whether that's something that would be a good thing for the people that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are some very, very difficult questions to answer, but I think we-and we are engaged in a serious program to understand both the technology and the policy issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I am-I would say this: We're the world's reserve currency, and that means that the dollar is used in transactions all around the world, far more than any other currency.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's because of our rule of law; our democratic institutions, which are the best in the world; our economy; our industrious people; all the things that make the United States the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, we have open capital accounts, which is essential if you're going to be the reserve currency.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those are the factors that make us the reserve currency.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I am-I'm less concerned that someone-that another country might have a digital currency first.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, ask yourself the question, does that mean that, if you were a company that's doing international business, would you then suddenly start to use that currency to use your-do your international transactions, or would you still do them in dollars, where, where- which is what everyone does?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is-it is a-it is a tricky set of questions that we have to navigate in a world where we already have, remember, a highly evolved payment system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Pretty soon everybody will be able to, to do what people do in other parts of the world, which is just use their phone to make immediately available payments all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what would be the role of a central bank digital currency in that kind of an environment?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Far more important to get it right than it is to do it fast or feel that we need to rush to reach conclusions because other countries are moving ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, that-what the China-the currency that's being used in China is not one that would-that would work here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's one that really allows the government to see every payment that's used-for which it is used in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's much more to do with things that are happening within their own financial system than it is, I think, to do with, with the global-you know, sort of global competition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation expectations before the pandemic hit-and here we think of survey, market based-survey being either households or, or economists and, and market based.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You look at all of those, and I would say that they were at the low end of what would have been consistent with a 2 percent inflation target, particularly our 2 percent inflation target, which calls for 2 percent average inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation expectations actually went down a bit at the beginning of the pandemic, and now they've just moved back up to levels broadly-that, that are where they were in 2018, or in some cases 2014, and, I would say, more consistent with our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we want them to be-we want them to be higher and-you know, on a persistent basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want inflation to run a little bit higher than it has been running for the last quarter of a century.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want it to average 2 percent, not 1. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And for that, we need to see inflation expectations that are consistent with that, really well anchored at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't really see that yet, but I would say that, that, you know, breakevens have moved up, in a way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Breakevens are based on CPI, of course, but they're, they're now at levels that are-that are pretty close to mandate consistent, whereas before, they were below.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We monitor inflation expectations very, very carefully, as you would obviously know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're, we're-inflation measures are always going to be a bit volatile.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We expect-as I mentioned, we expect core and, and headline PCE to move up because of base effects, and-you know, I-and we expect that to go away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we also expect these, these bottleneck effects to come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we think they'll-you know, it's a matter of, of when they will pass through, not whether they will pass through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we can't be confident about the exact timing of that or the size of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They don't seem especially large at the moment, but, you know, we, we don't know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, you know, this is-this is all about the reopening of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had it-we were in a deep, deep hole a year ago, and now, with a lot of help from fiscal policy, some additional help from monetary policy, and, you know, a great deal of help from vaccination, we're seeing a strong rebound in activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what's happening is, it's, it's-demand can be spurred with fiscal transfers and-the saved-up fiscal transfers and, and people going back to work and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The supply side will take a little bit of time to adapt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The supply of various inputs into the goods part of the economy will have to be brought back up to speed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That'll happen over a period of time, over coming quarters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You'll see some of the bottlenecks resolved, but the last one may not be resolved for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at-financial stability for us is really-we have a broad framework, so we don't just jump from one thing to another.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I know many people just look at asset prices, and they look at some of the things that are going on in the-in the equity markets, which, which I think do reflect froth in the equity markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But really, it-really, we try to stick to a framework for financial stability so we can-so we can talk about it the same way each time and so we can be held accountable for it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So one of the areas is asset prices, and I would say some of the asset prices are high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You are seeing, seeing things in the capital markets that, that are-that are a bit frothy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I won't say it has nothing to do with monetary policy, but it also-it has a tremendous amount to do with vaccination and reopening of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's really what has been moving markets a lot in the last few months is this turn away from what was a pretty dark winter to now a fast-a much faster vaccination process and a faster reopening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other-the other things, though-you know, leverage in the financial system, is it- is, is not a problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Leverage in the financial system is, is not an issue; we have very well capitalized large banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have funding risks for, for our largest financial institutions that are also very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do have some funding risk issues around money market funds, but I would say they're not systemic right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and the household sector is actually in pretty good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was in-it was in a very good shape as a relative matter before the financial crisis-sorry, the pandemic crisis hit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There were real concerns, of course, with high levels of unemployment and loss of wages and all of that, that the-that the household sector would, would, would weaken dramatically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, with the fiscal transfers, money that's on household balance sheets, they're in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see relatively low defaults and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the overall financial stability picture is mixed, but, on balance, it's-you know, it's manageable, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-by the way, I think it's appropriate and important for financial conditions to remain accommodative to support economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, 8½ million people who had jobs in February don't have them now, and, you know, there's a long way to go until we reach our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the federal funds rate has been well within target and-at target range, and money market funds-money market conditions are, are fine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have the ability to use our administrative tools to make sure that that remains the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do expect further downward pressure on, on rates through asset purchases and also the runoff in the-in the Treasury General Account.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, at this point, we didn't see a need for-to, to deploy our tools to, to support rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, we will do so if, if the need does arise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think capital requirements for banks are, to me-went up tremendously, really, over the course of the 10 years between the financial crisis and the arrival of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the banks really made it through a real stress test very well and passed three, three of our-two of our stress tests, and that is another one that's pending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So capital is, is in a good place, as far as I'm concerned, in the banking system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, to your point, what we saw was-so what, what kind of happened during the pandemic crisis that, that requires attention, and number one is money market funds and corporate bond funds where we saw run dynamics again, and we need to-we're, we're looking at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're looking at ways, and people around the world are looking at ways, to make those vehicles resilient so that they don't have to be, you know, supported by the government whenever there's, you know, severely stressed market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They, they need to have the wherewithal to stay in business and not just count on the Fed and others to-around the world to come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Dealers are committing less capital to that activity now than they were 10 or 15 years ago, and the need for capital is higher because there's so much more supply of Treasuries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so there are some questions about Treasury market structure, and there's a lot of careful work going on to understand whether there's something we can do about this, because we-you know, the U.S. Treasury market is probably the most single important-single most important market in, in the economy and the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It needs to function well for the good of our economy and the good of our citizens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not clear what, what-where that takes you, but we, we are taking a careful look-and the Treasury Department is, is really going to be leading this-at, at Treasury market structure and all of the various aspects of that to make sure that we do have a resilient, strong Treasury market that can work even in difficult times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As, as you know, at the very beginning of the financial-of the-of this recent crisis, there was such a demand for selling Treasuries, including by foreign central banks, that, really, the dealers couldn't handle the volume.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so what was happening was, the market was really starting to lose function, and that's-that was a really serious problem which we had to solve through really massive asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so we'd like to, we'd like to see if there isn't something we can do to-is-do we need to build against that kind of an extreme tail risk, and if so, what would that look like?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When will the economy be, be able to stand on its own feet?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not sure if-I'm not sure what the exact nature of that question is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have-you know, we've articulated our test for that, as you know, and that is just, we'll continue asset purchases at this pace until we see substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're, we're going to communicate well in advance of any decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to let, you know, the, the public know that that's what we're thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and so there'll be a lot of warning and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't have any, any external, virus- related specific requirement, although, again, I do think it'll-you know, the, the virus will need to continue to be controlled for us to achieve those economic goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we don't, we don't weigh in on specific fiscal bills or proposals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, basically, fiscal policy is the province of people who stand for democratic election and win, and they get to make those very difficult decisions, and they get to be accountable to the voters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't do any of that, and we don't have a seat at that table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's really something for Congress and the Administration to, to deal with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I mean, we're-we started buying MBS because the mortgage-backed security market was, was really experiencing severe dysfunction, and we've sort of, sort of articulated, you know, what our exit path is from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not meant to provide direct assistance to, to the housing market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was really just to keep that as-it's a very close relation to the Treasury market and a very important market on its own.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's, that's why we, we bought as we did during the Global Financial Crisis; we bought MBS too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, not, not an intention to send help to the housing market, which was, which was really not, not a problem this time at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and, you know, it's, it's a situation where we will, we will taper asset purchases when the time comes to do that, and those, those purchases will come to zero over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we articulated the "substantial further progress" test at our December meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, really, for the next couple of months, we made relatively little progress toward our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, remember, substantial further progress from December-from our December meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're hopeful that we will see along this path a way to that goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we believe we will; it just is a question of when.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, when that time-when the time comes for us to talk about talking about it, we'll do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're going to act on actual data, not on our forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're just going to need to see more data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if someone has the volume, they can turn it up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think the effect is proportional to the amount we buy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we have tried to create accommodative financial conditions to support economic activity, and we did that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we articulated the-you know, the, the tests for withdrawing that accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think, you know-so we're waiting to see those tests to be fulfilled both for asset purchases and for liftoff of rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, when the tests are fulfilled, we'll, we'll go ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did it in, in the last-after the last crisis, and, you know, we'll do it in, in maybe-we'll do it-as those tests are satisfied, we'll do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the-and the only thing that will guide us is, are the tests met?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, that, that's what we focused on: Is-have, have the macroeconomic conditions that we've articulated, have they been realized?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That will be the test for, for tapering asset purchases and for raising interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say, if you look at the labor market and you look at the demand for workers and the level of job creation and think ahead, I think it's clear, and I am confident, that we are on a path to a very strong labor market-a labor market that, that shows low unemployment, high participation, rising wages for people across the spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think that's, that's shown in our projections, it's shown in outside projections.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look through the current time frame and think one and two years out, we're going to be looking at a very, very strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of exactly what that means, we'll, we'll have to see how things evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we learned during the course of the last very long expansion, the longest in our history, that labor supply during a long expansion can exceed expectations, can move above its estimated trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and I have no reason to think that that won't happen again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we have seen-in terms of participation, we've seen a significant number of, of people retire.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we, we don't actually know exactly what labor force participation will be as we go forward, but I, I would tend to, to look at it and think that it-that it can return to high levels, although it may take some time to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But overall, this is-this is going to be, you know, a very strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the near term, you ask as well-so we see a couple of things, a few things that seem likely to be holding back labor supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are very large amounts of job openings, and there are a very large number of people who, who are unemployed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the pace of, of filling those jobs is-somehow feels slower than it might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'd point to a number of things, the first of which is just that most of the, the act of sort of going back to one's old job-that's kind of already happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is a question of people finding a new job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There may be something of a speed limit on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got to find a job where, where your skills match what, you know, what, what the employer wants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's just a lot that goes into the function of finding a job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, I would say that we, we look at, for example, a, a significant number of people still say that they're concerned about going back to work in jobs where there's a lot of public facing because of-because of COVID.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's clearly holding back some people, and that should diminish as vaccinations move ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as schools reopen and, and, and childcare/daycare centers open in the fall-in the fall, then we should see-we should see that supporting labor force participation by caretakers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Finally, unemployment insurance for something like 15 million people will either end or be diminished as we move through the summer and into, into, into the fall by the end of September, and I'd like some-that may also encourage some to go back in and take jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you would think that that would add to an increase in job creation as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you put all those together, I would expect that we would see strong job creation building up over the summer and going into-going into the fall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will also say, though, the last thing I'll say is, this is an extraordinarily unusual time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we, we really don't have a template or, or, you know, any experience of, of a situation like this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think we have to be humble about our ability to understand the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not a time to try to reach hard conclusions about the labor market, about inflation, about the path of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think, though, that we'll, we'll, we'll be seeing some things coming up in coming months that will-that will inform our, our thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So inflation has come in above expectations over the last few months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look behind the headline numbers, you'll see that the incoming data are, are consistent with the view that prices-that prices that are driving that higher inflation are from categories that are being directly affected by the recovery from the pandemic and the reopening of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, for example, the experience with, with lumber prices is, is illustrative of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The thought is that prices like that that have moved up really quickly because of the shortages and bottlenecks and the like, they should stop going up, and at some point, they, they, in some cases, should actually go down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we did see that in the case of lumber.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Another example where we haven't seen that yet is prices for used cars, which accounted for more than a third of the total increase in core inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Used car prices are going up because of sort of a perfect storm of very strong demand and limited supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do think that it makes sense that that would stop, and that in fact it would reverse over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That narrative seems, still seems quite likely to prove correct, although, you know, as I pointed out at the last press conference, the, the timing of that is, is pretty uncertain, and so are the, the effects in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But over time, it seems likely that these very specific things that are driving up inflation will be-will be temporary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be, you know, we're going to be looking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll, I'll also say that the labor market is going to be important, both for the maximum- employment goal, but also for inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and as I-as I mentioned, we expect and I expect that we'll see increases in supply over coming months as the factors that we believe have been suppressing supply abate, wane, move down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I can't give you an exact number or an exact time, but I would say that we do expect inflation to move down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the-if you look at the forecast for 2021 and-sorry, 2022 and 2023 among my colleagues on the, on the Federal Open Market Committee, you will see that people do expect inflation to move down meaningfully toward our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the full range of, of, of inflation projections for 2023 falls between 2 and 2. percent, which is consistent with our-with our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I expect that we'll be able to say more about timing as we see more data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Basically, there's not a lot of more light I can-I can shed on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you can think of this meeting that we had as the "talking about talking about" meeting, if you like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I now suggest that we retire that term, which has-which has served its purpose well, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So Committee participants were of the view that since we adopted that guidance in December, the economy has clearly made progress, although we are still a ways from our goal of substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And assuming that is the case, it will be appropriate to consider announcing a plan for reducing our asset purchases at a future meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So at coming meetings, the Committee will continue to assess the economy's progress toward our goals, and we'll give advance notice before announcing any decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The timing, of course, Ylan, will depend on the pace of that progress and not on any calendar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we do tend to look at the longer-term inflation expectations, because that's really, we think, what matters for, for inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So and, and, you know, the shorter-term ones do tend to move around based on, for example, gasoline prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you'll see if gasoline prices were to spike, you'll see the shorter-term inflation expectation measures, particularly the surveys, move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and that's, that's maybe not a good signal for future inflation if, if gas happens to spike and then go back down again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-yes, I think if, if you look at the broad range of longer-term inflation expectations, they've moved up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They moved down during the beginning of the pandemic, you know, sort of further exacerbating concerns that we might find ourselves where, for example, the ECB and the Bank of Japan have been, where you have expectations and inflation itself sliding down and you have a really hard time stopping that process once it begins.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it's good, actually, to see inflation-longer-term inflation expectations move back up to a range-it's a range that's consistent with what our objectives are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are not precise measures, and that's-and they, they contain risk premiums of various kinds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why we look at a broad range of them and tend to look at the movement of that broad range of, of, of indicators, which are from, you know, surveys of economists, surveys of the public, and also market based.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's, it's a wide index, as I'm sure you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at that, and we see them back in the range where they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, they've been broadly higher than that, somewhat modestly higher than that, not so many years ago, at a time when inflation was, was, was still anchored at around 2 percent or maybe even a little bit below.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the answer is, yes, I think they are anchored and they're at a good place right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's gratifying to see them having moved up off of their pandemic lows.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, as you know, it's, it's fundamental in our framework, our new framework, to, to assure that inflation-longer-term inflation expectations are anchored at a place that is consistent with our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, if inflation expectations are not anchored at a place that's consistent with your goal, it's not clear why you would expect to hit your goal over the longer term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On your first question, the judgment of when we have arrived at substantial further progress is one that the Committee will make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it would not be appropriate for me to lay out particular numbers that do or do not-that do or do not qualify.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is-that is, you know, the process that we're beginning now at the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will begin, meeting by meeting, to, to assess that progress and talk about what we-what we think we're seeing and, and just do all of the things that you do to sort of clarify your thinking around the process of deciding whether and how to adjust the pace and composition of asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the, the, the two hikes-so let me say a couple things first of all, not for the first time, about the-about the dot plot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we did not actually have a discussion of whether liftoff is appropriate at any particular year, because discussing liftoff now would be- would be highly premature, wouldn't make any sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
