text: If you look at the transcripts from five years ago, you'll see that sometimes people mention their rate path in their interventions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the last thing to say is, the dots are not a great forecaster of, of future rate moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's not because-it's just because it's so highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so dots to be taken with a-with a big, big grain of salt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: However, so let me talk about this, this, this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Committee spelled out, as you know, in our FOMC statements the conditions that it expects to see before an adjustment in the target range is made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, it's labor market conditions consistent with maximum employment, inflation at 2 percent and on track to exceed 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the projections, it gives some sense of how participants see the economy evolving in their most likely case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, honestly, the main message I would take away from the SEP is that participants-many, many participants are more comfortable that the economic conditions in the Committee's forward guidance will be met somewhat sooner than previously anticipated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If such outcomes materialize, it means the economy will have made faster progress toward our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the other thing I'll say is, rate increases are really not at all the focus of the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The focus of the Committee is the current state of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in terms of our tools, it's about asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The conditions for liftoff-we're very far from maximum employment, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the near-term thing is really-the real near-term discussion, discussion that will begin is really about the, the path of asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, we had a discussion about that today and expect to, in future meetings, continue to think about our progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our intention for this process is that it will be orderly, methodical, and transparent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I can just tell you, we, we, we see real value in communicating well in advance what our thinking is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, we'll, we'll give advance notice before announcing a decision to taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so all I can say is that we, we think it's important-we think where the balance sheet's concerned, a lot of notice, as much transparency as we can give, and as far-as far in advance as we can to give people a chance to adjust their expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we expect to be in that business until we reach substantial further progress and then have a-have a decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're a ways away from substantial further progress, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you can't say generally how far in advance you would signal?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, as we-as we approach that goal, we'll provide, you know, as much clarity as we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so as part of our year-and-a-half-long process, the review that we did and came out with at the end of that with the-with the new Statement on Longer- Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, we looked carefully at the idea.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've all read all the literature around different formulas for makeup and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we concluded-and, you know, I strongly agree-that it's not wise to, to wed yourself to a particular formulation of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we did adopt a discretionary-there's an element of discretion in it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it says that we will seek to-seek inflation that runs moderately above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's, it's meant to create a broad sense that we want inflation to average 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that under the old-under the old formula, under the old framework, what was happening was, 2 percent was a ceiling because all of the errors were below.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you were bouncing back and forth between 1½ and 2, and we wanted them to be centered around 2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were clear on that when we announced the framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on the-on the facility, we think it's doing its job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it's doing-the reverse repo facility is, is doing what it's supposed to do, which is to provide a floor under money market rates and keep the federal funds rate well within its-well within its range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's doing-you have an unusual situation where the Treasury General Account is, is shrinking and bill supply is shrinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so there's, there's downward pressure-we're buying assets-there's downward pressure on short-term rates, and that facility is, is doing what we think it's supposed to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's designed to keep the federal funds rate, you know, within the range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think it could have some effect on, on broader money market conditions below as it relates to, you know, the very low rates and the downward pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the funny thing, you would think that it would, but we'll have to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's possible that that would not be the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As, as you well know, there isn't one indicator we can look to, and there's no one number that we can therefore point to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at a range of indicators, and it's a very broad range, you can count to a high number just quickly-but, but, certainly, it will include things like unemployment and participation and wages and many different flavors of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're all going to be informed by what we saw in the last cycle, which was labor supply outperforming expectations over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, that hadn't happened in many other cycles, but this was a very long cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to have to be alert to see whether that can happen again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we have had a slew of retirements, and that may weigh on participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, that effect, though, should wear off in a few years and, and, you know, as you move through that window, because they would have-people would have retired anyway, and you'll be back where you, you would have been.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we're-I think that lesson number one is, is just to be careful about assessing maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if you-during the last cycle, there were-there were waves of concern that we were reaching full employment as early, you know, as, as 2012, when I arrived at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know-you know, nine years later- eight years later, we were still creating jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we understand this is a different economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the demographics are, people are getting older, and that should have a secular effect of, of reducing participation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have to be sensible about what, what can be done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think we're going to be-we're going to lean into that and be optimistic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's sort of a natural thing to be seeing in a strong economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we're seeing is-we don't see anything that's troubling in the sense of-what would be troubling would be, you know, very wide across the economy, wages at unsustainable levels without high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other words, wages in excess of productivity and inflation, you know, by a meaningful amount broadly across the economy, sort of forcing companies to keep raising prices and getting into a wage-price cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's the old formula for-one of the old formulas for having high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see them for, for people who are mostly new, you know, entering into new jobs, many of them in low-skilled jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, but we, we do think-you've got to-you've got to think in the labor market right now, where, where supply and demand are just not matched up well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we think it's a flexible economy and, and it will clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There will-there will be a level at which supply and demand meet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that'll-we think that'll, that'll be happening in coming months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but the last thing I'll say is, again, if you look at, at the forecasts, we are going to be in a very strong labor market pretty quickly here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're not going to forget about them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going-we're going to do everything we can to get people back into work and give them the chance to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's every reason to think that we'll be in a-in a labor market with very attractive numbers, with low unemployment, high participation, and rising wages across the spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's a little bit how we're looking at the-at the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't have anything to share with you in terms of the particulars or the timing right now, unfortunately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we've, we've always-our position has been for a long time and, and it is now that we'd, we'd like the leverage ratio to be a backstop to risk-based capital requirements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When leverage requirements are, are, are binding, it does skew incentives for firms to substitute lower-risk assets for high-risk ones.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And because of the substantial increase in reserves, Treasuries, and other safe assets in the banking system, the SLR is rapidly ceasing to become- ceasing to be the intended backstop for big firms that we want it to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do think it's appropriate to consider ways to adapt it to this new high-reserves environment, and, and we're looking hard at the issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would also, just to be really clear, we will take whatever actions are necessary to assure that any changes we do make or recommend do not erode the overall strength of bank capital requirements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, that is really not the problem we're having right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But- and, actually, people who work in commodity industries are very focused on that, because they know that, you know, they don't want to build, build capacity and then find out that it's not necessary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, really, the problem now is, is that demand is very, very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Incomes are high, people have money in their bank accounts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Demand for goods is extremely high, and it hasn't- it hasn't come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so you're seeing prices are moving back up off their lows there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in terms of, of overcorrecting, I mean, I think there, there is a possibility on the other side of this that, that inflation could be-could actually be quite low going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's not-that's not really where our focus is right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our focus right now is, we need to-our, our expectation is that these, these high inflation readings that we're seeing now will start to abate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it'll be like the lumber experience, and like we expect the used car experience to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With things like airplane tickets and hotels, which are the other two factors in the most recent CPI report that went up a lot, we expect that those prices will get back up to where they were, but there's no reason to think that they're going to keep going up a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no reason for supply and demand to be out of whack in the hotel business over any period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think in terms of the timing and the effects on inflation in the near term, there's a lot of uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The overall story is one that, that we think is right, and we think the incoming data support it and, you know, so do many, many forecasters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look at the forecasts on the FOMC, you will-you will see that as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we don't-we don't in any way dismiss the chance that it can work out that, that this goes on longer than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the risk would be that over time, it does begin to affect inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we see inflation expectations and inflation-or inflation moving up in a way that is really materially above what we-what we would see as consistent with our goals, and persistently so, we wouldn't hesitate to use our tools to address that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Price stability is half of our mandate, and we would certainly do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and in that we're joined by many other forecasters, but there's a lot to be humble about among forecasters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're, we're very much attuned to the risks and, and watching the data carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, I would say, you know, we should-as I mentioned earlier, there's so much uncertainty around this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's just a unique situation that we need to see how things evolve in coming months and, and see how that story holds up and act accordingly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you've seen with the pandemic is sharply declining cases, hospitalizations, and deaths.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, you, you also saw in the United Kingdom, which has, I think, at least as high if not higher vaccination rates, they've had an outbreak of the Delta variety.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-and it's causing them to have to-to have to react to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're not-you're not out of the woods at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it would be premature to-in my thinking, it would be premature to declare victory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Vaccination still has a ways to go to get to levels-it would be good to see it get to a substantially higher level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, look, I-but you're right, the statement language is evolving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you can expect us to drag our feet a little bit on that, because that's what you do with statement language.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say it is so great to see the reopening of the economy, though, and to see people out living their lives again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it appears to be safe, and I just would encourage people to continue to get vaccinated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think, clearly, since March what's happened is, people have grown more confident in these very strong outcomes, that they'll be achieved.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've also seen-we have seen inflation above target, though, and I think even though, you know, in, in our forecasters' case, they do see inflation coming back down over '22 and '23 into, into areas that are very consistent with our-with our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, the risk is, is something that can factor into people's thinking about appropriate monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The thing is, you know, these are 18 different forecasts, and I can't stand here and say exactly what was in all 18 people's minds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that, that is something that I think can factor into things as well-factor into our forecast as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we're seeing in the near term-again, our base case is that what we're seeing in the near term is, is principally associated with, with the reopening of the economy and not with a tight labor market or tight resource constraints, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When, when you get to-in, in the forecast, all of that, you know, supply and demand sides of the economy adapt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have a very highly adaptive, you know, flexible economy, more so than most.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And by 2023, those increases are really about, about, you know, rising resource utilization or, to put it a different way, you know, low unemployment, or high employment is a way to think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's about the kind of broad inflationary pressure that results from, you know, a really strong expansion tightening up resource utilization across the whole economy and lifting, lifting up inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why-that's why you would see it then, because by then, you know, in the forecast-and it's just a forecast, they're just individual forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, I think-there may be an element of the latter as well, because inflation expectations have continued to move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's all in people's individual thinking, and you can't-it's hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something the Committee debates in terms of, you know, what, what the outlook is for 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm, I'm a little bit speculating, which I shouldn't do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it wouldn't surprise me if there's an element for some people in, you know, seeing the inflation performance that we've had and thinking that I have more confidence that we could see inflation above 2 percent, that it may not be as hard to do that as we thought, and that inflation expectations may move up to a-to a level-they were-they were really at a level that was kind of a little below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They might move up as a consequence of this or, or, or as a consequence of, of, of the new framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we did see inflation expectations moving up in the-in the wake of the announcement of the framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, ultimately, I think it's consistent with both those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking at an economy that will not have the degree of, of fiscal support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The fiscal support in the forecast is much less than it was this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but you've, you've still got a very strong growth, well above the longer-run potential output of the- of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got-you've got growth meaningfully above that, and inflation is lower next year in all of our-in all of our forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the range of, of core PCE forecast for next year is 1. to 2. in 2022 and, and 2 to 2. in 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right, you're seeing-I, I can't remember the number, but it might be in the 3s-3, 3½ percent growth for next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's a really good year-coming on the back of a 7 percent growth year, that's a really good year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That'll see-you know, that'll cause significant job creation and, and it will-I mean, we would take 3½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't have a 3½ percent growth year-we didn't have a 3 percent growth year between the Global Financial Crisis and the end of the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, the economy's not, not decel-the economy is still growing, and growing at a, at a very healthy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our estimate-I mean, different people have different estimates-but, broadly speaking, economists think the economy has the potential to grow at around 2 percent per year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you're growing above that, then the unemployment rate should be declining, people should be being pulled into the labor force, wages should be going up, lots of things should be happening, businesses should be investing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I guess to answer your question a different way, is there a risk that inflation will be higher than we think?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I said earlier, you know, we, we don't have any certainty about the timing or the extent of these effects from reopening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And therefore we don't-we don't think that-we think it's unlikely that they would materially affect the underlying inflation dynamics that the economy has had for a quarter of a century.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The underlying forces around the globe that have created those dynamics are intact, and those are aging population, low productivity, globalization, all of those things that, that we think have, have, you know, really held down inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, when we get through this, we may well-we'll be facing those same forces.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, is there a risk that inflation will remain higher than we-than we thought?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if, if we see inflation moving above our goals in, in a time-sorry, to an extent, to a level or, or persistently-or persistently enough, you know, we would be prepared to use our tools to address that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A higher neutral rate would mean that interest rates would run higher by that amount.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and that would be a good thing from the standpoint of the economy, because it would give the Fed more room to cut rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The problem with, with interest rates being close to the lower bound, of course, is that it really cuts into our ability to react to a downturn-for example, a pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look, for example, at the European Central Bank, their, their policy rate was well below zero when, when the pandemic hit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't want to be in a place where we can't react.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A higher neutral rate would, would be-from that narrow standpoint, would be a good thing for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would give us more room and, therefore, then, that would tend to result in better outcomes for the economy over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, it's-you can't estimate it with great-with great precision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we would be alert to-I mean, studying r* is a-is a whole industry unto itself.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think we would be alert to factors that might raise r*, the neutral rate of interest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we, we try to keep up with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we're, we're, we're all thinking about that and the possibility of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, there are many-there are a lot of stories right now that could-that essentially could lead to higher productivity growth and higher r*.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know which of those stories will come true.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just there are-there are a lot of start-ups, a lot of early-stage companies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say, first, I think people misinterpret the framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the-there's nothing wrong with the framework, and there's nothing in the framework that would in any way, you know, interfere with our ability to pursue our, our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of our discussions and all of our thinking and planning are taking place in the context of our new framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're strongly committed to it, we think it's well suited to our goals, including in this-in this unique time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if you look at the-look at the forecasts that we've written down, you know, our Committee is solidly behind them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, your specific question, I guess, was, will we be behind the curve?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that's, that's not the situation we're facing at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The situation that we, we addressed in our-in our Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy was a situation in which employment was at very high levels, but inflation was low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we said was, we wouldn't raise interest rates just because unemployment was low and employment was high if there was no evidence of inflation or other troubling imbalances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the current situation, we have many millions of people who are unemployed, and we have inflation running well above our target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question we face with this inflation has nothing to do with our framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a very different, very difficult version of a standard investment-sorry, a central banking question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that is, how do you separate in inflation-how do you separate things that, that follow from broad upward price pressures from things that really are a function of, of sort of idiosyncratic factors in a particular-due to particular things?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, a classic example was, to pick a narrow example, was the cellphone price war back in 2017.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you remember, there was-prices were incredibly low, and it held down core PCE by three-tenths or something for a year, and then it fell out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, it's not-it's not easy to tell in real time which is which, but that's, that's the question you would face under, really, any framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've tried to, to explain that today about how we think about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we do think that these are temporary factors, and that they'll wane.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can't be absolutely certain about the timing of that, and we're prepared to use our tools as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Oh, you know, we will-we will taper when we feel that the economy has achieved substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will communicate very carefully in advance on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we're going to do, and, and we will follow through on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no-I mean, we will do what we can to avoid a market reaction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, when we achieve our macroeconomic goal, we will-we will taper as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-look, we have to balance the two-the two goals: maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Often they are-they do pull in the same direction, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But when we-when we raise interest rates to control inflation, there's no question that has an effect on activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's the channel-one of the channels through which we get to inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think that we're in a situation like that right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that the economy is recovering from a deep hole-an unusual hole, actually, because it's to do with, with shutting down the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It turns out it's a heck of a lot easier to create demand than it is to, you know, to bring supply back up to snuff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no reason to think that that process will last indefinitely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're going, you know, we're going to watch carefully to make sure that, that evolving inflation and our understanding of what's happening is, is, is right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, with maximum employment-unlike with, with price stability, where we can target a number of 2 percent on average-with maximum employment, there isn't a single number that we can target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That the- we monitor a broad range of, of, of data about different aspects of the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's unemployment, unemployment among different, different age groups, and such.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we look at all of it to try to arrive at a picture of what-of what is maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there isn't-I can't give you a, a, a set of numbers-for example, a numerical threshold like we used for a time back in 2012, I guess it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we said was substantial further progress toward our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we said was, we would keep, effectively, we'd-we would give advance warning as we-and, and, you know, more and more clarity-as, as we move forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'd say we have some ground to cover on, on the labor market side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're, we're some way away from, from having had substantial further progress with, with max-toward the maximum-employment goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So inflation is running well above our 2 percent objective and has been for a few months and is expected to run up certainly above our objective for a few months before we believe it'll, it'll move back down toward our objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question whether we've met that objective formally is really one for the Committee to make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's clear that, at this time, inflation is actually running above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, again, has been and will be, at least we expect it will, in coming months before returning down toward our target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you know, we're, we're in a process now where what we said is that as-at this meeting and in coming meetings, we're going to be continuing to assess the economy's progress toward our goals and give advance notice.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be-try to provide additional clarity about our thinking, both in the-in the postmeeting statement and in the minutes and in the public comments that people make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, our, our approach here has been to be as transparent as we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're not there, and we see our ways as having some-we see ourselves as having some ground to cover to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of-in terms of, of COVID and the Delta strain, I'll say a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, it will have significant health consequences for many.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we need to keep that in mind before we start-before we mention and move to the economic questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a-rising cases in, in a number of parts of the country, and some forecasts are for them to rise quite significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we've seen, though, is with successive waves of, of COVID over the past year and some months now, there has tended to be less economic-less in the way of economic implications from each wave.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will see whether that is the case with the Delta variety.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's, you know, it's a-it's certainly a-not an unreasonable expectation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it, it certainly is plausible if people would pull back from some activities because of the risk of infection.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We may just-we may see economic effects from some of that, or it might weigh on, on the return to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some people might choose-again, we, we don't have a strong sense of how that might work out, so we'll just be monitoring it-monitoring it carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, that would, again, be a question for the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would really say, the guidance that you're talking about is really the guidance to do with liftoff, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-what the guidance is for liftoff, we had to have labor market conditions consistent with full employment, inflation at 2 percent and on track to run-to run moderately above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're clearly a ways away from considering raising interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something that, that is on our radar screen right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so when we get to that question, when we start to get to the question of, of liftoff, which, which we are not at all at now or near now, that's when we'll ask that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is when that, that will become a real question for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For the first 15 seconds of your question, you froze.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's an-it's an important feature of this recovery is how uneven it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in many cases, that's related to the fact that some countries have had little in the way of access to, to vaccines.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so they're seeing significant outbreaks, and it's weighing on economic activity, whereas other countries-such as the United States, in particular-are having a very strong rebound.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and now Europe is having a stronger rebound as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One just is that, in general, economies-and through financial markets and through trade-are, are deeply interconnected now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so a stronger global economy will lead to more U.S. exports.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To the extent the global economy is weak and the United States is strong, it'll-we'll wind up, you know, we'll wind up exporting some of our demand through, through imports rather than having, having a lot of exports.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that is, as long as COVID is running loose out there, as long as there's time and space for the development of new strains, no one's really finally safe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These, these strains-there's no reason they just can't keep coming and one, you know, one more powerful than the next.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, as, as vaccinations rise, we can nonetheless get back to our economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, it, it is both the right thing to do and, and very much in our interest to make sure that vaccination happens broadly around the world, just for that reason.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look, again, if you look at the, the most recent inflation report, what you see is that it came in significantly higher than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But essentially all of the overshoot can be tied to a handful of categories.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It isn't the kind of inflation that's spread broadly across the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And each of those has a story attached to it that is-that is really about the reopening of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at that, and we think that those are temporary things because the, the supply side will respond.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have a very adaptive, adaptable, flexible economy and labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we think that inflation should move down over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, we don't have any-much confidence, let's say, in the timing of that or the size of the effects in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, in the near term, that the, the, the risks to inflation are probably to the upside.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I, I have some confidence in the-in the medium term, that inflation will move back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I, I will say, though, that, you know, we-inflation is half of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we were to see inflation moving up to levels persistently that were-that were above, significantly, materially above our goal and particularly if inflation expectations were to move up, we would use our tools to guide inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we won't have an extended period of, of high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that, that some of it will, will fall away naturally as the process of reopening the economy moves through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In any case, we will use our tools over time as appropriate to make sure that we do have inflation that averages 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so in terms of what's been happening in bond markets, I don't think there's a real consensus on, on what explains the moves between the last meeting and this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of it is a fall in real yields, which may have been connected to-some speculate-connected to sentiment around the, the spread of the Delta variant and concern about growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was also some decline in inflation compensation, which has significantly reversed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there, there are also so-called technical factors, which is where you put things that you can't quite explain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I, I don't see in any of that that there is really anything that challenges the credibility of our framework, if, if that's really your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are committed to achieving 2 percent average inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we said was that, in particular, when we see a very strong labor market, high levels of employment, low levels of unemployment, that won't be enough for us to raise interest rates until we see some inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, what we have today is kind of the opposite.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got, you know, 7 or 8 million people, fewer people, at work than were at work before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, you know, we're, we're a ways away from full maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we have high inflation, so it's kind of the opposite case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Any central bank has to deal with that by looking at the inflation and asking whether it is broad based and likely to be persistent and, and, and whether inflation expectations are implicated in a way that, that could cause them to rise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're monitoring that very carefully, and we're prepared to use our tools as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, I think our-I think our framework is pretty well understood.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and I think the real test of it will be down the road when it's time to think about raising interest rates and, and how we assess, assess that set of issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's a-there's a part in our Statement on Longer-Run Goals and, and Monetary Policy Strategy, which, Rich, I'm sure-I'm sure you're familiar with, which, which talks about that case in which the two goals are in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Most of the time, if you have high inflation, you also have high employment-they, they tend to go together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a situation where they're temporarily in different directions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not at full employment, but we are having high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We feel like we're going to be making good progress over the next-over the course of the next year, couple of years, really, toward maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the number of job openings compared to the number of unemployed, it's-we're, we're clearly on a path to a very strong labor market with high participation, low unemployment, high employment, wages moving up across the spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, that's, that's the path that we're on, and, and it shouldn't take that long in macroeconomic time to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's what I think is, is really the likely case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, it's not-it's not timely for us to be thinking about, about raising interest rates right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're doing is, we're, we're looking at our asset purchases and judging what is right for the economy and judging how we-how close we are to substantial further progress and then-and then tapering after that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question you asked about, would we raise rates if we hadn't finished cutting-hadn't finished the taper, hypothetical question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we'd, we'd face the circumstance at the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We could always just-you know, one thing one could do would be to just cut asset purchases all the way to zero if you wanted to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's, it's, it's just hard to-it's hard to answer what you would do without knowing a lot more about the situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ideally, you wouldn't be still buying assets and raising rates because, of course, you're adding accommodation by buying and, and removing accommodation by raising rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a-it's a really unusual situation to have-to have the ratio of vacancies to unemployed be this high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think there are a number of things at work there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Maybe the place to start is, is just to say that this is now not so much about people going back to their old jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there may be a bit of a speed limit on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There, there's research that suggests that there is a speed limit on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not like you can have millions of people at the beginning of the recovery going back in a single month because they're just going back to their old job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There may also be some factors that are-that are holding people back, and that's-this is what surveys say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are people who, who are reluctant to go back to work because they still feel exposed to COVID.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These could be jobs where, where there was a lot of, of interaction with the public and where perhaps there's a family member who's vulnerable or for whatever reason.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's also caretakers who are-where, where schools are not fully open and parents are at home or taking care of, of, of older people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's also been very generous unemployment benefits, which are now rolling off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They'll be-they'll be fully rolled off in a couple of months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we, we think we should see, because of that, we should see strong job creation moving forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, ultimately, it's unusual to see aspects like the job openings number in a context where there are that many unemployed people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That many job openings would typically suggest a tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, we hear from businesses all over the country that it's very hard to hire people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that may be because people, people are shopping carefully for their next job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I, I, I think the bottom line on this is, people want to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at where labor force participation can get, people will go back to work unless they retire.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, generally speaking, Americans want to work, and, and they'll find their way into the jobs that they want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you remember the, the summer wave last year of COVID, which was largely southern and western states, the economy just performed much better than anyone expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we were coming off the spring wave, where there were a lot of shutdowns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then this big second wave hit, and I think the natural thing to do is to expect that, that it would have a real impact on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People-what's happened is, first of all, many people are vaccinated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A lot of industries have, have kind of improvised their way around it-particularly, for example, buying a new home.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, that process of buying a new home very quickly moved to much more of a virtual process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so they were able to, you know, to, to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And other industries as well have gone to take-out and, you know, no-contact things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-so that can all-it seems like we've learned to, to handle this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, I think people would like to get back to, to, you know, the way things were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I, I hope to some extent, we will over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, of course, the big wave we had last winter did have significant employment effects, particularly in, you know, hospitality and leisure and other entertainment-other, other areas with a lot of direct contact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A lot of jobs were lost then because that was a very strong wave that happened in, in, in the winter months last year, just before the vaccines arrived.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So with Delta, we're just going to have to watch.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, with, with, with a reasonably high percentage of the country vaccinated and the vaccine apparently being effective-we're not experts on this-but it, it seems like the-a good-a good going-in estimate would be that the effects will probably be less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There probably won't be significant lockdowns and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, those, those are not decisions for us or, or, or-nor is it something we're be- we'd be expert in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the, the, the channels, you know, I-this is-this is kind of speculation, but it's pretty-it just is that people, you could imagine school districts deciding to wait a month or two for the-for the-for the Delta wave to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not saying this'll happen, but that it's easy to imagine that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also easy to imagine that some people might say, you know what?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm just going to-I'm just going to wait a couple of months before going back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, if schools don't open, then caretakers have to stay home.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if people don't go back into the labor force, then the job growth won't be as strong, those kinds of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't-it doesn't-it doesn't-again, sitting here today, not being able to really know the future-it doesn't seem as though the effects will be very large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they-it may be that the effect is to slow the economy down just for a period of months-or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are many parts of the country where it might not have an effect, and we're just going to have to, to see what the economic effects are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The concept of "transitory" is really this: It is that the increases will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It means that the increases in prices will happen, so there will be inflation but that the process of inflation will stop so that-so that there won't be further-when, when we think of inflation, we really think of inflation going up year upon year upon year upon year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When you have inflation for 12 months or whatever it might be-I'm just taking an example; I'm not making an estimate-then, then you have a price increase, but you don't have an inflation process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so part of that just is that, if it doesn't affect longer-term inflation expectations, then it's very likely not to infect-to affect the process of inflation going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what, what I mean by "transitory" is just something that doesn't leave a permanent mark on the inflation process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, we don't mean-I don't mean that, that, that, that, you know, producers are going to take those price increases back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So to the extent people are, are, are implementing price increases because raw materials are going up or labor costs or something's going up, you know, the question, really, for inflation really is, does that mean they're going to go up the next year by the same amount?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're going to be in a process where inflation, the inflation process, gets going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and that happens because people's expectations about future inflation move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, we have to watch this very carefully because this is-you know, we have two mandates: maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Price stability, for us, means inflation averaging 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we've got to be very careful about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, but I, I, I think it's a good point that it's, it's a term-what it really means is temporary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But then you've got to understand that it doesn't mean that the-that the increases will be taken back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of them will be, but, but that's not really what it means.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of-so we're, we're working virtually here, and we'll be coming back down the road in a couple of months, starting to bring people back here at the Board of Governors in Washington.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're going to follow public health guidance and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We really haven't made the fundamental decisions about exactly what that will look like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it'll depend on, to some extent, on what-on what, you know, CDC guidance looks like when we actually do bring people back in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in any decisions about the timing, and I did not-if I-if I said we're looking at wanting a couple more months of data, I wasn't-I'm not meaning to suggest anything about a particular time at which we might taper, because we really have not made that decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All I'm saying is, is, we're not at substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a range of views on, on what timing will be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those views ultimately track, track back to people's views about the economy and, and what will happen as we make progress towards, towards our-towards our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I-we will, of course, as we-you know, we're going to continue to try to provide clarity as appropriate on, on timing, pace, and composition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, today, I've, I've given you what I can give you because, again, this, this was the first, really, I would say, deep dive on the issues of timing, pace, and composition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but no decisions are made, and, and I'm just not in a position to, to give you much guidance, really any guidance, on the actual timing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we expect that, if, if things go well, then we will-we will reach that goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when we reach it and the Committee is comfortable that we have reached it, then, then we'll taper at that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't, I really-there's nothing I can say about Jackson Hole.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I'm in-we're in the process of writing that speech.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I am going to give a speech, and-but I, I, I wouldn't want to-I wouldn't want to say what will be in there at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-asset purchases were just a key part of our response to the critical phase of the crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They, they really helped us restore market function to these key markets, really, on which-on which, which are very, very important to our economy and the global economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then they were a big part of, of creating accommodative financial conditions to support demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was that commitment to continue asset purchases that provided strong support for the economy and, and has been a part of the story for why the economy is so strong right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we said we would taper when we-when we achieve substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, we're going to honor that commitment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it's-and, and, again, we're talking about it right now and meeting by meeting and, and moving in that direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll provide more, you know, more clarity on that as we go, as is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think strong capital requirements are essential for banks, particularly for the largest banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that an undercapitalized banking system, as we've seen, can be a real threat to the economy and most-mostly, or to, to the greatest extent, to people at the lower end of the income spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look back at not this previous-not this crisis but the previous one, the bank-the banking system was undercapitalized.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So higher capital requirements are, are, you know, are, are really a good thing because they allow banks to weather downturns and continue to perform the functions that they perform.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's other tools that we have to-and the Fed has some of these tools, Congress has some of these tools, other agencies have some of these tools-to assure or support the wide availability of credit, particularly to low- and moderate-income communities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're working on a-on a new CRA proposal right now with the other banking agencies, and we think it's going to be-it's going to be good and will support the flow of credit to low- and moderate-income households.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also the anti-anti- lending discrimination statutes that we enforce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's some of the programs that Congress has in place to support the flow of credit to low- and moderate-income communities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Strong capital is what enables banks to continue to serve their communities, including low- and moderate-income communities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So with inflation, as I mentioned, we're, we look not just at the headline number, but we look at all the components that go into the calculation of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you do that, if you look under the hood, what you see is not that, widely, across the whole range of goods and services that, that are in the economy, we're seeing upward, upward pressure on prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're seeing is a handful of things that are really-that really account for the, the overshoot of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, new, used, and rental cars have moved up in price because of the car shortage because of the semiconductor shortage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And housing-sorry, hotels and air, air fares have moved back up, but that really just is retracing the very large downward movement in prices that they had before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's a big, big part of, of why the inflation readings are so high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those don't-those, frankly, don't carry significant implications in the long run for the-for inflation or for the American economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what I said was, we, we're going to see whether these things-we don't need to see everything do what lumber prices have done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at lumber prices, they went up and then they went down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we want to see is these other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If they flatten out, then their, their contribution to inflation becomes zero over time so that they're not contributing to inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, if we start to see those things happen fairly widely among the-among the things that have really moved up quickly, then we'll, we'll-they won't all happen at once or happen quickly-but we'll know that our basic understanding of the situation is broadly correct.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't think it will take, or what I said was, I don't think it'll take a very long time to see whether that's the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It, it, it is probably the case that, frankly, the, the overall reopening of the economy is going to play out over a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a historic, world historical event, that the global economy is now reopening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's going to be very uneven, as we discussed before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think we will-we will know, you know, when we know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I do think that, that, if we see those things happening, we'll know that we have the story basically right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a number of participants raised that-the questions around MBS and tapering at, at today's meeting, as a matter of fact, and yesterday's meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'll just say that, generally speaking, I don't think and-I don't think that-I think that Treasury and MBS purchases affect financial conditions in very similar ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There may be modest differences in terms of, of contribution to housing prices, but it's, it's not something that's big.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-it's-so where I think we are is, there, there really is little support for the idea of tapering MBS earlier than Treasuries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we will taper them at the same time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The idea of reducing MBS purchases at a somewhat faster pace than Treasuries does have some attraction for some people-others, not so much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it's something that we'll be continuing to discuss.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on the standing repo facility, what is it going to do?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it's set at 25 basis points, so out of the money, and it's, it's there to help address pressures in money market-money markets that could impede the effective implementation of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, really, it's, it's to support the function of-functioning of monetary policy and its, its effectiveness.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Your question on, on the, the [ON]RRP, so we think it's doing what it's supposed to do, what we expect of it to do, which is to help provide a floor for money market rates and help ensure that the federal funds, funds rate stays within the target range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's essentially, essentially, what's happening is that it just results in a lower aggregate amount of Federal Reserve liabilities that are in banks in the form of reserves and a higher amount of Federal Reserve liabilities in money market funds in the form of overnight RRP balances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we expect it to be high for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's being driven, of course, by, by the relatively lower quantity of Treasury bills and, and, and also the onset of the debt ceiling and the decline in the TGA, things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't- we don't have a problem with, with what it's doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, money markets, private money market funds are, are choosing to, to invest because the rates are attractive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At some point, the rates will not be so attractive as, as the whole rate cluster normalizes, and, and you'll see it shrink back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Look, we-as you know, we're targeting a moderate overshoot of 2 percent inflation for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we want inflation expectations to be centered on, on 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We feel like they may be a little bit below that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the bigger picture is that, you know, that, that, that would be a healthy thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That was the kind of inflation we were thinking about that comes from, you know, from a very, very strong labor market and a-and a booming economy maybe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, that was the kind of inflation-this, this is something different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is really driven by the supply side, which is not able to hand-to handle this big spike in demand that we're seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As the economy reopens with vaccination and fiscal support and monetary policy support, the supply side-just all over the world, you're seeing the same thing, which is, it just can't keep up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are labor shortages in, in a lot of places, the same sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, there's, there's absolutely no sense of panic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just-I've explained, I think, several times here today that the best-my, my best estimate is that this is something that will pass.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's really a shock to the economy that will pass through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, if you-if you look at where forecasters are-people who actually write down a forecast for a living-very, very strongly they see it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, we-but, you know, are-we're actually responsible for this, though, so we have to take seriously the risk, the risk case, which is that inflation will be more persistent, that it might actually move inflation expectations up, and that we might-that the kind of things that might require a response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, we have to be on the alert for it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people have to understand and believe that we will react if, if we need to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: My base case is that-is, as I've said repeatedly, is that inflation will move back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And no, we're not-we, we have not at all changed our view, and I haven't changed my view that inflation running above 2 percent, moderately above 2 percent, is a desirable thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's also not the kind of inflation we were looking for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-a lot of it is driven at relatively low-paid jobs in the service industries as people come back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we, we don't see-there, there is a form of wage inflation that can lead to price inflation, and we're not seeing that right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that really is if what we call "unit labor costs" move up and, and, and, which really puts-move up in a way that is-that is hard for companies to manage and puts them in a situation where they have to accept substantially lower margins or raise prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, when it happens gradually, when that-if you-we've seen in a long expansion, sometimes unit labor costs do move up and, and put some pressure on margins.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In a long expansion, that's been happening late in the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The problem is if it happens in a way that pushes firms broadly into raising prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is something that was a feature of the high inflationary era of the Great Inflation, but it's not a feature now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is one of the reasons why we're watching so carefully to see whether labor force-whether people do come back and accept jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Given the very large number of job openings and the very large number of unemployed people, we'd like to see, you know, those- some matching going on there so people get back to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think labor supply would be- would be a healthy thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, but wages moving up across the spectrum, consistent with inflation and productivity, is a-is a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the test for beginning our taper is that we've achieved substantial further progress toward our goals of [2 percent] inflation and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And for inflation, we appear to have achieved more than significant progress-substantial further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that part of the test is achieved, in my view and in the view of many others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at a good number of indicators, you will see that, since last December, when we articulated the test, and the readings today, in many cases more than half of the distance, for example, between the unemployment rate in December of 2020 and typical estimates of the natural rate-50 or 60 percent of that road has been traveled.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many on the Committee feel that the "substantial further progress" test for employment has been met.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Others feel that it's close, but they want to see a little more progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess my own view would be that the test-the "substantial further progress" test for employment is all but met.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, once we've met those two tests, once the Committee decides that they've met [them]-and that could come as soon as the next meeting; that's the purpose of that language, is to put notice out that that could come as soon as the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Committee will consider that test, and we'll also look at the broader environment at that time and make a decision whether to taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you can see, the inflation forecasts have moved up a bit in the outyears.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really, I think, a reflection of-and they've moved up significantly for this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, I think, a reflection of the fact that the bottlenecks and shortages that are being-that we're seeing in the economy have really not begun to abate in a meaningful way yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those seem to be going to be with us at least for a few more months and perhaps into next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that suggests that inflation's going to be higher this year, and a number-I guess the inflation rates for next year and 2023 were also marked up, but just by a couple of tenths.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're looking at 2. and 2.1, you know, two years and three years out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are very, very-I don't think that households are going to, you know, notice a couple of tenths of an overshoot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we want to foster a strong labor market, and we want to foster inflation averaging 2 percent over time, and I think we're very much on track to achieve those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the framework, I see this as very consistent with the framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want inflation expectations to be anchored at around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want, we're-that's really the ultimate test of whether we're getting this done under the framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we do want inflation to run moderately above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't put too much on a couple of tenths over 2 percent in 2023 and '24-one-tenth in '24.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say that there's very broad support on the Committee for this plan, both as to the timing and as to the pace of the taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this was a unanimous vote today, and I'd say quite broad support for this approach.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're correct that there are some who would prefer to have gone sooner, and they've made their arguments publicly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is an approach that the Committee will broadly support, and it will put us having completed our taper sometime around the middle of next year, which seems appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the asset purchases, as I mentioned, were very, very important at the-in the early stages of the crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They were essential in restoring market function in the Treasury and other markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then, as the recovery got going, they supported aggregate demand, as they will do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now we're in a situation where they still have a use, but it's time for us to begin to taper them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Their usefulness is much less as a tool than it was at the very beginning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, this leaves the whole question of rate increases ahead, which is really where the framework-the framework is all about how we deal with rate increases and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think this is the appropriate way to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so, again, substantial further progress toward our goals is the test for beginning the taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're going to be well away from satisfying the liftoff test when we begin the taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in terms of the liftoff test, though, you know, it's what we adopted last September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And while we have interesting signs that, in many ways, the labor market's very tight, we also have lots of slack in the labor market, and we think that those imbalances will sort themself out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation at 2 percent and on track to achieve it, moderately higher inflation over 2 percent-you know, that really depends on the path of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If inflation remains higher during the course of 2022, then we may already have met that test by the time we reach liftoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I just think, if you look at what people are writing down for year-end 2022 numbers, some people are writing down very low unemployment rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's only one indicator, but it suggests a very strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think they're writing down in good faith what they see as meeting the test.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a range of perspectives about where the economy will be, but- by the way, all but one participants have us lifting off during 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not really an unusually wide array of views about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, no, I was not aware of the specifics of what they were doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me just say a couple things about this subject.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We understand very well that the trust of the American people is essential for us to effectively carry out our mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why I directed the Fed to begin a comprehensive review of the ethics rules around permissible financial holdings and activity by Fed officials.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those rules are, in many respects, the same as those for government agencies, plus a number of things that apply specifically to us because of our business.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One of those is-sort of, three things I would point to in terms of specific restrictures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One is, ownership of certain assets is not allowed, and that's bank securities and other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Secondly, there are times when we're not allowed to trade at all or to, you know, buy and sell financial assets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's the period immediately before and during an FOMC meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So all of these-everyone's, you know, ownership and activities are all disclosed on an annual basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I would have had to go back and read people's financial disclosures to know what their activities have been.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This has been our framework for a long time, and I guess you'd say it's served us well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other thing you would say-that it is now clearly seen as not adequate to the task of really sustaining the public's trust in us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need to make changes, and we're going to do that as a consequence of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to gather all the facts and look at ways to further tighten our rules and standards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Don't have a timeline yet; we can start with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, well, let me address the muni question, since that's in there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I personally owned municipal securities for many, many years, and in 2019, I froze that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Meaning I-they're no-I'm holding all those securities, my wife and I, to maturity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And munis were always thought to be a pretty safe place for a Fed person to invest because, as you know, the lore was that the Fed would never buy municipal securities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so then comes the, you know, the COVID crisis, and I reversed that policy, and I did it without hesitating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason was that the financial markets, including the municipal financial market, were very much on the verge of collapse.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we also checked with the Office of Government Ethics and-who looked carefully at it and said that I didn't have a conflict.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's one answer that I wanted to share with you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Secondly, you're right, though, as-we're going to be looking at all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't want to get ahead of the process here and speculate about particular outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But this, again, comprehensive and deliberate process-we're going to make changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I want to be able to look back on this years from now and know that we rose to meet this challenge and handled the situation well, and that what we did made a lot of sense and protected the public's interest and the institution that we're all a part of.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, and, of course, for the most part, we don't.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it was a real coincidence; I happened to pre-own these munis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we started buying munis as part of the Municipal Liquidity Facility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it was really not a-it just was an unforeseen event.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I couldn't sell them, so what I did was, I just held them, checked with the ethics people, and went ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, but as a general principle, yeah, that makes a lot of sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you're right, we have a-really, I'll call it a unique situation where, by many measures, the labor market is tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And 11 million job openings, very widespread reports from employers all over the economy saying it's quite difficult to hire people, wages moving up, and that kind-so, quite a tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our view, I think- widespread view a few months ago was that several things were coming together in the fall, including kids back to school, which would, you know, which would lighten caregiving duties, including the expiration of unemployment-extra unemployment benefits, and other things would come together to provide an increase in labor supply, and so we'd get out of this strange world where there're lots of unemployed people and a high unemployment rate but a labor shortage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you had this very sharp spike in Delta cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, so that affects-for example, when schools are open 60 percent of the time or when they're always at a threat of being closed because of Delta, the Delta variant, you know, you might want to wait.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Rather than going ahead and taking a job and starting work only to have to quit it three weeks later, you're going to wait until you're confident of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Also, people didn't, you know-as you know, hiring and spending in these face-to-face service industries, travel and leisure, it just kind of stopped during those months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-so that-really, the big shortfall in labor, in jobs, was largely in travel and leisure, and that's because of-clearly because of Delta.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's still-it may just be that it's going to take more time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it still seems that, inexorably, people will-these are people who were largely working back in February of 2020.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They'll get back to work when it's time to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're right, though-it didn't happen with any force in September, and a lot of that was Delta.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the-you asked also about the test for November.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if the economy continues to progress broadly in line with expectations, then I think-and also the overall situation is appropriate for this, then I think we could easily move ahead at the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Or not, depending on whether we feel like that, those tests are met.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, for me, it wouldn't take a knockout, great, super strong employment report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would take a reasonably good employment report for me to feel like that test is met.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And others on the Committee-many on the Committee feel that the test is already met.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we'll work it out as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that, in my own thinking, the test is all but met.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't personally need to see a very strong employment report, but I'd like to see a good-a decent employment report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
