text: I mean, it's not, it's, again, it's not to be confused with the test for liftoff, which is so much higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So Dodd-Frank created this position, Vice Chair for Supervision, and it's, there's actually a specific assignment in the Dodd-Frank language, as I'm sure you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, effectively, what it means is that the Vice Chair for Supervision is charged with setting the regulatory agenda.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in the 10 years, almost, that I've been at the Fed, that person has really done that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Dan Tarullo certainly did it, and Vice Chair Quarles did it as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I respect that that's the person who will set the regulatory agenda going forward, and I would accept that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, furthermore, you know, it's fully appropriate to look at-for a new person to come in and look at the current state of regulation and supervision and suggest appropriate changes, and I welcome that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of Vice Chair Quarles's term, we're not currently in that situation, and I actually don't have any updates for you on that today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right, so the point of the broad and inclusive goal was not to target a particular unemployment rate for any particular group.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, we look at a broad range of-a very broad range of metrics when we think about what maximum employment is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And one of the things we look at is unemployment rates and participation rates and wages for different demographic and age groups and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you look back, what were we really thinking?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we all saw the benefits of a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the last two or three years of, before the pandemic hit, you saw-after a lot of long progress, you saw a really strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you saw wages at the low end moving up faster than everywhere else-something that's great to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also saw the lowest unemployment rates for minorities of various, you know, for African Americans, for example, and also participation rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, we also-there was no reason why it couldn't continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There were no imbalances in the economy, and then along came the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were not-there was nothing in the economy that looked like a buildup of imbalances that could cause a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I was very much thinking that the country would really benefit from a few more years of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would have been-so we're all quite eager to get back to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also said we wouldn't raise rates just in response to very low unemployment, in the absence of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that was another aspect of it, because we saw that that really benefited labor market participants in a broad and inclusive way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have significant slack in the economy and inflation well above target, not moderately above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It isn't really just targeting the headline numbers, but it's about taking all of those things into account in your thinking about what constitutes maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, you really-I mean, first of all, ideally, there wouldn't be any gap, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a persistent gap, and it's very hard to explain based on typical metrics.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just, it's quite troubling, but it really is-you know, we have, you know, famously broad and blunt tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think eliminating inequality and racial discrimination and racial disparities and that kind of thing is really something that fiscal policy and other policies-frankly, education policies and that kind of thing-are better at focusing on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we've identified the part that we can do, and we'll do that part.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I've always been clear that it's going to take policies broadly across society to work on these problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I missed the first few words, but I think I got your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's just very important that the debt ceiling be raised in a timely fashion so that the United States can pay its bills when and as they come due.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The failure to do that is something that could result in severe reactions, severe damage to the economy and to the financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's just not something that we could contemplate, that we should contemplate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going to comment on particular tactics or things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm just going to say that I think we can all agree that the United States shouldn't default on any of its obligations-should pay them when and as due.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, you know, no one should assume that the Fed or anyone else can protect the markets or the economy in the event of a failure-fully protect in the event of a failure to, you know, to make sure that we do pay those debts when they're due.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I don't generally ever talk about the conversations I have with elected officials or other appointed officials.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, look, you can see that this is a major focus among those who have responsibility for it, and-including elected people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, of course, very closely monitoring Wells Fargo's efforts to fix its widespread and pervasive problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They represent a serious matter to us, and the firm is required to remediate them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will take appropriate supervisory action if the firm fails to meet our expectation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We continue to hold the firm accountable for its deficiencies with an unprecedented asset cap that will stay in place until the firm has comprehensively fixed its problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're not going to remove that asset cap until that's done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So bottom line is, we'll take strong supervisory action if a firm is engaging in unsafe and unsound practices or violating laws.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I can't speak to our confidential supervisory assessments of any individual bank.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So these, I don't need to tell you, we file, people file these reports annually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think they were just quite recently filed for 2020.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't have any reason to think people at the Board would have known about particular trading that's going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They will see that-there are people at the Fed who see the, you know, see the trading reports when they're, you know, when they're annually filed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, in terms of having confidence and that sort of thing, I think no one is happy, no one on the FOMC is happy to be in this situation, to be having these questions raised.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is an important moment for the Fed, and I'm determined that we will rise to the moment and handle it in ways that will stand up over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm very reluctant to get ahead of the process and speculate, though, about different things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, when we have things to announce, we'll go ahead and do that, but that's really what I have for today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, the five-year review that we do under this unusual provision of law where all of the Reserve Bank presidents are reviewed for reappointment at the same time every five years, that is really a broad review about their leadership of the institution, their performance on the FOMC, all of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if there were a concern-a public concern or a private concern-about something that someone had done, we wouldn't wait for the five-year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're right, though, these-as I mentioned, we have had a framework for a long time, and it's similar to what other government agencies have, only it's a little stricter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it is that you can trade financial instruments, but not specific ones like bank debt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can't trade during the FOMC period and during the meeting-the blackout period and then during the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then you disclose all this, and we have disclosed it for years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So all of these things have been going-to the extent they've been going on, they've been a matter of public record.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know-but, nonetheless-so that-you know, it was seeming to work just okay.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now you look at it, and you see this, and you think, "We need to do better."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you're right, but it has not been part of the process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I wouldn't blame the people who conduct that review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I really think, if someone had raised concerns or if we'd had concerns, then it would have been, but it wouldn't have been part of that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would have been raised instantly, rather than once every five years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're looking for conditions consistent with maximum employment to lift off, and those conditions can change over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're not necessarily bound by a particular level of the unemployment rate or the participation rate or anything else like that, which can change over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But more to your point, really, we actually have a paragraph in our framework, and something like this has been there for a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you're talking about a situation in which the two goals are not complementary; they're somehow in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we judge that's effect-that is the case, what it says is, we take into account the employment shortfalls and inflation deviations and the potentially different time horizons over which employment and inflation are projected to return to levels judged consistent with the mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, we used to call that the balanced-approach paragraph because it had those words.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a very difficult situation for any central bank to be-pardon me-to be in a situation where the two goals are in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that paragraph tries to address it by saying we would sort of weigh the equities between the two.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: How long will it take, and how big are the gaps, and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't really think we're in that-we're sort of in that situation, I'd say, in a short-term way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we think, we do expect that this is sort of-because of the COVID shock and the reopening and all that, you're seeing this temporarily.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Corporate defaults are very low in the United States right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Corporate leverage built up over the course of the long expansion that ended with the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were very concerned in the last year or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were concerned in the last year or so, and then I'd say very concerned at the beginning of the pandemic that, if you've got a highly leveraged company and your revenue stops for an uncertain period, as things happened at the beginning of the crisis, we were very concerned that there would be a wave of defaults.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It didn't happen, potentially-I mean, to a significant extent because of the CARES Act and the response that we undertook and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was a, you know, a much stronger response than we've ever had.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think for whatever reason now, you have very, very low default rates now among corporate debt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the Evergrande situation seems very particular to China, which has very high debt for an emerging market economy, really the highest that any emerging market economy has had.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the government has been working to get that under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The government put new strictures in place for highly leveraged companies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And Evergrande is dealing with those strictures, and it's something they're managing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the implications for us, there isn't, there's not a lot of direct United States exposure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, you would worry that it would affect global financial conditions through confidence channels and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I wouldn't draw a parallel to the United States corporate sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the phrase goes: "I have nothing for you on that today."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: -I'm focused on doing my job every day for the American people, and I don't have any comment on that, Brian.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So my thinking on this has been: Let's get through the taper decision, and then let's turn to those issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are a number of related issues that-you mentioned one, Greg, but, you know, and-which you need to start to think about, and we'll do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I want to get, we want to get through this taper decision, and then turn to those issues, rather than start, you know, thinking about them now and having the minutes discuss them and get people thinking that we are, you know, focused on those issues, because we're really not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we do have the experience of what we did last time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we'll be able to get to sensible decisions fairly expeditiously when it's time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The New York Fed survey, let me talk about that specifically, and this is from the New York Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's only an eight-year-old survey, and it does seem as though the, they're looking three years out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it seems like there's a high correlation between three-year and one-year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For the most part, surveys are showing that households expect higher inflation in the near term but not in the longer term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there are many, many different inflation measures, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why we have this thing called the CIE, which is the, it's an index of-it's market-based measures, it's professional forecasters, and it's household surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you just put them all-it's not, you know, it doesn't have a lot of grand theory about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You put them all in, and you measure the change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you should be-and, also, you measure things like the dispersion and that sort of thing, so you can look at all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it tells a story of inflation expectations moving up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many of the different measures will also show inflation expectations moving back up to where they were in, say, 2013, which was before the really-the drop in inflation expectations broadly happened in '14 and '15-around then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we did see them moving up in a troubling way and running persistently above levels that are really consistent with our mandate, then, you know, we would certainly react to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see more of a moderate increase that is-the first part of which is welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And because, you know, inflation expectations had drifted down, and it was good to see them get back up a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we can always-we haven't decided to taper yet, and we haven't decided the pace yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, it's not my expectation that we would have to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can certainly speed up or slow down the taper if we-if it becomes appropriate, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, back in '13, when we tapered, we always said we weren't on a preset course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy's much farther along than it was when we tapered in 2013.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it makes sense to allow the runoff to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, but we certainly have the freedom to either speed it up or slow it down if that becomes appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You wouldn't, no, because, you know, when you're-as long as you're buying assets, you're adding accommodation, and it wouldn't make any sense to, you know, then lift off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, what you would do is, you'd speed up the taper, I think, if that were the situation you're in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not-we don't expect to be in that situation, but I do think it would be wiser at that point to go ahead and speed up the taper, just because the two are then working in the same direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think it's really important that the central bank maintain a stable currency and payment system for the public's benefit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also live in a time of transformational innovation around digital payments, and we need to make sure that the Fed is able to continue to deliver to the public a stable and trustworthy currency and payment system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's extensive private innovation, a lot of which is taking place outside the regulatory perimeter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But where the public's money is concerned, we need to make sure that appropriate regulatory protections are in place, and today they really are not in some cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So with that in mind and with the creation of myriad private currencies and currency-like products, we're working proactively to evaluate whether to issue a CBDC and, if so, in what form.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have two broad workstreams, one of which is really technology, both at the Board and in the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston's work with MIT-the other of which is to identify, scope out, deal with, analyze the various public policy issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you mentioned, we do intend to publish a discussion paper soon that will be the basis for a period of public engagement- engagement with many different groups, including elected officials, around these issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it's our obligation to do the work, both on technology and public policy, to form a basis for making an informed decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The ultimate test we'll apply when assessing a central bank digital currency and other digital innovations is: Are there clear and tangible benefits that outweigh any costs and risks?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also, as you know, investing heavily right now in building a new settlement system for instant payments in the U.S.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll be the first such major expansion of our core payment system since the 1970s.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We found the case for this quite compelling-for consumers, businesses, and just ensuring that all financial institutions have access to that payment system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, bottom line, we haven't made a decision about the CBDC, but we will be issuing a discussion paper soon in order to form the basis of this public interaction that we'll have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's important that we get to a place where we can make an informed decision about this and do so expeditiously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's more important to do this right than to do it fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we're in a good place to make that analysis and make that decision-by the way, which will be a governmentwide decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would do this, we would have to have a meeting of the minds with the Administration and also probably with Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would really like to have broad support for this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we would need that to go ahead, and that's the process we're engaged in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We try to focus on what we can control-and that is how to communicate as clearly as possible, in this highly uncertain world, how we're thinking about the economic outlook and the balance of risks and how policy will evolve in that case and also in the cases, which are frequent, where the economy evolves in unexpected ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the focus at this meeting is on tapering asset purchases, not on raising rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is time to taper, we think, because the economy has achieved substantial further progress toward our goals, measured from last December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think it's time yet to raise interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There is still ground to cover to reach maximum employment, both in terms of employment and in terms of participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Getting to your question, our baseline expectation is that supply bottlenecks and shortages will persist well into next year, and elevated inflation as well, and that, as the pandemic subsides, supply chain bottlenecks will abate-and job growth will move back up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as that happens, inflation will decline from today's elevated levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, certainly, we should see inflation moving down by the second or third quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The time for lifting rates and beginning to remove accommodation will depend on the path of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If a response is called for, we will not hesitate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what I will tell you is, we will be watching carefully to see whether the economy evolves in line with our expectations, and policy will adapt appropriately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at the progress that we've made over the course of the last year, if that pace were to continue, then the answer would be: "Yes, I do think that that is possible."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we measure maximum employment based on a wide range of figures, but it's certainly within the realm of possibility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in particular, I would point to the employment compensation index reading that we got last Friday.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, in real terms, they've been-they had been running a little bit below inflation, so real wages were not really increasing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, with the ECI reading, it becomes close to maybe not increasing, but close to back to zero in terms of the real increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So wages moving up, of course, is how standard of living increases over the years for generation upon generation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the concern is a somewhat unusual case where, if wages were to be rising persistently and materially above inflation and productivity gains, that could put upward pressure on, or downward pressure on margins and cause companies to-or employers, really-to raise prices as a result, and you can see yourself, find yourself in what we used to call a wage-price spiral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, if you look back, we-so we'll be watching this carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that, at this point, we don't see troubling increases in wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't expect those to emerge, but we'll be watching carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm not sure I totally got your first question, but I would say-in fact, could you just quickly, succinctly, say your first question again?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, so, you know, this isn't the traditional Phillips curve situation where there's a direct tradeoff, where that's really what we're talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The inflation that we're seeing is really not due to a tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's due to bottlenecks, and it's due to shortages, and it's due to very strong demand meeting those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's not the classical situation where you have that precise tradeoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, in this situation, we do have a provision in our Statement on Longer-Run Goals, as you know, that says when those two things are in tension, what we do is, we take into account the employment shortfalls and inflation deviations and the potentially different time horizons over which employment and inflation are projected to return to levels judged consistent with the mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we used to call that the "balanced approach" paragraph.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to think about the amount of the deviation, we have to think about the time it will take, and we have to make policy in a world where the two goals are in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what it really boils down to is something that's common sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to be aware of the risks that we're-particularly now the risk of significantly higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see shortages and bottlenecks persisting into next year, well into next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see higher inflation persisting, and we have to be in position to address that risk should it become really a threat to-should it create a threat of more persistent, longer-term inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's what we think our policy is doing now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's putting us in a position to be able to address the range of plausible outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess, as I said in my opening remarks, assuming the economy performs broadly as expected, the Committee judges that similar reductions in the pace of net asset purchases will likely be appropriate each month, and we're prepared to deviate from that path if warranted by changes in the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm not going to give you a lot more detail on what that might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, if we do see something like that happening, if it becomes a question, then we'll communicate very transparently and openly about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I'm just going to leave it with the words that are in the statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I would just leave you with the words we have here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are prepared to speed up or slow down the pace of reductions in asset purchases if it's warranted by changes in the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, if we feel like something like that's happening, then we'll be very transparent about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll say, in light of this factor or these factors, we are considering doing this, and then we would either do it or not do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But so-but I'm not going to, you know, start making up examples of what that might be today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, first of all, it is our job to-and we accept responsibility and accountability for inflation in the medium term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're accountable to Congress and to the American people for maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The level of inflation we have right now is not at all consistent with price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: By the way, we're also not at maximum employment, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would want to assure people that we will use our tools as appropriate to get inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think it's a good time to raise interest rates, though, because we want to see the labor market heal further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have very good reason to think that that will happen as the Delta variant declines, so-which it's doing now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So "transitory" is a word that people have had different understandings of.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For some, it carries a sense of "short lived," and that's, you know, there's a real time component-measured in months, let's say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, for us, what "transitory" has meant is that if something is transitory, it will not leave behind it permanently or very persistently higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's why we, you know, we took a step back from "transitory."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We said "expected to be transitory," first of all, to show uncertainty around that-we've always said that, by the way, in other contexts; we just hadn't done it in the statement-but also to acknowledge, really, that it means different things to different people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we added some language to really explain more what we're talking about in paragraph two and paragraph three.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We said that "supply and demand imbalances related to the pandemic and the reopening of the economy have contributed to sizable price increases," and we said, "Progress on vaccinations and an easing of supply constraints are expected to support continued gains in economic activity and employment as well as a reduction in inflation."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're trying to explain what we mean and also acknowledging more uncertainty about "transitory."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, I mean, it's become a word that's attracted a lot of attention that maybe is distracting from our message, which we want to be as clear as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, the only other thing I would say is, look, we understand completely that it's particularly people who are living paycheck to paycheck or seeing higher grocery costs, higher gasoline costs-when the winter comes, higher heating costs for their homes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we will use our tools over time to make sure that that doesn't become a permanent feature of life.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, that's one of our principal jobs, along with achieving maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So maximum employment is, it's a broad-what would we say?-broad-based and inclusive goal that's not directly measurable and changes over time due to various factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's taking into account quite a broad range of things, and, of course, employment-levels of employment-[and] participation are a part of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in addition, there are other measures of what's going on in the labor market, like wages is a key measure of how tight the labor market is-the level of quits, the amount of job openings, the flows in and out of various states.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at so many different things, and you make an overall judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, the temptation at the beginning of the recovery was to look at the data in February of 2020 and say, well, that's the goal because we didn't know any-that's what we knew.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We knew that was achievable in a context of low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're in a, you know, we're learning that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to be humble about what we know about this economy, which is still very, you know, COVID-affected, by the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A lot of what we're seeing in the last 90 days is because of Delta.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were on a path to a very different place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, so I think we're going to have to-ideally, we would have, we would see further development of the labor market in a context where there isn't another COVID spike, and then we would be able to see, I think, a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would see whether-how does participation react in that world, in that sort of post-COVID world?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, people are staying out of the labor market because of caretaking [and] because of fear of COVID to a significant extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we thought that schools reopening and elapsing unemployment benefits would produce some sort of additional labor supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think there's room for a whole lot of humility here, as we try to think about what maximum employment would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to have to see some time post-COVID so that we know-or post-Delta, anyway-to see what is possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the learning for those of us who lived through the last cycle is that, over time, you can get to places that didn't look possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, what we also have now, though, is, we have high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have a completely different situation now where we have high inflation, and we have to balance that with what's going on in the employment market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a complicated situation, and I would say, we will, we hope to achieve significantly greater clarity about where this economy is going and what the characteristics of the post-pandemic economy are over the first half of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we reach maximum employment, when we reach a state where labor market conditions are at maximum employment in the Committee's judgment, it's very possible that the inflation test will already be met.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're aware that that language sounds, it sounds a little out of touch with what's going on, but, you know, we're not at maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When that is the case, we'll look to see whether the inflation test is met, and there's a good chance that it will be if you look at how inflation has evolved in the last year and a half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I'm really saying is, that question is not before us right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we had the question on when to taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've now answered that question and the speed of it and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have not focused on whether we meet the liftoff test, because we don't meet the liftoff test now because we're not at maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I'm saying is, given where inflation is and where it's projected to be, let's say we do meet the maximum-employment test.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then the Committee-the question for the Committee at that time will be, has the inflation test been met?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I don't want to get ahead of the Committee on that, but the answer may very well be "Yes, it's been met."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're not asking that question today, because we're not running a liftoff test.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did talk about the economy and the development of the economy, but we didn't ask ourselves whether the liftoff test is met, because, you know, it's clearly not met on the maximum-employment side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't actually define maximum employment as-we define it in terms of inflation, but, of course, there is a connection there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Maximum employment has to be a level that is consistent with stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think about maximum employment as looking at a broad range of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can't just look at- unlike inflation, where you can have a number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But with maximum employment, you could be in a situation, hypothetically, where the unemployment rate is low, but there are many people who are out of the labor force and will come back in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so you wouldn't really be at maximum employment, because there's this group that isn't counted as unemployed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the thing is, by many measures, we are at a very tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mentioned quits and job openings and wages and things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many of them are signaling a tight labor market, but the issue is, how persistent is that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Because you have people who are held out of the labor market, you know, of their own-they're holding themselves out of the labor market because of caretaking needs or because of fear of COVID, or, for whatever reason, they're staying out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's clear that there are, you know-with tremendous demand for workers and wages moving up, it does seem like we're set up to go back to a higher job- creation rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that would suggest that you're not at maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, at the end of the day, it is a judgment thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, of course, at the end of it, it also has to be a level of employment that's consistent with price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-I can't reduce it to an equation, but, ultimately, it's about risk management.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you want to be in a position to act, to cover the full range of plausible outcomes, not just the base case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For now, it appears to be skewed toward higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we need to be in a position to act in case it becomes necessary to do so or appropriate to do so, and we think we will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, though, that, judgmentally, too, it's appropriate to be patient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's appropriate for us to see what the labor market and what the economy look like when they heal further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that we were on a path to a different place, as I mentioned, when Delta arrived.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It stopped that transition away from a goods-focused economy where there's excess demand for goods because there-services are not available.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That transition itself could help bring inflation down, because, presumably, people would spend a little less on goods while they start spending more on travel and all sorts of travel services and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we want to see that healthy process unfold as we decide what the true state of the economy is, and we think it will evolve in a way that will mean lower inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We start to see that now with some of them, but, overall, they haven't gotten better overall, and, you know, we're very aware of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, we don't think it's time to raise rates now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, if we do conclude that it's necessary to do so, then we'll be patient, but we won't hesitate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's not a decision for bank regulators or for any agency.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we feel that any role that we have-and we do think we have a role in climate change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It relates to our existing mandates, and our existing mandates are, really, prudential regulation of financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We expect them, and the public will expect us to expect them, to understand and be in a position to manage their risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's physical risk, and it's transition risk for climate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, the large financial institutions are doing this already, and, you know, we think that's right within our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's also a financial stability question, the overall stability of the financial system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can try to help understand what will the pathways be through which climate change effects the economy-both physical risk and transition risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we can do, and that's what we will do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Within the frame of our existing mandates, we'll do it well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not the people who will decide the national strategy on climate change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That has to be elected people, and not so much us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We feel like we have that narrow mandate, and we will do it well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, you know, we-let me just say that this system, the ethics system we had in place had been in place for decades and had, as far as we know, served us well, and then that was no longer the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we had no moment of denial about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As a group, we stepped in, and we took the actions that we took.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, within one FOMC cycle, we announced a new set of rules to, you know, to try to put us back where we need to be, which is, we need to have the complete trust of the American people that we're working in their interest all the time-absolutely critical to our work, as it is for any government agency.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we reacted, I would characterize it, strongly and forcefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If there were other things that we could do that were reasonable, we would certainly do them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the overall authority for ethics around these issues in the federal government is the Office of Government Ethics, OGE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they have a long-held position which is not favorable to blind trusts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they think there are better ways to get at the things that need to be done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't know that there are any blind trusts, for that reason, because they are the, they're the regulator.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of laws broken, you know, I asked the inspector general to look to see whether there were rules broken and whether there were laws broken, and I won't speculate on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that is with the inspector general now and, of course, out of my hands.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so, let me say what's happened-and we're very, very straightforward about it-is that inflation has come in higher than expected, and bottlenecks have been more persistent and more prevalent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see that just like everybody else does, and we see that they're now on track to persist well into next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That was not expected-not expected by us, not expected by other macro forecasters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, let me say, you know, it's difficult enough to just forecast the economy in normal times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When you're talking about, you know, global supply chains in turmoil, it's a whole different thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you're talking about a pandemic that's holding people out of the labor force for reasons that we can sample, but we don't have a lot of experience with this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's very, very difficult to forecast and not easy to set policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so, to look at your question this way, I don't think that we're behind the curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I actually believe that policy is well positioned to address the range of plausible outcomes, and that's what we need to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think it would be premature to raise rates today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason is that there's still ground to cover to get to maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't want to stop that when there's good reason to think-there's still good reason to think, although it's been delayed, clearly, there's good reason to think that the economy will reopen, particularly if we do get past, you know, significant outbreaks of COVID.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's when we're really going to see what the characteristics of the labor market are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I think, you know, the bottlenecks that we're seeing in global supply chains around goods and, frankly, now at our own domestic ports, because demand is stronger than the capacity of those ports-those things are going to work themselves out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll take some time, but, you know, it took-you know, the experts managed to create a vaccine faster than, certainly, than I expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think this stuff will work itself out over the course of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is my baseline understanding, and that's a very widely held one among people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we are prepared for different eventualities, and we will use our tools to achieve price stability and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to let the data lead us to where we need to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our policy will adapt-and has already adapted-to the changing understanding of inflation and of bottlenecks and the whole supply-side story-which is also partly a demand story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our policy will continue to adapt as is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy is in quite a different place than when we tapered back in, I guess it was, 2013.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is an economy where demand is very, very strong, very strong, and job openings substantially exceed the number of unemployed people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the need for further stimulus is far less than it was in 2013, where we still had quite a ways to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, after we began that taper, it was still many years before we reached what I would characterize as conditions consistent with maximum employment, let alone price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is quite a different situation, and, you know, the Committee unanimously felt today that we had met the test that we'd articulated, and this was appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is faster than, you know, than what people had expected six months ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's earlier and faster, and that's because our, as I mentioned, our policy has been adapting to the situation as it evolves, as it's clarifying itself, and that's partly because we see inflation coming in higher-so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in terms of the balance sheet, those questions that you mention-we haven't gone back to them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now that we've tapered, I expect that that's exactly what we'll do in coming meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll do it in an orderly fashion, and we'll talk about reinvestment and all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't have to make decisions on those yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, typically, when we're doing a new subject like that, we'll have a series of briefings and discussions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the effect of asset purchases on the economy, so, there's a tremendous amount of research and scholarship on this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, you can kind of-you can find different people coming out with different views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say, the most mainstream view would be that you're at the effective lower bound, so how do you affect longer-term rates?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One, so you can't lower rates-let's say you can't lower rates any further, hypothetically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can say, we're going to keep the rates low for a period of time, either [for] a specific period, [or] until certain conditions are met.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The markets will do the math, and that'll have an effect on longer-term borrowings even, you know, 10, 30 years out kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other thing you can do is, you just go buy those securities, buy longer-term securities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That will drive down longer-term rates and hold them lower, and, you know, rates right across the, right across the rate spectrum matter for borrowers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So lower rates encourage more borrowing, encourage more economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's not different from what we do at the short end.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That was-I think Milton Friedman said that that was what you could do if you were pinned at the lower bound, many, many years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's quite hard to be precise about these things because, you know, you only have one economy, and you can't run two different economies right next to each other and do a scientific experiment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But most people find-most of the findings are that it does support economic activity in the way that you would expect, which is to say, at the margin, more economic activity with lower rates, which is why we do what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: More accommodative financial conditions lead to more economic activity, over time, with a lag.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that's the main finding I would say on QE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm not going to-I won't have any-I will answer your question, Paul, but I'm not going to have any comment whatsoever on the renomination process at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, though, that I have briefed Administration officials, and I've briefed people on Capitol Hill in detail about what we did and why we did it, and seeking their feedback, getting their reaction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, this is-part of my job is-Congress has oversight over the Fed, and we take that very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you're on our, one of the two committees that has oversight over us, then I'm in regular contact with you, probably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, when something like this comes up, I'm on the phone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm offering to meet with you and explain it to you and answer your questions and identify any concerns people might have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't have anything for you on supplemental leverage ratio right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are looking at ways to, if there are ways we can address liquidity issues through that channel.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also-we also have a-there's a working group headed by [the] Treasury about, over Treasury [securities] markets, and what happened in the acute phase of the pandemic, and what structural things may need to be done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that would be part of that workstream, and I know that there's a lot going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's one of the many issues that are part of that, along with things like central clearing of Treasuries, greater central clearing, and, you know, many other ideas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's important that we have a liquid Treasury [securities] market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a huge public benefit that we do, and, you know, I think we need to do those things that enable that, you know, while also assuring the safety and soundness of our largest financial institutions, who tend to be the main dealers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have to make sure that that's always a first order of concern as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going to answer who I spoke to at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just, I'm not going to give you any names, so don't take that as a "yes" or "no."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're quitting their jobs in all-time-high numbers-but, in many cases, going back into employment and getting higher wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a lot of the higher wages you're seeing are for job switchers rather than incumbents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's just, that's a sign of a really strong labor market, as opposed to people just running off and quitting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There have also been-there are a significant number of retirements, and we'll just have to see what that means.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, toward the end of the last cycle, which was the longest in our recorded economic history, we did see labor force participation moving up well above what economists estimate was the trend, and part of that was people staying in the labor force or just not retiring at the rates they were expected to retire.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I am a believer that, over time, you won't know how far-you won't know what can happen with labor force participation in advance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're just going to have to give it some time, because we saw that over and over again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are things that we can, where we can say, you know, this is where the limit is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Labor force participation is a much more flexible subject for me, and so I do think we need to be humble about what the limits are of labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know the pace at which it will do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in terms of full employment, as I discussed earlier, I think, at the very beginning of the recovery, the natural thing to do was to look back at labor conditions, labor market conditions in February of 2010, at the end of the longest expansion in our history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was so much to like about that labor market, a really historically good labor market-never perfect, but a good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The pandemic recession was the deepest, and the recovery has been the fastest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, real incomes were more than fully replaced by fiscal policy [support].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, an economy where inflation was driven by services is now inflation where-all the inflation is in goods, which have had negative inflation for a quarter-century.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we have to-I'm very open to the thought that it's going to be an empirical question of where it is located, and we're just going to learn more and more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, one thing we'll learn, I think, I hope we'll learn in the next, in the near term is, once the Delta variant really does continue to decline, what's going to happen to employment?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Are we going to start to see over the winter, you know, significant increases in jobs again?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look back, the three-, six-, and nine-month average job creation is between 550,000 and 600,000.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you think of that as a stronger-you don't have to think back to the million-job months of June and July.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can just think, okay, 550 to 600-if we should get back on that path, then we would be making good progress, and we like to see that, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So maximum employment, if you look at our Statement on Longer- Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, maximum employment is something that we look at a broad range of indicators.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those would include, of course, things like the unemployment rate, the labor force participation rate, job openings, wages, flows in and out of the labor force in various parts of the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'd also tend to look broadly and inclusively at different demographic groups and not just at the headline and aggregate numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a-that's a judgment for the Committee to make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Committee will make a judgment that we've achieved labor market conditions consistent with maximum employment when it makes that-it is, admittedly, a judgment call because it's a range of factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Unlike inflation, where we have one number that sort of dominates, it's a broad range of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, in my view, we are making rapid progress toward maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you see that, of course, in some of the factors that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on the first part of your question, which is, "Why not stop purchasing now?," I would just say this: We've learned that, in dealing with balance sheet issues, we've learned that it's best to take a careful sort of methodical approach to make adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we thought that this was-this was a doubling of the speed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're basically two meetings away now from finishing the taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we thought that was the appropriate way to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the question of long and variable lags is, is an interesting one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think that in this world, where everything is- where the global financial markets are connected together, financial conditions can change very quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And my own sense is that they get into-financial conditions affect the economy fairly rapidly, longer than the traditional thought of, you know, a year or 18 months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in addition, when we communicate about what we're going to do, the markets move immediately [in response] to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So financial conditions are changing to reflect, you know, the forecasts that we made and basically, which was, I think, fairly in line with what markets were expecting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But financial conditions don't wait to change until, until things actually happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't think it's a question of having to wait.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The sense of that, of course, being that buying assets is adding accommodation and raising rates is removing accommodation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Since we're two meetings away from completing the taper, assuming things go as, as expected, I think if we wanted to lift off before then, then, then what we-you would stop the taper potentially sooner.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I do-I do not think it would be appropriate, and we-and we don't find ourselves in a situation where we-where we might have to raise rates while we're still purchasing assets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we haven't made any decision of that nature.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, no, I wouldn't say that's our position at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say that we did talk today-We had our first discussion about the balance sheet, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we went through the way-the sequence of events regarding the runoff and that sort of thing with the balance sheet, last time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think people thought that was an interesting discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They thought that it was informative, but people pointed out that this is a significantly different economic situation that we have at the current time, and that those-the differences that we see now would tend to influence how we think about the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the same thing would be true about raising rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't-I don't foresee that there would be that kind of very extended wait at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I was here at the Fed when we lifted off the last time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the economy is so much stronger now, so much closer to full employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation is running well above target, and growth is well above potential.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There wouldn't be the need for that kind of long delay.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Having said that, I-you know, we'll make this decision in coming meetings, and it's not-it's not a decision that the Committee has really focused on yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-you know, the thing is, we're not going back to the same economy we had in February of 2020.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think early on, that was-the sense was that that's where we were headed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The post-pandemic labor market, and the economy in general, will be different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the maximum level of employment that's consistent with price stability evolves over time within a-within a business cycle and over a longer period, in part reflecting [the] evolution of the factors that affect labor supply, including those related to the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say: Look, we're, we're at 4. percent now and it's been-the unemployment rate has been dropping very quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The way in which-The important metric that has been disappointing really has been labor force participation, of course, where we had widely thought-I had certainly thought- that, last fall, as unemployment insurance ran off, as vaccinations increased, [and] as schools reopened, that we would see a significant surge, if you will, or at least a surge, in labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We certainly welcome the 2/10 improvement that we got in the November report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I do think that it's-it feels likely now that the return to higher participation is going to take longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in fact, that's, that's been the pattern in past cycles-that labor force participation has tended to recover in the wake of a strong recovery in unemployment, which is what we're getting right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you-it could well have been that this cycle was different because of the short nature of it and the very strong-the number of job openings, for example, you would have thought that that would have pulled people back in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, really, it's the pandemic, it's a range of factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the reality is, we don't have a strong labor force participation recovery yet, and we may not have it for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we have to make policy now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is something we need to take into-take into account.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is-this is not at all a decision that the Committee has made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you're really asking a question about how our framework works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, yes, there is a- there's a provision, it used to be called the "balanced approach" provision, that says, in effect, that in situations in which the pursuit of the maximum-employment goal and [the pursuit of] the price-stability goal are not complementary, we have to take account of the distance from the goal and the-and the speed at which we're approaching it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that is, in effect, an "off-ramp" which could, in concept, be taken and it's in our framework, it's been in our framework a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It, it is a provision that would enable us to, in this case, because of high inflation, move before achieving maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, we're-as I said, we're making rapid progress toward maximum employment in my-in my thinking, in my opinion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't at all know that we will-that we'll have to invoke that, that paragraph.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But just as a factual matter, that is part of our framework-and has been, really, for a very long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think there's a lot of uncertainty, which is why we-why we called it out in our statement, our postmeeting statement, as a risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-we, we follow the same experts and I-we, we talk privately to the same experts that everyone else does and read the same articles in the paper and the same research and, you know, so the-you mentioned the early assessment is highly transmissible, perhaps not as severe, some continuing protection from, from existing vaccines and also existing immunity from having had the disease.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're a long way from knowing what it will turn out to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It may well come to the United States and replace Delta as the dominant variant fairly quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's another step there, though-which is what's going to be the effect on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that will depend, you know, on how much it suppresses demand as opposed to suppressing supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is not clear how big the effects would be on either inflation or growth or hiring on top of what's already going on, which is quite a strong, you know, wave of Delta that's hitting large parts of the country across the northern United States and all the way to the eastern seaboard and now coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So coming in on top of that, again, it's very difficult to say what the economic effects would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think, wave upon wave, people are learning to live with this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So [vaccinated] people who get the new variant, it affects them much less than it tends to affect, in the aggregate, people who are not vaccinated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the more people get vaccinated, the less the economic effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it actually-it had an effect on global supply chains.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that sort of-that hurt the process of the global supply chains getting worked out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just think, at this point, we don't know much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll know a whole lot more in three weeks, and we'll know more than that in six weeks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, look, I think-if you look at the state of the economy and the amount-the strength of demand, the strength of just overall demand, and the strength of demand for labor, look at inflation, look at wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think moving, you know, moving forward the end of our taper by a few months is really-is really an appropriate thing to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, really, Omicron doesn't really have much to do with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would go back and-you know, it's been a continual process, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we had a view-it was very, very widely held in the forecasting community-that this would be temporary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was quite narrow, you know, a limited number of factors were causing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there was a decent amount of evidence to support that view, that it would be temporary or transitory, as we said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Certainly, we had five months of declining month on month-monthly readings of inflation, but we didn't see much in the way of progress on labor supply or on other supply-side issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then in September, I'd say after Labor Day, we started to see-it started to become clear that this was both larger in its effect on inflation and more persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, I said so on many occasions, and one of the consequences of that is that we move the taper forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We moved the taper forward and we-and it's a much faster taper than had been planned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've been adapting-I've been saying we're adapting our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So coming to your real question, we got the ECI reading on the eve of the November meeting-it was the Friday before the November meeting-and it was very high, 5. percent reading for the employment compensation index for the third quarter, not annualized, for the third quarter, just before the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I thought for a second there whether we-whether we should increase our taper, [We] decided to go ahead with what we had-what we had "socialized."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then, right after that, we got the next Friday after the meeting, two days after the meeting, we got a very strong employment report and, you know, revisions to prior readings and, and no increase in labor supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the Friday after that, we got the CPI, which was a very hot, high reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, honestly, at that point, really decided that I thought we needed to-we needed to look at, at speeding up the taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was essentially higher inflation and faster-turns out much faster progress in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, what's happening is the unemployment rate is catching up-seems to be catching up-with a lot of the other readings of a tight labor market, 6/10 [decline] over one cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's really what happened and, you know, widely supported in the Committee today, as you can see-unanimous vote-but beyond that I think widely, widely supported, you know, this, this move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's-so far, we don't see-wages are not a big part of the high-inflation story that we're seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you look forward, let's assume that the goods economy does sort itself out, and supply chains get working again, and maybe there's a rebalancing back to services and all that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what, what that leaves behind is the other things that can lead to persistent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In particular-we don't see this yet, but if you had something where wages were persistently- [increases in] real wages were persistently above productivity growth, that puts upward pressure on, on firms, and they raise prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would take something that was persistent and material for that to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But with the kind of hot labor market readings- wages we're seeing, it's something that we're-that we're watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the other thing, of course, is, is rents, which are very important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Unlike the things that are causing the inflation now, this is economically sensitive-and so would be expected to move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so as the-as some things go down, the question is: Where will we be when we come out the other side of this?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we need to keep our eyes on those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, as you know, you know, the SEP is not a plan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something we debate, negotiate over, or really discuss in terms of what the right answer should be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People write down their, their assumptions-their assessment of appropriate policy based on their economic forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so the median-what you're talking about, the three rate increases, that's the median of the Committee-the median of the Committee is also that growth will be 4 percent and then unemployment will be 3½ percent by the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, if the-if the economy turns out to be quite different from that, then so will the rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we-no one will say, "Oh, we can't change our policy because we wrote something down in December."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It will-the actual rate decisions we make will depend on our evolving assessment of the forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, for example, if, if the economy were to slow down significantly, then you would expect that that would have an effect of slowing down rate increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we'd have to-you know, we look at our two goals, maximum employment and price stability, and we make policy based on them, and not with respect to what we wrote down in a prior SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me start by saying that the inflation that we got was not at all the inflation we were looking for or talking about in the framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was to do with, you know, strong monetary policy and fiscal stimulus into an economy that was recovering rapidly, and in which there were these supply-side barriers which effectively led to, you know, in certain parts of the economy, what you might call a vertical supply curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, automobile purchases are very interest rate-sensitive, and you would think demand would drive up the quantity of cars, But it can't, because they don't have semiconductors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so that-it was a very different kind of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is not the inflation we were looking for under our framework at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And our-the way we've approached it is really nothing to do with our framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But coming to maximum employment, which is really your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think you look at, you know, prices and quantities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When you-if you want to look at maximum employment, you look at prices and quantities, and the main price you look at is wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's-So I mentioned a number of other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can get to 20, if you wanted to, easily, but labor force participation, the unemployment rate, different age groups of-you know, prime-age labor force participation, in particular, gets a lot of focus, the JOLTS data get a lot of focus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And wages, that's, that's really one of the great signals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The quits rate is really one of the very best indicators, according to a lot of labor economists, because people quit because they feel like they can get a better job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's, you know, record amounts, historically high levels of that going on-suggesting, again, that you've got a very tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on wages, that's the price indicator we look at to tell us, along with all the other data, whether we're-whether we have labor market conditions that are consistent with maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the-one of the complications is that, again, we've got to make policy in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Do we-if we think we can make labor, you know, participation might move up-if we, let's say we knew that it would start to move up in two years, would we wait two years when inflation is running way above target?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Probably not, you know, so you have to make an assessment that what's max-what is the level of maximum employment that is consistent with price stability in real time is, is one way to think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think-well, whether or not we- whether or not we say "we're at conditions-labor market conditions consistent with, with maximum employment" next year, we would all be open and I think expect, over time, that the level of maximum employment that's consistent with price stability would increase further over time-for example, through increasing participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-we would certainly-we would not, in any way, want to foreclose the idea that the labor market can get even better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, with inflation as high as it is, we have to make policy in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, the labor market is, by so many measures, hotter than it ever ran in the last-in the last expansion, if you think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the ratio of job openings, for example, to, to vacancies is at all-time highs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what would it take for labor force participation to move up more?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there, there are a bunch of answers, and all of them probably have some, you know, some validity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of it will be that people-for certain people, they don't want to go back in the labor force because either they're medically vulnerable or they're not comfortable going back while COVID is still everywhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The lack of availability of childcare made for caretakers is certainly part of it-not just for children, but for older people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has been pointed out by many that the stock market is high, people's portfolios are stronger-they may go back to being a one-income rather than a two-income family.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People buy-they have a mortgage, you know, with leverage, and the house price increases, the equity they have in their home might have doubled.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So they're-and people have savings on their balance sheet because of forced savings because they couldn't spend on travel and things like that and also because of, you know, because of government transfers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, for all of those reasons-and it's hard to know exactly the part each of them plays- we, we have a situation where we've had a shock to labor force participation that is not unwinding as quickly as, as many, as expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people-in effect, a good part of it is voluntary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, people-and this is how they want to maximize their welfare and that's, that's their, certainly their choice.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other cases, it's something that will abate very quickly if and when the pandemic gets under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the longer the pandemic goes on, you know, maybe the less likely that people will come back because they're-you know, they get used to their new life and they lose contact with their old jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, usually, in every other expansion, it's that there aren't enough jobs and people can't find jobs and, you know, we're stimulating demand and trying to get demand to come up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The problem is a supply-side problem, which-what it would take to work it out, I think it's going to be time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the number-one thing would, would really be to have the pandemic get under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
