text: That's what everyone would really like to see: What does the labor force- what does the labor market look like in a world without COVID?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That would be the thing that we'd really like to see but, you know, it doesn't look like that's coming anytime soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we actually got above the demographic trend at the end of the last expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-so one would expect over time that labor force participation would, would move down because an aging population, the older people are, the lower their participation rate is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you would expect that, that the trend would be lower and that, over time, participation would move down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question of how much we can get back up closer to where we were in February of 2020-and, indeed, for the year or so before that-is a good one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, I-What we can do is try to create the conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a lot of good for society when you have a tight but stable labor market, where people are coming in, they're getting into the labor force, they're getting paid well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the labor market we had before, we had, you know-the biggest wage increases were going to people at the bottom end of the wage spectrum for the last couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There were just a lot of really desirable aspects of a labor market like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, ultimately, we have the tools that we have, which are essentially to stimulate demand and also to control inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, really, it might be-one of the two big threats to getting back to maximum employment is actually high inflation, because, to get back to where we were, the evidence grows that it's going to take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we need is another long expansion, like the ones we've been having.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Over the last 40 years, we've had, I think, three of the four longest in our recorded history, including the last one, which was the longest in our recorded history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what it would really take to get back to the kind of labor market we'd like to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And to have that happen, we need to make sure that we maintain price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see consumer expense as very strong in this quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know, Edward, whether you're talking about more shopping online versus shopping in the store, but consumer demand is very strong, incomes are very strong, you know, because people are going back to work and they're getting wage increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Admittedly, some of the wage increases is being eaten away by inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, incomes, overall, are going up really significantly because of increased employment and spending is-has been strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There may be something in the seasonality that this year's holiday spending may have been pulled forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, there may be effects from, from Delta and there might be going forward from Omicron.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But fundamentally, though, the consumer is really healthy, and we expect personal consumption expenditures to be pretty strong in the fourth quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, actually, I'm looking at the SEP here, and the median forecasts for core and headline inflation did move up by 4/10 each.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a significant-you know, in an SEP, that's a pretty significant move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's, it's based on both of those things, I suppose.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think there's a broad expectation among forecasters, including our own, that the bottlenecks will alleviate sometime over the course of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at where Blue Chip forecasts are-which is, you know, a group of well-resourced, large forecasting operations with a long track record-they'll show inflation coming back down significantly toward the back-end of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, though, as well that our policy should begin to have an effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There will be a lag, but it should begin to have an effect on that as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess what-the thing I would want to say, though, is we can't act as though that's a certainty, and we're not going to act as though that's a certainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a real risk now, we believe, I believe, that inflation may be more persistent and that may be putting inflation expectations under pressure, and that the risk of higher inflation becoming entrenched has increased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think it's high at this moment, but I think it's increased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's part of the reason behind our move today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: [It] is to put ourselves in a position to be able to deal with that risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we are in a position to deal with that risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need to see how the inflation data and the-all the data evolve in coming months, but we are prepared to, you know, to use our tools to make sure that higher inflation doesn't get entrenched.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For one reason, as I-as I just mentioned, it's one of the two big threats, the other being the pandemic itself, to getting back to maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we have-we have had now for a decade and more a four-part financial stability framework that we use so we can-we can hold ourselves to the same kind of framework and, you know, not just treat each event individually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are four key areas: asset valuations, debt owed by households and businesses, funding risk, and leverage among financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say asset valuations-I'm going to go really superficially here, but asset valuations are somewhat elevated, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Debt owed by businesses, you know, and households-households are in very strong financial shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Businesses actually have a lot of debt, but their default rates are very, very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Funding risk is, by and large, low among, among financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do see money market funds as a vulnerability and, and, you know, would applaud the SEC's action this week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Leverage among financial institutions is low, in the sense that [their] capital is high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, you know, financial stability, that's how-I wouldn't make an overall characteristic, but we break it down into those pieces.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the things, you know, that we're-that we're looking for, looking at, you know, it's the-it's the things we've already talked about, to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's the emergence of a new variant that could, you know, that could lead to significant economic-if there were to be a variant, for example, [and if] that were quite resistant to vaccines, it could have another significant effect on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't have any basis for thinking that the new variant that we have is that one, but it's certainly one we're looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, you know, cyber risk, the risk of a successful cyberattack, is, for me, you know, always the most-you know, one that would be very difficult to deal with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we know how to deal with bad loans and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think more-a cyberattack that were to take down a major financial institution or financial market utility would be a really significant financial stability risk that we haven't actually faced yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I could go on with a list of "horribles," but I think that's a decent picture of where I would start.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think the concerns there are not so much current financial-stability concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, of course, would support the, the views expressed in the President's Working Group report on stablecoins.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Stablecoins can certainly be a useful, efficient, consumer-serving, part of the financial system, if they're properly regulated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and they have the potential to scale [up], particularly if they were to be, you know, associated with one of the very large tech networks that exist and you could have a payment network that was immediately systemically important-close to immediately systemically important that didn't have appropriate regulation and protections.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The public relies on the government-and [on] the Fed, in particular-to make sure that the payment system is safe and reliable, as well as the dollar and-you know, to provide a safe and reliable trusted currency.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of, you know, the more-the cryptocurrencies, you know, that are really speculative assets, I don't see them as a financial-stability concern at the moment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think they are risky, they're not backed by anything, and I think there's big consumer-issues for consumers who may or may not understand what they're getting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's certainly developments in the-in the markets that are worth following, which are really not in our jurisdiction, but things like, you know, the kind of leverage that's built into and those sorts of things is certainly worth, worth watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I actually think we are well positioned to deal with, with what's coming, with the range of plausible outcomes that can come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if you look at how we got here, I do think we've, we've been adapting to the incoming data, really all the way along, and, you know, noticing and calling out that, that the-both the effects and the persistence of inflation of bottlenecks and labor shortages and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've been calling out the fact that those were becoming longer, and more persistent, and larger.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now we're in a position where we're ending our taper within the next-well, by March, in two meetings, and we'll be in a position to raise interest rates as and when we think it's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we're going to be seeing a few more months of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think this was an important move for us to make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that the data that we got toward the end of the fall was a-was a really strong signal that inflation is more persistent and higher-and that the risk of it remaining higher for longer has grown.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't look at it that we're "behind the curve."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would look at it that we're actually in position now to take the steps that we'll need to take, you know, in a thoughtful manner to address all of the issues, including that of, of too-high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-you know, the, the asset purchases are a separate tool from interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Whereas raising interest rates starts to remove accommodation from what is a highly accommodative stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the extent to which they'll be separated in time is, is something we haven't really discussed at the Committee [meetings] yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think that, that-the last cycle, there was quite a long separation before interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think that's at all likely in this cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're in a very, very different place with high inflation, strong growth, a really strong economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, that-as I mentioned, the SEP medians are for 4 percent growth next year, 3½ percent- 3½ percent unemployment at the end of the year, and the, the-you know, headline inflation of 2. percent next year, core at 2.7.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is a strong economy, one in which it's appropriate for, for interest rate hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, with the balance sheet, we did have a balance sheet discussion, sort of a prelim-a first, first discussion of balance sheet issues today, [balance] sheet issues, at our meeting this week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll have another at the next meeting and another at the meeting after that I suspect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We looked back at what happened in the last cycle, and people thought that was interesting and informative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but to one degree or another, people noted that this is just a different situation, and those differences should inform the decisions we make about the balance sheet this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So [we] haven't made any decisions at all about, about when runoff would start, but we're-we'll be continuing to-you know, in relation to when either liftoff happens or the end of the taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But those are exactly the decisions we'll be turning to in coming meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, I'm not expressing any judgment about, about the stimulus in, in that comment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I'm saying is, there's a-there's a sense among some that "you wanted inflation, this is what you wanted, how do you like it?," you know?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the truth is, this is not the inflation that we were-what we were talking about in the-in the framework was inflation that comes from a tight labor market, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we had 3½ percent unemployment for a period, and we had inflation that was just barely getting to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-you know, I think, in that setting, our thinking was, we can afford to wait to raise rates until we see actual inflation rather than [acting] preemptive[ly] because, you know, no one had seen what 3½ percent unemployment would look like-with high labor force participation, by the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one had seen what it would look-really look like for an extended period, for decades.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It turned out there was barely 2 percent inflation-and no sense that it was gaining momentum and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, that's a situation where you had a very, very high level of employment and low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Or, you know, it has been the opposite, where we have very high inflation and we've had it since the labor market was in terrible shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It had nothing-so far, this inflation has really nothing to do with tightness in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It does have to do with, with strong demand, and strong demand was supported by the Fed, it was supported by Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not making any judgments on Congress, it's not my job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I will just say, we're coming out of a, you know, what we certainly hope will be a once in a lifetime, certainly historic-the first really global modern pandemic-which looked at the beginning like it might cause a global depression.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so we threw a lot of support at it [the economy].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what's coming out now is, is, you know, really strong growth, really strong demand, high incomes, and all that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, people will judge in 25 years whether we-whether we overdid it or not, but, you know, the reality is, we are where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we think our policy is, is the right one for the situation that we're in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think the short-end actions are easy to understand, which is, you know, they're basically very [monetary] policy-sensitive rates at the short end, and it makes sense that it's reacting to changes in expectations for policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think a lot of things go into the, you know, the long rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the place I would start is just look at global sovereign yields around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Look at JGBs, look at bunds, and they're so much lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can get-you can get, you know, a much higher yield on U.S. Treasuries by buying USTs rather than bunds and you can-you can hedge, hedge the currency risk back into yen, back into euros and still be way ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in a way, it's not surprising that there's a lot of demand for, for U.S. sovereigns in a world-you know, in a risk-free world where, where there's so much-they're yielding so much more than bunds are, than JGBs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also think, you know, there, there may be some assessment in there of what the neutral rate is or what the terminal rate is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-and I would just say that we, you know, we write down our own estimates of the-of the terminal rate or the neutral rate of interest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we'll make policy based on what we're seeing in the economy rather than based on what a neutral-what a model might say the neutral rate is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we all had the experience of the last cycle, where we all, through that cycle, were trying to estimate what the neutral rate was, and it turned out-you know, I think we learned a lot from seeing what happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We ended up cutting rates three times after raising them to 2¼ to 2½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm not troubled by where the long bond [rate] is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I mean, we're really focused on broader financial conditions, [and] we're focused on maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, we got the ECI reading just before the November meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We got the labor market report two days after the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, one week after that, I think on the 12th of November, we got the CPI reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was really the CPI reading, in concert with those two, and I, I just came to the view over that weekend that we needed to speed up the taper.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a full 10 days or so before the President made a decision of renominating me.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, honestly, it had-it had nothing to do with that at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I just thought this is what we got to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They were out talking about a faster taper before the President made his decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a decision that effectively was in-more than in train and, you know, to the point where people were talking about it publicly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it had absolutely nothing to do with it whatsoever.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're always going to just do what we think is the right thing, and I certainly will always just do what I think the right thing is for the economy and for the people that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason I didn't-and there was no-there was lots of talk about that, but not from the Fed, because that is not our job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are not the CBO, and we're not elected by anybody.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we take fiscal policy as it arrives at our front door, and we don't comment-you know, we make our own assessments inside the Fed, but it's really not our role.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, very important, that we stay out of that business, no matter who's in the White House, who's in Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just-it's just not our job and it's something we avoid pretty, pretty assiduously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I-as I referred to in my opening statement, it's-it is not possible to predict with much confidence exactly what path for our policy rate is going to prove appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, at this time, we haven't made any decisions about the path of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I stress again that we'll be humble and nimble.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to have to navigate crosscurrents and actually two-sided risks now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and, and I'll say also that we're going to be guided by the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, what I'll say is that we're going to be led by the incoming data and the evolving outlook, which we'll try to communicate as clearly as possible, moving steadily and transparency-transparently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So more to your question, we know that the economy is in a very different place than it was when we began raising rates in 2015.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation is running well above our 2 percent target, much higher than it was at that time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And these differences are likely to have important implications for the appropriate pace of policy adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just getting both, both parts of your question written down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say-and this view is widely held on the Committee-that both sides of the mandate are calling for us to move steadily away from the very highly accommodative policies we put in place during the challenging economic conditions that the economy faced earlier in the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say that most FOMC participants agree that labor market conditions are consistent with maximum employment in the sense of the highest level of employment that is consistent with price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, again, very broad support on the Committee for the judgment that it will soon be appropriate to raise the target range for the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other thing is, maximum employment will, will evolve over time and through the course of the business cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the particular situation we're in now, it may well increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Max-the level of maximum-of employment that's consistent with stable prices may increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we hope that it will, as more people come back into the labor market, as participation gradually rises.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the policy path that we're broadly contemplating would be supportive of that comment-that outcome as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the thing about the labor market right now is that there are-there are many millions of, of more job openings than there are unemployed people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you ask whether we can- whether we can raise rates and, and move to less accommodative, and even tight, financial conditions without hurting the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's quite a bit of room to raise interest rates without threatening the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is, by so many measures, a historically tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages are moving up at the highest pace they have in decades.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at surveys of workers, they find jobs plentiful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And all of those readings are at levels, really, that we haven't seen in a long time-and, in some cases, ever.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is a very, very strong labor market, and my strong sense is that we can-we can-we can move rates up without, without having to, you know, severely undermine it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also would point out that there are-there are other forces at work this year, which should also help bring down inflation, we hope, including improvement on the supply side, which will ultimately come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, fiscal policy is going to be less supportive of, of growth this year-not of the level of economic activity, but the fiscal impulse to growth will be significantly lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there are multiple forces-which should be working over the course of the year for inflation to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do realize that the timing and pace of that are, are highly uncertain and that inflation has persisted longer than we-than we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, we're prepared to use our tools to assure that higher inflation does not become entrenched.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm afraid to tell you that those are all great questions, and they're questions that the Committee is just turning to now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we had-we had a discussion, as you know, at the last meeting, an introductory discussion of the balance sheet and a teeing up of the issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At this meeting, we've gone through and carefully put together a set of principles at a high level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those are meant to guide the actual decisions we'll make about the pace and about all of the questions that you're, you're asking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I expect that this process will, will be something that we spend time on in coming meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-and then, you know, at the appropriate time, we'll provide additional information.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I did-the last cycle when we-when we went through balance sheet issues, we did find that over, over the course of two or three meetings, for example, we did come to interesting and better answers, we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And at the next meeting, we'll be turning to, you know, more of the details that you're-that you're asking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'd say it has a shorter duration than the last time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the economy's much stronger, and inflation is much higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and I think that leads you to-and I said, I've said this-being willing to move sooner than we did the last time and also perhaps faster.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But beyond that, it's really-it's really not appropriate for me to speculate exactly what that would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and-but I would point you to principle number one, which is "the Committee views changes in the target range for the federal funds rate as its primary means of adjusting the stance of monetary policy."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do want the federal funds rate-we, we want to operationalize that [as the primary means].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we want the balance sheet to be declining in a predictable manner, and we want it to be declining primarily by adjusting reinvestments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, we think of the balance sheet as, as moving in a predictable manner, sort of in the background, and that the active tool meeting to meeting is not both of them, it's the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are-there are rules of thumb-I'm reluctant to land on one of them-that, that equate this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but there's also an element of, of uncertainty around the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we have a much better sense, frankly, of how rate increases affect financial conditions and, hence, economic conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Balance sheet [policy] is, is still a relatively new thing for, for the markets and for us, so we're less certain about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, our-I think our-the pattern we'll follow is to-is to arrive at a, you know, a timing and a pace and composition and all those things and then announce that with advance notice, and, and it will-it will start in the background.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we'll look to have that just running in the background and have-and have the interest rates, again, be the active tool of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't tell you much more about any of the- any of the very good issues about size, pace, composition, those sorts of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we'll be turning to all of those at coming meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you know, the ultimate focus that we have is on the real economy: maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And financial conditions matter to the extent that they have implications for achieving the dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you also know that we, we look at broader financial conditions, not one or two things, one or two markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we're always asking ourselves is, are we seeing changes that are both persistent and material enough that-of a change in financial conditions-that they are inconsistent with the achievement of our goals?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't want to comment on today's financial conditions broadly, but we're not looking at any one market or, or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what we've seen, I would say this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, you know, we said at our last meeting we published the Summary of Economic Projections, the median of which-the median participant expected three rate increases this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's six weeks, seven weeks later now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you have seen that our communication channel with the markets is working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Markets are, are now pricing in a number of rate increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Surveys show that market participants are expecting a balance sheet runoff to begin, you know, at the appropriate time, sometime later this year perhaps.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we feel like the communications we have with market participants and with the general public are working and that financial conditions are reflecting in advance the decisions that we make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't made a decision yet, and we'll make that decision at the March meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll make a decision whether to raise the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that the Committee is, is of a mind to, to raise the federal funds rate at the March meeting, assuming that conditions are appropriate for doing so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have-we have our eyes on, on the risks, particularly around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do expect some softening in the economy from Omicron, but we think that that should be temporary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that the economy should-the underlying strength of the economy should, you know, should, should-show through fairly quickly after that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the path is highly uncertain and that we're committed to using our tools to make sure that inflation, high inflation that we're seeing, does not become entrenched.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a number of factors would be-it's not just monetary policy-a number of factors are supporting a decline in inflation, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Fiscal policy will be-will provide significantly less of an impulse to growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do expect this year-although we do expect now that it will come slower than, than we had expected and hoped-that there will be relief on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that, too, should-should lower the supply-side barriers, which are a big part of the story of why inflation is high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, monetary policy will be becoming significantly less accommodative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the question is-you know, we'll, we'll be asking this question all year long, and that will be, are things turning out as we expect?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a case that, for whatever reason, the economy slows more and inflation slows more than expected; we'll react to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, instead, we see inflation at a higher level or a more persistent level, then we'll react to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we're, we're well aware that this is a different economy than-than existed during the last tightening cycle, and our policy is going to reflect those differences.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me-let me-let me start by talking about that last paragraph.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you'll remember during the last cycle that this process of building up and then shrinking the balance sheet is a complicated one, and it involves, inevitably, surprises.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so during, during the years, during the prior cycle, we amended our balance sheet principles a number of times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we got a pretty robust paragraph there that says we're free to do this at any time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it doesn't mean we're going to, but if the situation turns out to be different than we had thought, we're not going to be-we're not going to stick with something that isn't working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's meant to be quite a general statement rather than a, a hint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I mean, I like to think that our, you know, our philosophy of the balance sheet is, is embodied in these principles.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, the idea that, for example, the federal funds rate is the primary means of adjusting the stance of policy, that we'll use-determine the timing and pace of reducing the size of the balance sheet to foster the dual mandate, that we'll begin to reduce the size after we begin the process of raising rates, and on and on like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, that- those are all the things that, that try to describe how we will proceed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But maybe at a higher level, to try to get at your question: You know, asset purchases were, were enormously important at the beginning of the recovery in terms of restoring market function, as they were at-right after the-in the critical phase of the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then after [that], they were a macroeconomic tool to support demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now the economy no longer needs this, this highly accommodative policy that we put in place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's time to stop asset purchases first and then, at the appropriate time, start to shrink the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, the balance sheet is, is substantially larger than it needs to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've identified the end state as-in amounts needed to implement monetary policy efficiently [and] effectively in the ample-reserves regime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's a substantial amount of, of shrinkage in the balance sheet to be done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so those are some of the ways that I would think this, this lays out our, you know, the way we-the way we're thinking about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the timing, I can't really help you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it just says after, after we get under way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're-I would say we are, we're going to have another discussion at, at the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And my guess is, we'll have at least one other discussion at the meeting after that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we'll, we'll tell you as we make progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll, you know, we'll start the process of allowing runoff and shrinking the balance sheet at what we find to be the appropriate time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we actually haven't even really had the, the important discussions on a lot of the details that we will have at coming meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-you know, the one risk is that inflation risks are still to the upside in the views of most FOMC participants and, certainly, in my view as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a risk that, that the high inflation we're seeing will be prolonged, and there's a risk that it will move even higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't-we don't think that's the base case, but you asked what the risks are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-we have to be in a position with our monetary policy to address all of the plausible outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we have an expectation about the way the economy is going to be evolved, but we've got to be in a position to, to address different outcomes, including the one where inflation remains higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, that is a risk to the-to the-to the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've been saying that what we need here is another long expansion, which is the kind of thing we saw over the last [one], which was a record long expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We saw wages persistently higher for people at the lower end, and there, there really was no obvious imbalance in the economy that threatened that expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It could have gone on for years were it not hit by the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'd love to find a way to get back to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's going to require price stability, and that's going to require the Fed to tighten interest rate policy and do our part in getting inflation back down to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And COVID can continue to evolve, and it's just-we have to accept that it's not over, and the risks to it can slow down growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that would be-that's sort of a downside risk from a growth standpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would point to-you know, another, another risk is just further, further problems in the supply chains, which could slow down activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you see the situation in China as a situation there where that's-their no-COVID policy may cause more lockdowns, is likely to, and that may play into-may play into more problems in supply chains.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, there's what's going on in Eastern Europe and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we, you know, we can't-we can't forget that there are risks on both sides.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I know you've been all over this issue with, with my colleagues, Craig, on the issue of, of information.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I hand- I asked the inspector general to do an investigation, and that is out of my hands.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't-I really-I can't help you here today on this issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'd say, you know, since, since the December meeting, I would say that the inflation situation is about the same but probably slightly worse.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'd be inclined to raise my own estimate of 2022 core PCE inflation-let's just go with that-by a few tenths today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're not writing, writing down an SEP at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's probably gotten just a-just a bit worse, and that's been the pattern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you look at the-the FOMC participants are-there's a range there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that range has been moving to the right for, for a year now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, if you look at other forecasters, essentially all other macro forecasters who do this for a living, you've seen the same pattern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think we, you know, we wrote down rate increases in the December meetings, each of us individually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think to the extent the situation deteriorates further, our policy will have to address that, if it deteriorates meaningfully further, either in the time dimension or in the size of the inflation dimension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-as I mentioned, though, I think it's-part of this will be that us, the Fed, moving away from a very highly accommodative policy to a substantially less accommodative policy and then, over time, to a policy that's not accommodative, in time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Another part of it is that fiscal policy provided an impulse to growth over the last two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That impulse will be less, in fact, will be-will be negative this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other one is, we will eventually get relief on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, what we're learning is, it's just taking much longer, so I think-longer than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, I think, does raise, raise the risk that high inflation will be more persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think we'll come off of the highs that we saw in the early part of this episode in the-in the spring last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, really, what's-the question is going to be, what is inflation running at?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, you know, we-our objective is to get inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also to provide enough support to keep the labor market healthy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market is very, very strong right now, and I think that that strength will continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see it particularly among production and nonsupervisory workers and people in the lowest quartile.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're also-you know, we realize, I think, as everyone does, that this outlook is quite uncertain and that we're going to have to adapt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to communicate as clearly as we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're going to have to be adaptable and, you know, move, move as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, we have not made these decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and what I can tell you now, though, is that we fully appreciate that this is a different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look back to where we were in 2015, '16, '17, '18 when we were raising rates, inflation was very close to 2 percent, even below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Unemployment was, was not at our estimates of the natural rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And growth was, you know, in the 2 to 3 percent range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, we have inflation running substantially above 2 percent and, and, you know, more persistently than we would like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have growth-even in forecasts, even in the somewhat reduced forecast for 2022-we still see growth higher than, substantially higher than what we estimate to be the potential growth rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we see a labor market where, by so many measures, it is historically tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the-you know, in a way, the least tight aspect of it is, is looking at the unemployment rate, which is still below our median estimate of, of [the unemployment rate consistent with] maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at things like quits and job openings, as I mentioned earlier, and wages, you're seeing-and, and just the ratio of job openings to unemployed-you're seeing a very, very tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, we also know that labor force participation is significantly lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's 1½ percentage points lower than it was in February of 2020.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Maybe a [full] percentage point of that is, is retirements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some part of those retirements are, are, you know, related to COVID rather than just regular retirements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think there's, there's a pool of people out there who could come back into the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's not happening very quickly, and it may not-it may continue to not happen very quickly as long as the pandemic is on[going].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't made-to your specific question-we really have not addressed those questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll begin to address them as we-as we move into the March meeting and meetings after that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it's more a matter of-I think the problem that we're-that we're talking about here is really that people who are on fixed incomes who are living paycheck to paycheck, they're spending most or all of their-of, of what they're earning on food, gasoline, rent, heating their-heating, things like that, basic necessities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so inflation right away, right away forces people like that to make very difficult decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't-I'm not aware of, you know, inflation literally falling more on, on different socioeconomic groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The point is, some people are just really in a-prone to suffer more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, for people who are economically well off, inflation isn't good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: High inflation is, is bad, but they're going to be able to continue to eat and keep their homes and drive their cars and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's more-so that, that's really how I think of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we, we have to control inflation for the benefit of all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But part of-part of it is just that it's particularly hard on people with fixed incomes and low incomes who spent most of their-of their income on necessities, which are-which are experiencing high inflation now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I would not say that I would expect the supply chain issues to be completely worked out by the end of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do not expect them, and I have not expected them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I would say, and I have been saying, is that I expect progress to be made in the second half of this year, mainly-progress because we're not making much progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at a ton of metrics, you can find some that suggest that delivery times are shorter and inventories in some industries moving up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, things like the semiconductor issue are going to-they're going to be quite a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of-so in terms of being too late, I would just say this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-our policy needs to be positioned to address the full range of plausible outcomes, as I said, and particularly the possibility that inflation will continue to run higher, more persistently than we'd expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think we are positioned to make the changes in our policy to do that, and, and we're committed to doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of your, your question about the, the size of rate increases, we haven't-we haven't faced those decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It isn't possible to sit down here today and tell you with any confidence what the-what the precise path will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in-as we work our way through this, meeting by meeting, we are aware that this is a very different, different expansion, as I've said a couple times, with higher inflation, higher growth, a much stronger economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think those differences are likely to be reflected in-in the policy that we implement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no-there's nothing in our framework about having inflation run below 2 percent so that we would do that, try to achieve that outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're trying to do is get inflation, keep inflation expectations well anchored at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do that in the service of having inflation-we get to that goal by having inflation average 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if inflation doesn't average 2 percent over time, then it's not clear why inflation expectations would be anchored at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it-what was the last part of your-of your question?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I would say you have a tremendously strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you have growth this year at-forecast to be well above-well above potential.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, people who are forecasting growth think potential growth is around 2 [percent].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Most forecasts [of actual growth] are significantly above that for 2022, and that's even with, with policy becoming substantially less accommodative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the labor market's going to be strong for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-ideally, what we're trying to achieve is inflation getting back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're trying to do that in a process that, that, that accomplishes-you know, that will also leave the labor market in a very strong position.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I would say that it isn't just monetary policy that's helping inflation get down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll be supply-side improvements, and it'll be less, less fiscal, you know, less fiscal impulse in all likelihood.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is our job to get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And a situation where, where the two goals are-the two goals can be in tension is a difficult one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I-but I don't really think they are here, though, because I think a really significant threat to further strengthening in the labor market in the form of higher participation over time is high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, high inflation is taking away the benefits of some of these larger wage increases that we're seeing now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do hope to achieve, and our plan is to achieve, both of those goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: State dependency was particularly around the thought that if we-if we saw a very strong labor market, we would wait to see actual inflation-actual inflation before we tightened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that was a very state-dependent thought because, for a long time, we'd been tightening on the expectation of high inflation, which never appeared.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that was the case for, for a number of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in this particular situation, we will be clearly monitoring incoming data as well as the evolving outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's too soon to write that history, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The-if you remember what it felt like at the beginning of the pandemic, literally the global economy shutting down in large part, including our own economy, and people going to their homes for weeks on end in masks, and there are no vaccines, and it could be a really long time to get them, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, you know, you have-economic activity drops by a shocking amount in one-so there was a real risk of lasting damage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think Congress responded remarkably with the-with the CARES Act, incredibly timely and very powerful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we were able to do was, you know, stave off a collapse of the financial system at the beginning and make time for what really needed to happen, which was the income replacement and then the recovery that Congress enabled with the CARES Act.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So now, that was a lot of-that was a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, now-so, what we have now is, we have the strongest recovery of any, any country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have-we have a recovery that looks completely unlike other recoveries that we've had, because we've, we've put so much support behind the recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're managing the, the relatively high-class problems that come with that, which are high inflation and a labor shortage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and these are serious problems, very serious problems that we, you know, we're working as hard as we can on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but look, in 25 years, we'll look back at this incident, which will be a, you know, 2-, 3-, 4-, 5-year period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll say, you know, we'll have a-we'll have a much better basis to make a judgment about the actions that people took.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it was all founded, though, in a-in a very strong reaction to a, you know, to a unique historical event.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I guess I'll have to leave it at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I look for-I hope I'll be around to see how that looks in 25 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we do monitor the slope of the yield curve, but we don't control the slope of the yield curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it is something that we watch, and, and you will know that from when we had this issue a few years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we take it into account, along with many other financial conditions, as we try to assess the implications of all those conditions for the economic outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you think about 2s to 10s, 2-year Treasury to 10-year Treasury, I think that's around 75 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's well within the range of a normal-of a normal yield-curve slope.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think of it as-I don't think of it as some kind of an iron law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do look at it and try to understand the implications and what it's telling us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-but it's one of many things that we monitor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Obviously, U.S. long-term sovereign debt is an-is an important global asset.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it-and the fact that our rates are so much higher than, than other risk-free sovereign rates around the world may put something of a ceiling on our-on our rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it would really depend on the- on the facts and circumstances at that time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is going to be a year in which we move steadily away from the very highly accommodative monetary policy that we put in place to deal with the-with the economic effects of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's going to involve and does involve finishing asset purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's going to involve additional rate increases as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we, we have-we're going to write down in March our next assessment of what that might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's going to continue to evolve as the data evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need to be quite adaptable, I think, in our understanding of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The last thing we're going to do is, we're going to have a couple more meetings, I think, to talk about allowing the balance sheet to begin to run off and [to] do so in a predictable manner.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's something that we will also be doing as appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I wouldn't-I don't think it's possible to say exactly how this is going to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're, we're going to need to be, as I've mentioned, nimble about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market is much, much stronger than it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And growth is above trend, even this year, let alone last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So all of those things are going to go into our thinking as we make-as we make monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what it shows is a number of, of positive aspects of financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you mentioned, really, [the behavior of] asset prices is one of the four.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So asset prices are somewhat elevated, and they reflect a high risk appetite and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't really think asset prices themselves represent a significant threat to financial stability, and that's because households are in good shape financially than they have been.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Defaults on business loans are low and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The banks are highly capitalized with high liquidity and quite resilient and strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are some concerns in the-in the nonbank financial sector around-still around money market funds, although the SEC is making-has made some very positive proposals there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we also saw some things in the Treasury market during the acute phase of the crisis, which, which we're looking at ways to address.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, overall, the financial stability vulnerabilities are manageable-are manageable, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would start by saying that, in my view, the probability of a recession within the next year is not particularly elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Aggregate demand is currently strong, and most forecasters expect it to remain so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the labor market, [you find that it is] also very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Conditions are tight, and payroll job growth is continuing at very high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so all signs are that this is a strong economy and, indeed, one that will be able to flourish-not to say withstand, but certainly flourish-as well in the face of less accommodative monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess that's how I would say I'm looking at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, the objective is to achieve price stability while also sustaining a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do feel the economy is very strong and well positioned to withstand tighter monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think that's a big piece of it, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think some of that is just an early assessment of the effects of spillovers from the war in Eastern Europe, which will hit our economy through a number of channels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Highly uncertain, but, you know, you're looking at higher oil prices, higher commodity prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll be-we think that will weigh on GDP to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think-I mean, I think, generally, monetary policy works with a lag, so some of that would also be in there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But remember, as well, that 2. percent is still very strong growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we think that the potential growth rate of the economy is somewhere between, somewhere around 1. percent, 2. percent is strong economic growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would have been one of the strongest years, in fact, of the last expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, while it's lower than last year's 5. percent, it's still quite strong growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, the way we're thinking about this is that every meeting is a live meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we do conclude that it would be appropriate to move more quickly to remove accommodation, then we'll do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't be perfectly specific about it, but that's certainly a possibility as we go through the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would say that at the-before the invasion of Ukraine by Russia-so let's go back to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would have said that the expectation was that inflation would peak sometime in the first quarter, maybe the end of the first quarter of this year, and then maybe stay at that level or a little bit lower and then start to come down in the back half of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So now we're, you know, we're getting-we're going-we're already seeing a little bit of short- term upward pressure in inflation due to higher oil prices, natural gas [prices] a little bit but not so much for us since we have our own natural gas supply, other commodities prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other thing is that you're seeing supply chain issues around shipping and around, you know, lots of countries and companies and people not wanting to touch Russian goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that could actually push out [in time] the relief we were expecting on supply chains generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would say that the expectation is still that inflation will begin to come down in the second half of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look at where I read the SEP headline median, we still expect inflation to be high this year, lower than last year, and then we expect-though, particularly with the effects of the war, but also the data we've seen so far this year-we expect inflation to remain high through the middle of the year, begin to come down, and then come down more sharply next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's one of many ways of capturing the situation, which is that we-the Committee really does understand that the time for rate increases and for shrinking the balance sheet has come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would just say, I would go back to "the economy is very strong," as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I-it's clearly time to raise interest rates and begin the balance sheet shrinkage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I just wanted to say that as I looked around the table at today's meeting, I saw a Committee that's acutely aware of the need to return the economy to price stability and [is] determined to use our tools to do exactly that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, if you look at the SEP, you've got people getting close to or even above, in many cases, their estimate of the longer-run neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I understand that doesn't do it for real rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you go out a year or two, many people are, in their forecasts, are having tight policy from a real interest rate standpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we don't know what's going to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do know that we're going to deploy our tools to achieve our goals-and that includes the price-stability goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So part of inflation coming down at the very beginning is clearly to do with factors other than our policy, and those would include, potentially, the supply chain is getting a little bit better, certainly base effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're lapping-as you know, when you look at a 12-month trailing window, you're lapping very high inflation in March, April, May, June of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there should be some effects from that in the 12-month picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really what we're looking for, though, is month-by-month inflation coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so it's really, it's all the things we've been talking about, you know, that really haven't helped much, including the shift away from goods and back to services, including supply chains getting better, including labor force participation-all those things that have been sticky and not happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But a big part of it is, though, is the base effects I mentioned as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think monetary policy starts to bite on inflation, and on growth, with a lag, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so you would see that more in '23 and '24.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But also, remember we started talking about rate increases last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For some months now, financial conditions have already incorporated a significant number of rate increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The effect, the moves are already priced into the market for a few months now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the clock is running on that, and I think some of that will be seen in the second half of the year as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on the regulatory portfolio, I would just say this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we have an obligation to carry out under the law in supervision and regulation, and we're doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what's happening is, things are coming to the full Board, and we're voting on them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've looked at, you know, a number of proposals for mergers and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we don't have a Vice Chair for Supervision, as you mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And a good number of things have come straight to the Board for approval.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't-Neil, I've never talked about my own SEP projection.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's in there, but I, you know, I think Fed Chairs have generally not done that, because we just haven't done it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's because we're, you know, we have to put together the consensus on the Committee and present that consensus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in terms of the pacing of it, I would just point out that that is-there's seven remaining meetings this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This isn't something we discuss or debate or agree on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's seven remaining meetings, and there's seven rate hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would add there's also the shrinkage of the balance sheet, which, you people do the math different ways, but that might be the equivalent of another rate increase just from the runoff of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't made any decisions on front-end loading or going steadily through the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, you know, if you look at the SEP, a good number of participants do see more than seven or eight increases this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I can't give you, I'm not going to try to give you a really specific test for what it would take to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I will say this, that we'll be looking at the data as they come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be looking to see whether the data show expected improvement on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be looking at the inflation outlook and making a judgement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we conclude that it would be appropriate to raise interest rates more quickly, then we'll do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have the tools that we need, and we're going to use them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as you can see, we have a plan over the course of this year to raise interest rates steadily and also to run off the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will take the necessary steps to ensure that high inflation does not become entrenched, while also supporting a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, if we conclude that it would be appropriate to move more quickly, we'll do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll leave it to others to make the judgment you asked for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, that's something we're watching report by report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're certainly, we noticed it in the last meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have expected services inflation to move back up to where it was, and that's part of what's happening is, in the case of some services, prices are still getting back up to where they were before the crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other cases, it's pretty clear that inflation has spread more broadly across services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meanwhile, we see some progress on the good side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, really, in this latest report, it was confined to vehicles, which is, admittedly, a large category.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, as I mentioned, the Committee acutely feels its obligation to move to make sure that we restore price stability and is determined to use its tools to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our, if you look, our-first of all, there is no-you're looking at medians.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But understand that there's no, it's not something we voted on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look, people do have their in-by the end of this year, broadly, people are at or close to or, in some cases, above their estimates of longer-run neutral interest rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that should stop pushing-that should, in other words, that should be a removal of accommodation for monetary policy, basically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we will have done significant balance sheet runoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the next year, and just looking at the median, you're now above the, you know, above the, what people estimate to be the longer-run median.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, in many people's forecasts, that actually amounts to, you know, tight policy under, in real rates as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One is the connection between-in the economy we had before the pandemic, the connection between inflation and the level of the unemployment rate was not very tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But this is-clearly, what this is is an expectation that, really it amounts to that, the idea that wage increases, which are now running above the level that would be consistent over the long run with 2 percent inflation, will move back down to levels which are still very attractive, full-economy kind of-full-employment kind of wages, but not to a point where they're pushing up inflation anymore.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, there are a lot of factors causing inflation to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the reality is, there are many, many moving pieces, and we don't know what will actually happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But no matter what happens, this is a Committee that is determined to use its tools to make sure that higher inflation does not become entrenched.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we are determined on that front, and we'll deal with what comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we'll deal with what comes, whether it's better or worse.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, if you take a look at today's labor market, what you have is 1.7-plus job openings for every unemployed person.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a very, very tight labor market- tight to an unhealthy level, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in principle, if you were-let's say that our tools work about as you described, and the idea is, we're trying to better align demand and supply, let's just say in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it would actually, if you were just moving down the number of job openings so that they were more like one to one, you would have less upward pressure on wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You would have a lot less of a labor shortage, which is going on pretty much across the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're hearing from companies that they can't hire enough people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's really the thinking there, is, you know, these are fairly well-understood channels, interest sensitive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, basically, across the economy, we'd like to slow demand so that it's better aligned with supply; give supply, at the same time, time to recover; and get into a better, you know, a better alignment of supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'll say again, though, you know, we don't have a perfect crystal ball about the future, and we're prepared to use our tools as needed to restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, without price stability, there-you really can't have a sustained period of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's our-one of our most fundamental obligations is to maintain and restore, in this case, price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, the plan is to restore price stability while also sustaining a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is our intention, and we believe we can do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what we saw in the last cycle was that, over the course of a long, steady expansion, labor force participation outperformed expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that was just a, you know, it was a tight labor market, but it wasn't-it was nowhere near as tight as this labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it was a tight labor market, and so people stayed in the labor force longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It wasn't so much people coming back in the labor force after retirement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's not something that happens, in the aggregate, very much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, more labor force participation is tremendously welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, our policy does not in any way preclude that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a situation where wages have moved up at the highest rate in a very long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people are able to quit their jobs and move to better-paying jobs in the same industry or different industries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And once, you know, as we get past COVID well and truly, it becomes an even more attractive one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we hope that that will lead to more labor supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it also will, we think, help relieve some of the wage pressures that do put inflation more at risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That last part is, we'll have to see whether, empirically, it winds up, works out that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in principle, it ought to help with inflation as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not the only thing we're looking for, though, from inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking for help from a number of different places and, most importantly, from our own policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's how it reaches the real economy-by just the mechanisms you mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And remember that the financial conditions we had for the last couple of years were a function not only of very aggressive, and appropriately so, fiscal policy, but also highly accommodative monetary policy-the monetary policy settings that we put in place at the worst parts of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is very appropriate to move away from those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, yes, that will lead to some tightening in financial conditions in the form of higher interest rates and just the sorts of things-we're not targeting any one or more of those things, but financial conditions generally should move to a more normal level so that-because we know the economy no longer needs, or wants, these very highly accommodative, this stance, which, you know, so it's time to move to a more normal setting of financial conditions, and we do that by moving monetary policy itself to more normal levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say, we look at a broad range of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, when we tighten monetary policy, we do expect that they will adjust in sync over time with monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not any particular financial condition, but a broad range of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They will reflect to some extent-they reflect any number of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, yes, we need our policy to transmit to the real economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it does so through financial conditions, which means that, as we tighten policy or remove accommodation so that it's at least less accommodative, that broader financial conditions will also be less accommodative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, at our meeting today and yesterday, we made excellent progress toward agreeing on the parameters of a plan to shrink the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'd say we're now in a position to finalize and implement that plan so that we'll actually begin a runoff at a coming meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that could come as soon as our next meeting in May.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that that's how well our discussions went in the last two days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be mindful of the broader financial and economic context when we make the decision on timing, and we always want to use our tools to support macroeconomic and financial stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to avoid adding uncertainty to what's a highly uncertain situation already.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So all of that will go into the thinking of the timing around this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't want to get too much into the details, because we're literally just finalizing them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the framework is going to look very familiar to people who are familiar with the last time we did this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, it's much sooner in a cycle than last time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would also say that there'll be-I'm sure there'll be a more detailed discussion of our-in the minutes to our meeting that come out in three weeks, where I expect that it will lay out, you know, pretty much the parameters of what we're looking at, which I think will look quite familiar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that is that nothing in our new framework or in the changes that we made has caused us to wait longer to raise interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we said in the framework changes was-and this was really a reflection of what had happened for the preceding couple of decades, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we said was, if we see, you know, low unemployment, high employment, but we don't see inflation, then we're not going to raise rates 'til we actually see inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we said, and that was the sense of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was no sense in which, if we got a burst of really high inflation, we would wait to raise rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The framework is all about anchoring inflation expectations at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
