text: So I do hear this, you know, that the framework-really, we can't blame the framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then it was the reaction to it, and it was what it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it was not in any way caused by or related to the framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think our vision on this on the Committee is very, very clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see a labor market with a lot of momentum, great job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, there are threats to growth from, you know, from what's going on in Eastern Europe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, but, nonetheless, in the base case, there's a pretty broad expectation of strong growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the help we've been expecting and other forecasters have been expecting from supply-side improvement, labor force participation, bottlenecks, all those things getting better-it hasn't come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're looking now to using our tools to restore price stability, and we're committed to doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you see that, I think, in the Summary of Economic Projections.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you see that in the decision we make, and you'll continue to see it in the decisions we make, going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The goal, of course, is to restore price stability while also sustaining a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have a dual mandate, and they're sort of equal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, as I said earlier, you know, price stability is an essential goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, it's a precondition, really, for achieving the kind of labor market that we want, which is a strong and sustained labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We saw the benefits of a long expansion, a sustained labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It pulled people back in, and there were really no imbalances in the economy that threatened the long expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It, just, the pandemic arrived; it was just a completely exogenous event.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, of course, want to achieve, you know, price stability with a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do understand also that, really, you can't have maximum employment for any sustained period without price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we need to focus on price stability particularly, because the labor market is so strong and the economy is so strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We feel like the economy can handle tighter monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I'd start by just assuring everyone that we're fully committed to bringing inflation back down and also sustaining the economic expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do understand that these higher prices, no matter what the source, have real effects on people's well- being.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's really, especially, on people who use most of their income to buy essentials like food, housing, and transportation, where-I mean, we've all seen charts that show, if you're a middle-income person, you've got room to absorb some inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you're at the lower end of the income spectrum, it's very hard because you're spending most of your money already on necessities, and the price is going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it has been a difficult time for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do anticipate that inflation will move back down, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It may take longer than we like, but I'm confident that we'll use our tools to bring inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the way that works, I would explain, is, as we raise interest rates, that should gradually slow down demand for the interest-sensitive parts of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so what we would see is demand slowing down, but just enough so that it's better matched with supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, as I just said, you know, I think we do understand very much, and we very much take to heart, that it's our obligation to restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we've had price stability for a very long time and maybe come to take it for granted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm old enough to remember what very high inflation was like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're strongly committed as a Committee to not allowing this higher inflation to become entrenched and to use our tools to bring inflation back down to more normal levels, which-our target is 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I just would want people to understand that, and that's-but the way we do that is by raising interest rates and by shrinking our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so financial conditions will become, at the margin, less supportive of various kinds of economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That will slow the economy, while also allowing the labor market to remain very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the good news is, the economy and the labor market are quite strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means the economy, we think, can handle interest rate increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I, you know, I say that our intention is to bring inflation back down to 2 percent, while still sustaining a strong labor market and that the economy is very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at where forecasts are, people are forecasting growth that's strong within the context of U.S. potential economic output.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And to the extent the data come in different, then, of course, our policy will adapt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do believe that our policy is the appropriate one for this forecast, and we believe that we can bring down inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We believe that we can do so while sustaining a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market is-it's not strong in the ordinary sense of the word.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have not seen a labor market where there are 1. job openings for every unemployed person or where there, if you add job openings to those who are employed, that's actually substantially a larger number than the size of the workforce, than the number of people who actually count themselves as in the workforce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is a situation where demand is higher than supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they-so we need to use our tools to move supply and demand back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't think we need to do this alone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we certainly are prepared to use our tools-and we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so, of course, central bankers around the world are generally very in favor of these sanctions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But let me say this: Sanctions are really the business of the elected government, and that's true everywhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the Administration and the Treasury Department, in particular, and other agencies-they create these sanctions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're there to provide technical expertise, but they're not, it's not our decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I'm reluctant to comment on sanctions really much because, again, they're not for us [to decide].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And these are really the province of elected governments, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the way I would say it is this: We, first of all, I would agree with the premise that wages moving up is a great thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, that's how the standard of living rises over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, generally, it's driven over long periods by rising productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what we have now, if you look at these, the wage increases that we have, we look at a-we're blessed with a range of measures of wages that all measure different things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But right now, they're all showing the same thing, which is that the increases-not the levels, but the increases-are running at levels that are well above what would be consistent with 2 percent inflation, our goal, over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that may be-we don't know how persistent that phenomenon will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really, I think, the sense of your question about a wage-price spiral; is that something that's going to start happening and become entrenched in the system?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can see, for example, in some sectors that got very high wage increases early on, those wage increases looked like they may have slowed down to a normal level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it comes back to, you know, what I'm saying here-which is, there's a misalignment of demand and supply, particularly in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that is leading to wages moving up at ways that are not consistent with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we need to use our tools to, you know, guide inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that would be in the context of an extraordinarily strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think this labor market can handle, as I mentioned, tighter monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, yes, wages are moving up faster than is consistent with 2 percent inflation, but it's good to see that moving up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it wouldn't be sustainable over too long of a period to see them moving up that much higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's because of this misalignment between supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We got more than we expected during the last cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do expect that we'll get people coming back in the labor market, particularly as COVID becomes less and less of a factor in many people's lives, something we all wish.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we are not-we don't have the luxury of 20/20 hindsight in actually implementing real-time decisions in the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, so the question is-the right question is, did you make the right decisions based on what you knew at the time?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's not the question I was answering, which is knowing what you know now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if we knew now-of course, if we knew now that these supply blockages, really, and the inflation resulting from them in collision with, you know, very strong demand, if we knew that that was what was going to happen, then in hindsight, yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, so, but that's a separate question from your other question, which is "behind the curve."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I don't have the luxury of looking at it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we are, we have our tools-powerful tools-and the Committee is very focused on using them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're acutely aware of the need to restore price stability while keeping a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what I saw today was a Committee that is strongly committed to achieving price stability, in particular, and prepared to use our tools to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're not going to wait so long that we have to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one wants to have to really put restrictive monetary policy on, in order to get inflation back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, frankly, the need is one of getting back up, getting rates back up to more neutral levels as quickly as we practicably can and then moving beyond that, if that turns out to be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as you can see, it is appropriate in the sense that, [in] people's [contributions to the] SEPs, they do write down levels of interest rates that are above their estimate of the longer-run neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's also a range of estimates, too, as you will see if you look at the details of the SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: percent unemployment is just about as low as it's been in 50 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say that I expect, and Committee members generally expect, that we'll get some additional participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people will be coming back into the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that will, of course, tend to hold the unemployment rate up a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would also expect, though, that job creation will slow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job creation has been, you know, more than half a million per month in recent months-very, very strong, particularly for this stage of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we think- with fiscal policy less supportive, with monetary policy less supportive, we think that job creation will slow as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is certainly possible that the unemployment would go down further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But so I would expect those to be relatively limited because of the additional supply and also just the slowing in job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Implications for inflation-really, the wages matter a fair amount for companies, particularly in the service sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages are running high, the highest they've run in quite some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they are one good example, or good illustration, really, of how tight the labor market really is, the fact that wages are running at the highest level in many decades.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's because of an imbalance between supply and demand in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think through our policies-through further healing in the labor market, higher rates, for example, of vacancy filling and things like that, and more people coming back in-we'd like to think that supply and demand will come back into balance and that, therefore, wage inflation will moderate to still high levels of wage increases, but ones that are more consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would say it this way: There's a path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a path by which we would be able to have demand moderate in the labor market and therefore have vacancies come down without unemployment going up, because vacancies are at such an extraordinarily high level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There're 1. vacancies for every unemployed person, 11. million vacancies, 6 million unemployed people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we haven't been in that place on the vacancy, sort of the vacancy/unemployed curve, the Beveridge curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't been at that sort of level of a ratio in the modern era.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in principle, it seems as though by moderating demand, we could see vacancies come down and, as a result-and they could come down fairly significantly and, I think, put supply and demand at least closer together than they are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that would give us a chance to get inflation down, get wages down, and then get inflation down without having to slow the economy and have a recession and have unemployment rise materially.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, I would say, I think we have a good chance to have a soft or softish landing or outcome, if you will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'll give you a couple of reasons for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One is, households and businesses are in very strong financial shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're looking at, you know, excess savings on balance sheets-excess in the sense that they're substantially larger than the prior trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market is, as I mentioned, very, very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so it doesn't seem to be anywhere close to a downturn.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Therefore, the economy is strong and is well positioned to handle tighter monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, but I'll say, I do expect that this will be very challenging; it's not going to be easy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it may well depend, of course, on events that are not under our control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But our job is to use our tools to try to achieve that outcome, and that's what we're going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a 75-basis-point increase is not something the Committee is actively considering.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we are doing is, we raised [the funds rate by] 50 basis points today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've said that, again, assuming that economic and financial conditions evolve in ways that are consistent with our expectations, there's a broad sense on the Committee that additional 50- basis-point increases should be on the table for the next couple of meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to make those decisions at the meetings, of course, and we'll be paying close attention to the incoming data and the evolving outlook as well as to financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, finally, of course, we will be communicating to the public about what our expectations will be as they evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the test is really just as I laid it out-economic and financial conditions evolving broadly in line with expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I think expectations are that we'll start to see inflation, you know, flattening out-and not necessarily declining yet, but we'll see more evidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen some evidence that core PCE inflation is perhaps either reaching a peak or flattening out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll want to really feel like we're making some progress there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to make these decisions, and there'll be a lot more information.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just think we want to see that information as we get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a very difficult environment to try to give forward guidance 60, 90 days in advance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are just so many things that can happen in the economy and around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we're leaving ourselves room to look at the data and make a decision as we get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we'd want to see evidence that inflation is moving in a direction that gives us more comfort.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I said, we've got two months now where core inflation is a little lower, but we're not looking at that as a reason to take some comfort.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think we need to really see that our expectation is being fulfilled-that inflation, in fact, is under control and starting to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, our expectation is, if we see what we expect to see, then we would have 50-basis-point increases on the table at the next two meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we talk about the neutral rate, we're really talking about the rate that neither pushes economic activity higher nor slows it down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the current estimates on the Committee are sort of 2 to 3 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's an estimate for an economy that's at full employment and 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, really, what we're doing is, we're raising rates expeditiously to what we see as the broad range of plausible levels of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we know that there's not a bright line drawn on the road that tells us when we get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to be looking at financial conditions, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our policy affects financial conditions, and financial conditions affect the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to be looking at the effect of our policy moves on financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we're going to be looking at the effects on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to be making a judgment about whether we've done enough to get us on a path to restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if that path happens to involve levels that are higher than estimates of neutral, then we will not hesitate to go to those levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, there's a sort of false precision in the discussion that we as policymakers don't really feel.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you're going to raise rates, and you're going to be kind of inquiring how that is affecting the economy through financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, if higher rates are required, then we won't hesitate to deliver them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't really see strong evidence of that yet, but that does not in any way make us comfortable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if you look at short-term inflation expectations, they're quite elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you can look at that and say, "Well, that's because people expect inflation to come down."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in fact, inflation expectations [at longer horizons] come down fairly sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Longer-term inflation expectations have been reasonably stable but have moved up to-but only to levels where they were in 2014, by some measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's a fair description of the picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see that companies have the ability to raise prices, and they're doing that, but there have been price shocks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I just think it takes you back to the basic point-was that we know we need to expeditiously move our policy rate up to ranges of more normal, neutral levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we need to look around and keep going if we don't see that financial conditions have tightened adequately or that the economy is behaving in ways that suggest that we're not where we need to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, you don't see those things yet, but I would say there's no basis for feeling comfortable about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just something that we can't allow to happen, and so we'll look at it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And to the extent we can't affect, really, oil prices or other commodity prices or food prices and things like that, so we can't affect those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that-you can see that in the labor market, where demand is substantially in excess of supply of workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you can see it in the product markets as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I guess I'm just pointing out that-a couple of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For both the situation in Ukraine and the situation in China, they're likely to, both, add to headline inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people are going to be suffering from that, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People almost suffer more from food and energy shocks then, but-even though they don't actually tell us much about the future path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the second thing is that they're both capable of preventing further progress in supply chains healing or even making supply chains temporarily worse.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So they're going to weigh on the process of global supply chain healing, which is going to affect broader inflation, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in a way, they're two further negative shocks that have hit really in the last, you know, 60 days, 90 days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I'll just say: For now, we're focused on doing the job we need to do on demand, and there's plenty to be done there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, if you look at it, it's essentially almost two to one, job vacancies to unemployed people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There're more than 5 million more employed plus job openings than there are the size of the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's an imbalance there that we have to do our work on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A very difficult situation-you know, you would look at core inflation, which wouldn't include the commodity price shocks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that's one of the reasons we would tend to focus on that, because we can have more of an effect on that, but it would be a very difficult situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we have to be sure that inflation expectations remain anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I mean, that's part of our job, too, so we'd be watching that carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it puts any central bank in a very difficult situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Okay, so in terms of the vacancies-to-unemployment ratio, we don't have a goal in mind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no specific number that we're saying, "We've got to get to that."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's really, you've got to get to a place where the labor market appears to be more in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that depends not only on the level of those things-it also, it depends on how well the matching functions in the labor markets are working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Because, you know, the longer these expansions go on, you can get very efficient with all of that, and the Beveridge curve shifts out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say we were- you know, I think, I think when we got to one-to-one in the, you know, in the late teens, we thought that was a pretty good number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we'd like to see is progress, but we're not really looking at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking at wages, and we're looking at, ultimately, inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, there are a bunch of channels through which policy works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can think of it as, you know, interest-sensitive spending, and then you can think of another big one as asset values broadly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there're big models with, you know, a lot of different channels that are related to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we don't focus on any one market-the equity market or the housing market-we focus on financial conditions broadly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we wouldn't be targeting any one market, as you suggest, for going up or down or taking a view on whether it's at a good level or a bad level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just would be looking at very broad measures of financial conditions-all the different financial conditions indexes, for example, which include equity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But they also include debt and other, many other things-credit spreads, things like that-too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, first, the first thing to say is that we understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And some of us are old enough to have lived through high inflation, and many aren't.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just something people don't-when they experience it for the first time, you're paying more for the same thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you're a normal economic person, then you probably don't have that much extra to spend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's immediately hitting your spending on groceries, on, you know, on gasoline, on energy, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's our job to make sure that inflation of that unpleasant, high nature doesn't get entrenched in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we're here for, one of the main things we're here for-perhaps the most fundamental thing we're here for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the way we do that is, we try to get supply and demand back in sync with each other, back in balance, so that the economy is under less stress and inflation will go down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, the process of getting there involves higher rates-so higher mortgage rates, higher borrowing rates, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Everyone- particularly people on fixed incomes and at the lower part of the income distribution are better off with stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we need to do everything we can to restore stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll do it as quickly and effectively as we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think we have a good chance to do it without a significant increase in unemployment or, you know, a really sharp slowdown.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, we think about the medium and longer term, and everyone will be better off if we can get this job done-the sooner, the better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we see, you know, household spending and business investment as fairly strong- and even in the first quarter, which was relatively slow on some other fronts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and the labor market-if you look at the labor market, for people who are out of work and looking, there are lots of job opportunities for-wages are moving up and at rates that haven't been seen in quite a long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a good time to be a worker looking to, you know, either change jobs or get a wage increase in your current job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a strong economy, and nothing about it suggests that it's close to, or vulnerable to, a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, of course, given events around the world and fading fiscal policy effects and higher rates, you could see some slower economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Certainly, it will not be-last year was an extraordinarily strong growth year as we recovered from the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But most forecasters have growth this year at, you know, at a solid pace above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and as I said, I think we have a good chance to restore price stability without a recession-without, you know, a severe downturn; without materially high, higher unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Businesses can't find the people to hire-they can't find them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there should be room, in principle, to reduce that surplus demand without putting people out of work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The issue will come that we don't have precision surgical tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have, essentially, interest rates, the balance sheet, and forward guidance, and they're famously blunt tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one thinks this will be easy, no one thinks it's straightforward, but there is certainly a plausible path to this, and I do think we've got a good chance to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, our job is not to rate the chances-it is to try to achieve it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are a range of opinions, though, and that's only appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's really the Fed that has responsibility for price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we take whatever arrives at the Fed in terms of fiscal activity, we take it as a given, and we don't evaluate it-it's not our job, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we look at it as our job, given all the factors that are happening, to try to sustain maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if Congress or the Administration has ways to help with inflation, I would encourage that, but I'm not going to get into making recommendations or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not, it's really not our role-we need to stay in our lane and do our job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we get inflation back under control, then maybe I can, you know, give other people advice [laughter].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, we need to focus on, just focus on doing our job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's certainly possible that we'll need to move policy to levels that we see as restrictive as opposed to just neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we do conclude that we need to do that, then we won't hesitate to do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll say again, there's no bright line, you know, that you're stepping over.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're really looking at what our policy stance is and what the market is forecasting for it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're looking at financial conditions and how that's affecting the economy and making a judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we won't be arguing about whose model of the neutral rate is better than the other one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's much more about a practical application of our policy tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I am, of course-who isn't an admirer of Paul Volcker?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I knew him just a little bit and have tremendous admiration for him.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I- But I would phrase it this way: He had the courage to do what he thought was the right thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was that he always did-he always did-what he thought was the right thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you read his last autobiography, that really comes through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, we do see, though-we see restoring price stability as absolutely essential for the country in coming years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Without price stability, the economy doesn't work for anybody, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so it's really essential, particularly for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you think about it, like if you look at the last cycle, we had a very, very-longest expansion cycle in our recorded history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the last two, three years, you had the benefits of this tight labor market going to people in the lower quartiles.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it was, you know, racial, wealth, and income-not wealth, but income gaps were coming down, wage gaps.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But to get back to anything like that place, you need price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, basically, we've been hit by historically large inflationary shocks since the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is, we have a pandemic, we have the highest unemployment, you know, in-since the Depression.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then we have this outsized response from fiscal policy and monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then we have a war in Ukraine, which is cutting the commodity, you know, patch in half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's been a series of inflationary shocks that are really different from anything people have seen in 40 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have to look through that and look at the economy that's coming out the other side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we need to somehow find price stability out of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's obviously going to be very challenging, I think, because you do have, you know, numerous supply shocks, which are famously difficult to deal with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I didn't-if I said "necessary," I meant to say "appropriate."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not going to be erecting a high barrier for this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the point is, we're a very long way from neutral now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're moving there expeditiously, and we'll continue to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The decision for about how high to go will be on the table to be made when we reach neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I expect we'll get there expeditiously, as I've mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not that we don't want to-making that decision today wouldn't really mean anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I'll say again, if we do believe that it's appropriate to go to those levels, we won't hesitate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was just, pick a date, you know, and that happened to be the date that we picked.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's not going to have any macroeconomic significance over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Sometimes we publish these calendars on the first day of the month, and that's what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the effect, I mean, I would just stress how uncertain the effect is of shrinking the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we run these models-and everyone does in this field-and make estimates of what will be, how do you measure, you know, a certain quantum of balance sheet shrinkage compared to quantitative easing?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, people estimate that, broadly, on the path we're on-and this will be taken, probably, too seriously-but sort of ¼ percent, one rate increase over the course of a year at this pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would just say, with very wide uncertainty bands-very wide.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are other estimates that are much smaller than that, by the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that it is part of returning to more normal, more neutral financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, our strategy is to set up a plan and have it operate and really have, you know, have the interest rate be the active tool of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of speaking to the American people, so I feel like sometimes I just want to remind us, really, that that's who we work for, and that it's inflation that people are feeling all over the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's very important that they know that we know how painful it is and that we are working hard on fixing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And a good example of why would be-in the fourth quarter of last year, as we started talking about tapering sooner and then raising rates this year, you saw financial markets reacting, you know, very appropriately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not to bless any particular day's measure, but the way financial markets, the forward rate curve has tightened in response to our guidance and our actions really amplifies our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-monetary policy is working through expectations now, to a very large extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look at financial conditions, the two-year [rate] is at 280 [basis points] now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In September, I think it was at 20 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that shows that the markets think that our forward guidance is credible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we want to keep it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so, as I mentioned, you can see places where the demand is substantially in excess of supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what you're seeing as a result of that is prices going up and at unsustainable levels, levels that are not consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so what our tools do is that as we raise interest rates, demand moderates: it moves down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Interest rates, you know-businesses will invest a little bit less, consumers will spend a little bit less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, getting those, getting supply and demand back, you know, back in balance, is what gives us 2 percent inflation, which is what gives the economy a footing where people can lead successful economic lives and not worry about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, so, yes, there may be some pain associated with getting back to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, the big pain over time is in not dealing with inflation and allowing it to become entrenched.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, look, I think what you've seen is-really, I would say, in the middle of last fall-there was a time when our policy stance was still pretty much in sync with what the data were saying.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you remember, there were a couple of weak jobs reports.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And inflation-month by month, inflation had come down till September, a few months in a row, stayed low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then around the end of October, we got three or four really strong readings that just said, no, this is a much stronger economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And by the way-then, with the restatement of the jobs numbers, it looked like the job market was much more even and stronger in the second half of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Anyway, we got an ECI reading-employment compensation, [employment cost] index reading-the Friday before the November meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think it became clear to the Committee that we needed to adjust and adapt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ever since then, really ever since then, we've been adapting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, you know-the Committee moved by the time of the December meeting to a median [in participants' 2022 projections] of three rate increases, then to a median of seven increases at the March meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why I say-and I actually mentioned this at the March meeting-that no one should look at any single SEP as sort of a real resting place for 90 days, because we're in a fast-evolving situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I told you the guidance-that broad support on the Committee to have 50-basis-point hikes on the table at the next couple of meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And by the way, other forecasters have been doing the same thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's just us adapting to the data and to the situation and using our tools to deal with it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So unemployment rates for all racial groups have come down a lot and are now much closer to where they were before the pandemic hit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the bigger point is this: I do not, at this time, see the two sides of the mandate as in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't, because you can see that the labor market is out of balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And companies can't hire, and wages are moving up at levels that would not, over time, be consistent with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, everyone loves to see wages go up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's a great thing, but you want them to go up at a sustainable level, because these wages are, to some extent, being eaten up by inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what that really means is, to get the kind of labor market we really want to get, we really want to have a labor market that serves all Americans, especially the people in the lower-income part of the distribution, especially them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've got to get back to price stability so that we can have a labor market where people's wages aren't being eaten up by inflation and where we can have a long expansion, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had-several of the longest expansions in U.S. history have been in the last 40 years, and that's because it's been a time of low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And long expansions are good for people and good for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to think in the, in the medium and longer term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think that the best thing for everyone is for us to get back to price stability to support, really, a sustained period of strong labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you know, we always aim to provide as much clarity as we can about our policy intentions subject to the inherent uncertainty in the economic outlook, because we think monetary policy is more effective when market participants understand how policy will evolve, when they understand our objective function, our reaction function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in the current highly unusual circumstances with inflation well above our goal, we think it's helpful to provide even more clarity than usual-again, subject to uncertainty in the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think over the course of this year, financial markets have responded and have, generally, shown that they understand the path we're laying out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's what we generally think about guidance, and that's why we offer it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, when we offered that-when I offered that guidance at the last meeting, I did say that it was subject to the economy performing about in line with expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also said that if the economy performed-if data came in worse than expected, then we would consider moving even more aggressively.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we got the CPI data and also some data on inflation expectations late last week, and we thought for a while, and we thought, well, this is the appropriate thing to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And do you wait six weeks to do it at the next meeting?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the answer is, that's not where we are with this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we decided we needed to go ahead, and so we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you take a step back, what we're looking for is compelling evidence that inflationary pressures are abating and that inflation is moving back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'd like to see that in the form of a series of declining monthly inflation readings- that's what we're looking for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by this point, we had actually been expecting to see clear signs of at least inflation flattening out and, ideally, beginning to decline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've said that we'd be data dependent, focused on incoming data, highly attentive to inflation risks-the things that I mentioned to Howard moments ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So contrary to expectations, inflation again surprised to the upside.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Indicators-some indicators of inflation expectations have risen, and projections of [inflation] this year have moved up notably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we thought that strong action was warranted at this meeting, and today we delivered that in the form of a 75 basis point rate hike, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the point of it, really, is this: We've been moving rates up expeditiously to more normal levels, and over the course of the seven months since we pivoted and began moving in this direction, we've seen financial conditions tighten, and appropriately so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the federal funds rate, even after this move, is at 1. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, the Committee is moving rates up expeditiously to more normal levels, and we came to the view that we'd like to do a little more front-end loading on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that the SEP gives you the levels that people think are appropriate at given points in time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This was really about the speed in which we would get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, 75 basis points today-I said the next meeting could well be about a decision between 50 and 75.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That would put us, at the end of the July meeting, in that range-in that more normal range, and that's a desirable place to be, because you begin to have more optionality there about the speed with which you would proceed going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just talking about the SEP for a second: What it really says is that Committee participants widely would like to see policy at a modestly restricted-restrictive level at the end of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's six months from now, and so much data [can accrue] and so much can happen, so remember how highly uncertain this is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But so that is generally a range of 3 to 3½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's where people are, and that's what they want to see, knowing what they know now and understanding that we need to be-we need to show resolve but also be flexible [in responding] to incoming data as we see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If things are better, we don't need to do that much, and if they're not, then we either do that much or possibly even more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in any case, it will be very data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then you're looking at next year, and what you're seeing is, people see more-a bit more tightening and a range of maybe 3½ to 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's generally what people see as the appropriate path for getting inflation under control and starting back down and getting back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So 75 basis points seemed like the right thing to do at this meeting, and that's what we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the question really is, how high does the rate really need to go?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is-the estimates on the Committee are in that range of 3½ to 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, you can think about the longer-run neutral rate, you can compare it to that, and we think that's in the mid-2s.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can look at asset prices, you can look at the effect they're having on the economy, rates, asset prices, credit spreads-all of those things go into that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can also look at the yield curve and ask, all along the yield curve, where is the policy rate?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So for much of the yield curve now, real rates are positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the short end of the yield curve in the early years, you don't have real-you have negative rates still.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that really is one data point-it's one part of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think-I have to look at it this way: We move the policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have, of course, ways-rigorous ways to think about it, but, ultimately, it comes down to, do we think financial conditions are in a place where they're having the desired effect on the economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that desired affect is, we'd like to see demand moderating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'd like to see the labor market getting better in balance between supply and demand, and that can happen [as a result of developments coming] both from supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, there's-demand is substantially higher than available supply, though, so we feel that there's a role for us in moderating demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are the things we can affect with our policy tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are many things we can't affect, and those would be, you know, the things-the commodity price issues that we're having around the world due to the war in Ukraine and the fallout from that, and also just all of the supply-side things that are still pushing upward on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's really how I think-how I think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's certainly in the range of plausible numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, honestly, though, that would be-you would have positive real rates, I think, and inflation coming down by then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you'd have positive real rates across the [yield] curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that the neutral rate is pretty low these days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would think it would, but you know what?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not going to be completely model driven about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be looking at this, keeping our eyes open, and reacting to incoming data both on financial conditions and on what's happening in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at a broad range of inflation expectations-so you've got the public, you've got surveys of the public and of experts, and you've also got market based.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if you look across that broad range of data, what you see is that expectations are still in the place, very much in the place, where short-term inflation is going to be high but comes down sharply over the next couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, as you get away from this episode, they get back down close to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so this is really very important to us-that that remain the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if you look for most measures, most of the time, that's what you see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we even see a couple of indicators that bring that into question, we take that very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do not take this for granted-we take it very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the preliminary Michigan [survey] reading-it's a preliminary reading; it might be revised-nonetheless, it was quite eye-catching, and we noticed that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also noticed that the index of common inflation expectations at the Board has moved up after being pretty flat for a long time, so we're watching that, and we're thinking, "this is something we need to take seriously."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that is one of the factors, as I mentioned-one of the factors in our deciding to move ahead with 75 basis points today was what we saw in inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're absolutely determined to keep them anchored at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That was one of the reasons-the other was just the CPI reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to-I'll just say, we're going to react to the incoming data and appropriately, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't want to put a number on what that might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The main thing is to get rates up, and then pretty soon, we'll be in an area where we're-I think as you get closer to the end of the year, you're in a range where you've got restrictive policy, which is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Forty-year highs in inflation-we think that policy is going to need to be restrictive, and we don't know how restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think we're- again, we're going, we're resolved to take this on, but we're going to be flexible in the implementation of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, the overall exercise is that we try to be-provide as much clarity about our policy intentions as we can, because we think that makes monetary policy work better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's always a tradeoff, because you have to live with that guidance, and so you do it, and it helps a lot of the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, frankly, think this year has been a demonstration of how well it can work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With us having really just done very little in the way of raising interest rates, financial conditions have tightened quite significantly through the expectations channel, as we've made it clear what our plans are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that's been a very healthy thing to be happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would hope that our-it's always going to be-any guidance that we give is always going to be subject to things working out about as we expect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in this particular situation, you know, we're looking for something specific, and that is progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to see-inflation can't go down until it flattens out, and that's what we're looking to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we don't see that, then that's the kind of thing that will-even if we don't see progress for a longer period, that could cause us to react.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Soon enough, we will be seeing some progress at some point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would like to think, though, that our guidance is still credible, but it's always going to be conditional on what happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is an unusual situation, to get, you know, some data late in, during blackout, pretty close to-very close to our meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Very unusual to [have] one that would actually change the outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I've only seen-in my 10-years-plus here at the Fed, I've only seen something like that, even close to that, one or two times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't think it's something that'll come up a great deal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what we want to see is a series of declining monthly readings for inflation, and we'd like to see inflation headed down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know-and right now, our policy rate is well below neutral, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, soon enough, we'll have our policy rate- let's assume the world works out about like the SEP says: The policy rate will be up where we think it should be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then the question would be: Do you slow down?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Does it make you- you'll be making these judgments about, is it appropriate now to slow down-from 50 to 25, let's say-or speed up?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's the kind of thinking we'll be doing, and, again, we're looking-ultimately, we're not going to declare victory until we see a series of these, really see convincing evidence, compelling evidence, that inflation is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's what I mean by-that's what it would take for us to say, "Okay, we think this job is done."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Because we saw-and, frankly, we saw last year-inflation came down over the course of the summer and then turned right around and went back up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we're going to be careful about declaring victory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But our-again, the implementation of our policy is going to be flexible and sensitive to incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I think that-I do think that our objective, and this is what's reflected in the SEP, but our objective, really, is to bring inflation down to 2 percent while the labor market remains strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that what's becoming more clear is that many factors that we don't control are going to play a very significant role in deciding whether that's possible or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there I'm thinking, of course, of commodity prices, the war in Ukraine, supply chain [developments], things like that, where we really-the monetary policy stance doesn't affect those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But having said that, there is a path for us to get there-it's not getting easier; it's getting more challenging because of these external forces-and that path is to move demand down, and you have a lot of surplus demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you have two job vacancies, essentially, for every person actively seeking a job, and that has led to a real imbalance in wage negotiating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You could get to a place where that ratio was at a more normal level, and you wouldn't-you would expect to see those wage pressures move back down to a level where people are still getting healthy wage increases, real wage increases, but at a level that's consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you could say the same thing about some of the product markets where there's just excess capacity and really where the strong demand has gone into-sorry, where they're capacity constrained, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you have, effectively, what we think of as a vertical supply curve or close to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So demand comes in, and it's very strong, and it shows up in higher prices-not higher quantities, not more cars, because they can't make the cars because they don't have the semiconductors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When demand comes down, you could see-and it's not guaranteed-but you could see prices coming down more than the typical economic relationships that you see in the textbooks would suggest, because of the unusual situation we're in on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is not going to be easy, and there-again, it's our objective, but, as I mentioned, it's going to depend to some extent on factors we don't control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the SEP, we have unemployment going up to 4 point-the median is 4. percent-of course, [there is] a range of actual forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would characterize that, if you were to get inflation down to, you know, on its way down to 2 percent and the unemployment rate went up to 4. percent, that's still a historically low level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We hadn't seen-we hadn't seen rates, unemployment rates below 4 percent until a couple years ago for-we'd seen it for, like, one year in the last 50.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a 4. percent unemployment rate with inflation well on its way to 2 percent-I think that would be-I think that would be a successful outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're not looking to have a higher unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that I would certainly look at that as a successful outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-again, we're not, we don't seek to put people out of work, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We never think, "Too many people are working, and fewer people need to have jobs."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we also think that you really cannot have the kind of labor market we want without price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have to go back and establish price stability so we can have that kind of labor market, and that's a labor market where workers are getting wage increases-maybe the workers at the lower end of the spectrum are getting the biggest wage increases, as they were before the pandemic-where participation is high, where there's lots of job opportunities, where it's just a really-I mean, the labor market we had before the pandemic was-that's what we want to get back to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you see disparities between various groups at historic lows.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, to get there-it's not going to happen with the levels of inflation we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have to restore that, and it really is in service, in the medium and longer term, of the kind of labor market we want and hope to achieve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're trying to achieve 2 percent inflation consistent with a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Clearly, it's our goal to bring about 2 percent inflation while keeping the labor market strong, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The SEP has inflation getting down to 2, a little above 2 percent in 2024, with unemployment at 4. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is a strong labor market-this is a good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, there are pathways to do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But those pathways have become much more challenging due to factors that are not under our control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, thinking here of the fallout from the war in Ukraine, which has brought a spike in prices of energy, food, fertilizer, industrial chemicals, and also just the supply chains more broadly, which have been larger and longer lasting than anticipated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the sentence that we deleted said that we believe that appropriate monetary policy, effectively alone, can bring about the result of 2 percent inflation with a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so much of it is really not down to monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just didn't-the sentence isn't-it kind of says on its face that monetary policy alone can do this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's not-that just didn't seem appropriate, so we took the sentence out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, yeah, I think you've seen-again, we've been expecting progress, and we didn't get that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I also think the situation, really-since the consequences of the Ukraine war become more and more clear, what you're seeing is the situation getting more difficult.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you look around the world-I mean, lots of countries are-lots of countries are looking at inflation of 10 percent, and it's largely due to commodities prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so-and we're seeing them here: gas prices at all-time highs, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is really-and, by the way, headline inflation, headline inflation is important for expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People-the public's expectations, why would they be distinguishing between core inflation and headline inflation?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Core inflation is something we [on the Committee] think about because it is a better predictor of future inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-expectations are very much at risk due to high headline inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's become-the environment has become more difficult, clearly, in the last four or five months, and hence the need for the policy actions that we took today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Hence our resolution to get rates up and, ultimately, get them to where we think they need to be in coming months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, of course, watching very, very carefully for that and looking at the retail-the big store numbers and all that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I-but I think the fair summary of what we see is, you see continuing shifts in consumption, you see some things getting-sales going down, but overall spending is very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no sign of a broader slowdown that I can see in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People are talking about it a lot-consumer confidence is very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's probably related to gas prices and also just stock prices to some extent for other people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see job growth slowing, but it's still at quite robust levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see the economy slowing a bit but still growth levels-healthy growth levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would be hard to watch anything much more closely than we watch consumer spending, but we watch everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We watch business fixed investment, which actually has softened a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Consumption is 60-some percent of the economy, two-thirds of the economy, so, naturally, we spend a lot of time on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, there's a lot going on-there are a lot of flows back and forth-but, ultimately, it does appear that the U.S. economy is in a strong position and well positioned to deal with higher interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, of course, like all central banks do, look very, very carefully at core inflation because it is-it's a much better predictor, and it's much-it's a much better predictor of where inflation is going, and it's also more relevant to our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, the parts that don't go into core are mostly outside the scope of our tools, so we look at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's-the current situation is particularly difficult because of what I mentioned about expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can't affect, really-I mean, the energy prices are set by global commodity prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And most of food-not all of it, but most food prices are pretty heavily influenced by global commodity prices, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we have to be mindful of the potential effect on inflation expectations [coming] from headline [inflation readings].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a very difficult situation to be in, and we- again, we can't do much about the difference between [headline and core inflation rates due to] the elements that make up headline that are not in core.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people had that in hand when they-when their SEPs were submitted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-in other words, it's not in addition to what's in the SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The SEP-everyone's SEP reflects their thinking about this rate increase and what's going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the role that we can play-maybe the way to get at this is to say that the role that we can play is around demand, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be able to see-the areas that we can affect are those associated with excess demand, and we'll be able to see our effect on, for example, job openings in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that would tell us what's-that would tell us about wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages are not principally responsible for the inflation that we're seeing, but, going forward, they would be very important, particularly in the service sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's always a risk of going too far or going not far enough, and it's going to be a very difficult judgment to make, or maybe not-maybe it'll be really clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I will say, the worst mistake we could make would be to fail, which-it's not an option.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We really do, because everything-it's the bedrock of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you don't have price stability, the economy's really not going to work the way it's supposed to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It won't work for people-their wages will be eaten up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think that it's affecting expectations in any kind of fundamental way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that the public generally sees us as very likely to be successful in getting inflation down to 2 percent, and that's critical.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's absolutely key to the whole thing that we sustain that confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And many people are experiencing it, really, for the first time, because we haven't had anything like this kind of inflation in 40 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they're experiencing that, and that's showing up in their-in surveys and in all kinds of ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we understand that, and we understand the hardship that people are experiencing from high inflation, and we're determined to do what we can to get inflation back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-I'm not-clearly, it's an incredibly unpopular thing, and it's very painful for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess what I'm saying is, the question, the really critical question from the perspective of doing our job is making sure that the public does have confidence that we have the tools and will use them and they do work to bring inflation back down over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It will take some time, we think, to get inflation back down, but we will do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, I think, in my opening statement, inflation has started-it started off in quite narrow, very directly pandemic-related areas, and it's spread now broadly across the economy and into the services sector as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was really in the goods sector at the beginning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, particularly, you're seeing in travel now, if you've flown on a plane lately-planes are very full, and plane tickets are very expensive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of that will be pass- through of energy prices, but it's-so you're experiencing services inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the question-and then you see the Cleveland measure going up, and many other measures are going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a time when we're not seeing progress and we want to see progress, and that's really another part of why we did what we did today and why the SEP looks like it does.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see it as appropriate to get the policy rate up to restrictive levels, which would be, in the thinking of the Committee, somewhere in the range of 3 to 3½ percent by year-end.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then after that, you see what the rest of the SEP says.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think what's in the SEP would certainly meet that test.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you see-you're looking at getting back down to almost a 2 percent inflation by 2024, and the unemployment rate is still as low as 4. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That would be-I would call that as meeting that test.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's-I think there's-I don't want to be the handicapper here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just-that is our objective, and I do think it's possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Like I said, though, I think that events of the last few months have raised the degree of difficulty, created great challenges.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, the answer to the question, can we still do it-there's a much bigger chance now that it'll depend on factors that we don't control, which is, fluctuations and spikes in commodity prices could wind up taking that option out of our hands.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we just don't know, but we're focused on-very, very focused on getting inflation back down to 2 percent, which we think is essential for the benefit of the public and also to put us on a path back to a sustainably strong labor market like the one we had before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, financial conditions have tightened over the last seven months, and that's a good thing, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the federal funds rate, even after this increase, is at 1. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's hard to see how that is too high of a rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And even if we did another-so we're going to get here by the end of the summer, somewhere in the 2s probably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's not a rate that is calculated to bring a recession on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll-by then, we'll have seen a whole lot more data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned a couple times, the Committee's views are around a modestly restrictive stance, which will be in the 3 to 3½ percent range by the end of this year, but that's conditioned on that being the appropriate thing to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we see data going in a different direction, it'll be reflected in our policy, as you see today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be watching-if things go in a direction we don't expect, then we're going to adapt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, this is a highly uncertain environment-extraordinarily uncertain environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, we've been looking very carefully and hard at why inflation picked up so much more than expected last year and why it proved so persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We- it's hard to overstate the extent of interest we have in that question morning, noon, and night.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For-really, the context is this: For decades before the pandemic and the reopening, you had a world where inflation was dominated by disinflationary forces such as declining population or aging demographics, let's call it that, globalization enabled by technology, other factors, low productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So and that's how all the models work is, decades and decades of data-they look at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a very flat Philips curve world, and the supply shocks tend to be transient, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have now experienced an extraordinary series of shocks, if you think about it: the pandemic, the response, the reopening, inflation, followed by the war in Ukraine, followed by shutdowns in China-the war in Ukraine potentially having effects for years here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're aware that a different set of forces are driving the economy-we have been, obviously, for quite a while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation is behaving differently, and, in our thinking, it really is a question of very strong demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you couldn't get this kind of inflation without a change on the supply side, which is there for anybody to see, which is these blockages and shortages and people dropping out of the labor force and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've done a lot of work internally on, and thinking about, what all that means.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You don't-the thing is, you don't know whether those forces are-to what extent are they going to be sustained?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other words, will we go back to a world where it looks a little more like the old world, or are we really going to be in a world where major supply shocks go on and on?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The history is, you see these waves of supply shocks, as you did in the '70s, and then they go away, and sort of there's a "new normal," and things settle down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, honestly, we don't know what that's going to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, we have to find price stability in this new world and maximum employment in this new world where, clearly, inflationary forces are-you're seeing them everywhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, if you look around the world at where inflation levels are, it's absolutely extraordinary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, we're sort of in the middle of the pack, although I think we have, of course, a different kind of inflation than other people have, partly because our economy is stronger and more highly recovered.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've done a lot of introspection and work on that and-sorry, on QT, we've communicated really clearly to the markets about what we're going to do there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're phasing in-Treasury [security] issuance is down quite a lot, quite a lot from where it's been, so I have no reason to think-markets are forward looking, and they see this coming.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I have no reason to think it will lead to illiquidity and problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It seems to be kind of understood and accepted at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
