text: So rates were very low-a good place to start is that rates were very, very low for quite a while because of the pandemic and the need to do everything we could to support the economy when unemployment was 14 percent and the true unemployment rate was well higher than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that was a-rates are low, and now they're coming back up to more normal, or above, levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in the meantime, while rates were low and while demand was really high, obviously demand for housing changed from wanting to live in urban areas to some extent to living in single-family homes in the suburbs, famously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we saw prices moving up very, very strongly for the last couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that changes now, and rates have moved up-we're well aware that mortgage rates have moved up a lot-and you're seeing a changing housing market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You would think over time-I mean, so there's a tremendous amount of supply in the housing market of unfinished homes, and as those come on line-whereas the supply of finished homes, inventory of finished homes that are for sale, is incredibly low, historically low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So prices may keep going up for a while even in a world where rates are up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say if you're a homebuyer, somebody or a young person looking to buy a home, you need a bit of a reset.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need to get back to a place where supply and demand are back together and where inflation is down low again and mortgage rates are low again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this will be a process whereby we-ideally, we do our work in a way that the housing market settles in a new place and housing availability and credit availability are at appropriate levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we did judge that a 75 basis point increase was the right magnitude in light of the data and in the context of the ongoing increases in the policy rate that we've been making.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'd say that we wouldn't hesitate to, to make an even larger move than we did today if the Committee were to conclude that that was-that that were appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was very broad support for the move that we made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we had said many times that we were prepared to move aggressively, more aggressively, if inflation continued to disappoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why we did move to a more aggressive pace at the June meeting, as we said we would do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At this meeting, we continued at that more aggressive pace, as inflation has continued to disappoint, in the form of the June CPI reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I'd start by saying we've been saying we would move expeditiously to get to the range of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: [percent], and that's right in the range of what we think is neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the question is, how are we thinking about the path forward?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So one thing that hasn't changed is that-won't change-is that our focus is continuing to-is going to continue to be on using our tools to bring demand back into better balance with supply in order to bring inflation back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also said that we expect ongoing rate hikes will be appropriate and that we'll make decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we'll be looking at the incoming data, as I mentioned, and that'll start with economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Are we seeing the slowdown that we-the slowdown in economic activity-that we think we need?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's some evidence that we are at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be asking whether we see the alignment between supply and demand getting better, getting closer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our mandate is for headline, of course; it's not for core.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we look at core because core is, is actually a better indicator of headline and of all inflation going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be looking at them for-at those both, really-for what they're saying about the outlook rather than just simply for, for what they say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we'll be asking: Do we see inflationary pressures declining?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in light of all that data, the question we'll be asking is whether the stance of policy we have is sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation back down to our 2 percent target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's also worth noting that these rate hikes have been large, and they've come-they've come quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's likely that their full effect has not been felt by the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's probably some additional tightening, significant additional tightening, in the pipeline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the best-I think the Committee broadly feels that we need to get policy to at least to a moderately restrictive level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And maybe the best data point for that would be what we wrote down in our SEP at the-at the June meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the median [federal funds rate] for the end of this year, the median would've been between 3¼ and 3½ [percent].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, then, people wrote down 50 basis points higher than that for 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-even though that's now six weeks old, I guess, that's-that's the most recent reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we'll update that reading at the-at the September meeting in eight weeks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, as it relates to September, I said that another unusually large increase could be appropriate, but that's not a decision we're making now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's one that we'll make based on the data we see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to be making decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it's-we think it's time to just go to a meeting-by-meeting basis and not provide, you know, the kind of clear guidance that we had provided on the way to neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm going to start by pointing out that it's very hard to say with any confidence in normal times-in normal times-what the economy's going to be doing in 6 or 12 months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And to try to predict what the appropriate monetary policy would respond- response would be-of course, we do that in the SEP, but, nonetheless, you've got to take any estimates of what rates will be next year with a grain of salt, because there's so much uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's significantly more uncertainty now about the path ahead than I think there ordinarily is, and, ordinarily, it's quite high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, I would-the best data, the only data point I have for you really is the June SEP, which I think is just the most recent thing that the Committee's done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Since then, inflation has come in higher; economic activity has come in weaker than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But at the same time, I would say that's probably the best estimate of where the Committee's thinking is still, which is that we would get to a moderately restrictive level by the end of this year-by which I mean somewhere between 3 and 3½ percent-and that when the Committee sees further rate increases in 2023, as I mentioned, we'll update that, of course, at the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's really the best I can do on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't say it was-I think we didn't expect a good reading, but this one-this one was even worse than expected, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't talk about my own personal estimate of, of what the terminal rate would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do-I will write down that in-it's going to evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Obviously, it has evolved over the course-I think, for all participants, it has evolved over the course of the year as we learn how persistent inflation's going to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And by the time of the September meeting, we will have seen two more CPI readings and two more labor market readings and a significant amount of readings about economic activity and perhaps geopolitical developments, who knows.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's an eight-week intermeeting period, so I think we'll see quite a lot of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll make our decision at that meeting based on that data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's hard to deal with hypotheticals, but I just would say this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, you know, we would look at both, and we would ask-we'd be asking ourselves, are we confident that inflation is on a path down to 2 percent?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be making-you know, our policy stance will be set at a level, ultimately, at which we are confident that inflation is going to be moving down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you would-it would depend on a lot of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, as I mentioned, core inflation is a better predictor of inflation going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in ordinary times, you, you look through volatile moves in commodities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The problem with the current situation is that, that if you have a sustained period of supply shocks, those can actually start to undermine or to work-to work on de-anchoring inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The public doesn't distinguish between core and headline inflation in their thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's something we have to take into consideration in our policymaking even though our tools don't really work on, on some aspects of this, which are the supply-side issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I-as I mentioned, we think it's necessary to have growth slow down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And growth is going to be slowing down this year for a couple of reasons, one of which is that you're coming off of the very high growth of the reopening year of 2021.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We actually think we need a period of growth below potential in order to create some slack so that-so that the supply side can catch up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also think that there will be, in all likelihood, some softening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that they're probably necessary if we were to have-to get inflation-if we were to be able to get inflation back down on a path to 2 percent and ultimately get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to be-again, we're going to be focused on getting inflation back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-as I've said on other occasions, price stability is really the bedrock of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can't have a strong labor market without price stability for an extended period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We all want to get back to the kind of labor market we had before the pandemic, where differences between, you know, racial and gender differences and that kind of thing were at historic minimums, where participation was high, where inflation was low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to get back to that, but that's not happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's not going to happen without, without restoring price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's something we see as, as something that we simply must do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that in the-we don't see it as a tradeoff with, with the employment mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see it as a way to facilitate the sustained achievement of the employment mandate in the longer term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're trying to do just the right amount, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that there's a path for us to be able to bring inflation down while sustaining a strong labor market, as I mentioned, along with-in all likelihood-some, some softening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is- that's what we're trying to achieve, and we continue to think that there's a path to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that the path has, has clearly narrowed, really based on events that are outside of our control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I do think-as I said just now-that restoring price stability is just something that we have to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There, there isn't an option to fail to do that because that is the thing that enables you to have a strong labor market over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Without restoring price stability, you won't be able, over the medium and longer term, to actually have a strong-a sustained period of very strong labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, we serve both sides of the dual mandate, but we actually see them as well aligned on this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let me put it this way: We do see that there are two-sided risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There would be the risk of doing too much and, you know, imposing more of a downturn on the economy than, than was necessary, but the risk-the risk of doing too little and leaving the economy with this entrenched inflation, it only raises the cost.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you fail to deal with it in the near term, it only raises the cost of, of dealing with it later to the extent people start to see it as just part of their economic lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They start to factor high inflation into their decisions-when that-on a sustained basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When that starts to really happen, and we don't think that's happened yet, but when that starts to happen, it just gets that much harder.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I really do think that it's important that we-that we address this now and get it done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't-I do not think the U.S. is currently in a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason is, there are just too many areas of the economy that are-that are performing, you know, too well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, I would point to the labor market, in particular.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, it's true that growth is slowing for reasons that we understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, the growth was extraordinarily high last year, 5½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look at the labor market, you've got growth-I think, payroll jobs averaging 450,000 per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a remarkably strong level for, for this state of, of affairs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The unemployment rate at near a 50-year low at 3. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of the wage measures that we track are running very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is a very strong labor market, and it's just not consistent with- you know, 2. million people hired in the first half of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't make sense that the economy would be in recession with, with this kind of thing happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't think the U.S. economy's in recession right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ah, haven't seen it, and, and we'll just have to see what it says.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't-I mean, I would say, generally, the GDP numbers do have a tendency to be revised pretty significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just-it's just that it's very hard-it's very hard to cumulate [to an estimate of] U.S. GDP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And a lot of-a lot of work and judgment goes into that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you tend to take first GDP reports, I think, with a-with a grain of salt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those are-those are the toughest rules in place, you know, at any comparable institution that I'm aware of.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think-you know, we've thought about this carefully, and we put them in place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're building the infrastructure so that-so that, you know, the enforcement will be tight, that, actually, you won't be able to make trades unless they're precleared.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the amount of trades you make, they'll have to be 45 days or more before any FOMC meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just-I think we've really, you know, created a very strong and robust set of rules that will, you know, support public trust in the institution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we're just now-the system is just now up and running.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm going to-I'm going to take that as a question about the next meeting and thereafter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, we're going to be looking at all of those things: activity, labor market, inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to be thinking about our policy stance and where does it really need to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I also mentioned that, as this process-now that we're at neutral-as the process goes on, at some point, it will be appropriate to, to slow down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we haven't made a decision when that point is, but intuitively that makes sense, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've been front-end-loading these very large rate increases, and now we're getting closer to where we need to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in terms of September, we're going-we're going to watch the data and the evolving outlook very carefully and factor in everything and make a decision in September about what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'm not really going to provide any specific guidance about what that might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, but I mentioned that we might do another unusually large rate increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's not a decision that we've made at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we are-you know, we're going to be guided by the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you can still think of the, the destination as broadly in line with the September-sorry, the June SEP, because it's only six weeks old.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think in this one-this one I would say is probably, probably the best guide we have as to where the Committee thinks it needs to get at the end of the year and then into next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we've, we've long used PCE because we think it's just better at capturing the inflation that people actually face in their lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that that view is pretty widely understood.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the difference really is because the CPI has higher weights on things like food, gasoline, motor vehicles, and housing than the PCE index does.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that accounts for a lot of the difference.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we-given the importance in the public eye of CPI, we are calling it out and noticing it and everything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The typical gap was really about 25 basis points for a very long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if it went-if it got to 40 basis points, that would be very noticeable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now it's-now it's much larger than that because of the things I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll be watching both, but, again, the one that we think is the best measure always has been PCE, at least since I think we-some 20 plus years ago-moved to PCE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, just talking about demand for a second: As I mentioned in my remarks, I think you pretty clearly do see a slowing now in demand in the second quarter- consumer spending, business fixed investment, housing, places like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, people widely looked at the first-quarter numbers and thought they didn't make sense and might have been misleading in terms of the overall direction of the economy-[that was] not, not true of the second quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But at the same time, you have this labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there are plenty of experiences where GDP has been reported as weak and the labor market as strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the economy has gone right through that and been fine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it used to happen-if you remember, in the first quarter of every year, for several years in a row, GDP was negative, and the labor market was moving on just fine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The truth is, though, we, we think that demand is moderating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are-there is a great deal of money on people's balance sheets that they can spend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's the kind of thing where you think that the-that the economy should actually be, be doing pretty well in the second half of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know that because you do see a marked slowing in the second quarter that does-that is fairly broad.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, as I mentioned, we do want to see demand running below potential for a sustained period to create slack and, and give inflation a chance to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think you're already seeing-you've seen, in the labor market, what you've seen is a decline from very high levels of job creation last year and earlier this year to modestly slower job creation-still, still quite robust, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're seeing some increase-some increase in initial claims from insurance, although that may actually have to do with seasonal adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's some evidence that wages-if you look at average hourly earnings, they appear to be moderating, not so yet from the other wage measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be getting the employment compensation index measurement, I think, on Friday, I guess.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's a very important one because it adjusts for compensation-composition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'd say you-and also, anecdotally, you hear much-the sort of level of concern on the part of businesses that they simply can't find workers is probably down a little bit from what it was, say, for example, late in the latter parts of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's a feeling that the labor market is moving back into balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at-if you look at job openings or quits, you see them moving sideways or perhaps a little bit down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think most-also, if you look at-I mean, once you start citing these things, you can't stop.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the household survey, you see much lower job creation, and the household survey can be quite volatile, but it has no jobs created in the last three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that might be a signal that job creation's actually a little bit slower than we're seeing in the-in the establishment survey.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So executive summary [is]: I would say there's some evidence that labor demand may be slowing a bit-labor supply, not so much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have been disappointed that labor force participation really hasn't moved up since January.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That may be related to yet another big wave of COVID.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-So we're not seeing much in the way of labor supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, I would say some, some progress on demand and supply getting back in alignment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we're looking-we're going to be looking at, at inflation as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, as I mentioned, we need to see inflation coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need to be confident that inflation is going to get back down to mandate-consistent levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, but we do think, though, that the labor market can adjust because of the huge overhang of job openings, of excess demand, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There should be able to be an adjustment that would have lower than-perhaps lower-than-expected increases in unemployment-lower than would be expected in the ordinary course of events because the level-the ratio of, of vacancies to unemployed is just out of keeping with historical experience.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as, as I mentioned, it doesn't seem that the U.S. economy is in recession right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you do see weakening, some slowdown-let's put it that way- in growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you see it across some of the categories that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's also just the very strong data coming out of the labor market, still.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, you would say that, in all probability, demand is still strong, and, and the economy is still on track to continue to grow this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're-you know, we're going to be watching that carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, you know, we've said since the beginning, I think, that, that having a soft landing is what we're aiming for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-I do think events-at the beginning, we said it was not going to be easy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was going to be quite challenging to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If there is a path to it, and we think there is, it is the one I mentioned, that the labor market actually is-has such a large amount of surplus demand that you could see-you could see that demand coming down in a way that didn't translate into a big increase in unemployment as you would expect in the ordinary course because, frankly, the imbalance is so much greater.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, this is a-this is a case of first impression.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So anyone who is really sure that it's impossible or really sure that it will happen is probably underestimating the level of uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I would certainly say it's an uncertain, uncertain thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, it's our goal to achieve it, and we'll keep trying to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: By all assessments, the markets should be able to absorb this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say the plan is broadly on track.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a little bit slow to get going because some of these trades don't settle until-for a bit of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess your second question was getting-the process of getting back down to the new equilibrium will take a while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that time, it's hard to be precise, but, you know, the model would suggest that it could be between two, two and a half years, that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is a much faster pace than the last time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we looked at this carefully, and we thought that this, this was the sensible pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a big piece of that is inflation expectations-you know, breakevens coming down, which, you know, is a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a good thing that markets do seem to have confidence in, in the Committee's commitment to getting inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we like to see market-based, you know, readings of inflation expectations come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, broader financial conditions have tightened, tightened a good bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the way this works is we, we set our policy, and financial conditions react, and then financial conditions are what affects the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're just going to do what we think needs to be done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to-we're going to get our policy rate to a level where we're confident that inflation will be moving back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, we'll be watching financial conditions to see that they are appropriately tight and that they're having the effect that we would hope they're having, which is to see demand moderate and inflationary pressures recede and, ultimately, inflation come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, yes, we said that we wouldn't lift off until we had basically achieved our dual-mandate goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason we did it in real time was that, the first look at the new framework that we'd rolled out, plenty of people were saying, "It's not credible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of our critics now who say inflation's too tight-too high were the same ones who were saying, "You'll never get to 2 percent."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we thought we needed to really make a strong statement with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The December '20 guidance was not part of our overall new framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One, I don't think that that has materially changed the situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I have to admit, I don't think I would do that again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-you know, ultimately, the situation evolved in a highly unexpected way for all of us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, maybe the learning is that leave a little more flexibility than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we-if you look at-I really don't think it did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not sure it would've mattered if we'd been raising rates three months earlier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, lots of central banks were raising rates three months earlier, and it didn't matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, this is a-this is a global phenomenon that's happening now-admittedly, different in the United States, but anyway.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we learned-there've been multiple taper tantrums, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's what happened at the December '18 meeting, where, you know, markets can ignore developments around the balance sheet for years on end and then suddenly react very sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we just had developed a practice of moving predictably and doing it in steps and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were-we were careful to, to take steps and communicate and all that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, we were trying to avoid a tantrum because they can be quite destructive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They can tighten financial conditions and knock the economy off kilter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, when it happens, you have to-really, in both '13 and '18, it really had consequences for the real economy, you know, two, three, four months later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I don't think that's-the real issue of 2020 and '21 was just trying to understand what was happening with the reopening economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, our view was that these supply-side issues would get better: that people would go back to work, that labor force participation would come back, everyone would get vaccinated, schools would open, kids would be in school, and labor force participation would jump back up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we were-that was very broadly thought to be the case: these supply-side issues would get solved reasonably quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's really the learning, I think, is around how complicated these supply-side issues can be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't seen this before in a long, long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's really, you know, what accounts for the pace at which we moved, and we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When inflation changed direction, really, in October, we've moved quickly since then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But before then, inflation was coming down month by month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we kind of thought we had the story-probably had the story right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But then, I think in October, you started to see a range of data that said "No.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a much stronger economy and much higher inflation than we've been thinking."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the Fed doesn't make a-doesn't make a judgment on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're focused on the dual mandate and using our tools to achieve maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't-we don't say "There is now a recession" and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would look at the data tomorrow-and no doubt, we'll look at it very carefully-and draw whatever implications we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, though, you know, if you think about what an inflation-sorry, what a recession really is, it's a broad-based decline across many industries that, you know, is sustained for more than a couple of months, and there are a bunch of specific tests in it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it just doesn't-this just doesn't seem like that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the real reason is that the labor market is just sending such a signal of economic strength that it makes you really question the GDP data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, that's not a decision that we-that we make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we won't-we won't reach a conclusion one way or another on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, broadly, a lot of economists think that the-that the natural rate of unemployment will have moved up to some significant extent above where we think it was before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason is there's-it's the usual matching issue, where matching has become less effective, and that kind of thing when you have the kind of turbulent downturn and the big switches in demand from services to goods and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And my own instinct is that the natural rate of unemployment is higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, I would add that we don't know it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can never know where these star variables are in real time with any confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say it must have moved up materially.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the other side of that is, as all these jobs get created and people go back to work and unemployment is so low, I think you could, in principle, you could see it coming back down pretty significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that would also, by the way, take pressure off of inflation because it's that gap-it's the gap between actual unemployment and the-and the natural rate that really is relevant for, you know, the negative slack we have in the economy with the overtight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's an unobservable, but you could actually be seeing inflationary pressures coming down if that does happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's something that, logically, if the pandemic and the disorder in the labor market caused the natural rate to move up, then as the labor market settles down, in principle, you should see it move back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, all I've really said is I don't think it's likely that the U.S. economy's in a recession now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's because you do see a very strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the public will see that as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, going forward, what we've seen is a-is a slowing in spending, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen the very beginnings of perhaps a slight lessening in the-in the tightness of the labor market, but it would only be the beginnings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and I mentioned that, that-I also said that our goal is to bring inflation down and have a so-called soft landing, by which I mean a landing that doesn't require a significant increase, a really significant increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I have said, on many occasions, that we understand that's going to be quite challenging and that it's got more challenging over recent months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, there are precedents for the FOMC moving very quickly- for example, in 1994, and in 1980, even more so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've been known to do that when it's the appropriate thing to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that, given how quickly we've moved, I'm gratified that while-that, basically, markets have been working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's been some volatility, but that's only to be expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For a financial stability perspective, you know, asset values are down, which in some-in some sense lowers vulnerabilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's when they're really high that you would worry that they're-that they're vulnerable to a fall, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you have-households are generally in about as strong as financial shape as they've been in a very long time or perhaps ever given the money that's on people's balance sheets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you have a pretty-from a financial stability standpoint, you have a pretty decent picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, the macroeconomic, there are plenty of macroeconomic issues that don't rise to the level of financial stability concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: By financial stability, you know, we think of that as things that might undermine the working of the financial system, so big, serious things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's not to say that people at the lower end of the income spectrum aren't, aren't suffering, because they are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're going to the-to the grocery store and finding that, in many cases, their paycheck doesn't cover the food they're accustomed to buying.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're seeing actual, you know, real declines in food consumption.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why we're-we're really committed to bringing down inflation-one of the reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess the first thing I would say to, to every household is that we know that inflation is too high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We understand how painful it is, particularly for people who are living paycheck to paycheck and spend most of that paycheck on necessities, such as food and gas and heating their homes and clothing and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do understand that, that those people suffer the most.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Middle-class and better-off people have some resources, where they can absorb these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are assigned uniquely and unconditionally the obligation of, of providing price stability to the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to use our tools to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, there will be some, in all likelihood, some softening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't want to-we don't want this to be bigger than it needs to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, if you think about the medium and longer term, price stability is the thing that, that makes the whole economy work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's what can-it can give us a strong labor market and wages that aren't being eaten up by high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you talk to people-again, people who are making, you know, wages, relatively low wages- they're the ones who are suffering the most from inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's all the more reason why we need to move, move on this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I will answer-I will answer your question directly, but I want to start here today by saying that my main message has not changed at all since Jackson Hole.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The FOMC is strongly resolved to bring inflation down to 2 percent, and we will keep at it until the job is done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the way we're thinking about this is, the overarching focus of the Committee is getting inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To accomplish that, we think we'll need to do two things, in particular: to achieve a period of growth below trend; and also some softening in labor market conditions to foster a better balance between demand and supply in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on the first, the Committee's forecasts and those of most outside forecasters do show growth running below its longer-run potential this year and next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the second, though, so far there's only modest evidence that the labor market is cooling off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job openings are down a bit, as you know; quits are off their all-time highs; there's some signs that some wage measures may be flattening out but not moving up; payroll gains have moderated but not much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in light of the high inflation we're seeing, we think we'll need to-and in light of what I just said, we think that we'll need to bring our funds rate to a restrictive level and to keep it there for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what will we be looking at, I guess, is your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, we'll want to see growth continuing to run below trend, we'll want to see movements in the labor market showing a return to a better balance between supply and demand, and, ultimately, we'll want to see clear evidence that inflation is moving back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of reducing rates, I think we'd want to be very confident that inflation is moving back down to 2 percent before we would consider that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, monetary policy does, famously, work with long and variable lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The way I think of it is, our policy decisions affect financial conditions immediately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, financial conditions have usually been affected well before we actually announce our decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then, changes in financial conditions begin to affect economic activity fairly quickly, within a few months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's likely to take some time to see the full effects of changing financial conditions on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why I noted in my opening remarks that, at some point, as the stance of policy tightens further, it will become appropriate to slow the pace of rate hikes while we assess how our cumulative policy adjustments are affecting the economy and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I should know better than to answer your second question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's very hard to say with precise certainty the way this is going to unfold.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, what we think we need to do and should do is to move our policy rate to a restrictive level that's restrictive enough to bring inflation down to 2 percent, where we have confidence of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what you see in the SEP numbers is people's views as of today, as of this meeting, as to the kind of levels that will be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, those will evolve over time, and I think we'll just have to see how that goes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There is a possibility, certainly, that we would go to a certain level that we're confident in and stay there for a time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Clearly, today we're, we've just moved, I think, probably, into the very lowest level of what might be restrictive, and, certainly, in my view and the view of the Committee, there's a ways to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right-in the SEP, there's what I would characterize as a relatively modest increase in the unemployment rate from a historical perspective, given the expected decline in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, really, that is what we generally expect because we see the current situation as outside of historical experience in a number of ways, and I'll mention a couple of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First-and you know these-but first, job openings are incredibly high relative to the number of people looking for work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's plausible, I'll say, that job openings could come down significantly-and they need to-without as much of an increase in unemployment as has happened in earlier historical episodes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, in this cycle, longer-run inflation expectations have generally been fairly well anchored, and, as I've said, there's no basis for complacency there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But to the extent that continues to be the case, that should make it easier to restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I guess the third thing I would point to that's different this time is that part of this inflation is caused by this series of supply shocks that we've had, beginning with the pandemic, and, really, with the reopening of the economy, and more recently amplified and added to by Russia's invasion of Ukraine-have all contributed to the sharp increase in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So these are the kinds of events that are not really seen in prior business cycles, and, in principle, if those things start to get better-and we do see some evidence of the beginnings of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not much more than that, but it's good to see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For example, commodity prices look like they may have peaked for now; supply chain disruptions are beginning to resolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those developments, if sustained, could help ease the pressures on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me just say, how much these factors will turn out to really matter in this sequence of events-it remains to be seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have always understood that restoring price stability while achieving a relatively modest decline-or, rather, increase-in unemployment and a soft landing would be very challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't know-no one knows whether this process will lead to a recession or, if so, how significant that recession would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's going to depend on how quickly wage and price inflation pressures come down, whether expectations remain anchored, and whether, also, do we get more labor supply, which would help as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, the chances of a soft landing are likely to diminish to the extent that policy needs to be more restrictive or restrictive for longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, we're committed to getting inflation back down to 2 percent-because we think that a failure to restore price stability would mean far greater pain later on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, vacancies are still almost a 2-to-1 ratio to unemployed people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That and quits are really very good ways to look at how tight the labor market is and how different it is from other cycles, where, generally, the unemployment rate itself is the single best indicator.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think those things have, for quite a time now, really added value in terms of understanding where the labor market is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so, again, we believe that we need to raise our policy stance overall to a level that is restrictive-and by that I mean, is meaningfully, putting meaningful downward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we need to see in the stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also know that there are long and variable lags, particularly as they relate to inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You look at broader financial conditions, as you know; you look at where rates are, real and nominal in some cases; you look at credit spreads; you look at financial conditions indexes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also, I would think-and you see this in the-this is something we talked about today in the meeting and talk about in all of our meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you see this, I think, in the Committee forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You want to be at a place where real rates are positive across the entire yield curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that would be the case if you look at the numbers that we're writing down and think about-you measure those against some sort of forward-looking assessment of inflation, inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you would see at that time-you'd see positive real rates across the yield curve, and that is also an important consideration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we make one decision per meeting, and the decision we made today was to raise the federal funds rate by 75 [basis points].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're right that the median for the year-end suggests another 125 basis points in rate increases, but there's also, there's another fairly large group that saw a 100 basis points addition to where we are today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to make that decision at the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't make that decision today; we didn't vote on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that we're committed to getting to a restrictive level for the federal funds rate and getting there pretty quickly, and that's what we're thinking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what we've seen is, inflation has-our expectation has been that we would begin to see inflation come down, largely because of supply-side healing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: By now we would have thought that we'd have seen some of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have seen some supply- side healing, but inflation has not really come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at core PCE inflation, which is a good measure of where inflation is running now, if you look at it on a 3-, 6-, and 12-month trailing annualized basis, you'll see that inflation is at 4. percent, 4. percent, and 4. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a pretty good summary of where we are with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's not where we expected or wanted to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what that tells us is that we need to continue, and we can-keep doing these, and we did today-do another large increase as we approach the level that we think we need to get to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But people are writing that down in their SEP where they think policy needs to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess core is at 2. in 2025-in the median-and headline is at 2.0, so that's pretty close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we write down our forecasts, and we figure out what the median is, and we publish it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not-I mean, I would say that if, actually, if the economy followed this path, this would be a pretty good outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you're right-it is a tenth higher than 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, as we said at the last press conference and in between that one and this one, we said that we would make our decision based on the overall data coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, if you remember, we got a surprisingly low reading in July and then a surprisingly high reading for August.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think you have to-you can't really-you never want to overreact too much to any one data point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at them together-and, as I just mentioned, if you really look at this year's inflation, 3-, 6-, and 12-month trailing, you see inflation is running too high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's running 4. percent or above; you don't need to know much more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If that's the one thing you know, you know that this Committee is committed to getting to a meaningfully restrictive stance of policy and staying there until we feel confident that inflation is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, what we said, as you know, was that we would consider that once balance sheet runoff is well under way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say it's not something we're considering right now and not something I expect to be considering in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just, it's something I think we will turn to, but that time, the time for turning to it, has not come and is not close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think a number of things might affect that decision, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The main thing is, we're not considering that decision, and I don't expect that we will any time soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, actually, my colleagues and I, a number of my FOMC colleagues and I, just got back from one of our frequent trips to Basel, Switzerland, to meet with other senior central bank officials from around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are in pretty regular contact, and we exchange, of course-we all serve a domestic mandate, domestic objectives-in our case, the dual mandate, maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we regularly discuss what we're seeing in terms of our own economy and international spillovers, and it's a very ongoing, constant kind of a process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we are very aware of what's going on in other economies around the world and what that means for us, and vice versa.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The forecasts that we put together, that our staff puts together, and that we put together on our own always take all of that-try to take all of that into account.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I can't say that we do it perfectly, but it's not as if we don't think about the policy decisions-monetary policy and otherwise-the economic developments that are taking place in major economies that can have an effect on the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is very much baked into our own forecast and our own understanding of the U.S. economy, as best we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't see-it's hard to talk about collaboration in a world where people have very different levels of interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you remember, there were coordinated cuts and raises and things like that at various times, but, really, we're all, we're in very different situations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I will tell you, our contact is more or less ongoing, and it's not coordination, but there's a lot of information sharing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we all, I think, are informed by what other important economies- economies that are important to the United States-are doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're right, of course-the labor market, in particular, has been very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there are-the sectors of the economy that are most interest rate sensitive are certainly showing the effects of our tightening, and, of course, the obvious example is housing, where you see declining activity of all different kinds and house price increases moving down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, through exchange rates, we're having an effect on exports and imports.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-so all of that's happening, but you're right, and we've said this: This is a strong, robust economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People have savings on their balance sheet from the period when they couldn't spend and where they were getting government transfers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's still very significant savings out there, although not as much at the lower end of the income spectrum-but still, some savings out there to support growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The states are very flush with cash, so there's good reason to think that this will continue to be a reasonably strong economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, the data sort of are showing that growth is going to be below trend this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think of trend as being about 1. percent, or in that range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're forecasting growth well below that, and most forecasters are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you're right-there's certainly a possibility that growth can be stronger than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's a good thing, because that means the economy will be more resistant to a significant downturn.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, of course, we are focused on the thing I started with, which is getting inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, if we were to fail to do that, that would be the thing that would be most painful for the people that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So for now, that has to be our overarching focus, and you see that, I think, in the SEP, in the levels of rates that we'll be moving to reasonably quickly, assuming things turn out roughly in line with the SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that there's a very high likelihood that we'll have a period of what I've mentioned is below-trend growth, by which I mean much lower growth, and we're seeing that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the median forecast, I think, this year among my colleagues and me was 0. percent growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a slower, that's a very slow level of growth, and it could give rise to increases in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think that's, so that is something that we think we need to have, and we think we need to have softer labor market conditions as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're never going to say that there are too many people working, but the real point is this: Inflation-what we hear from people when we meet with them is that they really are suffering from inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we want to set ourselves up, really light the way to another period of a very strong labor market, we have got to get inflation behind us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wish there were a painless way to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what we need to do is get rates up to the point where we're putting meaningful downward pressure on inflation, and that's what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we certainly don't hope, we certainly haven't given up the idea that we can have a relatively modest increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, again, our really tight focus now continues to be ongoing rate increases to get the policy rate up where it needs to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I said, you can look at this SEP as today's estimate of where we think those rates would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, for starters, people are seeing their wage increases eaten up by inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if your family is one where you spend most of your paycheck, every paycheck cycle, on gas, food, transportation, clothing, basics of life, and prices go up the way they've been going up, you're in trouble right away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You don't have a cushion, and this is very painful for people at the lower end of the income and wealth spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's what we're hearing from people is, you know, very much-that inflation is really hurting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, it would be nice if there were a way to just wish it away, but there isn't.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to get supply and demand back into alignment, and the way we do that is by slowing the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Hopefully, we do that by slowing the economy, and we see some softening in labor market conditions, and we see a big contribution from supply-side improvements, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In any case, we, our job is to deliver price stability, and I think-you can think of price stability as an asset that just delivers large benefits to society over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The United States had 2 percent inflation, didn't move around much, and that was enormously beneficial to the public that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have to get back to that and keep it for another long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To pull back from the task of doing that is, you're just postponing-the record shows that if you postpone that, the delay is only likely to lead to more pain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we're moving to do what we need to do and do our jobs, and that's what you see us doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it really depends on how long it takes for wages and, more than that, prices to come down for inflation to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so what you see in our projections today is that inflation moves down significantly over the course of next year and then more the next year after that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think once you're on that path, that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And things will start to feel better to people-they'll feel lower inflation, they'll feel that the economy is improving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, if our projections are close to right, you'll see that the costs in unemployment are, they're meaningful, and they're certainly very meaningful to the people who lose their jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we talk about that in our meetings quite a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, at the same time, we'd be setting the economy up for another long period-this era has been noted for very long expansions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had three of the four longest in measured history since we got inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when inflation is low and stable, you can have these 9, 10, 11-10-year, anyway, expansions, and you can see what we saw in 2018, '19, and '20, which was very low unemployment, the biggest wage gains going to people at the low end of the spectrum, the smallest racial gaps that we've seen since we started keeping track of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, to get there, we're going to have to get supply and demand back in alignment, and that's going to take tight monetary policy for a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Higher interest rates, slower growth, and a softening labor market are all painful for the public that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But they're not as painful as failing to restore price stability and then having to come back and do it down the road again and doing it at a time when, actually, now people have really come to expect high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If the concept of high inflation becomes entrenched in people's economic thinking about their decisions, then sort of getting back to price stability-the cost of getting back to price stability just rises, and so we want to avoid that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to act aggressively now and get this job done and keep at it until it's done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when I say "reset," I'm not looking at a particular, specific set of data or anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I'm really saying is that we've had a time of a red-hot housing market all over the country, where, famously, houses were selling to the first buyer at 10 percent above the ask, before even seeing the house.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there was a big imbalance between supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Housing prices were going up at an unsustainably fast level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the deceleration in housing prices that we're seeing should help bring sort of prices more closely in line with rents and other housing market fundamentals, and that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For the longer term, what we need is supply and demand to get better aligned so that housing prices go up at a reasonable level-at a reasonable pace-and that people can afford houses again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we-so we probably, in the housing market, have to go through a correction to get back to that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's also, there are also longer-run issues, though, with the housing market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, we're-it's difficult to find lots now close enough to cities and things like that, so builders are having a hard time getting zoning and lots and workers and materials and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But from a sort of business cycle standpoint, this difficult correction should put the housing market back into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that shelter inflation is going to remain high for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking for it to come down, but it's not exactly clear when that will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it may take some time, so I think, hope for the best, plan for the worst.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, on shelter inflation, you've just got to assume that it's going to remain pretty high for a while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you look, when we get to-if we-let's assume we do get to that level, which I think is likely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you're going to do is, you're going to adjust that for some forward-looking measure of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It could be-there are all kinds of different things you could pick and you get-but what you'll get is a positive number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In all cases, you will get forward inflation expectations in the short term, I think, that are going to be, assuming that we're doing our jobs appropriately, that will be significant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you'll have a positive [real] federal funds rate at that point, which could be 1 percent or so, but-I mean, I don't know exactly what it would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it would be significantly positive when we get to that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And let me say, we've written down what we think is a plausible path for the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is something that, as you can see, they've moved up, and we're going to continue to watch incoming data and the evolving outlook and ask ourselves whether our policy is in the right place as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do need to see inflation coming down decisively, and good evidence of that would be a series of down monthly readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, that's what we'd all love to see, but that's-I've never thought of that as the appropriate test for slowing the pace of increases or for identifying the appropriately restrictive level that we're aiming for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need to bring our policy stance down to a level that's sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to our 2 percent objective over the medium term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, we'll take into account the full range of analysis and data that bear on that question, guided by our assessment of how much financial conditions have tightened, the effects that that tightening is actually having on the real economy and on inflation, taking into consideration lags, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will be looking at real rates, for example, all across the yield curve and all other financial conditions as we make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what I want to do is put that question of pace in the context of our broader tightening program, if I may, and talk about the statement language along the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think you can think about our tightening program as really addressing three questions, the first of which was, and has been, how fast to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second is how high to raise our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the third will be, eventually, how long to remain at a restrictive level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on the first question-how fast to tighten policy-it's been very important that we move expeditiously, and we have clearly done so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've moved 3¾ percent since March, admittedly from a base of zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a historically fast pace, and that's certainly appropriate given the persistence and strength in inflation and the low level from which we started.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So now we come to the second question, which is how high to raise our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're saying that we'd raise that rate to a level that's sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation to our 2 percent target over time, and we put that into our postmeeting statement because that really does become the important question, we think now, is how far to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think there's some ground to cover before we meet that test, and that's why we say that ongoing rate increases will be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, incoming data between the meetings, both a strong labor market report but particularly the CPI report, do suggest to me that we may ultimately move to higher levels than we thought at the time of the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That level is very uncertain, though, and I would say we're going to find it over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, with the lags between policy and economic activity, there's a lot of uncertainty, so we note that in determining the pace of future increases, we'll take into account the cumulative tightening of monetary policy as well as the lags with which monetary policy affects economic activity and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say, as we come closer to that level, move more into restrictive territory, the question of speed becomes less important than the second and third questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why I've said at the last two press conferences that at some point, it will become appropriate to slow the pace of increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that time is coming, and it may come as soon as the next meeting or the one after that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is likely we'll have a discussion about this at the next meeting, a discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To be clear, let me say again [that] the question of when to moderate the pace of increases is now much less important than the question of how high to raise rates and how long to keep monetary policy restricted, which really will be our principal focus.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think I'm pleased that we have moved as fast as we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's-very difficult to make a case that our current level is too tight, given that inflation still runs well above the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that at this meeting, as in the last two meetings, as I've mentioned, I've said that we-that there would come a point, and this was a meeting at which we had a discussion about what that might mean.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we did discuss this, and, as I mentioned, we'll discuss it again in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's no-I don't have any sense that we've overtightened or moved too fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's been good and a successful program that we've gotten this far this fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Remember, though, that we still think there's a need for ongoing rate increases, and we have some ground left to cover here, and cover it we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is the question of, does the policy rate need to get above the inflation rate?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, there are a range of views on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would think you'd look more at a forward, a forward-looking measure of inflation to look at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think the answer is, we'll want to get the policy rate to a level where it is, where the real interest rate is positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do not think of it as the single and only touchstone, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you put some weight on that; you also put some weight on rates across the curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Very few people borrow at the short end-at the federal funds rate, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So households and businesses, if they're [borrowing]-[there are] very meaningfully positive interest rates all across the curve for them, credit spreads are larger, so borrowing rates are significantly higher, and I think financial conditions have tightened quite a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would look at that as an important feature.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'd put some weight on it, but I wouldn't say it's something that is the single, dominant thing to look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, one way to look at it is that it's a pretty stationary object and that when inflation runs-above that level, for sure-substantially above for some time, you'll see it move up, but the movement will be fairly gradual.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that's what the principal models would tend to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I wouldn't want to land on any one assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are many different-as you know, many different people publish an assessment of underlying inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would start by pointing to expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if we saw longer-term expectations moving up, that would be very troubling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they were moving up a little bit at the middle part of this year, and they've moved now back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Shorter-term inflation expectations moved up between the last meeting and this meeting, and we don't think those are as indicative, but they may be important in the wage-setting process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess the other thing I would say is that the longer we have-we're now 18 months into this episode of high inflation, and we don't have a clearly identified, scientific way of understanding at what point inflation becomes entrenched.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so the thing we need to do from a risk-management standpoint is to use our tools forcefully but thoughtfully and get inflation under control-get it down to 2 percent-get it behind us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we really need to do and what we're strongly committed to doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the way I would think about that is, it's commonly, for a long time, thought that monetary policy works with "long and variable lags," and that it works first on financial conditions and then on economic activity and then perhaps later than that even on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was an old literature that made those lags out to be fairly long.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The truth is, we don't have a lot of data [consisting] of inflation of [rates] this high in what is, now, the modern economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One big difference now is that it used to be that you would raise the federal funds rate, financial conditions would react, and then that would affect economic activity and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now financial conditions react well before in expectation of monetary policy [actions].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's the way it has moved for a quarter of a century-in the direction of financial conditions, then monetary policy-because the markets are thinking, what is the central bank going to do?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are plenty of economists that also think that once financial conditions change, that the effects on the economy are actually faster than they would have been before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess the thing that I would say is: It's highly uncertain-highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so from a risk-management standpoint-but we do need, it would be irresponsible not to, to ignore them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you want to consider them but not take them literally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's a very difficult place to be, but I would tend to be-want to be in the middle looking carefully at what's actually happening with the economy and trying to make good decisions from a risk-management standpoint, remembering, of course, that if we were to overtighten, we could then use our tools strongly to support the economy, whereas if we don't get inflation under control because we don't tighten enough, now we're in a situation where inflation will become entrenched and the costs, the employment costs in particular, will be much higher potentially.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So from a risk- management standpoint, we want to be sure that we don't make the mistake of either failing to tighten enough or loosening policy too soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think as we move now into restrictive territory, as we make these ongoing rate hikes and policy becomes more restrictive, it'll be appropriate now to be thinking more about lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we think about lags-the lags are just sort of a basic part of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we will be thinking about them, but we won't be-I think we'll be considering them but because it's appropriate to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let me say this: It is very premature to be thinking about pausing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people, when they hear lags, they think about a pause.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's very premature, in my view, to think about or be talking about pausing our rate hike.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our policy-we need ongoing rate hikes to get to that level of sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't-of course, we don't really know exactly where that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have a sense, and we'll write down in September-sorry, in the December meeting, a new Summary of Economic Projections, which updates that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would expect us to continue to update it based on what we're seeing with incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know that the channels through which policy works have changed that much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say a big channel is the labor market, and the labor market is very, very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
