text: So we go into this with a strong labor market and excess demand in the labor market, as you can see through many different things, and also with households who have strong spending power built up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it may take time, it may take resolve, it may take patience.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It may-I think you see, from our forecasts and others, that it will take some time for inflation to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, so we look at housing-of course, housing is significantly affected by these higher rates, which are really back where they were before the Global Financial Crisis-they're not historically high, but they're much higher than they've been.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you're seeing housing activity decline, and you're seeing housing prices growing at a faster rate and, in some parts of the country, declining.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I would say housing was-the housing market was very overheated for the couple of years after the pandemic as demand increased and rates were low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We all know the stories of how overheated the housing market was, prices going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many, many bidders and no conditions, that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the housing market needs to get back into a balance between supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: From a financial stability standpoint, we didn't see in this cycle the kinds of poor credit underwriting that we saw before the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Housing credit was very carefully-much more carefully managed by the lenders.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a very different situation and doesn't present potential financial-doesn't appear to present financial stability issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, no, we do understand that that's really where a very big effect of our policy is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we talk a lot about vacancies in the-vacancy-to-unemployed rate, but it's just one, it's just another data series.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been unusually important in this cycle because it's been so out of line.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at a very wide range of data on the unemployment-on the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'd start with unemployment, which is typically the single statistic you would look to, is at a 50-year low, 3½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had, I think, very small increase this year, which we had really thought, we thought we would get that back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Most analysts thought we would get some labor supply coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You mentioned wages, so I guess I would characterize that as sort of a mixed picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's true, with average hourly earnings, you see-so I would call it a flattening out at a level that's well above the level that would be consistent over time with 2 percent inflation, assuming a reasonable productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With the ECI reading this week, again, a mixed picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's some rays of light inside that if you look at private-sector workers-that did come down, that compensation did come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Overall, though, the broader picture is of an overheated labor market where demand substantially exceeds supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job creation still exceeds sort of the level that would hold the market where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Do we see-we keep looking for signs that sort of the beginning of a gradual softening is happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And maybe that's there, but it's not obvious to me, because wages aren't coming down-they're just moving sideways at an elevated level, both ECI and average hourly earnings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to see-we would love to see vacancies coming down, quits coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Vacancies are below their all-time high but not by as much as we thought, because-and the data series is volatile, we never take any one reading, we always look at two or three.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't see the case for real softening just yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we look at, I guess as I just showed you, we look at a very broad range of data on the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think wages have an effect on inflation and inflation has an effect on wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's always-going back and forth, the question is, is that really elevated right now?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think wages are the principal story of why prices are going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also don't think that we see a wage-price spiral, but, again, it's not something you can-once you see it, you're in trouble.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want wages to go up-we just want them to go up at a level that's sustainable and consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think we can-we do think that, given the data that we have, that this labor market can soften without having to soften as much as history would indicate through the unemployment channel.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we won't know that-that'll be, that'll be discovered empirically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, we, we keep close tabs on economic developments and also geopolitical developments that are relevant to the economy abroad.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're in very frequent contact with our foreign counterparts both through the IMF meetings and the regular meetings with central banks that we have, and I have one this weekend with many, many central bankers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess what-it's clearly a time, a difficult time in the global economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're seeing very high inflation in Europe, significantly because of high energy prices related to the war in Ukraine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're seeing China's having issues with the zero-COVID policy and much slower growth than we're used to seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we haven't-we take all of that into account in our models.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think about the spillovers and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Here in the United States, we have a strong economy, and we have an economy where inflation is running at 5 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Core PCE inflation-which is a really good indicator of what's going on for us, the way we see it-is running at 5. percent on a 12-month basis and sort of similar to that on a 3-, 6-, and 9-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we know that we need to use our tools to get inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The world's not going to be better off if we fail to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Price stability in the United States is a good thing for the global economy over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Price stability is the kind of thing that pays dividends for our economy-for decades, hopefully-even though it may be difficult to get it back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Getting it back is something that gives-that provides value to the people we serve for the long run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't directly affect, for the most part, food and energy prices, but the demand channel does affect them just at the margin.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The thing about the United States is that we also have strong-in many other jurisdictions, the principal problem really is energy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the United States, we also have a demand issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got an imbalance between demand and supply, which you see in many parts of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our tools are well suited to work on that problem, and that's what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't-the price of oil is set globally, and it's not something we can affect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think by the actions that we take, though, we help keep longer-term inflation expectations anchored and keep the public believing in 2 percent inflation by the things that we do, even in times when energy is part of the story of why inflation is high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right-the public's trust is really the Fed's and any central bank's most important asset, and any time one of us, one of the policymakers, violates or falls short of those rules, we do risk undermining that trust, and we take that very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So at the beginning of our meeting yesterday, actually, we had a Committee discussion of the full Committee on the importance of holding ourselves individually and collectively accountable for knowing and following the high standard that's set out in our existing rules with respect to both personal investment activities and external communications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've taken a number of steps, and I would just say we do understand how important those issues are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that our new investment program that we have is up now and running, and, actually, it was through that that the problems with President Bostic's disclosures were discovered, when he filed his new disclosure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We now have a central group here at the Board of Governors that looks into disclosures and follows them and approves people's disclosures and also all of their trades.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Any trade anyone has to make is covered, has to be approved, preapproved, and there's a lag-it has to be preapproved 45 days before it happens, so there's no ability to game markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-I think we all said to each other today- yesterday, actually, yesterday morning, we recommitted to each other and to this institution to hold ourselves to the highest standards and avoid these problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you know, I referred the matter concerning President Bostic to the inspector general, and once that happens, I don't discuss it with the inspector general or with anybody.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just-the inspector general has, he has the ability to do investigations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so we do monitor the near-term forward spread-you're right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think, just empirically, it dominates the ones that people tend to look at, which is 2s, 10s, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, also, you have to look at why things-why the rate curve is doing what it's doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It can be doing that because it affects-it expects cuts or because it expects inflation to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In this case, if you're in a situation where the markets are pricing in significant declines in inflation, that's going to affect the forward curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, what's happened is, time has passed, and we've raised interest rates by 375 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would not-I would not change a word in that statement, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think until we get inflation down, you'll be hearing that from me.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, if we overtighten-and we don't want to, we want to get this exactly right-but if we overtighten, then we have the ability with our tools, which are powerful, to, as we showed at the beginning of the pandemic episode, we can support economic activity strongly if that happens, if that's necessary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other hand, if you make the mistake in the other direction and you let this drag on, then it's a year or two down the road, and you're realizing, inflation behaving the way it can, you're realizing you didn't actually get it, you have to go back in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: By then, the risk, really, is that it has become entrenched in people's thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the record is that the employment costs-the cost to the people that we don't want to hurt-they go up with the passage of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think as we're farther along, we're now focused on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's the place, what's the level we need to get to rates?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't know what we'll do when we get there, by the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's been no decision or discussion around exactly what steps we would take at that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the first thing is to find your way there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I start by saying, I guess, that the measure that's in the CPI and the PCE, it captures rents for all tenants, not just new leases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that makes sense, actually, because for that reason-conceptually, that is-that's sort of the right target for monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the same thing is true for owners' equivalent rent, which comes off of-it's a reweighting of tenant rents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The private measures are, of course, good at picking up, at the margin, the new leases, and they tell you a couple things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One thing is, I think right now, if you look at the pattern of that series of the new leases, it's very pro-cyclical, so rents went up much more than the CPI and PCE rents did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what you're-the implication is that there are still, as people, as non-new leases roll over and expire, right, they're still in the pipeline, there's still some significant rate increases coming, okay?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But at some point, once you get through that, the new leases are going to tell you-what they're telling you is, there will come a point at which rent inflation will start to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that point is well out from where we are now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're well aware of that, of course, and we look at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that in terms of-the right way to think about inflation, really, is to look at the measure that we do look at, but considering that we also know that at some point, you'll see rents coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our message should be-what I'm trying to do is make sure that our message is clear, which is that we think we have a ways to go, we have some ground to cover with interest rates before we get to, before we get to that level of interest rates that we think is sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And putting that in the statement and identifying that as a goal is an important step.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's meant to put that question, really, as the important one now, going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've also said that we think that the level of rates that we estimated in September-the incoming data suggests that that's actually going to be higher, and that's been the pattern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I would have little confidence that the forecast-if we made a forecast today, if we were doing an SEP today, the pattern has been that, one after another, they go up, and that'll end when it ends, but there's no sense that inflation is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the-I have a table of the last 12 months of 12-month readings, and there's really no pattern there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would also say, it's premature to discuss pausing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the last thing I'll say is that I would want people to understand our commitment to getting this done and to not making the mistake of not doing enough or the mistake of withdrawing our strong policy and doing that too soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In theory, it was a headwind this year, but I do think the broader context is that you have households that have these significant amounts of savings and can keep spending even in-so I think those two things do tend to wage-to sort of counterbalance each other out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It appears, consumer spending is still positive-it's at pretty modest growth levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The banks that deal with retail customers and many retailers will tell you that the consumers are still buying and they're still-they're fine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't know how big the fiscal headwinds are, and they haven't shown up in the way that we thought they would in restraining spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it must have to do with the savings that people have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Demand is going to have some support from those savings and also from the strong demand that's still in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We still see pretty significant demand and a tightening labor market in some respects, although I think, overall, I would say it's not really tightening or loosening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we see those things, and what those things tell us is that our job is going to require some resolve and some patience over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's just-we take all that as a given, but we know what our objective is, and we know what our tools can do, and that's how we think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've always said it was going to be difficult, but I think to the extent rates have to go higher and stay higher for longer, it becomes harder to see the path-it's narrowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say the path has narrowed over the course of the last year, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I would say that the sort of array of data in the labor market is highly unusual and, to many economists, there is a path to- ordinarily there's a relationship to GDP going down and vacancies declining, translating into unemployment, or there's Okun's law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So all those things are relationships that are in the data, and they're very real.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Data's a little bit different this time, though, because you have this tremendously high level of vacancies and, we think, on a very steep part of the Beveridge curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All I would say is that the job losses may turn out to be less than would be indicated by those traditional measures, because job openings are so elevated and because the labor market is so strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think no one knows whether there's going to be a recession or not and, if so, how bad that recession would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And our job is to restore price stability so that we can have a strong labor market that benefits all over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just real quickly-why do you feel like the window has narrowed?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we would expect by now to have seen is that as the-really, as the supply-side problems have resolved themselves, we would have expected goods inflation to come down by now, long since by now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Actually, it has come down, but not to the extent that we had hoped.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, now you see services inflation, core services inflation moving up, and I just think that the inflation picture has become more and more challenging over the course of this year, without question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That means that we have to have policy be more restrictive, and that narrows the path to a soft landing, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, it is important that overall financial conditions continue to reflect the policy restraint that we're putting in place to bring inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that financial conditions have tightened significantly in the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those, in turn, affect economic activity, the labor market, and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we control is our policy moves in the communications that we make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would add that our focus is not on short-term moves, but on persistent moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And many, many things, of course, move financial conditions over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say it's our judgment today that we're not at a sufficiently restrictive policy stance yet, which is why we say that we would expect that ongoing hikes would be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would point you to the SEP again for our current assessment of what that peak level will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you will have seen, 19 people filled out the SEP this time, and 17 of those 19 wrote down a peak rate of 5 percent or more-in the 5s.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's our best assessment today for what we think the peak rate will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You will also know that, at each subsequent SEP during the course of this year, we've actually increased our estimate of what that peak rate will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And today we're-the SEP that was published shows again that, overwhelmingly, FOMC participants believe that inflation risks are to the upside.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I can't tell you confidently that we won't move up our estimate of the peak rate again at the next SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're writing down today is our best estimate of what we think that peak rate will be, based on what we know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Obviously, if data-if the inflation data come in worse, that could move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it could move down if inflation data are softer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I've been saying, as we've gone through the course of this year, as we lifted off and got into the course of the year and we saw the-how strong inflation was and how persistent, it was very important to move quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, the speed-the pace with which we're moving was the most important thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think now that we're coming to the end of this year, we've raised 425 basis points this year, and we're into restrictive territory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's far more important to think, what is the ultimate level?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then it's-at a certain point, the question will become, how long do we remain restrictive?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say the most important question now is no longer the speed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we'll make the February decision based on the incoming data and where we see financial conditions, where we see the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that'll be the key thing, but-I mean, for that decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, that question about how high to raise rates is going to be one that we make looking at our progress on inflation, looking at where financial conditions are, and making an assessment of whether policy is restrictive enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: [As] I've told you today, we have an assessment that we're not at a restrictive enough stance, even with today's move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've laid out our own-our individual assessments of what we would need to do to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At a certain point, though, we'll get to that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then the question will be, how long do we stay there?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there, the strong view on the Committee is that we'll need to stay there, you know, until we're really confident that inflation is coming down in a sustained way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at-you can break inflation down into three, sort of, buckets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first is goods inflation, and we see now, as we've been expecting, really, for a year and a half, that supply conditions would get better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, ultimately, supply chains get fixed, and demand settles down a little bit and maybe goes back to services a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're now starting to see that in this report and the last one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know the story there is that housing services inflation has been very, very high and will continue to go up, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As rents expire and have to be renewed, they're going to be renewed into a market where rates are higher than they were when the original leases were signed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we see that the new leases that are-that the rate for new leases is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, once we work our way through that backlog, that inflation will come down sometime next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The third piece, which is something like 55 percent of the index, PCE core inflation index, is non-housing-related core services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really a function of the labor market, largely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The biggest cost, by far, in that sector is labor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do see a very, very strong labor market, one where we haven't seen much softening, where job growth is very high, where wages are very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Vacancies are quite elevated, and, really, there's an imbalance in the labor market between supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that part of it, which is the biggest part, is likely to take a substantial period to get down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other-you know, the goods inflation has turned pretty quickly now after not turning at all for a year and a half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's an expectation, really, that the services inflation will not move down so quickly, so that we'll have to stay at it, so that we may have to raise rates higher to get to where we want to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really why we are writing down those high rates and why we're expecting that they'll have to remain high for a time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think it would qualify as a recession, though, because you've got positive growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The expectations in the SEP are basically as you said, which is, we've got growth at a modest level, which is to say that ½ percentage point, that's positive growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In that condition, labor market conditions are softening a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that many analysts believe that the natural rate of unemployment is actually elevated at this moment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not clear that those forecasts of inflation are really much above the natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that 4. percent is still a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look-you know, you've got-the reports we get from the field are that companies are very reluctant to lay people off, other than the tech companies, which is, you know, a story unto itself.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Generally, companies want to hold onto the workers they have because it's been very, very hard to hire.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you've got all these vacancies out there-far in excess of the number of employed people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That doesn't sound like a-you know, a labor market where a lot of people will need to be put out of work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that we-you know, there are channels through which the labor market can come back into balance with relatively modest increases in unemployment, we believe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: None of that is guaranteed, but that is what their forecast reflects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I haven't made a judgment on what size rate hike to make at the last meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, what you said is broadly right, which is, having moved so quickly and having now so much restraint that's still in the pipeline, we think that the appropriate thing to do now is to move to a slower pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that will allow us to feel our way and- you know, and get to that level, we think, and better balance the risks that we face.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It makes a lot of sense, it seems to me-particularly if you consider how far we've come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, I can't tell you today what the actual size of that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It will depend on a variety of factors, including the incoming data in particular, the state of the economy, the state of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As a-just a matter of practice, the SEP reflects any data that's-that comes out during the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And participants know that they have the-they know this-that they can make changes to their SEP during the meeting, you know, well in advance of the press conference so that we're not running around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's never the case that the SEPs don't reflect an important piece of data that came in on the first day of the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is more just that, you know, by now, we had expected-we've continually expected to make faster progress on inflation than we have, ultimately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why the peak rate for this year goes up between this meeting and the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see that-you see the fact that we've made less progress than expected on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why unemployment goes up, because we're having to tighten policy more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so it didn't go up by much in the meeting, I don't think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's the idea, is slower progress on inflation, tighter policy, probably higher rates probably held for longer just to get to where you-the kind of restriction that you need to get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And history would, you know, would say that, in a situation like this, the declines in unemployment would be more meaningful, I think, than what you see written down there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First just is that there's this huge overhang of vacancies, meaning that vacancies can come down a fair amount.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're hearing from many companies that they don't want to lay people off-so that they'll keep people because it's been so hard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think we've-it feels like we have a structural labor shortage out there where there are, you know, 4 million fewer people, a little more than 4 million who were in the workforce available to work than there's demand for workforce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the fact that there's a strong labor market, you know, means that companies will hold on to workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it means that it may take longer, but it also means that the costs in unemployment may be less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you do hear, you know, many, many labor economists believe that it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think that's why one of the reasons it went up was that core came in stronger this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you see is our best estimate, as of today-really, as of today-for how high we need to raise rates to-how much we need to tighten policy to create enough, you know, restrictive policy to slow economic activity and slow-soften the labor market and bring inflation down through those channels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, we'll make another estimate for the next SEP. And we'll, you know, of course, between meetings, we do the same thing, but we don't publish it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going into next year with higher inflation than we had thought, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're actually moving down to-the level that we're moving down to next year is still a very large drop in inflation from where inflation is running now, well more than 1 percent change in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But remember that the jump[ing]-off point at the beginning of the year is higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we-we're moving down still by a very large chunk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think it's having-I don't think the policy is having any less effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just starting from a higher level at the end of 2022.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: By the middle of next year, we should begin to see lower inflation from the housing services sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, you know, the big question is, when we-how much will you see from the largest, the 55 percent of the index, which is the non-housing services sector?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that's where you need to see-we believe you need to see a better balancing of supply and demand in the labor market so that you have-it's not that we don't want wage increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just want them to be at a level that's consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now that-if you put into-if you factor in productivity estimates, standard productivity estimates, wages are running, you know, well above what would be consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, our focus right now is really on moving our policy stance to one that is restrictive enough to ensure a return of inflation to our 2 percent goal over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that we'll have to maintain a restrictive stance of policy for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess I would say it this way: I wouldn't see us considering rate cuts until the Committee is confident that inflation is moving down to 2 percent in a sustained way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are not rate cuts in the SEP for 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Weaker output in China will push down on commodity prices, but it could interfere with supply chains ultimately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's very hard to say, you know, how much-how those two will offset each other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it doesn't seem likely, actually, that the overall net effect would be material on us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, to your point, China faces a very challenging situation in reopening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've seen, waves of COVID all around the world can interfere with economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They've- you know, they've backed away from their COVID restriction policies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It-but, again, it doesn't seem like it's likely to have material overall effects on us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the data that we've received so far for October and November, we don't have the-some of the-we have some remaining data to get in November, but they clearly do show a welcome reduction in the monthly pace of price increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned in my opening statement, it will take substantially more evidence to give confidence that inflation is on a sustained downward path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the way we think about this is this: This report is very much in line with what we've been expecting and hoping for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what it does is, it provides greater confidence in our forecast of declining inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, we've been expecting significant-forecasting significant declines in overall inflation and core inflation in the coming year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is the kind of reading that it will take to support that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, really, this gives us greater confidence in our forecasts rather than, at this point, changing our forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the pieces, we have been expecting goods inflation to come down as supply chain pressures eased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Housing services-as I mentioned, there's good news in the pipeline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As long as housing-new housing leases show declining inflation, that will show up in the measure around the middle of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the big piece, again, is core services, ex housing, which is very important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, that's the big-the more than half, as I mentioned, of PCE core index.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's very fundamentally about the labor market and wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at wages, look at the average hourly earnings number we got with the last payrolls report, you don't really see much progress in terms of average hourly earnings coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, there may be composition effects and other effects in that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't put too much weight on any one report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we will be looking for wages moving, you know, down to more normal levels where workers are doing well and, ultimately, their gains are not being eaten up by inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, one thing is to say is, I think our policy's in-getting into a pretty good place now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're restrictive, and I think we're-you know, we're getting close to that level of sufficient-we think-sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We laid out today what our best estimates are to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, it boils down to, how long do we think this process is going to take?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, we're-we welcome these better inflation reports for the last two months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the big story will really be the rest of it, and there's not much progress there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think my view and my colleagues' view is that this will take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll have to hold policy at a restrictive level for a sustained period so that, you know, two good-you know, two good monthly reports are, you know, very welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we need to be honest with ourselves that there's, you know, inflation-12-month core inflation is 6 percent CPI.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But let's just understand we have a long ways to go to get back to price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I would say this: You know, to the extent we need to keep rates higher and keep them there for longer and inflation, you know, moves up higher and higher, I think that narrows the runway.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But lower inflation readings, if they persist, in time, could certainly make it more possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I just-I don't think anyone knows whether we're going to have a recession or not and, if we do, whether it's going to be a deep one or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And certainly, you know, lower inflation reports, were they to continue for a period of time, would increase the likelihood of a- put it this way, of a return to price stability that involves significantly less of an increase in unemployment than would be expected given the historical record.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the largest amount of pain-the worst pain would come from a failure to raise rates high enough and from us allowing inflation to become entrenched in the economy so that the ultimate cost of getting it out of the economy would be very high in terms of employment, meaning very high unemployment for extended periods of time, the kind of thing that had to happen when inflation really got out of control and the Fed didn't respond aggressively enough or soon enough in a prior episode, you know, 50 years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's really-the worst pain would be if we failed to act.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're doing now is, you know, it's raising interest rates for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so people are paying higher rates on mortgages and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I wish there were a completely painless way to restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think, though, that-and markets are pretty confident, it seems to me-that we will get inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's just-so, changing our inflation goal is just something we're not thinking about, and it's something we're not going to think about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-we have a 2 percent inflation goal, and we'll use our tools to get inflation back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think this isn't the time to be thinking about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, there may be a longer-run project at some point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to keep our inflation target at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to use our tools to get inflation back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-I would go back to the labor market that we had in 2018, '19, '20.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what that looked like was, wage increases for the people at the lowest end of the income spectrum were the largest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The gaps between racial groups and gender groups were at their smallest in recorded history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-and all of that because of a tight labor market, a tight labor market which had inflation running, you know, just a tick below 2 percent and the economy growing right at its potential.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that seems like something that would be really good for the economy and for the country, if we could get back to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's what all of us want to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to get back to a long expansion where the labor market can remain strong over an extended period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a really good thing for workers in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, there's-in the near term, we have to use our tools to restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, you know, we can't-what we have to think about is the medium and longer term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you think about it, the country went through a difficult time-I think much more difficult than we can think it would happen here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it really set up our economy for several decades of prosperity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So price stability is something that really pays dividends for the benefit of the economy and the people in it over a very, very long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so when it is lost, for whatever reason, it has to be restored and as quickly as possible-which is what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at-it's our regular practice to talk about unemployment rates by different groups, including racial groups and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't want to get into too many hypotheticals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me just say that we have to use our tools to support maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've made it clear that right now, the labor market's very, very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're near a 50-year low where you're at or above maximum employment, a 50-year low in unemployment, vacancies are very high, wages-nominal wages are very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're missing by a lot on the inflation side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that means we need to really focus on getting inflation under control, and that's what we'll do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, as the economy heals, the two goals come more into play.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But right now, clearly, the focus has to be on getting inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what I meant by that, with "structural labor shortage," is, if you look at where we are now, as I mentioned, there-if you just look at demand for labor, you can look at vacancies plus people who are actually working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then you can take supply of labor by, "Are you in the labor market?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: "Are you looking for a job or have a job?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't see-despite very high wages and an incredibly tight labor market, we don't see participation moving up-which is contrary to what we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the upshot of all that is, the labor market is actually-it should-it's 3½ million people, at least, smaller than it should have been based on pre-pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just assume population and reasonable growth and aging of the population; our labor force should be 3½ million more than it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that-there're lots of easy ways to get to bigger numbers than that if you go back a few more years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People dropped out and aren't coming back at a higher rate than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of it is that we lost a half a million people who would have been work-close to half a million who would have been working died from COVID.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And part of it is that migration has been lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't prescribe-you know, it's not our job to prescribe things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, I think if you ask businesses, you know, pretty much everybody you talk to says there aren't enough people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I tried to identify that in my-in a speech I gave a month ago, but I stopped short of telling Congress what to do because, you know, they gave us a job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, what we do is, we make our forecasts, and we publish them quarterly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, if you look at those forecasts, those are forecasts for slow growth, for a softening labor market, by which I mean, unemployment goes up but not a great deal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are those forecasts, and that's really what they show.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-of course, we don't talk about, you know, this kind of a recession and that kind of a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The staff runs-and you will see this if you look at the old Tealbooks-runs alternative simulations of all different kinds at every meeting, and we look at those, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, that's a responsible practice that we've carried on for many decades.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, as I mentioned, you know, we wouldn't-I wouldn't see the Committee cutting rates until we're confident that inflation is moving down in a sustained way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't see us as having a really clear and precise understanding of what the neutral rate is and what real rates are so that it would mechanically happen like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would-really, it'll be a test of-for cutting rates, I think, in the event, it'll be a question of, do we actually feel confident that inflation is coming down in a sustained way?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is important that overall financial conditions continue to reflect the policy restraint that we're putting in place in order to bring inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, financial conditions have tightened very significantly over the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that our focus is not on short-term moves but on sustained changes to broader financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it is our judgment that we're not yet at a sufficiently restrictive policy stance, which is why we say that we expect ongoing hikes will be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, many things affect financial conditions-not just our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will take into account overall financial conditions along with many other factors as we set policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say it is a good thing that the disinflation that we have seen so far has not come at the expense of a weaker labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would also say that that disinflationary process that you now see under way is really at an early stage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you see is, really, in the goods sector you see inflation now coming down because supply chains have been fixed, demand is shifting back to services, and shortages have been abated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the other-in the housing services sector, we expect inflation to continue moving up for a while but then to come down, assuming that [rent increases associated with] new leases continue to be lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in those two sectors, you've got a good story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The issue is that we have a large sector called nonhousing service-core nonhousing services, where we don't see disinflation yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that, so far, what we see is progress but without any weakening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to write down new forecasts at the March meeting, and we'll see at that time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say that it is gratifying to see the disinflationary process now getting under way, and we continue to get strong labor market data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we did see-we've seen average hourly earnings and now the employment cost index abating a little bit still off of their highs of six months ago and more but still at levels that are fairly elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The job openings number has-in JOLTS, has been quite volatile recently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, I did see that it moved up-back up this morning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The ratio, I guess, is back up to 1. job openings to unemployed people, people who are looking for work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's an indicator, but nonetheless, we-you're right, we do see wages moving down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look across the rest of the labor market, you still see very high payroll job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, quits are still at an elevated level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So many, many-by many, many indicators, the job market is still very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the December meeting, we all wrote down our best estimates of what we thought the ultimate level would be, and that's obviously back in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the median for that was between 5 and 5¼ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the March meeting, we're going to update those assessments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did, however, continue to say that we believe ongoing rate hikes will be appropriate to attain a sufficiently restrictive stance of policy to bring inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think we've covered a lot of ground, and financial conditions have certainly tightened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say we still think there's work to do there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't made a decision on exactly where that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, we're going to be looking carefully at the incoming data between now and the March meeting and then the May meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't feel a lot of certainty about where that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It could certainly be higher than we're writing down right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we come to the view that we need to write down to, you know, to move rates up beyond what we said in December, we would certainly do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, if the data come in, in the other direction, then we'll, you know, we'll make data-dependent decisions at coming meetings, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I continue to think that it's very difficult to manage the risk of doing too little and finding out in 6 or 12 months that we actually were close but didn't get the job done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation springs back, and we have to go back in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now, you really do worry about expectations getting unanchored and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a very difficult risk to manage, whereas I-of course, we have no incentive and no desire to overtighten.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, you know, if we feel like we've gone too far, we can certainly-and inflation is coming down faster than we expect, then we have tools that would work on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do think that, in this situation, where we have still the highest inflation in 40 years, you know, the job is not fully done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I started to mention earlier, we have a sector that represents 56 percent of the core inflation index where we don't see disinflation yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: housing is still running at 4 percent on a 6- and 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the other two sectors representing, you know, less than 50 percent, you actually, I think, now have a story that is credible, that's coming together, although you don't actually see disinflation yet in housing services, but it's in the pipeline, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, for the third sector, we don't see anything here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it would be premature-it would be very premature to declare victory or to think that we've really got this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need to see-our goal, of course, is to bring inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are many, many factors driving inflation in that sector, and they should be coming into play to have inflation-the disinflationary process begin in that sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think until we do, we see ourselves as having a lot of work left to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can now say, I think, for the first time that the disinflationary process has started.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we see it, really, in goods prices so far.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-this is what we thought would happen since the very beginning, and now here it is actually happening, and for the reasons we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-you know, it's supply chains, it's shortages, and it's demand revolving back towards services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's, you know, around a quarter of the PCE price index-core PCE price index.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the second sector is housing services, and that's driven by very different things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-as I mentioned, with housing services, we expect, and other forecasters expect, that measured inflation will continue moving up for several months but will then come down, assuming that [rent increases associated with] new leases continue to be soft.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think that that's sort of in the pipeline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we actually see disinflation in the goods sector, and we see it in the pipeline for two sectors that amount to a little less than half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we note that when we say inflation is coming down that this is good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We expect to see that that disinflation process will be seen, we hope soon, in the core goods ex.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-you know, it's seven or eight different kinds of services, not all of them are the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we have a sense of what's going on in each of those different subsections.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Probably the biggest part of it, probably 60 percent of that is, you know, research would show is sensitive to slack in the economy and so the labor market will probably be important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of the other ones it's-the labor market is not going to be important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In any case, we don't see disinflation in that sector yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we need to see that it's the majority of the core PCE index, which is the thing that we think is the best predictor of headline PCE, which is [the price series that we associate with] our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not that we're not-we're neither optimistic nor pessimistic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're just telling you that we don't see inflation moving down yet in that large sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we will fairly soon, but we don't see it yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Until we do, I think we-you know, we see ourselves, we've got to be honest with ourselves, but we see ourselves as having perhaps more persistent-we'll see more persistent inflation in that sector, which will take longer to get down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're just going to have to-we have to complete the job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've-you know, we've raised rates 4½ percentage points, and we're talking about a couple of more rate hikes to get to that level we think is appropriately restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, of course, taking into account long and variable lags, and we're thinking about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It really-the story we're telling about inflation is to ourselves, and the way we understand it is basically the three things that I've just gone through a couple of times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we don't see it affecting the services sector ex.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, I mean, I think our assessment is that we're not very far from that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we're-you know, we're living in a world of significant uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would look across the rate-the spectrum of rates and see that real rates are now positive by- you know, by an appropriate set of measures are positive across the yield curve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're trying to make a fine judgment about how much is restrictive enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to-you know, that's why we're slowing down to 25 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be carefully watching the economy and watching inflation and watching the progress of the disinflationary process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-you know, you'll see that the minutes will come out in three weeks, and we'll give you a lot of detail.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-you know, we spend a lot of time talking about the path ahead and the state of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I wouldn't want to start to drive the-describe all the details there, but that was the sense of the discussion, was really talking quite a bit about the path forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're really asking about-you're asking about prioritization, in effect, is what-

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's only one way forward here, and that is for Congress to raise the debt ceiling so that the United States government can pay all of its obligations when due.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And any deviations from that path would be highly risky and that no one should assume that the Fed can protect the economy from the consequences of failing to act in a timely manner.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of our relationship with the Treasury, we are their fiscal agent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is a matter that's to be resolved between, really-it's really Congress' job to raise the debt ceiling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I gather there are discussions happening, but they don't involve us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the Committee obviously did not see this as the time to pause.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We judged that the appropriate, you know, thing to do at this meeting was to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we said that we continue to anticipate that ongoing increases in the target range will be appropriate in order to attain that stance of sufficiently restrictive monetary policy that will bring inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're going to write down new forecasts in March, and we'll-you know, we'll certainly be looking at the incoming data as everyone else will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think this is not something that the Committee is thinking about or exploring in any kind of detail.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In principle, though, you know, we used to-the thing we used to do was go every other meeting, if you remember, 25 basis points, and that was considered a fast pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I mean, you saw what the Bank of Canada did and, you know, they left it that they're willing to raise rates after pausing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But this is not something that the Federal Open Market Committee is on the point of deciding right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, on the forecast, if-you're right-if you take very short-term three-month, say, measures of PCE-core PCE inflation, they're quite low right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's because that's driven by, you know, significantly negative readings from goods inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Most forecasters would think that the significantly negative readings will be transitory and that goods inflation will move up fairly soon, back up to its longer-run trend of something around zero, something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a lot of forecasts would call for core PCE to go back up to 4 percent by the middle of the year, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, let's say inflation does come down much faster than we expect, which is possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, you know, obviously our policy is data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the non-sorry, the core nonhousing services, as I mentioned earlier, it's a very diverse sector, six or seven sectors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so sectors that represent 55 or 60 percent of that- subsectors of that sector are-we think are sensitive to slack in the economy, sensitive to the labor market in a way, but some of the other sectors are not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, for example, you know, financial services is a big sector that's really not driven by labor markets-wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's why I said there are a number of things that will affect-take restaurants, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, clearly, labor is important for restaurants but so are food prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, transportation services is going to be driven by fuel prices, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there are lots of things in that mix that will drive inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say overall, though, my own view would be that you're not going to have, you know, a sustainable return to 2 percent inflation in that sector without a better balance in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't know what that will require in terms of increased unemployment, your question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think there are a number of dimensions through which the labor market can soften.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so far, we've got-as I mentioned, in goods, we have inflation moving down without the softening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think most forecasters would say that unemployment will probably rise a bit from here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I still think-I continue to think that there's a path to getting inflation back down to 2 percent without a really significant economic decline or a significant increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's because the-you know, the setting we're in is quite different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The inflation that we originally got was very much a collision between very strong demand and hard supply constraints, not something that you really have seen in prior- you know, in prior business cycles.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so now we see goods inflation coming down for the reasons we thought, and we understand why housing inflation will come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think will-a story will emerge on the nonhousing services sector soon enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think there is- there's ongoing disinflation, and we don't yet see weakening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's because this is not like the other business cycles in so many ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It may well be that as-yeah, as-that it will take more slowing than we expect-than I expect to get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: My base case is that the economy can return to 2 percent inflation without a really significant downturn or a really big increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think many, many forecasters would say it's not the most likely outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do think you-most forecasts and, you know, my own assessment would be that that growth will continue-positive growth will continue but at a subdued pace as it did last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had growth of-GDP growth of 1 percent last year and also final sales growth, which we think is a better indicator, of about 1 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, most forecasts and certainly my assessment would be that growth will continue at a fairly subdued level this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are other factors, though, that need to be considered.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You will have seen that the global picture is improving a bit, and that will matter for us, potentially.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market remains very, very strong, and that's job creation, that's wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You also-state and local governments are really flush these days with, you know, money, and many of them are considering tax cuts or even sending checks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that's going to support-they're also spending a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a lot of spending coming in the construction pipeline, both private and public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think there's a good chance that those factors will help support positive growth this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's my base case, is that there will be positive growth this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't think there's, you know, going to be a light switch flipped or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, we'll be looking-by the time of the March meeting, we'll have two more employment reports, two more CPI reports, and we'll be looking at those carefully as all of us will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll be asking ourselves, what are they telling us?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And soon after that, we'll have another ECI wage report, which, as you know, is a report that we like because it adjusts for composition and it's very complete.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the one we got, I guess it was yesterday, was some-was constructive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-you know, it shows wages coming down but still at a high level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're still at a level that's way above-well above where they were before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't want to put a number on it in terms of months, but as the accumulated evidence comes in, it's going to be reflected in our assessment of the outlook, and that will be reflected in our policy over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I will say, though, we-you know, it is our job to restore price stability and achieve 2 percent inflation for the benefit of the American public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, I did that job for years but in one form or another.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we are strongly resolved that we will, you know, complete this task because we think it has benefits that will, you know, support economic activity and benefit the public for many, many years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the-so we, of course, expected goods inflation to start coming down by the end of 2021, and it didn't come down all through '22.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now it's coming down, and it's come down pretty fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say these are-this is not a standard business cycle where you can look at the last 10 times there was a global pandemic and we shut the economy down and Congress did what it did and we did what we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, our job is to deliver inflation back to target, and we will do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think we're going to be cautious about declaring victory and, you know, sending signals that we think that the game is won because, you know, it's-we've got a long way to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's most welcome to be able to say that we are now in disinflation, but that's great.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we just see that it has to spread through the economy and that it's going to take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so-again, my forecast and that of my colleagues as you will see from the SEP and-I mean, there are many different forecasts, but, generally, it's a forecast of slower growth, some softening in labor market conditions, and inflation moving down steadily but not quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in that case, if the economy performs broadly in line with those expectations, it will not be appropriate to cut rates this year, to loosen policy this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, other people have forecasts with inflation coming down much faster, that's a different thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, if that happens-inflation comes down much faster, you know, then we'll be seeing that, and it will be incorporated into our thinking about policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not particularly concerned about the divergence, no, because it is largely due to the market's expectation that inflation will move down more quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, as I just mentioned, we-you know, our forecasts- different participants have different forecasts, but, generally, those forecasts are for continued subdued growth, some softening in the labor market but not a recession, not a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have inflation moving down, you know, into the-somewhere in the mid-threes or maybe lower than that this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll update that in March, but that's what we thought in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They show inflation coming down, in some cases, much quicker than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have a different view and-a different view, it's a different forecast, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And given our outlook, I just-I don't see us cutting rates this year if we get-if our outlook turns true, as I mentioned just now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we do see inflation coming down much more quickly, that'll play into our policy setting, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Look, we understand-I personally understand well that COVID is still out there, but that it's no longer playing an important role in our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we've kept that statement in there for quite a while, and I think we just-we knew we would take it out at some point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's never a perfect time, but we thought that-you know, people are handling it better, and the economy and the society are handling it better now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't really need to be in a-you know, in the Fed's monthly, you know, postmeeting statement as an ongoing economic risk as opposed to, you know, a health issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the whole point is, you know, if you-once you see it, you have a serious problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That means that, effectively, in people's decisionmaking, inflation has become a really salient issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And once that happens- that's what we can't allow to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so that's why we worry that the longer we're at this and the longer people are talking about inflation all day long, every day, you know, the more risk of something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It always has been more of a risk than anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people are-you know, we pick that up in conversations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I've seen some data, too, that show people are, you know, gradually-they're glad that inflation is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as we see it coming down, that could also add a boost to economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You look at the sentiment surveys now, and they're very, very low with 3½ percent unemployment and, you know, high wage increases nominally by historical standards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think once inflation is seen to be coming down in coming months, even you will also see a boost to sentiment, I hope.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's what you're looking at most closely, is consumer expectations?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's at the very heart, is consumers and businesses that, you know, are the-essentially, we believe that expectations of future inflation are a very important part of the process of creating inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in this case, I would say, the risk eight months ago or so, longer-term inflation expectations had moved up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Expectations are-seem to be well anchored, including at the shorter end now, not just the longer end.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, the markets have decided, and the public has decided, that inflation is going to come back down to 2 percent and it's just a matter of us following through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's immeasurably helpful to the process of getting inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The fact that people now do generally believe that it will come down, that'll be part of the process of getting it down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Financial conditions didn't really change much from the December meeting to now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They mostly went sideways or up and down but came out in roughly the same place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's important that the markets do reflect the tightening that we're putting in place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As we've discussed a couple times here, there's a difference in perspective by some market measures on how fast inflation will come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I'm not going to try to persuade people to have a different forecast, but our forecast is that it will take some time and some patience and that we'll need to keep rates higher for longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Look, I-it's very hard to think about all the different possible ramifications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the answer is, basically, I don't think there's likely to be any important interaction between the two, because I believe Congress will wind up acting, and-as it will and must, in the end, to raise the debt ceiling in a way that doesn't risk, you know, the progress we're making against inflation and the economy and the financial sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, of course, will monitor money market conditions carefully as-you know, as the process moves on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For example, the Treasury General Account will shrink down, and then it will grow back up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we understand there'll be lots of flows between there and the overnight repo facility and reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I guess our view is that the banking system is sound and it's resilient-it's got strong capital [and] liquidity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We took powerful actions with [the] Treasury and the FDIC, which demonstrate that all depositors' savings are safe and that the banking system is safe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Deposit flows in the banking system have stabilized over the last week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the last thing I'll say is that we've undertaken-we're undertaking a thorough internal review that will identify where we can strengthen supervision and regulation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we considered-we did consider that in the days running up to the meeting, and you see the decision that we made, which I'll say a couple things about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, it was supported by a very strong consensus, and I'll be happy to explain why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, really, it is that the intermeeting data on inflation and the labor market came in stronger than expected and, really, before the recent events, we were clearly on track to continue with ongoing rate hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, as of a couple of weeks ago, it looked like we'd need to raise rates over the course of the year more than we had expected at the time of the SEP in December-at the time of the December meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are committed to restoring price stability, and all of the evidence says that the public has confidence that we will do so-that we'll bring inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is important that we sustain that confidence with our actions as well as our words.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we also assess, as I mentioned, that the events of the last two weeks are likely to result in some tightening credit conditions for households and businesses and thereby weigh on demand, on the labor market, and on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Such a tightening in financial conditions would work in the same direction as rate tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In principle, as a matter of fact, you can think of it as being the equivalent of a rate hike or perhaps more than that; of course, it's not possible to make that assessment today with any precision whatsoever.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our decision was to move ahead with the 25 basis point hike and to change our guidance, as I mentioned, from ongoing hikes to some, some additional hikes maybe-some policy firming may be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So going forward, as I mentioned, in assessing the need for, for further hikes, we'll be focused as always on the incoming data and the evolving outlook and, in particular, on our assessment of the actual and expected effects of credit tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, I think it's, it's meant to refer to our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, I would focus on, on the words "may" and "some," as opposed to "ongoing."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we clearly were-what we were doing there was taking onboard the-trying to reflect the uncertainty about what will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
