text: I mean, it, it's possible that this will turn out to have very modest effects-that these events will turn out to be very, very modest effects on the economy, in which case inflation will continue to be strong-in which case, you know, the path will look- might look different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also possible that this potential tightening will contribute significant tightening in credit conditions over time and, in principle, if that-that means that monetary policy may have less work to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, with our monetary policy, we're, we're really focused on macroeconomic outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In particular, we're focused on, on this potential credit tightening and what can that produce in the way of tighter credit conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think when we think about the situation with the banks, we're focused on our-on our financial stability tools, in particular our lending facilities, the debt-sorry, the discount window, and also the new facility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we have just come from an FOMC meeting and, you know, the people who write the minutes will be very carefully counting, but I'll tell you what I heard.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What I heard was significant number of people saying that they anticipated there would be some, some tightening of credit conditions and that would really have the same effects as, as our policies do, and that therefore they were including that in their assessment and that if that did turn out not to be the case, in principle you would need more rate hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So some people did reflect that in their FOMC-in their SEP forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there may also just have been- remember, this is 12 days ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're trying to assess something that just is so recent and it's people-you know, it's very difficult, there's so much uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So December was a good place to start, and we wound up with-we wound up with very similar outcomes for December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, in a way, the early-the data in the first part-the first five weeks of the intermeeting period pointed to stronger inflation and stronger labor markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then this, this latter part kind of-the possibility of credit conditions tightening really, really offset that, effectively.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we know that we have other, other tools in effect, but no, we think our monetary policy tool works, and we think, you know, many, many banks-our rate hikes were well telegraphed to the market, and many banks have managed to handle them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The issue was really not about those specific banks, but about the risk of a contagion to, to other banks and to the financial markets more broadly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So Vice Chair Barr is, is of course leading that review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And he's responsible for it in his capacity as Vice Chair for Supervision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-I realized, you know, right away that, that there was going to be a need for review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the question we're all asking ourselves over that first weekend was, how did this happen?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so what we did was, early Monday morning, we sat down and said, "Let's do this."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And he, he was obviously going to lead it in his capacity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't-my role was to announce it, and I get briefed on it, but I'm not involved in, in the work of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, what actually happened, Howard, was I got the question 12 times, so it's-maybe it's a feature, not a bug.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, so, but yeah, absolutely the same-the story is intact, so it's really three parts, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Goods inflation has been coming down now for six months; it's proceeding more slowly than we would have liked, but it's certainly proceeding.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Housing services is, is really a matter of time passing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We continue to see the new leases being signed at much lower levels of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's 44 percent of the-of the core PCE index, where you've got a story that's ongoing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Where we didn't have in February, and we still don't have now, is a sign of progress in the nonhousing services sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that is, you know, that's just something that will have to come through softening demand and perhaps some softening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's of course 56 percent of the index.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say that the inflation data that we got, to your point, really pointed to stronger inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's really just a question of not knowing at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a great deal of literature on the connection between tighter credit conditions, economic activity, hiring, and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question is, how significant will this credit tightening be and how sustainable it will be?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't really see it yet, so, so people are making estimates, you know, people are publishing estimates, but it's very kind of rule-of-thumb guesswork almost at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we think it's, it's potentially quite real and that argues for, you know, being alert as we go forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As we think about further rate hikes for us, we'll be paying attention to the actual and expected effects from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say what, what I think happened, and then I'll come to the questions around supervision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, at a basic level, Silicon Valley Bank management failed badly-they grew the bank very quickly, they exposed the bank to significant liquidity risk and interest rate risk, didn't hedge that risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We now know that supervisors saw these risks and, and intervened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that SVB experienced an unprecedentedly rapid and massive bank run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is a-this is a very large group of connected depositors-concentrated group of connected depositors in a very, very fast run, faster than historical record would suggest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as for us-so for our part, we're doing a review of supervision and regulation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: My only interest is that we identify what went wrong here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then make an assessment of what are the right policies to put in place so that it doesn't happen again, and then implement those policies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would be inappropriate for me at this stage to offer my views on what the answers might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Vice Chair Barr is leading this, and I think he's testifying next week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the review is going to be thorough and transparent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is clear-really to your last question-it's clear that we do need to strengthen supervision and regulation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I assume that there will be recommendations coming out of the report, and I, I plan on supporting them and supporting their implementation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are not weaknesses that are-that are at all broadly through the banking system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This was-this was a bank that was an outlier in terms of both its percentage of, of uninsured deposits and in terms of its holdings of duration risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And again, supervisors did get in there, and, and they were, as you know, obviously, you know they were- they were on this issue, but nonetheless, this, this still happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's really the nature of the interview-sorry, of the review-is to discover that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we published an SEP today, as you will have seen, and it shows that basically participants expect relatively slow growth, a gradual rebalancing of supply and demand in the labor market, with inflation moving down gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In that most likely case, if that happens, participants don't see rate cuts this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just say: As always, the path of the economy is uncertain, and policy is going to reflect what actually happens rather than what we write down in the SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Remember, we're looking-for purposes of our monetary policy tool, we're looking at what's happening among the banks and asking, is there going to be some tightening in credit conditions?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we're thinking about that as effectively doing the same thing that rate hikes do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, the key is, we have to have-policy has got to be tight enough to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't all have to come from rate hikes: It can come from, you know, from tighter credit conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're looking at, and we, we-it's highly uncertain how long the situation will be sustained or how significant any of those effects would be, so we're just going to have to watch.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, you know-obviously, at the end of the day, we will do enough to bring inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we're well aware of the concentrations people have in commercial real estate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the banking system is, is strong, it is sound, it is resilient, it's well capitalized, and I really don't see that as at all analogous to this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I welcome-it's 100 percent certainty that there will be independent investigations and outside investigations and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't give advice to the fiscal authorities, and we assume that-we take fiscal policy as, as it comes to our front door, stick it in our model along with a million other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and we will get inflation down to 2 percent in time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You have to look at, at the impulse from spending because spending was, of course, tremendously high during the pandemic, and then, as the pandemic programs rolled off, spending actually came down, so the-this sort of fiscal impulse is actually not what's driving inflation right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was-it was at the beginning perhaps part of what was driving inflation, but that's not really the story now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So 13(3) seemed like the right-we have a little more flexibility under section 13(3).

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've done quite a lot under the discount window as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We needed to do a special facility that was designed a certain way, so we did it under 13(3).

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's only available in unusual and exigent circumstances, and it has to be- meet certain requirements, but it seemed to be the right place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So with the FDIC, we're just, we're lending to the, in effect, we're-we're lending to the bridge bank.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's where the funds came from, and it's-it's a loan that's 100 percent guaranteed by the FDIC, so there's no risk in it for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, we, if we need to raise hike-raise rates higher, we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think for now though we, we-as I've mentioned, we see the likelihood of, of credit tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that can have, you know, an effect on the macroeconomy, on demand, on labor market, on inflation, and we're-we're going to be watching to see what that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll also be watching what's happening with inflation and in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll be watching all those things, and of course we will-we will eventually get to [a] tight enough policy to bring inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-People think of QE and QT in different ways, so let me be clear about how I'm thinking about these recent developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the recent liquidity provision that has increased the size of our balance sheet but the intent and the effects of it are very different from what we-from when we expand our balance sheet through purchases of longer-term securities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Large-scale purchases of long-term securities are, are really meant to alter the stance of policy by pushing down-pushing up the price and down the rates, longer-term rates, which supports demand through channels we understand fairly well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The balance sheet expansion is really temporary lending to banks to meet those special liquidity demands created by the recent tensions; it's not intended to directly alter the stance of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's having its intended effect of bolstering confidence in the banking system and thereby forestalling what might otherwise have been an abrupt and outsized tightening in financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the distribution of reserves, we, we don't see ourselves as, as running into reserve shortages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we think that our program of allowing our balance sheet to, to run off predictably, predicatbly and passively is working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And of course we're, we're always prepared to, to change that if that changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, to be honest, I don't-I don't recall the specifics of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, but I will tell you, though, that we have-there have been presentations about, about interest rate risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not a surprise that there are institutions that have-that have had unhedged long positions in long- duration securities that have lost value as, as longer-term rates have gone up due to our rate increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think, as you know, as is now in the public record, the supervisory team was apparently engaged, very much engaged with the bank repeatedly, and was escalating but, you know, nonetheless, what happened happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's really the purpose of-one way to think about the review that Vice Chair Barr is conducting is to try to understand how that happened and try to understand how we can do better and what policies we need to change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, one thing is the speed of the-I'll come back to that, the speed of the run, it's very different from what we've seen in the past, and it does kind of suggest that there's a need for possible, you know, regulatory and supervisory changes just because supervision and regulation need to keep up with what's, what's happening in the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will have to come back to you on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but what I'm saying is you've seen that we have the tools to protect depositors when there's a threat of serious harm to the economy or to-or to the financial system, and we're prepared to use those tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think depositors should assume that their-that their deposits are safe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we-that was really the Swiss government that we of course were, were following it over the course of the weekend, and we were engaged with their authorities in the way that you would expect, all the ways that you would expect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It seems to have been a positive outcome in the sense that the transaction was agreed to, and it has been- the markets have accepted it, and it seems to have gone well, and I think there was a concern that it might not go well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So coming into the middle of this week, yes, I would say that that is going well so far.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's just-that's an estimate of what will happen as demand slows and as conditions soften in the labor market and it's just-it's a highly uncertain estimate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, I was really-we have to bring inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The costs of bringing it down-there are real costs to bringing it down to 2 percent, but the costs of failing are much higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you read your history, as I'm sure you have, you can see that if the central bank doesn't get inflation back in place, get inflation-make sure that inflation expectations remain anchored, you can have a long series of years where inflation is high and volatile, and it's hard to invest capital, it's hard for an economy to perform well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're looking to avoid that and, you know, to get back to where we need to be-back to where we were for a quarter century, and get there as quickly as we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, it depends on whether you-so recessions tend to be nonlinear, and so they're very hard to model.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the models all work in a kind of linear way-if you have more of this, you get more of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But when a recession happens, the reactions tend to be nonlinear and that's what-so we don't know whether that'll happen this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know-if so, we don't know how significant it will be, and so, you know, we're very focused on getting inflation down because we know in the longer run that that is the thing that will most benefit the people we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's how we can have a long-you know, we've had very strong labor markets through these long expansions that we've had.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Four of the five longest, or three of the four longest expansions in U.S. history have been really since the high-inflation period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason was inflation wasn't forcing the central bank to come in and stop an incipient or, or, you know, an expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can have very, very long expansions without high inflation, and we had several of those, and they're very good for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see late in an expansion-you see low unemployment, you see the benefits of wages going to people at the lower end of the wage spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just a place that we should try to get back to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know it's, it's too early to say, really, whether these events have had much of an effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's hard for me to see how they would have helped the possibility-but I guess I would just say, it's too early to say whether there really have been changes in that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the question will be how long this period is sustained.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The longer it's sustained, then the greater will be the likely declines in-or tightening in credit standards, credit availability, so we'll just have to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do still think, though, that there's a-there's a pathway to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that pathway still exists and, you know, we're certainly trying to find it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But those are serious-those are serious regulatory, in particular immediate attention, and that's-and I guess there were six of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and getting to the seriousness of it, how are you going to ensure that banks comply with these citations, take them seriously-how will you enforce them?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is a great question and is right in the heart of what the review will be doing under Vice Chair Barr's leadership.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, I think that's where-that's what you think about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What can we do to make sure that-but, again, that's not for me to answer today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well I, I-see, if I did, I wouldn't share them because I, I really, you know, this review is going on, and, you know, I want nothing other than us to find out what happened and why, figure out what we can do to do better, and then implement those changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-For me to be giving you my half-formed, or partially informed, thoughts, it, you know, just isn't appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a real serious review going on with, with people from all over the Federal Reserve System who are not connected to this, you know, to this work, not connected to this bank, and under, again, Vice Chair Barr's leadership, and I'm confident that it will produce a satisfactory result.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we haven't really talked about changing the balance sheet implementation-that's not something we've discussed yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, we're always willing to change that if we conclude that it's appropriate, but we're really not seeing any signs there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Sorry, then the question before that was, just give me a-

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So financial conditions seem to have tightened-and probably by more than the traditional indexes say, because traditional indexes are focused a lot on [interest] rates and [prices of] equities, and they don't necessarily capture lending conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there are other measures which, if they're focused on, you know-bank lending conditions and things like that-they show some more tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question for us, though, is, how significant will that be and how, you know-what will be the extent of it and what will be the duration of it?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then-and then, you know, once you have-once you know that, there's a fair amount of research about how that, with broad uncertainty bands-how that works its way into the economy [and] over what period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, you know, we'll be looking to see the first part of that-like how serious is this, and does it look like it's going to be sustained, and if it is, you know, it could easily have a significant macroeconomic effect, and we would factor that into our policy decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mentioned with rate cuts, rate cuts are not in our base case, and, you know, so that's all I have to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, taking your question-of course, today our decision was to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A, a decision on a pause was not made today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You will have noticed that in the-in the statement from March, we had a sentence that said the Committee anticipates that some additional policy firming may be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That sentence is, is not in, in the statement anymore.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We took that out, and instead we're saying that, in determining the extent to which additional policy firming may be appropriate to return inflation to 2 percent over time, the Committee will take into account certain factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-that's a- that's a meaningful change that we're no longer saying that we anticipate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we'll be driven by incoming data meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we'll approach that question at the June meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-the staff's forecast is-so let me say-start by saying that that's not my own most likely case, which is really that, that the economy will continue to grow at, at a modest rate this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's-so different people on the Committee have different forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's my own assessment of the most likely path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: [The] staff produces its own forecast, and it's independent of the forecasts of, of the participants, which include the Governors and the Reserve Bank presidents, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think this is a healthy thing- that the, the staff is writing down what they really think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're not especially influenced by what the Governors think, and vice versa.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Governors are not taking what the staff says and just writing that down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's actually good that the, the staff and individual participants can have different perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, broadly, the forecast was for a mild recession, and by that I would characterize as one in which the rise in unemployment is smaller than is-has been typical in modern-era recessions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't want to characterize the staff's forecast for this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll, we'll leave that to the minutes-but broadly, broadly similar to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't want to speculate specifically, but I will say this: These are fiscal policy matters, for starters, and they're, they're for Congress and the Administration-for the elected parts of the government to deal with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: From our standpoint, I would just say this: It's essential that the debt ceiling be raised in a timely way, so that the U.S. government can pay all of its bills when they're due.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'd be in uncharted territory, and the-and the consequences to the U.S. economy would be highly uncertain and could, could be quite a[d]verse.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just would point out that it-that it's very important that this be done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the, the other point I'll make about that, though, is that no one should assume that the Fed can protect the economy from the potential, you know, short- and long-term effects of a failure to pay our bills on time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we- it's, it would be so uncertain that it's just as important that, that this-we never get to a place where we're actually talking about or even having a situation where the U.S. government's not paying its bills.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We talk a lot about risks to the-to the outlook, and that will-that come up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A number of people did raise that as a risk to the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't say that it was important in today's monetary policy decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the February 14 presentation-I didn't remember it very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But now, of course, I've gone back and looked at it very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was an informational briefing of the whole Board- the entire Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it was about interest rate risk in the banks and, and lots of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there was one page on Silicon Valley Bank, which talked about, you know, the amount of losses they-or mark-to-market losses they had in their portfolio.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was nothing in it about-that I recall, anyway, about, about the risk of a bank run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it was-I think the takeaway was, they were going away to do a-an assessment, a vertical-sorry, horizontal assessment of, of banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It wasn't-it, it wasn't presented as an urgent or alarming situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was presented as a-as an informational, nondecisional kind of a thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I thought it was a good presentation and, and, as I said, did remember it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what we're doing-of course, I think banks themselves are, are-many, many banks are now, are attending to liquidity and taking opportunity now, really, since, since the events of, of early March, to build liquidity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I- you know, like so many things, it, it's very useful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I, I think in this particular case, we have found that the monetary policy tools and the financial stability tools are not in conflict.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've used our, our financial stability tools to support banks through our lending facilities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, at the same time, we've been able to use our monetary policy tools to foster maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was-they're pointing out something that they're working on and that they're on the case-that, that, you know, that-I'm not sure whether they mentioned-I think they did, actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They mentioned that they had taken regulatory action matter-or supervisory action in the form of matters requiring attention.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it was to say: Yes, this is a bank, and there are many other banks that are experiencing this-these things, and we're on the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, you know, we certainly don't-and I don't have an agenda to further consolidate banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's been-consolidation has been a factor in the U.S. banking industry really since interstate banking and before that even-it goes back more than 30 years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You-when I was in the government a while back, I think there were 14,000 banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I personally have long felt that having small-, medium-, and large-size banks is a, a great part of our banking system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the community banks serve particular customers very well; regional banks serve very important purposes, and the various kinds of G-SIBs do as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's healthy to have a, you know, an arrange-a range of different kinds of banks doing different things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Is it a financial-so I would just say, in terms of J.P. Morgan buying First Republic, the FDIC really runs the process of closing and selling a closed bank completely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, that is their role, so I really don't have a comment on, on that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, there's an exception to the deposit cap for a failing bank.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the FDIC, I believe, is bound by law to take the bid that is the least-cost bid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think it's probably good policy that we, we don't want the largest banks doing big acquisitions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but this is-this is an exception for a failing bank.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think it's actually a good outcome for the banking system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It also would have-would have been a good-a good outcome for the banking system had one of the regional banks bought, bought this company.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, we have to follow the law in our agencies, and the law is, it goes to the, the least-cost bid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-I think I follow that up by saying, it's, it's quite impossible to have a precise estimate of the words to that effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, when we-we've been raising interest rates, and that raises the price of credit, and that, in a sense, restricts credit in the economy, working through the price mechanism.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, when banks raise their credit standards, that can also make credit tighter in a kind of broadly similar way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It isn't-it isn't possible to make a kind of clean translation between one and the other, although firms are trying that and, you know, we're trying it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, we have to be-we have to be honest and humble about our ability to make a precise assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it does complicate the task of achieving, you know, a sufficiently restrictive stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think, conceptually, though, we think that, you know, interest rates-in principle, we won't have to raise the rates quite as high as we would have had this not happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The extent of that is so hard to predict because we don't know how persistent these, these effects will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know how large they'll be and how long they'll take to be transmitted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's, that's what we'll be watching carefully to find out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's that-this is just something that we have to factor in as we-as we want to find ourselves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would say it this way: The assessment of, of the extent to which additional policy firming may be appropriate is going to be an ongoing one, meeting by meeting, and we're going to be looking at the factors that I mentioned that-they're listed in, in the statement, the obvious factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's the way we're going to be thinking about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I say, it does complicate-we, we have, you know, a broad understanding of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But translating it into, into rate hikes is uncertain, let's say-it adds even further uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, we'll be able to see what's happening with credit conditions- what's happening with lending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we'll, we'll factor that into our decisionmaking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to need data to accumulate on that-not an assessment that we've made, as-that, that would mean we think we've reached that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I just think it's, it's not possible to say that with confidence now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, you, you will know that the Summary of Economic Projections from the March meeting showed that in-at that point in time, that the median participant thought that this was- this was the appropriate level of the-of the ultimate high level of rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-you know, we're just going to have to- before we really declare that, I think we're going to have to see data accumulating and, and, you know, make that-as I mentioned, it's an ongoing assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to release the results of this SLOOS on May 8, in line with our usual time frame.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would just say that the SLOOS is broadly consistent, when you see it, with how we and others have been thinking about the situation and what we're seeing from other sources.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You will have seen the Beige Book and listened to the various earnings calls that indicate that midsize banks have-some of them had been tightening their lending standards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Banking data will show that lending has continued to grow, but the pace has been slowing really since the second half of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, we-the reason is that we-again, with our monetary policy we're try-trying to reach and then-and then stay at a, for an extended period, a level of policy-a policy stance that's sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that's what we're trying to do with our-with our tool.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think it's enabled us to see more data, and it will continue to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I-you know, we really-you know, we have to balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We always have to balance the risk of not doing enough and, and not getting inflation under control against the risk of maybe slowing down economic activity too much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we thought that this rate hike, along with the meaningful change in, in our policy statement, was the right way to balance that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, as I mentioned, I would just say that this assessment will be an ongoing one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You-you know, you can't-with, with economic data, you, you can't-you've, you've seen-take inflation for a minute.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen inflation come down-move back up two or three times since March of 2021.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen inflation have a few months of coming down and then come right back up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think you're going to want to see that-you know, that a few months of data will, will persuade you that you've-that you've got this right, kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we, we have the luxury: We've raised 500 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think real rates are probably-that you can calculate them many different ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But one way is to look at the nominal rate and then subtract a, a reasonable estimate of, of, let's say, one-year inflation, which might be 3 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's meaningfully above what most people would-many people, anyway, would, would assess as, you know, the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you also begin to see it more and more in, in other activities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you-if you put the-you put the credit tightening on top of that and the QT that's, that's ongoing, I think, I think you feel like, you know, we're, we may not be far off-we're possibly even at-that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Look-I think we're always going to have 2 percent as our, our target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's-let me just say, that's not what we're looking for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking for inflation going down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we-that's, that's not a question that's in front of us, and it would depend on so many other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, we're not looking to get to 3 percent and then drop our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have a, a goal of getting to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I think we're going to-we're going to need to stay at this for a while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think they, they-you know, they, they will both matter equally at that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, you have a labor market that's still extraordinarily tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You still got 1. job openings, even with the lower job openings number, for every unemployed person.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do see some evidence of softening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages-you all will have seen that the wage number from late last week, and it's-whenever it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's, it's a couple of percentage points above what would be-what would be consistent with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do see some softening; we see new labor supply coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the labor market is very, very strong, whereas inflation is, you know, running high-well above our-well above our goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And right now, we need to be focusing on bringing inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Fortunately, we've been able to do that so far without unemployment going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think-you know, I know what's printed in the Summary of Economic Projections and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think you can deduce exactly what you said about what participants think, because you don't know what they were thinking for first- quarter GDP at that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They could have been thinking about a fairly low number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Anyway, in any case, I'll just say, I, I continue to think that it's possible that this time is really different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason is, there's just so much excess demand, really, in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's interesting, as, you know, we've raised rates by 5 percentage points in 14 months, and the unemployment rate is 3½ percent, pretty much where it was-even lower than where it was when we started.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see-by surveys and much, much [other] evidence-that, that conditions are cooling gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it wasn't supposed to be possible for job openings to decline by as much of the-as they've declined without unemployment going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it just seems that, to me, that it's possible that we can continue to have a cooling in the labor market without having the big increases in unemployment that have gone with many, you know, prior episodes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I do think that it-that this, that the situation in the labor market, with so much excess demand, yet, you know, wages are actually-wages have been moving down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wage increases have been moving down, and that's a good sign-down to a more sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-you know, I think, you know, the, the case of, of avoiding a recession is, in my view, more likely than that of having, having a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's not-it's not that the case of having a recession is-I don't rule that out, either.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's possible that we will have what I hope would be a mild recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at a range of wage, wage measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then-so you assume wages should be equal to productivity increases plus inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so you can-you can look at, you know, the employment compensation index, average hourly earnings, the Atlanta wage tracker, compensation per hour-basically, those four and many others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you can-you can look at, at what the-what they would have to run at over a long period of time for that to be consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there is a feature of long expansions where they do go down-where labor gets a bigger share toward later, later in a recession-sorry, later in an expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the-you know, and we calculate those, and you have to take the precision with a degree of-a degree of salt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that what they will show is that, you know, if, if the-if wages are running at 5 percent, 3 percent is closer to where they need to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wage increases and closer to 3 percent, roughly, is what it would take to get-to be consistent with inflation over a longer period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-by the way, I don't want to-I do not think that wages are the principal driver of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, I've never said that, you know, that-that wages are really the principal driver, because I don't think that's really right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So higher profits and higher margins are what happens when you have an imbalance between supply and demand: too much demand, not enough supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've been in a situation in many parts of the economy where, where supply has been fixed or, or not flexible enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, you know, the way the market clears is through higher prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So to get, I, I think-as goods pipelines have, have gotten, you know, back to normal so that we don't have the long waits and the shortages and that kind of thing-I think you will see inflation come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you'll see-you'll see corporate margins coming down as a result of return of full competition, where there's enough supply to meet demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then it's-then it's, then you're really back to full competition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we look at a combination of data and, and forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, the whole idea is to-is to create a good forecast based on what you see in the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, and it will-of course, it'll be the obvious things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll be readings on wages, on economic growth, on the labor market, and all of those many things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think a particular focus for us going-now, over the past six, seven weeks now and going forward is going to be, what's happening with credit tightening?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Are small and medium-sized banks tightening credit standards, and, and is that having an effect on, on loans, on lending?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so we can begin to assess how that fits in with monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's- again, I would just point out, we've raised rates by 5 percentage points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now we have credit conditions tightening-not just in the normal way, but perhaps a little bit more, due to what's happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have to factor all of that in and, and make our assessment of-you know, of whether our policy stance is sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have to do that in a world where policy works with long and variable lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we, we will make our best assessment, and that's what we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we on the Committee have a-have a view that inflation is going to come down-not so quickly, but it'll take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in that world, if that forecast is broadly right, it would not be appropriate and-to cut rates, and we won't cut rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you have a different forecast and, you know, markets-or have been, from time to time, pricing in, you know, quite rapid reductions in inflation, you know, we'd, we'd factor that in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, the history of the last two years has been very much that inflation moves down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Particularly now, if you look at nonhousing services, it really, really hasn't moved much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so we think we'll have to-demand will have to weaken a little bit, and labor market conditions, conditions may have to soften a bit more to begin to see progress there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, in that world, it wouldn't be-it wouldn't be appropriate for us to cut rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we looked at that very carefully, as you would imagine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the-it's, it's really not contributing, we don't think, now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it moved up-moved down and then moved back up to where it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What happened in the-when, when there were the big deposit flows, which, by the way, have really stabilized now-what happened was, institutional investors took their uninsured deposits and put them in government money market funds, which bought paper from the Federal Home Loan Banks and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Over the course of, of maybe the last year, retail investors had been gradual-as they do in every tightening cycle, they've been gradually moving their deposits into higher-yielding places such as CDs and, and other things, including money market funds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a gradual process that is quite natural and happens during a, a tightening cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What was unusual, really, was the institutional investors moving their uninsured deposits and spreading them around and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it doesn't seem to have had any-any effect overall on the overnight repo facility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is really there to, to help us keep rates where they're supposed to be, and it's, it's serving that purpose very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just say, it's -I, I don't really think we should be- we shouldn't even be talking about a world in which the U.S. doesn't pay its bills.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and again, I would just say, we don't-no one should assume that the Fed can do-can really protect the economy and the financial system and our reputation globally from, from the damage that such, such an event might inflict.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I didn't-I didn't take part in creating the report or doing the work, but I do-I have read it, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I would say it this way: A, a very large-a large bank, not a very large bank-a large bank failed quite suddenly and unexpectedly in a way that threatened to spread contagion into the financial system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the only thing that, that I'm really focused on is to understand what went wrong, what happened, and, and identify what we need to do to address that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of that is-may, it may just have been technology evolving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we have to keep up with all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But some of it may be our policies, and-supervisory and regulatory, whatever.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What our job is now is, identify those things and implement them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's kind of the only thing I care about is-and I think-I feel like I am accountable for doing everything I can to make sure that that happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would-I guess I would say it this way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There were three large banks, really, from the very beginning that were at the heart of the stress that we- that we saw in early March, the severe period of stress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those have now all been resolved, and all the depositors have been protected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that the resolution and sale of, of First Republic kind of draws a line under that period of-is an important step toward drawing a line under that period of, of severe stress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also think we are very focused on what's happening with credit availability, particularly, you know, with what you saw in the-in the Beige Book, and you will see in the SLOOS, is, is small and medium-medium-sized, small and medium-sized banks who are feeling that they need to tighten credit standards-build liquidity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: More broadly, we, we will continue to very carefully monitor what's going on in the banking system, and we'll factor that assessment into our decisions in an important way, going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say, first of all, I've been Chair of the Board for five-plus years now, and I fully recognize that we made mistakes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we've learned some new things as well, and we need to do better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, I thought the report was unflinching and appropriately so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do feel that I'm personally accountable to do what I can to foster measures that will address the problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on, on the Vice Chair for Supervision, you know, the place to start is, is the statutory role, which is quite unusual.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Vice Chair, it says, shall deploy policy recommendations-"develop policy recommendations for the Board regarding supervision and regulation of depository institution .

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: , and shall oversee the supervision and regulation of such firms."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is Congress establishing a four-year term for someone else on the Board-not, not the Chair-as Vice Chair for Supervision who really gets to set the agenda for supervision and regulation for the Board of Governors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Congress wanted that person to be-to have political accountability for developing that agenda.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the way it works-the way it has worked in practice for me is, I've had a good working relationship.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I give my, my counsel, my input privately, and that's-I offer that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I have good conversations, and I try to contribute constructively.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I respect the authority that Congress has deferred on that person, including working with, with Vice Chair Barr and, and his predecessor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's the way it's supposed to work, and that's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know-but, but it isn't-I wouldn't say it's a matter of complete deference.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's more, I have a-I have a role in, in presenting my views and discussing-having an intelligent discussion about what's going on and why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, that person does get to set the agenda and gets to take things to the Board of Governors and really, in supervision, has sole authority over supervision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, you know, who doesn't look back and think that you could have done things differently?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As one of my great mentors used to always say, "Control the controllable."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we control now is, make a fair assessment, learn the right lessons, figure out what the fixes are, and implement them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and I think that, that Vice Chair Barr's report is an excellent first step in that, but we've got to follow through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So support for the 25 basis point rate increase was very strong across the board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say there are a number of people-and, you know, you'll see this in the minutes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't want to try to do the head count in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But people did talk about pausing, but not so much at this meeting, you know, that we're-I mean, there's a sense that we're, we're-that, you know, we're much closer to the end of this than to the beginning, that-you know, as I mentioned, if you-if you add up all the tightening that's going on through various channels, it's-we, we feel like we-you know, we're getting close or, or maybe even there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that, again, that's going to be an ongoing assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and we're going to be looking at those factors that we listed and-to determine whether there's, there's more to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just think we're-I think we-look, I think we've moved a long way fairly quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we can afford to look at the data and, and make a careful assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I just would start with something that's changed, really, which is this-the run on Silicon Valley Bank was out of keeping with the speed of runs through history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that now needs to be reflected in some-in some way in regulation and in supervision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It-we know-now that we know it's possible, I think we didn't-no one thought that was possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one-I'm not aware of anybody thinking that this could happen so-quite so quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that, you know, that will play through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I, you know-it will be up to Vice Chair Barr to really take the lead in designing the ways to address that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then, you know-that we're going to- obviously, we're going to revisit [this].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's pretty clear we need-to me, anyways-clear that we need to strengthen both supervision and regulations for banks of this size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'm, I'm thinking that we're on the-on track to do that as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Can you be any more specific on stress testing or looking at banks that have specific concentrations in certain parts of the economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-see, that's, that's what Vice Chair Barr's role really is, and he'll take the lead on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I guess I would-I guess I would go back to the beginning of this tightening cycle to address that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as we started our rate hikes early last year, we said there were three issues that would need to be addressed kind of in sequence-that of the speed of tightening, the level to which rates would need to go, and then a period of time over which we'd need to keep policy restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So at the outset, going back 15 months, the key issue was how fast to move rates up, and we moved very quickly by historical standards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then last December, after four consecutive 75 basis point hikes, we moderated to a pace of 50-of a 50 basis point hike and then this year to three 25 basis point hikes at sequential meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it seemed to us to make obvious sense to moderate our rate hikes as we got closer to our destination.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the decision to consider not hiking at every meeting and ultimately to hold rates steady at this meeting, I would just say it's a continuation of, of that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The main issue that we're focused on now is determining the extent of additional policy firming that may be appropriate to return inflation to 2 percent over time-so that the pace of the increases and the ultimate level of increases are separate variables, given how far it-we have come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It may make sense for rates to move higher but at a more moderate pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I want to stress one more thing-and that is that the Committee decision made today was only about this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't make any decision about going forward, including what would happen at the next meeting, including-we did not decide or really discuss anything about going to an every-other-meeting kind of an approach or, or really any other approach.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We really were focused on what to do at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So again, we didn't-we didn't make a decision about July.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, of course, it, it came up in the-in the meeting from time to time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But really, the focus was, was on what to do today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say about, about July two things: (1) [the] decision hasn't been made, (2) I do expect that it will be a "live" meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're, you're right that the data came in, I would say, consistent with, but on the high side of, expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you go back to the old-the former SEP-the last SEP in March, you will see that [compared with March, projected real GDP] growth moved up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are not huge moves, but growth estimates moved up a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, all three of those kind of point in the same direction-which is, you know, that perhaps more [monetary policy] restraint will be necessary than we had thought at the last meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So although the level, frankly, is, is pretty-the level of 5.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: [percent] is pretty consistent, if you think about it, where the [expected] federal funds rate was trading before the bank incidents of early March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So your question is, where's the-where's the disinflation going to come from?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, you know, I don't think the story has really changed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-the Committee has consistently said and believed that the process of getting inflation down is going to be a gradual one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you go back to the-to the three-part framework for [analyzing] core PCE inflation-which is, we think, as good an indicator as you can have for where inflation is going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With goods, we need to see continued healing in supply conditions-supply-side conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They've definitely improved a substantial amount, but if you talk to people in business, they will say it's not back to where it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that should enable goods prices to continue-goods, goods inflation to continue to come down over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and you are seeing there that new rents in new, new leases are, are coming in at low levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's really a matter of time as that goes through the pipeline.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, I think any forecast that people are making right now about inflation coming down this year will, will contain a big dose of-this year and next year-will contain a, a good amount of, of disinflation [coming] from that source.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and that's, again, probably going to come slower than we would [previously have expected it to come into] effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That leaves, you know, the big sector, which is a little more than half, pardon me, of the-of core PCE inflation that's not housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we see only the earliest signs of disinflation there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say [that,] in a number of the parts of that sector, the largest cost would be wage cost.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's the service sector, so it's, it's heavily labor intensive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think many analysts would say that the key to getting inflation down there is to have a continuing loosening in labor market conditions-which we have seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have actually seen, you know-I go through a number of indicators suggesting there has been some loosening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would almost say that the, the conditions that we need to see in place to get inflation down are, are coming into place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that would be [real GDP] growth meaningfully below trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would be goods pipelines getting healthier and healthier and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There, there-the things are in place that we need to see, but the process of that actually working on inflation is going to take some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-first, I would say that the, the question of speed is a separate question from the question-from the-from, from that of level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and I think if you look at the SEP, that is our estimate-our individual-it's, it's really a cumulation of our individual estimates of how far to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I mentioned how, how we got to those numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of speed, it's, it's what I said at the beginning, which is, speed was very important last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As we get closer and closer to the destination-and, according to the SEP, we're not so far away from the destination, in most people's accounting-it's, it's reasonable-it's common sense to go a little slower, just as it was reasonable to go from 75 basis points to 50 to 25 at every meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so the Committee thought overall that it was appropriate to moderate the pace, if only slightly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it allows the economy a little more time to adapt as we-as we make our decisions going forward, and we'll get to see, you know-we haven't really-we don't know the full extent of, of the consequences of the banking turmoil that we've seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we-it would be early to see those, but we don't know what the extent is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it's, it's just the idea that we're trying to get this right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is-if you think of the two things as separate variables, then I think-I think that the skip-I shouldn't call it a skip-the, the decision makes sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think you're adding that to the, the data that we've seen since the last meeting, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we-since we chose to maintain rates at this meeting, it'll really be a three-month period of data that we can look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's a full quarter, and I think you can-you can draw more conclusions from that than you can from any six-any six- week period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll look at all the data, the evolving outlook, and we'll make a decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I-I mean, on the first part, I just think we're following the data and also the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy is-the labor market, I think, has surprised many, if not all, analysts over the last couple of years with its extraordinary resilience, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really, if you think about it-that's what's driving it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's supporting spending, which in turn is supporting hiring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's, it's really the engine, it seems, that is-that is driving the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of, you know-we, we always write down at these meetings what we think the appropriate terminal rate will be at the end of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's based on our, our own individual assessments of what the most likely path of the economy is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It can be-it can actually, in reality, wind up being lower or higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's-it is-it's, it's what people think as of today, and as the-as the data come in, it, it can move around during the intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't-I can't tell you that that I ever have a lot of confidence that we can see where the-where the federal funds rate will be that far in advance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I, I would say again that I think that, over time, the balance of risks, as we move from very, you know-from interest rates that are effectively zero now to 5 percentage points with, with an SEP calling for additional hikes-I think we've moved much closer to our destination, which is that sufficiently restrictive rate, and I think that means by-almost by definition that the-that the risks of, of sort of overdoing it and under, underdoing it are, are getting closer to being in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I still think, and my, my colleagues agree, that, that the risks to inflation are to the upside still.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't-we don't think we're there with inflation yet because we're just looking at the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look at the-at the full range of, of inflation data, particularly the core data, you just-you just aren't seeing a lot of progress over the last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Headline, of course, inflation has come down materially, but, as you know, we look at core [inflation] as a better indicator of where inflation overall is going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Sufficiently-so I think, you know, what, what we'd like to see is credible evidence that inflation is topping out and then beginning to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's what we want to see- of course that's what we want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think it's-it's also-we understand that there are lags, but remember that it's, it's more than a year since financial conditions began tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's-I think the reason we're, we're comfortable pausing is that we are still-much of the tightening took place over last summer and later into the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it's, it's reasonable to think that some of that may come into effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, you know-I think stretching out into a more moderate pace is appropriate to, to allow you to make that judgment of sufficiency, you know, more-with more data over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's sort of standard thinking that monetary policy affects economic activity with long and variable lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, these days, financial conditions begin to tighten well in advance of actual rate hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you-if you look back when we were lifting off, we started talking about lifting off-by the time we had lifted off, the two-year [interest rate], which is a pretty good estimate of where [monetary] policy is going, had gone from 20 basis points to 200 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in that sense, tightening happens much sooner than it used to in a world where- where news was in newspapers and not, you know, not on, on the wire.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's still the case that what you see is interest-sensitive spending is affected very, very quickly-so housing, and durable goods, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But broader demand, and spending, and, and asset values, and things like that-they just take longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you can pretty much find research to support whatever answer you would like on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's not any certainty or agreement in the profession on how long it takes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, then that makes it challenging, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, it's one of the main reasons why it makes sense to go at a slightly more moderate pace now as we seek that, that ultimate-I can't point to-that ultimate endpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we'll see it when we see inflation, you know, really, really flattening out reliably and then starting to soften.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, ideally, by, by taking a little more time, we won't go well past the level where we need to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it's too early still to, to try to assess the full extent of what that might mean.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that's something we're going to be watching, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, if we were to see what, what we would view as significant tightening beyond what would normally be expected because of, of this channel, then, you know, we would factor that into account on, on-in, in making rate decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we've-remember, we've-we're two and a half years into this-or two and a quarter years into this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And forecasters, including Fed forecasters, have consistently thought that inflation was about to turn down and, you know, traditional-you know, typically forecasted that it would and been wrong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you-I think if you look at the-at core PCE inflation overall-look at it over the last six months-you're just not seeing a lot of progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's running, and it's running at a level, you know, over 4½ percent-far above our, our target and not really, you know, moving down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, you know, of course, we're going to get inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we don't want to do-we, we want to do that with the minimum damage we can to the economy, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we have to get inflation down to 2 percent, and we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, hence, you see today's policy decision: both, both to write down further rate hikes by the end of this year but also to, you know, to take-to, to moderate somewhat the pace with which we're moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm, I'm not going to comment on any particular paper, but I, I would say that the-I think the overall picture is that at the beginning in, you know, early 2021, inflation was really becoming from very strong demand for-largely for goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They had money in the bank, and they wanted to spend-they spent a lot on goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, at the same time-and because of that high demand, to some extent, supply chains got all snarled up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that was the, the origin, and it wasn't really particularly about the labor market or wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as you-as you moved into-through '21, into '22, and now in '23, I think many, many analysts believe that it will be important-an important part of getting inflation down, especially in the nonhousing services sector, to getting wage inflation back to a level that is sustainable, that is consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We actually have seen wages broadly move down but just at a quite gradual pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So- and that's, you know, that's a little bit of the finding of the Bernanke paper with Blanchard of a few weeks ago, which is very consistent with, with what I, I would think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I don't want to deal with, with hypotheticals about different ways data might move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, we, you know-we of course-we're not-we don't go out of our way to surprise markets or the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, our main focus has to be on getting the policy right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's what we're doing here, and that's what we'll do for the upcoming meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say the July meeting will be "live," and we'll just have to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you'll, you'll see the data, you'll hear Fed people talking about it, and, and markets will have to make a- make a judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I, I think if you look at-if, if you just look at-I'll just point you to the forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So inflation is running-core PCE inflation is running at about 4½, a little higher than 4½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the, the median FOMC participant thinks it will go down to 3. on a 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's a pretty significant decline for half a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we'll-we do try to be transparent in our reaction function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say, first of all, on the Treasury part of it-if I can talk about that and then go back to the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on that-of course, we've been very focused on that for a couple of months, as everyone has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we all saw-I saw the Secretary's comments yesterday to the effect that [the] Treasury has consulted widely with market participants about how to avoid market disruption and that they're going to watch carefully for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's from the Treasury, which actually sets the, you know, the, the borrowings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the Fed, we'll be monitoring market conditions carefully as the Treasury refills the, the TGA.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The adjustment process is very likely to involve both a reduction in the RRP facility and also in reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's really hard to say at the-at the beginning of this which will be-which will be greater.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are starting at a very high level of reserves-and still elevated over RRP take-up, for that matter-so we don't think reserves are likely to become scarce in the near term or even over the course of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's-that's the-that's the Treasury part of the answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will, of course, continue to monitor conditions in money markets, and we're prepared to make adjustments to make sure that, that monetary policy transmission works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we have a number of-I would say the [ON] RRP [facility] doesn't look like it's, it's pulling money out of-out of the banking system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't think-that's not something, something we've thought about a lot over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't really look like that's, that's something that we would do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's-I think it's a tool that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are other tools we can-we can use to address money market issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I wouldn't say that that's something that's likely that we would do in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So certainly housing-very interest sensitive, and it's the first place, really, or one of the first places, that's either helped by low rates or, or that is held back by, by higher rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we certainly saw that over the course of the last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We now see housing putting in a bottom and maybe even moving up a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think we-we will see rents, rents and, and house prices filtering into, into housing services inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I do see them kind of-kind of wandering around at a relatively low level now, and that's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, you know, the way it works is the individual participants sit in their offices all over the country, and they write down their forecast and-including their most likely forecasts-including their rate forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then they send it in on Friday afternoon, and we cumulate it, and then we publish it for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I don't know that housing is, is itself going to be driving the rates picture, but it's part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-we hope and expect that other policymakers will respect our independence on, on monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't see ourselves as, as, you know, the judges of appropriate fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, and many of my predecessors have said, that we're on an unsustainable fiscal path and, and that needs to be addressed over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think trying to get into, into that with lawmakers would be-would be kind of inappropriate, given our independence and our need to stick to our knitting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I continue to think-and this really hasn't changed-that there is a path to getting inflation back down to 2 percent without having to see the kind of sharp downturn and, and large losses of employment that we've seen in so many past instances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A-in a way, a strong labor market is-that, that gradually cools could, could aid that along-it could aid that along.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
