text: But I, I guess I want to come back to the, the main thing, which is, though, simply this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we see-the Committee- as you can see from the SEP, the Committee is completely unified in the need to get inflation down to 2 percent and will do whatever it takes to get it down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we, we understand that allowing inflation to get entrenched into the-in the U.S. economy is the thing that we cannot, cannot allow to happen for the benefit of today's workers and families and businesses but also for the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Getting price stability back and, and restored will benefit generations of people as long as it's sustained.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and you should understand that that is our top priority.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, if you look two and three years out with, with the forecast-first of all, I wouldn't-I wouldn't put too much weight on forecasts even one year out because they're, they're so highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what they're showing is that as inflation comes down in the-in the forecast, if you don't lower interest rates, then real rates are actually going up, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So just to maintain a real rate, the nominal rate at that point-two years out, let's say-should come down just to maintain real rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if-and actually, you know, since we're, we're probably going to-we're, we're having real rates that are going to have to be meaningfully positive and significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So for us to get inflation down, that probably means- that, that certainly means that, that it will be appropriate to cut rates at such time as inflation is coming down really significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And again, we're talking about a couple of years out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, as, as anyone can see, not a single person on the Committee wrote down a rate cut this year, nor do I think it is at all likely to be appropriate, if you think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has-it has not so far reacted much to our-to our existing rate hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we are, of course, worried about-there are-there are long- standing differences in racial and ethnic groups across, across our labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a factor that we don't-we can't really address with our tools.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do consider that when we're thinking about what constitutes maximum employment-it is, for us, a broad and inclusive goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But remember, all unemployment, including Black unemployment, has been bouncing around right near historic lows-historic modern lows here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're still talking about, I mean, what is as strong a labor market as we've seen in, you know, a half- century here in the United States.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So overall unemployment of 3. percent is, is higher-three- tenths higher than it was measured to be at the last-a month ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't say-that's, you know-as a factual matter, that's correct.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do need to see, you know, rents bottom out here or at least stay quite low in terms of their increases because we want-we want the, you know, we want inflation to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And rental is, is a very large part of the CPI-about a third-and it's about half of that for the PCE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't say it's the decisive part, but take a step back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you see is- look at-look at core inflation over the past six months, a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're just not seeing a lot of progress-not the kind of progress we want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the Committee-people on the Committee-the median went up significantly, so that the median participant now thinks that core PCE inflation on a 12-month basis will be 3. percent this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, once again, every year for the past three years, it's gone up over the course of the year, and that's doing that again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we see that, and we see that inflation forecasts are coming in low again, and we see that-that that tells us that we need to do more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're-that's why you see the SEP with-where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we, you know-what we're talking about is having wage increases still at a very strong level but at a level that's consistent with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I, I think we've seen some progress-all, all of the major measures of wages have, have moved down from extremely elevated-not extremely elevated-highly elevated levels a year or so ago, and they're, they're moving back down but, but quite gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, we want to see that, that process continue gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, it's great to see wage increases, particularly for people at the lower end of the income spectrum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we want that as part of the process of getting inflation back down to 2 percent, which benefits everyone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, inflation hurts those same people more than anyone else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People on a fixed income are hurt the worst, and the fastest, by high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the topic of wages in the labor market and dynamics in the labor market could-is about as central a topic to our discussions as, as anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it's, it's very-labor economics, you know, and the labor market are utterly central.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we spend a lot of time talking about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, we-there, there are structural issues that are really not for the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we don't spend a lot of time- although we take notice of, of what's going on, but we're not, you know-we're not involved in discussions or debates over, over strikes and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we-you know, we, we look, and we see what's going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're making judgments about what it will take to get inflation down to 2 percent in the aggregate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as I said, don't think that was about-I didn't-most folks would say now it wasn't really about that-about wages at the beginning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's becoming more about that as we-as we get into really service-sector inflation, which is the part of the economy where we have seen the least progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a substantial amount of commercial real estate in the banking system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A, a large part of it is in smaller banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's well distributed-to the extent it's well distributedthen, then the system could, could take losses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do expect that there will be losses, but they'll be-they'll be banks that have concentrations, and those banks will experience larger losses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it feels like-it feels like something that will be around for some time, as opposed to, you know, something that will suddenly hit and, and, you know, work its way into systemic risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of nonbank financials-financial sector-there's been a ton of work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, clearly in the-in the pandemic, it really was-it was the nonbank financial sector where, where issues really arose.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there's a lot of work going on in-with the Administration, in particular, leading that to try to address issues in the Treasury market and, and in all kinds of areas in the nonbank financial market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but, you know, our jurisdiction at the Fed is over banks-actually bank holding companies and some banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, in terms of the events of March-as I mentioned earlier, we will be carefully monitoring that situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, our, our job generally involves worrying about a lot of things that may go wrong, and that would include the banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It might be hard for me to identify something that we don't worry about rather than that we do worry about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as we see things unfold-as we see what's happening with credit conditions and, and also all the individual banks that are out there, you know, we'll be able to take, to the extent it's appropriate, we can take, if they're macroeconomic implications, we can take that into account in our rate setting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-and, and I was-I guess I meant to address that by saying as we-as we watch, we'll see what's happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we-if we're seeing the kind of tightening of conditions that, that you could be referring to, then we can factor that-because really, we're-we use our-our rate tool is, is, you know, is-it really has macroeconomic purposes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we have responsibility for financial stability as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that also is a factor that we're always going to be considering.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we haven't made a decision to go to every other meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be going meeting by meeting, and as we go into each meeting, we're going to be asking ourselves the same questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we haven't made any decisions about, about any future meetings, including the pace at which we'd consider hiking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're going to be assessing the need for further tightening that may be appropriate-you read the language-"to return inflation to 2 percent over time."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that the intermeeting data came in broadly in line with expectations: Economic activity remained resilient, job creation remains strong while cooling a bit, and the June CPI report actually came in a bit better than expectations for a change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the June CPI report, of course, was welcomed, but it's only one report, one month's data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We hope that inflation will follow a lower path, as was-that will be consistent with the CPI reading, but we don't know that, and we're just going to need to see more data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, it will be the broader, the whole broader picture, and starting with-we're looking for moderate growth, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking for supply and demand through the economy coming into better balance, including, in particular, in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be asking ourselves, does this whole collection of data, do we assess it as suggesting that we need to raise rates further?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we make that conclusion, then we will go ahead and raise rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's how we're thinking about the next meeting and, you know, how we're thinking about meetings going forward potentially, but, you know, we're now mainly thinking about the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will also say, since we're talking about it, between now and the September meeting, we get two more job reports, two more CPI reports.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we have an ECI report coming later this week-which is [an] employment compensation index-and lots of data on economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of that information is going to inform our decision as we go into that meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say it is certainly possible that we would raise funds again at the September meeting if the data warrant it, and I would also say it's possible that we would choose to hold steady at that meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be making careful assessments, as I said, meeting by meeting, and I'll close by saying we've raised the federal funds rate now by 525 basis points since March 2022.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Monetary policy, we believe, is restrictive and is putting downward pressure on economic activity and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm just going to go back to what I said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have eight weeks now until the September meeting, and all that data that I recited, we're going to be looking at all that and making that assessment then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it really-we did have the one good reading, and, of course, we welcome that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, we've seen-we've seen this before in the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many forecasts call for, for rates-for, for inflation to remain low, but we just don't know that until we see the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say it this way: The overall resilience of the economy, the fact that, that we've been able to achieve disinflation so far without any meaningful negative impact on the labor market, the strength of the economy-overall, that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also-you see consumer, consumer confidence coming up and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the margin, stronger growth could lead, over time, to higher inflation, and that would require an appropriate response for monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll be watching that carefully and seeing how it evolves over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you go back to what we're trying to do here, we're trying to achieve a stance of policy that's sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the last meeting, we wrote down our individual estimates of that would take-of what that would take, and the median of that was, was an additional two rate hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say, we looked at the interim intermeeting data and, as I mentioned, broadly consistent, not perfectly consistent, but broadly consistent with expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as a result, we went ahead and, and took another step.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, you know, a labor market that continues to be strong but, but gradually slowing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mentioned that the inflation report was actually a little better than expected, but, you know, we're, we're going to be careful about taking too much signal from, from a single reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's how we look at it, and, and so we did take that step today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's hard to pick the pieces apart and say, you know, how much of this and how much of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we'll, of course, we'll be looking to see whether the signal from June's CPI is replicated or, or the opposite of replicated or whether it's somewhere in the middle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be looking at the labor market data very closely, of course, and making an overall judgment about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's the totality of the data, I think, but with a particular focus on, on making progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm just going to tell you again what we're going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In September, we're going to look at, at two additional job reports, two additional CPI reports, lots of activity data, and that's what we're going to look at, and we're going to make that decision then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that decision could, could mean another hike in, in September, or it could mean that we decide to maintain at that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, the question we're going to be asking ourselves is, is the overall signal one that we need to do more, that we need to tighten further?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we get that signal, whenever we get it, then-and that's the collective judgment of the Committee- then we will move ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we don't, you know, then, then we'll have the option of maintaining policy at that level, but it's, it's, you know, it's really dependent so much on the data, and we just don't have it yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I'd say it this way: First, it is-it is a good thing that headline inflation has come down so much, because that's really what the public experiences.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and I would say that having headline inflation move down that much almost creates a-it will strengthen the broad sense that, that the public has that inflation is coming down, which will in turn, we hope, help inflation continue to move down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we-I'd say it this way: It's really a question of, how do you balance the two risks, the risk of doing too much or doing too little?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I would say that, you know, we're coming to a place where, where there really are risks on both sides.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's hard to say exactly whether, whether they're in balance or not, but as our-as our stance has become more restrictive and inflation moderates, we do increasingly face that risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we, we need to see that inflation is durably down that far, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, we think, and most economists think, that core inflation is actually a better signal of, of where headline inflation is going, because headline inflation is affected greatly by volatile energy and food prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we would want core inflation to be coming down, because that's what we think-that's-core is signaling where headline is going to go in the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's reason to think it can come down now, but it's, it's still quite elevated, and so we think we need to stay on task, and we think we're going to need to hold, certainly, hold policy at a restrictive level for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we need to be prepared to raise further if that-if we think that's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is-it is a very positive thing that, actually, the unemployment rate is the same as it was when we lifted off in March of '22, at 3. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a real blessing in that we've been able to achieve some disinflation, and we don't seek to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not that we're aiming to, to raise unemployment, but I would just say, the historical record-we have to be honest about the historical record, which does suggest that when central banks go in and slow the economy to bring down inflation, the result tends to be some softening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that is still the, the likely outcome here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we hope that that's as little as possible, but we have to be honest that that is-that is the likely outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The worst outcome for everyone, of course, would be not to deal with inflation now, not get it done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Whatever the short-term social costs of getting inflation under control, the longer- term social costs of failing to do so are greater, and the historical record is very, very clear on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go through a period where inflation expectations are not anchored, inflation is volatile, it interferes with people's lives and with economic activity, and, you know, that's the- that's the thing we, we really need to avoid and will avoid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'll just say again, the broader picture of what we want to see is, we want to see easing of supply constraints and normalization of pandemic-related distortions to demand and supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to see economic growth running at moderate or modest levels to help ease inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to see continued restoration of supply and demand balance, particularly in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And all of that should lead to declining inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now what we see is, we see those pieces of the puzzle coming together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're seeing evidence of those things now, but I would-I would say that what, what our eyes are telling us is that policy has not been restrictive long, restrictive enough for long enough to have its full desired effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we intend, again, to keep policy restrictive until we're confident that inflation is coming down sustainably to our 2 percent target, and we're prepared to further tighten if that is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think the process, you know, still probably has a, a long way to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think-we think, you know, today's rate hike was appropriate, and I think we're going to be looking at the incoming data to inform our decision at the next meeting about, is the incoming data telling us that we need to do more?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if it does tell us that-collectively, if that's our view-then we will do more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a more gradual pace doesn't go immediately to [moving] every other meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It could be-it just means if you're slowing down, the point really was to slow down the decision cycle as, as we get closer and closer to, we think, our destination.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I wouldn't want to go automatically to [moving] every other meeting, because I just don't think that's-we don't-I think it's not an environment where we want to provide a lot of forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just want to keep moving at what we think is the right pace, and I do think it makes all the sense in the world to slow down as we now make these finely judged decisions, and so that's what we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's possible that we would move at consecutive meetings-we're not taking that off the table-or we might not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's really going to depend on what the data tell us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're-look, I think we're going to-we're going to make a decision about the next meeting, and then we're going to make a decision about the one after that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's a long-running debate about the lags between changes in financial conditions and the response to those changes from economic activity and inflation, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we know that in the modern era, financial conditions move in anticipation of our decisions, and that has clearly been the case in this cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in a sense, the clock starts earlier than it-than it used to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that doesn't necessarily change the process from that point on, and it's not clear that it has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also-this is-I'll tell you what we know and then what we don't know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that financial conditions affect economic activity and inflation with a lag that can be long and variable, or lags, plural, that can be long and variable-a lot of uncertainty around the length of the lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, that's just one component of the broader uncertainty that we face.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'll tell you how I-how I think about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First, the first thing to say is, we're determined to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time, and we will use our tools to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The real federal funds rate is now in meaningfully positive territory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you take the nominal federal funds rate, subtract the mainstream estimate of near-term inflation expectations, you get a real federal funds rate that is well above most estimates of the longer-term neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say, monetary policy is restrictive, more so after today's decision, meaning that it is putting downward pressure on economic activity and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll keep monetary policy restrictive until we think it's not appropriate to do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, if I sum it up, I would say: We've come a long way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are resolutely committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent goal over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation has proved, repeatedly, has proved stronger than we and other forecasts-forecasters have expected, and at some point, that may change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to be ready to follow the data, and given how far we've come, we can afford to be a little patient, as well as resolute, as we let this unfold.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess that the SLOOS will come out early next week, and I would just say it's broadly condition-consistent with what you would expect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got lending conditions tight and getting a little tighter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got weak demand, and, you know, it, it gives a picture of pretty tight credit conditions in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's really hard to tease out whether-how much of that is from this source or that source, but I think what matters is, the overall picture is of tight and tightening lending conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me start by saying that the inflation surge that we saw in the pandemic resulted from a collision of elevated demand and, and constrained supply, both of which followed from the unprecedented features of the pandemic and the response from fiscal and monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've always expected that the disinflationary process would stem from, both from the normalization of those broad pandemic- related supply and demand conditions and from restrictive, restrictive monetary policy, which would help return the balance between supply and demand by restraining demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So to go, break it down a little further: Of course, headline inflation has come down sharply from elevated levels as energy and food prices have come down, mostly due to [a] reversal of the effects [on those prices that resulted] from the war in Ukraine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's a good thing, and the public experiences that, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For core inflation, I'd say there also-there has been a role for, for most-for, for both factors, both that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Clearly, for goods, normalization of supply conditions is playing an important role, as is the reversal, the beginning of the reversal, of spending-back into services and away from goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The combination of an increase in sales and inventories, while, while vehicle inflation has decelerated, points to a substantial role for supply, but there's also a role for demand, as, you know, the loans and things like that are more expensive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I would say, monetary policy is working about as we expect, and we think-we think it'll play an important role going forward, in particular in nonhousing services, where, really, we think that's, that's where the labor market will come in as a very, very important factor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think both of those-both of those sources of disinflation are playing an important role.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think monetary policy is going to be important going forward because we, we're sort of reaping now the benefits of the-of the reversal of some of the very specific pandemic things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're seeing that with goods, in particular, with supply chains and shortages moving, and we're seeing-so I think going forward, monetary policy will be important, particularly in that, in the sector, in the nonhousing services sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that, as it relates to goods, it's really an indication that supply chains and, and shortages are easing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think what we're-what we're looking for is a broad cooling in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're still at levels what would-that would be consistent over a long period of time with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And by so many indicators, labor market demand is cooling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can-you can look at surveys by workers and businesses who see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can look at just job creation in the, the establishment survey has, you know-it's still at a high level, but it was at, really, an extraordinarily high level for most of the last two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you see cooling, particularly in private sector, in the last, you know, in the last report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we see that, and it's happening at a gradual pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's actually not a bad thing, in a sense, because if, if what we see is a labor market, very strong demand for labor, which is really the engine of the economy-people are getting hired, many people going back to work, getting wages, spending money-and that's really what's driving the economy but that it's gradually slowing, it's gradually cooling, that's a good prescription for getting where we want to get.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we monitor these things, and we'll keep an eye on them, but, really, that's something that's, that's handled at that level and not-

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you'd take everything into account when you start cutting rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would-it would depend on the whole, on a wide range of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when, when people are writing down rate cuts next year, you know, it just is a sense that inflation is coming down, and we're comfortable that it's coming down, and it's time to start cutting rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-but I mean, there's a lot of uncertainty between what happens, you know, in the next meeting cycle, let alone the next year, let alone the year after that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it's hard to say exactly what happens there, what's motivating people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm saying we would-we'd be comfortable cutting rates when we're comfortable cutting rates, and that won't be this year, I don't think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would be-you know, many people wrote down rate cuts for next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's just going to be a judgment that we have to make then, a full year from now, and it'll be about how confident we are that inflation is, in fact, coming down to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it has been my view consistently that we do have a shot, and my base case is that we will be able to achieve inflation moving back down to our target without the kind of really significant downturn that results in high levels of job losses that we've seen in some past-in some past instances, many past instances of tightening that look like ours.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, you know, that that's sort of consistent with, with what I see today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but it's a long way from assured, and, and, you know, we have a lot left to go to see that happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the staff now has a noticeable slowdown in growth starting later this year in the forecast, but given the resilience of the economy recently, they are no longer forecasting a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just want to note that it's-that our staff produces its own forecast, which is independent of the forecasts that we as FOMC participants produce.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Having an independent staff forecast as well as the individual participant forecasts is really a strength of our-of our process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's just a lot of, I think, constructive diversity of opinion that, that helps us make- informs our deliberations-helps us make, I hope, better decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would-I would say, though, that there's a pathway, and, yes, that's, that's a good way to think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've, we've seen so far the beginnings of disinflation without any real costs in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just also say the historical record suggests that there's very likely to be some softening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And consistent with having a soft landing, you would-you would have some softening in labor market conditions, and that's still likely as we-as we go forward with this process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's a good thing to date that we haven't- we haven't really seen that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen softening through other-not through unemployment, not through higher unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen softening through, you know, job openings coming down part of the way back to more normal levels; the quits rate, so people are not quitting as much; we've seen participation-people coming in, and so labor supply has, has improved, which has lowered the temperature in the labor market, which was quite overheated, you know, going back a year or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're seeing that kind of cooling, and that's, that's very healthy, and, you know, we hope it continues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the idea that we would keep hiking until inflation gets to 2 percent-it would be a prescription [for a policy] of going way past the target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's clearly not the appropriate way to think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and in fact, if you look at our forecast, we, we-the median participant-and, again, these are forecasting out years, so take them with a grain of salt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But people are cutting rates next year because, because, you know, the federal funds rate is at a restrictive level now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if we see inflation coming down credibly, sustainably, then we don't need to be at a restrictive level anymore.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can, you know, we can move back to a-to a neutral level and then below a neutral level at a certain point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we would, you know, we would-we, of course, would be very careful about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'd really want to be sure that inflation is coming down in a sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's hard to make-I'm not going to try to make a numerical assessment of when and where that would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's the way I would think about it, is you'd start-you'd stop raising long before you got to 2 percent inflation, and you'd start cutting before you got to 2 percent inflation, too, because we don't see ourselves getting to 2 percent inflation until-you know, all the way back to 2-until 2025 or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't want to comment on any particular merger proposal, but I will say, things have settled down for sure out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Aggregate bank lending was stable quarter over quarter and is up significantly year over year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we're still watching, you know, the situation carefully and monitoring, you know, monitoring conditions in, in the banking sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the, the actual effect on-if you think of a particular set of banks that were, were affected because of their size and business model and things like that, that were more affected by the turmoil in March than others, it's very hard, as I mentioned; it's very hard to sort of tease out the effects on this very large economy of ours from them tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They may be tightening a little bit more, probably are, than other banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The SLOOS has been telling us for more than a year that banking conditions are tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That process is ongoing, and that will restrain economic growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think-I think we have to take a step back from "I can't separate those anymore."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-I think, basically, we're just looking at the overall picture, which is one of tightening credit conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we-that goes-that's-an expected result of tightening interest rate policy is that-is that bank credit conditions-bank lending conditions would tighten as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so the question is, is it more effective this time because of what happened in May?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're looking at the current data in GDP, and we're seeing strong spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're seeing a strong economy, and it's made us confident that we can go ahead and raise interest rates now for the third time since the March events.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-it seems like the economy is weathering this well, but, of course, we're watching it carefully and, and expect to continue to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, [growth in nominal] wages in excess of inflation means [that increases in] real wages are positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we want wages to be going up at a level that's consistent with, with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, [increases in] nominal wages have been coming down gradually, and that's what we want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's just more of what's consistent over a longer period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't really think that, that wages were an important cause of inflation in the first year or so of the outbreak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that wages are probably an important issue going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Labor market conditions broadly are going to be an important part of, of getting inflation back down, and that's why we think we need some further softening in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, you know, we have a job assigned to us by Congress to get inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think the, the single most important thing we can do to benefit those very families, especially families at the lower end of the income spectrum, is to get inflation sustainably under control and restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that is the most important thing we can do now, and we're determined to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would just point out that the people who are the most hurt by inflation right away are people who are on a low fixed income, who, you know, when you're talking about travel or, you know, transportation costs, heating costs, clothing, food, things like that, those-if you're just making it through each month on your paycheck and prices go up, you're in trouble right away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Even middle-class people have some resources and can absorb inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People, people on the lower end of the income spectrum have a harder time doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the record is clear that if we-if we take too long or if, if we don't succeed, that the pain will only be greater.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's how I would explain what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Look, I would say there's a range of views on the Committee, and when you see the minutes in three weeks, you'll see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a range of views about what we should do at this meeting and what we should do at the next meeting, and it's a-it's a process that we go through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many times when we go into a meeting, the decision is not, you know, fundamentally in doubt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, we have the meeting, and some-some-some meetings are, you know, less uncertain than others, and I'll just leave it at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we monitor, of course, financial conditions, broad financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's the dollar and equities, but-and, you know, we're, of course, very focused on rates and our own policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we will-we're going to use our policy tools to-working through financial conditions-to get inflation under control The implication is, you know, we will do what it takes to get inflation down, and in principle, that, that could mean that if financial conditions get looser, we have to do more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what tends to happen, though, is, financial conditions get in and out of alignment with what we're doing, and, and, ultimately, over time, we get where we need to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question is, you know, is that consistent with, with-so if you think about both of them as normalization, imagine it's a world where things are okay, and it's time to bring rates down from what are restrictive levels to more normal levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Normalization, in the case of, of the balance sheet, would be to reduce QT or to continue it, depending on where you are in the cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, really, the active tool of monetary policy is rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you can imagine circumstances in which it would be appropriate to have them working in what might be seen to be just different ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, yes, banks are now working to see that they are ready to use the discount window, and we are strongly encouraging them to do that-banks broadly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did find, as you know, during the events of March and that, you know, that it's a little clunkier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It can be a little clunkier and not as quick as it needs to be sometimes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So why not be in a situation where, where you're just much more ready in case you-in case you need to access the discount window?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we've got a ways to go to get back to balance, really, for the reasons that you talked about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With existing homes, you know, there are many people who have low-rate mortgages, and whereas they might want to sell in a normal situation, they're not going to because they have such, so much, value in their mortgage, whch means that supply of existing homes is really, really tight, which is keeping prices up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other hand, there's, you know, there's a lot of supply coming on line now, and, and there are people coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A lot of the buyers are, are, you know, first-time buyers coming in, buying at, you know, with these, you know, with these relatively elevated mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think this will take some time to work through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Hopefully, more supply comes on line, and, you know, we, we work through it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're still living through the, you know, the aftermath of the-of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The withdrawal from the Black Sea Grain Initiative does raise concerns about global food security, particularly for poorer countries that import a large share of their food.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Grain prices did go up on this news, but they remain well below their peaks of last spring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the moves that we've seen so far, I would say, are not expected to make a significant contribution to U.S. inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you don't think it would have a big effect on Fed policy at this point?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You wouldn't say so looking at what we-what we know now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would characterize the, the situation a little bit differently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we decided to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate where it is-at 5¼ to 5½ percent-while continuing to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we say we're committed to achieving and sustaining a stance of monetary policy that's sufficiently restrictive to bring down inflation to 2 percent over time-we said that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the fact that we decided to maintain the policy rate at this meeting doesn't mean that we've decided that we have or have not at this time reached that-that stance of monetary policy that we're seeking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you looked at the SEP, as you-as you obviously will have done, you will see that a majority of participants believe that it is more likely than not that we will-that it will be appropriate for us to raise rates one more time in the two remaining meetings this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it's something where we're-by, by-we're not making a decision by, by deciding to-about that question by deciding to just maintain the rate and await further data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not saying-yeah, no, no-clearly, we're just-what we decided to do is maintain a policy rate and await further data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to see convincing evidence, really, that we have reached the appropriate level, and then, you know, we're- we've-we've seen progress, and, and we welcome that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we need to see more progress before we'll be willing to-to reach that conclusion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say it this way: First of all, interest rates-real interest rates are, are positive now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need policy to be restrictive so that we can get inflation down to target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we need- we're going to need that to remain to be the case for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, you know- remember that the-of course, the SEP is not a plan that is negotiated or discussed, really, as a plan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a cumulation, really, and what you see are the medians.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a cumulation of individual forecasts from 19 people, and then what you're seeing are the medians.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't want to, you know, bestow upon it the idea that, that it's really a plan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what it reflects, though, is that economic activity's been stronger than we expected-stronger than I think everyone expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and so what you're-what you're seeing is, this is what people believe, as of now, will be appropriate to achieve what we're looking to achieve, which is progress toward our-toward our inflation goal, as you see in the SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the proposal at the meeting was to-was to maintain our current policy stance, and, and I think there was obviously unanimous support for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But this, of course, is an SEP meeting, and so people write down what they think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you've got-you have some-you saw, I think-seven wrote down no hike at this-at this meeting-or between now and the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think 12 wrote down another single hike in one of the next two meetings that we have between the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it wasn't like we were arguing over that-people just stating their positions-and, really, what, what people are saying is, "Let's see how the data come in."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we want to see-you know what we want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to see that, that this, this-these good inflation readings that we've been seeing for the last three months-we want to see that it's more than just three months, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to see, you know-the, the labor market report that we received, the last one that we received, was a good example of what we do-of what we do want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was a combination of, of, you know, of-across a broad range of indicators, continuing rebalancing of the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those are the two things-so those are our two mandate variables, and, and that's, that's the progress that we want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think people-they want to be convinced, you know-they want to be careful to-not to jump to a conclusion, really, one way or the other-but just be convinced that the data, you know, support that conclusion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why, given how far we've come and how quickly we've come, we're actually in a position to be able to proceed carefully as we assess the incoming data and the evolving outlooks and risks and make these decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, you, you can make the argument that one hike one way or the other won't matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, for us, we're, we're trying-obviously, as a group, it's a pretty tight cluster of, of where we think that, that policy stance might be, but we're always going to be learning from data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've learned all through the course of the last year that, actually, we needed to go further than we had thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go back a year-and what we thought, what we wrote down-it's actually gotten higher and higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we don't really know until-and that's why, again, we-we're in a position to proceed carefully at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A year ago, we proceeded pretty quickly to get rates up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now-now we're fairly close, we think, to where we need to get.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's just a question of reaching the right stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't attribute huge importance to one hike in, in macroeconomic terms.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, you know, we need-we need to get to a place where we're confident that we have a stance that will bring inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we need to get to, and we've been-you know, we've been moving toward it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As we've gotten closer to it, we've slowed the pace at which we've moved.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now that we're getting closer, we, we- again, we have the ability to proceed carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I guess I would point more to-rather than pointing to a sense of inflation having become more persistent, I wouldn't think-that's not-we've, we've seen inflation be more persistent over the course of the past year, but I wouldn't say that's something that's appeared in the recent data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if, if I had to attribute one thing-again, we're, we're picking medians here and trying to attribute one explanation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think, broadly, stronger economic activity means, means rates- we have to do more with rates, and that's what-that's what that meaning is, is telling you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of, of what the neutral rate can be-you know, we-we know it by its works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can't-we can't-you know, the, the models and, and-that we use, you-ultimately, you only know when you get there and by, by the way the economy reacts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, that's another reason why we're-why we're moving carefully now, because, you know, there are lags here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it, it may-it may, of course, be that the-that the neutral rate has risen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You do see people-you don't see the median moving-but you do see people raising their estimates of, of the neutral rate, and it's certainly plausible that the neutral rate is higher than, than the longer-run rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Remember-what we write down in the SEP is the longer-run rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is certainly possible that, you know, that the-that the neutral rate at this moment is higher than that, and that-that's part of the explanation for why the economy has been more resilient than, than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is a-it is a good thing that we, we've seen now meaningful rebalancing in the labor market without an increase in unemployment, and that's, that's because we're seeing that rebalancing in other places-in, for example, job openings and in the jobs-worker gap.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, though, we still-I still think, and I think, broadly, people still think, that there will have to be some softening in the labor market that can come through more supply, as we've seen as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Also, remember, the natural rate, we think, is, is coming down, which is a supply-side thing, so that the, the gap between any given unemployment rate that's lower than that and the natural rate comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a way for supply-that's a way for the labor market to achieve a better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're right-in, in the median forecast, we don't see a big increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do see an increase, and-but that's-that really is just "playing forward" the trends that we've been seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There, there may come a time when unemployment goes up more than that, but that's, that's really what we've been seeing is, progress without higher unemployment for now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I would just say-what, what would I say about that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've always thought that the soft landing was, was a plausible outcome-that there was a path, really, to, to a soft landing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've thought that, and I've said that since we lifted off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also possible that, that the path has narrowed, and it's widened, apparently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, it-this may be decided by factors that are outside our control at the end of the day.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know-I also think, you know, this is why we're in a position to, to move carefully again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we know that we have to do that, and we know the public depends on us doing that, and we know that we have to do it so that we can achieve the kind of labor market that we all want to achieve, which is an extended period-sustained period of strong labor market conditions that benefit all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The fact that we've come this far lets us really proceed carefully, as I keep saying.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, you know, that's, that's the end we're trying to achieve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't want to handicap the likelihood of it, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, yes-we, we understand that it's a real rate that will matter and that needs to be sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, I would say, you know-you know "sufficiently restrictive" only when you see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You-it's not something you can arrive at with confidence in a model or, or in various estimates, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're seeing, you know, through a combination of the, you know, the unwinding of the pandemic-related demand and supply distortions and monetary policy's work in suppressing demand or, or, you know, alleviating very high demand-the combination of those two things is actually working.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You begin to see effects of it in nonhousing services as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think, you know-as we've said, we, we want to reach that-we want to reach something that we're confident gets us to that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think confidence comes from seeing, you know, enough data that you feel like, "Yes, okay, this feels like it-we can-we can, for now, decide that this is the right level and just agree to stay here."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not permanently deciding not to go higher, but, but we would-let's say, if we get to that level-and then the question is, how long do you stay at that level?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For now, the question is trying to find that level where we think we can stay there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we haven't-we haven't gotten to a point of confidence about that yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's what we're-that's, that's the stage we're at, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The decision that we make at, you know, at each meeting and, certainly, at the-at the last two meetings this year-it's going to depend on the totality of all the data: so, the inflation data, the labor market data, the growth data, the, the balance of risks, and the other events that are happening out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll make-we take all of that into account, so I can't really answer a hypothetical about one piece of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll-it'll be trying to reach a judgment over whether we should move forward with another rate hike overall and whether that would increase our confidence that, that, yes, this is an appropriate move, and it will help, help us be more confident that we've gotten to the level that we need to get to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When-so when I answer these questions about hypotheticals about, about cutting, I'm never intending to send a signal about timing; I'm just answering them as, as the question is expressed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so please-I, I wouldn't want to be taken that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so we're-as we go into next year, that's the question we'll be asking is-you know, taking into account lags and, and everything else we know about the economy and everything we know about monetary policy, the, the time will come at some point, and I'm not saying when, that it's-that it's appropriate to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of that may be that real rates are rising because inflation is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of it just may be that-it'll be all the factors that we see in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that time will certainly come at some point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you-what you see is us writing down, you know, a year ahead, estimates of what that might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there's-you know, there's so much uncertainty around that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In, in- when we-in the moment, we'll do what we think makes sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one will look back at this and say, "Hey, we made a plan."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-this is-these are estimates made a year in advance that are highly uncertain, and that's how it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on, on your first question-I mean, we're looking at GDP very, very carefully to try to understand really what's the direction of it-what's, what's driving it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's, it's a lot of consumer spending, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is, you know, that's how we're looking at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think the question will be-GDP is not our mandate, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question will be, is, is the level-is GDP-is the-is the heat that we see in GDP-is it really a threat to our ability to get back to 2 percent inflation?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-it's not a question about GDP on its own.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, you-you know, you're expecting to see the-this improvement, you know-continued rebalancing in the labor market and inflation moving back down to 2 percent in a sustainable way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to have confidence in that, and, you know, we'd be-we'd be looking at GDP just, just to the extent that it threatens one or both of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there is a-there is a long list, and you hit some of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it- you know, it's, it's the strike, it's government shutdown, resumption of student loan payments, higher long-term rates, oil price shock.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you could-there are a lot of things that you can-you can look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know-so, what we try to do is assess all of them and, and handicap all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, ultimately, though, there's so much uncertainty around, around these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, to, to start with the strike-first of all, we absolutely don't comment on the strike, as we have no view on the strike one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, we do have to make an assessment of its economic effects to do our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, the, the thing about it is-so uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economic effects-it could affect-you've looked-we've looked back at history-it could affect economic output, hiring, and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's really going to depend on how broad it is and how long it's sustained for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-and then it also depends on how quickly production can make up for, for lost production.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and we'll be learning, I think, over the course of the next intermeeting period, much more about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we-I don't know if you mentioned shutdown; I think of all of these as being on the list.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, energy prices being higher-that's-that is a significant thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A sustained period of higher-of higher energy prices can affect consumer expectations about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We tend to look through short-term volatility and look at-look at core inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But so the question is, how long are, are higher prices sustained?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to-we have to take those macroeconomic effects into account as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-I mean, ultimately, you know, you're, you're coming into this with an economy that appears to have significant momentum.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we-but we do have this collection of risks that you mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To begin: A soft landing is a primary objective, and I did not say otherwise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, that's, that's what we've been trying to achieve for all this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the real point, though, is-the, the worst thing we can do is to fail to restore price stability, because the record is clear on that: If you, you don't restore price stability, inflation comes back, and you go through-you can have a long period where the economy's just very uncertain, and it will affect growth; it will affect all kinds of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It can be a miserable period to have inflation constantly coming back and the Fed coming in and having to tighten again and again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the best thing we can do for everyone, we believe, is to restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think now, today, we actually-you know, we, we have the ability to be careful at this point and move carefully, and that's what we're planning to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we fully appreciate that-you know, the benefits of being able to continue what we see already, which is rebalancing in the labor market and inflation coming down without seeing, you know, an important, large increase in unemployment, which has been typical of other tightening cycles.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if I-if I understood your question, it's-I would say it this way: I think we knew from the time-from before when we lifted off, but certainly by the time we lift-we knew that bringing inflation back down was going to take, as I call it, the unwinding of these distortions to both supply and demand that happened because of the pandemic and the response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was going to help supply side heal by, by cooling demand off and, just in general, better aligning supply with demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those two forces were always going to be important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I do think both of them are at work now, and I think they're at work in a way that shows you the progress that we-that we are seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Forecasters are a humble lot with much to be humble about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But to get to, to your question, though-what's happened is, growth has come in stronger, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Unemployment, you know-you also see that the, the ultimate unemployment rate is not as high, but that-that's really because of what we've been seeing in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen more and more progress in the labor market without seeing significantly higher unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of inflation, you, you are seeing-the last three readings are, are very good readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-we're well aware that we need to see more than three readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look at June, July, and August, you're looking at, you know, really significant declines in core inflation, largely in the goods sector-also to some extent in housing services and just a little in nonhousing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Headline inflation, of course, has come way down, largely due to lower energy prices, some of which is now reversing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think-people should know that, that economic forecasting is very difficult, and these are highly uncertain forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, they're, they're-we have very high-quality people working on these forecasts, and I think they stand up well against other forecasters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But just the nature of the business is, the economy is very difficult to forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I, I think we have come very far very fast in, in the, the rate increases that we've made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it was important at the beginning that we move quickly, and we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and I think as we get closer to the rate that we think-the stance of monetary policy that we think is appropriate to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time, you know, the risks become more two sided, and the risk of overtightening and the risk of, of undertightening becomes more equal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the, the natural, commonsense thing to do is, as you approach that, you move a little more slowly as you get closer to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're taking advantage of the fact that we have moved quickly to move a little more carefully now as we-as we sort of find our way to, to the right level of restriction that we need to get inflation back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on that, we're, you know, we're looking at just monthly, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can look at just monthly readings and see what the increase was from the prior month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right-when you go back 3, 6, and 12 months, you get base factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of not getting data-you know, again, we don't-we don't comment on government shutdowns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It-it's possible-if, if there is a government shutdown and it lasts through the, the next meeting, then it's possible we wouldn't- we wouldn't be getting some of the data that we would ordinarily get, and we-you know, we would just have to deal with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's hard for me to say in advance how that would affect that meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would depend on all kinds of factors that I don't know about now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's certainly a reality that, that that's a possibility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, if you're looking-if-we, we can tell how much inflation has gone up in a given month, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I think-I think what we're really looking at is, there's a tendency to look at, you know, shorter and shorter maturities, but they're incredibly volatile, and they can be misleading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think, in this situation-where it looks like we've had a bit of a turn in inflation starting in June-we're also looking at six months, and even three months, but really six months' inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're looking at it over that period and over longer periods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't-we don't need to be in a hurry to-in, in getting to a conclusion about what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, energy prices are very important for the consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, gas prices are one of the big things that, that affects consumer sentiment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It, it really comes down to how persistent-how sustained these energy prices are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The reason why we look at core inflation, which excludes food and energy, is that energy goes up and down like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it doesn't-energy, energy prices mostly, mostly don't contain much of a signal about how tight the economy is, and hence don't tell you much about where inflation's really going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: However, we're well aware, though, that, that, you know, if energy prices increase and stay high, that'll have an effect on spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and it may have an effect on, on consumer expectations of inflation-things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, to, to finish my prior thought, I was saying that's why we tend to look through energy moves that we-that we can see as, as short-term volatility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, turning to consumer credit, you know-of course, we watch that carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Consumer distress- measures of distress among consumers were at historic lows quite recently, you know, after- during and after the, the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, at this point, these, these readings are not at troublingly high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're, they're just kind of moving back up to what was the typical [level] in the pre-pandemic era.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's always hard to say precisely, but it's-most, most people do a common decomposition of the increase, and they'll, they'll-the view will be, it's not-it's not mostly about inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's mostly about other things, you know-either term premium or real yields- and it's, it's hard to be precise about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, everyone's got models that'll give you a very precise answer, but they give you different answers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but, essentially, they're, they're moving up because-it's not because of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's because probably-it'll probably have something to do with stronger growth, I would say-more, more supply of Treasuries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the common explanations that you hear in the markets kind of make sense.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on the supply point-of course, supply is very important over time in, in setting house prices and, and, for that matter, rents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in terms of, of where inflation's going in the near term, though, as, as you obviously know, a lot of it is, is leases that are running off and then being re-signed or re- leased at a level that's, that's not as-it won't be that much higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A year ago, it would have been much higher than it was a year before; now it may be below or at the same level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as those leases are rolling over, we're, we're seeing what we expect, which is measured housing services inflation coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think we look at the-I would look at the lock-in, the, the idea being that people are in, in very low mortgage-very low-rate mortgages, and if-even if they want to move now, they-it would be hard because the new mortgage would be so expensive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's explaining some of the-that's one of the explanations for what's happening broadly in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Would that play a role in, in our future decisions-in a-in a future tight- in a future loosening cycle about whether we would cut rates?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I don't think that's-I, I think we'd be looking at, what, you know, fundamentally, what, what rates does the economy need?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, in, in an emergency like the pandemic or during the Global Financial Crisis, you, you know, the, the-you have to cut rates to the point that-you have to do, do what you can to support the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't-I wouldn't think that that would be a reason for us not to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something we're thinking about at all right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a good thing that the economy has been able to hold up under, under the tightening that we've done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the only concern-it, it just means this: If the economy comes in stronger than expected, that just means we'll have to do more in terms of monetary policy to get back to 2 percent-because we will get back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I guess, on the other hand, would you worry that that could contribute to an economic slowdown or even a recession?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, concern number one is, is restoring price stability, because in the long run, that's, that's something we have to do so that we can have the kind of economy we really want, which is one with sustained period of tight labor market conditions that benefit all, as I-as I've said a couple times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that, that said-of course, you know-we, we also now, given how far we've come with our rate hikes and how quickly we've come here, we do have the ability to be careful as we move forward because of that consideration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what-I guess it's fair-it's fair to say that the economy has been stronger than many expected, given, given what's been happening with, with interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One, one is just that household balance sheets and business balance sheets have been stronger than we had understood, and so that, that spending has held up-and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The savings rate for consumers has come down a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That could-it could just mean that the-that the date of effect is, is later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It could also be that for other reasons, the neutral rate of interest is, is higher for-for various reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It could also just be that policy hasn't been restrictive enough for long enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to, in, in all this uncertainty, make policy, and I, you know, I feel like what we have right now is what's still a very strong labor market-but that's coming back into balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think by many forecasts-many, many, many forecasts call for growth to, to moderate over the course of the next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's where we are, and, you know, we have to-we have to deal with what comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On your second question, which was- sorry, your second question was distributional, but can you-can you be a little clearer about that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so the point I would make there is that we're trying to get inflation back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The people who are most hurt by inflation are the people who are on a fixed income.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you're a person who spends all of your income, you don't really have any meaningful savings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You spend all your income on the basics of life-clothing, food, transportation, heating-the basics-and prices go up by 5, 6, 7 percent, you're in trouble right away, whereas even, even middle-class people have some savings and some ability to absorb that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is for those people as much as for anybody that we need to restore price stability, and, and we, we want to do it as quickly as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'd like the current trend to continue, which is that we're making progress without seeing the kind of increase in unemployment that we've seen past-in past things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we raise rates, people who are, you know, living on credit cards and, and borrowing are going to feel that more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, people with, with lots of savings also have a-have a much lower marginal propensity to consume, and so they're not going to-it's not going to affect them as much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's an idea we can-we can take away and think about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of how low and moderate Americans-you know, they're clearly-were suffering from, from high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think during the pandemic, the, the government transfers that happened were very meaningful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, if you know the-the surveys that we take showed that-showed that low- and moderate-income people were actually in very, very strong financial condition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think now it's a very "hot" labor market, and you're seeing high [growth in] nominal wages, and you're starting to see [that growth rates of] real wages are now positive by most-by most measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think, overall, households are in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So surveys are showing dissatisfaction, and I think a lot of that is just, people hate inflation-hate it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, that causes people to say, "The economy's terrible."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Their behavior is, is not exactly what you would expect from the surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's kind of a, a guess at what the answer might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, I think there's a lot of good things happening on household balance sheets-and, certainly, in the labor market and with wages.
