speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The biggest wage increases having gone to relatively low- wage jobs-and now [with] inflation coming down-you're seeing [increases in] real wages, which is a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I'll talk about bond yields, but I want to take a second and just sort of set the broader context in which we're looking at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, if you-if you look at the situation-let's look at the economy first.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation has been coming down, but it's still running well above our 2 percent target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market has been rebalancing, but it's still very tight by many measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: GDP growth has been strong, although many forecasters are forecasting, and they have been forecasting, that it will slow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As for the Committee, we are committed to achieving a stance of monetary policy that's sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time, and we're not confident yet that we have achieved such a stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is the broader context into which this, this strong economy and all the things I said-that's the context in which we're looking at this question of rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, obviously we're monitoring, we're attentive to the increase in longer-term yields and-which have contributed to a tightening of broader financial conditions since the summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, persistent changes in broader financial conditions can have implications for the path of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In this case, the tighter financial conditions we're seeing-[coming] from higher long-term rates, but also from other sources, like the stronger dollar and lower equity prices-could matter for future rate decisions, as long as two conditions are satisfied.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first is that the tighter conditions would need to be persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Things are fluctuating back and forth-that's not what we're looking for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: With financial conditions, we're looking for persistent changes that are material.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second thing is that, that the longer-term rates that have moved up-they can't simply be a reflection of, of expected policy moves from us that we would then-that if we didn't follow through on them, then the rates would come back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and I would say on that, it does not appear that an expectation of higher near-term policy rates is causing the increase in longer-term rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in the meantime, though, perhaps the most important thing is that these higher Treasury yields are showing through to higher borrowing costs for households and businesses and those higher costs are going to weigh on economic activity to the extent this tightening persists and the mind's eye goes to the 8 percent-near 8 percent mortgage rate, which could have pretty significant effect on housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, to say it a different way: We haven't made any decisions about, about future meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have not made a determination, and we're not-I will say that we're not confident at this time that we've reached such a stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not confident that we haven't; we're not confident that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-that is-the way we're going to be going into these future meetings is to be, you know, just determining the extent of any additional further policy tightening that may be appropriate to return inflation to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, let me start by saying we haven't made a decision about September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're going into December meeting-we'll get, as you know, two more inflation ratings, two more labor market readings, some data on, on economic activity, and so we'll be taking-and also the broader situation, the broader financial condition situation and broader world situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be looking at all those things as we make a decision in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, though, that, that the idea that if you-the idea that would-difficult to raise again after stopping for a meeting or two, it's just not right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the Committee will always do what it thinks is appropriate at the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we haven't made any decisions about- at all about December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't even-we didn't talk about making a decision in December today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, it was a decision for this meeting and understanding broader things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I don't want to answer your question about the-about the recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think I have to answer it, since we did publicly say in the minutes-you'll know anyway in the [next] minutes-the staff did not put a recession back in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it would be hard to see how you would do that if you look at the-look at the activity we've seen recently, which is not really indicative of a recession in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of how to think about translation into rate hikes, I think it's just too early to be doing that, and the main reason is we just don't know how persistent this will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Different kinds of news will affect the level of rates, and I think any kind of an estimate that was precise would hang out there and have a great chance of looking wrong very quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think what we can say is that financial conditions have clearly tightened, and you can see that in the rates that, that consumers and households and businesses are paying now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just don't know how persistent it's going to be, and it's tough to try to translate that in a way that I'd be comfortable communicating into how many rate hikes that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I just-that's, you know, the way our policy works is-and sometimes it works with lags, of course, which can be long and variable, but ultimately, if you raise interest rates, you do see those effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You'll see, if you look at surveys of people, it's not a good time they think to buy durable goods of various kinds because rates are so high now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mention again, we're getting reports from housing that the effects of this-of this could be quite significant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are a number of possible reasons why that may be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our job is to-is to achieve maximum employment and price stability, and so we take the economy as it comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has been resilient, so we just-we take it as it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those were not meant to be the only factors or a specific test that we're going to be applying with some metrics behind it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, we're going to be looking at the broader picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what's happening with our progress toward the 2 percent inflation goal?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Is the labor market continuing to, broadly, cool off and achieve a better balance?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, growth-we look at growth insofar as it has implications for our two mandate goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at that, and we look at broader financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll be looking at all of those things as we reach a judgment, you know, whether we need to further tighten policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, if we do reach that judgment, then we will further tighten policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's, it's-the fact is the Committee is not thinking about rate cuts right now at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're still very focused on the first question, which is, have we achieved a stance of monetary policy that's sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time sustainably?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The next question, as you know, will be, for how long will we remain restrictive?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we've said there is that we'll keep policy restrictive until we're confident that inflation is on a sustainable path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That'll be the next question, but honestly, right now we're really tightly focused on the first question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question of rate cuts just doesn't come up because I think the first-it's so important to get that first question, you know, as close to right as you can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say-I mean, the language, looking at it here, "In determining the extent of additional policy firming that may be appropriate to return inflation to 2 percent over time."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't used that term, but it's fair to say that's the question we're asking is, should we hike more?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-it's not, you know-that is the question, and you're right that, in September, we wrote down one additional rate hike.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know-and we'll [each] write down another forecast, as you know, in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, there are significant issues out there, as you point out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that goes for the war in Ukraine; it goes for the war between Israel and Hamas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our job is to monitor those things for their economic implications.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, the UAW strike, as you point out is-appears to be coming to an end.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess they've gone down a little bit from their earlier peak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Another one is the possibility of government shutdown; we don't know about that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would go back to-the bigger picture from our standpoint is, we've got a very strong economy, strong labor market, making progress on the labor market, making progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're very focused on getting confident that we have achieved a stance of monetary policy that is sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I was very impressed by York as a town with a real strategy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say it's very impressive what the people there have put together in the face of, you know, some difficult longer-run trends about offshoring of manufacturing and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They've done a great job as a city, I think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what you hear-and it's consistent there-which is people are really suffering under high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We talked to some people who, you know, were feeling that in their businesses and other people who were feeling it in their home lives as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's painful for people-particularly people who don't have a lot of extra financial resources who are spending most of their incoming, you know, income on the essentials of life.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that did come through very clearly in, in the conversations we had in York, and, you know, I walked away from that even-you know, I mean, just thinking that we really-the best thing we can do for the U.S. is to restore price stability-fully restore price stability and not fail in that task and do it as quickly as possible, but also with the least damage we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think everyone has been very gratified to see that we've been able to achieve, you know, pretty significant progress on inflation without seeing the kind of increase in unemployment that has been very typical of rate hiking cycles like this one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's a historically unusual and very welcome result.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've been saying that we need to see below-potential growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And growth has been strong, but yet we're still seeing this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think I still believe, and my colleagues for the most part I think still believe, that is likely to be true.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is still likely to be true-not a certainty-but likely that we will need to see some slower growth and some softening in the labor market-in labor market conditions to get, you know, to fully restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but it's only a good thing that we haven't seen it, and I think we know why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, since, since we lifted off, we, we have understood that there are really two processes at work here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One of them-one of which is the unwinding of the distortions to both supply and demand [that arose] from the pandemic and the response to the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the other is, is, you know, restrictive monetary policy, which is moderating demand and giving the supply side time to recover-time and space to recover.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you see those two forces now working together to bring down inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's that first one can bring down inflation without the need for higher unemployment or slower growth, it's just-it's supply-you know, supply-side improvements like shortages and bottlenecks and that kind of thing going away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's getting, you know, a significant increase in the size of the labor market now, both from labor force participation and from immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a big supply-side, you know, gain that is really helping the economy, and it's part of why-part of why GDP is so high is because we're getting that supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think those things will run their course, and we're probably still going to be left-we think, and I think-we'll still be left with some ground to cover to get back to full price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's where monetary policy and what we do with demand is still going to be important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I continue to think it's very hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's been one year at this meeting-one year ago, this was the fourth of our 75 basis points hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we are seeing the effects of, of all the hiking we did last year and this year-we're seeing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's very hard to know exactly what that might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you can, for example-an example where you wouldn't have felt this yet is, is debt that had been termed out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's going to come due and have to get rolled over next year or the year after.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and there are little things like that where the effects have just taken time to get into the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't-I think we have to make monetary policy under great uncertainty about how long the lags are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think trying to make a clear-get a clear answer and say, "I'm just going to assume this is really not a good way to do it."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is one of the reasons why we have slowed the process down this year, was to give monetary policy time to get into the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, doing-slowing down is giving us, I think, a better sense of, of how much more we need to do, if we need to do more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the dot plot is a picture in time of what the people in the Committee think is likely to be appropriate monetary policy in light of their own personal economic forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In principle, when things change, it's not-that's not, like, planned that anybody's agreed to or that we will do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a forecast that would change, for example-I mean, many things could change that would cause people to say, "I wouldn't write down that dot six weeks later."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Think of the number of things that could change your mind on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the efficacy of the dot plot probably decays over the three-month period between that meeting and the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't- we do personally update our forecast, but we don't formally update the dot plot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I think we try to be as transparent as we can about the way we're thinking about these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're laying out there our thinking, and, you know, as we approach the meeting, we'll all be- my colleagues and I will be talking about how we're processing that data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of-so we're not really changing the way-in terms of growth, what I said was "below potential."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what you have here recently is growth that is-that is temporarily- potential growth is elevated for a year or two right now over its trend level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the right way to think about it is, what's potential growth this year?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People think trend growth over a long period of time is a little bit less than 2 percent, or I would say just around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what we've had is, with the-with the, you know, improvement in the size of the labor force, as I mentioned, through both participation and immigration, and with the, the, you know, the better functioning in the labor market and with the-with the, you know, the unwinding of the supply chain and shortages and those kinds of things, you're seeing actually elevated potential growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means that if you're growing-you could be growing at 2 percent this year and still be growing below the increase in the potential output of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I don't know that I want to just accept anybody's characterization, but I'll tell you how we're doing this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're asking ourselves whether we've achieved a stance of policy that is sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking at the full range of economic data, including financial conditions and all of those things that we look at, and then we're, we're-you know, we've, we've come very far with this rate hiking cycle, very far.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you saw the spread at the September meeting of-you know, it's a relatively small spread of-people think one or two additional hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're close to the-to the end of the cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-that was an impression as of, I believe, as of September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not a promise or a plan of the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're going into these meetings one by one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're proceeding carefully because we can proceed carefully at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see its effects, particularly in interest-sensitive spending and other channels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the Committee is not considering changing the pace of balance sheet runoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something we're talking about or considering, and I know there are many candidate explanations for why rates have been going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It may be playing a relatively small effect, although I would say at $3.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: trillion in reserves, it's not-I think-I think it's hard to make a case that reserves are even close to scarce at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's not something that we're-that we're looking at right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We won't get those comments until the end of, well, into next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll say what, what I do expect is that we will-we will come to a-we're a consensus-driven organization.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll come to a package that has broad support on the Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at a very wide range of financial conditions and, in fact, as you'll know, different organizations publish different financial conditions' indexes, which can have, you know, 7 or 8 variables, or they can have 100 variables, so there's a very rich environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we tend to look at a few of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going to give you the names, but, you know, they're a few of the common ones that people look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so they're looking at things like the level of the dollar, the level of equity prices, the level of rates, the credit spreads.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Sometimes they're pulling in credit availability and things like that, so it isn't any one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would never look at, for example, long-term Treasury rates in isolation, nor would we ignore them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we would look at them as part of a broader picture, and they do play a role, of course, in many of the major standard financial condition indexes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, we, we did have-there were issues with interest rate risk and also funding uninsured deposits in the March-the things we went through in March and thereafter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we've been working a lot with financial institutions to make sure that they have good funding plans and good-and that they have a plan for how to deal with the kind of portfolio, unrealized, losses that they have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do think the banking system is quite resilient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had, you know, a handful of bank failures but-so that's, that's what we're out there doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't have any reason to think that this-that these rate hikes are materially changing that picture, which is one of a strong banking system and one where there's a strong focus by banks and by supervisors on liquidity, on funding, and those sorts of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We put a proposal out for comment, is what we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, this is a job that Congress assigned us, as you, of course, know, in Dodd-Frank, and all we can really do is faithfully implement the statute.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a 90-day comment period, and we typically don't comment on these things once they're out for-out for comment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do hope that stakeholders-and we know that they will use this opportunity to express their views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's critical and that's, that's what I can say about that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the progress is probably going to come in lumps and be bumpy, but we're making progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think the core PCE [inflation rate] came down by almost 60 basis points in the third quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the best thing I could point you to would be the September SEP where, you know, the expectation was that, that inflation by the end of next year, on a 12-month trailing basis, would be well into the 2s and the year after that, further into the 2s.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's-if you look historically, that's, that's sort of consistent with the way inflation comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It does take some time, and as you get-you know, as you get further and further from those highs, it may actually take longer time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the good news is, you know, we're making progress and monetary policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we feel like we're on a path to make more progress, and it's essential that we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we know that, if we fail to restore price stability, the risk is that expectations of higher inflation get entrenched in the economy, and we know that that's really bad for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a-that's a prescription for misery, and, and so we're really committed to not letting that happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, for the first year or so of our tightening cycle, the risk was all on the side of not doing enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, you know, we're- we've come far enough that, that the risks, you know, have gotten more two sided.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can't identify that with a lot of precision, but it does feel like the, the risks are more two sided now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but we're committed to getting inflation back down to our target over time, and we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't really-we haven't really been thinking about that yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-you know, it's November 1, and that's a decision we'll be making in the first quarter of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the, the, the, you know, the UM thing got blown out of proportion a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was actually a preliminary estimate that got revised away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I said it was preliminary in it, but that didn't get picked up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So really, look across the broad array of surveys and also market-based estimates, and, you know, we do that really carefully at every meeting and between meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there's-it's just clear that inflation expectations are in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The public does believe that inflation will get back down to 2 percent over time,.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can always find one reading that is a little bit out of whack, but, honestly, the bulk of them are just very clear that the public believes that inflation will come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, of course-we believe that's critical in winning the battle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So first thing to say is that it's very important.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a very important variable in, in the way we think about monetary policy, but you can't identify it with any precision in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you have to just take that-you have to take your estimate of it with a grain of salt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we know now is, you know, within a range of estimates of the neutral rate policy, is restrictive, and it's therefore putting downward pressure on economic activity, hiring, and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's not any debate or attempt to, you know, to sort of agree as a group on what-whether r* has moved or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some people think it has, some people haven't said-that don't think it has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, it's unknowable, and so really again, what we're focused on is, you know, looking at the data and giving ourselves a little more time now to look carefully at the data by being careful in our moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Does it-does it feel like monetary policy is restrictive enough to bring inflation down to 2 percent over time?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, years from now economists will be revising their estimates of r* as it existed on November 1, 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can't-we can't really wait for that in making policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to look-we have to have those models and look at them and think about them, and, ultimately, we've got to look at the effects that policy is having, accounting for the lags, which makes it difficult.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, if you look at the-look at the broad range of wages, they have- wage increases have really come down significantly over the course of the last 18 months to a level where they're substantially closer to that level that would be consistent with 2 percent inflation over time, making standard assumptions about productivity over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's true of the ECI, which is the one that's-the one that we got this week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's true of average hourly earnings and compensation per hour, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and all of them are kind of saying that, which is great.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you have to look at a group of them because any one of them can be idiosyncratic from-in any given reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so what you saw with the ECI reading was, if you look back a couple-it comes out four times a year-if you look back a couple of quarters, you'll see it was much higher, then it came down substantially in June.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then the September reading was more or less at the same level as the June reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in a way, it's just validating that decline, and it was very close to our expectations internally, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Also I would say it isn't-in my thinking, it's not the case that, that wages have been the principal driver of inflation so far, although I think it's all-I do think it's fair to say that, as we go forward, as monetary policy becomes more important relative to the supply-side issues I've talked about in the unwinding of the pandemic effects, it may be that the labor market becomes more important over time, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as I mentioned, I think for much of the last year and a half, the concern was not doing too, too-not doing enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was not getting rates high enough in time to avoid having inflation expectations-higher inflation expectations become entrenched.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we've reached, you know, now more than 18 months into this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can see by the fact that we have slowed down, although we're still-we're still-we're still trying to gain confidence in what the appropriate stance is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think, and I think, that the risks are getting more balanced.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The risk of doing too much versus the risk of doing too little are getting-are getting more- closer to balance, because policy is I think clearly restrictive at 5¼ to 5½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That range, if you take off a mainstream estimate of the expected inflation, take one year inflation, you're going to see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're going to see a real policy rate that is well above mainstream estimates of a neutral policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't really-the proof is really in how the economy reacts, but I would say that we're in a place where those risks are getting closer to being in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you said the proof is how the economy reacts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What are you looking at to be sure you're not overshooting?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think what we're looking at is are we still-is inflation still broadly cooling?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Do we-is it sort of validating the path we saw over the summer, where inflation was clearly cooling and coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now we've seen periods like that before, and they've just-there hasn't been follow-through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second thing is, in the labor market, what we've seen is a very positive rebalancing of supply and demand, partly through just much more supply coming online.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And with labor demand still clearly remaining very strong-when you have the kind of job growth we've had over the last quarter, it's still very strong demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and you see wage increases coming down as we discussed but coming down in a kind of gradual way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that's-we want to see that, that whole set of processes continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't say there's been a structural change in consumption.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We may have underestimated the balance sheet strength of households and small businesses, and that may be part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There may be-you know, we've been, like everyone else, trying to estimate the number-the amount of savings that households have from the pandemic when they couldn't spend on services really at all, or in-person services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there can still be more of that than we think, although at a certain point we have to-we're going to be getting back to pre-pandemic levels of savings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The dynamic has been really strong job creation with now wages that are-that are higher than inflation, in the aggregate anyway, and that raises real disposable income, and that raises spending, which continues to drive more hiring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so you've had a really-that whole-that whole dynamic has been, and also at the same time, the pandemic effects are wearing off, so that goods availability, automobile availability is better-or was better, I think it still is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, from a business standpoint, there are more people to hire.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the whole thing has led to more growth, more spending, and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's been-you know, it's been good, and the thing is, we've been achieving progress on inflation in the middle of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I just think this-the existence of this second set of factors at this time, which is the unwinding of the pandemic effects, that's what makes this cycle unique, I think, and, you know, we're still learning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That took longer for that process to begin than we thought, and we're still learning about how it plays out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't want to speculate too much, but I'll just say so-you know, really the question there is, does the war spread more widely and does it start to do things like affect oil prices in particular, since this is the Middle East we're talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The price of oil has really not reacted very much so far to this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As the-you know, as the Fed-as the Federal Open Market Committee, our job is really to talk about [and] to understand the economy and economic effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it isn't clear, at this point, that the conflict in the Middle East is going to-is on track to have significant economic effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That doesn't mean it isn't incredibly important and something for people to, you know, to take really important notice of, but it may or may not turn out to be something that matters for the Federal Open Market Committee as an economic body.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-so what the Financial Stability Report does is it "calls out" risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's what it's doing-[it] is calling out a risk of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The war in Ukraine did have, immediately, very significant macroeconomic implications because of the connection to commodities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-specifically on "any": We do say that "in determining the extent of any additional policy firming that may be appropriate," so "any additional policy firming"-that sentence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we added the word "any" as an acknowledgement that we believe that we are likely at or near the, the peak rate for this cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Participants didn't write down additional hikes that we believe are likely, so that's what we wrote down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But participants also didn't want to take the possibility of further hikes off the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, I don't comment on, on any other officials, even those who work at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I'll-but I'll try to answer your question more broadly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the way- the way we're looking at it is, is really this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we started out, right, we said the first question is, how fast to move, and we moved very fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second question is, you know, really, how high to raise the policy rate?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really the question that we're still on here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're very focused on that, as I-as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People generally think that we're at or near that and, and think it's not likely that we will hike, although they don't take that possibility off the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-when you get to that question, and that's your answer, there's a natural-naturally, it begins to be the next question, which is when it will become appropriate to begin dialing back the amount of policy restraint that's in place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's really the next question, and that's what people are thinking about and, and talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are seeing, you know, strong growth that is-that appears to be moderating; we're seeing a labor market that is coming back into balance by so many measures; and we're seeing inflation making real progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're moving carefully in making that assessment of whether we need to do more or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, of course, the other question, the question of when will it become appropriate to begin dialing back the amount of policy restraint in place, that, that begins to come into view and is clearly a discussion-topic of discussion out in the world and also a discussion for us at our meeting today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So many people mentioned what their-what their rate forecast was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there was no back-and-forth, no attempt to sort of reach agreement like, "This is what I wrote down; this is what I think," that kind of thing, and a preliminary kind of a discussion like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, and I would say, there's a general expectation that this will be-this will be a topic for us, looking ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't do the head count for you in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you can say that there's little basis for thinking that the economy is in a recession now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's, there's always a probability that, that there will be a recession in the next year, and it's a meaningful probability no matter what the economy is doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I have always felt, since the beginning, that there was a possibility, because of the unusual situation, that the economy could cool off in a way that enabled inflation to come down without the kind of large job losses that have often been associated with high inflation and tightening cycles.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what many forecasters, on and off the Committee, are seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's certainly possible that, that the economy will behave in an unexpected way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has done that repeatedly through the post-in the post-pandemic period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, where we are is, is we see the things that I-that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think forecasters generally, if you go back a year, were very broadly forecasting a recession for this year, for 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And not only did that not happen-that includes Fed forecasters and really, essentially, all forecasters; a very high proportion of forecasters predicted very weak growth or a recession-not only did that not happen, we actually had a very strong year, and that was a combination of, of strong demand but also of real gains on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this was the year when labor force participation picked up, where immigration picked up, where the distortions to supply and demand from the pandemic-you know, the shortages and the bottlenecks-really began to unwind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we had significant supply-side gains with strong demand, and we got what looks like a 2½ percent-plus, or a little more than that, growth year at a time when potential growth this year might even have been higher than that, just because of the healing on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the inflation forecast is roughly, roughly what people wrote down a year ago, but in a very different setting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say the labor market, because of the stronger growth, has also been significantly better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look back at the SEP from a year ago, there was a significant increase in, in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've seen, you know, strong growth, still a tight labor market but one that's coming back into balance with the-with support from the supply side, a greater supply of labor.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a-you know, that's, that's what we see, and I think that combination was, was not anticipated broadly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The SEP really is, is a bottoms-up-built from the bottom up, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think people are looking at what's happening in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if you look at the big difference from September in the SEP, [it is that] the expectations for inflation this year, both headline and core, have come down, you know, really significantly in three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, [real GDP] growth has turned out to be very strong in the third quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've got-we've had several labor market reports, which suggest, again, significant progress toward greater balance across a very-a broad range of indicators.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're seeing so many of the indicators coming back to normal, not all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But so I think that people look at that, and they write down their-basically, each individual writes down a forecast and a rate forecast that goes with that forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so it's not-it isn't-you ask about real rates, I take it?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, that's-that is-that is something that we're very conscious of, and aware of, and monitor, and it's certainly a big part of-it's a part of how we think about things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as you well know, it's so hard to know exactly, you know, what the-what the real rate is or exactly how tight policy is at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you couldn't follow that like it was a rule and think that you would get the right answer all the time, but it's certainly something that we're focused on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, indeed, if you look at the projections, I think the expectation would be that the real rate is declining as we-as we move forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think about what's the right thing to do for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The minute we start thinking about those things-you know, we just can't do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll do the things that we think are right for the economy at the time we-when we think is the right time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One of the things we're moving carefully about is that decision over-that assessment, really-over whether, whether we've done enough, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you see that people are not writing down rate hikes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's us thinking that we have done enough but not, not feeling that really strongly, confidently and not wanting to take the possibility of a rate hike off the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, it's not the base case anymore, obviously, as it was, you know, 60, 90 days ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, as I mentioned, we wrote down this SEP, and it talks about-people have individual assessments of when it will be appropriate to, you know, to start to dial back on, on the tight policy we have in place, and that's a discussion we'll be having going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's another assessment that we're going to make very carefully, so as time goes forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this last year has been remarkable for the, the sort of seesaw thing, the back-and-forth we've had over the course of the year of markets moving away and moving back and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and what I would just say is that we, we focus on what we have to do and how we need to use our tools to achieve our goals, and that's what we really focus on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people are going to have different forecasts about the economy, and they're going to-those are going to show up in market conditions, or they won't, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in any case, we have to do what we think is right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, in the long run, it's important that financial conditions become aligned or are aligned with what we're trying to accomplish, and, in the long run, they will be, of course, because we will do what it takes to get to our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, ultimately, that will mean that financial conditions will, will come along.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in the meantime, there can be back-and-forth, and, you know, I'm just focused on what's the right thing for us to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's, it's really good to see the progress that we're making.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if you look at the 12-month-look at the 6-month measures, you see very low numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at 12-month measures, you're still well above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're actually above 3 percent on core, through November, PCE [inflation].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That isn't to say- I'm not, you know, calling into question the progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need to see, you know, continued further, further progress toward getting back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, our-it's our job to restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that-it's one of our two jobs, along with maximum employment, and they're equal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're very focused on, on, you know, doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're pleased with the progress, but, but we see the need for further progress, and I think-I think it's fair to say there is a lot of uncertainty about going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen the economy move in surprising directions, so we're just going to need to see more further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll, we'll look at the totality of the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Growth is one thing, so is inflation, so is labor market data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As we-as we make decisions about policy changes going forward, we're going to be looking at all those things and, particularly, about the-as they affect the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's ultimately all about the outlook and the balance of risks as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we have stronger growth, you know, that'll be good for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It might actually mean that it takes a little longer to get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will get it down to 2 percent, but, you know, if we see stronger growth, we'll-we will set policy according to what we actually see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's only a problem insofar as it makes it more difficult for us to achieve our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, if you have-if you have growth that's robust, what that will mean is probably it will keep the labor market very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It probably will, will place some upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That could mean that it takes longer to get to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That could mean we need to keep rates higher for longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It could even mean, ultimately, that we would need to hike again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just is- it's the way, the way our policy works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on, on the better-balance side, there are just a lot of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's- you see-you see job growth still strong but moving back down to more sustainable levels, given population growth and labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The things that are not quite-but let me go on with that list.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at surveys of businesses, they're, they're- sort of the era of this frantic labor shortage, [those kinds of worker shortages] are behind us, and they're seeing a shortage of labor as being significantly alleviated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at shortages of workers, whereas they thought job, job availability was the highest that it'd ever been or close to it, that's now down to more normal levels by so many measures-participation, unemployment-so many measures: the unemployment-job openings, quits, all of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So wages are still running a bit above what would be consistent with 2 percent inflation over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if wages are running around 4 percent, that's still a bit above, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I guess there, there are just a couple of other-the unemployment rate is very, very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And these are-but, but I would just say, overall, the development of the labor market has been very positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been a good time for workers to find jobs and get solid wage increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A common theme is that, while inflation is coming down, and that's very good news, the price level is not coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Prices of some, some goods and services are coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But overall, in the aggregate, the price level is not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people are still living with high prices, and that's, that's not-that is something that people don't like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so what will happen with that is, wages are now-[changes in] real wages are now positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So [nominal] wages are now moving up more than inflation, as inflation comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that might help improve the mood of people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do see those-we see those public opinion surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The thing that we can do is to do our jobs, which is to use our tools to foster price stability, which has such great benefits over such long periods of time, and which is the thing that really enables us to work for and achieve an extended period of high employment, which is so beneficial for, you know, families and, and companies around the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Obviously, we're hoping to, to see something very different-which is a continuation of what we have seen, which is the labor market coming into better balance without a significant increase in unemployment, inflation coming down without a significant increase in unemployment, and growth moderating without a significant increase in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we're, we're trying very much to achieve and not something that we're looking to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, obviously, what we'll do is we'll look at the totality of the data, as I've mentioned a couple times, and, certainly, the labor data would be important in that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, if you-if you can describe a situation like that where if, if there were the beginning of a recession or something like that, then, yes, that would certainly weigh heavily on that decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're aware of the risk that we would hang on too long.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we know that that's a risk, and we're very focused on not making that mistake.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do regard the two-you know, we've come back into a better balance between the risk of overdoing it and the risk of underdoing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not only that, we were able to focus hard on the-on the price-stability mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're getting back to the point where-which is what you do when you're very far from, from one of them, one of the two mandates-you're getting now back to the point where both mandates are important, and they're, they're more in balance, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we'll be-we'll be very much keeping that in mind, as we make policy going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the things we'll be looking at, I've already described.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're, we're obviously looking hard at what's happening with demand, and what we see?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see the same thing other people see, which is a strong economy, which really put up quite a performance in 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see good evidence and good reason to believe that growth will come in lower next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the median growth-median participant wrote down 1. percent growth, but, you know, we'll have to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll also be looking to see progress on inflation and, you know, the labor market remaining strong but, but ideally, without seeing the kind of large increase in unemployment that happens sometimes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't typically tried to articulate, with one exception, really specific target levels, which was if you-some of you will remember the thresholds that we used in, I guess, 2013.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't-the answer is, these are things that we haven't, you know, really worked out yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're sort of just at the beginning of, of that discussion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It wouldn't, if that were to-first of all, let me just say, that isn't a plan.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's not something-you know this, but allow me to say it again: We don't debate or discuss what the right, you know, whose SEP is right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just say what they are, and we tabulate them and publish them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So and it's, you know, it's important for people to know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it wouldn't need to be a sign of-it could just be a sign that the economy is normalizing, and it doesn't need the tight policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It depends on-the economy can evolve in many different ways, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So but, but it could be more of what I just described.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, that's what we're finding out, and we've, you know, we've seen real progress in, in core inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has been sticky, and famously, the service sector is thought to be stickier, but we've actually seen reasonable progress in nonhousing services, which was the area where, where you would expect to see less progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in fact, all three of the categories of core [prices] are now contributing: goods, housing services, nonhousing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're all contributing in different-at different levels, you know, meeting by meeting-or, rather, report by report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we got-we got CPI the morning of the first day, and we got PPI the next day, which informs the, you know, the translation into PCE [inflation].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's very late in the game, you know, to-but nonetheless, participants are allowed to, encouraged to update their SEP forecast until probably midmorning today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: After that, so staff has to-has to cumulate all of that and create the documents that you see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So until about midmorning, a little, maybe late morning, it's okay to update, and I believe some people did update their forecast based on what we saw today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question of whether there have been fundamental structural shifts is, is really hard to know the answer and a very interesting one right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The one that would affect-the one that comes to mind, though, is just the question of where the neutral rate of interest is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, for example, if it's risen, and I'm not saying that it has, but if it were to have risen, that would mean that, that interest rates would need to be a little bit higher to convey the same level of restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The thing is, we're not really going to know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, people will be writing papers about that 10 years from now and still fighting about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to be making policy in this, you know, difficult, uncertain, really unprecedented environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some-someone once said that you know the-you know the natural rate of interest by its works, and that's really right, but that's very difficult because policy operates with a lag.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's one of the reasons why we slowed down this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We started slowing down at this meeting last year, reducing the pace at which we were adding restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, over the course of this year, we really slowed down a lot to give those lags time to work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of demand, has demand shifted more away from services into goods?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's- you can make a case for that, that the shift back into services has not been complete, and it doesn't look like it's ongoing, but I don't know if that's right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Maybe people just bought so much stuff that they temporarily don't want any more stuff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the reason you wouldn't wait to get to 2 percent to cut rates is that policy would be, it would be too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, you'd want to be reducing restriction on the economy well before 2 percent because-or before you get to 2 percent so you don't overshoot, if we think, think of restrictive policy as weighing on economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it takes-it takes a while for policy to get into the economy, affect economic activity, and affect inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look at what's in the-in the SEP, and, you know, I think you'll see a reasonable estimate of the time lags and things like that that it would take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't want to-I wouldn't want to identify any one precise point, because I would be able to look back then and probably find out that it turned out not to be right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we'll be looking at it and, and looking at the broad collection of factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we felt since the beginning that it would be a combination of two factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first factor is just the unwinding of, of what happened in the pandemic: the distortions of supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the second thing would be our policy, which was weighing on aggregate demand and actually making it easier for the supply side to recover because of lower demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We thought those two things were going to be necessary.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Sorry, say your-say the last part of your question again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not that-it may or may not be about "different," the U.S. economy being different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that this inflation was not the classic demand overload, pot-boiling-over, kind of inflation that we [typically] think about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was a combination of very strong demand, without question, and unusual supply-side restrictions, both on the goods side but also on the labor side, because we had a-we had a participation shock.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we had the view-my colleagues and I broadly had the view-that we could get a lot of-you know, you had essentially a vertical supply curve, because you ran into the limits of, of capacity at very low levels, because there weren't workers and because people couldn't-the supply chains were all broken.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we had the view that you could come straight down that vertical supply curve to the extent demand [was] lowered, reduced.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question is, you know, once, once that part of it runs out-and we think it has a ways to run; we definitely think that the sort of supply chain and shortages side has some, some ways to run-does labor force participation have much more to run?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Immigration could help, but it may be that, at some point-at some point, you will run out of supply-side help, and then it gets down to demand, and it gets harder.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But to say with certainty that the last mile is going to be different, I'd be reluctant to, you know, to suggest that we have any certainty around that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's so far, so good-although we kind of assume that it will get harder from here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're not talking about altering the pace of QT right now, just to get that out of the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the balance sheet seems to be working pretty much as expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we've been seeing is, you know, that we're allowing runoff each month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The reverse repo facility [take- up] has been coming down quickly, and reserves have been either moving up or-as a result-or holding steady.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At a certain point, you know, there won't be any more to come out of, or there'll be a level where [take-up at] the reverse repo facility levels out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, at that point, reserves will start to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we still have-you know that we intend to reduce our securities holdings until we judge that the quantity of reserve balances has reached a level somewhat above that consistent with ample reserves, and we also intend to slow and then stop the decline in size of the balance sheet when reserve balances are somewhat above the level judged to be consistent with ample reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not at those levels, you know, with, with reserves close to 3. trillion [dollars].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-we don't think we're at those [levels judged consistent with ample] reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so far-so far, it's working pretty much as expected, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're asking, though, the question, I guess you're implying the question of can you continue with QT at such time-QT, which is a tightening action-at such time as policy is still tight?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, if you're-if you're-if you're cutting rates because you're going back to normal, that's one thing, [and distinct from] if you're cutting them because the economy is really weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you can imagine, you'd have to know what the reason is to know whether it would be appropriate to do those two things at the same time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what are we looking for to get greater confidence?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-we're looking for greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Implicitly, we do have confidence, and it has been increasing, but we want to get greater confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-we're looking at continuation of the good data that we've been seeing, and a good example is inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question really is, that six months of good inflation data-is it sending us a true signal that we are, in fact, on a path-a sustainable path down to 2 percent inflation?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the answer will come from some more data that's also good data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't-it's not that the six-month data isn't-isn't low enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just a question of, can we take that with confidence that we're moving sustainably down to 2 percent?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, if you take a step back, we've had strong growth-very strong growth [in real GDP] last year-going right into the fourth quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And yet we've had a very strong labor market, and we've had inflation coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think-whereas a year ago, we, we were thinking that we needed to see some softening in economic activity-that hasn't been the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we, we look at-we look at stronger growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, at this point, we want to see strong growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking for inflation to continue to come down, as it has been coming down for the last six months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, I think it's-I, I would say it, it seems-it seems to be the likely case that, that we will achieve that confidence, but we have to achieve it, and we haven't yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you can-and you know this-you can look behind those numbers, and you can see that a lot of it's been coming from goods inflation, for example, and goods inflation running significantly negative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a reasonable assumption that, over time, goods inflation will flatten out-probably approximate zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That would mean the services sectors would have to contribute more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in other words, what we care about is the aggregate number-not so much the composition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We need to see more evidence that sort of confirms what we think we're seeing and that tells us that we are on-gives us confidence that we're on, on a path to-a sustainable path down to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you know, almost every participant on the Committee does believe that it will be appropriate to reduce rates and for, for-partly for the reasons that you say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we feel like inflation is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-what we're trying to do is identify a place where we're really confident about inflation getting back down to 2 percent so that we can then begin the process of dialing back the restrictive level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, I think-I think people do believe-and, as you know, the median participant wrote down three rate cuts this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think to get to that place where we feel comfortable starting the process, we need some confirmation that inflation is, in fact, coming down sustainably to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I-look, I think, as you know, we consult the range of Taylor rules and, and non-Taylor kind of rules.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're in our, our Tealbook, and, and they're in all the materials that we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, I don't think we've ever been at a-at a place where we were-where we were setting policy by them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there-depending on the rule, it will tell you different things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Another way to think about it is, implicitly, is-so, in theory, of course, real rates go up if-holding all else equal-as inflation comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that doesn't mean we can mechanically adjust policy as real rates-sorry-as inflation comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't mean that at all, because, for one thing, we, we don't know-we, we look at more than just the fed funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in addition, we don't know with great confidence where the neutral rate of interest is at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that also doesn't mean that we wait around for-to see, you know, the economy turn down, because that would be too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're really in a risk-management mode: of managing the risk-as I mentioned in my opening remarks-managing the risk that we move too soon and move too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think to move, which is-which is where almost everyone on the Committee is-is in favor of, of moving rates down this year-but the timing of that is going to be linked to our gaining confidence that inflation is on a sustainable path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, I, I don't know that we've worked out the particulars- statement language and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just say, if you look at-you know, look at where, where 12-month inflation is, and it's, you know, it's still well above-core is 2. percent, for example-12-month-which is way down from where it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Very, very positive development-very fast decline-and, and, you know, the, the case is likely that it will continue to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're, you know, we're wanting to see, you know, more data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say that we're not looking for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, yes, if you think about, you know-in, in the base case, the economy is performing well-the labor market remains strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we saw an unexpected weakening in, in-certainly in the labor market, that would certainly weigh on cutting sooner.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we saw inflation being stickier or higher or those sorts of things-would argue for moving later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the base case, though, where, where the economy is healthy and we have, you know, we have ongoing growth-solid growth-we have a strong labor market-we have inflation coming down-that's what people are writing their SEP [submissions] around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in that case, what we're saying is, based on that, we think we can and should take advantage of that and, and be careful as we approach that question of when to begin to dial back restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're- we're-there was no proposal to cut rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some people did, you know, talk about their view of the rate path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would point you to the [December 2023] SEP as, as, you know, as good evidence of where people are, although it is-it is [now] one [FOMC meeting] cycle later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we're not-we're not at a place of, of really working out those kinds of details, because we weren't actively considering, you know, a-moving, moving the federal funds rate down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, there is a-there is a wide disparity-a healthy disparity-of views, and you see that in public, public statements, in the minutes, and the transcripts when they're released every five years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do have a healthy set of differences, and I think that's actually essential for making good policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also able to reach agreement, generally, because we listen to each other- we, we compromise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And even though not everybody loves what we do, they're able to-for the most part-able to join in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so we're not-you know, it's not the pandemic, so we can actually rely on more, more traditional forms.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're getting wages, and, and the economy has largely reopened and is broadly normalizing, as you see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't say we're looking at that, that sort of more innovative data as much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, we follow the, the components of inflation very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Which would be: Goods inflation-I talked about that a little bit; you mentioned housing inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the question is, when will these lower market rents find their way into measured rents, as measured, measured in PCE inflation?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that's coming, and we know it's coming.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just a question of when and, and how big it'll be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But at the same time, we think goods inflation will probably-it's been giving a lot of disinflation to the effort-and probably that declines over time, but it may well have some, some more time to run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, these-the supply chains are not perfectly back to where they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, it takes time for the, the healing process to get into prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at the things that relate to our mandate very carefully, and-as you would imagine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think we have-we have a ways to go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation is still-you know, core inflation is still well above target on a 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we're, we're not-we're not declaring victory at all at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-I think you, you do see in the interest-sensitive parts of the economy-you do see, for example, housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Your, your second question, though, really, I think, is important, and that is, a lot of this has come through-a lot of the disinflationary process has come through the healing of supply chains and also of the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you've seen the-you know, that other set of factors is really different from other cycles and has brought that working with tighter, tighter policy, which has enabled the supply side to recover-I think is that, that mixture has been behind what has enabled this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, no-we really do think that we're having an effect broadly across the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would point to the interest-sensitive parts of the economy as well as spending, generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-so I think it's, it's-of course, you know that it's not something you can identify with any precision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you-a standard approach would be to take the nominal rate-5.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: percent, let's say-and subtract sort of a, a forward measure of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you do that-and there are many, many ways to calculate the neutral rate-but that's one I like to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, you're going to get to something that is materially above mainstream estimates of neutrality-of the neutral rate-you will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but at the same time, you look at the economy, and you say, "This is an economy that grew 3. percent last year."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and you say, "What does that tell you about the neutral rate?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's happening, though, is, the supply side has been recovering in the middle of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a lot of the growth we're seeing is not-is-it isn't just a tug of war between, between interest rates and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're getting, you know, more activity because of the-of labor market healing and supply chains healing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the question is, when that peters out, I think the, the, you know, the, the restriction will show up probably more, more sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think the labor market by many measures is at or nearing normal-but not totally back to normal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, you know, job openings are not quite back to where they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages-wage increases, rather, are not quite back to where they-to where they would need to be in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the economy is broadly normalizing, and so is the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So wage setting is something that happens-it's, it's-you know, probably will take a couple of years to get all the way back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do see-you saw today's ECI reading-you know, the evidence is that, that wage increases are still at a healthy level-very healthy level-but they're gradually moving back to levels that would be more associated-given, given assumptions about productivity, are more typically associated with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's an ongoing process-a healthy one- and, and, you know, I think we're, we're moving in the right direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the, the labor market is-it-I don't know if I'd-it's rebalancing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Clearly, that the-there was a fairly severe imbalance between demand for workers and supply at the beginning of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we lost several million workers at the beginning of the pandemic from people dropping out of the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then when the economy reopened-you remember 2021-you had a severe labor shortage, and it was just-it was everywhere-panic on the part of businesses-couldn't, couldn't find people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what's happened is-we expected labor-the labor supply-labor market to come back quickly, and it didn't.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And 2022 was a disappointing year, and, you know, we were kind of thinking, "Well, maybe we won't get it back."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then 2023, we did, as you know-so labor force participation came back strongly in '23, and so did immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and so those two forces have significantly lowered the temperature in the labor market to what is still a very strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's still a good labor market for wages and for finding a job, but it's getting back into balance, and that's what we want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, one great way to look at that is what's happening with, with wage increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you see it now across the, the major things that we-that we track.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It isn't every quarter, but, overall, there's a clear trend-still at high levels, but back down to where-what would be consistent with, with where we were before the pandemic and with 2 percent inflation.
