speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, I think that that is a risk-the risk that inflation would, would reaccelerate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the, the greater risk is that it would-that it would stabilize at a level meaningfully above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, if-if inflation were to surprise by moving back up, that would-we would have to respond to that, and that would- that would be a surprise at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I have to tell you, that's why we keep our options open here and why we're not, you know, rushing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think both of those are risks, but I think the more likely risk is the one that I mentioned, which is, you've had six good months-very good months-but what, what's really going to "shake out" here?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, where-what will- when we look back, what will we see?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Will, will inflation have dipped and then come back up?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Are the last six months flattered by factors that are-that are one-off factors that won't repeat themselves?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't-you know, that's not what we think, but that's the question we are asking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to ask [that], and we want to get comfort on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, how to-your first question-how to describe where we are?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would just say this-executive summary would be that growth is solid to strong over the course of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had just about two years now of, of unemployment under 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've got six months of good inflation data and an expectation that there's more to come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's looking in the rearview-the outlook-we do expect growth to moderate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we have expected it for some time, and it hasn't happened, but we do expect that it will moderate as supply chain and labor market normalization runs its course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, 12-month inflation is, is above target and getting, you know, getting down closer to target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not guaranteed, but we do seem to be getting on track for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those are the risks and, and questions we have to answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-the thing is, we're not looking for inflation to tap the 2 percent base once.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking for it to settle out over time at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the same thing is true if we have a month or two of lower-and we have that now-of, of inflation that's annualized at a-at a lower level-that wouldn't be good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-you know, we're not looking to have inflation anchor below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if we do face those circumstances, then we'll have to deal with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-I think as of now, you know, the, the question, which-we want to take advantage of this situation and finish the job on inflation while keeping the labor market strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'll point you to that language on your first question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we included that language in the statement to signal clearly that-with strong growth, strong labor market, inflation coming down-the Committee intends to move carefully as we consider when to begin to dial back the restrictive stance that we have in place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you take that to the current context-current context, we're going to be data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be looking at this meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Based on the meeting today, I would tell you that I don't think it's likely that the Committee will reach a level of confidence by the time of the March meeting to identify March as the time to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't call-you know, when you say-when you ask me about "in the near term," I'm hearing that as March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say I don't think that's-that's, that's probably not the most likely case or what we would call the base case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The whole thing is, this is going to depend on the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be looking at the economic data as it affects the outlook and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to make our decisions based on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it could wind up-you know, we'll, we'll have another SEP at the March meeting, and, and people will write down what they think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in the end, it's really going to depend on how the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We talked about, there are risks that would cause us to go slower-for example, stronger inflation-more, more persistent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are risks that would cause us to-if they happen-that would cause us to go faster or-and sooner.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that would be a weakening in the labor market or, for that matter, very, very persuasive lower inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're just-we're just going to be reacting to the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's the- that's really the only way we can do this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think-my, my own view is-I think if you look, look back to the pandemic, you, you saw a spike in productivity as workers were laid off, and, and activity didn't decline as fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, over the last-you saw high productivity last year, in '23.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're, we're basically in the throes of getting through the pandemic economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the question will be, what, what is it that has changed the-you know, the productivity tends to be based on, you know, fundamental aspects of our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Is there-is there a case-will it be the case that we come out of this more productive on a sustained basis?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would take-you know, people talk about AI, but I would-my guess is that we may shake out and be back where we were, because I don't-I'm not sure I see-work from home doesn't seem like it's a big productivity increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Or AI, artificial intelligence- generative it may be, but probably not in the short run-probably, maybe in the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm not-I'm not seeing why it would, but, you know, right-you know, right now I would say that productivity is kind of what falls out of the, the broader forces that are driving people in and out of the labor force and, and activity returning and supply chains getting fixed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when we think about, you know-our, our statutory goals are maximum employment and price stability, and that's what we're targeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not targeting housing price inflation, the cost of housing, or any of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But they're not-you know, those are not the things we're targeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also well aware that when we cut rates at the beginning of the pandemic, for example, the housing, housing industry was helped more than any other industry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when we raise rates, the housing industry can be hurt, because it's a very interest-sensitive sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On top of that, we have longer-run problems with the availability of housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we have a, a built-up set of cities, and, and, you know, people are moving further and further out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And these are not-these are not things that we have any tools to address.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, where it comes into play very specifically in our work is inflation, which is a combination.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're taking owners' equivalent rent and then actual rent paid by tenants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what that's telling you is that market rents are increasing at a much lower rate or even being flat and that that will show up in inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has to as long as that remains the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And just real quick-what is your response to the letter that was sent to you by some members of Congress asking the Fed to lower interest rates to make housing more affordable?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: My response is what I started with, which is that our, our job-the job Congress has given us is price stability and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Price stability is absolutely essential for people's lives, most importantly for-well, not most importantly-most, mostly for people at the lower end of the income spectrum who are living at the edges-at the margins.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so someone-for someone like that, high inflation in the-in the necessities of life-right away, you're in trouble, whereas even middle-class people have some, you know, some scope to absorb higher costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's what society has asked us to do, is to get inflation down, and the tools that we use to do it are interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would start by saying that balance sheet runoff so far has gone very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as the process has continued, you know, we're getting to that time where questions are beginning to come into greater focus about the pace of runoff and all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So at this meeting, we did have some discussion of the balance sheet, and we're planning to begin in- depth discussions of balance sheet issues at our next meeting in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those, those questions are all coming into scope now, and we're focusing on them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're, we're at the beginning of that process, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so they don't-for example, if you're-if you're normalizing policy, you might be reducing rates but continuing to run off the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In both cases, that's normalization, but from a strict monetary policy standpoint, you could say we're loosening along with tightening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something we're planning or thinking about, but right now, we're thinking about getting to a place where-we're going to see the balance sheet runoff to continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're watching it carefully, and, as I said, we'll-we'll be looking into that as a Committee starting in March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm, I'm not in a position to put a number on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm just going to say-and it's not that we don't have any confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we have growing confidence, but not to the point where we-where we feel like-it's a highly consequential decision to start the process of, of dialing back on restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we want to get that right, and we feel like the strong economy, strong labor market, inflation coming down-it gives us the ability to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that's the best way we can serve the public, because, ultimately, we, we've made a lot of progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just want to make sure that we do get the job done in a sustainable way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of when that'll be, you know, that, that'll all come out of our communications, and, you know, we won't-we won't keep that a secret.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not a decision that we've made, but I, I wouldn't think we'd, we'd be-we wouldn't be taking a position that it's got to go to zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, if it-if it were to stabilize at a different level-but that's, that's not a decision that we've made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's what we'll be talking about at the March meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A whole range of issues will be briefed up, and the Committee will get into-get into all of the issues that will be arising over the course of the next, let's say, year or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have-this year is going to be a highly consequential year for, for the Fed and for monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're, all of us, very buckled down, focused on doing our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-you know, we're going to do-we'll update our, our inflation forecasts at the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's, you know, three months old [by March], so it might be lower now, given the data we've gotten.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, look, as I mentioned, we're going to be reacting to the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, if we get-if we get very strong inflation data and it, it kicks back up, then it'll-then we'll go slower or later or both.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we got really good inflation data soon, that would matter for both the-that, that would tell us that, that we could go sooner and perhaps go faster.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're just going to be-but, of course, we'll weigh that with all the other factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're setting policy based on the totality of, of the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think if we-if we came to the view that, that inflation were-that the six-month inflation numbers, which are very close to 2 [percent], were, in "PCE world"-if we came to-if that's-if we thought that is really where we're going to be, then, yes, our policy would be in a different place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, that's the whole point is, we're trying to get comfortable and gain confidence that that is where-that inflation is on a sustainable path down to 2 percent or toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so it's been-it's been interesting that confidence surveys have been weak, at a time when unemployment has been low-very low, historically low-for a couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, one obvious answer-we don't pretend to have perfect wisdom on this-is-but one obvious answer is that the price level is high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So prices went up much more than 2 percent for year-per year for a couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people are going to the store, and they're paying much more for the basics of life than they were two years ago-three years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's fine that inflation is coming down, but the price-the prices they're paying are still high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that, that is what-that, that has to be some part of why people are unhappy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, this is why we need to keep price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's why we need to do our jobs-so that people don't have to deal with things like this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In, in recent, recent surveys, a couple of-you've seen a couple of significant increases in, in consumer confidence or, or happiness with the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it is-it is a fact that we have seen, you know, a meaningful increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think levels of confidence are still maybe not as high as they've been at various times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we do meet with outside groups who come from all different parts of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I always feel like you-I mean, I spent most of my life in the private sector looking at companies-individual companies-individual management teams-and then building out from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, starting with GDP data is-and working into what's actually affecting people's lives is-is challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, as you know, the 12 Reserve Banks have really the best network of anyone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In all their Districts, they're talking to, you know, not just the business community, but the educational, medical, all, all-you know, nonprofit community.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so when they come back-that's what goes into the Beige Book.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But they come back, and what each Reserve Bank president does is, during the outlook go-around, they'll say, "In my District .

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they'll talk about 100 conversations they-not-they won't talk-they, they will give you input, based on 100 conversations that they've had with people of all different walks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-I personally find it very helpful in understanding what's going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, I think you hear things before they show up in the data sometimes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, if you-if you look back at the last-not this Beige Book, but the one before, it was more-there was a lot of "slower activity."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that, that what you're hearing now is, is, things are picking up a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're hearing-not, not in every District and not every, every person that we talk to, but you're-overall, it feels like you're hearing things picking up at the margin.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's-again, we've had inflation come down without a slow economy and without, you know, important increases in, in unemployment, and there's no reason why we should want to get in the way of that process, if it's going to continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I am-you know, I think-I think declining inflation-continued declines in inflation are, are really the main thing we're looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we want the labor market to remain strong, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got a, a maximum-employment mandate and a, a price-stability mandate, and those are the two things we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Growth only matters to the extent it influences our achievement of those two-of those two mandates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What it means is that, you know, we've seen incoming-as I pointed out in my opening remarks, we did mark up our growth forecast and so have many other forecasters, so the economy is performing, performing well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the inflation data came in a little bit higher is a separate matter, and I think that caused people to write up their inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But nonetheless, we continue to make good progress on bringing inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're strongly committed to bringing inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is-that is our goal, and we will achieve that goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they should believe that, because that's what-that's what will happen over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think we're, we're making projections that do show that happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're committed to that outcome, and we will bring it about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think there's some confidence that the market rents-lower market rent increases that we're seeing will show up in measures of housing services inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a little bit of uncertainty about when that will happen, but there's real confidence that they will show up eventually over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will get aggregate inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and I would assume that we'll continue to see is-we'll see goods prices coming into a new equilibrium where they're going down perhaps not as quickly as they had been earlier this year, where housing services inflation will come back down as, as current market rents are suggesting will happen and where nonhousing services will move back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some combination of those three things-and it may be different from the combination we had before the pandemic-will be achieved and will bring inflation back down to 2 percent sustainably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's more-I would put it more in the context of what I said in our- in my opening remarks that the risks are really two-sided here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-we're in a situation where, you know, if we ease-if we ease too much or too soon, we could see inflation come back, and if we ease too late, we could do unnecessary harm to employment and people's working lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, you know, we do see the risks as two-sided, so it is consequential.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, fortunately, with the economy growing, with the labor market strong, and with inflation coming down, we can approach that question carefully and let the data speak on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I want to start by being-saying I always try to be careful about dismissing data that we don't like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you need to check yourself on that, and I'll do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But- so I would say the January number, which was very high-the January CPI and PCE numbers were quite high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's reason to think that there could be seasonal effects there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, we don't want to be completely dismissive of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The February number was high, higher than expectations, but we have it at currently well below 30 basis points core PCE, which is not terribly high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I take the two of them together, and I think they haven't really changed the overall story, which is that of inflation moving down gradually on a sometimes-bumpy road toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also don't think that those readings added to anyone's confidence that we're moving closer to, to that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we didn't-the last thing I'll say is we didn't excessively celebrate the good inflation readings we got in the last seven months of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you heard us saying was that we needed to see more that we could, you know-we wanted to be careful about that decision, and we're not going to overreact, as well, to these two months of data, nor are we going to ignore them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we didn't make any decisions about future meetings today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are going to depend on our ongoing assessment of the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I really don't have anything for you on any specific meeting, looking forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll take-you know, things can happen during an intermeeting period, if you look back-unexpected things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't want to-I wouldn't want to dismiss anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I just would say that the Committee wants to see more data that gives us higher confidence that inflation is moving down sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also mentioned-and we don't see this in the data right now, but if there were a significant weakening in the data, particularly in the labor market, that could also be a reason for us to begin the process of reducing rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I don't-there's nothing in the data pointing at that, but those are the things that we'll be looking at, at coming meetings and-without trying to refer to any specific meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was an uptick in the longer-run rate, and also there's a 25 basis point increase in '25 and '26.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of, are rates going to be higher in the longer run, if that's really your question, I don't think we know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's, it's-we think that rates were generally low during the pre-pandemic post-Global Financial Crisis era for reasons that are mostly, you know, important, slow-moving, large things like demographics and productivity and that sort of thing-things that don't move quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, my instinct would be that rates will not go back down to the very low levels that we saw, where, all around the world, there were long- run [real interest] rates that were at or below zero in some cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't see rates going back down to that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that that higher year-end number reflects the data we've seen so far this year because you're now-you're now in this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that-sorry, say your last part of your question again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, you know, I think, if you look at the SEP, what it says is that it is still likely in most people's view that we will achieve that confidence and that there will be rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's really going to depend on the incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other thing is, in the second half of the year, you have some pretty low readings, so it might be harder to make progress as you move that 12-month window forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, we're looking for data that confirm the kind of low readings that we had last year and give us a higher degree of confidence that what we saw was really inflation moving sustainably down to 2 percent-toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so, if what we're getting is a lot of supply and a lot of demand, and that supply is actually feeding demand because workers are getting paid and they're spending and that's, you know-what you would have is potentially kind of what you had last year, which is a bigger economy where inflationary pressures are not increasing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you can have that if you have a continued supply-side activity that we had last year with-both with supply chains and also with, with growth in the size of the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we saw-you saw last year very strong hiring and inflation coming down quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We now have a better sense that a big part of that was supply-side healing, particularly with, with growth in the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in and of itself, strong job growth is not a reason, you know, for us to be concerned about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think-there are many different financial conditions indicators, and you can kind of, you know, see different answers to that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, we do think that financial conditions are weighing on economic activity, and we think you see that in-a great place to see it is in the labor market, where you've seen demand cooling off a little bit from the extremely high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there I would point to job openings, quits, surveys, the hiring rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are also supply-side things happening, but I think those are demand-side things happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we saw-that's been a question for a while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did see progress on inflation last year-significant progress, despite financial conditions sometimes being tighter, sometimes looser.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I see the Committee looking at the two months of data and asking the same question you're asking and saying we're just going to have to see what the data show.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, you can look at January, which is a very high reading and you can-and I think many people did see the possibility of seasonal adjustment problems there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, you don't want to-you've got to be careful about dismissing the parts of the data that you don't like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So then February wasn't, wasn't as high, but it was higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the question is, what are we going to see?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we tend to see a little bit stronger-this is in the data-a little bit stronger inflation in the first half of the year, a little bit less strong later in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to- we're going to let the data show.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think we really know whether this is a bump on the road or something more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, the economy is strong, the labor market is strong, inflation has come way down, and that gives us the ability to approach this question carefully and feel more confident that inflation is moving down sustainably at 2 percent when we take that step to begin dialing back our restrictive policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It certainly hasn't improved our confidence-it hasn't raised anyone's confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that the story is really essentially the same and that is of inflation coming down gradually toward 2 percent on a sometimes-bumpy path, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got nine months of 2½ percent inflation now, and we've had two months of kind of bumpy inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were saying that we'll-it's going to be a bumpy ride.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now here are some bumps, and the question is, are they more than bumps?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is very important for everyone that we serve that we do get inflation sustainably down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the historical record, it's-every situation is different, but the historical record is that you need to approach that question carefully and try to get it right the first time and not have to come back and raise rates again perhaps if you cut inappropriately- prematurely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Have they-well, first of all, I respect our-you know, in our system of government, it is Congress that has oversight responsibility over the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We place a tremendous amount of importance on our engagements with Congress and always treat them with great respect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In this case, I would say, those are, you know-our mandate is for maximum employment and price stability and the other things that we do, and that's what we're trying to accomplish.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're trying to do that in a way that sustains the strong growth we're seeing, the strong labor market we're seeing, but allows us to make further progress with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's how we can best serve the public and leave the other issues, which in many cases are incredibly important, such as those you mentioned, leave those to the people who have responsibility for those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We receive these letters with respect, and we write careful responses and address concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We listen, again, because we're talking to the people who, in our system of government, have oversight over our activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-but at the end of the day, we take that on board, but we have to make our judgments, and we have to "stick to our knitting"- which is maximum employment, price stability, supervise and regulate the banks, work on the payment system: the things that we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're a very consensus-oriented organization, and we do try to achieve consensus and, ideally, unanimity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-and so I-you know, you respect thoughtful dissents very much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's like, you may not agree with some arguments, but you really want to understand them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you may read a book that takes a position that you have long opposed, just to understand [the position of] that book.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, of course, monitor-it's one of our two goal variables.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, you know-we follow all the possible stories that are out there about, about there being cracks, but the overall picture really is a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The extreme imbalances that we saw in the early parts of the pandemic recovery have mostly been resolved.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're seeing strong wage growth, but wage growth is gradually moderating down to more sustainable levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In many, many respects, the things are returning more to their state in 2019, which we can think of as normal for this purpose.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And surveys of workers and businesses are always interesting on this: You know, how tight is the-how easy is it to find a job?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: How hard is it-how easy it is to find a worker?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you do see things like the low- the low hiring rate, and people have made the argument that if, if layoffs were to increase, that would-that would mean that the net would be fairly quick increases in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's something we're watching, but we're not seeing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, initial claims are very, very low and, if anything, have tracked down a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when I say something-I, I use the term "unexpected" weakening of the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we do expect the unemployment rate to-the forecast is that it would move up, I think, closer to what we see as the longer-run sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is what we're discussing essentially is-and we're not discussing all the other many other balance sheet issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what we're really looking at is slowing the pace of runoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There isn't much runoff among MBS-in MBS right now, but there is in Treasuries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't want to give you a specific number because we haven't made a-haven't had an agreement or decision, but that's the idea.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't want to try to be more specific than that, but you get the idea.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The idea is-and this is in our longer-run plans-that we may actually be able to get to a lower level, because we would avoid the kind of frictions that can happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there can be times when, in the aggregate, reserves are ample or even abundant, but not in every part.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those parts where they're not ample, there can be stress, and that can cause you to prematurely stop the process to avoid the stress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then it would be very hard to restart, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking at what would be a good time and what would be a good structure, and "fairly soon" is words that we use to mean fairly soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that-our, our longer-run goal is to return to a balance sheet that is mostly Treasuries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do expect that, once we're through this, we'll come back to the other issues about the composition and the maturity and revisit those issues, but it's, you know, not urgent right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to get this, this decision made first and then we can, when the time is right, come back to the other issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But one of the reasons we're slowing down-we will soon enough, fairly soon I should say, slow down-is that we want to avoid any, any kind of that turbulence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wasn't thinking particularly about the banking- sector turbulence, but we-and we had some indicators the last time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is our second time in doing this, and I think we're going to be paying a lot of attention to the things that started to happen and that foreshadowed what eventually happened at the end of that tightening cycle where we wound up in a short[-of-]reserves situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think now we have a better sense of what are the indicators.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It isn't-it wasn't so much in the banking system as it was around, for example, where federal funds are trading relative to the administered rates and where secured rates are relative to the administered rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will always be watching the banking system for similar signs, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think we broadly think that, once [take-up at] the overnight [reverse] repo [facility] stabilizes, either at zero or close to zero, that, as the balance sheet shrinks, we should expect that reserves will decline pretty close to dollar-for-dollar with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's sort of ironic that, by going slower, you can get farther.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The idea is that, with a smoother transition, you won't-you'll run much less risk of kind of liquidity problems, which can grow into shocks, and which can cause you to stop the process prematurely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-in terms of how it ends, we're going to be monitoring carefully money market conditions and asking ourselves whether they-what they're telling us about reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Are they-right now, we would characterize them as "abundant," and what we're aiming for is "ample" and, you know, which is a little bit less than abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there isn't a- you know, there's not a dollar amount or a percent of GDP or anything like that where we think we have a really pretty clear understanding of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be looking at what these- what's happening in money markets, in particular-a bunch of different indicators, including the ones I mentioned, to tell us when we're getting close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then, though, you reach a point ultimately where you stop allowing the balance sheet to run off and you-but then, from that point, there's another period in which nonreserves-nonreserve liabilities grow organically, like currency, and that also shrinks the reserves at a very slow pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you have a, you know, a slower pace of runoff, which we'll have fairly soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then you have another time where you effectively hold the balance sheet constant and allow nonreserve liabilities to expand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then that ultimately brings you, ideally, in for-brings it into a nice, easy landing at a level that is above-you know, above what we think the lowest possible ample number would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to have a cushion, a buffer, because we know that demand for reserves can be very volatile.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't want to, again, find ourselves in a situation where there aren't reserves, and we have to turn around and buy assets and put reserves back in the banking system the way we did in 2019 and '20.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Chair Powell, you said you're waiting to become more confident that inflation's getting to your 2 percent goal before you cut rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Can you just sum up more specifically what data you're looking at that would give you that confidence?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're-most importantly, we're looking at the incoming inflation data and the contents of it and what they're telling us, so that'll be-and also the various components-so obviously that's what we want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want more confidence that inflation is coming down sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, of course we'll also be looking at all the other things that are happening in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll look at the totality of the data, including everything essentially as we make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the most important thing will be the inflation data coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, are there things that you would give more weight to, like wages?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we would look to the fact that wages are still coming in very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, but they've been-wage increases, that's to say-wage increases have been quite strong, but they're, they're gradually coming down to levels that are more sustainable over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think that-the inflation was not originally caused-we think, I don't think, by mostly by wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do think that, to get inflation back down to 2 percent sustainably, we'd like to see, you know, continuing gradual movement of wage increases at still high levels but back down to levels that are more sustainable over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess I'd put it this way: The-if you look at the incoming inflation data that we've had for January and February, I think very broadly that suggests that we were right to wait until we're more confident.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, I think-I didn't hear anyone dismissing it as not information that we should look at or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, generally speaking, it does go in the direction of saying, yes, it's appropriate for us to be careful as we approach this question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we've been pretty transparent on this, but I will- I'll try harder.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we are not getting ready to-we haven't proposed-we haven't come to a conclusion that we should propose, or anything like that, that Congress consider legislation to authorize a digital dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it would take legislation by Congress signed by the President to give us the ability to do what we think of as a CBDC, which is really a retail CBDC with the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we are doing, and I think what every major central bank is doing, is we're trying to stay in the frontiers of what's going on in digital finance, and it has many, many different areas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has applications in wholesale finance, in the payment system, and so we need-to serve the public-these issues have become very front burner in the last five or six years-we need to be knowledgeable about all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we actually do have people trying to understand things that are-but it's wrong to say that we're working on a CBDC and that we've secretly got a lab here where we've got one, and we're just going to spring it on Congress at the right moment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I haven't at all, in my own mind, made a decision that I think this is something the U.S. should be doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just think it's something we need to be-we need to understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do have people who are keeping up with that, as part of the broader payments landscape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I generally think-I mean, this movement actually started 30 years ago-30 years ago, when some academics posited that a more transparent central bank, if the public understands your reaction function, the markets will do your work for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so it all happens that way and so there's been a march toward greater and greater transparency.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that-certainly Chairman Bernanke advanced that, Chairman Greenspan did, Chair Yellen did, and I.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so we went from four press conferences a year to eight, so now every meeting really is "live" now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we have an annual supervision report, Financial Stability Report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, there's a long list of things that we've done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you-I mean, nothing comes to mind as really desperately in need of doing at this moment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have no shortage of FOMC participants speaking to the public through the media.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's generally broadly helped and made things better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say my main message at that-in those two days of hearings was really that the Committee needs to see more evidence to build our confidence that inflation is moving down sustainably toward our 2 percent goal, and we don't expect that it will be appropriate to begin to reduce rates until we're more confident that that is the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I said that any number of times, so those were kind of the main part of the message.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also-to the language you mentioned, I, I really pointed out that we had made significant progress over the past year, and what we're looking for now is confirmation that that progress will continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had a series of inflation readings over the second half of last year that were really much lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, we'll just have to see how the data come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would, of course, love to get great inflation data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We got really good inflation data on the second-in the second part of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We said we needed to see more, and we said it would be bumpy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now we have January and February, which I've talked about a couple of times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we're looking for more good data, and we would certainly welcome it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do think the evidence shows, you know, pretty clearly that policy is restrictive and is weighing on demand, and there are a few places I would point to for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So demand is still strong-the demand side of the labor market, in particular-but it's cooled from its extremely high level of a couple years ago, and you see that in job openings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw it-more evidence of that today in the JOLTS report, as you'll know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it has been coming down both in the Indeed report and the JOLTS report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The same is true of quits and hiring rates, which have essentially normalized.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I also look at the-we look at surveys of workers and-pardon me-surveys of workers and businesses, and [they] ask workers, "Are jobs plentiful?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you've seen that the answers to those have come back down to pre-pandemic levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You also see in interest-sensitive spending, like housing and investment-you also see that higher interest rates are weighing on those activities.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do think it's clear that, that policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say that we believe it is restrictive, and we believe [that] over time it will be sufficiently restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That will be a question that, that the data will have to answer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I don't want to get into complicated hypotheticals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that, you know, we're committed to retaining our current restrictive stance of policy for as long as is appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's unlikely that the next policy rate move will be a hike.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, our policy focus is really what I just mentioned, which is- which is how long to keep policy restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think we'd need to see persuasive evidence that our policy stance is not sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation sustainably down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's not-that's not what we think we're seeing, as I-as I mentioned, but that's-something like that is what it would take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'd look at the totality of the data in answer to that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That would include inflation, inflation expectations, and all the other data too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think, again, the test-what I'm saying is, if we were to come to that conclusion that policy weren't tight enough to achieve that, so it would be the totality of all the things we'd be looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, if we-if we reach that conclusion-and we don't see evidence supporting that conclusion-that's what it would take I think for us to take that step.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, obviously, our decisions that we make on our policy rate are going to depend on the incoming data, how the outlook is evolving, and the balance of risks, as always.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, and we think, that policy is well positioned to address different paths that the economy might take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've said that we don't think it would be appropriate to dial back our restrictive policy stance until we've gained greater confidence that inflation is moving down sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, for example, let me take a path: If we did have a path where inflation proves more persistent than expected and where the labor market remains strong, but inflation is moving sideways and we're not gaining greater confidence, well, that would be a case in which it could be appropriate to hold off on rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's also other paths that the economy could take, which, which would cause us to want to consider rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those would be-two of those paths would be that we do gain greater confidence, as we've said, that inflation is moving sustainably down to 2 percent, and another path could be, you know, an unexpected weakening in the labor market, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those are paths in which you could see us cutting rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it really will depend on the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of peak rate, you know, I think, really, it's the same question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think the data will have to answer that question for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, it's, it's-we've set ourselves a test that we-for us to begin to reduce policy restriction, we'd want to be confident that inflation is moving-you know, moving sustainably down to 2 percent, and, for sure, one of the things we'd be looking at is the performance of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But clearly, incoming, incoming inflation data would be at the very heart of that decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we'll be able to look back, you know, from down the road and look back and understand it better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, what we've seen so far this year in the first quarter is growth coming in about consistent with where it was last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I know GDP came in lower, but you don't see an acceleration in growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the thought would be that financial conditions loosened in, in, December, and that caused an uptick in activity, and that caused inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you see is economic activity at a level that's roughly the same as, as last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we'll, we'll have a better sense of that over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know that there's an obvious connection there, though, with easing of financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Rates are certainly higher now and have been for some time than they were before the December meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that's appropriate, given what inflation has done in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I just want to be careful that we don't target wage growth or the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And remember what we saw last year: very strong growth, a really tight labor market, and a historically fast decline in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and that's because we know there are two forces at work here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's the unwinding of the pandemic-related supply-side distortions and demand-side distortions, and there's also monetary policy, you know, restrictive monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't rule out that something like that can continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I wouldn't give up, at this point, on further things happening on the supply side either because, you know, we do see that companies still report that there are supply-side issues that they're facing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, even when the supply-side issues are solved, it should take some time for that to affect economic activity and ultimately inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't like to say that either strong-either growth or, or a strong labor market, in and of itself, would automatically create problems on inflation, because, of course, it didn't do that last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The point with wages is, of course, we, like everyone else, like to see high wages, but we also want to see them not eaten up by high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's really what we're trying to do, is to cool the economy and work with what's happening on the supply side to bring-to bring the economy back to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of that will probably be having wage increases move down incrementally toward levels that are more sustainable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the-what we said is that we need to be more confident, and we've said-my colleagues and I today said that we didn't see progress in the first-in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I've said that it appears, then, that it's going to take longer for us to reach that point of confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I can just say that when we get that confidence, then rate cuts will be in scope.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what, what-so I thought it was appropriate to reserve judgment until, until we had the full quarter's data, until we saw the March data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see strong economic activity, we see a strong labor market, and we see inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see three inflation readings, and so I think you're at a point there where you should take some signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't like to react to one or two months' data, but this is a full quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it's appropriate to take signal now, and we are taking signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the signal that we're taking is that it's likely to take longer for us to gain confidence that we are on a sustainable path down to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we will-you know, we will put the thing-we have put the thing under a microscope.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, nothing is going to come out of that that's going to change the view.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that, in fact, we didn't gain confidence and that it's going to take longer to get that confidence-but-confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's happened since December is you've seen higher goods inflation than expected, and you've seen higher nonhousing services inflation than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those two are working together to, to sort of be higher than we had thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are stories behind how that happened, and, you know, we-I think-I think my expectation is that we will, over the course of this year, see inflation move back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think my confidence in that is lower than it was because of the data that we've seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also continue to expect, and I continue to expect, that housing services inflation, given where market rents are, those will show up in measured housing services inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just-it looks like the lag-that there are substantial lags between when, you know, lower market rates turned up and-for new tenants and when it shows up for existing tenants or for in-housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the active tool of monetary policy is, of course, the interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is-this is a long-a plan we've long had in place to slow, really not in order to, you know, provide accommodation to the economy but to-or to be less restrictive to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It really is to ensure that the process of shrinking the balance sheet down to where we want to get it is a smooth one and doesn't wind up in-with financial market turmoil the way it did the last-the last time we did this and the only other time we've ever done this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on your first question, I don't have a probability estimate for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But all I can say is that, you know, we've said that we didn't think it would be appropriate to cut until we were more confident that inflation was moving sustainably down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't get our confidence, in that [it] didn't increase in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in fact, what really happened was we came to the view that it will take longer to get that confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think there are-you know, I think it's-the economy has been very hard for forecasters broadly to predict-to predict its path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there are paths to, to not cutting, and there are paths to cutting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the employment mandate, to your point, if you go back a couple of years, our, our sort of framework document says that, when you look at the two mandate goals, and if one of them is further away from goal than the other, then you focus on that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It actually-it's the time to get back there times the, you know, times how far it is from the goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As-and this is what we referred to in the statement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As inflation has come down, now to below 3 percent on a-on a 12-month basis, it's become-we're now focusing [on] the other goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there are-there are paths that the economy can take that would involve cuts and there are paths that wouldn't.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't have great confidence in which of those paths-I think I would say my personal forecast is that we will begin to see further progress on inflation this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're going to have to let the data lead us on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess I would say I was around for stagflation, and it was, you know, 10 percent-10 percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now we have-and very slow growth-so right now we have 3 percent growth, which is, you know, pretty solid growth I would say, by any measure, and we have inflation running under 3 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't-I don't really understand where that's coming from.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in addition, I would say most forecasters, including our forecasting, was that last year's level of growth was very high-3.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: percent in, I guess, the fourth quarter, you know- and probably not going to be sustained and would come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That would still be to a very healthy level of growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, with inflation, you know, our-we will return inflation to 2 percent, and that won't be-so I don't see the "stag" or the "flation," actually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think I would take that question this way: We saw a year of very high productivity growth in 2023, and we saw a year of, I think, negative productivity growth in 2022.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's hard to draw from the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the question is, will productivity run-there are two questions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One is: Will productivity run persistently above its longer-run trend?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of potential output, though, that's a separate question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had a-what amounts to a, a significant increase in the potential output of the economy that's not about productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was about having more labor, frankly, both through-in 2022, both through participation and also through immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're very much-like other forecasters and economists-getting our arms around what that means for potential output this year and next year-and last year for that matter, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think-in that case, I think you really do have a significant increase in potential output, but you've also got-so you've got more supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But those people also come in, they work, they have jobs, they spend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it-there may be-it may be that you get more supply than you get demand at the beginning, but, ultimately, it should be neither inflationary nor disinflationary over, over a longer period.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we, we believe our policy stance is in a good place and is appropriate to the current situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We believe it's restrictive, and, you know, we-our evidence for that, I went over earlier.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see it in inflation-sensitive spending, where demand has clearly come down a lot over the past few years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's more from monetary policy, whereas the supply side of things that are happening are more on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, of course we're not satisfied with 3 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: [Laughter] So we will return inflation to 2 percent over time but over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think our policy stance is, is appropriate to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if we were to conclude that policy is not sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation sustainably down to 2 percent, then that would be what it would take for us to want to increase rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the policy focus has been on-has really been on what to do about, about holding the current-the current level of restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, these are- these are going to be judgment calls.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, clearly restrictive monetary policy needs more time to do its job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, that is pretty clear, based on what we're seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: How long that will take and how patient we should be is going to depend on the totality of the data, how the outlook evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're always going to do what we think the right thing for the economy is when we come to that consensus view that it's the right thing to do for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's hard enough to get the economics right here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are difficult things, and if, if we were to take on a whole, another, set of factors and use that as a new filter, it would reduce the likelihood we'd actually get the economics right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that we'll do what we think is the right thing, when we think it's the right thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I can't say it enough, that we just don't-we just don't go down that road.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go down that road, where do you stop?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're on the road where we're serving all the American people and making our decisions based on the data and how those data affect the outlook and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: -a significant difference between an institution that takes into account all sorts of political events and one that doesn't.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's where the significant difference is, and, you know, we're-we just don't do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, you can go back and read the transcripts for every-this is my fourth election, fourth presidential election here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Read all the transcripts, and see if anybody mentions, in any way, the pending election.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we start down that road, again, I don't know how you stop.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you go back to where wages peaked-wage increases peaked a couple, three years ago-essentially all wage measures have come down substantially [when compared] to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But they are not, not down to where they were before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you'll note the ECI reading from Tuesday was-it was expected to be-to have come down, and, essentially, it was flat year over year, you know, I think roughly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So yeah, I mean, it's-that part of it is bumpy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we don't target wage increases, but, you know, in the longer run, if you have-if you have wage increases running higher than productivity would warrant, then, you know, there will be inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Employers will raise prices over time if that's the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has been inconsistent, but we have seen a substantial decline overall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, the thing that hurts everybody, and particularly people in the lower-income brackets, is inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you're a person who's living paycheck to paycheck, and suddenly all the things you buy-the fundamentals of life-go up in price, you, you are in trouble right away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, with those people in mind, in particular, what we're doing is, we're using our tools to bring down inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will bring inflation back down to 2 percent, and then people won't have to worry about it again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we're doing, and we know that it's painful and inconvenient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the dividends will be paid and will be very large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and everyone will share in those dividends, and we've made quite a lot of progress if you can think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think core-I think headline-core PCE [inflation] peaked at 5.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Quick follow-up-are current interest rates really doing that much, though, to fight inflation right now for those consumers?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think-I think that restrictive monetary policy is doing what it's supposed to do, and it's-but it's also, in this case unusually, working alongside and with the healing of the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This, this-what was different this time was that a big part of the source of the inflation and the reason why we're having this conversation is that we had this supply-side kind of collapse, with shortages and bottlenecks and all that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so-and this was to do with the shutting down and reopening of the economy and other things that, that really raised demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think now you see those two things working together, the reversal of those supply and demand distortions from the pandemic and the response to it, along with restrictive monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those two things are working to bring down inflation, and we've made a lot of progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got work left to do, but we're not looking at the very high inflation rates that we were seeing two years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, essentially, there are-there are a number of places in the economy where there are just lag structures built into the inflation process, and housing is one of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when you have-when, when someone goes to-a new person goes to rent an apartment, that's called market rent, and you can see market rents are barely going up at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what happens is, those market rents take years, actually, to get all the way into rents for tenants who are rolling over their leases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Landlords don't tend to charge as much of an increase to a rollover tenant, for whatever reason.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what that does is it builds up a sort of an unrealized portion of increases when there have been big increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what happens is, you know-it's complicated, but the story is it just takes some time for that to get in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now I am confident that, as long as market rents remain low, this is going to show up in measured inflation, assuming that market rents do remain low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We now think significantly longer than we thought at the beginning, and so confident that it will come but not so confident in the timing of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that, that may happen, and, you know that we all serve domestic mandates, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the difference between the United States and other countries that are now considering rate cuts is that they're just not having the kind of growth we're having.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They have-their inflation is performing about like ours or maybe a little better, but they're not experiencing the kind of growth we're experiencing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we actually have the luxury of having strong growth and a strong labor market, very low unemployment, high job creation, and all of that, and we can be patient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will-we'll be careful and cautious as we approach the decision to cut rates, whereas I think other jurisdictions may go before that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the implications, you know, I think obviously markets see it coming.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think the markets and economies can adapt to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think, you know, we haven't seen-in addition, for the emerging market economies, we haven't seen the kind of turmoil that was more frequent 20 years ago, 30 years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, I think, partly because emerging market countries, many of them have much better monetary policy frameworks, much more credibility on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we thought, and most people thought, there would have to be probably significant dislocations somewhere in the economy, perhaps the labor market, to get inflation all the way down from the very high levels it was at at the beginning of this episode.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're very, of course, gratified and pleased that that hasn't happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, if you look at the dynamics that enabled that, it really was that this, the-that so much of the gain was from the unwinding of things that weren't to do with monetary policy but the unwinding of the distortions to the economy, you know, supply problems-supply-side problems and also some, some demand issues as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, as I've said, I'm not giving up on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think-I think it is possible that, that those forces will still work to help us bring inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're-you know, we're trying to use our tools in a way that keeps the labor market strong, and the economy strong, but also helps bring inflation back down to 2 percent sustainably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We hope we can do it without, you know, without significant dislocations in the labor market or elsewhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I said "an unexpected weakening" is what I-the way I characterized it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know-and I'm not going to try to define exactly what I mean by that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, it would be-it would have to be meaningful and get our attention and lead us to think that the labor market was really significantly weakening for us to want to react to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A couple of tenths in the unemployment rate would be-would probably not do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But a broader-it would be a broader thing that would-that would suggest that it would be appropriate to consider cutting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think whether you decide to cut will depend on all the facts and circumstances, not just that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me-let me start by saying that the Fed is committed to, you know, completing this process and carrying out Basel III Endgame in a way that's faithful to Basel and also comparable to what the other large comparable jurisdictions are doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't made any decisions on, on policy or on process at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll say again, though, if we conclude that re-proposal is appropriate, we won't hesitate to insist on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say that the, you know, the Basel III process is by far the most important thing and really is, I think, occupying us at this time in terms of what's, what's-what we're moving ahead with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you listen to, and you all do, listen to my 18 colleagues on the FOMC, you'll see that we do not lack for a diversity of voices and perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's one of the great aspects of the Federal Reserve System.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have 12 Reserve Banks around the country where they have their own economic staff, not the people who work here at the Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, and so each, each Reserve Bank has its own culture around monetary policy and its own approach and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-and, in terms of-in terms of dissents, you know, we have dissents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, a thoughtful dissent is a good thing, if someone really makes you think, that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But all I can say from my standpoint is I try-I listen carefully to people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I try to incorporate their thinking or do everything I can to incorporate their thinking into what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think many people, if they feel that's happening, you know, that for most people most of the time, that'll be enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but I'm not-I mean, it's, it's not, you know, frowned upon or illegal or against the rules or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I mean, I think we have a very diverse group of rounded people-frankly, more diverse than it used to be in many dimensions, more diverse from the obvious gender and demographic ways, but also we have more people who are not Ph.D. economists.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have people from business and law and academia and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we actually do have quite a good diverse perspective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think all of us read these stories about the lack of diversity, and we look around the room and say, "I don't understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what's going on there is that we had very low readings in the second half of last year-June through December, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as you go through the 12-month window, a very low reading drops out, and a new reading comes in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's just a, a slight element of conservativism that we're, we're assuming a certain level of-of, you know, incoming monthly PCE and core PCE numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you put that on top of where we are now, you get a very slight increase in the 12-month-in the 12-month, you know, reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just the kind of conservative way for forecasting things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we were to get more readings like today's reading, then, of course, that wouldn't be the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, I think-let me say that we welcome today's reading and then hope for more like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think we've, we've-what we said is that we don't think it'll be appropriate to, to reduce rates and begin to loosen policy until we have more confidence that inflation is moving back down to 2 percent on a-on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know that-I think if we-I don't know that this rules that in or out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, really, it's, it's a forecast-a fairly conservative forecast month by month that would lead to slightly higher, you know, 12-months rates by the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we get, you know, good-better readings than that, then you will see that come down or, or remain the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: [percent], you know, that's, that's a really good place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as far as the SEP part of that is concerned-as you know, I talk to-I talk to all of the other participants on the FOMC every cycle, and we talk about their Summary of Economic Projections and, and the dot plot-and, you know, their dot plot and everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what you-what I hear and see is that people are looking at, at, you know, a range of plausible outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in many cases, they're-they're thinking, "I don't really"- you know, "I can't really distinguish between two of these.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are very close calls, but we ask them to write down the most likely one-so they do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as, I think, you've, you've-as you've said, there's 15 of the 19 are, are kind of clustered around one or two.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think I would look at, at all-I'd look at all of them as plausible, but I'd look at-so I think that does tell you kind of what the Committee thinks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what everyone agrees on is, it's going to be data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one-no one brings to this or takes away from it that is on the Committee a really strong commitment to a particular rate path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's actually just their forecast and their-it's a combination of their forecast and their own reaction function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, everyone would say that this is very data dependent, and I don't hold it with high confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think if you're looking for-and, and don't really think that they're-they're not trying to send a strong signal that "this is what I think is the right thing."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just what they think at a given moment in time, subject to data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
