text: In terms of, you know, future meetings, we haven't, you know-we don't-we don't try to-we don't make decisions about future meetings until we get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think in terms of what we need to see, I mentioned it earlier-we, we want to-we want to gain further confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going to be specific about how many because, you know, really, it's going to be not just the inflation rating-readings-it's going to be the totality of the data: what's happening in the labor market, what's happening with the balance of risks, what's happening with the forecast, what's happening with growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You look at all of that, and you ask, "Are we confident?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Have we reached an appropriate level of confidence that inflation is moving down sustainably to 2 percent, or, alternatively, do we see really unexpected signs of weakness in the labor market that would call for a response?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-we do see today's-we see today's report as, as progress and as, you know, building confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, we don't see ourselves as having the confidence that would warrant-you know, that would warrant beginning to, to loosen policy at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-this happens too often, but it, it does happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just is, you know-data came-I think it happened a couple of meetings ago-a few meetings ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when that happens-when there's an important data print during the meeting, first day or second day- what we do is, we, we make sure people remember that they have the ability to update.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I'm not going to get into the specifics, but you have the ability to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that, you know-what's in the SEP actually does reflect the data that we got today to the extent you can, you know, reflect it in one day.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll know more about the PCE [inflation] reading as the month goes on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the initial CPI reading and its, you know, kind of first-level translation to, to PCE [inflation] we did have this morning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were briefed about it, and people were able to consider whether they should make changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I said, you know, some people generally do, but most people generally don't.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So by, by so many measures, the labor market was, was kind of overheated two years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've seen it gradually move back into much better balance between supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen labor force supply come up quite a bit through immigration and through recovering participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But still, we've had some increases in prime-age labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of on the demand side, you know, we've seen-well, we've seen quits moving down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen wage increases moving from very, very high levels a couple of years ago back down to more sustainable levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have seen unemployment creep up now sixth-tenths over the course of, of a year or so very, very gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you put all that together-what you have is still-low unemployment, still 4 percent unemployment-historically low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's moved up a little bit-it's softened a bit-and, and, you know, that's an important statistic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, but more than that, you've got strong job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You, you have payroll jobs still coming in strong, even though, you know, there's an argument that they may be a bit overstated but still they're, they're still-they're strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we watch the labor market, of course, and the economy as a whole-but the labor market very carefully-and that's what we see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're monitoring it carefully for signs of, of something more than that, but we really don't see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You just have to, have to-have to look at it and, and try to understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why it always makes sense to look at a series, you know, in 6-in 3, 6, and 12 months of things rather than just one report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you're right to point to the last report, where it was your-job losses in the household survey-job gains, big job gains in the establishment survey.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I mean, we're left with ambiguous results, and we have to deal with that uncertainty around data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, the overall picture is one of a strong and gradually cooling-gradually rebalancing labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job openings, while they've come way down, are still, you know, greater than the number of unemployed people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The jobs-workers gap is still a significantly positive number-greater than it was before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, we're looking at what is still a very strong labor market but not the superheated labor market of two years ago or even one year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the inflation forecast moved up several tenths for the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, as I mentioned earlier, in the, you know-what, what did we take away from this?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had really, really good inflation data in the second half of last year, then kind of a pause in progress in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we took away from that was that it's probably going to take longer to get the confidence that we need to begin to loosen policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the sense of that is that rate cuts that might take place in-might've taken place this year-take place next year, you know?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we-there are-there are fewer rate cuts in the median this year, but there's one more next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so you really-if you look at year-end 2025 and '26, you're, you're almost exactly where you would have been, just it-just it's moved later because of that progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll have to see where the data light the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're, we're-the economy has, you know, repeatedly surprised forecasters in both directions, and today was certainly a better inflation report than almost anybody expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll just have to see what, what-what the incoming data flow brings and, and how that affects the outlook and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So two things about that-one, one is this-you're right, it did move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, but I want to remember to point out that the long-run neutral rate of interest is, is a long-run concept.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It, it really is a theoretical concept-can't be directly observed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what it is is the, the interest rate that would hold the economy at equilibrium-maximum employment and price stability-potentially, potentially years in the future where there are no shocks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's- it's a little bit-it's not something we observe today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Today we've got a very specific economy with all kinds of shocks we're still getting over from the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-I, I don't think that the, the concept of r-star-it's a very important concept in economics and in what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, honestly, it doesn't really get you where you need to be to think about what appropriate policy is in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, I-back to your original question, people have been gradually writing it up because I just think people are coming to the view that rates aren't-are less likely to go down to their, their pre-pandemic levels, which were, you know, very low by recent history measures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's an interesting dispute and discussion to have now, but, ultimately, we think that things like the neutral rate are driven by longer-run, slow-moving forces.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there's a really good question about whether, whether those really have changed or whether, instead, rates and the economy are experiencing a, a series of persistent but, ultimately, temporary shocks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in the meantime, we're making policy with the economy that we have-with the distortions that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I also-to your other point, I, I think it is-it is the case that as time has gone by, the question of "How restrictive is policy?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: has become one that everyone's asking, and we're asking it, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, my answer has been that policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question of whether it's sufficiently restrictive is going to be one we, we know over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think for the reasons I've talked about at the last press conference and, and other places, I think the evidence is pretty clear that policy is restrictive and is having, you know, the effects that we would hope for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think this is about, you know, looking at the incoming data and asking, "How much progress are we making on inflation, and how is the rest of the economy doing?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you can-you can translate it into the-into the language you're talking about, but, to me, the focus is more on, we have a goal, which is price stability, and another goal, which is maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think we've got a good, strong labor market still.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think we've been making progress toward the price- stability goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we look at today's thing, and we think, "Well, that's a good reading, and we hope we get more like that."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, in the meantime, we're asking, "Is our policy stance about right?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're prepared to adjust that as appropriate, but we think-we think we're getting the things that we would want to get, broadly speaking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's why we've been at this policy rate now for almost a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, you know, it's been coming-where's it been coming from- let's start with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, clearly a lot of what-some of what we've been getting is just the reversal of the-the unwinding of the pandemic-related distortions to both supply and demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that is, you know-that is complemented by and amplified-supported by restrictive monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've also had a very positive supply shock on the labor side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, also, you get-you get a positive supply shock when the-when the supply conditions unwind and return to normal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you've had, you know, above-trend potential growth and, and high growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And yet you've had the benefit of, of inflation coming down, you know, really fast, actually, last year, and you will see what the rest of this year brinks-brings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So these dynamics can continue as long as they continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, ultimately, the question is, ultimately, are you down to demand?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, if we see more like that-you know, we don't-we can't know what the future holds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in the meantime, we've made pretty good progress on inflation with our current stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think, ultimately, that if you-if you just set policy at a restrictive level, eventually you will see real weakening in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's always been the thought is that, you know, since we raise rates this far, we've, we've always been pointing to cuts at a certain point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not to eliminate the possibility of hikes, but, you know, no one has that as their base case, so-no one on the Committee does.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But so that's, that's-you know, that's how we think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we've been getting is good progress on inflation, with growth at a-at a, a good level and with a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, ultimately, we think rates will have to come down to continue to support that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that's why we're watching so carefully for signs of weakness.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We kind of see what we wanted to see, which was gradual cooling in demand-gradual rebalancing in the labor market while we're continuing to make progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On housing-you know, the housing situation is a complicated one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you can see that's a place where rates are really having, having a significant effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, ultimately, the best thing we can do for the housing market is to bring inflation down so that we can bring rates down so that the housing market can continue to normalize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There will still be a national housing shortage, as there was before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There will still be one, but the distortions that we see now with lock-ins and things like that-you know, low mortgages-in terms of banks, the banking system has been, you know, solid, strong, well capitalized.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had the turmoil earlier last year, but, you know, banks have been focusing on bringing up their liquidity, bringing up their capital, and having a risk-risk-management plans in place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the banking system, you know, seems to be-seems to be in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think it's true that housing-that inflationary pressures have come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know-and I think you can see it in, in various places in-you know, in some parts of, of nonhousing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see elevated inflation still-and that's probably to do with-it could be to do with wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's been a surprising increase in, in import prices on goods, which is kind of hard to understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, may, may-we've taken some signal from that, but, you know-and, and, of course, housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're seeing-you're continuing to see high readings there to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, the labor market has come into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages are still running, you know, I would say, above a, a sustainable path, which would be that of trend inflation and trend productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we haven't thought of wages as being the principal, you know, cause of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But at the same time, getting back to 2 percent inflation is likely to require a return to a more sustainable level, which is somewhat below the current level of increases in the aggregate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if, you know-if you look back in 5 or 10 years and, and try to pull out the significance to the U.S. economy of one 25 basis point rate cut, you'd, you'd have quite a job on your hands.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's not how we look at it-you know, really, the whole rate path matters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I do continue to think that when-you know, when we do start to loosen policy, that will show up in a significant loosening in financial market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the market will price in what it prices in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't-I have no way of saying-we're, we're not at that stage, so I don't know what we'll be thinking about at that time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, you want to-you want to get it right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, fortunately, we have a strong economy, and we, we have the ability to, you know, approach this question carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will approach it carefully while we're very much keeping an eye on, you know, downside economic risks, should they-should they emerge.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we always want to avoid the tendency to dismiss the parts of inflation that we-that we don't like and just make it go away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but we had a quarter where inflation was running higher, and, yes, I could stand here and say, "It's stuff we shouldn't have taken signal from."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you, you have to-you know, low inflation is low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: High-so if you have a quarter where it's higher-we tried not to take signal from the first couple of months, but we got a third month, and we said, "Okay, the signal we're taking is that, you know, we think it's going to take longer to get confidence that inflation is moving sustainably down to 2 percent."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now we have today's inflation reading, which is very different-very much more positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to have to see what the trend is-what's, what's going to be the data going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking for something that gives us confidence that inflation is, is moving sustainably down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And readings like today's, you know-that's a step in the right direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, one reading is-isn't-it just-it's only one reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You don't want to-you don't want to be too motivated by any single data point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, you know-I, I don't think anyone knows-has a definitive answer why people are, are not as happy about the economy as they might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't tell people how they should think or feel about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All I can tell you is what the-what the data show, which is, we've got an economy that's growing at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got a very strong labor market with unemployment at 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been a long time since we've had, you know, a long stretch of time with unemployment at or below 4 percent-very long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-inflation has come down really significantly, and we're doing everything we can to-you know, to bring that inflationary episode fully to a halt and fully restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in the meantime, you know, it's going to be painful for, for people, but the ultimate pain would be a, a period of long, high-a long period of high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is people who-lower-income people-people who are at the margins of the economy who, who have the worst experience-who experience the most pain from inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, it's for those people-for all Americans, but particularly for those people-that we're doing everything we can to bring inflation back down under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, you know, I, I don't have a precise date for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what we said is that we, we want to make sure that we're confident that inflation is actually moving back down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when we are, then we can look at loosening policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So having that kind of confidence that inflation will be at 2 percent just-it just pays benefits to the whole economy, to all Americans, for a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We very much want to get back to a place where people can, can not think about inflation-it's just not a concern in the everyday economic decisions that they make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We were there for a long time, and our goal is to get back to that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've made good progress, and we're just-we're in the phase now of just, you know, sticking with it until we get it done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, encouraging has been that growth-you know, the growth, clearly, that we had last year, particularly the second half of last year, and we continue to see still-strong growth-solid growth this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go back a year, there was a real concern about, you know, very much slowing growth and, and a recession-many forecasters had that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Instead, we-the U.S. is, anyway, and it's in-it's in sharp distinction with many other advanced economies around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say that the, the-today's inflation report is encouraging, but it comes after, you know, several reports that were not so encouraging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You asked about-your second question was really about shelter inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you go back a couple of years-we, we know that there were renters, and then there are, you know, people who own their houses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so when market-based rents go up sharply, as they did at the beginning of the-of the-when the economy reopened, they really went up sharply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those play into rollover rents much more slowly for existing tenants than they do for new tenants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and so what we-so we, we've found now that there are big lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's sort of a-there's a bulge of high past increases in, in market rents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has to get worked off, and that may take, you know, several years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, as long as market rents remain-are going at-up at relatively low levels-and they still are-you know, this, this is just going to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just is going to happen more slowly than we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we also do sort of this thing where we impute a rental value to, to owned homes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-you know, many countries around the world do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's something that the-you know, that the, the price experts have regularly looked at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is not something that we're the only country that does, and it's not something we're looking at changing or would look at changing, you know, anytime soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's one of the very hardest things in, in inflation and in prices is how to think about, you know, the services that someone is getting by living in a home that they could rent, but they're actually living in it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's not our-that's not how we do inflation here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we do it the way we do it, and we've been very transparent about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's true that we're-we're seeing delays in, in realizing what-what's happening economically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we understand that-you know, we understand that very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we monitor all the things you mentioned and more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what we're seeing is, basically, spending was going up faster than disposable income during big parts of next year, so-last year, rather-and so what that-you'd expect to see is people spending more on their credit cards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They couldn't go out to spend money; they could spend money from home.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we see the same data that everybody else sees, but you've still got a household sector that's in-that's in pretty good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know-but, nonetheless, it's not in the kind of shape it was in a year or two ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not growing at the pace it was growing at a year or so ago, but, but it's still-it's still growing solidly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, by the way, other parts of the economy are picking up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Spending on equipment and intangibles is-has picked up quite a bit, you know, in the wake of all the construction that we saw of new tech- you know, tech plants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, the economy is exhibiting solid growth, and, you know- something around 2 percent-which is-which is, you know, good-a good pace of growth for the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we do see the same thing other people see, which is, you know, increasing financial pressures on, you know, more lower-income people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, the best thing we can do is, is to foster a very strong jobs economy, which we think we have done-ultimately to get inflation under control, because those people experience inflation, you know, very directly-very painfully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, once, once we get inflation under control, rates can come down-which, which will also improve things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know-you know, when I say "unexpectedly," the first thing is more than, kind of, is in our forecast or in common forecasts-so, something more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we'll-the, the labor market, you know, has the ability-has, has the tendency sometimes to, to weaken quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So waiting for that to happen is, is not what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're watching very carefully; we're looking at the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I always point out the balance of risks, so-and, and also the fact that we look at, at all of it-the whole situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, a decision to begin to-you know, to loosen policy could have several reasons associated with it at a given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, you know, I would just- you know, we monitor all the-all the labor market data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we saw troubling-weakening more than-more than expected, then that would be something we'd consider responding to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we'd look at the-we look at the broader context of what's going on, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going to-yeah, I mean, I, I can think of things that would- many things would make it on that list, but I don't think I'll, I'll utter them here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I, I don't actually have that kind of mechanical thing in, in my thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I get that, you know-as many good ones as we had bad ones-but it's not like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's going to be the totality of the data-[including] labor market data, the growth data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of inflation, you know, you'd, you'd want to see real progress that builds your confidence that we're-that we are on a path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I don't want to try to give you specific numbers of things, because that points to dates, and I, I just don't think-we're not at a point of being able to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't-actually, it's our-it's our finance ministry, the Treasury Department, that has a responsibility for thinking about and, and, if it sees fit, doing things about the level of the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you're right-the dollar has been-has exhibited, exhibited some strength over the course of the last year or so because the U.S. economy is very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think of it as benefiting or hurting the U.S. We don't-again, we don't manage the level of the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know-and for, for our economy, what, you know, we're trying to foster is maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we feel like we've made good progress on, on both of those goals over the course of the past year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know-so we are-we're well aware of the two-sided risks here, let me just say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we understand that if we wait too long, that could come at the cost of economic activity, of employment, of the expansion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We understand that if we move too, too quickly, we could end up undoing a lot of the good that we've done and have to then start over, and it could be very disruptive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're, we're extremely aware of both of those risks and, and just basically trying to manage them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we said is that we'll-that we're-we don't think it'll be appropriate to, to begin to loosen policy until we're more confident that inflation is moving down to 2 percent over time on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Or there's another test, which is, you know, an unexpected deterioration in labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that's, that's the right way for us to think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got growth-all forecasts are very commonly around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market continues to print jobs at a pretty high rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have the ability now to approach this question carefully, and that's, that's what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's not what we're-that's not our plan is to wait for things to break and then try to fix them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're trying to balance these two goals in a way that is consistent with our framework, and we think we're doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-what, what we've been thinking is that we would announce and commence the review later or late in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, as that time approaches, we will be devoting a lot of careful thought and planning to the contours of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-I'm not going to say that we'll look at this or that particular thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And all the other details, you know-we're just-we don't want to get prematurely into a conversation until it's really time to have it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, you know, I'm going to leave pretty much everything else to, to later in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't-there isn't any one thing-one variable, like housing prices moderating, that would really decide or decide against what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got an overall test, which is greater confidence that inflation is moving down to 2 percent on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Or, alternatively, we see unexpected weakening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, you know, we're not- we're not looking at any one price in any one sector and saying, "That's the one."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we target aggregate prices and overall employment, so- NANCY MARSHALL-GENZER.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if housing prices remain sticky, could that slow down the pace of rate cuts?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you'd look at the over-we'd be looking at the aggregate numbers and, and asking ourselves, "What's going on here with inflation in the-at the aggregate level?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know-and, of course, if, if-any price that contributed to ongoing inflation would, would matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Any price that contributed to ongoing disinflation would matter, too, but I wouldn't single out housing as having a, a special role there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we have made no decisions about future meetings, and that includes the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The broad sense of the Committee is that the economy is moving closer to the point at which it will be appropriate to reduce our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In that, we will be data dependent but not data point dependent, so it will not be a question of responding specifically to one or two data releases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question will be whether the totality of the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks are consistent with rising confidence on inflation and maintaining a solid labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If that test is met, a reduction in our policy rate could be on the table as soon as the next meeting in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would just say, again, that the broad sense of the Committee is that we're getting closer to the point at which it will be appropriate to reduce our policy rate but that we're not quite at that point yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I guess I would-I would think about it this way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll give an example of, of cases in which it would be appropriate to cut and maybe that it wouldn't be appropriate to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if we were to see, for example, inflation moving down quickly or more or less in line with expectations, growth remains, let's say, reasonably strong, and the labor market remains, you know, consistent with its current condition, then I would think that a, a rate cut could be on the table at the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, if inflation were to prove, you know, sticky and we were to see higher readings from inflation, disappointing readings, we would weigh that along with the other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think it's going to be not just any one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's going to be the inflation data, it's going to be the employment data, it's going to be the balance of risks as we see it-it's going to be the totality of all of that that would help us make this decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think it's just a question of seeing more good data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have seen-the last couple of readings have, have certainly added to confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've seen progress across all three categories of core PCE inflation-that's goods, nonhousing services, and housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's really just-you know, we had a quarter of poor inflation data at the beginning of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then we saw some more good inflation data; we had seven months at the end of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we just want to see more and, and gain confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I said, we have-we did gain confidence, and more good data would cause us to, to gain more confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so I would just say, really, the path ahead is going to depend on the way the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I can't really give you any, any better forward guidance on it than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't, of course, do an SEP at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just say, I can-I can imagine a scenario in which there would be everywhere from zero cuts to several cuts, depending on the way the economy evolves, and I wouldn't want to lay out a baseline path for you there today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've said what I-what I can say about September and about today, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is the very reason that we're thinking about-that we've said in our-in our statement that we're going back to looking at both mandates and that we think the risks are coming back into balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think what the data broadly show in the labor market is an ongoing, gradual normalization of labor market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've seen that over a period of a couple of years and a move, really, from overheated conditions to more normal conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are watching the labor market conditions quite closely, and that's what we're seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we-if we start to see something that looks to be more than that, then we're well positioned to respond.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have, we have-growth isn't one of our three.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market, maximum employment is one, and stable prices is another.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we weigh-we weigh those two things equally under the law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we were far away from our inflation mandate, we had to focus on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now we're back, back to a closer to even focus, so we'll be looking at labor market conditions and asking whether we're getting what we're seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I said, we're prepared to respond if we see that it's-that it's not what we wanted to see, which was, you know, a gradual normalization of conditions-if we see more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it wouldn't be any one statistic, although, of course, the unemployment rate is generally thought to be, you know, a single-a good single statistic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we'd be looking at wages, we'd be looking at participation, we'd be looking at all the things-surveys, quits, hires, all of those things-to determine the overall status of the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, again, I think you're back to conditions that are close to 2019 conditions, and that was not an inflationary economy-broadly similar labor markets then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think inflation was actually-core inflation was actually running below 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't think-I don't now think of the labor market in its current state as a likely source of significant inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would-I would not like to see a material further cooling in the labor market, and that's part of what's behind our thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other part, of course, is that we have made real progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're-we've got growing confidence there that we are not quite there yet, but we're more confident that we're on a-that we're on a sustainable path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those two things are working together, and we're factoring those both into our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't say I wouldn't want to see any other cooling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we-if we'd be looking at this and if we see something that looks like a more significant downturn, that would be something that we would-we would have the intention of responding to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in terms of-I don't think of it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think of it as, you know, we're actually in a good place here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're balancing these two risks of, you know, go too soon, and you undermine progress on inflation; wait too long or don't go fast enough, and, and you put at risk the recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's the nature of having two mandates, and I think we-this is how we balance them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a rough balance, but it does feel like, again, the labor market feels like it's in a place where it's just a process of ongoing normalization; 4. percent unemployment is still historically low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we'll just have to see what the data show us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think all of the data points continue to point to kind of the direction we would want to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that was taken as, you know, there was a decline in job openings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Today's ECI reading was a little softer than expected, so that's, that's a good reading.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It shows that wage increases are still at a strong level but that that level continues to come down to more sustainable levels over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's exactly the pattern that we want to be seeing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think the data-the data we've been seeing in the labor market are broadly consistent with that normalization process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, we're closely monitoring to see whether it starts to show signs that it's more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're-we- we've seen significant movement in the labor market, and, you know, we're very mindful of this question of, is it just normalization or is it more?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it's just normalization, but we want to be in a position to, to support the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we actually got to this-we raised rates a year ago at the July meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look at the situation in the economy a year ago, unemployment-sorry, inflation was over 4 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now we've made a lot of progress, and the labor market-I think unemployment was in the 3s, mid-3s, so it's a different economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it's time, it's coming to be time, to adjust that so that we support this continued process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The thing we're trying to do is-you know that we have, we've had this really significant decline in inflation, and unemployment has remained low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is a really unusual and historically, historically unusual and such a welcome outcome for the people we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're thinking about all the time is, how do we keep this going?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think we don't need to be 100 percent focused on inflation because of the progress we've made: 12-month headline at 2½ [percent], core at 2.6.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The job is not done on inflation, but, nonetheless, we can afford to begin to dial back the restriction in our policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what that looks like, I mean, I think most rate-you would think, in a base case, that policy rates would move down from here, but I don't want to try to give specific forward guidance about when that might be, the pace at which it might happen, because I think that's really going to depend on the economy, and that's highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Actually, what we're seeing now is a little better than what we saw last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Last year, as we pointed out late in the year, a whole lot of the progress we saw last year was from goods prices, which were going down at an unsustainable rate, disinflating at an unsustainable rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This has goods prices coming down, but it's also-we're also now seeing progress in the other two big categories: nonhousing services and housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, the thing is, we've only-you've got one quarter of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had seven months of low inflation; you got one quarter of this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say the quality of this is, is higher, and it's good, but so far, it's only a quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, you know, we need to see more to know that we're-to have more confidence that we're on, on a good path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as I mentioned, our confidence is growing because we've been getting good data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And things like the ECI report and, frankly, the softening in the labor market conditions, you know, give you more confidence that the economy's not overheating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't look like an overheating economy, and it looks like an economy that's normalizing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the thing about-if what it is is seasonality, and it could just be- it's very, very hard to, you know, to do appropriate seasonal adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If that's what it is, then that actually implies that, that other months were underreporting too low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at 12 months because that takes all of that out, all those effects out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is so much better than where we were even a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I want to stress that, and we're committed to getting the job-inflation sustainably under 2 percent, but we need to take note of that progress, and we need to weigh the risks to the labor market and the risks to our inflation target now more equally than we did a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I-you know, I think that we've been given an assignment by Congress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is how we serve the American people is by achieving maximum employment and price stability, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so in our, you know, quasi-constitutional document, the Statement on Longer-Run Goals and Monetary Policy Strategy, we look at the two goals, and if one of them is farther away than the other-the two variables, inflation and employment-if one is farther away from its goal than the other, then you, you concentrate on the one that's farther away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you take account of the time to reach the goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, for the last couple of years, the best service we could do to the American people was to focus on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as inflation has come down-and I think the upside risks to inflation have decreased as the labor market has cooled off, and now the labor market has softened-you know, probably the inflation, inflation's probably a little farther from its target than is employment, but I think the downside risks to, to the employment mandate are, are real now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have to weigh all that, and if you think about where that takes us is we have a restrictive policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been the rate we've had in place for a full year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the time is coming-as other central banks around the world are facing the same question-the time is coming at which it will begin to be appropriate to dial back that level of restrictions, restriction so that we may address both mandates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: "Certainty" is not a word that we have in our-in our business.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we get-we get a lot of data between now and September, and it isn't going to be one data read or even two.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's going to be the totality of the data, all of the data, and not just-and then how is that affecting the outlook?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we'll, we'll all look carefully at the employment report, but so much other data coming in and so much happening between now and the September meeting, and we'll, you know, we'll make a judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen some, some tendency to have a narrowing base of job creation in some months going back, but then we've had some months where, where job creation was broader.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, you know, the headline number of jobs has come down, so-but you look at the whole thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you do look at private demand extra carefully, to your point about, about government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll just be looking at, at all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so look, the objective is to balance the two risks, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's the risk of going too soon and the risk of going too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've been-you know, we, we had seven months of good inflation data at the end of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We said-we pointed out that too much of this was coming from goods, and, sure enough, the first quarter wasn't, wasn't great-inflation data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now we've got another quarter-a quarter that is good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're balancing the risk of going too soon against the risk of going too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a very difficult judgment call, but this is-this is how we're making it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but in terms of today, your question about today, we did have a-you know, we had a nice conversation about, about this issue today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The overall sense of the Committee, as I mentioned, is that we're getting closer to the point at which it will be appropriate to begin to dial back restriction, but we're not quite at that point yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there was a real discussion back and forth of what the case would be for, for moving at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the lags have kind of showed up here in the last six months, by the way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You, you really do now see the restriction, whereas, I mean, even a few months ago, people were questioning how restrictive policy was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't say it's extremely restrictive, but it's certainly effectively restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yes, there-the lag should, should be on the way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It should take some time to get into-to get into the full economy, affect financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that affects economic activity, hiring and that kind of thing, and, ultimately, inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't-it's not instantaneous, although it's faster than it used to be because markets move now in anticipation of our moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we-just to make it clear, you know, it's a very difficult, challenging judgment, and we don't want to go too soon, and we don't want to go too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're certainly very well positioned to respond to weakness with the policy rate at 5. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We certainly have a lot of room to respond if we were to see weakness.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're seeing-look at the-look at the first-half growth numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Look at PDFP at 2. percent for the first half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Labor market-admittedly, the unemployment rate has moved up seven-tenths, and we're seeing-we're seeing normalization there, but wage, wage increases are still at a high level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Initial claims have moved up, but they're pretty stable, and they're historically not high at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the total scope of the data suggests a normalizing labor market, and, again, we are carefully watching to see that that continues to be the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We-so I would just say, the question really is, is one of, are we worried about a sharper downturn in the labor market?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and the answer is, we're watching really carefully for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're aware of that rule, which is really a, you know, a-I would call it a statistical, statistical thing that has happened through history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not like an economic rule where it's telling you something must happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at-we look at all the things we're seeing, and what it looks like is a normalizing labor market-again, job creation at a pretty decent level, wages moving up at a strong level but coming down gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job vacancies have come down, but they're still high by historical standards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, I've been through some of the data already, but what we think we're seeing is, is a normalizing labor market, and we're watching carefully to see if it-if it turns out to be more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If it starts to show signs that it's more than that, then we're well positioned to respond.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, history doesn't repeat itself; it rhymes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You never assume it's going to be just the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: An example would be, is there a trend increase in the level of vacancies?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are many, many examples, so it's never exactly the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Also, let's remember that this pandemic era has been one in which so many, you know, apparent rules have been flouted, like the inverted yield curve for starters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, many, many received-pieces of received wisdom just haven't worked, and it's because this situation really is unusual or unique in that so much of this inflation came from the shutdown of the economy and the resulting supply problems in the face of, admittedly, very strong demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the whole-the whole situation is not the same as many of the other prior inflation or downturns that we've seen or business cycles that we've seen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're having to, to be very careful about the judgments that we make, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't assume that these regularities will, will just repeat themselves automatically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do take that seriously, and the Beige Book is great.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's even greater is hearing the Reserve Bank presidents come in and talk about their conversations with, with businesses and business leaders and workers and people in the nonprofit sector in their Districts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I'll tell you, it's a pretty-the picture is, is not one of a slowing or, you know, a really bad economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's one of there are spots of weakness, and there are regions where growth is stronger than other regions, but, overall, it's-again, look at the aggregate data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The aggregate data is-particularly PDFP, private domestic final purchases-is 2. percent, and that's a good indicator of private-of private demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we listen to all of that, and it does, does-I think it's important to listen to anecdotal data and not just look at the aggregate data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Especially, you know, it's very hard-GDP data can be volatile quarter to quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I look at both, but I wouldn't say that the-that the anecdotal data is uniformly downbeat.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I absolutely do, and I think it's-first of all, we haven't made any decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say it this way: haven't made any decision about any future meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know what the data will reveal or how that will affect the appropriate path of our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you take a step back, the current situation, again, is inflation has come down much closer to our goal, and that's happened while unemployment has remained low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're very tightly focused on using our tools to try to foster that state of affairs continuing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's at each of our meetings and all of our decisions, our focus is strictly on that and really on nothing else-doing our part, whatever that part may be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We follow the many commentators who bless us with their commentary [laughter], but we don't change anything in our approach to address other factors, like the political calendar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Congress has, we believe, ordered us to conduct our business in a nonpolitical way at all times, not just some of the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll say this, too: We never use our tools to support or oppose a political party, a politician, or any political outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The bottom line is, if we do our very best to do our part and we stick to our part, that will benefit all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we get it right, the economy will be stronger.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's what we believe, and that's how we will always act.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can tell you this is how we think about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So anything that we do before, during, or after the election will be based on the data, the outlook, and the balance of risks and not on anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't act as though we know, and we just can't do that, you know?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-we can run simulations of different potential policies, but we would never try to make policy decisions based on the outcome of an election that hasn't happened yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would just-that would just be a line we would never cross.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't want to be involved in any-in politics in any way, so we wouldn't do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we talk a lot before, during, and after the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do have a very robust discussion of these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're right that in, in most cases, people, if they feel heard and they feel that they've-that their position has been given serious consideration, for most people, most of the time, that's going to be enough.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No single person has a veto, so it just is a question of, who will vote for and against?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't had so many during the pandemic era, and it just may be that we, we felt more united because we felt under a lot of pressure to get things right, but before the pandemic, we had plenty of dissents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's nothing wrong with dissents, and if it happens, it happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I don't want to say-I don't want to be really specific about what we're going to do, but that's, that's not something we're thinking about right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we haven't made any decisions at all as of today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so, you know, the way the meeting is set up, the first day there's a discussion of financial stability because it's every other meeting we have that, and then we have an opportunity to comment on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, this morning, we have the monetary policy go-round.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think in people's economic or in their monetary policy go-round, people express their views about this, and, you know, there's a range of views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People-as you will know from the speeches that they give-people have different ways of thinking about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, in the minutes, we'll lay this out in a much-in a much better way than I can do off the cuff, but there's a range of perspectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know-but I do think that we are, we're a consensus-driven organization.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, at the end, everyone, everyone supported the outcome-not just the voters, but everyone.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would also say, some people examined the possibility, you know, the case for moving at this meeting, but, overwhelmingly, the sense of the Committee was not at this meeting but as soon as the next meeting, depending on how the data come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, assuming that the totality of the data supports such an outcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that the time is, is- it's approaching, and if we do get the data that we-that we hope we get, then a reduction in our policy rate could be on the table at the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is the judgment that we have to make, and we're, we're well aware of the judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-as I've said, we have to weigh the risk of going too soon against the risk of going too late.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we go too soon, we can-we had a lot of advice, you know, to go ahead and cut after the seven good months of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen one quarter of good inflation, and we've seen the labor market move quite a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, I don't think it needs to cool off anymore for us to get the inflation results that are related to the labor market-not all inflation is, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's a difficult judgment to make, and what you see is the judgment of the Committee is that that time is drawing near.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That time could be in September if, if the data support that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think this is-you don't see any reason to think that this economy is either overheating or sharply weakening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's in the data right now is an economy that's growing at a-at a solid pace, a labor market that has cooled off, but, nonetheless, inflation-sorry, unemployment is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-it's neither an overheating economy, nor is it a sharply weakening economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's kind of what you would want to see, but, of course, the job is never done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're, we're watching to see, you know, which way the economy heads.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we're-if we are to respond to weakness, we're certainly, you know, well equipped to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're seeing is strong economic activity and, you know, a good labor market and inflation coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, I mean, I think the reality is that, that forecasters-and this isn't just the Fed by any means-forecasters have been continually surprised by, for example, the strength of the economy last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we had to be pretty humble about, about giving forward guidance about this, that, and the other thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, when you're saying you're going to be data driven, of course, it's always what the data-how they affect the outlook and the balance of risks, but it's-nobody has great vision deep into the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of a reaction function, that's a-that's a long-time discussion that people have had forever.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think people have understood for a long time, actually, that we were very focused on bringing down inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The data have, you know- again, we've seen significant improvement in inflation just for the last quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not so much-it's not really what we're going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's more just that the data keep coming in, and markets are very, very responsive to that data right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something that comes up at all with the-in the FOMC.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, more broadly, digital finance is an area that's having-that has really significant implications for payments generally, instant payments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's something that's going to really change the way-it's going to make more efficient and, hopefully, safer and all those things- the way payments are made around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we have people who are researching that and trying to keep up to speed, because we play an important role in the payments sector, both as a convener and as an operator, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of a CBDC, there's really nothing new going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-we don't have the authority to issue a CB-a retail CBDC that's available to the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we're doing is keeping up with-keeping up with developments there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Pretty much every major central bank in the world is at least doing, doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some of them are actually seriously looking at implementing a CBDC.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're really just evaluating, you know, the story and what's happening out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's work that we need to be doing, which could be very beneficial down the road, but we don't have-on a CBDC, we don't have any plan to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would need to go to Congress, and we have no plan to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-no one here has decided that we think it's a good idea yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, since the last meeting-okay, the last meeting we have had a lot of data come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've also had two inflation reports, including one that came in during blackout.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had the QCEW report, which suggests that maybe-that not maybe, but suggests that the payroll report numbers that we're getting may be artificially high and will be revised down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've also seen anecdotal data, like [the data collected in] the Beige Book.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we took all of those, and we went into blackout.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we thought about what to do, and we concluded that this was the right thing for the economy, for the people that we serve, and that's, that's how we made our decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A good place to start is the-is the SEP, but let me start with what I said, which was that we're going to be making decisions meeting by meeting based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the SEP, you'll, you'll see that it's, it's a process of recalibrating our policy stance away from where we had it a year ago, when inflation was high and unemployment low, to a place that's more appropriate given where we are now and where we expect to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's nothing in the-in the SEP that suggests the Committee is in a rush to get this done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know, as I mentioned in my remarks, that the actual things that we do will depend on the way the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I would point you to the SEP as just an assessment of where-what the Committee is thinking today-what the individual members, rather, of the Committee are thinking today, assuming that their particular forecasts take-you know, are realized.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it would-the way I would really characterize it is this: I think people write down their estimate, individuals do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think every single person on the Committee, if you asked them, what's your level of certainty around that, they would say there's a wide range where that could fall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are model-based approaches and empirically based approaches that estimate what the neutral rate will be at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that leaves us in a place where we'll be-where we expect, in the base case, to be continuing to remove restriction, and we'll be looking at the way the economy reacts to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that'll be guiding us in our thinking about the question that we're asking at every meeting, which is, is our policy stance the appropriate one?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know-if you go back, we know that the policy stance we adopted in July of 2023 came at a time when unemployment was 3½ percent and inflation was 4. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Today, unemployment is up to 4. percent; inflation's down to a few tenths above 2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we know that it is time to recalibrate our policy to something that is more appropriate given the progress on inflation and on employment moving to a more sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is the beginning of that process I mentioned, the direction of which is toward a sense of neutral, and we'll move as fast or as slow as we think is appropriate in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you have is our individual-accumulation of individual estimates of what that will be in the base case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, if you go back, I talked about this at Jackson Hole, but I didn't address the question of the size of the cut and left it open, and I think we left it open going into blackout.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so there was a lot of discussion back and forth, good diversity of-excellent discussion today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there was also broad support for the decision that the Committee voted on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would add, though, look at the SEP. All 19 of the participants wrote down multiple cuts this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Seven of the-seven of them wrote down three or more and-sorry, 17 of the 19 wrote down three or more cuts, and 10 of the 19 wrote down four or more cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, there is a dissent, and there's a range of views, but there's actually a lot of common ground as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to take it meeting by meeting, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no sense that the Committee feels it's in a rush to do this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We made a good, strong start to this, and that's really, frankly, a sign of our confidence-confidence that inflation is, is coming down toward 2 percent on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To me, the logic of this, both from an economic standpoint and also from a risk-management standpoint, was clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think we're going to go carefully, meeting by meeting, and make our decisions as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, the labor market is actually in solid condition, and our intention with our policy move today is to keep it there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's growing at a solid pace, inflation is coming down, the labor market is in a strong pace, we want to keep it there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do not think-we think this is timely, but I think you can take this as a sign of our commitment not to get behind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's about-we come into this with a policy position that was put in place, as you know, I mentioned, in July of 2023, which was a time of high inflation and very low unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've been very patient about, about reducing the policy rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Other central banks around the world have cut, many of them several times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've waited, and I think that that patience has really paid dividends in the form of our confidence that inflation is moving sustainably under 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that is what enables us to take this, this strong move today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do not think that anyone should look at this and say, "Oh, this is the new pace."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you have to think about it in terms of the base case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so, in the base case, what you see is-look at the SEP, you see cuts moving along.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The sense of this is we're recalibrating policy down over time to a more neutral level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're moving at the pace that we think is appropriate given developments in the economy and the base case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy can develop in a way that would cause us to go faster or slower, but that's what the base case is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in the current situation, reserves have really been stable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So reserves are still abundant and expected to remain so for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, the shrinkage in our balance sheet has really come out of the overnight RRP [facility].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think what that tells you is, we're not thinking about, about stopping runoff because of this at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that these two things can happen side by side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In a sense, they're both a form of normalization, and so, for a time, you can have the balance sheet shrinking but also be cutting rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think what we're seeing is, clearly labor market conditions have cooled off by any measure, as I talked about in Jackson Hole, and-but they're still at a level- the level of those conditions is actually pretty close to what I would call maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're close to mandate, maybe at mandate, on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Clearly, clearly payroll job creation has moved down over the last few months, and this bears watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many- By many other measures, the labor market has returned to or below 2019 levels, which was a very good, strong labor market, but this is more sort of 2018, '17.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the labor market bears close-bears close watching, and we'll be giving it that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But ultimately, we think-we believe, with an appropriate recalibration of our policy, that we can continue to see the economy growing, and that will support the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, if you look at the growth in economic activity data, retail sales data that we just got, second-quarter GDP-all of this indicates an economy that is still growing at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that should also support the labor market over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're-that's-you know, our plan, of course, has been to begin to recalibrate and we're-as you know, we're not seeing rising claims, we're not seeing rising layoffs, we're not seeing that, and we're not hearing that from companies that that's something that's getting ready to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're not waiting for that, because, you know, there is-there is thinking that the time to support the labor market is when-is when it's strong and not when we begin to see the layoffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have, in fact, begun the cutting cycle now, and we'll be watching-and that'll be one of the factors that we consider.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we're going to look at the totality of the data as we make these decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be watching all of the data, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if-as I mentioned in my remarks, if the labor market were to slow unexpectedly, then we have the ability to react to that by, by cutting faster.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also going to be looking at our other mandate, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are more-we have greater confidence now that inflation is moving down to 2 percent, but, at the same time, our plan is that we will be at 2 percent, you know, over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and policy, we think, is still restrictive, so that should still be happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, what I would say is, we don't think we need to see further loosening in labor market conditions to get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we have a dual mandate, and I think you can take this whole action as-take a step back, what have we been trying to achieve?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're trying to achieve a situation where we restore price stability without the kind of painful increase in unemployment that has come sometimes with disinflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think you can take today's action as a sign of our strong commitment to achieve that goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll start with unemployment, which is the single most important one probably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, you know-I know it's higher than we were used to seeing, numbers in the mid- and even below mid-3s last year, but, if you look back over the sweep of the years, that's, that's a low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And anything in the low 4s is, is a really-is a good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, you know-we've had-we're right-adjusted for demographics for aging, participation's at pretty high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages are still a bit above what would be their-wage increases, rather, are still just a bit above where they would be over the very longer term to be consistent with 2 percent inflation, but they're very much coming down to what that sustainable level is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Vacancies over-per unemployed is back to what is still a very strong level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That number reached two to one, two vacancies for every unemployed person.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's still-that's still a very good number, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, quits have come back down to normal levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question isn't the level; the question is that there has been change, particularly over the last few months, and, you know, so what we say is, as the risks, the upside risks, to inflation have really come down, the downside risks to employment have increased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and because we have been patient and held our fire on cutting while, while inflation has come down, I think we're now in a very good position to manage the risks to both of our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we get a-we might, actually- we get two-we get a second jobs report on the day of the meeting, I think, or no, no, on the Friday before the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's always a question of, look at the incoming data and ask what are the implications of that data for the evolving outlook and the balance of risks and then go through our process and think, what's the right thing to do?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Is policy where we want it to be to foster the achievement of our goals over time?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's what it is, and that's what we'll be doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on the job creation, it depends on-it depends on the inflows, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, if you're having millions of people come into the labor force then, and you're creating 100,000 jobs, you're going to see unemployment go up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it really depends on what's the trend underlying the volatility of people coming into the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We understand there's been quite an influx across the borders, and that has actually been one of the things that's, that's, that's allowed the unemployment rate to rise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the other thing is just the slower hiring rate, which is something we also watch carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it does depend on what's happening on the supply side.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
