text: On the Beveridge curve question, yes, so we all felt, on the Committee, not all, but I think everyone on the Committee felt that job openings were so elevated that they could fall a long way before you hit the part of the curve where job openings turned into higher unemployment, job loss.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And yes, I mean, I think we are-it's hard to know that-you can't know these things with great precision, but certainly it appears that we're very close to that point, if not at it, so that further declines in job openings will translate more directly into unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we've seen a lot of, of tightness come out of the labor market in that form without it resulting in lower employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is a question-and you mean after we get through all of this?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just-great question that we just, we can only speculate about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Intuitively, most-many, many people anyway, would say we're probably not going back to that era where there were trillions of dollars of sovereign bonds trading at negative rates-long-term bonds trading at negative rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it looked like the neutral rate was-might even be negative, so-and it was-people were issuing debt at negative rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: My own sense is that we're not going back to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, it feels-it feels to me that the neutral rate is probably significantly higher than it was back then.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so, you know, this is my fourth presidential election at the Fed, and, you know, it's always the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're always-we're always going into this meeting, in particular, and asking, what's the right thing to do for the people we serve?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do that, and we make a decision as a group, and then we announce it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nothing else is discussed, and I would also point out that the things that we do really affect economic conditions for the most part with a lag.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our job is to support the economy on behalf of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, if we get it right, this will benefit the American people significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this really concentrates the mind, and, you know, it's something we all take very, very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if you start doing that, I don't know where you stop.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just say that, you know, the U.S. economy is in a good place, and, and our decision today is designed to keep it there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: More specifically, the economy is growing at a solid pace, inflation is coming down closer to our 2 percent objective over time, and the labor market is still in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our intention is really to maintain the strength that we currently see in the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll do that by returning rates from their high level, which has really been-the purpose of which has been to get inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're going to move those down over time to a more normal level over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So inflation, you know-what we say is we want inflation-the goal is to have inflation move down to 2 percent on a sustainable basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're not really-we're close, but we're not really at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we're going to want to see it be, you know, around 2 percent and close to 2 percent for some time, but we're certainly not doing-we're not saying "mission accomplished" or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I have to say, though, we're encouraged by the progress that we have made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So housing inflation is the-is the one piece that is kind of dragging a bit, if I can say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that market rents are doing what we would want them to do, which is to be moving up at relatively low levels, but they're not rolling over-the leases that are rolling over are not coming down as much and OER is coming in high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we now understand that it's going to take some time for those lower market rents to get into this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, the direction of travel is clear, and as long as market rents remain, you know, relatively low inflation, over time that will show up, just the time it's taking now, several years rather than just one or two cycles of annual lease renewals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-I think we understand that now, but I don't think the outcome is in doubt again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As long as market rents remain under control, the outcome is not as in doubt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say it's-the rest of the portfolio-or of the elements that go into core PCE inflation have behaved pretty well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will get down to 2 percent inflation, I believe, and I believe that, ultimately, we'll get what we need to get out of the housing services piece, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The housing market, it's hard to-it's a game that-the housing market is in part frozen because of lock-in with low rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, because they have a very low mortgage, it would be quite expensive to refinance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As rates come down, people will start to move more, and that's probably beginning to happen already.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But remember, when that happens, you've got a seller, but you've also got a new buyer in many cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not, you know, obvious how much additional demand that would make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the real issue with housing is that we have had, and are on track to continue to have, not enough housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's hard to find-to zone lots that are in places where people want to live.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-all of the aspects of housing are more and more difficult, and, you know, where are we going to get the supply?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is not something that the Fed can, can really fix.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think, as we normalize rates, you'll see the housing market normalize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, ultimately by getting inflation broadly down and getting those rates normalized and getting the housing cycle normalized, that's the best thing we can do for house holders.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then the supply question will have to be dealt with by the market and also by government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right about lags, but I would just point to the overall economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You have an economy that is growing at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at forecasters or talk to companies, they'll say that they think 2025 should be a good year, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's no sense-the U.S. economy is basically fine if you talk to market participants, I mean, you know, business people who are actually out there doing business.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, you know, I think our move is timely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I said, you can-you can see our, our 50 basis point move as a commitment to make sure that we don't fall behind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're really asking about-your second question, you're asking about July.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I guess if you ask if we'd gotten the July report before the meeting, would we have cut?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't make that decision, but we might well have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that's not-you know, that doesn't really answer the question that we ask ourselves, which is, let's look, you know-at this meeting we're looking back to the July employment report, the August employment report, the two CPI reports, one of which came, of course, during blackout, and all of the other things that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're looking at all of those things, and we're asking ourselves, what's the right-what's the policy stance we need to move to?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We knew-it's clear that we-clearly, literally, everyone on the Committee agreed that it's time to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just how big-how fast do you go, and what do you think about the paths forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this decision we made today had broad support on the Committee, and I've discussed the path ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-from our standpoint, I can't really speak to mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say that'll depend on how the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our intention, though, is-we think that our policy was appropriately restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that it's time to begin the process of recalibrating it to a level that's more neutral, rather than restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We expect that process to take some time, as you can see in the projections that we released today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as-if things work out according to that forecast, other rates in the economy will come down as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: However, the rate at which those things happen will really depend on how the economy performs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We can't see-we can't look a year ahead and know what the economy is to be doing-going to be doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, what I can say to the public is that we had the highest-we had a burst of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many other countries around the world had a similar burst of inflation, and, when that happens, part of the answer is that we raise interest rates in order to cool the economy off in order to reduce inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something that people experience as pleasant, but, at the end, what you get is low inflation restored, price stability restored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And a good definition of price stability is that people in their daily decisions, they're not thinking about inflation anymore.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's where everyone wants to be, is back to what's inflation, you know?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we're going through now really restores-it will benefit people over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Price stability benefits everybody over a long period of time, just by virtue of the fact that they don't have to deal with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's what's been going on, and I think we've made real progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I completely-we don't tell people how to think about the economy, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, people are [still] experiencing high prices, as opposed to high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're always going to try to do what we think is the right thing for the economy at that time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we will continue to look at that broad array of labor market data, including the payroll numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we'll certainly look at those, but we will mentally tend to adjust them based on the QCEW adjustment, which you referred to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it will be-the unemployment rate's very important, of course, but there isn't a single statistic or single bright line over which that thing that might move that would dictate one thing or another.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll look at-each meeting, we'll look at all the data on inflation, economic activity, and the labor market, and we'll make decisions about, is our policy stance where it needs to be to foster over the medium term our mandate goals?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I can't-I can't say we have a bright line in mind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So countries that are-democracies around the world, countries that are sort of like the United States, all have what are called independent central banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason is that people have found over time that insulating the central bank from direct control by political authorities avoids making monetary policy in a way that favors maybe people who are in office as opposed to people who are not in office.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's the idea, is that- you know, I think the data are clear that countries that have independent central banks, they get lower inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're, we're not-we do our work to serve all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not serving any politician, any political figure, any cause, any issue, nothing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just maximum employment and price stability on behalf of all Americans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's how the other central banks are set up, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a good institutional arrangement, which has been good for the public and I hope-and I hope and strongly believe that it will continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the answer to your question is that, yes, those, those changes were negotiated between the agencies with my support and with my involvement, with the idea that we were going to re-propose, re-propose the changes that Vice Chair Barr talked about and then take comment on them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't have a-we don't have a calendar date for that, and, as for the other agencies, you know, the idea is that we're all moving together, we're not moving separately, so that-I don't know exactly where that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the idea is that we will move as a group to put this, again, out for comment, and then, you know, it'll-the comments will come back 60 days later, and we'll dive into them, and we'll try to bring this to a conclusion sometime in the first half of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I would-I would bounce that question to Vice Chair Barr.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a good question, but I don't have that today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, I think-I think, and we think, they are now roughly balanced.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you go back for a long time, the risks were on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was a severe labor shortage, so very hot labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, that said to us, concentrate on inflation, concentrate on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we did for a while, and we kept at that, that the stance that we put in place 14 months ago was a stance that was focused on bringing down inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of bringing down inflation, though, is cooling off the economy and a little bit cooling off the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You now have a cooler labor market, in part because of our activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what that tells you is, it's time to change our stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The sense of the change in the stance is that we're recalibrating our policy over time to a stance that will be more neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And today was-I think we made a good strong start on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it was the right decision, and I think it should send a signal that we, you know, that we're committed to coming up with a good outcome here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't-there's-as I look-well, let me look at it this way: I don't see anything in the economy right now that suggests that the likelihood of a recession-sorry, of a downturn is elevated, okay?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see-you see growth at a solid rate, you see inflation coming down, and you see a labor market that's, that's still at very solid levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say that in the near term, the election will have no effects on our policy decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, many, many things affect the economy, and anyone who writes down forecasts in their job will tell you that the economy is quite difficult to forecast, looking out past the very near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Here, we don't know what the timing and substance of any policy changes will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We therefore don't know what the effects on the economy would be-specifically, whether and to what extent those policies would matter for the achievement of our goal variables: maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't-we don't guess, we don't speculate, and we don't assume.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, just in principle, it's possible that any Administration's policies or, or policies put in place by Congress could have economic effects over time-over time that would matter for our pursuit of our dual-mandate goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, we-along with countless other factors, forecasts of those economic effects would be included in our models of the economy and would be taken into account through that channel.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've watched the, the run-up in bond rates, and it's, it's nowhere where it was, of course, a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess that, you know, the long- run rates are well below that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Things have been moving around, and we'll see where they settle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's too early to really say where they settle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, I'm sure we've all read these decompositions of what, you know-and I certainly have, but it's not really our job to provide our specific decomposition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, though, that it appears that the moves are not, not principally about higher inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're really about a sense of more likely to have stronger growth and perhaps less in the way of downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If they-if they're persistent and if they're material, then we'll certainly take them into account in our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say we're not at-we're not at that stage right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, these things don't really have mainly to do with, with Fed policy, but to do with other factors in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-you get halfway through the cycle between the last set and the next set.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I wouldn't want to comment one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, people are-let's talk about the data we've gotten since the last meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in the main, the economic activity data have been stronger than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Certainly, the September employment report was stronger; the October report, not stronger; retail sales, stronger.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, though, I think you take away a sense of, of some of the downside risks to economic activity having, having been diminished, with the NIPA revisions in particular, and so, overall, feeling, feeling good about economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we got one inflation report, which was-it wasn't terrible, but it was- it was a little higher than expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, by December we'll have-we'll have more data: I guess one more employment report, two more inflation reports, and lots of other data, and, you know, we'll make a decision as we get to December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't fill out a-we don't fill out an SEP, and I can't characterize one that wasn't filled out today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I can't really speak for kind of exactly where the-where the Committee is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just say, for December, we're going to be-again, in every meeting-we're going to be looking at the incoming data and how that affects the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, we're in the process of recalibrating from a fairly restrictive level at 5. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're, we're asking ourselves, "Is that where we need to be?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know that we're, we're trying to steer between the risk of moving too quickly and perhaps undermining our progress on inflation or moving too slowly and allowing the labor market to weaken too much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're trying to, to be on a middle path where we can maintain the strength in the labor market while also enabling further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that's where we are, but that's the question we're going to be asking in September and, and in other meetings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, I can't really update you on the Committee's thinking, because we don't fill out an SEP at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I'm going to wait-we're going to wait and see how things come in in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I-it's just-I would put it this way: We're on a path to a more neutral stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're just going to have to see where the-where the data lead us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have, you know, a whole six weeks of data to look at to make that decision in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Obviously, I'm not ruling it out or in, but, but, you know, I would say-you know, I would say that, you know, again, we didn't update the SEP, so I'm not going to characterize, you know, where the Committee would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the test of gaining further confidence was a-was our test for the first rate cut, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we, we met that test in September, and therefore we take that test out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you leave it in, then it's new forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to say "yes" or "no" at every meeting whether we've made further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The point is we have gained confidence that, that we're on a sustainable path down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that, I would tell you, is, is what that's really all about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Neither of those is meant to send a further signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, saying "further progress" it becomes a test where we don't want to be-we don't think it's a good time to be doing a lot of, of forward guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're-there's a fair amount of uncertainty in that-in what I've said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The path that we're on, we do know what-where the destination is, but we don't know the right pace, and we don't know exactly where the destination is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-the-the point is to find that, to find the right pace and the right destination as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think there's a fair amount of uncertainty about that, and, you know, you don't want to tie yourself up with, with guidance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You want to be able to make sensible decisions as you go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't comment on fiscal policy, and, again, I don't have a lot more to say on, on what's driving bond yields.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of, of policy changes, though, let me give you a sense of how this, this works in the ordinary case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let's say Congress is considering a rewrite of the tax laws; it doesn't matter what's in the content.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At a certain point, we'd, we'd think we see the outline, so we'd start to model it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we'd wait, and we'd wait, and, at a certain point, the staff would brief the FOMC and say, you know, "This is-these are the likely effects."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's lots and lots of literature on the effects of tax policy changes on various parts of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then the law actually passes, and, you know, you'd start to put it-you'd probably run an alternative simulation before that happens, just to keep people trying to understand it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then, then when it actually passes, it goes into the model, along with a million other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, a law change of some kind would go in there, but-it would go in, but it would-you know, it's a process that takes some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, the real question is not the effect of that law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's the net effect and, you know, the overall effect on the economy at any given time?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think that's a-that's a process that takes a lot of time and that we go through all the time with every Administration, constantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, right now, we're-there's nothing to-there's nothing to model right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know what the policies are, and once we know what they are, we won't-we won't have a sense of, you know, when they'll be implemented or, or all those sorts of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: -we're not doing that now, and all that will take time, and it will be very much regular order when we do do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-look, I just think-the first question is, how long will they be sustained?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you remember the 5 percent 10-year, people were drawing massively important conclusions only to find, you know, three weeks later that the 10-year was 50 basis points lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, it's material changes and financial conditions that last, that are persistent, that really matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're doing the decompositions and reading others, but right now it's not a major factor in, in how we're thinking about things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, and as you mentioned, the latest economic data have been strong, and that's, of course, a great thing and highly welcome.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, of course, our mandate is maximum for employment and price stability, and we think that even with today's cut, policy is still restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We understand it's not possible to say precisely how restrictive, but we feel that it is still restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look at our goal variables, the labor market has cooled a great deal from its overheated state of two years ago and is now essentially in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is continuing to cool, albeit at a-at a modest rate, and we don't need further cooling, we don't think, to achieve our inflation mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation has moved down a great deal from its higher-its highs of two years ago, and we judged, as I mentioned, that it's on a sustainable path back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look at those two things, we judged in September that it was appropriate to begin to recalibrate our policy stance to reflect this progress, and today's decision is really another step in that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Overall, as I mentioned, we believe that with an appropriate recalibration of our policy stance, we can maintain strength in the labor market even as our policy stance enables further progress toward our inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we haven't, you know, made any decision like that at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're-so we're in the process, as I mentioned, of moving policy down-our stance down over time to a more neutral level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as a general matter, as we move ahead, we are prepared to adjust our assessments of the appropriate pace and destination as the outlook evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, for example, if we were to see the labor market deteriorating, we'd be prepared to move more quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Alternatively, as we approach levels that are plausibly neutral or close to neutral, it may turn out to be appropriate to slow the pace at which we're dialing back restriction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, haven't made any decisions about that, but that's certainly a possibility.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you- you can think of it as similar to what we do with asset purchase-with asset runoff with QT.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we reach a point where we slow the pace, much like an airplane reaching the airport slows down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, you know, it-we're thinking about it that way, but it's, it's something that we're just beginning to think about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so I think if you look at the 3- and 6-month-you're quoting the 12-month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look at three- and six-month core PCE, you'll see they're around 2. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we look at-we also-we look at 12 as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what it's telling us is that we really have made significant progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For example, you know, the, the last three months of last year, the core PCE readings were very, very low-probably unsustainably low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's why you see-that's why forecasts generally see a couple of upticks toward the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other hand, the January reading certainly looks like an example of residual seasonality, so that we saw last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when that falls out of the 12-month calculation in February, we should see it staying down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there will literally be a bump up and then down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Overall, you see the progress on inflation, and you also look at the economy, and you say, "What's-what is the inflation story now?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One is the nonhousing services and goods, which together make up 80 percent of that- of the core PCE index, are back to the levels they were at the last time we had sustained 2 percent inflation, which happens to be in the early 2000s for a period of five, six, seven years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's going on there is, you know, market rents, newly signed leases, are experiencing very low inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what's happening is older, you know, leases that are turning over are taking several years to catch up to where market, market leases are-market rent leases are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not really reflecting current inflationary pressures; it's reflecting past inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other thing is, I'd say look at the labor market-not a source of inflationary pressures.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see that catch-up inflation also in insurance and in several other areas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're seeing-we're not, not declaring victory, obviously, but we feel like the story is very consistent with inflation continuing to come down on a bumpy path over the next couple of years and settling around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That story is intact, and it won't be one or two really good data months, or bad data months aren't going to really change the pattern at this point, now that we're this far into the process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nothing in the economic data suggests that the Committee has any need to be in a hurry to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are seeing ongoing strength in the labor market; we're watching that carefully, but we do see maintaining strength there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we think that the right way-the right way to find neutral, if you will, is carefully, patiently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, that's not meant to have a specific meaning other than we-to the extent-to the extent the economy remains strong, we have the ability to, to take advantage of that as we try to navigate that middle path between the two risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on your first question, I'm not going to talk about anything that relates directly or indirectly to the election.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the second one, you're-you know, this is the great question, and it's the one we think about all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we know is that the unemployment rate is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also know that it's come down significantly-sorry, moved up significantly from a year or so ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It appears that the-I wouldn't say that the labor market has fully stabilized, because I do think it's continuing to very gradually cool, but it seems to be in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And our policy, of course, is designed to keep it in that good place, to maintain the strength in the labor market, while also enabling further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you mentioned a bunch of, of indicators, and you're right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the openings to unemployment rate is back to a normal level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages are still running just a bit above where they would need to be to be consistent with 2 percent inflation, unless productivity is going to remain at this high level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we see the-if we see productivity, you know, more sustainably at these high levels, then that would sustain higher wage gains.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say-in fact, you can say it the other way, that, that wage increases are now consistent with 2 percent inflation given current productivity readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, of course, you know, the lore on productivity readings is whenever you see high readings, you should assume they're going to revert pretty quickly to the longer-term trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, it may be that-we're now five years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the NIPA revisions that came out a month ago, we're five years into, into a nice set of productivity readings, which are sustained and very healthy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we don't want the labor market to, to soften much from here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think we need that to happen to get inflation back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's hard to characterize a, you know, really interesting set of discussions we had, and, of course, you'll see them in the minutes in three weeks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, the comments from our Reserve Bank colleagues and from the CEOs that they talk to are pretty constructive on the economy right now-pretty constructive, feeling that the labor market is, is, you know, back to normal to the point where it's no longer that much of a discussion topic in their world, whereas two years ago, it was all they were talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, you're seeing, what, 2. percent growth in the third quarter estimated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's actually remarkable how well the U.S. economy has been performing with, you know, strong growth, a strong labor market, inflation coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, you know, really performing better than any of our global peers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that is reflected in what you hear from-what I hear people hear from CEOs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't get to talk to a lot of CEOs in my job, but I hear what others summarize from those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, I hear the Reserve Bank presidents do a lot of that, and it's pretty constructive overall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, that's not to say-there are areas of caution and things like that but, ultimately, overall pretty positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's-you know, it's things like-clearly, geopolitical risks around the world are elevated, and just as clearly, they've had relatively little effect on the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, that can change through the price of oil or otherwise, but people talk about those as, you know, something that's on the horizon all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, ultimately, if you look at the U.S. economy, its, its performance has been very good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's what we hear from businesspeople, an expectation that that will continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If anything, people feel next year-I've heard this from several people-that next year could even be stronger than this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, I have said many times no more, no less than what the predecessors you mentioned have said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what that is is that the U.S. fiscal-federal government's fiscal path-fiscal policy is on an unsustainable path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The level of our debt relative to the economy is not unsustainable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, you've got a very large deficit at-you're at full employment, and that's expected to continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's important that we-you know, that that be dealt with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I was not referring to, to the new Administration's policies at all, nor will I today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-what I'm just saying is, as we look ahead, we know-and I mentioned this in my statement-that the risks are two sided.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess I should start by saying that we think that the economy and we think our policy are both in a very good place, a very good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but as you look forward, you say, "What are the risks?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And one risk is that we would move too quickly and find ourselves having moved too quickly, and inflation comes back, and we-and we lost our chance to get inflation back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, that-to avoid that risk, that means you want to move carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other risk is that we move too slowly and that we allow the labor market to weaken too much and do unnecessary damage to the labor market and to people's working lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So these are two-these two things are the two risks that we have to manage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We try to be in the middle and deal with both of the-manage both of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, the idea is to maintain support, the strength that we have in the labor market and in the economy, but also with somewhat less restrictive but still restrictive policy, enable further progress toward our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so there's-you know, there- this is the thing: Meeting by meeting, we're going to be making our assessment of what the right path is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's not as important-the precise timing of these things is not as important as the overall arc of them, and the arc of them is to move from where we are now to a sense of neutral, a more neutral policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know exactly where that is; we only know it by its works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as we move further, there will be more uncertainty about where that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to move carefully as, as this goes on so that, you know, we can increase the chances that we will get it right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we would be concerned if we saw-if we thought we saw longer-term inflation expectations anchoring at a higher level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're still seeing between surveys and market readings broadly consistent with-you know, I, I looked at the five-year, five-year earlier today, and it's probably moved, but it's just not-it's just-it's kind of right where it's been, and also it's pretty close to consistent with 2 percent PCE inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's one that's been a traditional one that we look at a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, overall, expectations seem to be-and really have throughout this-in a place that's consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you're right to say we watch that very carefully, and we will not allow inflation expectations to drift upward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's, that's really why we reacted so sharply back in 2022 was, was to avoid that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right that, you know, we say that the economy is performing well, and it is, but we also know that people are still feeling the effects of high prices, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we went through-the world went through a global inflation shock, and inflation went up everywhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it, it stays with you because the price level doesn't come back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what that takes is it takes some years of real wage gains for people to feel better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we're well on the road to creating that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages are moving up but, but at a sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's just-I think-I think what needs to happen is happening and, for the most part, has happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it'll be some time before people, you know, regain their confidence and feel that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we don't tell people how to-how to feel about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And just a quick follow-up-President-elect Trump has been critical of your performance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going-I'm not going to get into the-any of the political things here today, but thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's a-you know, the whole plan is not to have stagflation, so we don't have to deal with it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: [Laughter] You know, it's, of course, a very difficult thing because you're-you know, you're-anything you do with interest rates will, will hurt one side or the other, either the inflation mandate or the-or the employment mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would just say that, you know, we've, we've been able to see inflation come down a whole lot, you know, much closer to our goal without the kind of sharp increase in unemployment that has often accompanied programs of disinflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So knock on wood, we've gotten this far without seeing a real weakening in, in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we believe we can complete the inflation task while also keeping the labor market strong, and that, of course, is exactly what we're trying to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Can you rule out an interest rate hike next year?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't rule anything out or in that far away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, our baseline expectation is that we'll continue to move gradually down towards neutral, that the economy will continue to grow at a healthy clip, and that the labor market will remain strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at our-look at our-that will not change from the September SEP. You know, that is our baseline forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, short of some exogenous event, it will-that will continue to be our forecast for the foreseeable future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So- but, ultimately, you know, it's-we're not in a-we're not in a world where we can afford to rule, rule things out a full year in advance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-we do not have-we do not think it would be appropriate to deliberately undershoot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, part of the problem there is that low inflation can be a problem, too, in a way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's not part of our framework, and it's not something we're going to be-going to be looking at in our framework review.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so let, let me start by saying why we-why we cut today and then-and then move to 2025.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say today was a-was a closer call, but we decided it was the right call because we thought it was the best decision to foster achievement of both of our goals, maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see the risks as two-sided: moving too slowly and needlessly undermine economic activity and the labor market, or move too quickly and needlessly undermine our progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're trying to steer between those two risks, and, on balance, we decided to go ahead with a further cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Downside risks to the labor market do appear to have diminished, but the labor market is now looser than pre-pandemic, and it's clearly still cooling further, so far in, in a gradual and orderly way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think we need further cooling in the labor market to get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job creation is now well below the level or certainly below the level that would hold unemployment constant, the job-finding rate is low and declining, and other measures-such as surveys of workers and businesses, quits, things like that-broadly show a, a much cooler labor market than there was, than we had in 2019.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation, we see that story as still broadly on track, and, and I'll tell you why.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Twelve-month core inflation, as I mentioned, through November is estimated at 2. percent, down from a high of 5. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Twelve-but 12-month inflation has actually been moving sideways, as we are "lapping" very low readings of late last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Housing services inflation actually is steadily coming down now, albeit at a slower pace than we might like, but it has now come down substantially and it is making progress, slower than hoped.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we, we've had recent high readings from nonmarket services and some bumpiness for goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'll just say, we, we-so remember that we couple this decision today with the "extent and timing" language in the postmeeting statement that signals that we are at or near a point at which it will be appropriate to slow the pace of further adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think that the lower-the slower pace of cuts for next year really reflects both the higher inflation readings we've had this year and the expectation that inflation will be higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw in the SEP that risks and, and uncertainty around inflation we see as higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, we, we see ourselves as, as still on track to continue to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the actual cuts that we make next year will not be because of anything we wrote down today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's just the general sense of what the Committee thinks is likely to be appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're-to, to cut further after this point, I, I would say it this way: We've reduced our policy rate now by 100 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At 4. percent and "change," we believe policy is still meaningfully restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as for additional cuts, we're going to be looking for further progress on inflation as well as continued strength in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as long as the economy and the labor market are solid, we can be cautious about-as we consider further cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And all of that is reflected-to your question-in the December SEP, which shows a median forecast of down [to] two cuts next year, compared to four in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I'd say-I'd, I'd point to five or six things, and, and I'd start-let me start by saying that we think the economy's in a really good place, and we think policy's in a really good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let's remember that the economy's growing 2½ percent this year, that inflation has come down by 50 percent to, to-from 5. percent to 2. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But since, you know-so, so what's really driving the, the slower rate-cut path?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, the economy grew faster in the second half of 2024, so far, than we had expected and is expected to be above what our expectations in September next year as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Unemployment is lower, and, you know, in the SEP, you'll see that participants think that the-that the downside risks are less and uncertainty is less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'd also point out that we're, we're closer to the neutral rate, which is another reason to be cautious about, about further moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And-but then getting to your-to your point, there's also, there's uncertainty-uncertainty around inflation, I pointed out, is actually higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also-it's also, in the case of some people, some people-the way I'd say it is this: Some people did take a very preliminary step and start to incorporate highly conditional estimates of economic effects of policies into their forecast at this meeting and said so in the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some people said they didn't do so, and some people didn't, didn't say whether they did or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have people making a bunch of different approaches to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But some did identify policy uncertainty as one of the reasons for their, their writing down more uncertainty around inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the point of that uncertainty is, it's kind of commonsense thinking that when the path is uncertain you go a little bit slower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not unlike driving on a foggy night or walking into a dark room full of furniture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that may have affected some of the people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as, as I said, there's a range of-range of approaches on the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's happened is that our forecast for inflation for this year, I think, are five-tenths higher than they were in September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you've got-you had two months of higher inflation, September and October.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, once again we've, you know, we've had a year-end projection for inflation and it's kind of fallen apart as we've approached the end of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is certainly a large factor in people's thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can tell you that might be the single biggest factor is inflation has once again underperformed relative to expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's still, you know, going to be between 2½ and 3 [percent].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we really want to see progress on inflation, to, to, you know, as I mentioned, as we think about further cuts, we're going to be looking for progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have been moving sideways on 12-month inflation as the 12-month window moves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's in part because inflation was very, very low measured in, in the 4th quarter of 2023.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, as we go forward, we're going to want to be seeing further progress on bringing inflation down and keeping a solid labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I do think that the 2018, the September 2018 Tealbook alternative simulations are a good place to start.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I happened to have brought them here with me today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're, they're a good starting point, and, and I would just say, you know, it's six-years-old analysis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But nonetheless, this is still, I think, I think the right, the right questions to ask.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there, there were two simulations: one was-one was "seeing through," one was not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I point you to, you'll- there's some language in the-in the "see- through" paragraph.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It says, you know, it considers situations in which it might be appropriate to "see through" inflation and then, and then names some conditions that in, in which it might not be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In any case, this is not a question that's in front of us right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we won't face that question-we don't know when we'll face that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What the Committee's doing now is, is discussing pathways and understanding, again, the ways in which tariff-driven inflation can affect-tariffs can affect inflation and the economy, and, and how to think about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, we're, we're-we've done a bit of, good bit of work, all of us have, each of us has, and, you know, it puts us in position, when we finally do see what the, what the actual policies are, to be, to make, you know, a more, more careful, thoughtful assessment of what might be the appropriate policy response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the, the main thing is-and this is also a point in these alternative simulations-is that there're just many, many factors that go into what, what-how much tariffs will, will even go into consumer inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, so, we just-we just don't know, really, very much at all about the actual policies, so it's very premature to try to make any kind of conclusion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know what'll be tariffed, from what countries, for how long, and what size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know whether there'll be, you know, retaliatory tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know what the, you know, the transmission of any of that will be into consumer prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To your-to your point as well, I don't-I wouldn't say that we know whether the last episode is or is not a good model for what happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You pointed out we've just been through a period of high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was also quite a bit of diversion of trade away from China to other countries, since that, that may-that may have affects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just think we, we need to take our time, not rush, and make a very careful assessment, but only when we've actually seen what the policies are and how they're implemented.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're just-we're just not at that stage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're at the stage of doing what other forecasters are doing-which is kind of thinking about these questions, but not, not trying to get to definitive answers for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have-we have inflation coming down, core inflation coming down to 2½ [percent] next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that does take on board that we want to see real progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, we, you know, we'd be seeing meaningful progress to get inflation down to that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That wouldn't be all the way to 2 percent, but that would be, it would be, you know, better than this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we also have to think about the, the, you know, the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And while we, we have the labor market forecast as being in good shape, we are also mindful that it is still out there very gradually cooling, so far in an orderly, gradual way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's also something we need to keep our eye on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's not the-that's not any decision that we've made at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the, the sense of that wording is to make clear that if the economy does evolve about as anticipated, we're at a point at which it would be appropriate to slow the pace of rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So "extent," that just relates to how, how much further we can reduce our policy rate consistent with getting to a neutral stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we're going to be looking for further progress on inflation, as well as a strong labor market, to make those cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: "Timing" just suggests, again, that we're at a place where we, we, assuming the economy develops as expected, we're at or near a level that will make it appropriate to slow the pace of adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not trying to make decisions about the longer run.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we are, we're trying to make sensible policy as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I just would emphasize the uncertainty, which is, it's just-it's just a function of the fact that, that we expect significant policy changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we need to, we need to see what they are and see what the effects they will have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll, we'll have a much clearer picture, I think, you know, when that happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the, the risks that you-sorry, the rates that you talked about are, are really longer-run rates, and they're affected, they are affected to some extent by Fed policy, but they're also affected by many other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And longer rates have actually gone up quite a bit since September, as, as you well know, and those are the things that drive, for example, mortgage rates more than short-term rates do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at that, but we look at all financial conditions, and then we look at what's happening in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we see happening in the economy, again, is, you know, most forecasters have been calling for a slowdown in growth for a very long time, and it keeps not happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have-we're now well into another year of growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Third and-second and third quarters were right about at the same level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the U.S. economy is just performing very, very well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I-there's no reason to think a downturn is, is any more likely than it-than it usually is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to stay on task, though, and continue to have restrictive policies so that we can get inflation down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're also going to be looking out for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to keep the labor market pretty close to where it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're pretty close to estimates of the, the natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job creation is, is a little below the, the level that would keep it there but, nonetheless, close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So confidence was our test for raising rates, and, you know, we've made-look, look at the broader suite: We've made just a great deal of progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, you know, we're well into the 2's in, in core inflation and around 2½ [percent]-or even lower than that, we have been-for headline inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I would say I'm confident that inflation has come down a great deal, and I, I'm confident in the story about why it's come down and why that portends well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You, again, you do see with housing services inflation, which is one that we've really worried, worried about, it really has come down now quite steadily, at a slower pace than we thought, you know, two years ago, but it's nonetheless steadily coming down as, as market rents, you know, market rents start to equilibrate better with, you know, new leases that turn over.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that, that's happening; that process is ongoing pretty much as we expect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Goods inflation, which is another big piece of it, has returned right to the range where it was before the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Just for some months this year it kind of moved up in a bumpy way because of used cars and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we think, overall, that should generally be in the range it was in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then that leaves nonhousing services, and market-based nonhousing services are in, in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's nonmarket services, and those are-those are services that are imputed rather than measured directly, and they, they don't, we, we think they don't really tell us much about the, you know, about tightness in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, a good example is financial services, which is really done off of asset prices, and that just-so that, that's how that inflation works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the overall picture, the story of why inflation should be coming down, is still intact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it is cooler by so many measures now-modestly cooler than it was in 2019, a year when inflation was well under 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not to say there aren't regional and, and, you know, particular professions where labor is tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, overall, you're not getting inflationary impulses of any significance from the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The story is still just, we're unwinding from these large shocks that the economy got in 2021 and '22 in, for example, housing services, and now also in, in insurance, in particular, where costs went up, and those are now being reflected later in housing insurance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's real inflation, but it doesn't portend persistently high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we and most other forecasters still feel that we're on track to, you know, to get down to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It might take another year or two from here, but I, I'm confident that that's the path we're on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, our policy will do everything it can to assure that that is the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the unemployment rate has now-is now the same as it was in July: 4. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's moved up and down, but it's now the same as July.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And job creation is, is lower than it has been, but it's been-it's been steady-it's not-it's not declining.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been steady at a level which, as I pointed out a couple times, is actually below the level that would hold the unemployment rate constant, but it's not so far below.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you might-you might-if, if we have the, the breakeven level right, and if jobs continue-job creation continues at that level in the establishment survey, then you would get a tenth maybe every other month kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we don't have that kind of precision in this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, but you're right, though, and I, I read out some of the reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we do think the labor market is still cooling by many measures, and we're watching that closely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's not cooling in a-in a quick or in a way that really raises concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, you pointed out participants in the FOMC really thought that the risks and uncertainty had improved relative to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's because of, because things have just gotten a little bit better, it doesn't-the unemployment rate flat and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I-what I said is, we don't think we need further softening to get to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, if you had a situation where inflation's moving around by a tenth every few months, that's, you know, we'd have to weigh that against the fact that inflation has in recent months been moving sideways in the 12-month window.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we've got to weigh them both, at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, for a while there we were only really focused mainly, mainly focused on, on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've now gotten to a place where, where the risks of the two are what we think are broadly, roughly in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, no, I, I would say we, we are, though, in, in a new phase in the process, as I said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and that's just because we've reduced-we've reduced our policy rate by 100 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We still think where we are is meaningfully, meaningfully restrictive, and I think from this point forward, you know, it's appropriate to move cautiously and look for progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've, you know, we've done a lot to support economic activity by cutting 100 basis points, and that's a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think it would-I support the decision, and, and I think it was the right decision to make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think from now we are in a place where the risks really are in balance, and we need to see progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We moved pretty quickly to get to here, and I think going forward, obviously, we're going to be moving slower, which is consistent with, with the SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, yeah, we always try to be careful about not throwing out the numbers we don't like, you know?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just a, an occupational hazard is, is to [say], "Look, those high months are wrong."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've got, we have a very low month, potentially, in November.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's estimated by many to be in the mid-teens for core PCE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We try to look-we try to look at not just a couple or three months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We shouldn't have-our, our position shouldn't change based on two or three months of good or bad data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have a long string now of inflation coming down gradually over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, 12-month, I think it's 12-month headline's 2½; 12-month core is 2.8.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We still have some work to do, though, is how we're looking at it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we need policy to remain restrictive to, to get-to get that work done, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we do look carefully at financial conditions, of course; that's part of what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we, we really look carefully at is the performance of our- of our goal variables and, and how are we affecting the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we've seen over the course of-just take the last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we've seen inflation-well, over the last couple of years-come down a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've seen the labor market cool off quite a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've, we can also look more directly at, at the parts of the economy that are affected by-that, that are interest sensitive, like particularly housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Housing activity is, is very low, and that's partly, significantly because of our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's transmitting, and it's having the effects on our goal variables that we would want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, a lot of things move financial conditions around, as you know, and we don't really control those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I'd say we, we see the effects we're hoping to see on, on the goal variables and, and the places where we'd expect to see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we, we're not allowed to own Bitcoin.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Federal Reserve Act says what we can own, and we're, we're not looking for a, a law change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's the kind of thing for Congress to consider, but we are not looking for a law change at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think growth this year has, has been solid, it really has.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: PDFP, private domestic final purchases, which, which we think is the best indicator of private demand, is looking to come in around 3 percent [real growth] this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-when we, in these international meetings that I attend, this has been the story, is that how well the U.S. is doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if you look around the world, there's just a lot of slow growth and continued struggles with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I feel-I feel very good about where the economy is and the performance of the economy, and we want to keep that going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, overall, if you look at it, prime-age participation is still very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What, what's going on in the labor market is that the hiring rate is low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you-if you have a job, you're doing very well, and layoffs are very low, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people are not losing their jobs in large numbers, unusually large numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you are looking for a job, though, the hiring rate is low, and that's a signal of, of lower demand, and it has come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look for signs like that, and that, that's clearly a sign of softening, further softening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I didn't mention it earlier, but I, I think you can see a, an ongoing gradual softening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, not something we need to see to get 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that's part of the reason that explains why we moved ahead today with, with our, with the action, with, with an additional cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, but you take a step back, the level of unemployment is very low-again, participation is high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Wages are at a healthy and, and ever more sustainable level-wage growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so the labor market-this is a good, a good labor market, and, you know, we want to keep it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we can't know that with any tremendous certainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I will say that we think that, that our policy balances the risks-we think the risks are roughly in balance as between the two mandates, and we think the labor market is, is in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And when I say it's softening or cooling, it's very gradual process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, job creations are, are meaningfully positive; wages are, you know, if anything, a little, still a bit above what would be sustainable if productivity were to revert to its longer-run trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you, if you take into account the high productivity readings we've had, then wages are already at a sustainable level relative to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, I, I don't want to overstate the downside in the labor market, because the downsides clearly appear to have diminished.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, it's, it's one of our mandate goals, and, you know, we pay close attention to it, and it's, it's worth noting that it is still gradually cooling-gradually and in an orderly way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, that's, that's how I would characterize it, and that's why we're paying careful attention.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it, it breaks down into a long answer, if you want, but it just has been a little bit more stubborn.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if you go back two or three years, many people were saying that to get this far down we would've had to have a, had a deep recession and, you know, high unemployment by now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, that has not been the case, so, you know, the, the path down has actually been much better than many predicted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we've managed to, to have the unemployment rate remain essentially at its longer-run natural rate, while inflation has come down from-you know, core PCE inflation has come down from 5. percent to 2. percent on a 12-month basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One reason is that, that-just a technical issue around the way we calculate housing services, and that, that process has been slower than-market rents have, are showing up more slowly in that measure than we might have thought three, two, two years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there are other, other parts of the story, but, you know, the, the-what, what I think people are feeling right now is the effect of high prices, not high inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we understand very well that prices went up by a great deal, and people really feel that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's prices of food and transportation and heating your home and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's tremendous pain in, in that burst of inflation that was very global.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This was everywhere in all the advanced economies at the same time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So now we have-inflation itself is way down, but people are still feeling high prices, and that is-that is really what people are feeling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The best we can do for them-and that's who we work for-is to get inflation back down to its target and keep it there so that people are earning, you know, big, real wage increases so that their, their wages are going up, their, their compensation is going up faster than inflation year upon year upon year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's what will restore people's good feeling about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what it will take, and that's what we're aiming for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I feel-I feel very good about where the economy is, and, honestly, I'm very optimistic about, about the economy, and it's-we're, we're in a really good place; our policy's in a really good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First of all, when we, when we write- the thing we write down in the Summary of Economic Projections is the longer-run neutral rate, which is the neutral rate at a time when supply and demand are in balance, the full economy's in balance, and no shocks are hitting the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when we're making monetary policy at the Fed, that's not the question we're asking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you can't do a straight read between those longer-run numbers that we write down and what we think the appropriate policy should be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, basically, at any given time, various shocks are hitting the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so what we're doing in, in real time is we're looking at our policy stance, and we're looking at the way it's hitting the economy, and, particularly, we look at the effects it's having as we try to move the economy toward maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the answer can be that there are things that affect the economy that are-that are lasting but not permanent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the, the ones that are permanent are the ones that would be in r*.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The ones that are, could be lasting, but, but nonetheless go away over time, they could actually affect what, what's sort of technically the appropriate neutral stance in near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're looking at that, and, you know, we don't-we don't know exactly where it is, but as I like to say, we know it by its works, and I think what, what we know for sure is that we're 100 basis points closer to it right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are many estimates of where that might be, and we know we're a lot closer to it, and I think we're in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think from here it's a new phase, and we're going to be, you know, cautious about, about further cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, I mean, honestly, we-you know, there are countless models of what-of what a neutral rate might be at any given time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There, there are empirical models, there are theoretical models, there are things that combine them, and they have as many different answers as you'd like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, it's, it's actually a good thing to know that we don't know exactly where it is, so you're not-you're not tempted to think, "Oh, I think this model or this estimate is right."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You, you just have to be open to, you know, the empirical data that are coming in and also how it's affecting the outlook.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's not made any easier by the fact that, you know, that our policy works with long and variable lags.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, that is the job we have, and so we're, we're- I think we need- it's appropriate for us-for us now to proceed cautiously, now that we're 100 basis points closer to, to neutral, and we'll do so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Meanwhile, the economy seems to be in, in good shape, and these cuts will certainly help to support economic activity and the labor market while we can still make progress on inflation, because policy is still meaningfully restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and as, as I imagine you know, the, you know, the goal overall is headline inflation, because that's what people experience.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People don't experience core inflation; they experience inflation, and that includes food and energy costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, as we know, headline inflation contains energy and food, and those prices can fluctuate for reasons that are not related to tightness in the economy and therefore are not really good predictors of future inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it turns out that core inflation is, is a better predictor of overall inflation than overall inflation is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at core inflation because it's a better measure of what future inflation is like to be, likely to be, because it's a better measure of, of what inflation pressures exist.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's, that's-it's complicated, but ultimately, we, you know, our goal is headline, not core.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so headline can, again, it can be affected by energy prices and food prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that, there, there will be things in, in the headline forecasts that are to do with forecasts of energy prices, whereas core will be-if, if you look at core going out a full year, then it'll be much more driven by things like tightness in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
