text: So it-that, that's why the two can go in different directions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Headline has been lower, as you know, most of this year, but that's because energy prices have been coming down, which is a great thing for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But energy prices will come down, and then they will go up, and it won't really be telling us anything about how tight the economy is and how, how future inflation will perform.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we monitor geopolitical risks really quickly, but, you know, but-really carefully, rather.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, I would say so far those risks haven't really- nothing has come out of those risks that really, has really been important for the United States economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The single thing that you would look to is the price of oil, given that we're talking about the Middle East and Ukraine, and, you know, and-but that, that is a good summary statistic for the kind of thing that could go wrong in, in, with global turmoil.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the price of oil's been coming down, and, for, because of supply conditions, global supply conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't-the U.S. is not feeling, really, the effects of geopolitical turmoil, but we are at, certainly, at a time of elevated geopolitical turmoil.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so inflation-again, we don't overreact to a couple of months of higher readings or a couple months of lower readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we, what we had was-we had four months of really nice readings, and then September and October were higher, but then November is much lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't really think the public is experiencing that as a surprising upside risk to inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What the public is feeling, and they're right about it, is that prices are, are just-the price level went up, because of the past inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is going to take some time to, for real wages to recover, over a period of years in which your, your real compensation is growing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in other words, your compensation's growing meaningfully faster than inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's exactly the kind of economy we have now, and we just want to hold onto it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, that process will probably take some years, but that's, that's what's going on right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't think that, you know, a, a couple of months of higher inflation really signal that, anything of the nature you're suggesting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You previously predicted hitting the 2 percent inflation target in 2026.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You said you're focused on enabling further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Are you confident that target isn't going to move further out?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're talking about-when you're projecting the economy, you know, three years out, two years out, you're talking about high uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we really-at that point it, it's not, it's not possible to confidently predict where the economy is going to be in three years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we're doing is we're looking at what's happening now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're kind of projecting that the same kinds of things are happening-so we, we keep a strong labor market, housing services inflation comes down, goods and services-goods inflation settles down, and, you know, nonmarket services return to their, their prior level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of those things should happen over time, and, and, you know, those pieces come together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, but you're not wrong, though, that, you know, we've, the- it's been a bit frustrating because the-while we've made progress, it has been slower than we had hoped.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I think if you'd-if two, two years ago, you'd said, "we were [going to be] at 4. percent unemployment and 2. percent inflation," people would be, would say, "I'll take that."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, that, that's a pretty good interim place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job's not done, but, but I think we're, we're feeling good about where we are and where we're headed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're, we're, you know, we certainly have every intention and expectations that we'll get inflation back sustainably to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has taken longer, but it's, you have to be-you know, we are making progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll continue to do so and get back to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In that case, can you rule out a rate hike next year?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You don't rule things completely in or out in this-in this world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's meaningfully restrictive, and I, I think it's a well-calibrated rate for us to continue to make progress on inflation while, while keeping a, a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I, I'm not going to have-I'm not going to have any, any response or comment whatsoever on, on what the President's said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The public should be confident that we will continue to do our work as we always have-focusing on using our tools to achieve our goals, and really keeping our heads down and doing our work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've gotten more strong data, but we've also seen rates move up at the long end, which could represent a tightening in financial conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if we look back over the past year or so, we can see that policy is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the effect of high rates on interest-sensitive spending-for example, in housing-and if you look at the achievement of our goal variables, we're seeing the economy move toward 2 percent inflation and, and has moved largely to maximum employment, so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Though we literally look at the-at the-at movement toward the goal variables to make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, policy is meaningfully less restrictive than it was before we began to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And for that reason, you know, we're going to be focusing on seeing real progress on inflation or, alternatively, some weakness in the labor market before we-before we consider making adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I, I think our policy stance is very well calibrated, as I mentioned, to balance the achievement of our two-of our two goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we want to-policy to be restrictive enough to continue to foster further, further progress for our 2 percent inflation goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we don't need to see further weakening in the labor market to achieve that goal, and that's kind of what we've been getting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market has really been broadly stable; the unemployment rate has been broadly stable now for six months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, look at the last couple of inflation readings and you see we don't-we don't overreact to two good readings or two bad readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, nonetheless, the last couple of readings have suggested, you know, more positive readings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think we're-I think policy's well, well positioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, so let me look-if you just look at the first paragraph, we did a little bit of language cleanup there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We took out a reference to "since earlier in the year" as it related to the labor market, and we just chose to, to shorten that sentence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I, I mean, if you look at the sort of intermeeting data was good, and, and there was-there was another inflation reading, I guess, just before the December meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, we've got two, two good readings in a row that are consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, we're not going to overinterpret two good or two bad readings, but this was not meant to send a signal other than this: You know, you, you can take away from all of this that we remain committed to achieving our 2 percent inflation goal sustainably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well I, I'd say you, you see expectations moving up a little bit, at the short end-but not at the longer run, which [is] where it really matters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those could be related to-could be related to what you mentioned, some of the new policies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think where the Committee is very much in the mode of waiting to see what policies are enacted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, and we, we don't know what will happen with, with tariffs, with immigration, with fiscal policy, and with regulatory policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're only just beginning to see-actually, are not really beginning to see much, and I think we need to-we need to let those policies be articulated before we can even begin to make a, a plausible assessment of what their implications for the economy will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to be watching carefully and, and, as we always do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is no different than any other set of policy changes at the beginning of a-of an Administration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll patiently watch and understand and, and, you know, kind of not be in a hurry to, to get to a place of understanding what our policy response should be until we see how it plays out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, at all times-at all times, forecasts are conditional, at a minimum, on just a set of expectations, and, and they're highly uncertain in both directions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we know that economic forecasting is, is really difficult, beyond just a month or two out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in the current situation, there's probably some elevated uncertainty because of, of, you know, significant policy shifts in those four areas that I mentioned: tariffs, tariffs, immigration, fiscal policy, and, and regulatory policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's probably some additional uncertainty, but that should be passing; we should go through that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we'll be back to the regular amount of uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what, what forecasters are doing-not just us, but everybody's doing-is they've got sort of just a set of assumptions about what might happen, but they're really kind of in the nature of a placeholder, and-meaning, you know, plausible, could be, but honestly you wouldn't stand behind it because you just don't know, and so you're just-you're just on hold, waiting to see what comes down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's, it's a very large economy, and policies affect it at the margin, but we'll, you know, we're going to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're-we're looking-it's more the other-the way- the way it works is, we are looking at the data to guide us in what we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And right now, we feel like we're in a very good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy's in, in quite a good place, actually, as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what, what we do expect is to see further progress on inflation, and, you know, as I mentioned, as we see that-or if we were to see weakening in the labor market that could foster-we could then be in a position of, of making further adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, right now, we, we don't see that, and we see things as in a really good place for policy and for the economy, and so we feel like we don't need to be in a hurry to, to make any adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say, "yes," in answer to your first question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, to the second question, I want to say this: We are, like others, we're reviewing the orders and the associated details as they are made available.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as has been our practice over many Administrations, we are working to align our policies with the executive orders as appropriate and consistent with applicable law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I want to add that I'm not going to have anything more specific for you today on this whole set of issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I did-I did mention "consistent with applicable law," right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I've-as I've said countless times over the years, this is-this is who we are; this is what we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We study the data, we, we analyze how it will affect the outlook and the balance of risks, and we use our tools to try to give it our best understanding, our best thinking, try to achieve our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-you know, lots of research shows that's the-that's the best way for a central bank to operate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That'll give us the best possible chance to achieve these goals for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people should have confidence in that, as I-as I said a few minutes ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So one of the things our, our staff does is they, they look at a range of possible outcomes, and, and they, they tend to go from really good to really bad, and, you know, it's, it's one of the best things that they do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in each Tealbook-you can look at the five-year-old Tealbooks and see their alternative simulations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They, it'll be a baseline, and then they'll show six or seven alternative scenarios, including really good ones and, and not-so-good ones.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what those do is they spark, you know, the, the policymakers to sort of think and understand about the, you know, the, the uncertainties that surround this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, yes, we, we-staff does that, and we, we're all well aware that there are-that the range of possibilities is always broad, and-not just now, but always.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you have to-it's hard to be open to just how, how broad the possibilities are for an economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, no one saw the pandemic coming, and it was-you know, it changed everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So things happen, and-but yes, we do-we do do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's, it's one thing to do that to make assessments about what might happen and begin to think about what you might do in that case, but you don't act until you-until you see much more than we see now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we want to see, you know, further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it's-we're just going to have to see the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the end of the day, it, it comes down to 12-month inflation, because that takes out the seasonality issues that may exist.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're, we're just going to need to see that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think that-we think we see the pathway for that to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One, one example-a key example-is that you now do see owner's equivalent rent and, you know, housing services-the way it's calculated for PCE [prices], you see that coming down pretty steadily now, and that's the-that's the place where the, most of the remaining gap is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, a big part of the overrun, as you will know, was [coming] from nonmarket services [prices], which don't tend to send much signal [about future inflation].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you can look through all that and, and think, "Okay, that then we seem to be set up for further progress."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But being seem to set up for it is one thing; having it is another.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we're going to want to see further, further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Remember, we're not, you know, we're, we're under-2 percent, but our goal is 2 percent, and we do mean to get back sustainably to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we look at, of course, a very broad range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, so, it starts with unemployment-sorry, with, yeah, with the unemployment rate, employment participation, wages, job quits-are people quitting?-that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at all those things, and you, you put your finger, though, on-it's a low-it's a low-hiring environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you have a job, it's all-it's all good, but if you-if you have to find a job, the job-finding rate-the hiring rates have come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's more typical of a-let's say-let's say that the unemployment-that the-that the labor market is at a sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think we need it to cool off anymore.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, yeah, I, I'd say we watch those things quite carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But nonetheless, overall, look at the aggregate data in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It does seem to-the labor market does seem, seem to be pretty stable and broadly in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When you've got a, an unemployment rate that is-that has been pretty stable now for, for a, a full half a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so what's happening is that the, the flows across the border have decreased very significantly, and there's every reason to expect that to continue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so-but job creation has come down a bit, too, so, you know, if those two things come down together, that, that sort of can be a reason for the unemployment rate to stabilize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In other words, a breakeven rate-as, as population growth slows, the breakeven rate that you need in new jobs to make-to, to make jobs for, for workers declines as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You, you do see a very-a very flat unemployment rate at a time when you've seen significant declines [in job growth].

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we run a very careful budget process where we're fully aware that what, that, you know, we owe the-we owe that to the public, and we believe we do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Chris, I'm not going to-I'm not going to react or discuss anything that, that any elected politician might say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we considered this, you know, really at length, and we did decide to withdraw from the NGFS.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, really, the reason is that the, the work that the NGFS does has broadened very significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Think about nature-related risks and biodiversity and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, the, the work of the NGFS is, is, in, in significant part intended to-and this is a quote-"mobilize mainstream finance to support the transition toward a sustainable economy."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we joined to get the benefit of understanding what other central banks were doing and, and seeing research and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think this is just way beyond any plausible mandate that you could attribute to the Fed, and so we have a quite narrow role, as I've-as I've said many times, and I think that, that the activities of the NGFS are not a good fit for the Fed, given our current mandate and authority.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, and I just think it was time to acknowledge that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the process-this process dates back-thinking about it dates back a couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I made the decision to bring this to the Board, you know, some months ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just-it just-the process just took time to get here, and, and this is when- this is when we, we got in and voted on it, so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'm aware of how it can look, but it was really not driven by politics; it was driven by kind of the disconnect between the work of the NGFS and our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Other central banks have different mandates and belong to the NGFS.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, 2 percent-inflation down to-inflation down to 2 percent sustainably is what, what we're trying to achieve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're, we're somewhat above that, as you know, and, you know, we, we want to see, you know, serial readings that suggest that we're making further progress on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And consumers will, will pick that up, of course, in the things that they buy at the grocery store or at the store.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I like to say, that you know that-you know the neutral rate by its works.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, you know, at 4. percent we're, we're above pretty much everyone on the Committee's estimates of the longer-run neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think our eyes are telling us that our policy is having the effects on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you can consult models, empirical models, theoretical models.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You really have to just look out the window and see how your-how your policy rate is affecting the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we see that it's having meaningful effects in bringing inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has helped bring the labor market into balance as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I am-I, I have no illusion that, that anyone knows precisely how much that is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, but it, you know-not knowing that, and having cut 100 basis points, means that it's appropriate that we-that we not be in a hurry to make further adjustments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's been-it's been our practice, as I mentioned, to work to align our policies to those that are mentioned in, in the executive orders.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, I'm not going to-I'm not going to go any deeper than that or, or get into any deeper into this set of issues today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we just-so first of all, thing, things are a little different now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've just come through a high-inflation period, and you can argue that both ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can- you can say that companies have figured out that they do like to raise prices, but, but we also hear a lot from companies these days that consumers have really had it with price increases, and so I don't know how that shakes out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, you're coming through a situation where we're not quite back to 2 percent, and that, that's just different.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, you know, the trade-the kind of footprint of trade is, has changed a, a lot, as trade is now spread around the, you know-it's not as concentrated in China as it was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so there were differences, and I just think the, the range of possibilities is, is very, very wide.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just don't know, and I, I don't want to start speculating, as tempting as it is, because we really don't know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we didn't know, by the way, in, I guess, 2018.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it, you know, the-again, the range of possibilities, very, very wide.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know for how long or how much, what countries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know how it's going to transmit through the economy to consumers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, there are lots of places where that-where that-where that price increase from the tariff can show up between the manufacturer and a consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're just going to have to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the best we can do is what we've done, which is study up on this and, you know, look at historical experience, read the literature, and think about the factors that might matter, and then we'll just have to see-have to see how it-how it goes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the most recent data do suggest that reserves are still abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Reserves remain roughly as high as they were when runoff began.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the federal funds rate has been very steady within the target range.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We track a, a bunch of metrics, and they do tend to point to, to reserves being abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do intend to reduce the size of our balance sheet to a level that's consistent with implementing monetary policy efficiently and effectively in our ample-reserves regime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're closely monitoring a, a range of indicators to assess conditions, and that should provide signals whether reserves are approaching a level that could be judged as, quote, "somewhat above ample."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I don't have anything to say to you about particular dates; it's just that's the process, and what we see is, is that, that rates do appear to be abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As always, we stand ready to take appropriate action to support the smooth transition of monetary policy, including to adjust the details of our approach for reducing the size of the balance sheet in light of economic and financial developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On, on AI, it's a big event in, in the stock market and in particular parts of the stock market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, what, what really matters for us is macro developments, and that means substantial changes in financial conditions that are persistent for a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't put that label on, on these events, although of course we're all watching it with interest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you know, as we've reduced our, our policy rate 100 basis points, longer rates have gone up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Not because of expectations-not principally because of expectations about our policy or about inflation; it's more a term premium story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, and, you know, it's long rates that matter for, for housing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I don't think-I think these higher rates are going to-they're, they're probably hold back housing activities to some extent, if they're persistent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we, we are-we control an overnight rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Generally, it, it propagates through the whole family of asset prices, including interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in this particular case, it's all happened at a time when, for reasons unrelated to our policy, longer rates have moved up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we've never said we need to be all the way at target to reduce rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At, at any time, what we're doing is we're looking at the economy and asking whether our policy stance is the right one to achieve maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think if-we would want to see further progress, but we think our-we think our-as I mentioned, we think that our policy stance is restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I would think we need to see further progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't say all the way back down to 2 percent on a sustainable basis, although we'd love to see that, of course, and we will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we-I want to avoid commenting, even indirectly, on the conduct of tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's not our job, and it's not our job to comment on the moves that people make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I wouldn't want to criticize anything that's happening or really comment on it one way or another-praise it, for that matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think that-you know, we found in, in 2018, [when] there was a lot of work done on trade policy uncertainty, trade policy uncertainty, if it's large and persistent, can start to matter for businesses making investment decisions and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and it's one, you know, one of many things we'll be watching.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we, we look-we look at, from a financial stability perspective, at asset prices generally, along with things like leverage in the household sector, leverage in the banking system, funding risk for banks, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's just one of the four things, asset prices are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, yeah, I, I'd say they're elevated by, by many metrics right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A good part of that, of course, is this thing around tech and AI, but we, we look at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we also-we look at how resilient the households and, and businesses and the financial sector are to those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at that mainly from our financial stability perspective, and we think that there's a lot of resilience out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Banks have high capital, and households are actually, overall-not all households, but in, in the aggregate, households are in pretty good shape financially these days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, you know, we, we also-we look at overall financial conditions, and you've got-you can't just take-you can't just take equity prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got to look at rates, too, and that, you know, that represents a, a tightening in conditions, with higher rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, financial conditions are probably still somewhat accommodative, but it's a mixed bag.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One, one is, is that there's a low hiring rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that if, if there were to be a spike in layoffs, if companies were to start to reduce headcount, you would see unemployment go up pretty quickly, because the hiring rate is quite low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's also-it's worth pointing out that for lower-income households, they are- they're under significant pressure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in the aggregate, the numbers are good, but we know that people at the lower end of the income spectrum are, are struggling with, with costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, really, it's, it's high inflation for the basics of life.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not so much the inflation now; it's the price level, because inflation has raised prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation is now closer-much closer to target, but people are really feeling that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, overall, this is a good labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's just a really good level, and you've been solidly there now for six, seven months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And job creation is pretty close to a level that will hold the unemployment rate there, given, given that, you know, there'll be much slower population growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we hear anecdotal reports, but I, I don't see-there's nothing in the data yet on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you do-you hear-you hear that kind of thing about construction, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, businesses that are dependent on immigrant labor are, are saying that it's, it's suddenly gotten harder to, to get people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, again-I know-you don't see that in the aggregate data yet, but yes, you, you hear it anecdotally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess I'd say this: Uncertainty is, is with us all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, it is human nature, apparently, to underestimate the-how fat the tails are, in a way, that, you know, the, the possibility-we think of things in a normal distribution, and in the economy it's not a normal distribution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The tails are very fat, meaning things can happen way out of your expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't-you know, if you-if you think about it- think about the first few months of the pandemic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Are we going to be able to reopen the economy?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have the economy growing at, you know, 2 to 2½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation's come down to, to now the, you know-the headline inflation number was 2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at-we look at core because it's a better indicator of future inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, yes, the price level went up a lot for inflation, and people are feeling that, and, and they're not wrong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I-so the kind of uncertainty we have is just a, a usual level of uncertainty about the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But then policies-which are, you know, not for us to criticize or, or praise, really-those are-those are policies which people are, have been elected to implement.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're implementing them with a view to, to making a better economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I, I don't think-I wouldn't call this out as, as a- as one of those times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't compare it to the Global Financial Crisis or anything like that, given that we have actually a very good economy right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as, as I mentioned, the economy's strong, the labor market's solid, downside risks to the labor market appear to have abated, and we think disinflation continues on a slow and sometimes bumpy path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That tells me and the other members of the Committee-the broad sense of the Committee, actually, is that we don't need to be in a hurry to adjust our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's one of those things we'll know it when we see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But more, more the-the expectation is that we will make continued progress, and, you know, that's what we want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we-it, it's going to have to be something that isn't just idiosyncratic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're going to want to see, you know, continued progress with housing services inflation; you're going to want to see inflation behaving in a way that builds confidence that we are really making progress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, is, is that better than our expectations?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we expect to see that, it's just a question of when.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think to-I think that goal has served us well over a long period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that if, if a central bank wanted to look at changing that, you wouldn't do it at a time when you're not meeting it anyway.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would not look at changing it anyway, but I certainly wouldn't look at, at it at a time when you're not-when you're not meeting it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, there's just no interest at all in changing it, if, if I'm being at all unclear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not-we're not going to change the inflation goal any time soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we really said was that we wouldn't-we wouldn't look at a-at a strong labor market and raise rates unless we saw some evidence of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the thought was that we'd seen really low levels of inflation-sorry, of unemployment-with no sign of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So why would you preemptively want to-want to put people out of work in the absence of, of any kind of-any evidence that suggested that, that this was not a sustainable level?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was a way of, of acknowledging how much humility we have about, about the starred variables, especially u*, the natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That'll be one of the many things that we discuss.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We didn't-you know, we, we-what we said was that, you know, in-at times when inflation persistently undershot 2 percent, we, we would likely allow inflation to run moderately above 2 percent for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That was- turned out not to be relevant to what actually happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was the pandemic, and it happened, and, you know, our framework permitted us to act quite vigorously, and we did once we decided that that's what we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our framework had really nothing to do with the decision to-we, we looked at the inflation as, as transitory, and-right up to the point where the data turned against that, and when the data turned against that in late '21, we changed our, our view, and we raised rates a lot, and here we are at 4. percent unemployment and inflation way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the framework was, was more irrelevant than anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the, that part of it-that part of it was irrelevant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The rest of the framework worked just fine as, as we used it, as it supported what we did to bring inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so our, our role with Bitcoin, really, is to look at-with crypto, really, is to look at the banks, and, and, you know, we, we think it's-you know, banks are perfectly able to serve crypto customers, as long as they understand and can manage the risks and its safe, safe and soundness.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many of our-a good number of our banks that we regulate and supervise do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the threshold has been a little higher for banks engaging in crypto activities, and that's because they're so new, and, you know, we don't want to make the mistake you're-if you-if you're making a choice to conduct that activity inside a bank which is inside the federal safety net, with deposit insurance, then you want to be pretty sure that, that it's a safe and sound activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we're, we're not against innovation, and we certainly don't want to, to take actions that would cause banks to, you know, to terminate customers who are perfectly legal just because of, of excess risk aversion maybe related to regulation and supervision, so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, you know, that's, that's kind of a-it's not really our, our bailiwick.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You want people to be knowledgeable about the financial engagements that they have, and that's why we have, you know, the securities law, laws that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's why, you know, if you read a mutual fund prospectus or individual stock prospectus, you, you want households to have the chance to understand the risk that they're taking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I, I do think it would be helpful if there were a greater regulatory apparatus around crypto, and I think that, that's something Congress was working on quite a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've actually spent a lot of time, you know, with members of Congress working together with them on, on various things, and I, I think that would be a very constructive thing for, for Congress to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say that it is going to be very difficult to have a precise assessment of how much of inflation is coming from tariffs and from, from other-and that's already the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You may have seen that goods inflation moved up pretty significantly in the first two months of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Trying to track that back to actual tariff increases, given what was tariffed and what was not-very, very challenging.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So some of it-the, the answer is clearly some of it-a good part of it is, is coming from tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we'll be-we'll be working, and so will other forecasters, to try to find the best possible way to separate nontariff inflation from tariff inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the, the-your, your sort of looking-through question, too soon to say about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As, as I've mentioned, it, it can be the case that it's appropriate sometimes to look through inflation if it's going to go away quickly without action by, by us, if it's transitory.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that can be the case in the case of, of tariff inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that would depend on the, the tariff inflation moving through fairly quickly and would depend critically, as well, on inflation expectations being well anchored-longer-term inflation expectations being well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think-I think that's kind of the base case, but, as I said, it's- we really can't know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to have to see how things actually, actually work out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the fact that there wasn't much change-I think that's, that's partly because, you know, you see-you see weaker growth but higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, frankly, a little bit of inertia when it-when it comes to changing something in this highly uncertain environment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you're-you, you know, I think there is a level of inertia where you just say, "Maybe I'll stay where I am."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our inflation expectations-of course, we do monitor inflation expectations very, very carefully-basically, every source we can find, and, you know-short- term, long-term, households, businesses, forecasters, market-based.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the picture, broadly, is this: You do see increases widely in short-term inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people who fill out surveys and answer, you know, questionnaires are pointing to tariffs about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look-in the survey world, if you look a little further out, you, you really-you really don't see much in the way of an increased longer-term inflation-inflation expectations are mostly well anchored, if you look at the [series maintained by the Federal Reserve Bank of] New York, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Then you have market based, and it's the same pattern.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, people and markets are pricing in and, and breakevens, some higher inflation over the next year must be related to tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look out five years or five-year, five- year forward, you'll see that breakevens have-are either flat or, actually, slightly down in the case of a longer-term one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at that, and we will be watching all of it very, very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's at the very heart of our framework: anchored inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we do see pretty solid hard data still.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So growth looks like it's maybe moderating a bit, consumer spending moderating a bit, but still at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Job creation, most recently, has been at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation has started to move up now, we think partly in response to tariffs, and there may be a delay in further progress over the course of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The, the survey data, [in the case of] both household and businesses, show significant rise in uncertainty and significant concerns about downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned the other day, as you pointed out, the relationship between survey data and actual economic activity hasn't been very tight.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There have been plenty of times where people are saying very down-downbeat things about the economy and then going out and buying a new car.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we don't know that that will be the case here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will be watching very carefully for signs of weakness in the real data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, I-you know, given where we are, we think our policy's in a good place to react to, to what comes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think that the right thing to do is, is to wait here for, you know, for greater clarity about, about what, what the economy's doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In fact, I used it at the recent conference where I spoke.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think a world where, where people can make their daily economic decisions, and businesses, and they're not having to think about the possibility of significantly high inflation-we know inflation will bounce around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think we were getting closer and closer to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think with the arrival of, of the tariff inflation, further progress may be delayed, if the SEP doesn't really show further downward progress on inflation this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, that's really due to the tariffs coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, delayed, but if you look at our forecast, we do see ourselves getting back into the low 2s in '26 and then down to 2 [percent] by '27-of course, highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I see progress having, having been made toward that, and then progress in the future.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that progress is probably delayed for the time being.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, people wrote down two cuts the last time, and they look at-they look at the-you know, the-and they wrote down, you know, meaningful decline in growth out from 2. to 1. in 2025, a tick up in the unemployment rate, so not much there, but core inflation up by three-tenths.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so those two kind of-those kind of balance each other out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people-not everybody, but, on balance, people wrote down similar numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other-the other factor, though, as I mentioned, is just really high uncertainty.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it's just-it's really hard to know how this is going to work out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, we think our policy's in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it's a good place where we can move in the direction that-where we need to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in the meantime, we, we-it's, it's really appropriate to wait for further clarity, and, of course, you know, the costs of doing that, given that the economy is still solid, are very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so that's a feature of the-has been for some time, a feature of this labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got wages that are consistent with 2 percent inflation, assuming that we're going to keep getting, you know, relatively high productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got unemployment, you know, pretty close to its natural level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But job-the hiring rate is quite low, but so is the layoff rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're not seeing people losing their jobs, but you're seeing that people who don't have a job having to wait longer and longer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the question is, which way does that break?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we were to see a meaningful increase in layoffs, then that would probably translate fairly quickly into unemployment, because people are-you know, it's, it's not a-it's not a big hiring market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've been watching that, and it's just not in the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we've had is, is a low-firing, low-hiring situation, and it seems to be in balance now for, you know, for the last six, seven, eight months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, it's a labor market that's in balance, and, you know, we, we watch it very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, you know, only in a-kind of an early way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, for example, the, the layoffs that are happening here are, you know, they're certainly meaningful to the people involved, and they may be meaningful to a particular neighborhood or region or area, but at the national level, they're not-they're not significant yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mentioned that-you, you saw it-we've had two, two very strong goods inflation readings in the last two months, which is very unexpected, and, I think, hard to trace it to specific tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it must have-it must have something to do with-it's either noise and it'll come back, and that-that's very possible, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if it is persistent, then it must be to do with, you know, people buying ahead of tariffs, or raising prices ahead of tariffs, and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That-those kinds of things happen, and they're very, very hard to capture because so much of it is indirect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A great example is there-washing machines were tariffed in the last, last round of tariffs, and prices went up, but prices also went up on, on dryers, which were not tariffed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the manufacturers just, you know, they just kind of followed the crowd and, and raised it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So things happen very indirectly, and so there'll be a lot of work done in the coming months to, to try to trace all that through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, though, it's too soon to be seeing significant effects in economic data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When you say "last time," are you talking about the last-

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You could have been talking about the last time there were tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's, it's still the truth, if, if there's an inflationary impulse that's going to go away on its own, it's not the right policy to, to tighten policy, because by the time you have your effect, you're-you know, you're-an effect that by-by design, you are lowering economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if that's not necessary, you don't want to do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In real time, as we know, it's hard to make that judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and, and we're well aware, you know, of what happened, obviously, with, with the pandemic inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, I mean, we have to look at this as a-as a different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we haven't had real price stability fully reestablished yet, and we have to keep that in mind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we also have-we hear that people are very reluctant to take on-to, you know, to, to allow prices to go up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we hear that businesses are intending to pass many of these prices through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's hard to say how this is going to work out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have maximum employment and price stability, and we have to balance those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, there can be situations in which they are in tension, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have, actually have a provision in our-in our consensus statement that says what we should do in that case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a very challenging, you know, situation for, for any central bank, and certainly for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, what we say that we'll do is, we'll, we'll look how far each of those two goals is-each of those two measures is from its goal, and then we'll ask how long we think it might take to get back to the goal for each of them, and we'll make a judgment, because our, you know, our tools work in one direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Let me say, we don't have that situation right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's not what the-that's not where the economy is at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know any mainstream forecast that really shows significant problems like that, so-

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, there's always an unconditional probability-possibility of, of a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It might be broadly in the range of one in four at any time, if you look back through, through the years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It-there could be, within 12 months, a one in four chance of a recession.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the question is, is whether that-whether this current situation, those possibilities are elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say this: We don't-we don't make such a forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at outside forecasts, forecasters have, have generally raised-a number of them have raised their possibility of a-of a recession somewhat, but still at relatively moderate levels-you know, still in the region of, of the traditional, because they were extremely low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go back two months, people were saying that the, the likelihood of a recession was extremely low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think I, I did answer that question in this very room some time ago, and I, I [have] no desire to change that answer and have nothing new for you on that today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I mentioned it back then, but in no way did I place a huge weight on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it, it-that was an ex post story, but it wasn't the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's also-this is-that, that Michigan, the one you're referring to, the longer-term thing-you know, we look at it, and we don't dismiss data that we don't like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it is an outlier compared to market-based and compared to other survey-based assessments of longer-run inflation expectations, so we've got to keep that in mind.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I-again, I, I would just say, we look at-we look at all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that one-that one's kind of an outlier, but, you know, nonetheless, we, we take notice of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, look, we're, we're aware of the-we're well aware of how things are going to evolve and the time frames and all that, and, you know, we will-we will use our tools to foster achievement of our goals to the-to the best we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, we're going to try to be timely with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we are obviously aware of the soft sentiment data and high uncertainty, and we're watching that carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think it's a, a good time for us to wait for further clarity before we consider adjusting our, our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're-these decisions are going to be made, and they're going to be implemented, and then we'll know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At that point, we'll know what the decisions are, and we'll have to make assessments then about their, their implications for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A lot of them will happen over the course of, you know, in coming months, certainly over the course of this year, and we'll be adapting as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when we say "separating the signal from the noise," that's just a way of saying that things are highly uncertain and that, you know, you're reading about developments-the news is full of developments of tariffs being put on and taken off and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's-some of that is noise in the sense that it's, it's not really telling you anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're trying to extract a signal from that, and the signal is what's going to be the effect on economic activity, on inflation, on employment, and all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so that's really when we say "signal and noise."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's sort of a, a special case of that-of, you know, with the idea being-and I think-do think that the first two months of this year are a great example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got high readings for goods inflation after a string of readings that averaged close to zero, and you have to ask-it's coming during tariffs, but, you know, you-it's very hard to, actually, scientifically go back and match up those increases and say, "Yes, I can prove that that's from tariffs."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it kind of has to be, to some extent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There can be idiosyncratic readings in various categories, which will shortly reverse, and that, that happens, too, and that could be a big piece of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In a couple of months, we'll know whether those were-you know, where that really was from.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's a-that's another case where I think it's going to be very, very challenging to unpack the inflation that we see over the course of this year and be able to say with confidence how much of that came from inflation and how much of it-sorry, from tariffs-and how much of it didn't.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be doing that, and so will everybody else, and we'll all be trying very hard to, to make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I, I'm sure we will make a lot of progress on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it would depend on what we're talking about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, obviously, you're looking for direct evidence that, that particular pieces of, of inflation are, are- or are clearly not-caused by tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For example, something that was, you know, in the service sector that was far away from anything that's tariffed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You, you might think, okay, well that is- like, frankly, housing services inflation-which, which, by the way, has been behaving well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know-which, for, for some time, was kind of our problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now it's been-it's slow, but it's definitely, you know, moving down in a-in a very good way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's more now with goods and, to some extent, with, with nonhousing services inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was inflation in '21, '22, and '23, and prices went up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's, they're unhappy-and, and they're not wrong to be unhappy-that prices went up quite a bit, and they're paying a lot for those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-I think that is the fundamental fact and has been for a long time-a couple years-why people are unhappy with the-with the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've got 2 percent growth, and, you know, it's, it's a pretty good economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And just to follow up: Why are you still projecting two rate cuts this year if your own projections show inflation higher for longer?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Does that mean you see a slowdown in economic growth as a real threat?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think if you-yeah, I mean, remember, we came into this with-at the December meeting, and the median was two cuts, the median was.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so you come in, and you see, broadly speaking, weaker growth but higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they kind of balance each other out, so you think-and, and unemployment is really, really only, only a one- tenth change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-there's just not a big change in the forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Modest, you know, meaningfully higher growth and meaningfully higher inflation, which call for different responses, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So they cancel each other out, and people just said, "Okay, I'm going to stay here."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Is just-you know, we're sitting here thinking-and we, we obviously are in, in touch with businesses and households all over the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have an extraordinary network of contacts that come in through the Reserve Banks and put it in the Beige Book-and also through contacts at the Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we get all that, and we, we do understand that sentiment has fallen off pretty sharply, but economic activity has not yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would tell people that the economy seems to be- seems to be healthy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We understand that, that sentiment is, is quite negative at this time, and that probably has to do with, you know, turmoil at the beginning of an Administration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's making, you know, big changes in, in areas of policy, and that's probably part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think the underlying unhappiness people have about the economy, though, is more-is more about the price level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so, in the SEP, you'll see that there's not further progress on core inflation this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't ask people to say-to write down how much of this is from tariffs and how much of it is not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that tariffs are coming, and we know that they're probably already-all, all forecasters have tariff inflation affecting core PCE inflation [and] core CPI inflation this year, without exception.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't tell you how much of that it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of the balance sheet-so, yeah, we-I think-I guess the way I'd say it is, you know, it was the flows in and out of the, the TGA that got us thinking about it, but as we, you know, as we thought about it, we really came to the view that this was a good time to, to make the move that we made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, broadly, Committee came around-came around to the view that we, we would do the same thing we'd already done, which is, once we-I guess in June, we- was it June?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Whenever it was, we, we lowered the pace of QT, and we're just going to do that again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the sense of that is, if you're cutting the pace of QT roughly in half, then the runway is probably doubled, okay?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can think of it like a plane coming in for a landing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As we get closer and we-by the way, we still think that reserves are abundant, although you begin to see some of the-some of the things we look at begin to react a little bit, but we still think that they're abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, now, the TGA is emptying out, so reserves are, are higher now, so you can't really see the underlying signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we came around to the view, and, and it had a lot of appeal, and so we did it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It really-it has no implications at all for monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It has no implications at all for the ultimate size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It isn't sending a signal in any hidden way that you can try to tease out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, we're basically-it's very consistent with our plans and our practices that we've published and that we've followed since we began this-what is a very successful, you know, rundown of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, [this is] the second time that we've slowed the pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've said that we would stop when we were somewhat above the level [of reserves] we judge as ample.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, clearly, we're not at that level yet, but we're going to be approaching it more slowly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a commonsense kind of a- kind of a thing, and it had-it had pretty broad appeal, I will say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So when we-when we talk about inflation expectations being well anchored, we're talking about longer-run inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they really haven't moved much, I mean, if at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There, there's one reading that everyone's focusing on that's higher, but the other survey readings and the market-based readings all show relatively, you know, well- anchored inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You would expect that expectations of inflation over the course of a year would move around, because conditions change, and in this case, we have tariffs coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't know how big, what's-there's so many things we don't know, but we kind of know there are going to be tariffs, and they tend to bring growth down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They tend to bring inflation up at the-in the first instance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so I would say, you, you know, I'm not dismissing what we're seeing in short-term inflation expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But when we say expectations are well anchored, we're really looking at, you know, longer term, five year and out, and there's really no story to tell five years and out, either in market based or, or in surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we're not, you know, we're, we're not going to miss any evidence that longer-term or medium-term inflation expectations are, are moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We talked about that over the course of the last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There were-there were some good number of months and times when a lot of the job creation was, was concentrated in, you know, educational institutions, health care, state governments, things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There were also times when private-sector job growth has been moving, moving in a healthy frame-and they're all-they're all jobs, but-and remember, we're, you know, we're at very low unemployment for, you know, for, for quite a time now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think it's a good labor market, but it's-look, it's something that we monitor carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I, you know-the, the elected government is entitled to have-you know, we, we don't have policies that address different kinds of employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, but the elected government has a-has a different role, and they can-they, they can have those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we may or may not stop MBS runoff, though, because, you know, we can-we can-we, we want to stop runoff in net at some point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't made any decisions about that, but, you know, we, we want the-we want the MBS to roll off our balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We really, strongly desire that, so-but we haven't made any decisions about that, you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we will-we-I think we'd, we'd look carefully at letting that keep going, but hold the overall size of the balance sheet in, you know, constant, at some point-a point that we're not at yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm confident that we're well positioned in the sense that we're, we're well positioned to move in the direction we'll need to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I mean, I, I don't know anyone who has a lot of confidence in their forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, the point is, we are-we are at, you know, we're at a place where we can cut or we-or we can hold what is a clearly a restrictive stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Forecasting right now, it's-you know, forecasting is always very, very hard, and in the current situation, I just think it's-uncertainty is, you know, remarkably high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, like, I, I think we're not going to be in any hurry to move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, I think we're, we're well positioned to wait for further clarity, and not in any hurry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, sometimes with language they-it, it lives its, its useful life, and then we take it off, and we- and, and that was the case there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Over the past year, you know, conveying this sense of the balance of risks was important that they be in balance or close to being in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That was useful as we approach liftoff, if you remember.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I actually would say that the more important thing now about risks-and this is in, in pages like 10, 11, 12 of the SEP-if you look, participants widely raised their estimate of, of the risks to our-of uncertainty, but also of the risks to growth in our employment and inflation mandates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's a more salient point now than whether they're-whether they're in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So financial conditions matter to us because, you know, financial conditions are the main channel to the real economy through which our policy has its effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what matters from, from a Fed standpoint for the macroeconomy is material changes to overall financial conditions that are persistent, that last for a while-long enough to actually affect economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I'm not going to opine on the appropriate level of any market-equity, debt, commodities, or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would just point you to the-to the bigger picture again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the real economy, the, the hard data are still in, in reasonably good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's the soft data-it's the surveys that are showing, you know, significant concerns, downside risks, and those kind of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're watching it carefully, but, you know, we, we don't want to get ahead of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we, we want to focus on the hard data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This-if it's-if that's going to affect the hard data, we should know it very quickly, and, and, of course, we'll, we'll understand that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, fortunately, we're in a situation where we have seen inflation move down from, you know, higher levels to pretty close to 2 percent, while the unemployment rate has remained very consistent with full employment, 4. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we now have inflation coming in from an exogenous source, but the underlying inflationary picture before that was, you know, basically 2½ percent inflation, I would say, and 2 percent growth, and 4 percent unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't see any reason to think that we're looking at, at a replay of the '70s or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, inflation-underlying inflation is, is, you know, still running in the 2s, with probably a little bit of a pickup associated with tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I don't think we're facing-I, I wouldn't say we're in, in a situation that's remotely comparable to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I-it's not-it's not appropriate for me to speculate on political ideas or, or fiscal policy, for that matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm going to-I'm going to pass on that one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, since the very beginning, we've had kind of a placeholder-the staff has a placeholder of-range of-really a range of possible outcomes from tariffs, and from trade policy generally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's, that's kind of baked into the numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What happens-it will be complicated, and there will be some retaliation and some not and, and all that, but, ultimately, they're trying to, with the placeholder, give us a broad sense of what this might look like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This-when we know-when we actually know the specifics, we'll be able to, to have still uncertain but, you know, better-informed forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so we, we looked at pausing, and we looked at, at slowing, and, really, people came together very strongly behind slowing, not pausing, for a variety of reasons.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so people really came to be, you know, pretty strongly in favor of, of this move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It slows down the path and probably lengthens it-you know, doubles it, effectively, by slowing it by half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's, that's-people thought that's, that's a good place to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It'll, it'll, you know, help us assure that this path is, is a smooth one as we get closer and closer to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it was-it was actually-it was the, the TGA flows- Treasury General Account flows that got us thinking about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the more we thought about it, we came around to this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, it, it is-yes, it was provoked.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think what we came up with, though, was broader than that and different than it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It does address that issue, but it really is also-it fits in really nicely with our principles and our plans, and the things we've done before, and the things we've said we would do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'd just say it's, it's nothing to do with monetary policy, nothing to do with the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just kind of a commonsense adjustment as you get closer and closer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, that way, we'll be more and more confident that we're getting where we need to get.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're shrinking the balance sheet every month, and we think that's-we think it was a good play and, as I mentioned, well supported.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so, as we noted in our-in our statement-postmeeting statement, we've judged that the risks to higher employment and higher inflation have both risen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this, by the way, of course, is compared to March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think we can say, you know, which way this will shake out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think there's a great deal of uncertainty about, for example, where tariff policies are going to, to settle out and also, when they do settle out, what will be the implications for the economy for growth and for employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I mean, ultimately, we think our policy rate is in-is in a good place to stay as we await further clarity on tariffs and, ultimately, their implications for the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have an economy that, if you "look through," you know, the sort of distortions in Q1 GDP, you've still got an economy that looks like it's growing at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's an economy that's been resilient and is in good shape, and our policy is sort of modestly or moderately restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's 100 basis points less restrictive than it was last fall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we think that leaves us in a good place to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think we need to be in a hurry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The data may move quickly or slowly, but we do think we're in a good position, where we are, to, to let things evolve and become clearer in terms of what should be the monetary policy response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's what you see, which is inflation now running a bit above 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've had basically decent readings in housing services and nonhousing services, which is a big part of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that part, I think is, is moving along well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-and we're in a good position to wait and see, is the thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy is-has been resilient and is doing fairly well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The costs of waiting to see further are fairly low, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The Administration is entering into negotiations with many countries over tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll know more with each week and month that goes by where-about where tariffs are going to land-you know, land, and we'll know what the effects will be when we start to see those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, for now, it does seem like it's, it's, it's a fairly clear decision for us to wait and see and watch.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, as I said, we're-we are comfortable with our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think the right-we're in the right place to wait and see how things evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't feel like we need to be in a hurry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, when things develop-of course, we have a record of-we can move quickly when that's appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we think right now, the appropriate thing to do is to wait and see how things evolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you talk to businesses or market participants or forecasters, everyone is just-is just waiting to see how developments play out, and then we'll be able to make a better assessment of what the appropriate path for monetary policy is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're not in that place, and, you know, as that develops-and I can't really give you a time frame on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, let me say-I mean, so let's, let's, let's look back and see where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had-we've had, you know, unemployment in the low 4s for more than a year, we've had inflation coming down in the-now in the mid-to-low 2s, and we've had an economy growing at 2½ percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that is-that is the economy as we see it now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What looks likely, given the scope and scale of the tariffs, is that we will see the-certainly, the risks to higher inflation, higher unemployment have increased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if that's what we do see, if-and if the tariffs are ultimately put in place at those levels, which we don't know, then, then we will see-we won't see further progress toward our goals, but we might see a delay in that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think in the-you know, in our thinking, we would get-we would never-we never do anything but keep achieving those goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what we would-at least for the next, let's say, year, we would-we would not be making progress toward those goals, again, if that is-if that's the way the tariffs shake out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's so much uncertainty about the scale, scope, timing, and persistence of the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of preemption, you know, I think you can look back at the 2019 cuts as preemptive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
