text: I wouldn't say that what we did last fall was at all preemptive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the situation was, you had a weakening economy, and you had inflation at 1. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we have an expectation conditional on what happens that we'll see upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at where forecasters are, they're all forecasting an increase in inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it makes it-and then we've also got, you know, forecasts of weakening in the economy, and some have recession forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't make a-we don't make-publish a forecast about, about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't publish a forecast that assesses how likely a recession is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in any case, it's not a situation where we can be preemptive, because we actually don't know what the right response to, to the data will be until we see more data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so first of all, we don't see that yet, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have 4. percent unemployment, good participation, wages behaving very well, participation, I mentioned, at a good level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, with the labor market, we would look at the totality of the-of the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We would look at the whole huge array of labor market data to, to get a sense of whether conditions are really deteriorating or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, at the same time, we'd be looking at the other side of the mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We could be in a position of having to balance those two things, which is, of course, a very-a difficult balancing judgment that we'd have to make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, let's just say this is a-this would be a complicated and challenging judgment that we would have to make if-and this is-we're not in this situation, but the situation is if the two goals are in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let's say that unemployment is moving up in an uncomfortable way and so is inflation-not the situation we're in-hypothetically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we would look at how far they are from the goals, how far they're expected to be from the goals, what's the expected time to get back to their goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'd look at all those things and make a difficult judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's-we haven't had-we haven't faced that question in a very long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, again, difficult, difficult judgment to make, and not one that we face today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we have to be keeping it in our thinking now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you have to just take a step back and realize this is-this is why we are where we are, is, you know, we are going to need to see how this evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are cases in which it would be appropriate for us to cut rates this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are cases in which it wouldn't, and we just don't know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Until we know more about how this is going to settle out and what the economic implications are for employment, for-and for, for inflation, I couldn't confidently say that I know what the appropriate path will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-you know, we're always going to do the same thing-which is, we're going to use our tools to foster maximum employment and price stability for the benefit of the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're always going to consider only the economic data, the outlook, the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it really doesn't affect either our job or the way we do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: My gut tells me that uncertainty about the path of the economy is extremely elevated [laughter] and that the downside risks have increased.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The risk is-as we pointed out in our statement, the risks-the risks of higher unemployment and higher inflation have risen, but they haven't materialized yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're not, really not in the data yet, so that-and that tells me more than by intuition because I think-I think it's obvious, actually, that the right thing for us to do is to-we're in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our policy's in a very good place, and the right thing to do is, is await further clarity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-you know, there's- usually, things clarify, and that-the appropriate direction becomes clear.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, it's very hard to say what that would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's 100 basis points less restrictive than it was in, you know, last summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think it's-we think it's in a good place, and we think the appropriate thing is for us to wait and see and get more clarity about, about the direction of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you know, we all look at all these sentiments and read many, many individual comments just to get a better feel.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it-you know, businesses and households very broadly are concerned and, you know, postponing economic decisions of various kinds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, yes, if that continues and nothing, nothing happens to sort of alleviate those concerns, then you would expect that to begin to show up in economic data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It wouldn't maybe show up overnight, but it would show up over weeks and months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that may be what happens, but it hasn't happened yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, there are things that can happen that will-that will change that narrative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, they haven't happened, but it's possible to imagine things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in the meantime, yes, we're watching it extremely carefully, like everyone is, but don't see really much evidence of it in the actual economic data yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And by the way, consumers keep spending, credit card spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-you know, it's still-it's still a healthy economy, albeit one that is shrouded in some very downbeat sentiment on the part of people and businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-well, I mean, there are a couple-that's not really beyond the confines of our mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-look, I would say this: We-you know, we did things-essentially, we were on an emergency footing for a couple of years in the pandemic, and it's very fair and very welcome for people to look back over what we did and say, "Hey, you could have done this better and different."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And one thing we hear a lot is, we could have explained the QE a little better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did think we were explaining it in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I completely accept the, the thought that we could have explained it better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a lot of thinking that we went on too long with QE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can tell you that the reason we did was, we were-we were concerned that we didn't want a tightening of-a sharp tightening in financial conditions at a time when we thought the economy was still vulnerable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we did hold on for a long time to QE.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we immediately went into QT, and, you know, we've-we're down a couple of trillion.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I get the-that, you know, we, we certainly, with the benefit of hindsight, could have tapered earlier or faster.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's, it's-you know, we knew, doing this in real time, that we weren't going to get it perfect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those kind of-those kind of, you know, after-action kind of looks are essential.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're doing the same thing in-you know, in our review, so-on some issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, okay, on climate, you've heard me say over and over again that we will not be climate policymakers and that our role on climate is a very, very narrow one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You can say that was-that little bit that we've done was too much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I wouldn't want to give any impression that, that, you know, we take-that we've taken climate in and it's something that we're spending a lot of time and energy on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did one thing, one guidance for the banks, and then we did one-a one-time stress analysis, climate stress analysis, and that's it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we dropped out of the Network for Greening the Financial System.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we didn't do much on climate, but-and I do think, and I've said this publicly several times, I think it's, it's a real danger for us to try to take on a mandate like that, which is very narrow application to our work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the risk is, if you-if you go for things that are really not on your mandate, you know, then why are you independent?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I do think we've done a whole lot less on climate than some people seem to think we did.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we said-what we said was that we never targeted any unemployment rate for individual racial or demographic groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we said was that maximum employment was a broad and inclusive goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think what we meant by that was, we're going to consider the totality of the country as we look at our maximum- employment goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we were never going to target on any individual group with that, but I think some people, you know, wanted to hear it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-so that's just not a correct reading of our-but I can see how, you know, maybe people found that confusing, and, you know, we have to take that into consideration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, you know, so we really don't see in the data yet big economic effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We see-we see sentiment, their concerns that higher prices may be coming, or things like that, but-so people, they're worried now about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're worried about, you know, a shock from the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Okay, so, you know, we're going to be looking at not just the sentiment data, but also the real economic data as we assess what it is we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One of them would be weakening economy-weakening economic activity, which translates into higher unemployment, and the other would be potentially higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, to say it again, the timing, the scope, the scale, and the persistence of those effects are very, very uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not at all clear what the appropriate response for monetary policy is at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're- you know-and by the way, our policy's in a good place, so we think we can wait and move when it is clear what the right thing to do is; really not at all clear what it is we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people are feeling stress and concern, but unemployment hasn't gone up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, people are not-layoffs are-people are not getting laid off at high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, initial claims for unemployment are not increasing, you know, in any kind of impressive way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the economy itself is still, you know, in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we don't do a Summary of Economic Projections at every meeting, as you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so this was the meeting when we didn't do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I-you know, we don't also kind of poll people, so I really-I really wouldn't want to try to make a specific projection for where we are relative to that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will-in six weeks, we have the June meeting, and you'll have another SEP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not going to hazard a guess here today what-as to what it would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, what I would say is that we think our policy rate is in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think it leaves us well positioned to respond in a timely way to potential developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's where we are, and that-depending on the way things play out, that could include rate hikes-sorry, rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it could include us holding where we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just are going to need to see, you know, how things play out before we make those decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, you just captured the-this is the issue with the two goals being in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, there can be a case in which one goal is very far-one variable's very far from its goal, much farther than the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, frankly, that was the case-well, it wasn't a case where they were really in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you go back to 2022, it was very clear that we needed to focus on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market was also super tight, so it wasn't really a tradeoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, if-I think you know what our-what our framework document says.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It says we'll look at how far each goal-each variable is from its goal and also we'll factor in the time it would take to get there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, that's going to be a-potentially, a very difficult judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the data could break in a way that it's not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And right now, there's no way to-no need to make a choice and no real basis for doing so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-they're going to do-we take what they do as a given, and we put it in our models and in our assessment of the economy, so I wouldn't want to, you know, speculate on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, I think we do know that the debt is on an unsustainable level-on an unsustainable path-not on an unsustainable level, but an unsustainable path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's on Congress to figure out how to get us back on a sustainable path, and, you know, it's not up to us to give them advice.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think they don't need my advice and our advice on how to do fiscal policy any more than we need their advice on monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What was happening last year is that over the space of six, eight, seven months, the unemployment rate went up by almost a full percentage point, and it was click, click, click, click, click each month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, everywhere, people were talking about downside risks to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, payroll job numbers were getting softer and softer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there was a really obvious concern about downside risk to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so at Jackson Hole and then in September, you know, we wanted to address that forthrightly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We wanted to show that we were there for the-I mean, we had been there for inflation for a couple of years, and we wanted to show also that we're there for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Fortunately, since then, the labor market has really-and the unemployment rate have really been moving sideways at a level that is, you know, well in the range of mainstream estimates of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now we have a situation where, you know, the risks to higher inflation and higher unemployment have both gone up, as we noted in our statement, and we've got to monitor both of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We actually have a potential situation where there may be a tradeoff or tension between the two potentially.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't have it yet, and we may not have it, but that's what we [may] have, and that's why I think it's a very different, different situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I can't give you a-you know, a-I'm not going to try to give you a specific number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll just say, we've got-we have to now be looking at both variables and which of them is, is, you know, demanding-if one of them is demanding our focus more than the other, that would tell us what to do with policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If they're more or less this, you know, equally distant and equally-or not distant, then we don't have to make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm not going to try to be really specific about what we need to see in terms of the number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if-look, if we did see, you know, significant deterioration in the labor market, of course that's one of our two variables, and we would look to be able to support that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You'd hope that it wasn't also coming at a time when inflation was getting very bad.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're just going to have to wait and see how the-how it plays out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, these are not talks that we're in any way involved in, so I really can't comment directly on them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but what I will say is this: You know, we had-coming out of the March meeting, we, we-the public generally had an assessment of where tariffs were going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then April 2 happened, and it was really substantially larger than anticipated in the forecasts that I've seen and in our forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and now we-and now we have a different-we're in a new phase where-it seems to be we're entering a new phase where the Administration is entering into beginning talks with a number of our important trading partners.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-that has the potential to change the picture materially or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think it's going to be very important how that shakes out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I-you know, we simply have to wait and see how it works out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It certainly could change the picture, and we're mindful of not trying to make conclusive judgments about what will happen at a time when the-you know, when the facts are changing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I don't want to get my-we're not-we shouldn't be involved, even verbally, in questions about the timing of these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I know they're- as you can see, they're, again, having-beginning to have talks with many nations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that has the potential to change the picture materially, so we'll just have to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Okay, so, I mean, I think we-I think we think that the-you know, there was a big spike in imports-right?-very big, historically large, really, and-to beat tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now that should actually reverse so that it's-you know, it's the difference between-it's exports minus imports, so-and imports were huge, and so then it conveyed a very negative contribution to U.S. GDP-annualized GDP in the first quarter, as we all know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that could, in the second quarter, be reversed so that we have, you know, an unusually large contribution to- unusually positive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You could also have-you know, very likely you'll have restatements of the-of the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think it's going- this whole process is going to, a little bit, make it harder to make a clean assessment of U.S. demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mentioned private domestic final purchases, which doesn't have inventories, government, or-inventories, government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that, that, too, probably was flattered a little bit by-you know, by strong demand for imports to be tariffed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a really good reading, 3 percent PDFP in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not really going to-I don't think it's going to affect our decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will just say, though, that it's a little confusing and it's probably less confusing to us than it would be to the general public as we try to explain this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's complicated, and, you know, GDP is sending a signal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think we understand what's going, and it's not really going to change things for us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, it's-look, the-look at the state of the economies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's no real cost to our waiting at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Also, the sense of it-the sense of it is, we're not sure what the right thing will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so until we know- potentially call for different responses-and so, you know, until we know more, we have the ability to wait and see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think, going back a number of years, the link between sentiment data and consumer spending has been weak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other hand, we haven't had a move of this, you know, speed and size.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it wouldn't be the case that we're looking at this and just completely dismissing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're right that we had a couple of years during the pandemic where people were saying-just very downbeat surveys and going out and spending money.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that can happen, and that may happen to some degree here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is an outsized change in sentiment, though, and so none of us are looking at this and saying that we're sure one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, we don't have, you know, the kind of tools that are good at dealing with supply chain problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's a-that's a job for the Administration and for the private sector more than anything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, what we can do with our interest rate tool is, we can support-be more or less supportive of demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's- that'd be a very inefficient way to try to fix supply chain problems.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we don't see-we don't see the inflation yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're, of course, reading the same stories and watching the same data as everybody else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, right now, we see inflation, you know, kind of moving sideways at a fairly low level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: My whole focus is on- and my colleagues' focus is all on, you know, trying to navigate this tricky passage we're in right now, trying to make the right decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we want to make the best decisions for the people that we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is a challenging situation, and that's, that's 100 percent of our focus right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've never asked for a meeting with any President, and I never will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's never a reason for me to ask for a meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's always an initiative-I-you know, I don't think it's up to a Fed Chair to seek a meeting with the President, although maybe some have done so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've never done so, and I can't imagine myself doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-I think it's always-comes the other way: A President wants to meet with you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think once you have a direction-a clear direction, you can make a-we can make a judgment about how fast to move and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's- really, the harder question is the timing, I think, and when will that become clear?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, fortunately, as I mentioned, we have our policy in a good place, the economy's in a good place, and it's really appropriate, we think, for us to be patient and wait for things to unfold as we get more clarity about what we should do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've had three months of, of favorable inflation readings since the high readings of January and February, and that's, of course, highly welcome news.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Part of that just is that services, core services-both housing services and nonhousing services have really been grinding down toward levels that are-that are consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had goods inflation just moving up a bit, and, of course, we expect-as you-as you point out, we, we do expect to see more of that over the course of the summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It takes some time for tariffs to work their way through the chain of distribution to the end consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A good example of that would be, goods being sold at retailers today may have been imported several months ago-before tariffs were imposed-so we're beginning to see some effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do expect to see more of them over coming months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do-we do also see price increases in some of the relevant categories like personal computers and audio-visual equipment-things like that that are attributable to tariff increases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, we look at surveys of businesses, and there, there are many of those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and, you, you do see a range of things, but, but many, many companies do expect to-to, to put all or-some or all of the effect of tariffs through to the next, next person in the-in the chain and, ultimately, to the consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Today-you know, the amount of these-the, the amount of the tariff effects, the size of the tariff effects, their duration, and the time it will take are all highly uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that, that is why we think the appropriate thing to do is to hold where we are as we learn more, and we think our policy stance is, is in a good place-where we're well positioned to react to incoming developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you look at the forecast, you will see that people do generally expect inflation to move up and then to come back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, we don't know that, and, you know, our, our job is to make sure-one of our jobs-to make sure that a one-time increase in inflation doesn't turn into an inflation problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that, again-that will depend on the size of the effects, how long it takes for them to come in, and, and, ultimately, on, on keeping inflation expectations anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would focus most on the-on the nearer term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you think-as you get out to the-to the later years, it's hard to-it's hard for anybody to know where the economy is going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You didn't see people moving their longer-term, you know, estimate of the neutral rate, for example, at this meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think-I think if you look at what's happening here since March-this is since March, right?- you see a little slower growth, just a tiny tick up, one-tenth tick up, in, in unemployment, and you see inflation moving up three-tenths.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And by the way, it was-it was a similar move from the December SEP to the March.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we learned in April, after the March meeting, that substantially higher tariffs were likely, and then since then, the estimates of where the tariffs will be have actually moved back down, although still at an elevated level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're adapting in real time, and what you see is, you know, an, an accumulation of individual assessments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we said was that uncertainty has, has-uncertainty about the economic outlook has diminished but remains elevated.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and, and, that's-that's actually a line from the Tealbook, which you can see in five years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No-but if you think of that, tariff uncertainty-uncertainty really peaked in April and since then has come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do-we do, of course, monitor all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think if you look at the overall picture, you know, what you're seeing is 4. percent unemployment and an economy that's growing at a-at a rate hard to know, given the, the unusual flows in the first quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it appears to be 1½, 2 percent-maybe a little better than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Sentiment has come up off of its very low levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, you can-you can point to things-the housing market is a longer-run problem and also a short-run problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think it's indicative of-you know, basically, the situation is, we have a longer-run shortage of housing, and we also have high rates right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the best thing we can do for the housing market is to restore price stability in a sustainable way and, and create a strong labor market, and that's the best thing we can do for the housing market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You asked about the job market-again, look at labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I would say you can see perhaps a very, very slow continued cooling, but nothing that's troubling at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we watch it-we watch it very, very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, again, the current stance of monetary policy leaves us well positioned to respond in a timely way to economic developments, and-for now-and we'll be watching the data carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this is very much the conversation we had today and yesterday.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There, there are many, many different scenarios-many combinations of scenarios where inflation does or doesn't prove out to be at the levels we think and where the labor market does or doesn't soften.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think what, what you see people doing is looking ahead at a time of very high uncertainty and writing down what they think the most likely case is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No one holds these, these rate paths with a great deal of conviction, and everyone would agree that they're all going to be data dependent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that-you can make a case for, for any of the rate paths, I think, that you see in, in the SEP. And, you know, we do this once a quarter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-it's a hard thing to do at this-particularly at this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it does reflect-you know, if you see somebody writing down, you know, a, a rate path that involves cuts, that's them saying, "Yes, I think we will get to a place, more likely than not, where cuts will be appropriate."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it could be-it could be a joint probability of a number of possible outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's-it's-again, it's very, very hard to say when that will happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that the time will come; it come-could come quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As long as the economy is solid, though-as long as we're seeing the kind of labor market that we have and reasonably decent growth and inflation moving down, we feel like the right thing to do is to be where we are, with where our policy stance is, and just learn more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in particular, we feel like we're going to learn a great deal more over the summer on tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do-we hadn't expected them to show up much by now, and they haven't, and we will see whether-the extent to which they do over, over coming months.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's going to inform our thinking, for one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, meanwhile, we'll be watching, watching the labor market very carefully for signs of weakness and strength and tariffs for signs of, of what's going to happen there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, there are many developments ahead, you know, even in the near term-developments are expected on tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we, we don't yet know with any confidence where they will settle out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have an estimate, and it's a pretty-I think all estimates are now pretty close together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, what you start with is, is-what's the effective tariff rate overall?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, the, the pass-through of tariffs to consumer price inflation is a whole process that's very uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, as you know, there are many parties in that chain: There's the manufacturer, the exporter, the importer, the retailer, and the consumer, and each one of those is going to be trying not to be the one to, to pay for the tariff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But together, they will all pay for it together-or maybe one party will pay it all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that process is very hard to predict, and we haven't been through a situation like this, and I think we have to be humble about our ability to forecast it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's why we need to see some actual data to have-to make better decisions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We, we'd like to get some, some more data, and, and, again, in the meantime, we can do that because the economy remains in solid condition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right, we-and, as is often the case, we have a pretty healthy diversity of views on the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We did have strong support for today's decision and broad agreement that our policy stance does leave us in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would point to two factors, and you mentioned them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The first is just that parties have a diversity of forecasts, and, and they do align with, with where-with where their dots are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you have a higher inflation forecast, you're going to be less likely to be writing down, you know, more, more cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as-remember, as we see more data, we're going to learn more about where inflation is headed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means when it is time to look at, at normal-at sort of, at, you know- resuming our normalization process, the differences you may-you see should be smaller because we'll have seen actual data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, it's just a forecast in a very foggy time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Secondly, people can look at the same data, and they can evaluate the risks differently, as you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that includes, you know, the, the risk of higher inflation, the risk it'll be more persistent, the risk that the labor market will weaken-people are going to have different assessments of that risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those are the two ways that, that-the two things, I think, that drive these things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Remember, though, with-as I mentioned earlier- with uncertainty as elevated as it is, no one holds these rate paths with a lot of conviction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a function of those things, and I think as the data come in, you should see those differences diminish.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you just look backward at the data, that, that's what you would say, but that's not-we have to be forward looking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the thing that every forecaster-every outside forecaster and the Fed is saying is that we expect a meaningful amount of inflation to arrive in coming months, and we have to take that into account.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think a backward-looking look would, would lead you to a neutral stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we, we can't-we have to-we have to look at that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And because the economy is still solid, we can take the time to actually see what's going to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It, it's, you know, the-there's a range of possibilities on how, how large the, the inflation effects and the other effects are going to be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll make smarter and better decisions if we just wait a couple of months or however long it takes to get a sense of, of really what, what is going to be the pass-through of inflation and what're-what's going to be the effects on spending and on hiring and all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What everyone on the FOMC wants is a good, solid American economy with a strong labor market and, and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think our policy is well positioned to-right now to, to deliver that and, and to be able to respond in a timely way as the data lead us around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy's been resilient, and part of that is our stance, and, again, we think we're-we're in a good place on that to respond to significant economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is what matters to us-pretty much, that's all that matters to us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What-one way to get at that from an economic standpoint-we, of course, don't comment on immigration policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what you see is a-an, an unemployment rate that has been really solid and at a low level-not really increasing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been in a-in a good range and well within the range of mainstream estimates of maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means, like, part of that is that labor demand and labor supply are kind of moving down at the same rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Labor demand is, is softening-you see that in job creation-but it's still kind of at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And labor supply is, is diminishing because the, the immigration numbers that we see are, are much lower than they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-those two factors, supply and demand-that's what has kept the, the unemployment rate in a reasonably, you know, stable place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we, we've said that we would finish that and announce it by the end of the summer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've had the meetings that we need to have, and we're now going to be going into [cough]-pardon me-into discussions about, you know, specific changes to language.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The second part of it is our communications tools and practices [cough]-pardon me-and that, that part comes next, okay?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's what we're going to do in the meetings this fall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Actually, what we did at this meeting, though, is we, we sort of prepared the ground for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had a-we had a meeting where we talked at a high level about a number of ideas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The SEP is part of it-you know, other-many, many other ideas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-it's sort of- how do we think our communications can be improved?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Number of ideas-but we're-we're going to look at those with staff briefing and a lot of thought in the fall.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, when it comes to changing communications, you know, I would only do-I would only support things really that only-implement things that have very broad support.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, you want to be really careful, because I think our communications are pretty well received.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're not broken, so more is not necessarily better-but better is better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to be looking at ways to do-to do things that will improve the clarity of what we do for the benefit of, of the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, the, the forecast for inflation in December was 2½ core PCE for 2025-the forecast was 2½ percent-which is a good inflation forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think what we've learned is that-and this was long before we had any idea of what the actual policies would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've learned the tariffs are going to be substantially larger than, than forecasters generally thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we, we don't-our, our forecasts are generally not particularly different from those of other, you know, well-resourced forecasting operations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what we learned-and particularly in April-was that substantially larger tariffs were coming and that that would mean higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so you-now you see-you saw 2½ percent forecast in December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw 2. percent in March, and you see 3. percent now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's six-tenths higher inflation for 2025, and that's-that's a big part of, of the change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-that's due to the effects of, of the tariffs that are-you know, we, we don't know where they're going to land, but it's pretty apparent they're going to land higher than outside forecasters were really guessing at the end of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: My follow-up to that-I think consumers-right?-were looking for relief on rates when it comes to mortgages-car loans.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When you look at the cumulative inflation over the past five years, prices have risen over 20 percent-it's been a rough road.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what is the tipping point, then, for the wait-and-see approach in terms of how much it's going to help versus when it hurts the American consumer?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I mean, we're trying to restore price-the best thing we can do for the-for the public that we serve is restore price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we can, and we will, restore price stability, meaning 2 percent inflation on a durable, sustainable basis-that and also maximum employment-and if we, we restore those things, that's the best thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The best thing we can do for the American people-for, for households and businesses- that is the ultimate thing that we can deliver.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they can make their decisions without having to think about inflation all the time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, in the meantime, we have to keep rates high to keep-to get inflation all the way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say policy is modestly or moderately-probably modestly now-restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at the economy, it's not performing as though it were performing under very strict monetary policy-very restrictive monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say probably modestly restrictive-and so what it will take is, is confidence that inflation is coming down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, I would say, without tariffs, that confidence would be building because if you-if you see what's happening with nonhousing services and housing services, which are the other two big pieces other than goods, those are coming down really nicely now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we have to learn a little more about, about tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know-I don't know what the right way for us to react will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's hard to know with, with any confidence how we should react until we see, really, the size of the effects-then we can start to make a better judgment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's what we're doing, and I think we can-we can take the time to do that, because unemployment is 4. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Real wages are moving up at a-at a healthy clip now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a good economy, and a solid economy with decent growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, from our standpoint, what I can say is that the, the U.S. economy is in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a- it's a good-job creation is at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Unemployment, again, as I said, low-labor force participation at a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're waiting for to reduce rates is, is to understand what will happen with, with, really, the tariff inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Every forecaster you can name who, you know-who is a professional, you know, forecaster with, with adequate resources and forecasts for a living is forecasting, you know, a pretty significant-everyone that I know is forecasting a meaningful increase in inflation in coming months from tariffs because someone has to pay for the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it will be someone in that chain that I mentioned: Between the manufacturer, the exporter, the importer, the retailer- ultimately, somebody putting it into a, a good of some kind or just the consumer buying it-and, you know, all through that, that chain, people will be trying not to be the ones who, who pick up the cost.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, the cost of the tariff has to be paid.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And some of it will fall on the end consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know that because that's what businesses say-that's what the, the data say from past-so we know that's coming.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we just want to see, see a little bit of that before we make judgments prematurely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, I mean, you're-monetary policy has to be forward looking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got to be looking-I always-we always talk about the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We say that over and over and over again, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, if you know-at the very beginning of the pandemic, you know, we cut rates to zero immediately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just knew that it was going to be really bad, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we took very aggressive forward looking-because we knew things were going to be unusually difficult.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, this, this is something we, we sort of know is coming-we just don't know the size of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, the economy seems to be in solid shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the labor market's not crying out for a rate cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Businesses, you know, were in a bit of shock after April 2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you see business sentiment-you talk to business people now-there's a very different feeling now that people are working their way through this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they, they understand how they're going to go, and it's-it, it feels much more positive and constructive than it did three months ago, let's say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, again, we think that our current stance of monetary policy is in a good place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't see them at all as, as in tension.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so I was asked, "Is the Fed overstaffed?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, and I sort of said as a pun, "Overworked, but not overstaffed."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People do work extremely hard at the Fed, and I know they work hard at Bloomberg, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say this-so we are careful stewards of public resources, and sometimes you need to show that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there've been several times in our history-modern history-where the Fed has said, "You know what?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to demonstrate that we are good stewards of public resources."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we thought-and I, I thought- that this is a time when we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we've-we grow about-our headcount has grown at about 1 percent a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So over the course of a couple of years, we're going to-we're doing a careful scrub of the Board and all of the Reserve Banks, and we're going to find 10 percent of employees who can do something else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Where, where we can-we can streamline our operations-and we, we think we can get there in a year, in a couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think the-we think the, the-this is, this is without taking risk to carrying out our critical missions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you do it, again, respecting that we have critical missions to carry out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I've had experience-a lot of experience-in my prior careers, you know, with headcount reductions and things like that, and this is how you do it professionally.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You do it carefully-thoughtfully-with a lot of planning, and you do it over a period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I, I think it's-I think the Fed will be fine.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think no one will notice any decline in our ability to carry out our missions, and I think it's just us wanting to demonstrate to the public that we are actually good stewards of their-of their resources.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-we're effectively wiping out 10 years of headcount growth with this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I mean, we just-we wanted to show that, you know-that we're good stewards.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think many organizations find that they can-that they can do this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You don't want to do it every year or anything, but you can do it at intervals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you, you wind up not, you know-not interfering with your ability to perform your jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so, you know, we don't-we don't sit around and debate or really discuss-we, we take fiscal policy as fully exogenous.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we, we actually, you know, really didn't talk about, about the bill or the contents of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, when, when it gets close-closer-remember also we have a very, very large economy, and that the effects will be at the margin.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I, I expect that they'll-they may already be in- but they will be in by the next meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's not a major thing; it's nothing that we discuss.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It, it may have been mentioned a couple of times-but as something that's coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think the outcome is-you know, we don't know the outcome yet there-so, hard to be real specific.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, two things-one, the data we get right now-we, we can do our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The point, really, is that we are starting to see, you know, layoffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and important gatherers of data are saying that they're-they're having to cut back on the size of their surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's going to lead to more volatility in the surveys.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, from our standpoint-and I think the standpoint of businesses and governments and everyone-having really good data on the state of the economy at any given time is a huge public good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It helps the government, it helps Congress, it helps the executive branch.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They need to know what's going on in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The United States has been a leader for many, many years in this whole project of measuring and understanding what's happening in, in our very large and dynamic economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I hate to see-I hate to see us cutting back on that because it, it is a real benefit to the general public that people in all kinds of jobs have the best possible understanding of what's happening in the economy and, and, hence, what's likely to happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's very hard to measure what's going on in the U.S. economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If, if you read-there was a book called-well, it's really remarkable how many things you need to understand to estimate U.S. GDP.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Very, very difficult-and it's so important that we get it right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I just would-I just would say it's not a place to-I would want to keep investing in that, you know, for the good of the general public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the framework goes back to-the framework document goes back to 2012, and it's-it's the Committee's document.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not like we're going to invent a brand new way to do things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-it's been an evolving document, so it shouldn't depend on who the Chair is at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It should depend on what's happening in the economy and what the Committee wants to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, yeah, it isn't really tied to any particular Chair, and, you know, we used to renew it every year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-but I, I don't think anybody- I've never heard anyone raise this issue that, you know, a new Chair might want to come in and go in a completely different direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, that's not-not going to be up to me to decide.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, we're watching-like everybody else is-what's going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, possible that, that we'll see higher energy prices-what's tended to happen is, when there's turmoil in the Middle East, you may see a spike in energy prices-but tends to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those things don't generally tend to have lasting effects on inflation, although, of course, in the 1970s, they famously did, because you had a series of very, very large shocks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The U.S. economy is far less dependent on foreign oil than it was back in the 1970s.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The question really is, will AI be more augmenting labor or replacing labor?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I wouldn't-I, I-we all see those announcements, including one today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't overread a, a couple of data points, because, you know, AI should be creating jobs at the same time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Anyone who's done any work with it-with AI-will, will have been a little bit stunned at how capable it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think this is something that certainly has transformational potential-and probably we're in the very early stages of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They say what you're seeing now compared to what you'll see in two years is, is going to be very different and even more effective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, of course, there are optimists who feel like it's going to make everybody much more, you know-much more productive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are those who think it's going to replace an awful lot of jobs right across the income spectrum-you know, white collar, blue collar, and everything.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But this is-this is going to be a very important question for some time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-it's certainly a time of real change-you know, from a geopolitical standpoint, from a trade standpoint, from an immigration standpoint-you see this not just here, but everywhere.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't change the way we do monetary policy in the near term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, but-and it doesn't change our objectives or what we need to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, these, these things are not really our issues-they're really issues for elected governments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's no question it's a time of, of real, real change-and very hard to see where that goes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Will it be-there have been many, many things written about how it's going to be a more inflationary time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, AI could cut in a very other direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: AI could make people much more productive and-and push in the other direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you're right, but, honestly, our focus is, is a much more practical one, and that is, how do we keep inflation low and, and employment high in the near term?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't, you don't see-you don't really see unemployment going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You don't see increased slack, really-I mean, at the margin.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That, that was for many, many years-that was an extremely low level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It happens to have come up off of an even lower level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As we came out of the pandemic, we were as low as 3. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But 4. percent is probably at the low end of estimates of the longer-run, you know, sustainable level of natural rate of unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, in terms of wages-you know, real wages after inflation have been moving up sort of more than was consistent with 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're still moving up at a-at a healthy clip-and I think much more consistent with 2 percent inflation, given, given a, a reasonable assessment of, of trend productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, you're right that the level of job creation has come down, but so has the supply of workers-the change in the supply-the, the new supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you've seen-you've seen the unemployment rate remain pretty stable at 4.2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been as high as 4.3, but, you know, those are-those are good numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's-the thing is, there's-a more concerning thing is, there's not-there are not a lot of layoffs, but there are not a lot of, of job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The number-if you're out of work, it's-it's hard to find a job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But very few people are being laid off at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-an equilibrium we watch very, very carefully, because if there were to be, you know, significant layoffs and the job-finding rate were to remain this low, you would have a lot-you would have an increase in unemployment fairly quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're-so the U.S. economy has defied all kinds of forecasts for it to, to weaken, really, over the last three years, and it's been remarkable to see-just again and again when people think it's going to weaken out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Eventually it will, but we don't see signs of that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there are a number of people on the Committee who wrote down no cuts this year but some cuts next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, look, I think, you know, people are writing down their most likely path, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're not saying there's zero possibility of other things, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, it's-think of it as the least unlikely path in a situation like this where uncertainty is very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I think-again, people write-they write down their, their rate paths, and they do not have, like, a really high conviction that this is exactly what's going to happen over the next two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They feel like, "What am I going to write down?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not easy to, to be-to do that with confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't rule things in or out-certainly, a hike is not the base case at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in the meantime, we do the best we can with these forecasts, and I, I think they're-they're representative of, you know, of the different forecasts and different reaction functions that people on the Committee have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you know, today we decided to leave our policy rate where it's been, which-where I would characterize as modestly restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Inflation is running a bit above 2 percent, as I mentioned, even excluding tariff effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Financial conditions are accommodative, and the economy is not-the economy is not performing as though restrictive policy were holding it back inappropriately.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it seems to, to me and to almost the whole Committee that the economy is not performing as though restrictive policy is holding it back inappropriately, and modestly restrictive policy seems appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All that said, there's also downside risk to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In coming months, we'll receive a good amount of data that will help inform our assessment of the balance of risks and the appropriate setting of the federal funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do have-this is an, an, an intermeeting period when we'll get two full rounds of employment and inflation data before the time of the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have made no decisions about September-we don't do that in advance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be taking that information into consideration and all the other information we get as we make our decision at the September meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, essentially, the statement in the-in the-in our statement about uncertainty reflects what's gone on since the last meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, at the time of the last meeting, uncertainty had, had, had moved down a little bit, but it was more or less even this time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we took out, you know, "had diminished" because it didn't diminish further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, I think we're still-so you're right, it's been a very dynamic time for these trade negotiations, and lots and lots of events in the intermeeting period, but we're still, you know, a ways away from seeing where things settle down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I think at this point, people's estimates, our estimates, outside estimates of the-of the likely, you know, effective, effective level of tariffs is, is not moving around that much at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But at the same time, there are many, many uncertainties left to resolve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't feel like we're very close to the end of that process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, that's not for us to judge, but it does-it feels like there's much more to come, you know, as well looking ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the GDP and PDFP numbers came in pretty much right where we expected them to come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, certainly, as I mentioned in my opening remarks, economic activity data, GDP, private domestic final purchases-which we think is a narrower but better signal for future, for where the economy is going-has come down to a little better than 1 percent, 1. percent I think, in the case of GDP for the first half, whereas it was 2½ last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you look at the labor market, what you see is, by many, many statistics, the labor market is kind of still in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's things like quits, you know, job openings, and-let alone the unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're all very-by many measures, very similar to where they were a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you do not see a weakening in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You do see a slowing in job creation, but also in a slowing-a slowing in the supply of workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you've got a labor market that's in balance, albeit partially because both demand and supply for workers has-is coming down at the same pace, and that's why the unemployment rate has remained roughly, roughly stable, which is why I said there-we do see downside risk in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, our two-our two mandate variables- right?-are inflation and maximum employment-stable prices and maximum employment, not so much growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And even if you-if you look through the tariff effects, we think it's still a bit above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, as I mentioned, you know, downside risks to the labor market are certainly apparent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the, the main number you have to look at now is the unemployment rate, because if, if-it's true that the, you know, demand for workers in the form of, let's call it-say-just say, payroll jobs-that number has come down, but so has the breakeven number, kind of in tandem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, as long as the-that puts the labor market in, in balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The fact that it's getting into balance due to declines in both supply and demand, though, I think does-it is suggestive of downside risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So on, on the dissents, you know, what you-what you want from everybody and also from a dissenter is a clear explanation for-of what your thinking is and what are the arguments you're making.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think, basically, this was-this was quite a good meeting all around the table where people were-you know, thought carefully about this and put their positions out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, you know, the, the-sort of the majority of the Committee was of the view that inflation's a bit above target, maximum employment is at target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That calls for modestly restrictive-in my way of thinking, a modestly restrictive stance of policy for now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we had two dissenters who, I think-you know, you want that clear thinking and, and, and, you know, expression of your thinking, and we certainly had that today, I think all around the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of-you asked about the June SEP. You know, I wouldn't-you're right that that's what it-that's what it says, and that may-that may well-I, I couldn't point to it six weeks later as, as expressing people's thought-you really can't do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't run an SEP, and I don't like to substitute in my own estimate of what the SEP might be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'll just say that, you know, we, we haven't made any decisions about September.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We'll be monitoring all the incoming data and asking ourselves whether the federal funds rate is in the right place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me say, my own estimate is modestly restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there are-there are a range of views of what the neutral rate is at this moment for, for our economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so others may say it's more restrictive or less restrictive even.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're-we're going to be-at some point, when we return to moving toward a more neutral stance, we'll be making that judgment as we go.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not so mechanical as saying, you know, "We've derived with great confidence the neutral rate, and that is our destination," because, really, we understand that no one actually knows what the neutral rate is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We know it by its works, and that will be how-the way the economy reacts over time to-you know, to slightly looser policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you have to think of this as still quite early days.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I think what we're seeing now is substantial amounts of tariff revenue being collected, on the order of $30 billion a month, which is, you know, substantially higher than, than before.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the evidence seems to be, mostly not paid, but paid only to a small extent, through exporters lowering their price.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And companies or retailers, sort of people who are upstream-institutions that are upstream from the consumer, are paying most of this for now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, in the June report, we expect to see more of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we know from surveys that companies feel that they have every intention of, of, of putting this through to the consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, the truth is, they may not be able to in many cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's-we're just going to have to watch and learn empirically how much of this and over what period of time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we've learned that the process will probably be slower than, than expected at the beginning, but we never expected it to be fast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think we have a long way to go to really understand exactly how we'll be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You could argue we are, a bit, "looking through" goods inflation by not raising rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I don't think-I think the base case-I said-as I said, a reasonable base case is that these are one-time-one-time price effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, in the end, there, there will not be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This will not turn out to be inflation, because we'll make sure that it's not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We will, through our tools, make sure that this does not move from being a one-time price increase to serious inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means we want to do it-if you-if you move too soon, you wind up maybe not getting inflation all the way fixed, and you have to come back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you move too late, you might do too-unnecessary damage to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there won't be, in the end, a big inflationary problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we're trying to do is accomplish that in a way that is efficient.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in the end, there should be no doubt that we will do what we need to do to keep inflation under control.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, let me just-ritual disclaimer that we don't express any judgments or anything, right, on, on fiscal legislation or other legislation, for that matter.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say, when you think that, you know, the biggest part of the bill was, was making permanent existing law on, on taxes, I don't think we see it as particularly stimulative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There should be some stimulative effect, but it shouldn't be significant over the next couple of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: No, that's-you know, we, we have a mandate, and that's maximum employment and price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it is-it's not something we do, to consider the cost to the government of our rate changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to be able to look at the goal variables Congress has given us-use the tools they have given us to achieve those goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-we don't consider the fiscal needs of the federal government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it wouldn't be good for-if we did do that, it would be good neither for our credibility nor for the credibility of U.S. fiscal policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's just not something we, we take into consideration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, we had a-we had a nice visit with the President.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not something that happens very often at the Federal Reserve-to have the President come over, let alone to visit a building-but it was-it was a good visit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we-this project was hatched and conceived almost a decade ago now, and we went through the very long process of clearing it through historic preservation at the National Capital Planning Commission and a lot of back-and-forth there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We started out to do the work, and we're very well along on that work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I was quite pleased to have the President say multiple times that what he really wanted to see was, was us getting this construction completed as soon as possible.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is our focus, and that's what we're going to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So inflation-when you talk about these 12-month inflation measures, you're always battling residual seasonality.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll have, for example, two months of high inflation, sometimes early in the year, and then inflation turns lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And a lot of that may just be an artifact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-look, I think inflation is most of the way back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, for example, all the insurance costs that are now-they're only now going through inflation, but they actually reflect inflationary pressures from two, three years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, now we have, you know, three- or four-tenths of inflation in core inflation from tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're not going to have a separate, you know, kind of inflation that isn't the tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're always going to be dealing with the whole-all of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, if you go back to the last couple of years, it was all about services inflation, which was being very sticky.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Goods inflation was well behaved before, and now goods inflation is going up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also partially because we had restrictive policy in place, and we-and we've seen that-the result of that gradually work its way through the services economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think-as I've said, I think that we-you know, we're, we're getting the data that we need to do our jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it's really important that, that good data helps not just the Fed-it helps the government, but it also helps the private sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, people in the economy-they, they use this data a lot, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's quite important for our economy and, certainly, for the Fed's work and other government agencies' work that we-that we continue to get better at data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's very hard to accurately capture in real time the output of a $20-plus trillion economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the United States has been a leader in that for 100 years, and we really need to continue that, in my view.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, what, what may be giving-it's not our policy stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What may be giving-some companies will certainly be taking advantage of the fact of the tariffs and all of the discussion of how they're going to-you know, companies will raise prices when and as they can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you-so you saw it famously in the-in the-in the first Administration of President Trump, during those tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Price-the price of dryers went up, too, just like washing machines.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So companies will often just take-they'll cross the street in a group, if you know what I mean.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, what we see now is basically the very beginnings of whatever the effects turn out to be on goods inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I'll say again, they may be-they may be less than, than people estimate or more than people estimate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we're just going to have to, to see it through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, so the housing-the housing is a-is a special case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our-we don't set-we don't set mortgage rates at the Fed, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We set an overnight rate, and the rates that go into mortgages are longer-term rates, like Treasury rates-it might be 30-year rates, it might be shorter than that, but it's not the overnight Fed's rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do have an effect, but we're not the main effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are other things go-though, going on in the housing sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And one of those is just, there's kind of a long-term housing shortage that we have.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is not something the Fed can help with, but then that'll be the case even after things normalize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I, I think the best thing that we can do for housing is to have 2 percent inflation and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are lots of other jobs to do for the private sector and Congress, but that's what we're trying to get to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, I mean, we've made a lot of progress toward that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're in-we have a very good labor market right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're seeing some goods inflation move us away but, so far, not very far away.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, ultimately, it's-it could be any-it could be any of those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, but, you know, if you saw that the risks to the two goals were moving into balance, if they were fully in balance, that would imply that you should move toward a more-a more neutral stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is-this is the special situation we're in, which is, we have two-sided risk, risk to both of our goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we paused, inflation was above target, and the labor market was pretty good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, so, you know, that was a time when policy-policy was restrictive when we paused.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And to be restrictive is to be-to be supporting a return to our inflation target, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So as the two targets get back into balance, you would-you would think you'd move in, in, in a way closer to neutral and that the next-the next steps that we take are likely to be in that direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it'll just take-it'll be the totality of the evidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I mentioned, there's quite a lot of data coming in, which, before the next meeting, will it be dispositive of that?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's-as I mentioned, you know, a pretty reasonable base case is that this will be a one-time price increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, in the end, we'll make sure that that's the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
