text: We're-and "efficiently" means getting the timing right so we don't-again, if we go-if we cut rates too soon, maybe we didn't finish the job with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you cut too late, then maybe you're doing unnecessary damage to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're trying to-we're trying to get that timing right, and that's effectively what we're doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this goes back to the division of labor between the Fed and the Treasury-as you, I'm sure, know-and, you know, the, the, the Treasury only speaks to the- speaks to the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-it's not something that's been a topic of, of, you know, major discussion at all at, at-at the-at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The [FOMC meeting] transcripts, when they come out in a few years-they'll probably reflect some mentions of the dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We do, of course- I mean, as you know, during the pandemic, we looked at a whole lot of new kinds of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People are looking at big data sets that you can get from all sorts of places.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But at the same-we really need-the government data really is the gold standard in data, and we need it to be-you know, to be good and be able to rely on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're not going to be able to substitute for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if-we have to make do with what we have, but I certainly hope that we get what we need.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'll just say that-so I, I think that having an independent central bank has been an institutional arrangement that has served the public well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as long as it serves the public well, it should continue and be respected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If it didn't serve the public well, then, then it wouldn't be something that we should just automatically defend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But what it gives us and other central banks-what it gives you is the ability to make these, these very challenging decisions that-in ways that are focused on the data and the evolving outlook, the balance of risks, and all the things we talk about, and not political factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so governments all over the advanced-economy world have chosen to put a little bit of distance between direct political control of those decisions and the decisionmakers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you-if you were-if you weren't-if you were not to have that, that would be a great temptation, of course, to, to use interest rates to affect elections, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's something that, that we don't want to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Consumer spending had been very, very strong for the last couple of years and had-repeatedly, forecasters, not just us, had been forecasting it would slow down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say, you know, if you talk to credit card companies, for example, they will tell you that the consumer is in solid shape and that spending is at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not growing rapidly, but it's at a healthy level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-so, generally-and if you look at the banks and when the banks talk about in their earnings calls, their-the performance of credit has been good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, essentially, you, you have a consumer that's in good shape and is spending, not at a rapid rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it was, again, right in line with what we expected, the GDP data that we got this week.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and I think it's still a little bit difficult to interpret, because you have these massive swings in net exports, which, which may also be affecting-you know, some of that can be affected by-can affect consumer spending as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Look, we-it's one of the data points that we pay most careful attention to, and there's no question that it's slowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we also watch the labor market and the performance of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are our two-those are our two variables that we're assigned to maximize.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I'm not going to talk about any individual's-you know, any individual's comments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, look, I think what we know is that private- sector job creation, you know, certainly in the last report-we'll see on Friday-but had come down a bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, and if you-if you take the QCEW adjustment seriously, with it-it may be even low-maybe close to zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, what that's telling you is that, that, you know, demand for workers is slowing, but so is the supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've got a very low unemployment rate, and it's kind of been there for a year as job creation has moved down, but also we know that, you know, because of immigration policy really, the flow into our labor forces is just a great deal slower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those two things have slowed more or less in tandem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at things, like I mentioned, quits, look at wages-wages are gradually cooling-look at vacancies to unemployment, those things have been pretty stable for-they haven't really moved a lot in a full year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think if you take the totality of the labor market data, you've got a solid labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think you have to see that there are downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not-you don't see weakening in the labor market, but I think you've got downside risks in a world where unemployment's being held down because both demand and supply are declining.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that's-it's worth paying close attention to it, and we are.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we have-we have an economic go-round, where people talk about the economy, and then the next-to-then to-that's yesterday.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then today, we have a monetary policy go-round, all the way around the table-everyone gives their views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the discussion around policy was-the majority view was, was still what it has been, which is that inflation is running above target, maximum employment is right at target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That means policy, policy should be a little bit restrictive, somewhat restrictive, because we want-we want inflation to, to move all the way back to its target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Two of our members felt that the time had come to cut and that they-for the reasons that they're-they're going to express.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They-they'll issue some kind of a-of a thing in the next day or so.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, you know, well argued, very thoughtfully argued all around the table, good arguments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy is in-is in, you know, good shape, but it's an unusual situation where you have risks to both your employment mandate and your inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's probably not surprising that there would be differences and different perspectives on that as well as different views of where the neutral rate is, so they-different views of how tight policy is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I will say, what you hope is that people, you know, explain their, their positions very thoughtfully and clearly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we absolutely had that today all the way around the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would call it one of the better meetings I can recall from that standpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you've said you're waiting to be confident inflation is heading toward your 2 percent target before you start cutting rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When you do get that confidence, would you be in-would you be in favor of lowering rates right away?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not, not quite the way I would put it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I said that's why we think policy should, should be restrictive, is because, you know, inflation is above target.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we-when we have risks to both goals-one of them is farther away from goal than the other, and that's inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you have to-that means policy should be tight because tight policy is what brings inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you came to the view that the risks to the two were more in balance, that would imply that policy shouldn't be restrictive, it should be more neutral-more, more, you know, a neutral stance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that would be somewhat lower than where we are now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're going to be obviously looking at a lot of data in the next cycle.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It is one of the cycles where we have two employment and two inflation reports, and we'll see where that takes us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's going to be the total-hard to answer that specifically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: PDFP, I think, for the first half-private domestic final purchases, or final sales, as people call it-was 1. on the first half.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, GDP is bumpy quarter to quarter, half to half, and often gets revised, you know, after the fact.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market data, we, we still think, is- continue to think, is the best data we have on the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It shows wages, you know, still at a healthy level, but moving ever closer to what we would regard as long-run sustainable, consistent with longer-run productivity and 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And tariffs-so we're watching all of that and, again, trying to-trying to do the right thing in what is a challenging situation, because you're being pulled in two directions and you have to decide which of those it took to go in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, actually, at some point, if they're-if they're sort of equally at risk, then you really want to be at a neutral policy stance, which we're not right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I, I, I just think we're going to need to see the data, and it can go in many different directions-the inflation data and, and the employment data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll just-we're going to make a judgment based on all of the data and based on that balance-of-risks analysis that I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we did welcome a new Committee member today, as we always do, and the Committee remains united in pursuing our dual-mandate goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're strongly committed to maintaining our independence, and beyond that I really don't have anything to share.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we're beginning to see-we have begun to see [increased] goods prices showing through into higher inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, actually, the increase in goods prices accounts for most of the increase in inflation or, perhaps, all of the increase in inflation over the course of this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do expect them to continue to build over the course of the rest of the year and into next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's also possible that there may be effects on employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I would say, if you're looking at why employment is doing what it's doing, that's much more about the change in immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the supply of workers has, obviously, come way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's very little growth, if any, in the supply of workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And at the same time, demand for workers has also come down quite sharply and to the point where we see what I've called a "curious balance."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Typically, when we say things are "in balance," that sounds good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in this case, the balance is because both supply and demand have come down quite sharply, now demand coming down a little more sharply because we see-we now see the unemployment rate edging up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we can say is this: that over the course of this year, we've kept our policy at a restrictive level-and people have different views, but a clearly restrictive level, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we were able to do that over the course of this year because the labor market was in very solid condition, with strong job creation and all those things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think if you go back to April and now look at the revised job-creation numbers for May, June, July, and August, you can kind of-I can no longer say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what that means is that the risks, which-the risks were clearly tilted toward inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Maybe they're not quite at equality-we don't need to know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we do know that they've moved meaningfully toward greater equality-the risks between the two goals-and that suggests that we should be moving in the direction of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There wasn't widespread support at all for a 50 basis point cut today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I think we've done-we've done very large rate hikes and very large rate cuts in the last five years, and you tend to do those at a time when you feel that policy is out of place and needs to move quickly to a new place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I feel like our policy has been doing the right thing so far this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we were right to wait and see how tariffs and inflation and the labor market evolved.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're now reacting to the much lower level of job creation and other evidence of softening in the labor market and saying, well, those risks are maybe not fully balanced but moving in the direction of balance now, and so that warrants a change in policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, I think you could think of this, in a way, as a risk-management cut, because if you look at the SEP, actually the projections for growth this year and next actually ticked up just a little bit and inflation and unemployment didn't really move.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What's different now is that you see a very different picture of the risks to the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've seen-you know, we were looking at 150,000 jobs a month at the time of the last meeting, and now we see the revisions and we see the new numbers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I didn't-I don't want to put too much emphasis on payroll job creation, but it's just one of the things that suggests that the labor market is really cooling off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that tells you that it's time to take that into account in our, you know, in our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We fully understand and appreciate that we need to remain fully committed to restoring 2 percent inflation on a sustained basis, and we will do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we've got to weigh the risks to the two goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say since-really, since April, to me the risks of higher and more persistent inflation have probably become a little less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's partly because the labor market has softened, GDP growth has slowed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I would just say that the risks there have been less than one might think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And in terms of the labor market, what we're seeing is, unemployment is still low-it's still at a relatively low rate, but we're seeing downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I was-I was saying that what's happening in the labor market has more to do with immigration than it has to do with tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't say that all of what's happening in the labor market is due to tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, you clearly have a slowing due to immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You clearly have a slowing in demand, which is now perhaps more than that in supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we know that because the unemployment rate has ticked up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It does say we're going to get to 2 percent inflation in 2028-at the end of '28.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But that's-you know, that's literally how you put the projections together.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You're writing down a rate path which is designed to create, over the course of the SEP, you know, time frame, 2 percent inflation, and maximum employment too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we don't-no one really knows where the economy will be in three years, but the nature of the exercise is to write down policy that you believe would return to the 2 percent goal over the-at least by the end of the exercise.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So our expectation, and you can see this consistently through the year, has been that inflation will move up this year, but that the-basically, because of the effects on goods prices from tariffs-but that those will turn out to be a one-time price increase, as opposed to creating an inflationary process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to-our job is literally to make sure that that is what happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Right now, the situation we're in is that we see inflation-we continue to expect it to move up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Maybe not as high as we would have expected it to move up a few months ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The pass-through into-of the tariffs into inflation has been slower and smaller.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the case for there being a persistent inflation outbreak is less.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's why we think it's time for us really to acknowledge that the risks to the other mandate have grown, and that we should move in the direction of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we have two mandates, and we try to balance them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: For a long time, our framework says that when our two goals are in tension-this is quite an unusual situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we do is we ask, which is farther from-how far is each from the goal, and how long is it expected to get to the goal?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So and then that's-we think about those things, and we see-as I mentioned, we have been-our policy had been really skewed toward inflation for a long time, really.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now we see that there's downside risk clearly in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're moving in a direction of more neutral policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And obviously we think it's appropriate that we reduce our rates so that we become more neutral, which will be-which, presumably, will be better for the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see people who are sort of more at the margins-so kids coming out of college and younger people, minorities-are having a hard time finding jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the concern is that if you start to see layoffs, the people who are laid off won't-there won't be a lot of hiring going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In a healthier economy, healthier labor market, there would be jobs for those people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's been a growing concern over the last few months, and it's one of the reasons why we think it's appropriate that we begin to shift our policy focus toward a more balanced one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we are-we're in a meeting-by-meeting situation, and we're going to be looking at the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, let me say a word about the SEP, really, here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What the SEP is, it's an accumulation-a cumulation of the individual projections of 19 people showing what they believe at a particular moment in time to be the most likely path for the economy and, thus, the appropriate path for monetary policy as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as you know, we don't-we don't debate or try to agree on what that is; we just write them down and cumulate them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we always say we're not on a preset path, and we really mean that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The actual decisions we make are going to be based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks at the time the decisions are actually made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you will have seen that we have 10 participants out of 19 who wrote down two or more cuts for the remainder of the year, and 9 who wrote down fewer than-in fact, in a good number of cases no more cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So rather than looking at-so rather than looking at this as certainty, I would encourage people, as always, to look at the SEP as-through the lens of probability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so there are-there are different possible outcomes and likelihoods rather than "this one is certain, and this one isn't happening."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ordinarily, when the labor market is weak, inflation is low; and when the labor market is really strong, that's when you've got to be careful about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have a situation where we have two-sided risk, and that means there's no risk-free path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's not at all surprising to me that you have a range of views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not so much about having different views for the path of the economy, but-it's partly that, but it's also partly about what's the right thing to do in light of this-of the tension between the two goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it would actually be surprising if you didn't have a pretty wide range of views based, you know, in this kind of highly unusual situation, and we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we get together, we discuss-we have a great discussion, and then we decide what to do and we act.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you're right that it is-it's a wide dispersion of views, and I think that's understandable and natural in the current situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Look, it's deeply in our culture to do-to do our work based on the incoming data and never consider anything else.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's just-everybody here who's at the Fed really feels strongly about that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, you'll know it by the way we talk about what we're doing, by the speeches that people give, by the decisions that we make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You'll know that we're just still going to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we don't-we don't frame these questions at all or see them in terms of political outcomes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think when you get to another part of Washington, everything is seen through the lens of, does it help or hurt this political party, this politician?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think people find it hard to believe that that's just-that is not at all the way we think about things at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're trying to, you know, serve the American people as best we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think- I think you would be able to tell.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't-I don't believe we'll ever get to that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I would say we're doing our work exactly as we always have now, and people are- they're making their arguments, and we're having, really, a great discussion around these challenging issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I see it as a court case that it would be inappropriate for me to comment on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, on the QCEW, the revision that we saw was almost exactly what we expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the reason for that is for the last bunch of quarters, there's been a-almost a predictable overcount.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the, you know, the Bureau of Labor Statistics really does understand this, and they're working hard to fix it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's got to do-of course, it has something to do with low response rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's also got to do with what's called the birth-death model, because a good amount of job creation happens around new companies, and how many go out of business, how many are founded.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's quite difficult to do, especially when the economy is undergoing big changes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they've been working on that and are making progress on it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, the data we get is still well good enough for us to do our work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To the extent we have issues around data right now, it's about low response rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Response rates are just lower to surveys now, both in and out of the government.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we want higher response rates, and we need those to have, you know, less volatile data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the way to get that is to make sure that the agencies that collect the data have sufficient resources to drive higher response rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other thing I'll say, Edward, is in the case of the job creation, the first-the response rate is quite low for the first month, or lower for the first month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: By the time you get to the second or third month, you're still collecting responses for that last month-for that prior month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you get to the place where the data are much more reliable by the second, and certainly the third, month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not that we don't get the data-it's just that we get it a little later.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we have to live life looking through the windshield rather than the rearview mirror, as you know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And all I can tell you is we see where we are now, and we take appropriate action.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I hadn't say that I thought a ¼ point would make a huge difference to the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you've got to look at the whole path of rates, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the market has already-has already been baking in expectations.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it's important that we use our tools to support the labor market when we do see signs like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I did mention that, you know, you see minority unemployment going up, you see younger people-people who are more vulnerable economically, more susceptible to economic cycles.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's one of the reasons, in addition to just overall lower payroll job creation, that shows you that at the margin the labor market is weakening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some part of the significant decline in labor force participation over the last year has probably been cyclical in nature, rather than just the usual aging process.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we put all those together, and we see that the labor market is softening, and we don't need it to soften any more, don't want it to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it starts with a 25 basis point rate cut, but we-you know, the market's also pricing in a rate path.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Those are two-we're getting unusually large amounts of economic activity through the AI build-out and corporate investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of spending, you saw the consumer spending numbers were well above expectations, and that may well be skewed toward higher-earning consumers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, I mean, I think the economy is-you know, it's moving along.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Economic growth is going to be 1½ percent or better this year, maybe a little better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So labor market is- unemployment is low, but-you know, downside risks-but it's still a low unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-of course, I'm not going to comment on anything the secretary says or, really, any other officer says.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in terms of reform at the Fed, you know, we just-we just went through a lengthy and I think very successful process of updating our monetary policy framework.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say there's a lot of work going on behind the scenes around the assets we have in the Federal Reserve System and at the Board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're actually going through a 10 percent head count reduction through the whole Fed, including the Board and all the Reserve Banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Employment at the Fed at the end of that will be basically at the same level it was more than 10 years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we will have had zero job growth for more than a decade when we're finished with that, and I think we'll probably do more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think we're certainly open to constructive criticism and ways to do our jobs better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're certainly open to, you know, to always trying to do better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think my view-which is also a bit of a guess, but widely shared I think-is that you are seeing some effects, but it's not the main thing driving it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so a particular focus on young people coming out of college and, yeah, there may be something there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It may be that companies or other institutions that have been hiring younger people right out of college are able to use AI more than they had in the past.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also part of the story, though, that, you know, job creation more broadly has slowed down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, if you-you can take goods-just sort of the broad goods category, and last year goods inflation was negative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you go back 25 years, that was the typical thing was that goods inflation was-goods prices generally went down, even adjusting for quality.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that was not the case during the pandemic, of course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we had essentially returned to zero or slightly negative inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, I think goods inflation over the course of the past year is 1. percent, which doesn't sound like a lot, but it's a big change.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we think-I mean, analysts have different views, but we think it's contributing, you know, 0. or 0.4, something like that, to the current core PCE inflation reading, which is 2. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What seems to be happening is that, you know, the tariffs are not-mostly not being paid by exporters, mostly being paid by, really, the companies that sit between the exporter and the consumer.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you buy something and you sell it through retail or you use it to make a product, you're probably taking a lot of those costs on and not able to pass it fully along to the consumer yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: All of those companies and entities in the middle, they'll tell you that they have every intention of passing that through in time, but they're not doing that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's been slower and later-slower and smaller than we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the evidence is very clear that there's some pass-through.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's 12 voters-19 participants, of whom 12 vote, as you know, on a rotating basis.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So no one voter, you know, can really-the only way for any voter to really move things around is to be incredibly persuasive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the only way to do that, in the context in which we work, is to make really strong arguments based on the data and one's understanding of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that is the way the institution-that's in the DNA of the institution.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our response is we're going to do everything we can to use our tools to achieve the goals that Congress has given us.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think there's quite a wide assessment that the situation has changed with respect to the labor market, whereas we could still say-and did say-in July, at the time of the July meeting, that the labor market was in solid condition, and we could point to 150,000 jobs per month, and many other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think that the new data that we've had-and it's not just payrolls, it's other things as well-suggests that there really is meaningful downside risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I said there was downside risk then, but I think that that downside risk is now a reality.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, some wrote down-almost everyone wrote down support of this cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And some supported more cuts, and some didn't, as you will see from the dot plot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's just the way-that's just the way it is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, people have-you have people who take this work very seriously, think about it all the time, do their work, discuss it with our colleagues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we have a meeting where we put it all out on the table.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you're right, there is a-there's a range of views in the dots.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think that's, like I said, very unsurprising given the quite unusual-historically unusual nature of the challenges that we face.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's not a bad economy, or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But from a policy standpoint, the standpoint of what we're trying to accomplish, it's challenging to know what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are, as I mentioned earlier, there are no risk-free paths now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, we cannot ignore and must keep our eye on maximum employment, which is-those are our two equal goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you will see that there are just a range of views on what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Nonetheless, we came together today at the meeting and acted with a high degree of unity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, so there are many different ways to calculate it and none of them is perfect, but, you know, it's clearly come way down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are-you could say it's somewhere between zero and 50,000, and you'd be right or wrong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, there's just many different ways to do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So wherever it was-150,000, 200,000 a few months ago-it's come down quite significantly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's because a very-a lower amount of people are joining the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor force is really not growing much at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's a lot of where the supply of labor was coming from over the last three-two or three years, so we're not getting that now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's interesting that supply and demand have really come down together so far, except now we do have inflation-sorry, unemployment ticking up outside, just one tick outside of the range where it's been for a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Four point three percent is still a low level, but, you know, I think this level of-this speedy decline in both supply and demand has certainly gotten everyone's attention.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't know that you see a big tension there, but it's gratifying to see that economic activity is holding and-you know, so it's a good, a good bit from consumption.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It looks like consumption was stronger than expected-what we got earlier this week, I guess.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also we're getting, you know-a fairly narrow sector is producing a lot of economic activity, which is the AI build-out and, you know, business investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say we-you know, we did move up, the median for growth for this year actually moved up in the SEP between the June and September SEPs, so-and, really, the inflation and labor market didn't change much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's really the risks that we're seeing to the labor market that were the focus of today's decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, housing is an interest-sensitive activity, so it's at the very center of monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When the pandemic hit and we cut rates to zero, the housing companies were incredibly grateful and it was really-they said that was the only thing that kept them going was that we cut so aggressively and provided credit and things like that, and they were able to finance because we did that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other side of that is when inflation gets high and we raise rates-and you're right, it does burden the housing industry.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so rates have come down a bit, and as that happens we don't set the-we don't set mortgage rates, but our policy rate changes do tend to affect mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that'll, of course, raise demand, lower borrowing rates for builders, will help, you know, get builders-will help supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think most analysts think that it would have to be pretty big changes for it to matter a lot for the-big changes in rates to matter a lot for the housing sector.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, the other thing is by-you know, by achieving maximum employment and price stability, that's a strong economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then the last thing I'll say is, you know, there's a deeper problem here that is not a cyclical problem that the Fed can address, and that just is a pretty much nationwide housing shortage, or a lot of places in the country just don't have enough housing for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, all of the areas around metropolitan areas-like Washington, for example-are very built up, and so you're having to build farther and farther out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, forecasting is very difficult, even in placid times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I've mentioned before, forecasters are a humble lot, with much to be humble about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think right now is a particularly challenging time, even more uncertain than usual.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so I don't know any forecaster anywhere really-ask any of the forecasters whether they have great confidence in their forecast right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think we're-you know, we're cutting the size of our balance sheet quite marginally now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As you know, with the balance sheet, we're still in an abundant- reserves condition.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've said that we would stop somewhat above a-somewhat above an ample-reserves level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't think that that has, at all, significant macroeconomic effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are pretty small numbers moving around inside a giant economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the level of runoff is not very large.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I wouldn't attribute macroeconomic consequences to that, at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we always think of it as the dual mandate, maximum employment and price stability, for a long time, because we think moderate, long-term interest rates are something that will result from stable inflation-low and stable inflation and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we don't-we haven't thought about that for a very long time as a third mandate that requires independent action.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's no thought of-as far as I'm concerned, there's no thought of considering that, you know, considering that we somehow incorporate that in as something in a different way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think default rates have been kind of ticking up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're not at a level-I don't believe they're at a level where, overall, they're, you know, terribly concerning.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know that one rate cut will have, you know, a visible effect on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But over time, you know, a strong economy with a strong labor market is what we're-what we're aiming for, and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we take the actions that we take with an eye on those goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, I would say it's a mixed picture, but households are in good shape, banks are in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Overall, households are still in good shape in the aggregate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I know that people at the lower end of the income spectrum are under pressure, obviously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But from a financial stability perspective, we monitor that picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't have a view that there's a right or wrong level of asset prices for any particular financial asset, but we monitor the whole picture, really looking for structural vulnerabilities, and I would say those are not elevated right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, as you said, shorter-term inflation expectations have tended to respond to near-term inflation, so if inflation goes up, inflation expectations will predict that it takes just a little while to get back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Fortunately, throughout this period, longer-term inflation expectations, both breakeven in the markets and almost all of the longer-term surveys-Michigan being a bit of an outlier lately-have been just rock solid in terms of, you know, running at levels that are consistent with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We actually assume that our actions have a real effect on that, and that, you know, we need to, you know, continually show and also mention/discuss our commitment to 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, we're-as I mentioned, it's a difficult situation because we have risks that are both affecting the labor market and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When they're both at risk, we have to balance them, and that's really what we're trying to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't- the latter part of your question was about independence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I don't see market participants-I don't see that that's something they're factoring in right now in terms of setting interest rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, as I just mentioned, a further reduction to the policy rate at the December meeting is not a foregone conclusion, as I've just said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I would say that that needs to be taken on board.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had-you know, I would just say this-19 participants on the Committee, everyone works very hard at this and takes their obligations to serve the American people very seriously.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And at a time when we have tension between our two goals, we have strong views across the Committee.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, they were strongly differing views today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the "takeaway" from that is that we haven't made a decision about December, and we're going to be looking at the data that we have, how that affects the outlook and the balance of risks, and I'll just say that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the way we have been thinking-the way I've been thinking about it is the risks to the two goals-for a very long time, the risk was clearly of higher inflation, and then that has changed now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as we saw the-particularly after we saw-after the July meeting, we saw downward revisions in job creation, we saw a very different picture of the labor market and suggested that there were higher downside risks to the labor market than we had thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that suggested that policy, which we had been holding at a, I would say, "modestly"-other people would say "moderately"-restrictive level, needed to move more in the direction, over time, of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If the two goals are sort of equally at risk, then you ought to be at neutral, because one of them is calling for you to hike, and one of them is calling for you to cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if that got back into balance, then you'd want to be roughly at neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in that sense, it was a [case of] risk management, and I would say the same about today-sort of the same logic.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But as I mentioned, going forward is a different thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't say that's a-that's a factor in everyone's assessment of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't say it's a driving factor, I don't think, for anybody.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I guess I would say it this way: Once again, I would just point out that we have the situation where the risks are to the upside for inflation and to the downside for employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It can't do both of those-you can't address both of those at once.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So they'll feel-they'll forecast faster or slower progress on one or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And people-some will be more averse to inflation overruns, and some will be more averse to underruns of employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so you put that together, and as you can see from the SEP and from the public discussion that goes on between the meetings when participants go out and talk, they're very disparate views.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they were reflected in strongly differing views in today's meeting, as I pointed out in my remarks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's what leads me to say that, that we haven't made a decision about December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I always say that it's a fact that we don't make decisions in advance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But this is-I'm saying something in addition here, that it's not-it's not to be seen as a foregone conclusion-in fact, far from it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That could be one of the factors, but the reality is that we've seen- the things that we've seen, higher repo rates and the federal funds rate moving up, these are the very things that we-that we look for.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We actually have a framework for looking at the place we're trying to reach.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What we said for a long time now is that when we feel like we're a little bit or a bit above what we consider a level that's ample that we would freeze the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, reserves will continue to decline from that point forward as nonreserve liabilities grow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this happened, some of it-some things have been happening for some time now, showing a gradual tightening in money market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Really, in the last, call it, three weeks or so, you've seen more significant tightening and I think a clear assessment that we're at that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The other thing is, we're-the balance sheet is shrinking at a very, very slow pace now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We've reduced it by half twice, and so there's not a lot of benefit to be-to be holding on for it to get the last few dollars, because, again, when the balance sheet-reserves are going to continue to shrink as nonreserves grow.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there was support on the Committee, as we thought about it, to go ahead with this and announce effective December 1 that we will be freezing the size of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the December 1 date gives the markets a little bit of time to adapt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, I mean in principle if you were to see data that suggested that the labor market is strengthening or even that it's stabilizing, that would certainly play into our decisions going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The labor market is a place where we get-for example, we get the state-level data on initial claims, which are sending sort of a signal of more of the same.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We also get job openings, and we'll get lots of survey data, we'll get the Beige Book and things like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll have a-we'll have a picture of what's going on in the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the fact that we're not seeing an uptick in claims or a downtick, really, in openings suggests that you're seeing maybe continued very gradual cooling, but nothing more than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll-we get-I mentioned what we get in the labor area.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We get some data in inflation, some data in economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we'll get-we'll have a picture of what's going on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say we're not going to be able to have the detailed feel of things, but I think if there were significant or material change in the economy one way or another, I think we'd pick that up through this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in terms of how it might affect December, it's really hard to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If there is a very high level of uncertainty, then that could be an argument in favor of caution about moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I was referring to the discussion about-to the extent it related to December.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You saw we had two dissents, one for 50 and one for no cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that was a strong, solid vote in favor of this cut.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The strongly differing views were really about the future, what does that look like?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think people are saying-they're noticing stronger economic activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Forecasters generally, broadly, have raised their economic growth forecast for this year and next year, in some cases quite materially.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the meantime, we see a labor market that's kind of-I don't want to say "stable," but it's not clearly in motion, it's not clearly declining quickly in any case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, people have different-they have different forecasts and expectations about the economy and different risk tolerances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so there's-you read the SEP, you read the speeches, you know there are differing views on the Committee and to the point where I said what I said.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The place we'll be on December 1 is that the size of the balance sheet is frozen, and as mortgage-backed securities mature, we'll reinvest those in Treasury bills, which will foster both a more Treasury balance sheet and also a shorter duration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's-in the meantime, if you freeze the size of the balance sheet, the nonreserve liabilities-currency, for example-they're going to continue to grow organically.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, because the size of the balance sheet is frozen, you have further shrinkage in reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And reserves is the thing that we're-that we're managing that has to be ample.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that'll happen for a time, but not a tremendously long time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But at a certain point, you'll want to start-you'll want to start reserves to start gradually growing to keep up with the size of the banking system and the size of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we'll be adding reserves at a certain point, and that's the last point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Even then we'll be-we didn't make decisions about this today, but we did talk today about the composition of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And there's a desire that the balance sheet be-right now it's got a lot more duration than the outstanding universe of Treasury securities, and we want to move to a place where we're closer to that duration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We haven't made a decision about the ultimate endpoint, but we all agree that we want to move more in the direction of a balance sheet that more closely reflects the outstanding Treasuries, and that means a shorter-duration balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, this is something that's going to be-take a long time and move very, very gradually, and I don't think you'll notice it in market conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, okay, so the September CPI report, we didn't get PPI after that, which is-which is important for translation into what we look at, which is PCE inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we can still make a pretty good assessment of what that will be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But so directionally, it was a little softer than expected, and we always break it down into the three components.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, basically, you've seen goods prices increasing, and that's really due to tariffs, and that's due-that's compared to a longer-run trend of very, very mild deflation in goods.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the other side of that, good news- housing services inflation has been coming down and is expected to continue to come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you remember, a year-a couple years ago, that's the one that just, we kept expecting it to do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now it's doing-it's been doing that for some time, and we expect to continue that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That leaves-the biggest category is services other than housing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's kind of been moving sideways over the last few months, but a significant part of that is nonmarket services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't take a lot of signal about the tightness of the economy from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you add all that up, a couple of things to say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One is that inflation away from tariffs is actually not so far from our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We estimate-people have different estimates of what that is, but it might be five- or six-tenths, and so if it's 2.8, then core PCE, not including tariffs, might be 2. or 2.4, in that range, something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that-we look at that, and the thing about tariff inflation is the base case is that it will come, and it probably will increase further.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it is that it will be a one-time increase, and we've been very focused for all of this year at making sure that that's the case and thinking carefully about what are the-what are the pathways through which it could become something else, troublesome inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: One of those would be a really tight labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's-it's not the case that we're just assuming that it's going to be a one-time inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We understand fully that this is a risk we have to monitor and ultimately manage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, again, the part of services inflation that is-that isn't coming down as we would like it to is the nonmarket part of nonhousing services.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, overall, that's just something that we expect will come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It largely reflects higher stock prices and financial services that are imputed, rather than actually paid, is a big part of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But also, just-we think policy is still modestly restrictive in my telling.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's the kind of thing that should lead to a gradually cooling economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's one of the reasons you see a gradually cooling labor market, [it] is because Fed policy is modestly restrictive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I want to say, though, we're absolutely committed to returning inflation to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at longer-term surveys or market pricing, you will see that that's a credible commitment, and there should be no question that that's where we're going.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't-I don't think that the-you're right, there's a-there's a lot of data centers being built and other investments being made around the country and around the world.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And big U.S. companies are just investing a lot of resources in thinking about how AI, which will be based on those data centers, run through data centers, is going to affect their businesses.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think that the spending that happens to build data centers all over the country is especially interest sensitive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's based on longer-run, it's-longer-run assessments that this is an area where there's going to be a lot of investment and that's going to drive higher productivity and that sort of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know how those investments will work out, but I don't think they're particularly interest sensitive compared to some of the other sectors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it doesn't replace government data, but you know all of these, it's-I'll just mention some of the many, many names: PriceStats, Adobe, and others.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On spending-you're going to ask about spending at some point-there are lots of other things that we look at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's, again, it's, it's many, many different sources and, again, including what we get out of the Beige Book, which will be sort of-come out mid-cycle as always.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it doesn't replace the government data, but it gives us a picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I think if something material were happening, if there were material developments, I think we would pick that up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't think we'll be able to have a very granular understanding of the economy while this-while this data is not available.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're going to do our jobs, we're going to collect every scrap of data we can find, evaluate it, and think carefully about it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you ask me, "Could it affect the December meeting?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: ", I'm not saying it's going to, but, yeah, you could imagine that-what do you do if-what do you do if you're driving in the fog?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't know how that's going to play into things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But there's a possibility that it would make sense to be more cautious about moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I'm not- I'm not committing to that, I'm just saying it's certainly a possibility that you would say, "We really can't see, so let's slow down."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So those are-those are both things that we're watching very, very, very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To start with the layoffs, you're right-you see a significant number of companies either announcing that they are not going to be doing much hiring or actually doing layoffs, and much of the time they're talking about AI and what it can do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, yes, it could absolutely have implications for job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We don't really see it in the initial claims data yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, it's not a surprise that we don't-it takes some time for it to get in there-but we're watching that really carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, again, don't see it yet in the-in the initial claims data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: On the K-shaped economy thing, I would say the same thing, or similar thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We are- if you listen to the earnings calls or the reports of big, public, consumer-facing companies, many, many of them are saying that there's a bifurcated economy there and that consumers at the lower end are struggling and buying less and shifting to lower-cost products, but that at the top, people are spending at the higher income and wealth, and they're-so much, much anecdotal data on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, perspectives of people on the Committee that we've now moved 150 basis points and that we're down into-you're into that range between 3 and 4, where most estimates of-many estimates of the neutral rate live in that 3 to 4 percent area.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think there are people on the Committee who have higher estimates of the neutral rate, and that's-you can argue these positions since it can't be directly observed, the neutral rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think for some part of the Committee, it's time to maybe take a step back and see whether there really are downside risks to the labor market, or see whether, in fact, the growth-that the stronger growth that we're seeing is real.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ordinarily, the labor market is a better indicator of the momentum of the economy than the spending data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So people just have-again, we've cut 50 more basis points in the last two meetings and there was a sense, from some, "let's pause here" kind of thing, and a sense from others wanting to go ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-look, everybody on the Committee is deeply committed to doing the right thing to achieve our goals: maximum employment and stable prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as I mentioned, some of that is different forecasts, but a lot of it is also different risk aversions to the two different variables, which is common through, through all federal reserves, they're-people just have different risk tolerances, let's say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You will know that from the speeches you've been listening to from my colleagues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we're at a place now where we have, in fact, cut two more times, and now we're 150 basis points closer to neutral, wherever that may be, than we were a year ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so there's a growing chorus now of feeling like maybe this is where we should at least wait a cycle, something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's-and, again, you've seen it in the September Summary of Economic Projections.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You've seen this in the public remarks of FOMC participants.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And now I'm telling you that's what-that's what you can expect in the minutes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I'm just telling you that's what happened in the meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the-I think there are two things affecting the job market, and one of them is just a dramatic reduction in the supply of new workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So and that's two things- that's declining labor force participation, which is a cyclical thing, and then there's declining immigration-which is just a big policy change that actually began in the last Administration and has been accelerated now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a big part of the whole story is that supply-side story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, labor demand has declined, and so the labor-the unemployment rate has gone down, meaning that demand for workers has gone down a little more than supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's what's going on, and-but it is mostly a supply function.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's mostly a function of the change in supply, I think and many people think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the question then is, what does-what does our tool do, which supports demand?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so-and I would just say, when you're in a situation where job creation, if you adjust for likely overcounting in the way that BLS does its work, is pretty close to zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So maximum employment doesn't, on a sustainable basis, doesn't-if you're making, creating zero jobs, if it's in equilibrium, if it's in balance, it's a pretty, as I said before, pretty curious balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I thought, and many of my colleagues thought-in fact, you've seen the last two meetings that it was appropriate for us to react by supporting demand with our rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've done that-we've reduced so that rates are looser.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't say that they're accommodative right now, but they're meaningfully less tight than they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that should help so that at least the labor market doesn't get worse.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a complicated situation, and some people argue that this is supply and we really can't affect it much with our tools, but others argue, as I do, that there is an effect from demand, and that we should use our tools to support the labor market when we see this happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the basic expectation is that there will be some additional increased inflation because it takes a while for tariffs to work their way through the production chain and finally get to consumers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we see this now from the tariffs that were put in place now many months ago-we see those effects.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if you put tariffs in effect-and they've been coming into effect consistently in February, March, April, May-and that's all happening, so that'll continue to happen for some time, probably into the spring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They may be big increases on a particular product that's been tariffed, but, overall, these are fairly modest.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think some projections-we're at 2. percent inflation-you might get two or three more tenths, or four more tenths maybe.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But then, as all the tariffs are in, they stop generating inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As long as you're not-at least this is the theory, this is how we believe and hope that it will work out-once the last tariff is put on something, at that point it becomes a higher price level, but it stops going up, if you will, prices stop going up, they'll just be at that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then measured inflation will come back down to non-tariff inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as I mentioned, non- tariff inflation is not so far from 2 percent now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: More than that, the reason they're so unhappy about inflation is the inflation that we had in 2021, '22, '23- because you can say that prices aren't going up as much, but that doesn't mean people aren't feeling those higher prices from the inflation we had two or three years ago.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's, I think, a large part of why the public-you sample people, inflation is still very much making people quite unhappy, even-and it's nice that prices are not going up as fast as they were, but they're still much higher than they were.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it'll take some time for that effect to wear off.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As real incomes rise, it will feel better over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we don't look at any one asset price and say, "Hey, that's wrong."

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at the overall financial system, and we ask whether it's stable and whether it could withstand shocks, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So banks are well capitalized, while some households are clearly under stress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the aggregate, households are in good shape financially-relatively, relatively manageable levels of debt.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the lower-income spectrum, you are seeing rising defaults, particularly in subprime auto, but, nonetheless, in the aggregate pretty good.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you don't see-so you don't see too much leverage in the banking system or the financial system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's a mixed picture, but it's not an overly troubling picture.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, again, I'm not-it's not appropriate-we don't set asset prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, I don't-I don't think interest rates are an important part of the AI-the data center story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think-people think there are great economics in building these data centers, and they're making a lot of money building them, and I think they have very high present value and all that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's not really-it's not about 25 basis points here or there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We use our tools to support the labor market and to create price stability.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're here to-by lowering rates at the margin, that will support demand, and that will support more hiring.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, no 25 basis point or even 50 basis point hike is going to be a dispositive thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, ultimately, lower rates will support more demand, and that'll support hiring over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, we also have to be careful about this, which is what we've been doing because we know where inflation is and we know-I've told you the story, this complicated story, but this is the best assessment that we can make and-but because there's uncertainty around inflation and the path ahead for inflation, that's why we're going-that's why the pace we're going has been a careful one.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is-this is different in the sense that these companies-the companies that are so highly valued-actually have earnings and stuff like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you go back to the '90s and the dot-com [period], they were-these were ideas rather than companies.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we're-so there's a clear bubble there, whereas the-I won't go into particular names, but they actually have earnings, and it looks like they have business models and profits and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the investment we're getting in equipment and all those things that go into creating data centers and feeding the AI, it's clearly one of the big sources of growth in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Consumer spending also, though, has been-is much bigger than that and has been growing and has defied a lot of, you know, negative forecasts, continuing to do so this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, it is-it may be mostly higher-end consumers or maybe skewed that way, but the consumer spending-and that's a big, big chunk of what's going on in the economy, bigger than-substantially bigger than AI.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You could point to growth-I mean, actually, maybe-growth as opposed to level, but consumer spending is a much bigger part of the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, what's happened is that the supply of workers has dropped very, very sharply due to mainly immigration, but also lower labor force participation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that means there's less need for new jobs, because there's-there isn't this flow into the pool of labor where people need jobs because there aren't those people now, so there's not a supply of workers showing up for jobs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In addition, demand has also gone down and so has-labor force participation has declined, which is more of a sign, in this case, of demand as well as trend.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The economy is growing at a slower rate than it was-2.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: percent last year, we think around 1. percent this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It could have been a couple of tenths higher if not for the shutdown.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, that will reverse, but you've still got the economy growing at a moderate pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, well, we'll know when we face that question-if we face that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I've said a couple times here that if you-if you really aren't getting information, you really don't know, and the economy looks like it's solid and stable and hasn't really changed, there will be an argument, I don't know how persuasive it will be, but there will be an argument that you slow down in a-when you can't see as far ahead.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Others may argue-I'm not sure where this argument will come, but you're perfectly right that you could also argue, things haven't really changed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you might not know that, so I don't know whether we'll face this or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I hope by the time of the December meeting, we're getting a better flow of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But if we-we're going to have to do our jobs one way or the other.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's discussions going on, I think, among the agencies, and I don't want to get ahead of those discussions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I continue to think that the level of capital, when I said that in 2020, was about right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, of course, there's been much capital added since then, through various mechanisms, but I look forward to-I know these discussions are really just getting going, they haven't come to the point where they're-where they've got a whole plan and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I really don't have much to say on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do not see the weakness, as you put it, the weakness in the job market accelerating.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, then again, we don't have-we didn't get the September employment report, payroll report, but we do get-we look at the unemployment insurance claims, initial claims are reported at the state level, and we still get those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we can cumulate them and get the national number, and there's really-I mean, there's no story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Same thing with the job openings we get from Indeed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you don't see anything that says that the job market-or, really, any part of the economy-is making a significant deterioration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You see more things, like I mentioned, though, which is that you see big companies making announcements of either layoffs or of the idea that they can-they won't need to hire.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Their number of employees is not expected to go up over a number of years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There may be different people working there then- they say that too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You don't see it in the aggregate numbers-the layoff numbers have not gone up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the job-finding rate for people who are unemployed is very low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the unemployment rate is very low as well, 4. percent is a low employment-unemployment rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, we can't-our tools don't allow us to target any demographic or any income level and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I do think that people-we saw this during the Global Financial Crisis and the long recovery.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you have a long period of very strong labor market conditions, it benefits people at the lower end the most.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The last two or three years of that long expansion, people at the lower part of the income spectrum were getting the biggest benefits, and lots of things were happening in that space, demographically, which were very constructive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But so, yeah, a stronger labor market is the best thing we can do for the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it is absolutely the best thing we can do for people, along with keeping prices stable.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, inflation also hurts people on fixed incomes more than other people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's a process that we go through, under the law.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The way the law works is, we have a reappointment process every five years for all of the-all of the Reserve- each of them and all of them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're in the middle of that process, and we're going to complete it in a timely way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you-you have to take what comes, and what comes right now is a pretty challenging situation where we have-first of all, we have 4. percent unemployment, we have an economy that's growing close to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in terms of our policy, we have upside risks to inflation, downside risks to employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And this is a very difficult thing for a central bank, because one of those calls for rates to be lower, one calls for rates to be higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we have to balance the two, and so it's a challenging thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as we have worked our way through this process, you would expect that there would be a range of views across the Committee on what to do and the speed with which we should do it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: These are-all of these people are people who take their jobs very seriously, work very hard at this, and just want to do what's right for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's an honor to work among people who care that much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I don't feel that it's unfair or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just-it's a time when we're making quite difficult judgments in real time, and I believe we'll get through this, and I think we've done sort of the right things so far this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we were-it was appropriate for us to be careful about this.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it would not be appropriate to just ignore or assume away the inflation issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, I think the risk of higher, more persistent inflation has declined significantly since April.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And if we do wind up resuming rate cuts at some point-we will at some point-I think we're trying to get to the end of this cycle with the labor market in a good place and with inflation on its way to 2 percent or at 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So that's all we're trying to do, and we're doing it under quite challenging circumstances and doing the best we can.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, we're-obviously we watch these things very carefully, credit conditions very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
