text: You're right-you've seen rising defaults in subprime credit for some time now, and now you've seen a number of subprime credit-automobile credit institutions having significant losses, and some of those losses are now showing up on the books of banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't see, at this point, a broader credit issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't seem to be something that has very broad application across financial institutions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we're going to be-we're going to be monitoring this quite carefully and making sure that that is the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there is some-there is some relationship there, but, remember, the more wealth someone has, the lower an additional dollar of wealth matters.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So your marginal propensity to consume declines quite dramatically as you reach-as you reach levels of stock market wealth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the stock market-it would affect spending if the stock market went down, but it wouldn't drop-it wouldn't drop sharply unless there were quite a sharp drop in the stock market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People at the lower end of income and wealth have a much higher marginal propensity to consume an incremental dollar of income or wealth, but they don't have the stock market wealth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I think it's certainly a factor supporting consumption right now, but-and you would see it if you saw material corrections in spending.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it wouldn't be-you shouldn't think that it'll, dollar for dollar, stop consumption, because that wouldn't be the case.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, yes, the adjustments since September bring our policy within a broad range of estimates of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as we noted in our statement today, we are well positioned to determine the extent and timing of additional adjustments based on the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That new language points out that we'll carefully evaluate that incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, also, I would note that having reduced our policy rate by 75 basis points since September and 175 basis points since last September, the fed funds rate is now within a broad range of estimates of its neutral value, and we are well positioned to wait to see how the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So a number of things are driving what's happening in the forecast.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I would say, if you look broadly at outside forecasts, you do see a pickup in growth in many of those now, too.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it is-it's partly that consumer spending has held up.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: To another degree, it is that AI-spending on data centers and related to AI has been holding up business investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, overall, the baseline expectation for next year is, at least at the Fed and I think with outside forecasters, too, is a pickup in growth from today's relatively low level of 1. percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mentioned that the SEP median is 1. for this year-growth-and 2. for next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So you can take two-tenths out of 2026 and put it in 2025.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it looks like the baseline would be solid growth next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to get a great deal of data between now and the January meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that will-the data that we get are going to factor into our thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, yes, we have-if you go back, we held our policy rate at, you know, 5. percent for more than a year because inflation was high, very high, and unemployment-and the labor market was really solid at that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what happened is, over last summer-summer of '24-inflation came down and the labor market began to show real signs of weakness.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we decided, as our framework tells us to do, that when the risks to the two goals become more equal, you should move from a stance that favors really dealing with one of them-in that case, inflation-to a more balanced, more neutral setting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we did that, and we did some cutting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then we paused for a while to work our way through what was happening in the middle of the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we've cut now three-we've now cut a total of 175 basis points.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, as I mentioned, you know, we feel like where we're positioned now puts-we're well positioned to wait and see how the economy evolves from here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It just-also, I think productivity has just been almost structurally higher for several years now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if you start thinking of it as 2 percent per year, you can sustain higher growth without more job creation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Of course, higher productivity is also what enables incomes to rise over long periods of time, so it's basically a good thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So let me just say, as I mentioned-and as I've mentioned here before-the situation is that our two goals are a bit in tension, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, interestingly, everyone around the table at the FOMC agrees that inflation is too high and that we want it to come down and agrees that the labor market has softened and that there's further risk.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Where the difference is is, how do you weight those risks and what does your forecast look like and where do-ultimately, where do you think the bigger risk is?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, it's very unusual to have persistent tension between the two parts of the mandate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think it's actually what you would expect to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Meanwhile, the discussions we have are as good as any we've had in my 14 years at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we come together and we reach-we reach, you know, a place where we can make a decision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's not like the normal situation where everyone agrees on the direction and what to do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In terms of what it would take, you know, we all have an outlook in terms of what's going to come, but I think, ultimately, having cut 75 and, you know, the effects of the 75 basis points will only begin to be coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: As I've said before a couple of times, we're well positioned to wait to see how the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we will get, as you know, quite a bit of data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I should mention on the data, as long as I'm talking about it, that we're going to need to be careful in assessing particularly the household survey data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are very technical reasons about the way data are collected in some of these measures, both in, you know, inflation and in labor-in the labor market, so that the data may be distorted.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that's-and that's really because data was not collected in October and half of November.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're going to get data, but we're going to have to look at it carefully and with a somewhat skeptical eye by the time of the January meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Notwithstanding that, we will have a lot of the December data by the time of the January meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we expect to see a lot more, but I'm just saying that the-what we get for, for example, CPI or for the, you know, household survey, we're going to look-we're going to look at that really carefully and understand that it may be distorted by very technical factors.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I wouldn't-I don't feel that we're at that point at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would say, again, these are good, thoughtful, respectful discussions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you hear people say- and you'll hear many outside analysts say the same thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to make decisions, and we-you know, we always hope that the data will give us a clear read.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But in this situation, you have competing-if you look-if you look through the SEP, you'll see that a very large number of participants agree that risks are to the upside for unemployment and to the upside for inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: How, how-what size moves do you make and that kind of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think we're in a good place to, as I mentioned, to wait and see how the economy evolves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't think that a rate hike is anybody's base as the next thing- is anybody's base case at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What you see is some people feel we should stop here and that we're at the right place and just wait.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Some people feel like we should cut once or more this year and next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But the-but when people are writing down their estimates of policy of where it should go, it is either holding here or cutting a little or cutting more than a little.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I don't see that as-I don't see the base case as involving that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, of course, you know, a data set of two, now three, is not a big data set.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you are right about those two three-cut times in the '90s.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, yeah, the idea is that with now having cut 75 basis points more now and having policy, you know, I'd call it in a broad range of plausible estimates of neutral, that that will be a place which will enable the labor market to stabilize or to only kick up one or two more tenths.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we won't see, you know, any kind of a sharper downturn, which we haven't seen any evidence of at all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, policy is still in a place where it's not accommodative, and we feel like-we feel like we have made progress this year in nontariff- related inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And as tariffs come through, as they flow through, that'll show through next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, as I said, we're well past-well placed to wait and see how that turns out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That is our expectation, but, you know, we're going to start to see the data, and it'll tell us whether we were right or not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So in October, I said that there was no certainty of moving.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I said it's possible you could think about it that way, but I was careful to say other people could look at it differently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, I would say-point to a couple of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: First of all, gradual cooling in the labor market has continued.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We think there's an overstatement in these numbers by about 60,000, so that would be negative 20,000 per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And also, just to point out one other thing, surveys of households and businesses both showed declining supply and demand for workers, so I think you can say that the labor market has continued to cool gradually, maybe just a touch more gradually than we thought.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, in terms of inflation, we are-it's come in a touch lower.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think the evidence is kind of growing that what's happening here is services inflation coming down, and that's offset by increases in goods, and that goods inflation is entirely in sectors where there are tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so far, it's only a story that this is-that the goods inflation, which is really the source of the excess at this point, that that-almost more than half the source of the excess inflation is goods-is tariffs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you've got to say then, "So what do we expect from tariffs?"

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-I would say that is, to some extent, down to looking for broader economic, you know, heat.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It doesn't feel like a hot economy that wants to generate, you know, a Phillips curve kind of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we look at all those things, and we say that this was a decision to make.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, overall, that was the judgment that we made, and that's the action we took.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So what really happened is this: Balance sheet shrinkage, sometimes called QT, went on.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had a framework in place for monitoring it, and nothing happened.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The overnight reverse repo facility went down pretty much close to zero.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And then, beginning in mid-September, the federal funds rate started to tick up within the range, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it ticked up almost all the way to interest on reserve balances.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: What that's telling you is that we're actually in a reserves-in an ample-reserves regime.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we knew this was going to come.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When it finally did come, it came a little quicker than expected, but we were, yeah, absolutely there to take the actions that we said we would take.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, we announced that we're resuming reserve management purchases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's just we need to keep an ample supply of reserves out there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The answer to that is, you know, if you look ahead, you will see that April 15th is coming up, and our framework is such that we want to have ample reserves even at times when reserves are at a low level temporarily.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: People pay a lot of money to the government, reserves drop sharply and temporarily.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So this seasonal buildup that we'll see in the next few months was going to happen anyway.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It was going to happen because April 15th is April 15th.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's also a secular ongoing growth of the balance sheet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We have to keep reserves, call it, constant as a-as it relates to the banking system or to the whole economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that alone calls for us to increase about $20 [or] $25 billion per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also happening in the context of a temporary few month front-loading to get reserves high enough to get through the, you know, the tax period in mid-April.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's before the courts, and we think our-we don't think that we help matters by trying to engage as a public discussant of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So I did think that in 2019, when we cut three times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: This is-it's not the 1970s, let's put it that way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so that's just unique in my time at the Fed and I think going back a long ways.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our framework, as you know, says that when that's the case, that we try to, you know, take a balanced approach to the two things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We look at how far they are and how long it would take to get them back to-each of them back to the goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it just tells you you've got to-and I think, ultimately, what it says is, when they're broadly equally threatened or equally at risk, you should be kind of neutral because if you're either accommodative or tight, you're favoring one or the other goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we've been trying to- we've been sort of moving in the direction of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We're in the high end of the range of neutral, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, as I've said, we think we're well positioned to wait and see how the economy performs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So with tariff inflation, you know, it takes-there's the announcement of a tariff and then there's-you know, they start to take effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Goods may have to be shipped from other parts of the-you know, it may take, you know, quite a while for an individual tariff to take its full effect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But once it's had that effect, then the question is, isn't that just a one-time price increase?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we've actually-we actually look at all of the announcements.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what you get from all that, you see sort of a-for each one of them, there's a time period and then it's fully in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So if there are no new tariff announcements-and we don't know that, but let's assume there are no major new tariff announcements-inflation from goods should peak in the first quarter or so, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we haven't been able to predict this with any precision.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But call it the first quarter or so of next year should be the peak.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And from here, it should be-it shouldn't be big, it should be a couple tenths or even less than that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, after that, again, if there are no new tariffs that are being announced that will take nine months to get fully in-and nine months is also an estimate-then you should start to see that coming down in the back half of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we're looking at the real economy and focusing on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And you have-you've got-when the long bonds move around, you've got to look at why they're moving around.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you look at inflation compensation, it's very-that's one part of it is inflation compensation breakevens, and, you know, they're at very comfortable levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They're at levels consistent-past-once you get out past the very short term now, breakevens are at a, you know, at quite-levels that are quite consistent with 2 percent inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So there's nothing happening with rates going up out there that suggests concern about inflation in the long term or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Surveys are all saying that the public understands our commitment to 2 percent and expects us to get back there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It must be, you know, an expectation of higher growth or something like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I mean, you saw a big move, you know, toward the end of last year, which was not to do with us, it was to do with other developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we-as you know, we have a network of contacts in the U.S. economy which is really unmatched if you go through the 12 Reserve Banks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we hear loud and clear how people are experiencing, really, costs.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And a lot of that is not the current rate of inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: A lot of that is just embedded higher cost due to higher inflation in 2022 and '23.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so the best thing we can do is restore inflation to its 2 percent goal-and our policy is intended to do that-but also have a strong economy where real wages are going up, where people are getting jobs and earning money.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And they're- we're going to need to have some years where real compensation is higher, you know, it's positive, significantly positive, so wages-nominal wages are higher than inflation for people to start feeling good about affordability-the affordability issue.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We want to-we're trying to keep inflation under control but also support the labor market and strong wages so that people are earning enough money and feeling economically healthy again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Everyone should understand, and the surveys show that they do, that we're committed to 2 percent inflation and we will deliver 2 percent inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's a complicated, unusual, difficult situation where the labor market is also under pressure, where job creation may actually be negative.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Now, supply of workers has also gone way down, so the unemployment rate hasn't moved that much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, it's a labor market that seems to have significant downside risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: That's their jobs, that's their ability, if they get laid off or if they're entering the labor force, to find work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The story with inflation-and, you know, we're well aware that this is a story at this point-is that if you get away from tariffs, inflation is in the low 2s, right?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it's really tariffs that's causing the-most of the inflation overshoot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we do think of those as likely to, in the current situation, as likely to be a one-time, you know, one-time price increase.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Our job is to make sure that it is, and we will do that job.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, right now, you've got this difficult balance, and there are risks to both sides.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If we were-if we-you know, if it was just inflation and the labor market was just really strong and then we'd-rates would be higher, as they were for more than a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, we didn't have to worry about inflation- sorry, about the labor market, because the labor market, unemployment was very low, if you remember, when inflation was very high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was a labor shortage, so we could focus entirely on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I think we're doing the best we can for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And the best thing we can do there is both to support economic activity but also, you know, make sure that when tariff inflation goes down and disappears, inflation lands around 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's a-it's very difficult to estimate job growth in real time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so we expect it and they correct it twice a year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So the last time they corrected it, we thought the correction would be 800,000 or 900,000.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so there was an overcount in the payroll job numbers, we think, continuing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't have the exact month in my head right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-and that's just-I don't- again, I think forecasters generally understand that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So-and we think it's about 60,000 a month, so 40,000 jobs could be negative 20.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, that could be wrong by 10 or 20 in either direction.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, in any case-but the thing is, that's, that's job creation, in a way, that's demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, if you had a world where they're just-there's just no growth in workers and you really don't need a lot of jobs to have full employment, some people argue that's what we're looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I think a world where job creation is negative, I just think we need to watch that situation very carefully and be in a position where we're not, you know, pushing down on job creation with our policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, you know, for example, if you look at-you can't miss the big announcements of layoffs and also companies saying that they're not going to hire anybody for a long time, and they cite AI-that's all clearly happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: At the same time, people are not filing for unemployment insurance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And since job creation-job-finding rates are extremely low, if there were big numbers of layoffs, you'd expect the continuing claims to go up, and you'd expect new claims to go up, but they really haven't much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But longer term, though, you know, the question is, what are we going to see here?

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But it's-you know, there's a-it may be that, in past technology, really significant technology and innovation eras, you have seen some jobs destroyed and other jobs made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Ultimately, what's happened for a couple hundred years is, when you get through all that, you have higher productivity, and you have new jobs, and there are enough jobs for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, it's-every time we have a wave of technology, we think, "Oh, this could put a lot of people out of work.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the past, there's always been more work and higher productivity, and incomes have risen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But right now is such early days, we don't think we see much-it's certainly not showing up in layoffs yet.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The views are more varied on each-in each group as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There's some of that, but I would say there are also Governors and there are people in both-on both sides in both groups.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It would depend on-it would depend on a whole bunch of things we don't know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So we do, through our vast network of contacts and just through our observation of what's going on in the economy, we hear about this a lot.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: If you listen to the earnings reports for consumer-facing companies that tend to deal with low- and moderate- income people, they'll all say that we're seeing people, you know, tightening their belts, you know, changing products that they buy, buying less and that sort of thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's also clearly a thing that, you know, asset values, housing values, and securities values are high, and they tend to be owned by people more at the higher end of the income and wealth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, as to how sustainable it is, I don't know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Most of the consumption does happen by people who have more means.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think, you know, the top third accounts for way more than a third of the consumption, for example.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: You know, the best we can do is to have, you know, price stability and a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And what we saw-for example, what we saw at the end of the, you know, the very, very long expansion that ended with the outbreak of the pandemic, we saw that it was 10 years and 8 months or something like that-the longest one in recorded history.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: In the last two years, most of the job-the largest part of the wage gains were going to people in the bottom quartile, the bottom part of the low and moderate income.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, you know, having a strong labor market for a long period of time is really, really good from a social standpoint.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It's helping people at the lower-income levels, and that's what we all want to get back to.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But we've got to have price stability, and we've got to have, you know, full employment, maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Yeah, so the housing market faces some really significant challenges.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And I don't know that, you know, a 25 basis point decline in the federal funds rate is going to make much of a difference for people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Many people have very, very low-rate mortgages from the pandemic period, and they kept refinancing and caught the really low.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, we're a ways away from that changing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Also, we're just-we haven't built enough housing in the country for a long time, and so a lot of estimates suggest that we just need more housing of different kinds.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So housing is going to be a, you know, a problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And, you know, really the tools to address it are-we can raise and lower interest rates, but we don't really have the tools to address, you know, a secular housing shortage-a structural housing shortage.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Well, I think the risk of inflation is pretty clear to see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And that is, you know, we see higher inflation, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And we think, we estimate, we expect-most of us-that inflation will be a one-time price increase and then come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We just came off an experience where inflation turned out to be much more persistent than anyone had expected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: The risk is either that tariff inflation just turns out to be more and more persistent, maybe because companies who are now holding back from passing through the tariffs will just keep doing that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think the other possibility is less likely, and that is just that, you know, the labor market gets tight or the economy gets tight and you see, you know, just traditional inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But-so I think-you know, again, you know, all across the Committee, people see the picture pretty similarly but see the risks quite differently.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But you've got to make an assessment, and this is the assessment we made.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So, yeah, I mean, I never thought I would see a time when we had, you know, five, six years of 2 percent productivity growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think you-I also think if you look at what AI can do and if you use it in your personal life, as I imagine many of us have, you can see the prospects for productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it makes people who use it more productive.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: It may make other people have to find other jobs, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: So it could have productivity implications while also having, you know, social and labor market implications that we don't have the tools to deal with.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But, yes, I think we are seeing-we're definitely seeing higher productivity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I don't-I think it's a little quick to be saying it's generative AI.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: But I don't know-you know, the pandemic may have induced people to do more automation and do more things with computers to replace people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There are many, many things pushing in different directions on where the neutral rate would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I-my thought is that I really want to turn this job over to whoever replaces me in-with the economy in really good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I want inflation to be under control, coming back down to 2 percent, and I want the labor market to be strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And all of my efforts are to get to that place.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: They have been all along, but, ultimately, that's what I want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And it's-you know, I don't have time to think about bigger things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I have, I hope, many years ahead to worry about that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: Again, I'm focused on-I'm focused on my remaining time as Chair.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I haven't got anything new on that to tell you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I would-I wouldn't agree that that's collateral damage of our-I mean, over time, we do what we do in order to create price stability and maximum employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And those things are hugely valuable to all of the people we serve.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: When we raise rates to bring inflation down, you know, that does work by slowing the economy, but we've moved back our rate-our policy back down to where it's not-it's certainly not strongly restrictive at this point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think it's sort of in the range of neutral.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: I think what people are feeling is the effect of higher prices.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: There was a global wave, sort of every large economy in the world-sort of every large open economy, market-based economy in the world had a wave of inflation that looked an awful lot like ours.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: We had higher growth, we had a better labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
text: And so, you know, all of us who work in economics jobs are really fortunate to have the U.S. economy.
